TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always rewrite both numbers with the same number of decimal places
  and read them as hundredths ("50 hundredths and 45 hundredths"); use money
  (paise) and a metre stick marked in centimetres; draw the number line between
  two whole numbers before rounding. Harder: order sets that mix fractions and
  decimals (3/4, 0.7, 0.8, 4/5), find decimals between 0.35 and 0.36, round to
  the nearest 10 and to the nearest tenth, and make the largest and smallest
  decimals from digit cards such as 4, 0, 7.

================================================================================
TOPIC 4.27 - ROMAN NUMERALS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - The seven Roman symbols: I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500,
    M = 1000. There is no symbol for zero.
  - ADD when a symbol is followed by a smaller or equal one: VI = 5 + 1 = 6,
    XV = 15, LX = 60, MDC = 1600.
  - I, X, C and M can be repeated, but at most three times in a row (III = 3,
    XXX = 30, CCC = 300, MMM = 3000). V, L and D are never repeated.
  - SUBTRACT when a smaller symbol comes before a larger one. Only six pairs are
    allowed: IV = 4, IX = 9, XL = 40, XC = 90, CD = 400, CM = 900.
  - Number to Roman: split the number into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones
    and write each part: 1994 = 1000 + 900 + 90 + 4 = M CM XC IV = MCMXCIV.
  - Roman to number: read from the left, adding, but take away a symbol that
    stands before a bigger one: XLIX = 40 + 9 = 49.
  - The biggest number with these rules is 3999 = MMMCMXCIX.
  - Roman numerals are used on clock faces, for chapters, classes, kings and
    queens, and for years on buildings and in films: MMXXVI = 2026.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Dadaji's wall clock has Roman numerals. Read the numbers on the clock face
    from 1 to 12.
                  XII
             XI         I
           X               II
           VIII            IV
             VII        V
                  VI
    Answer: I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII, VIII, IX, X, XI, XII.
    Teacher explains: Start at the top: XII is 12 (10 + 1 + 1). Going clockwise:
    I, II, III are 1, 2, 3 made of ones. IV is 5 - 1 = 4, V is 5, and VI, VII,
    VIII are 5 + 1, 5 + 2, 5 + 3. IX is 10 - 1 = 9, X is 10, and XI is 10 + 1.
    Some old clocks show IIII instead of IV for 4; this is a clock-maker's
    custom, but the correct numeral is IV. Now you try: the short hand points at
    VII and the long hand at XII. What time is it? (7 o'clock)

D2. Why is VIII equal to 8, XVI equal to 16 and LXII equal to 62?
    Answer: When symbols go from biggest to smallest we add them:
    VIII = 5 + 3 = 8, XVI = 10 + 5 + 1 = 16, LXII = 50 + 10 + 2 = 62.
    Teacher explains: Read from left to right. If each symbol is the same as or
    bigger than the one after it, just add all the values. Say the values aloud
    as you point: "fifty, sixty, sixty-one, sixty-two". This is the ADDING rule.
    Now you try: LXXVII and CLVI. (77; 156)

D3. Why do we write 4 as IV and not IIII?
    Answer: Because I placed before V means "one less than five":
    IV = 5 - 1 = 4. A symbol may not be repeated four times.
    Teacher explains: When a SMALLER symbol stands just before a BIGGER one, we
    subtract it. So IV = 4 and VI = 6: the I on the left takes one away, the I
    on the right adds one. In the same way IX = 10 - 1 = 9, and XI = 11. This
    SUBTRACTING rule keeps numerals short. Now you try: write 9 and 14. (IX;
    XIV)

D4. Rohan wrote 49 as IL (one less than fifty). Why is this wrong? What is the
    correct numeral?
    Answer: Only six subtraction pairs are allowed, and IL is not one of them.
    49 = 40 + 9 = XL + IX = XLIX.
    Teacher explains: The allowed pairs are IV (4), IX (9), XL (40), XC (90), CD
    (400) and CM (900). I can only go before V and X; X only before L and C; C
    only before D and M. To write 49, split it by place value: 40 and 9. 40 = XL
    and 9 = IX, so 49 = XLIX. Check: 50 - 10 + 10 - 1 = 49. Now you try: 99.
    (XCIX, not IC)

D5. A new school building has the year it was built on the wall. It was built in
    2026. How is 2026 written in Roman numerals?
        Thousands | Hundreds | Tens | Ones
           2000   |    0     |  20  |  6
            MM    |  (none)  |  XX  |  VI
    Answer: MMXXVI.
    Teacher explains: Split by place value: 2026 = 2000 + 20 + 6. 2000 = MM,
    there are no hundreds (Roman numerals have no zero, so we write nothing),
    20 = XX and 6 = VI. Put them together: MMXXVI. Check:
    1000 + 1000 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 1 = 2026. Now you try: 2008. (MMVIII)

D6. What year is MCMXCIV?
    Answer: 1994. M + CM + XC + IV = 1000 + 900 + 90 + 4 = 1994.
    Teacher explains: Break the numeral into chunks from the left. M = 1000.
    Next C is before M, a bigger symbol, so CM is a pair: 900. Then X before C:
    XC = 90. Then I before V: IV = 4. Add the chunks:
    1000 + 900 + 90 + 4 = 1994. Underline each subtraction pair first; then
    everything else is just adding. Now you try: MCMLXXXV. (1985)

D7. Sonu says VV = 10 and XXXX = 40. What rules has he broken?
    Answer: V, L and D are never repeated (10 is X). No symbol is repeated more
    than three times (40 is XL).
    Teacher explains: Two fives make ten, and there is already a symbol for ten:
    X. In the same way LL would be C and DD would be M. For 40, four X's are too
    many; use the subtraction pair XL (50 - 10). So the numbers 1 to 10 go I,
    II, III, IV, V, VI, VII, VIII, IX, X, and the tens go X, XX, XXX, XL, L, LX,
    LXX, LXXX, XC, C. Now you try: correct CCCC. (CD = 400)

D8. A storybook has Chapters XIV, XIX and XXIV. What are these numbers? Which
    chapter comes after Chapter XXXIX?
    Answer: XIV = 14, XIX = 19, XXIV = 24. After XXXIX (39) comes XL (40).
    Teacher explains: XIV = X + IV = 10 + 4. XIX = X + IX = 10 + 9.
    XXIV = XX + IV = 20 + 4. For the next chapter after 39: 40 is not XXXX but
    XL. Watch out when counting in Roman numerals at 4, 9, 40, 90, 400 and 900:
    those are the places where the subtraction pairs come in. Now you try: which
    chapter comes after LXXXIX? (XC = 90)

D9. Which of these are NOT correct Roman numerals: XC, IC, XLV, IIV, VX, MMM?
    Answer: IC, IIV and VX are not correct. (XC = 90, XLV = 45, MMM = 3000 are
    correct.)
    Teacher explains: IC: I may only go before V or X, so 99 must be XCIX. IIV:
    only one small symbol can be taken away, so 3 is III. VX: V is never used
    for subtracting, so 5 is just V. Check any numeral by changing it to a
    number and back: if you do not get the same numeral, it is not correct. Now
    you try: is XIIII correct? (no, 14 = XIV)

D10. What is the biggest number you can write with Roman numerals using these
     rules? Can you write 0?
     Answer: 3999 = MMMCMXCIX. There is no Roman numeral for 0.
     Teacher explains: M can be repeated only three times: MMM = 3000. Then the
     biggest hundreds is CM (900), the biggest tens XC (90) and the biggest ones
     IX (9): MMMCMXCIX = 3000 + 900 + 90 + 9 = 3999. The Romans had no zero;
     that is why places with no value are simply left out, as in MMXXVI. Our
     Hindu-Arabic numerals, with the zero that came from India, make place value
     and calculation much easier. Now you try: 3888. (MMMDCCCLXXXVIII)

D11. India became independent in 1947. Write 1947 in Roman numerals. How many
     years is it from 1947 to 2026? Write that in Roman numerals too.
     Answer: 1947 = MCMXLVII. 2026 - 1947 = 79 = LXXIX.
     Teacher explains:
     1947 = 1000 + 900 + 40 + 7 = M + CM + XL + VII = MCMXLVII. For the years in
     between, subtract in ordinary numbers: 2026 - 1947 = 79. Then
     79 = 70 + 9 = LXX + IX = LXXIX. Also: 1950 (the Republic) = MCML. Now you
     try: 1857. (MDCCCLVII)

D12. Work out XXIV + XVIII and write the answer in Roman numerals.
     Answer: 24 + 18 = 42 = XLII.
     Teacher explains: Adding Roman numerals directly is very hard, so change
     them into our numbers first: XXIV = 24 and XVIII = 18. Add: 24 + 18 = 42.
     Change back: 42 = 40 + 2 = XL + II = XLII. This is why the place-value
     system we use today replaced Roman numerals for calculating. Now you try:
     L - XIII. (50 - 13 = 37 = XXXVII)

M12. Work out a) to h) and write the answer in Roman numerals. For i) to p)
     write <, > or =.
     a) XIV + XXVI = __          b) L - XIII = __
     c) XXIV + XVIII = __        d) C - I = __
     e) XII x III = __           f) L / V = __
     g) MMXXVI - MCMXLVII = __   h) CD + CD = __
     i) XC __ CX                 j) XLIX __ LI
     k) MCM __ MM                l) IX __ XI
     m) CDXC __ CDIX             n) XL __ LX
     o) MMXXVI __ MMXXIV         p) DCCC __ CM
     Answers:
       a) 14 + 26 = 40 = XL
       b) 50 - 13 = 37 = XXXVII
       c) 24 + 18 = 42 = XLII
       d) 100 - 1 = 99 = XCIX
       e) 12 x 3 = 36 = XXXVI
       f) 50 / 5 = 10 = X
       g) 2026 - 1947 = 79 = LXXIX
       h) 400 + 400 = 800 = DCCC
       i) XC < CX (90 < 110)
       j) XLIX < LI (49 < 51)
       k) MCM < MM (1900 < 2000)
       l) IX < XI (9 < 11)
       m) CDXC > CDIX (490 > 409)
       n) XL < LX (40 < 60)
       o) MMXXVI > MMXXIV (2026 > 2024)
       p) DCCC < CM (800 < 900)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: make cards for I, V, X, L, C, D, M and build numbers with them;
  first master 1 to 12 on a clock face, then 1 to 50; always split the number by
  place value before writing (47 = 40 + 7 = XL + VII) and underline subtraction
  pairs before reading. Harder: convert years of famous events and film credits,
  find the longest numeral below 100 (LXXXVIII), explain why IIII, IC and VX are
  wrong, and write their own age, birth year and today's date in Roman numerals.

================================================================================
TOPIC 4.28 - PERIMETER OF POLYGONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - PERIMETER is the total length of the boundary of a closed shape: the
    distance all the way round. Add the lengths of ALL the sides.
  - Square: 4 equal sides, P = 4 x side. Rectangle: opposite sides are equal, P
    = l + b + l + b = 2 x (l + b). Equilateral triangle: P = 3 x side.
  - A REGULAR polygon has all sides equal: P = number of sides x side (pentagon
    5, hexagon 6, octagon 8, decagon 10).
  - An IRREGULAR polygon: add every side. Keep a tick on each side as you add it
    so none is missed or counted twice.
  - Find a missing side from the perimeter: square side = P / 4; rectangle: the
    other side = P / 2 - the known side; any shape: missing side = P - (sum of
    the other sides).
  - Rectilinear (L-shaped) figures: find missing sides from the opposite sides
    first (the lengths going across on top add up to the length across the
    bottom).
  - On a grid, count the unit edges round the outside.
  - Perimeter is a LENGTH, so it is measured in mm, cm, m or km. Change to the
    same unit before adding: 1 m = 100 cm.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A rectangular garden is 12 m long and 8 m wide. How much fencing is needed
    to go all the way round it? If fencing costs ₹25 per metre, what is the
    cost?
                  12 m
           +----------------+
           |                |
        8 m|                |8 m
           |                |
           +----------------+
                  12 m
    Answer: 40 m of fencing, costing ₹1000. P = 2 x (12 + 8) = 40 m;
    40 x 25 = 1000.
    Teacher explains: Walk round the garden in your mind: 12 m, then 8 m, then
    12 m, then 8 m. Add: 12 + 8 + 12 + 8 = 40 m. Because opposite sides are
    equal, we can add one length and one breadth and double:
    2 x (12 + 8) = 2 x 20 = 40 m. Or 2 x 12 + 2 x 8 = 24 + 16 = 40. Cost: 40 m x
    ₹25 = ₹1000. Now you try: a 15 m by 10 m field. (50 m)

D2. Riya puts lace round a square photo frame of side 15 cm. How much lace does
    she need?
    Answer: 60 cm. P = 4 x 15 = 60 cm.
    Teacher explains: A square has 4 equal sides, so instead of
    15 + 15 + 15 + 15 we multiply: 4 x 15 = 60 cm. Remember the unit: the answer
    is a length, 60 cm. Now you try: a square tile of side 25 cm. (100 cm)

D3. A triangular park has sides 5 m, 7 m and 9 m. What is its perimeter? What is
    the perimeter of an equilateral triangle with sides of 6 cm?
    Answer: 5 + 7 + 9 = 21 m. The equilateral triangle: 3 x 6 = 18 cm.
    Teacher explains: For any triangle, add the three sides: 5 + 7 + 9 = 21 m.
    An equilateral triangle has three EQUAL sides, so multiply: 3 x 6 = 18 cm.
    Check: 6 + 6 + 6 = 18. Now you try: a triangle with sides 12 cm, 9 cm and
    15 cm. (36 cm)

D4. Honeycomb cells are regular hexagons. If each side is 4 mm, what is the
    perimeter of one cell? What is the perimeter of a regular pentagon with
    sides of 7 cm?
    Answer: Hexagon: 6 x 4 = 24 mm. Pentagon: 5 x 7 = 35 cm.
    Teacher explains: "Regular" means all sides are equal. A hexagon has 6
    sides, so P = 6 x 4 = 24 mm. A pentagon has 5 sides, so P = 5 x 7 = 35 cm.
    The rule for any regular polygon is: number of sides x length of one side.
    Count the sides carefully on a drawing first. Now you try: a regular octagon
    of side 3 cm. (24 cm)

D5. A farmer's field has five straight sides of 12 m, 15 m, 9 m, 11 m and 13 m.
    How long is the path all round it?
    Answer: 60 m. 12 + 15 + 9 + 11 + 13 = 60.
    Teacher explains: The sides are all different, so there is no short cut: add
    all five. Tick each side on the drawing as you add it. Look for easy pairs:
    9 + 11 = 20 and 12 + 13 + 15 = 40, so the total is 20 + 40 = 60 m. A common
    mistake is to leave out one side. Now you try: sides 8 cm, 6 cm, 10 cm,
    7 cm. (31 cm)

D6. The perimeter of a square is 36 cm. How long is each side?
    Answer: 9 cm. 36 / 4 = 9.
    Teacher explains: A square has 4 equal sides, and together they make 36 cm.
    Share 36 into 4 equal parts: 36 / 4 = 9 cm. Check: 4 x 9 = 36. Finding the
    side is the opposite of finding the perimeter, so we divide instead of
    multiply. Now you try: a square of perimeter 100 m. (25 m)

D7. A rectangle has a perimeter of 30 cm. Its length is 9 cm. What is its
    breadth?
    Answer: 6 cm. 30 / 2 = 15, and 15 - 9 = 6.
    Teacher explains: The perimeter is 2 lengths and 2 breadths. Half of the
    perimeter is 1 length + 1 breadth: 30 / 2 = 15 cm. The length is 9, so the
    breadth is 15 - 9 = 6 cm. Check: 2 x (9 + 6) = 30. A common mistake is
    30 - 9 = 21, forgetting that there are two lengths. Now you try: perimeter
    50 m, breadth 10 m. (length 15 m)

D8. A triangle has a perimeter of 25 cm. Two sides are 8 cm and 10 cm. How long
    is the third side?
    Answer: 7 cm. 25 - (8 + 10) = 25 - 18 = 7.
    Teacher explains: The three sides add up to 25. The two we know add up to
    8 + 10 = 18. The missing side is what is left: 25 - 18 = 7 cm. Check:
    8 + 10 + 7 = 25. The same idea works for any polygon: missing side =
    perimeter - the sum of the other sides. Now you try: a quadrilateral with
    perimeter 40 cm and sides 12, 9 and 11 cm. (8 cm)

D9. Find the missing sides p and q of this L-shaped room, and then its
    perimeter. (All corners are right angles.)
                      6 m
               +------------+
               |            | 3 m     p
           8 m |            +--------+
               |                     |
               |                     | q
               |                     |
               +---------------------+
                         10 m
    Answer: p = 10 - 6 = 4 m, q = 8 - 3 = 5 m. Perimeter =
    6 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 10 + 8 = 36 m.
    Teacher explains: Look at the lengths going ACROSS: the bottom is 10 m, and
    the top is made of two parts, 6 m and p. So 6 + p = 10, and p = 4 m. Now the
    lengths going UP and DOWN: the left side is 8 m, and the right side is made
    of two parts, 3 m and q. So 3 + q = 8, and q = 5 m. Now add all six sides:
    6 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 10 + 8 = 36 m. Notice that 2 x (10 + 8) = 36 too: an L-shape
    has the same perimeter as the rectangle round it. Now you try: top 5 m, drop
    2 m, bottom 9 m, left 6 m. (p = 4, q = 4, P = 30 m)

D10. Each small square on the grid has sides of 1 cm. What is the perimeter of
     this shape?
         +--+--+--+
         |        |
         +        +
         |        |
         +  +--+--+
         |  |
         +  +
         |  |
         +--+
     Answer: 14 cm. Count the unit edges all round the outside.
     Teacher explains: Put your finger on a corner and walk round the outside,
     counting each 1 cm edge: across the top 3, down the right 2, back to the
     left 2, down 2, across the bottom 1, and up the left side 4.
     3 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 4 = 14 cm. Mark the corner where you started so you
     know when to stop. Do not count the lines inside the shape. Now you try: a
     3 by 3 square on the grid. (12 cm)

D11. A table top is 2 m long and 75 cm wide. What is its perimeter in
     centimetres, and in metres?
     Answer: 550 cm = 5 m 50 cm = 5.5 m. 2 x (200 + 75) = 550.
     Teacher explains: The sides are in different units, so change them to the
     same unit first: 2 m = 200 cm. Then P = 2 x (200 + 75) = 2 x 275 = 550 cm.
     Since 100 cm = 1 m, 550 cm = 5 m 50 cm = 5.5 m. Adding 2 + 75 = 77 would be
     a big mistake. Now you try: a rectangle 1 m by 40 cm. (280 cm = 2.8 m)

D12. Ravi says a rectangle 6 cm by 4 cm has a perimeter of 10 cm. Meena says it
     is 24 cm. Who is right?
     Answer: Neither. P = 2 x (6 + 4) = 20 cm.
     Teacher explains: Ravi added only two sides, 6 + 4 = 10: that is only half
     the way round. Meena multiplied, 6 x 4 = 24: that is the AREA (the number
     of 1 cm squares inside), not the perimeter. The perimeter is
     6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20 cm. Draw it on squared paper and walk round it with a
     finger. Now you try: a rectangle 7 cm by 3 cm. (20 cm)

PART B - MATHEMATICAL ONLY

M1. Find the perimeter of each square. (P = 4 x side.)
    a) side 1 cm    b) side 3 cm    c) side 5 cm    d) side 7 cm

    i) side 15 cm   j) side 20 cm   k) side 25 cm   l) side 11 m

             m) 4 x 30 = 120 m   n) 4 x 45 = 180 m   o) 4 x 100 = 400 m
             p) 4 x 50 = 200 m

M2. Find the perimeter of each rectangle. (P = 2 x (l + b).)
    a) l = 9 cm, b = 4 cm     b) l = 6 cm, b = 3 cm     c) l = 10 cm, b = 5 cm
    d) l = 8 cm, b = 2 cm     e) l = 12 cm, b = 7 cm    f) l = 15 cm, b = 10 cm
    g) l = 7 cm, b = 1 cm     h) l = 20 cm, b = 11 cm   i) l = 5 cm, b = 4 cm
    j) l = 14 cm, b = 6 cm    k) l = 25 m, b = 15 m     l) l = 30 m, b = 20 m
    m) l = 11 m, b = 9 m      n) l = 18 m, b = 12 m     o) l = 40 m, b = 25 m
    p) l = 100 m, b = 50 m
    Answers:
      a) 2 x (9 + 4) = 2 x 13 = 26 cm
      b) 2 x (6 + 3) = 2 x 9 = 18 cm
      c) 2 x (10 + 5) = 2 x 15 = 30 cm
      d) 2 x (8 + 2) = 2 x 10 = 20 cm
      e) 2 x (12 + 7) = 2 x 19 = 38 cm
      f) 2 x (15 + 10) = 2 x 25 = 50 cm
      g) 2 x (7 + 1) = 2 x 8 = 16 cm
      h) 2 x (20 + 11) = 2 x 31 = 62 cm
      i) 2 x (5 + 4) = 2 x 9 = 18 cm
      j) 2 x (14 + 6) = 2 x 20 = 40 cm
      k) 2 x (25 + 15) = 2 x 40 = 80 m
      l) 2 x (30 + 20) = 2 x 50 = 100 m
      m) 2 x (11 + 9) = 2 x 20 = 40 m
      n) 2 x (18 + 12) = 2 x 30 = 60 m
      o) 2 x (40 + 25) = 2 x 65 = 130 m
      p) 2 x (100 + 50) = 2 x 150 = 300 m

M3. Find the perimeter of each triangle.
    a) 5 cm, 7 cm, 9 cm          b) 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm
    c) 6 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm         d) 10 cm, 10 cm, 12 cm
    e) 7 cm, 7 cm, 7 cm          f) 4 cm, 9 cm, 11 cm
    g) 12 cm, 5 cm, 13 cm        h) 15 cm, 15 cm, 20 cm
    i) 8 cm, 6 cm, 11 cm         j) 9 cm, 9 cm, 9 cm
    k) 20 cm, 25 cm, 30 cm       l) 13 cm, 14 cm, 15 cm
    m) equilateral, side 6 cm    n) equilateral, side 11 cm
    o) equilateral, side 25 cm   p) equilateral, side 40 cm
    Answers: a) 5 + 7 + 9 = 21 cm   b) 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 cm   c) 6 + 8 + 10 = 24 cm
             d) 10 + 10 + 12 = 32 cm   e) 7 + 7 + 7 = 21 cm
             f) 4 + 9 + 11 = 24 cm   g) 12 + 5 + 13 = 30 cm
             h) 15 + 15 + 20 = 50 cm   i) 8 + 6 + 11 = 25 cm
             j) 9 + 9 + 9 = 27 cm   k) 20 + 25 + 30 = 75 cm
             l) 13 + 14 + 15 = 42 cm   m) 3 x 6 = 18 cm   n) 3 x 11 = 33 cm
             o) 3 x 25 = 75 cm   p) 3 x 40 = 120 cm

M4. Find the perimeter of each regular polygon.
    a) regular pentagon, side 7 cm        b) regular hexagon, side 4 cm
    c) regular octagon, side 3 cm         d) regular decagon, side 5 cm
    e) equilateral triangle, side 12 cm   f) square, side 9 cm
    g) regular hexagon, side 10 cm        h) regular pentagon, side 11 cm
    i) regular octagon, side 12 cm        j) regular dodecagon, side 2 cm
    k) regular nonagon, side 6 cm         l) regular heptagon, side 5 cm
    m) regular decagon, side 10 cm        n) regular hexagon, side 25 cm
    o) regular octagon, side 15 cm        p) regular pentagon, side 20 cm
    Answers: a) 5 x 7 = 35 cm   b) 6 x 4 = 24 cm   c) 8 x 3 = 24 cm
             d) 10 x 5 = 50 cm   e) 3 x 12 = 36 cm   f) 4 x 9 = 36 cm
             g) 6 x 10 = 60 cm   h) 5 x 11 = 55 cm   i) 8 x 12 = 96 cm
             j) 12 x 2 = 24 cm   k) 9 x 6 = 54 cm   l) 7 x 5 = 35 cm
             m) 10 x 10 = 100 cm   n) 6 x 25 = 150 cm   o) 8 x 15 = 120 cm
             p) 5 x 20 = 100 cm

M5. Add the sides to find the perimeter of each polygon (all lengths in cm).
    a) 6, 8, 5, 9               b) 12, 7, 12, 9
    c) 4, 4, 6, 6, 5            d) 10, 3, 8, 4, 6
    e) 7, 9, 11, 13             f) 2, 5, 2, 5, 2, 5
    g) 15, 20, 25, 10, 30       h) 6, 6, 8, 8, 10, 10
    i) 9, 14, 9, 14             j) 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8
    k) 25, 18, 30, 22           l) 11, 11, 11, 11, 16
    m) 5, 12, 8, 7, 9, 3, 6     n) 20, 35, 15, 40, 30, 10
    Answers:
      a) 6 + 8 + 5 + 9 = 28 cm
      b) 12 + 7 + 12 + 9 = 40 cm
      c) 4 + 4 + 6 + 6 + 5 = 25 cm
      d) 10 + 3 + 8 + 4 + 6 = 31 cm
      e) 7 + 9 + 11 + 13 = 40 cm
      f) 2 + 5 + 2 + 5 + 2 + 5 = 21 cm
      g) 15 + 20 + 25 + 10 + 30 = 100 cm

M6. The perimeter of a square is given. Find its side. (side = P / 4.)
    a) P = 36 cm    b) P = 20 cm    c) P = 48 cm    d) P = 100 cm

M7. The perimeter of a rectangle and one side are given. Find the other side.
    (other side = P / 2 - known side.)
    a) P = 30 cm, one side = 9 cm     b) P = 24 cm, one side = 8 cm

M8. The perimeter and all but one side of a polygon are given. Find the missing
    side.
    a) P = 25 cm; sides 8, 10 cm and __
    b) P = 30 cm; sides 9, 12 cm and __
    c) P = 40 cm; sides 12, 9, 11 cm and __
    d) P = 21 cm; sides 7, 7 cm and __
    e) P = 50 cm; sides 10, 15, 5, 12 cm and __
    f) P = 18 cm; sides 5, 6 cm and __
    g) P = 60 cm; sides 20, 15, 10 cm and __
    h) P = 36 cm; sides 9, 9, 9 cm and __

      g) 60 - (20 + 15 + 10) = 60 - 45 = 15 cm
      h) 36 - (9 + 9 + 9) = 36 - 27 = 9 cm
      i) 45 - (8 + 12 + 6 + 9) = 45 - 35 = 10 cm
      j) 100 - (25 + 30 + 20) = 100 - 75 = 25 cm
      k) 33 - (11 + 11) = 33 - 22 = 11 cm
      l) 24 - (4 + 5 + 6 + 3 + 2) = 24 - 20 = 4 cm
      m) 70 - (18 + 22) = 70 - 40 = 30 cm
      n) 54 - (10 + 8 + 12 + 6 + 9) = 54 - 45 = 9 cm

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: walk round the edge of a table, a rug or the classroom and count
  steps; lay string round a shape and then measure the string; mark a dot where
  you start and tick each side as you add it; draw shapes on squared paper.
  Harder: find missing sides of shapes with 8 or more sides, find all the
  rectangles with whole-number sides and perimeter 20 cm, work backwards from
  perimeter for regular polygons, and find the perimeter of shapes drawn on
  dotty paper.

================================================================================
TOPIC 4.29 - AREA BY COUNTING SQUARES; AREA OF RECTANGLE = LENGTH x BREADTH
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - AREA is the amount of flat surface inside a shape. We measure it by counting
    how many UNIT SQUARES cover it with no gaps and no overlaps.
  - A square 1 cm long and 1 cm wide has an area of 1 SQUARE CENTIMETRE, written
    1 cm^2 (or 1 sq cm). A square 1 m by 1 m has an area of 1 m^2 (used for rooms,
    floors and fields). Length is in cm or m; area is in cm^2 or m^2.
  - Counting squares: count the whole squares; two half squares make one whole
    square. For a curved shape, ESTIMATE: count a square if half or more of it
    is inside, leave it out if less than half is inside.
  - A rectangle is ROWS of equal squares, so area = number of rows x squares in
    each row, that is AREA = LENGTH x BREADTH (6 cm by 4 cm gives 6 x 4 = 24
    cm^2). A square: AREA = SIDE x SIDE.
  - Know the areas of squares with sides 1 to 12: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64,
    81, 100, 121, 144.
  - Missing side: if you know the area and one side, divide: breadth = area /
    length (area 40 cm^2, length 8 cm, so breadth = 40 / 8 = 5 cm).
  - Area is NOT perimeter: perimeter is the distance round the edge (add the
    sides), area is the space inside (multiply length by breadth).

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Meera covers part of her floor with square tiles. Each # is one tile and
    each . is bare floor. How many tiles are there? What is the area of the
    tiled part?
        # # # # .
        # # # # .
        # # # # #
        . . . # #
    Answer: Area = 15 square units (15 tiles).
    Teacher explains: Count row by row and write the number at the end of each
    row: row 1 has 4, row 2 has 4, row 3 has 5, row 4 has 2. Add: 4 + 4 + 5 + 2
    = 15. Tick each square as you count so you never count one twice. The area
    is 15 square units, because 15 unit squares cover it. Now you try: a shape
    with rows of 3, 5, 5 and 2 squares (15 square units).

D2. On a squared page, Arjun draws this shape. # is a whole square and / is half
    a square (a square cut along its diagonal). What is its area?
        # # # /
        # # # #
        / # # /
    Answer: 9 whole squares and 3 halves: 9 + 1 1/2 = 10 1/2 square units.
    Teacher explains: First count the whole squares: 3 + 4 + 2 = 9. Then count
    the half squares: 3. Two halves make one whole, so 3 halves = 1 whole and 1
    half. Total 9 + 1 + 1/2 = 10 1/2 square units. A common mistake is to count
    every half as a whole square (that gives 12, too much). Pair the halves with
    a pencil line: "these two make one". Now you try: 6 whole squares and 4
    halves (8 square units).

D3. Why do we measure area with squares? Why not with circles, like one-rupee
    coins?
    Answer: Squares fit together with no gaps and no overlaps, so they cover a
    shape exactly. Circles always leave gaps between them.
    Teacher explains: Let the child cover a notebook with coins: there are gaps
    between the coins, so the count does not tell us the true space. Then cover
    it with square paper tiles or sticky notes: they fit edge to edge. That is
    why the unit of area is a unit SQUARE. The size of the square must be the
    same every time, which is why we use 1 cm^2 or 1 m^2. Now you try: can
    triangles cut from a square tile cover a floor without gaps? (yes, 2 halves
    make each square)

D4. A photo is 6 cm long and 4 cm wide. Mark it into 1 cm squares. How many
    squares are there? Can you find it without counting one by one?
        # # # # # #
        # # # # # #
        # # # # # #
        # # # # # #
    Answer: Area = 24 cm^2. There are 4 rows of 6 squares: 4 x 6 = 24.
    Teacher explains: Every row has the same number of squares: 6 (the length).
    There are 4 rows (the breadth). So instead of counting 24 squares we
    multiply: 4 rows x 6 = 24. This is why AREA OF A RECTANGLE = LENGTH x
    BREADTH. Write the unit: cm^2 (square centimetres), not cm. Draw a 5 cm by 3
    cm rectangle on squared paper and check by counting that 5 x 3 = 15. Now you
    try: a card 7 cm long and 5 cm wide (35 cm^2).

D5. A classroom floor is 8 m long and 6 m wide. What is its area?
    Answer: Area = 8 x 6 = 48 m^2.
    Teacher explains: Length x breadth = 8 m x 6 m = 48 m^2. Picture the floor
    marked into squares of 1 m by 1 m: 6 rows of 8 squares. Metres times metres
    gives SQUARE metres, m^2. For a big floor we use m^2, for a page we use cm^2.
    Ask: "Would the area of a floor in cm^2 be a big or a small number?" (very
    big: 1 m^2 = 100 x 100 = 10,000 cm^2). Now you try: a hall 12 m long and 9 m
    wide (108 m^2).

D6. A square handkerchief has sides of 9 cm. What is its area?
    Answer: Area = 9 x 9 = 81 cm^2.
    Teacher explains: A square is a rectangle whose length and breadth are
    equal, so area = side x side = 9 x 9 = 81 cm^2. A common mistake is 9 x 4 =
    36 (that is the perimeter, in cm). Learn the square areas 1, 4, 9, 16, 25,
    36, 49, 64, 81, 100, 121, 144 for sides 1 to 12 - they are the square
    numbers. Now you try: a square tile of side 12 cm (144 cm^2).

D7. A vegetable garden has an area of 60 m^2. It is 12 m long. How wide is it?
    Answer: Breadth = 60 / 12 = 5 m.
    Teacher explains: Area = length x breadth, so 12 x __ = 60. Ask: "12 times
    what is 60?" 12 x 5 = 60, so the breadth is 5 m. This is the same as 60 / 12
    = 5. Check: 12 x 5 = 60. Draw a bar: 60 squares in rows of 12 make 5 rows.
    Watch the unit: the answer is a LENGTH, so it is 5 m, not 5 m^2. Now you try:
    a rug of area 56 m^2 that is 8 m long (7 m wide).

D8. Ravi says the area of a rectangle 5 cm by 3 cm is 16 cm^2. What did he do
    wrong?
    Answer: He found the perimeter: 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm. The area is 5 x 3 =
    15 cm^2.
    Teacher explains: Draw the rectangle and mark it into squares: 3 rows of 5 =
    15 squares. Then walk a finger round the edge: 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm.
    Perimeter is the FENCE around the field (cm); area is the GRASS inside
    (cm^2). Say "fence: add, grass: multiply". The numbers 15 and 16 are close
    here only by chance. Now you try: the area and the perimeter of 6 cm by 2 cm
    (12 cm^2 and 16 cm).

D9. Priya traces a leaf on 1 cm squared paper. # means a square fully inside the
    leaf, o means a square that is half or more inside, . means less than half
    inside. Estimate the area of the leaf.
        . o o .
        o # # o
        # # # #
        o # # o
        . o . .
    Answer: About 8 + 7 = 15 cm^2.
    Teacher explains: For a curved shape we cannot get the exact area by
    counting, so we ESTIMATE. Count the full squares: 8. Count the squares that
    are half or more inside: 7 - count each as 1. Leave out the squares that are
    less than half inside (they roughly make up for the bits we added).
    Estimate: 8 + 7 = 15 cm^2. Say "about 15 cm^2". Now you try: a shape with 12
    full squares and 6 squares more than half inside (about 18 cm^2).

D10. A verandah is 4 m long and 3 m wide. It is covered with square tiles of 1 m
     by 1 m. Each tile costs ₹250. How many tiles are needed and what is the
     cost?
     Answer: Area = 4 x 3 = 12 m^2, so 12 tiles. Cost = 12 x ₹250 = ₹3,000.
     Teacher explains: Each tile covers 1 m^2, so the number of tiles is the area
     in m^2. Step 1: area = 4 x 3 = 12 m^2, 12 tiles. Step 2: cost = 12 x 250.
     Work it as 10 x 250 = 2,500 and 2 x 250 = 500, total ₹3,000. Draw the
     verandah as 3 rows of 4 tiles to check the 12. Now you try: a floor 5 m by
     4 m with ₹300 tiles (20 tiles, ₹6,000).

D11. Which has the bigger area: a rectangle 7 cm by 5 cm or a square of side 6
     cm? By how much?
     Answer: The square: 6 x 6 = 36 cm^2, the rectangle 7 x 5 = 35 cm^2. The
     square is bigger by 1 cm^2.
     Teacher explains: Find both areas, then compare. Rectangle: 7 x 5 = 35 cm^2.
     Square: 6 x 6 = 36 cm^2. 36 - 35 = 1 cm^2. Both shapes have the same
     perimeter (24 cm), but not the same area - we meet this idea again in topic
     4.30. You cannot tell the bigger area by looking at the longest side. Now
     you try: rectangle 9 cm by 4 cm or square of side 6 cm? (the same: 36 cm^2)

D12. A rug is 4 m by 3 m. What happens to its area if the length is doubled?
     What if both the length and the breadth are doubled?
     Answer: Length doubled: 8 x 3 = 24 m^2 (twice 12). Both doubled: 8 x 6 = 48
     m^2 (4 times 12).
     Teacher explains: Draw it on squared paper. The first rug is 3 rows of 4 =
     12 squares. Doubling the length puts a second copy beside it: 2 copies, 24
     m^2. Doubling both makes 2 copies across and 2 copies down: 4 copies, 48 m^2.
     Many children think doubling both sides doubles the area - the picture
     shows it is 4 times. Now you try: a 2 cm by 5 cm card with both sides
     tripled (6 x 15 = 90 cm^2, 9 times 10).

M4. Find the area of the square with the given side.

    Answers: a) 1 cm^2   b) 4 cm^2   c) 9 cm^2   d) 16 cm^2   e) 25 cm^2   f) 36 cm^2

M6. The area and one side of a rectangle are given. Find the other side.
    a) A = 24 cm^2, side 6 cm     b) A = 35 cm^2, side 5 cm
    c) A = 42 cm^2, side 7 cm     d) A = 56 cm^2, side 8 cm
    e) A = 72 cm^2, side 9 cm     f) A = 30 cm^2, side 3 cm
    g) A = 48 cm^2, side 4 cm     h) A = 63 cm^2, side 9 cm
    i) A = 80 cm^2, side 10 cm    j) A = 96 cm^2, side 12 cm
    k) A = 54 cm^2, side 6 cm     l) A = 132 cm^2, side 11 cm
    m) A = 100 cm^2, side 25 cm   n) A = 60 cm^2, side 15 cm
    o) A = 45 cm^2, side 45 cm    p) A = 84 cm^2, side 7 cm
    q) A = 120 cm^2, side 8 cm    r) A = 7 cm^2, side 7 cm
    s) A = 1 cm^2, side 1 cm      t) A = 200 cm^2, side 40 cm
    Answers: a) 4 cm   b) 7 cm   c) 6 cm   d) 7 cm   e) 8 cm   f) 10 cm
             g) 12 cm   h) 7 cm   i) 8 cm   j) 8 cm   k) 9 cm   l) 12 cm
             m) 4 cm   n) 4 cm   o) 1 cm   p) 12 cm   q) 15 cm   r) 1 cm
             s) 1 cm   t) 5 cm

M9. Which rectangle has the larger area, and by how many cm^2? (All lengths in

M10. True or false? Correct the false ones.
     a) 4 cm x 5 cm rectangle: area = 20 cm^2

     c) square of side 10 cm: area = 100 cm^2
     d) 3 cm x 8 cm rectangle: area = 22 cm^2

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: let the child build rectangles with square tiles or cut paper
  squares, count them one by one, then count the rows and the squares in a row,
  and only then write length x breadth. Always say the unit aloud ("square
  centimetres"). Keep separate the words "round the edge" (perimeter) and
  "inside" (area). Harder: measure real things (a table top, a notebook, the
  classroom) and find their areas; find how many 1 m^2 tiles a room needs and the
  cost; find all the rectangles with area 36 cm^2 (topic 4.30); estimate the area
  of a hand traced on squared paper.

================================================================================
TOPIC 4.30 - AREA VS PERIMETER: SAME AREA DIFFERENT PERIMETER AND VICE VERSA
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - PERIMETER is the distance round the edge (in cm or m). AREA is the space
    inside (in cm^2 or m^2). For a rectangle: perimeter = 2 x (length + breadth),
    area = length x breadth.
  - SAME AREA, DIFFERENT PERIMETER: 24 squares can make rectangles 1 x 24
    (perimeter 50), 2 x 12 (28), 3 x 8 (22) and 4 x 6 (20). The long thin one
    has the biggest perimeter; the one closest to a square has the smallest.
  - SAME PERIMETER, DIFFERENT AREA: with perimeter 20 we can make 1 x 9 (area
    9), 2 x 8 (16), 3 x 7 (21), 4 x 6 (24) and 5 x 5 (25). The square has the
    biggest area; the long thin one the smallest.
  - To find ALL the rectangles with a given area, use the factor pairs of the
    area (topic 4.13). To find all the rectangles with a given perimeter, halve
    the perimeter: length + breadth = half the perimeter.
  - A rectangle with whole-number sides always has an EVEN perimeter.
  - A bigger area does not always mean a bigger perimeter, and a bigger
    perimeter does not always mean a bigger area. Always work both out.
  - Moving or adding squares in a shape can change the perimeter even when the
    area stays the same.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A farmer wants a rectangular pen for his goats with an area of 24 m^2. The
    sides must be whole metres. Which rectangles can he make? Which needs the
    least fencing?
    Answer: All the rectangles have area 24 m^2:
        length  breadth  area   perimeter
        24 m    1 m      24 m^2  50 m
        12 m    2 m      24 m^2  28 m
        8 m     3 m      24 m^2  22 m
        6 m     4 m      24 m^2  20 m
    The 6 m by 4 m pen needs the least fencing: 20 m.
    Teacher explains: List the factor pairs of 24 in order, so none is missed: 1
    x 24, 2 x 12, 3 x 8, 4 x 6. The next would be 6 x 4, which is the same pen
    turned round, so stop. For each pen, perimeter = 2 x (length + breadth): 2 x
    (24 + 1) = 50, 2 x (12 + 2) = 28, 2 x (8 + 3) = 22, 2 x (6 + 4) = 20. Same
    area, very different fences! The fatter the rectangle, the less fence. Now
    you try: area 18 m^2 (1 x 18: 38 m, 2 x 9: 22 m, 3 x 6: 18 m; least 3 x 6).

D2. Ananya has 20 m of rope to mark a rectangle for a game of kabaddi practice.
    The sides must be whole metres. Which rectangle gives the biggest playing
    area?
    Answer: Length + breadth = 20 / 2 = 10 m.
        length  breadth  perimeter  area
        9 m     1 m      20 m       9 m^2
        8 m     2 m      20 m       16 m^2
        7 m     3 m      20 m       21 m^2
        6 m     4 m      20 m       24 m^2
        5 m     5 m      20 m       25 m^2
    The 5 m by 5 m square gives the biggest area: 25 m^2.
    Teacher explains: The rope goes all round, so the perimeter is 20 m. Two
    sides (one length and one breadth) use half of it: 10 m. So look for pairs
    that add to 10: 9 + 1, 8 + 2, 7 + 3, 6 + 4, 5 + 5. Multiply each pair for
    the area: 9, 16, 21, 24, 25. Same perimeter, different areas, and the square
    wins. A common mistake is to use pairs adding to 20 - that would need 40 m
    of rope. Now you try: perimeter 16 m (7 x 1 = 7, 6 x 2 = 12, 5 x 3 = 15, 4 x
    4 = 16; biggest 4 x 4).

D3. Four square tiles of side 1 m are placed in a row, and then as a 2 x 2
    square. Do the two shapes have the same area? The same perimeter?
        row:       square:
        # # # #    # #
                   # #
    Answer: Same area: 4 m^2 each. Different perimeters: the row has 4 + 1 + 4 +
    1 = 10 m, the square has 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 m.
    Teacher explains: The tiles are the same, so the area (space covered) does
    not change: 4 m^2. But the edge changes. In the row, the tiles touch along
    only 3 edges; in the square, they touch along 4 edges, and every edge that
    is shared is hidden inside, not part of the perimeter. More hidden edges
    means a smaller perimeter. Let the child move real tiles and count the
    outside edges. Now you try: 6 tiles as a 1 x 6 row and as a 2 x 3 rectangle
    (both 6 m^2; perimeters 14 m and 10 m).

D4. Tanvi says, "If a rectangle has a bigger area, it must also have a bigger
    perimeter." Is she right?
    Answer: No. A 10 cm by 1 cm strip has area 10 cm^2 and perimeter 22 cm. A 4
    cm by 4 cm square has a bigger area (16 cm^2) but a smaller perimeter (16
    cm).
    Teacher explains: To show a statement is wrong, one example that breaks it
    is enough (a counter-example). Work out both measures for each shape and put
    them in a table: strip 10 cm^2, 22 cm; square 16 cm^2, 16 cm. The square wins
    on area, the strip wins on perimeter. So area and perimeter are different
    measures and must each be worked out. Now you try: compare 12 x 1 and 5 x 5
    (areas 12 and 25, perimeters 26 and 20).

D5. A school garden must have an area of 36 m^2 and whole-metre sides. Fencing
    costs ₹100 a metre. Which shape is cheapest to fence, and which is dearest?
    Answer: Cheapest: 6 m by 6 m, perimeter 24 m, ₹2,400. Dearest: 36 m by 1 m,
    perimeter 74 m, ₹7,400.
    Teacher explains: Factor pairs of 36: 1 x 36, 2 x 18, 3 x 12, 4 x 9, 6 x 6.
    Perimeters: 74, 40, 30, 26, 24 m. The square uses the least fence. Cost =
    perimeter x ₹100: 24 x 100 = ₹2,400 and 74 x 100 = ₹7,400. Point out the
    pattern: as the sides get closer together, the perimeter gets smaller. Now
    you try: area 16 m^2 at ₹50 a metre (4 x 4: 16 m, ₹800; 1 x 16: 34 m,
    ₹1,700).

D6. Rahul bends a 16 cm piece of wire into a rectangle with whole centimetre
    sides. List all the rectangles. Which one has the biggest area?
    Answer: 7 x 1 (7 cm^2), 6 x 2 (12 cm^2), 5 x 3 (15 cm^2), 4 x 4 (16 cm^2). The 4
    cm square has the biggest area.
    Teacher explains: Half of 16 is 8, so length + breadth = 8. Go down in
    order: 7 + 1, 6 + 2, 5 + 3, 4 + 4. Multiply for the areas: 7, 12, 15, 16.
    The wire (perimeter) is always 16 cm, but the space inside grows as the
    shape gets more square. Let the child bend a piece of string round pins on a
    board to see it. Now you try: a 12 cm wire (5 x 1 = 5, 4 x 2 = 8, 3 x 3 = 9
    cm^2; the square).

D7. Sita has 12 square tiles. She wants to arrange all of them into one
    rectangle. How many different rectangles can she make? Which has the
    shortest border?
    Answer: Three: 1 x 12 (perimeter 26), 2 x 6 (perimeter 16) and 3 x 4
    (perimeter 14). The 3 x 4 has the shortest border.
    Teacher explains: 12 tiles: rows x tiles in a row = 12, so use the factor
    pairs 1 and 12, 2 and 6, 3 and 4. (4 x 3 is the 3 x 4 turned.) Every
    rectangle has area 12 square units. Perimeters: 2 x 13 = 26, 2 x 8 = 16, 2 x
    7 = 14. With 7 tiles, only one rectangle is possible (1 x 7), because 7 is
    prime. Now you try: 20 tiles (1 x 20: 42, 2 x 10: 24, 4 x 5: 18).

D8. An L-shape is made of 3 squares of side 1 cm. One more square is added to
    fill the corner. What happens to the area and to the perimeter?
        before:    after:
        # .        # #
        # #        # #
    Answer: Area goes up from 3 cm^2 to 4 cm^2, but the perimeter stays 8 cm.
    Teacher explains: Count the outside edges one by one, going round: the L has
    8 edges of 1 cm, and the 2 x 2 square also has 8. The new square adds 2 new
    outside edges but hides 2 old ones, so the perimeter is unchanged. If
    instead the new square is stuck on the end of a row (touching one edge), it
    adds 3 edges and hides 1: the perimeter grows by 2. So adding area can leave
    the perimeter the same or make it bigger. Now you try: add a square to the
    end of a row of 3 (area 3 -> 4, perimeter 8 -> 10 cm).

D9. Two carpets both have a perimeter of 18 m. One is 7 m by 2 m; the other is 5
    m by 4 m. Which carpet covers more floor?
    Answer: The 5 m by 4 m carpet: 20 m^2 against 14 m^2 - 6 m^2 more.
    Teacher explains: Check the perimeters first: 2 x (7 + 2) = 18 and 2 x (5 +
    4) = 18. Same border! Now the areas: 7 x 2 = 14 m^2 and 5 x 4 = 20 m^2. The
    same length of border can hold different amounts of floor. Ask: "Can you
    find a carpet with perimeter 18 m that covers even more?" (no whole-metre
    one: 4 + 5 is the closest pair to equal). Now you try: perimeter 22 m: 9 m
    by 2 m or 6 m by 5 m? (6 x 5 = 30 m^2, more than 18 m^2)

D10. Can a rectangle with whole-number sides have a perimeter of 15 cm? Explain
     why.
     Answer: No. Perimeter = 2 x (length + breadth), which is always an even
     number. 15 is odd.
     Teacher explains: Every length appears twice (top and bottom) and every
     breadth twice (left and right). A number used twice gives a double, and all
     doubles are even. So perimeters like 10, 12, 14 cm are possible, but 15 cm
     is not (with whole-number sides). With half-centimetres, like 4 1/2 cm by 3
     cm, it can happen. Now you try: can the perimeter be 30 cm? (yes, e.g. 10 x
     5; half is 15)

D11. A square of side 4 cm has area 16 cm^2 and perimeter 16 cm. Are the area and
     the perimeter equal?
     Answer: No. The NUMBERS are equal, but 16 cm^2 is a space and 16 cm is a
     length - they cannot be compared. Only the numbers happen to match.
     Teacher explains: Change the unit to show it: in millimetres the square is
     40 mm by 40 mm, area 1,600 mm^2 and perimeter 160 mm - no longer the same
     number! There is one more whole-number rectangle whose numbers match: 6 by
     3 (area 18, perimeter 18). Let the child test other rectangles and see that
     the numbers usually differ. Now you try: a 5 x 5 square: area and perimeter
     numbers? (25 and 20)

D12. For a rangoli competition, Kavya can decorate a square card of side 5 cm or
     a rectangular card 8 cm by 3 cm. She puts ribbon round the edge and paint
     inside. Which card needs more ribbon? Which needs more paint?
     Answer: Ribbon (perimeter): square 20 cm, rectangle 22 cm - the rectangle
     needs more. Paint (area): square 25 cm^2, rectangle 24 cm^2 - the square
     needs more.
     Teacher explains: Ribbon goes round the edge, so find perimeters: 4 x 5 =
     20 cm and 2 x (8 + 3) = 22 cm. Paint covers the inside, so find areas: 5 x
     5 = 25 cm^2 and 8 x 3 = 24 cm^2. The shape with more paint has less ribbon!
     Always ask first: "Is this about the edge or about the inside?" Now you
     try: square of side 6 cm or rectangle 9 cm by 4 cm (ribbon 24 and 26 cm;
     paint 36 and 36 cm^2).

      g) A 20, 21: second; P 42, 20: first
      h) A 64, 64: same; P 32, 40: second
      i) A 20, 20: same; P 18, 24: second
      j) A 30, 30: same; P 22, 26: second
      k) A 11, 18: second; P 24, 18: first
      l) A 81, 72: first; P 36, 36: same

M9. Fill in the table (lengths in cm, areas in cm^2).
         length  breadth  perimeter  area
    a)  6       4        __         __

    Answers: a) P 20, A 24   b) length 7, A 21   c) breadth 5, P 26

     (cm) of each shape.
     a)           b)       c)         d)       e)       f)
     # # # # #    # # #    # # # #    # # #    # # .    # # #
                  # # #    # . . .    . # .    . # #    # . #

     g)       h)         i)         j)             k)           l)
     . # .    # # # #    # . . .    # # # # # #    # . # . #    # # # #

M11. True or false?
     a) Rectangles with the same area always have the same perimeter.
     b) Rectangles with the same perimeter can have different areas.
     c) 3 x 8 and 4 x 6 have the same area.
     d) 3 x 8 and 4 x 6 have the same perimeter.
     e) 2 x 7 and 4 x 5 have the same perimeter.
     f) For area 36, the 6 x 6 square has the smallest perimeter.
     g) For perimeter 24, the 1 x 11 rectangle has the largest area.
     h) A whole-number rectangle can have perimeter 21.
     i) A bigger perimeter always means a bigger area.
     j) A 4 x 4 square: area and perimeter are the same number.
     k) A 6 x 3 rectangle: area and perimeter are the same number.
     l) Area 7 can be made only as 1 x 7 (whole numbers).
     m) Perimeter 10 can be made as 4 x 1 and 3 x 2.
     n) Filling the corner of an L of 3 squares changes the perimeter.
     Answers:
       a) false
       b) true
       c) true
       d) false (22 and 20)
       e) true (18)
       f) true
       g) false (6 x 6, area 36)
       h) false (always even)
       i) false (e.g. 9 x 1: P 20, A 9; 4 x 4: P 16, A 16)
       j) true (16)
       k) true (18)
       l) true (7 is prime)
       m) true
       n) false (stays 8)

M12. For a square with this side (cm), find P (cm) and A (cm^2). Then say for
     which side P and A are the same number, for which P is bigger, and for
     which A is bigger.
     a) side 1               b) side 2               c) side 3
     d) side 4               e) side 5               f) side 6
     g) side 7               h) side 8               i) side 9
     j) side 10              k) side 11              l) side 12
     m) P = A when side is   n) P > A when side is   o) A > P when side is
     Answers: a) P 4, A 1   b) P 8, A 4   c) P 12, A 9   d) P 16, A 16
              e) P 20, A 25   f) P 24, A 36   g) P 28, A 49   h) P 32, A 64
              i) P 36, A 81   j) P 40, A 100   k) P 44, A 121   l) P 48, A 144
              m) 4   n) 1, 2, 3   o) 5 and more

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: work with square tiles or matchsticks on squared paper. Build a
  shape, count the squares (area) and then walk a finger round the outside edges
  counting them (perimeter). Use two colours: one for the edge, one for the
  inside. Keep to small numbers (areas up to 12, perimeters up to 16). Harder:
  find all rectangles for areas up to 100 and spot which areas give only one
  rectangle (the primes) and which give a square (the square numbers); make a
  table of length, breadth and area for perimeter 40 and draw a bar graph of the
  areas; design a garden with the most area for 30 m of fence (7 x 8 or, with
  half metres, 7 1/2 x 7 1/2).

================================================================================
TOPIC 4.31 - AREA OF COMPOSITE (L-SHAPED) FIGURES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A COMPOSITE (rectilinear) figure is made of rectangles joined together, like
    an L, a T or a U. All its corners are right angles.
  - METHOD 1 - SPLIT AND ADD: cut the shape into rectangles with a straight
    line, find each area, and add. An L can be cut ACROSS or DOWN; both ways
    give the same total.
  - METHOD 2 - SUBTRACT: draw the big rectangle round the whole shape, find its
    area, and take away the area of the missing piece.
  - MISSING LENGTHS: the sides facing one way add up to the long side facing the
    same way. In an L, the bottom = top + step, and the left side = the two
    right-hand parts added.
  - Never count a piece twice: the rectangles you split into must not overlap.
  - Perimeter of an L-shape = perimeter of the rectangle round it (2 x (length +
    breadth)). Find all the missing sides first and add them.
  - A PATH or BORDER round a rectangle: area of path = area of the big rectangle
    - area of the inside rectangle. A path w m wide adds 2 x w to each side.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Here is the plan of an L-shaped room. Find its area by cutting it ACROSS
    into two rectangles.
                   4 m
              +-----------+
              |           | 3 m
              |           |     ?
              |           +-----------+
          7 m |                       | 4 m
              |                       |
              +-----------------------+
                         9 m
    Answer: Area = 12 + 36 = 48 m^2.
            +-------+
            |  A    |  A = 4 x 3 = 12 m^2
            +-------+-----------+
            |     B             |  B = 9 x 4 = 36 m^2
            +-------------------+
    Teacher explains: Draw a line across, along the bottom of the step. The top
    rectangle A is 4 m wide and 3 m tall: 4 x 3 = 12 m^2. The bottom rectangle B
    is the full width 9 m and 4 m tall: 9 x 4 = 36 m^2. Add: 12 + 36 = 48 m^2.
    Shade the two parts in two colours so the child can see they fit together
    with no gap and no overlap. Now you try: an L with top 5 m, step 3 m down,
    bottom 8 m, right side 4 m, left side 7 m (5 x 3 + 8 x 4 = 15 + 32 = 47 m^2).

D2. Sunil cuts the same room (from D1) DOWN instead of across. Does he get the
    same area?
    Answer: Yes. Left part: 4 x 7 = 28 m^2. Right part: 5 x 4 = 20 m^2. Total 28 +
    20 = 48 m^2 - the same.
    Teacher explains: Cut down along the step. The left rectangle is 4 m wide
    and the full height 7 m: 4 x 7 = 28. The right rectangle needs its width:
    the step is 9 - 4 = 5 m, and its height is 4 m: 5 x 4 = 20. Total 48 m^2. The
    area of the room does not change with the way you cut it, so doing it both
    ways is a good CHECK. Now you try: the L in D1's "Now you try", cut down (5
    x 7 + 3 x 4 = 35 + 12 = 47 m^2).

D3. Find the area of this shape by SUBTRACTING.
                   6 m
              +-----------+
              |           | 2 m
              |           |    4 m
              |           +-----------+
          7 m |                       | 5 m
              |                       |
              +-----------------------+
                        10 m
    Answer: Big rectangle 10 x 7 = 70 m^2. Missing corner 4 x 2 = 8 m^2. Area = 70
    - 8 = 62 m^2.
    Teacher explains: Imagine the shape is a full rectangle with a corner bitten
    off. The full rectangle is 10 m by 7 m = 70 m^2. The bitten corner is 4 m
    wide (the step) and 2 m tall (the drop): 8 m^2. Take it away: 70 - 8 = 62 m^2.
    Check by splitting across: 6 x 2 = 12 and 10 x 5 = 50, and 12 + 50 = 62.
    Same! Now you try: a 12 m by 8 m rectangle with a 5 m by 3 m corner missing
    (96 - 15 = 81 m^2).

D4. Two sides of this L-shaped plot are not marked. Find them, then find the
    area.
                   6 m
              +-----------+
              |           | ?
              |           |     ?
              |           +-----------+
         10 m |                       | 4 m
              |                       |
              +-----------------------+
                        15 m
    Answer: Step = 15 - 6 = 9 m. Drop = 10 - 4 = 6 m. Area = 6 x 10 + 9 x 4 = 60
    + 36 = 96 m^2.
    Teacher explains: Look at the sides going across: the bottom (15 m) is as
    long as the top (6 m) and the step together, so the step is 15 - 6 = 9 m.
    Now the sides going up and down: the left side (10 m) is as long as the two
    right-hand pieces together, so the drop is 10 - 4 = 6 m. Now cut down: 6 x
    10 = 60 and 9 x 4 = 36, total 96 m^2. Check by subtracting: 15 x 10 = 150,
    150 - 9 x 6 = 150 - 54 = 96. Now you try: bottom 12 m, top 5 m, left 9 m,
    right 3 m (step 7 m, drop 6 m; area 5 x 9 + 7 x 3 = 45 + 21 = 66 m^2).

D5. What is the perimeter of the L-shaped room in D1? Why is it the same as the
    perimeter of the 9 m by 7 m rectangle round it?
    Answer: Perimeter = 4 + 3 + 5 + 4 + 9 + 7 = 32 m, and 2 x (9 + 7) = 32 m
    too.
    Teacher explains: First find every side: top 4, drop 3, step 5, right 4,
    bottom 9, left 7. Add them: 32 m. Now push the step up and out to the
    corner: the step (5 m) moves up to join the top, making 9 m, and the drop (3
    m) moves right to join the right side, making 7 m. The edge is just as long,
    but now it is the rectangle 9 by 7. So for an L, perimeter = 2 x (bottom +
    left). But the AREA does change: 48 is less than 63. Now you try: the L in
    D3 (2 x (10 + 7) = 34 m).

D6. A school garden is shaped like a T. Find its area.
                        12 m
              +-----------------------+
              |                       | 3 m
              +-------+       +-------+
                      |       |
                      |       | 6 m
                      |       |
                      +-------+
                         4 m
    Answer: Top bar 12 x 3 = 36 m^2. Stem 4 x 6 = 24 m^2. Area = 36 + 24 = 60 m^2.
    Teacher explains: Split the T where the stem meets the bar. The bar is a
    rectangle 12 m by 3 m: 36 m^2. The stem is 4 m wide and 6 m tall: 24 m^2. Add:
    60 m^2. A common mistake is to use 3 + 6 = 9 m as the height of the whole T
    and multiply 12 x 9 = 108 - that counts the two empty corners beside the
    stem. Now you try: a T with bar 10 m by 2 m and stem 3 m wide, 5 m tall (20
    + 15 = 35 m^2).

D7. A school building is shaped like a U round a courtyard. The whole block is
    12 m by 8 m; the gap (the courtyard) is 4 m wide and 5 m deep. Find the area
    of the building.
                4 m      4 m      4 m
              +-----+         +-----+
              |     |    5 m  |     |
              |     |         |     |
              |     +---------+     |
          8 m |                     |
              |                     |
              +---------------------+
                       12 m
    Answer: Area = 12 x 8 - 4 x 5 = 96 - 20 = 76 m^2.
    Teacher explains: Subtracting is quickest here. The big rectangle is 12 x 8
    = 96 m^2. The gap is a rectangle 4 m by 5 m = 20 m^2. 96 - 20 = 76 m^2. Check
    by splitting: two arms 4 x 8 = 32 each, and the middle piece under the gap
    is 4 m wide and 8 - 5 = 3 m tall: 12. 32 + 32 + 12 = 76. Same! Now you try:
    a U 10 m by 6 m with a gap 2 m wide and 4 m deep (60 - 8 = 52 m^2).

D8. A lawn 10 m by 6 m has a path 1 m wide all round the outside. What is the
    area of the path?
        +---------------------------+
        |       path 1 m wide       |
        |   +-------------------+   |
        |   |        lawn       |   |
        |   |     10 m x 6 m    |   |
        |   +-------------------+   |
        |                           |
        +---------------------------+
    Answer: Outside rectangle 12 m by 8 m = 96 m^2. Lawn = 60 m^2. Path = 96 - 60
    = 36 m^2.
    Teacher explains: The path adds 1 m on EACH side, so the length grows by 1 +
    1 = 2: 10 + 2 = 12 m, and the breadth grows by 2: 6 + 2 = 8 m. The most
    common mistake is to add only 1 m. Lawn and path together: 12 x 8 = 96. Take
    away the lawn: 96 - 60 = 36 m^2. Check: two long strips 12 x 1 = 12 each and
    two short strips 6 x 1 = 6 each: 12 + 12 + 6 + 6 = 36. Now you try: a pond 8
    m by 5 m with a 1 m path round it (10 x 7 - 40 = 30 m^2).

D9. A photo 20 cm by 15 cm is put in a frame that is 2 cm wide all round. What
    is the area of the frame?
    Answer: Outside: 24 cm by 19 cm = 456 cm^2. Photo: 20 x 15 = 300 cm^2. Frame =
    456 - 300 = 156 cm^2.
    Teacher explains: Add 2 cm on both sides: 20 + 4 = 24 and 15 + 4 = 19. Work
    out 24 x 19 with the area model: 24 x 20 = 480, minus 24 = 456. The photo is
    300 cm^2. Frame = 456 - 300 = 156 cm^2. Draw it to see the frame as a border
    and the photo as the hole in the middle. Now you try: a 10 cm by 8 cm card
    with a 1 cm frame (12 x 10 - 80 = 40 cm^2).

D10. Carpet for this L-shaped hall costs ₹200 for each m^2. How much will it cost
     to carpet the hall?
                    5 m
               +-----------+
               |           | 2 m
               |           |    3 m
               |           +-----------+
           6 m |                       | 4 m
               |                       |
               +-----------------------+
                          8 m
     Answer: Area = 5 x 2 + 8 x 4 = 10 + 32 = 42 m^2. Cost = 42 x ₹200 = ₹8,400.
     Teacher explains: Two steps: first the area, then the cost. Cut across: top
     part 5 x 2 = 10, bottom part 8 x 4 = 32, total 42 m^2. Check by subtracting:
     8 x 6 = 48, missing corner 3 x 2 = 6, and 48 - 6 = 42. Then cost: 42 x 200
     = 8,400, so ₹8,400. Now you try: an L of 30 m^2 at ₹150 per m^2 (₹4,500).

D11. For the room in D1, Neha found 4 x 7 = 28 and 9 x 4 = 36, and added them to
     get 64 m^2. What went wrong?
     Answer: Her two rectangles overlap: the bottom-left 4 m by 4 m square (16
     m^2) was counted twice. 64 - 16 = 48 m^2, the correct area.
     Teacher explains: Draw her two rectangles on the plan in two colours. The
     tall left one (4 x 7) and the wide bottom one (9 x 4) share a corner piece
     4 m by 4 m. The pieces we add must fit together like a jigsaw, with no
     piece used twice. Fix it by making the second rectangle only the part NOT
     yet covered: 5 x 4 = 20, and 28 + 20 = 48. Now you try: an L with top 3,
     drop 2, step 4, right 3 (bottom 7, left 5). What is wrong with 3 x 5 + 7 x
     3? (the 3 x 3 corner is counted twice; 15 + 12 = 27 m^2)

D12. On squared paper, Aman draws a staircase shape. Each # is 1 cm^2. Find the
     area using rectangles, then check by counting.
         # # # . . . . . .
         # # # . . . . . .
         # # # # # # . . .
         # # # # # # . . .
         # # # # # # # # #
         # # # # # # # # #
     Answer: Rows in pairs: 3 x 2 + 6 x 2 + 9 x 2 = 6 + 12 + 18 = 36 cm^2.
     Teacher explains: Cut the staircase into three flat rectangles, one for
     each step. Top step: 3 wide, 2 tall: 6. Middle step: 6 wide, 2 tall: 12.
     Bottom step: 9 wide, 2 tall: 18. Total 36 cm^2. Counting row by row: 3 + 3 +
     6 + 6 + 9 + 9 = 36. Or subtract: the full 9 by 6 rectangle is 54 cm^2, the
     empty part above the steps is 6 x 2 + 3 x 2 = 18 cm^2, and 54 - 18 = 36 cm^2.
     Now you try: steps 2, 4, 6 wide, each 1 tall (2 + 4 + 6 = 12 cm^2).

M8. A rectangle with a rectangular hole (like a garden with a pond). Outer
    rectangle, then hole. Find the area that is left.
    a) 10 x 8, hole 4 x 3       b) 12 x 10, hole 6 x 5
    c) 20 x 15, hole 10 x 5     d) 9 x 9, hole 3 x 3
    e) 15 x 12, hole 5 x 4      f) 30 x 20, hole 12 x 10
    g) 8 x 6, hole 2 x 1        h) 25 x 10, hole 5 x 5
    i) 14 x 11, hole 7 x 3      j) 40 x 25, hole 20 x 15
    k) 6 x 5, hole 1 x 1        l) 100 x 50, hole 30 x 20
    Answers: a) 80 - 12 = 68   b) 120 - 30 = 90   c) 300 - 50 = 250
             d) 81 - 9 = 72   e) 180 - 20 = 160   f) 600 - 120 = 480
             g) 48 - 2 = 46   h) 250 - 25 = 225   i) 154 - 21 = 133
             j) 1,000 - 300 = 700   k) 30 - 1 = 29   l) 5,000 - 600 = 4,400

M9. A path of width w runs round the OUTSIDE of a rectangle l by b. Find the
    outer rectangle and the area of the path.
    a) l 10, b 6, w 1    b) l 8, b 5, w 1     c) l 12, b 8, w 2
    d) l 20, b 10, w 1   e) l 6, b 6, w 1     f) l 15, b 10, w 2
    g) l 9, b 4, w 1     h) l 30, b 20, w 5   i) l 7, b 3, w 2
    j) l 16, b 12, w 3   k) l 5, b 5, w 5     l) l 25, b 15, w 2
    Answers: a) 12 x 8 - 60 = 36   b) 10 x 7 - 40 = 30   c) 16 x 12 - 96 = 96
             d) 22 x 12 - 200 = 64   e) 8 x 8 - 36 = 28   f) 19 x 14 - 150 = 116
             g) 11 x 6 - 36 = 30   h) 40 x 30 - 600 = 600   i) 11 x 7 - 21 = 56
             j) 22 x 18 - 192 = 204   k) 15 x 15 - 25 = 200
             l) 29 x 19 - 375 = 176

M10. A border of width w runs round the INSIDE edge of a rectangle l by b (like
     a frame). Find the inner rectangle and the area of the border.
     a) l 12, b 8, w 1      b) l 20, b 15, w 2     c) l 10, b 10, w 1
     d) l 24, b 18, w 3     e) l 30, b 20, w 2     f) l 16, b 12, w 1
     g) l 9, b 7, w 1       h) l 40, b 30, w 5     i) l 14, b 10, w 2
     j) l 50, b 40, w 5     k) l 8, b 6, w 2       l) l 100, b 60, w 10
     Answers:
       a) inner 10 x 6; 96 - 60 = 36
       b) inner 16 x 11; 300 - 176 = 124
       c) inner 8 x 8; 100 - 64 = 36
       d) inner 18 x 12; 432 - 216 = 216
       e) inner 26 x 16; 600 - 416 = 184
       f) inner 14 x 10; 192 - 140 = 52
       g) inner 7 x 5; 63 - 35 = 28
       h) inner 30 x 20; 1,200 - 600 = 600
       i) inner 10 x 6; 140 - 60 = 80
       j) inner 40 x 30; 2,000 - 1,200 = 800
       k) inner 4 x 2; 48 - 8 = 40
       l) inner 80 x 40; 6,000 - 3,200 = 2,800

M11. Find the missing lengths (?) and the area of each figure. In c) the whole T
     is 12 m tall.

                7 m

M12. Work backwards. The area A of each L-shape is p x u + r x s. Find the
     missing length.
     a) p 4, u 8, r 5, s ?, A 52       b) p 6, u 7, r 3, s ?, A 51
     c) p 5, u ?, r 4, s 3, A 47       d) p 3, u ?, r 6, s 2, A 30

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw every shape on squared paper and colour the rectangles you
  split it into in different colours; count the squares to check. Cut L-shapes
  out of card and physically cut them into two rectangles. Write the missing
  lengths on the drawing before doing any area. Harder: find the area of the
  classroom floor minus the cupboards, or a wall minus its door and window;
  design an L-shaped garden with area exactly 50 m^2; find the area of a
  plus-shaped (cross) figure and a staircase with 4 steps; find the cost of
  tiling a path round a pool.

================================================================================
TOPIC 4.32 - ANGLES: RIGHT, ACUTE, OBTUSE; MEASURING WITH A PROTRACTOR
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - An ANGLE is made by two ARMS meeting at a point called the VERTEX. It
    measures the amount of TURN from one arm to the other, not the length of the
    arms. We measure angles in DEGREES ( degrees).
  - A full turn is 360 degrees, a half turn 180 degrees, a quarter turn 90 degrees (a right angle), a
    three-quarter turn 270 degrees.
  - ACUTE: less than 90 degrees. RIGHT: exactly 90 degrees (a square corner, marked with a
    small square). OBTUSE: more than 90 degrees but less than 180 degrees. STRAIGHT: exactly
    180 degrees. REFLEX: more than 180 degrees but less than 360 degrees.
  - Using a PROTRACTOR: put its centre point on the vertex, lay the base line
    along one arm, find the scale (inner or outer) that reads 0 on that arm, and
    follow THAT scale round to the other arm. The two numbers at any mark add up
    to 180 (e.g. 40 and 140), so first decide if the angle is acute or obtuse.
  - Angles on a STRAIGHT LINE add up to 180 degrees. Angles all the way round a POINT
    add up to 360 degrees.
  - Clock: the 12 numbers split 360 degrees into 12 equal parts, so each hour gap is
    30 degrees. At 3 o'clock the hands make 90 degrees, at 6 o'clock 180 degrees.
  - Estimate before measuring: compare with a right angle (90 degrees), half a right
    angle (45 degrees) and a straight angle (180 degrees).

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. What kind of angle is made by: a) the corner of a book, b) a slice of pizza
    at its tip, c) a laptop screen opened wide to 110 degrees, d) the hands of a clock
    at 6 o'clock?
    Answer: a) right angle (90 degrees)   b) acute   c) obtuse   d) straight angle
    (180 degrees)
        acute     right     obtuse       straight
           /      |         \
          /       |          \
         /        |           \
        +-----    +-----       +-----    -----+-----
    Teacher explains: Compare each angle with a square corner (fold a paper
    twice to make a right-angle tester). If the opening is smaller than the
    tester, it is ACUTE ("a cute little angle"). If it fits exactly, it is
    RIGHT. If it is bigger than the tester but not yet a straight line, it is
    OBTUSE. If the arms make a straight line, it is a STRAIGHT angle (180 degrees). The
    size of an angle does not depend on how long the arms are drawn. Now you
    try: the hands at 2 o'clock, a door opened a little, a set square corner
    (acute, acute, right).

D2. How do you measure an angle with a protractor? The arm OA lies along the
    base line, on the side where the INNER scale starts at 0. The arm OB passes
    the mark that reads 65 on the inner scale and 115 on the outer scale. What
    is the angle?
    Answer: Angle AOB = 65 degrees.
    Teacher explains: Steps on the board: (1) Put the small centre hole of the
    protractor exactly on the vertex O. (2) Turn the protractor so the base line
    lies along arm OA. (3) Find the 0 that sits on OA - here it is on the inner
    scale. (4) Follow the inner scale 10, 20, 30 ... up to where OB crosses: 65.
    The angle is 65 degrees. Look first: the angle is smaller than a right angle, so
    the answer must be less than 90 - 115 cannot be right. Reading the wrong
    scale is the most common mistake; the two numbers always add to 180 (65 +
    115 = 180). Now you try: OA on the outer 0, OB at the mark "inner 30, outer
    150" (150 degrees, obtuse).

D3. Riya measured an angle that is clearly smaller than a right angle and wrote
    140 degrees. What should it be?
    Answer: 40 degrees. She read the wrong scale: 180 - 140 = 40.
    Teacher explains: Always ESTIMATE first. The angle is acute, so it is less
    than 90 degrees. At every mark the two scales add to 180, so the other number at
    her mark is 180 - 140 = 40. Teach the child to say "acute, so small number"
    or "obtuse, so big number" before writing the answer. Now you try: an obtuse
    angle measured as 75 degrees (105 degrees).

D4. A ladder leans against a wall. It makes an angle of 70 degrees with the ground on
    one side. What angle does it make with the ground on the other side?
    Answer: 110 degrees, because angles on a straight line add up to 180 degrees: 180 - 70 =
    110.
                    /
                   /
             110 degrees /  70 degrees
          --------+---------  ground
    Teacher explains: The ground is a straight line, which is a half turn: 180 degrees.
    The ladder splits it into two angles that together make 180 degrees. So the second
    angle is 180 - 70 = 110 degrees. Check: 70 + 110 = 180. One angle is acute, the
    other obtuse - that always happens unless both are 90 degrees. Now you try: one
    angle on a straight line is 35 degrees (145 degrees).

D5. A round cake is cut from the centre into 3 pieces. Two of the angles at the
    centre are 120 degrees and 150 degrees. What is the third angle?
    Answer: 90 degrees, because angles round a point add up to 360 degrees: 360 - 120 - 150 =
    90.
    Teacher explains: A full turn round the centre is 360 degrees. Add the angles we
    know: 120 + 150 = 270. The rest is 360 - 270 = 90 degrees. So the third piece has a
    right angle at its tip. Check: 120 + 150 + 90 = 360. Now you try: four
    slices of 100 degrees, 80 degrees, 110 degrees and __ (70 degrees).

D6. Why is the angle between the hands at 1 o'clock 30 degrees? What is it at 3
    o'clock?
    Answer: 360 degrees / 12 = 30 degrees for each hour gap. At 3 o'clock the hands are 3 gaps
    apart: 3 x 30 = 90 degrees.
    Teacher explains: The 12 numbers are spread evenly round a full turn of
    360 degrees. Each gap is 360 / 12 = 30 degrees. At 1 o'clock the minute hand is on 12 and
    the hour hand on 1: one gap, 30 degrees. At 3 o'clock: 3 gaps, 90 degrees, a right angle.
    At 6 o'clock: 6 gaps, 180 degrees, a straight line. Make a paper clock and mark
    30 degrees, 60 degrees, 90 degrees ... Now you try: 4 o'clock (4 x 30 = 120 degrees, obtuse).

D7. At 7 o'clock, what angle do the hands make? There are two angles between the
    hands - find both.
    Answer: Smaller angle: 5 gaps (from 7 on to 12) = 5 x 30 = 150 degrees. The other
    angle (the reflex angle) = 360 - 150 = 210 degrees.
    Teacher explains: Count the gaps the SHORT way round: from 7 to 12 going on
    is 5 gaps (7 -> 8 -> 9 -> 10 -> 11 -> 12), 5 x 30 = 150 degrees. Going the long way from
    12 to 7 is 7 gaps, 7 x 30 = 210 degrees. Together they make a full turn: 150 + 210
    = 360. When we say "the angle between the hands" we usually mean the smaller
    one. Now you try: 8 o'clock (120 degrees and 240 degrees).

D8. A dancer spins a three-quarter turn clockwise. How many degrees is that? How
    many right angles?
    Answer: 3/4 of 360 degrees = 270 degrees, which is 3 right angles.
    Teacher explains: A quarter turn is 90 degrees (one right angle), because 360 / 4 =
    90. A three-quarter turn is 3 quarter turns: 3 x 90 = 270 degrees. Turn together in
    class: face the board, turn 90 degrees (face the window), another 90 degrees (180 degrees, face
    the back), another 90 degrees (270 degrees). A full turn is 4 x 90 = 360 degrees. Now you try: a
    half turn (180 degrees, 2 right angles).

D9. Fold a square paper corner in half through the corner. What angle do you
    get? Why?
    Answer: 45 degrees, because folding the 90 degrees corner in half gives 90 / 2 = 45 degrees.
    Teacher explains: A square corner is 90 degrees. Folding it exactly in half splits
    it into two equal angles: 45 degrees + 45 degrees = 90 degrees. This 45 degrees is a useful benchmark:
    an angle that looks about half a right angle is about 45 degrees. Half of 45 degrees is
    about 22 degrees, and a right angle and a half is 90 + 45 = 135 degrees. Use these to
    estimate before measuring. Now you try: what is two right angles and a half?
    (90 + 90 + 45 = 225 degrees)

D10. At 2 o'clock the hands make a 60 degrees angle. What is the reflex angle between
     the hands?
     Answer: 360 - 60 = 300 degrees.
     Teacher explains: The two angles between the hands together make a full
     turn, 360 degrees. The small one is 2 gaps x 30 degrees = 60 degrees. The big one, going the
     long way round, is 360 - 60 = 300 degrees (or count 10 gaps: 10 x 30 = 300). A
     REFLEX angle is bigger than 180 degrees. Draw both angles and shade the reflex
     one. Now you try: 5 o'clock (smaller 150 degrees, reflex 210 degrees).

D11. How do you DRAW an angle of 75 degrees with a protractor?
     Answer: Draw arm OA, put the protractor centre on O with the base line on
     OA, find 75 on the scale that starts at 0 on OA, make a dot, and join O to
     the dot.
                          B
                         .
                        /
                       /
                      /
                   O +----------- A
     Teacher explains: Step 1: draw a straight line OA with a ruler. Step 2:
     place the centre of the protractor on O and the base line along OA. Step 3:
     find which scale reads 0 at A; go round THAT scale to 75 and make a small
     dot B. Step 4: remove the protractor and join O to B. Step 5: check - 75 degrees
     is acute, a bit less than a right angle, so the picture should show that.
     (In a text drawing the slope cannot be exact.) Now you try: draw 130 degrees
     (obtuse; check it opens wider than a square corner).

D12. A geometry box has two set squares. One has angles 45 degrees, 45 degrees, 90 degrees; the other
     has 30 degrees, 60 degrees, 90 degrees. Which angles can you make by putting two corners side by
     side?
     Answer: One corner from each set square: 45 + 30 = 75 degrees, 45 + 60 = 105 degrees, 90
     + 30 = 120 degrees, 45 + 90 = 135 degrees, 90 + 60 = 150 degrees, 90 + 90 = 180 degrees.
     Teacher explains: Angles that sit side by side with a shared arm and the
     same vertex ADD. Take each corner of the first set square (45, 45, 90) with
     each corner of the second (30, 60, 90): 45 + 30 = 75, 45 + 60 = 105, 45 +
     90 = 135, 90 + 30 = 120, 90 + 60 = 150, 90 + 90 = 180. You can also
     SUBTRACT by laying one corner on top of another: 45 - 30 = 15 degrees and 60 - 45
     = 15 degrees. Let the child make each one and check with a protractor. Now you
     try: which two corners make 105 degrees? (45 degrees and 60 degrees)

M4. Two angles make a straight line (180 degrees). One is given; find the other.

    g) 10 degrees    h) 179 degrees   i) 100 degrees   j) 65 degrees    k) 88 degrees    l) 135 degrees
    m) 1 degrees     n) 60 degrees    o) 155 degrees   p) 30 degrees    q) 112 degrees   r) 45 degrees

M5. Angles round a point add up to 360 degrees. Find the missing angle.
