TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw the triangle every time, mark the right angle and ring the
  hypotenuse before writing anything; say "longest side: add the squares;
  shorter side: subtract"; keep a table of squares 1^2 to 30^2 in the notebook;
  start with the 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 families and cut out squares of centimetre
  paper to check 9 + 16 = 25. Harder: prove the converse (build a right-angled
  triangle with legs a and b; its hypotenuse is c, so the two triangles are
  congruent by SSS); show that (m^2 - n^2, 2mn, m^2 + n^2) always works by
  expanding; find all triples with hypotenuse 25 ((7, 24, 25) and (15, 20, 25));
  find the diagonal of a cube of side s (ssqrt3); investigate Garfield's trapezium
  proof.

================================================================================
TOPIC 6.22 - QUADRILATERALS AND POLYGONS: PROPERTIES, INTERIOR/EXTERIOR ANGLE
             SUMS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - PARALLELOGRAM: both pairs of opposite sides parallel and equal; opposite
    angles equal; neighbouring angles add up to 180 degrees; the diagonals BISECT each
    other (cut each other in half).
  - RECTANGLE = parallelogram with four right angles; its diagonals are also
    EQUAL. RHOMBUS = parallelogram with four equal sides; its diagonals are
    PERPENDICULAR and bisect the corner angles. SQUARE = both a rectangle and a
    rhombus, so it has every one of these properties.
  - TRAPEZIUM: exactly one pair of parallel sides; the two angles along each
    slanting side add up to 180 degrees. In an ISOSCELES trapezium the slanting sides
    are equal, the base angles are equal and the diagonals are equal. KITE: two
    pairs of equal NEIGHBOURING sides; one pair of opposite angles equal;
    diagonals perpendicular, and one of them is a line of symmetry.
  - The INTERIOR angles of a polygon with n sides add up to (n - 2) x 180 degrees,
    because diagonals from one corner cut it into n - 2 triangles: triangle
    180 degrees, quadrilateral 360 degrees, pentagon 540 degrees, hexagon 720 degrees, octagon 1080 degrees,
    decagon 1440 degrees, 20-gon 3240 degrees.
  - The EXTERIOR angles (one at each corner, made by extending a side) of ANY
    convex polygon add up to 360 degrees - one full turn. At each corner
    interior + exterior = 180 degrees.
  - REGULAR polygon (all sides and all angles equal): each exterior angle is
    360 degrees / n; each interior angle is 180 degrees - exterior, which equals
    (n - 2) x 180 degrees / n. Backwards: n = 360 degrees / exterior angle; if this is not a
    whole number, no such regular polygon exists.
  - Missing angles: add the known angles and subtract from the angle sum; with
    algebra, write "sum of the expressions = angle sum" and solve for x.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. In parallelogram ABCD, AB = 9 cm, BC = 5 cm and angle A = 65 degrees. The diagonals meet
    at O and AO = 4 cm. Find the other sides, the other angles, the perimeter
    and the length of diagonal AC.
    Answer: CD = 9 cm, DA = 5 cm; angle B = 115 degrees, angle C = 65 degrees, angle D = 115 degrees;
    perimeter = 28 cm; AC = 8 cm.
    Teacher explains:
            D +-----------------+ C
             /  .           .  /
           /    .       .    /
        A +-----------------+ B
    Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal: CD = AB = 9 cm and
    angle B are co-interior angles (topic 6.19) and add up to 180 degrees:
    angle B = 180 degrees - 65 degrees = 115 degrees. Opposite angles are equal: angle C = 65 degrees, angle D = 115 degrees.
    Check: 65 + 115 + 65 + 115 = 360.
    The diagonals BISECT each other, so O is the midpoint of AC:
    AC = 2 x 4 = 8 cm. Common mistake: thinking the diagonals of every
    parallelogram are equal - that is only true for rectangles. Now you try:
    angle A = 108 degrees. (angle B = 72 degrees, angle C = 108 degrees, angle D = 72 degrees)

D2. Rectangle ABCD is 8 cm long and 6 cm wide, and its diagonals AC and BD meet
    at O. How long is each diagonal, and what kind of triangle is AOB? How does
    a carpenter use this to check that a frame is truly rectangular?
    Answer: Each diagonal is 10 cm (sqrt(64 + 36) = 10). OA = OB = 5 cm, so
    triangle AOB is isosceles. A carpenter measures both diagonals: in a
    rectangle they must be equal.
    Teacher explains: A rectangle is a parallelogram, so its diagonals bisect
    each other. Its diagonals are also EQUAL: triangles ABC and BAD are
    congruent by SAS (AB common, BC = AD, both right angles), so AC = BD. By
    Pythagoras AC^2 = 8^2 + 6^2 = 64 + 36 = 100, AC = 10 cm, and
    OA = OB = OC = OD = 5 cm.
    A frame that has been pushed out of shape is a parallelogram: its sides are
    still equal in pairs, but one diagonal becomes longer than the other. So
    "equal diagonals" is the test for a right-angled frame. Now you try: a
    rectangle 12 cm by 5 cm. Find a diagonal and OA. (13 cm, 6.5 cm)

D3. The diagonals of a rhombus are 12 cm and 16 cm. Find the length of a side,
    the perimeter and the area.
    Answer: Side 10 cm, perimeter 40 cm, area 96 cm^2.
    Teacher explains:
                  .
                / | \
              /   8   \       diagonals cross at 90 degrees
            /  6  |  6  \     halves: 6 cm and 8 cm
            \     |     /
              \   8   /
                \ | /
                  .
    The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other AT RIGHT ANGLES. So they cut
    the rhombus into 4 congruent right-angled triangles with legs 12 / 2 = 6 cm
    and 16 / 2 = 8 cm. Each side is a hypotenuse: sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt100 = 10 cm, and
    the perimeter is 4 x 10 = 40 cm.
    Area: the four triangles each have area 1/2 x 6 x 8 = 24 cm^2, total
    4 x 24 = 96 cm^2. Shortcut: area = 1/2 x d_1 x d_2 = 1/2 x 12 x 16 = 96. This
    works for every quadrilateral with perpendicular diagonals (rhombus, square,
    kite). Now you try: diagonals 10 cm and 24 cm. (side 13 cm, area 120 cm^2)

D4. Riya says, "A square is a rhombus, but a rhombus is not always a square." Is
    she right? Explain with the family tree of quadrilaterals.
    Answer: Yes. A square has four equal sides, so it is a rhombus. A rhombus
    need not have right angles (for example angles 60 degrees, 120 degrees, 60 degrees, 120 degrees), so it
    need not be a square.
    Teacher explains:
                       QUADRILATERAL
                    /        |        \
            TRAPEZIUM  PARALLELOGRAM   KITE
                         /       \     /
                   RECTANGLE    RHOMBUS
                         \       /
                          SQUARE
    Read the tree downwards: each shape is a SPECIAL CASE of every shape above
    it joined by lines, and it has all their properties. A square is a rectangle
    (four right angles), a rhombus (four equal sides), a parallelogram and even
    a kite. Reading upwards needs care: a parallelogram is not always a
    rectangle.
    To decide "Is every A a B?", check whether the DEFINITION of B is true for
    every A. Common mistake: thinking a square is "not a rectangle" because it
    looks different. Now you try: true or false - every rectangle is a
    parallelogram. (true)

D5. Kite ABCD has AB = AD and CB = CD, with angle A = 120 degrees and angle C = 50 degrees. Find angle B and
    Answer: angle B = angle D = 95 degrees. angle S = 110 degrees and angle R = 125 degrees.
    Teacher explains: KITE: the diagonal AC is a line of symmetry, so the angles
    B and D on either side of it are equal. The angle sum is 360 degrees:
    angle B + angle D = 360 degrees - (120 degrees + 50 degrees) = 190 degrees, and each is 190 degrees / 2 = 95 degrees. Note: angle A
    and angle C (between the unequal pairs of sides) are NOT equal.
    TRAPEZIUM: PS and QR cross the parallel sides, so the two angles on each
    slanting side are co-interior and add up to 180 degrees: angle S = 180 degrees - 70 degrees = 110 degrees and
    angle R = 180 degrees - 55 degrees = 125 degrees. Check: 70 + 55 + 125 + 110 = 360. Common mistake:
    pairing the angles along a PARALLEL side (P and Q) instead of along a
    slanting side. Now you try: an isosceles trapezium has one base angle 64 degrees.
    Find the other three. (64 degrees, 116 degrees, 116 degrees)

D6. Why do the interior angles of a polygon with n sides add up to
    (n - 2) x 180 degrees? Find the angle sum of a 15-sided polygon.
    Answer: From one corner, draw all the diagonals: they make n - 2 triangles,
    each with angle sum 180 degrees. For n = 15: (15 - 2) x 180 degrees = 2340 degrees.
    Teacher explains:
       sides n     3     4     5     6     7      8      9     10
       triangles   1     2     3     4     5      6      7      8
       angle sum  180   360   540   720   900   1080   1260   1440
    From corner A you cannot draw a diagonal to A itself or to its two
    neighbours, so there are n - 3 diagonals, cutting the polygon into n - 2
    triangles. The angles of these triangles fit together exactly into the
    angles of the polygon. So the sum is (n - 2) x 180 degrees.
    A second way: join the centre to all n corners. That gives n triangles,
    n x 180 degrees, but the angles round the centre (360 degrees) are not polygon angles:
    n x 180 degrees - 360 degrees = (n - 2) x 180 degrees. For n = 15:
    15 x 180 - 360 = 2700 - 360 = 2340. Each extra side adds 180 degrees. Now you try:
    a 20-sided polygon. (3240 degrees)

D7. Find each interior angle and each exterior angle of a regular 12-sided
    polygon (a dodecagon).
    Answer: Interior 150 degrees, exterior 30 degrees.
    Teacher explains: Method 1: angle sum (12 - 2) x 180 degrees = 1800 degrees; the 12 angles
    are equal, so each is 1800 degrees / 12 = 150 degrees. Exterior = 180 degrees - 150 degrees = 30 degrees.
    Method 2 (faster): the exterior angles add up to 360 degrees, so each is
    360 degrees / 12 = 30 degrees, and the interior angle is 180 degrees - 30 degrees = 150 degrees. For large n
    this is much easier.
       n           3     4     5     6     8     9    10    12
       exterior   120    90    72    60    45    40    36    30
       interior    60    90   108   120   135   140   144   150
    Common mistake: dividing 360 degrees by n and calling it the INTERIOR angle. Now
    you try: a regular 20-sided polygon. (interior 162 degrees, exterior 18 degrees)

D8. Meena walks once round a park shaped like a pentagon. At the five corners
    she turns left through 70 degrees, 60 degrees, 80 degrees, 75 degrees and 75 degrees. What is her total turn,
    and why?
    Answer: 70 degrees + 60 degrees + 80 degrees + 75 degrees + 75 degrees = 360 degrees: one full turn. She ends facing
    the way she started.
    Teacher explains: The angle she TURNS at each corner is the EXTERIOR angle.
    After walking all the way round she faces her starting direction again, so
    the turns together make exactly one complete turn, 360 degrees. This is true for
    every convex polygon, whatever its number of sides.
    Proof with algebra: at each corner interior + exterior = 180 degrees, so all n
    corners give n x 180 degrees. The interior angles take (n - 2) x 180 degrees of this,
    leaving n x 180 degrees - (n - 2) x 180 degrees = 2 x 180 degrees = 360 degrees for the exterior angles.
    Now you try: five exterior angles of a hexagon are 50 degrees, 60 degrees, 70 degrees, 40 degrees and
    80 degrees. Find the sixth. (60 degrees)

D9. A regular polygon has each exterior angle 24 degrees. How many sides has it? Is
    there a regular polygon with each interior angle 130 degrees?
    Answer: 360 degrees / 24 degrees = 15 sides. No: the exterior angle would be 50 degrees, and
    360 / 50 = 7.2 is not a whole number.
    Teacher explains: Work backwards through the exterior angle, because the
    exterior angles of a regular polygon are n equal parts of 360 degrees:
    n = 360 degrees / exterior. From an interior angle, first find the exterior:
    180 degrees - interior. For example interior 156 degrees gives exterior 24 degrees, so n = 15
    again.
    For interior 130 degrees: exterior 180 degrees - 130 degrees = 50 degrees, and 360 / 50 = 7.2. A polygon
    cannot have 7.2 sides, so no regular polygon has angles of 130 degrees. The
    exterior angle must be a FACTOR of 360. Now you try: each interior angle is
    165 degrees. How many sides? (24)

D10. The angles of a hexagon are x, x + 10 degrees, x + 20 degrees, x + 30 degrees, x + 40 degrees and
     x + 50 degrees. Find x and the angles.
     Answer: x = 95 degrees; the angles are 95 degrees, 105 degrees, 115 degrees, 125 degrees, 135 degrees, 145 degrees.
     Teacher explains: Angle sum of a hexagon: (6 - 2) x 180 degrees = 720 degrees. Add the
     expressions: six x's and 10 + 20 + 30 + 40 + 50 = 150. So
        6x + 150 = 720
              6x = 570     (subtract 150 from both sides)
               x = 95      (divide both sides by 6)
     Check: 95 + 105 + 115 + 125 + 135 + 145 = 720. Always check that every
     angle is sensible (for a convex polygon each is less than 180 degrees). Common
     mistake: using 360 degrees for every polygon. Now you try: a pentagon has angles
     2x, 3x, 3x, 4x and 3x. (x = 36 degrees; angles 72 degrees, 108 degrees, 108 degrees, 144 degrees, 108 degrees)

D11. Floor tiles in many Indian homes are squares or hexagons. Which regular
     polygons can cover a floor with no gaps (tessellate) on their own? Can
     regular octagons do it?
     Answer: Only equilateral triangles (6 x 60 degrees = 360 degrees), squares
     (4 x 90 degrees = 360 degrees) and regular hexagons (3 x 120 degrees = 360 degrees). Octagons alone
     cannot (360 / 135 is not whole), but two octagons and a square fit:
     135 degrees + 135 degrees + 90 degrees = 360 degrees.
     Teacher explains: Where tiles meet at a point, their angles must add up to
     exactly 360 degrees. So the interior angle must divide 360 exactly. Pentagon:
     108 degrees, and 3 x 108 = 324 leaves a gap, 4 x 108 = 432 overlaps. Any regular
     polygon with more than 6 sides has an interior angle between 120 degrees and 180 degrees,
     so 2 tiles are too few and 3 are too many.
     Mixing shapes gives more patterns: octagon-octagon-square is common on
     bathroom floors. Now you try: can two regular 12-gons and one equilateral
     triangle meet at a point? (yes, 150 + 150 + 60 = 360)

D12. In a parallelogram two opposite angles are (3x + 10) degrees and (5x - 30) degrees. Find
     x and all four angles.
     Answer: x = 20; the angles are 70 degrees, 110 degrees, 70 degrees, 110 degrees.
     Teacher explains: Choose the right property FIRST. Opposite angles of a
     parallelogram are equal, so
        3x + 10 = 5x - 30
             40 = 2x          (add 30, subtract 3x on both sides)
              x = 20
     Then 3 x 20 + 10 = 70 and 5 x 20 - 30 = 70 (equal, as they must be).
     Neighbouring angles add to 180 degrees, so the other two angles are
     180 degrees - 70 degrees = 110 degrees each. If the two angles were NEIGHBOURS instead, the
     equation would be (sum) = 180. Now you try: two neighbouring angles are
     (2x + 15) degrees and (3x - 5) degrees. (x = 34; 83 degrees and 97 degrees)

PART B - MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Pa = parallelogram, Re = rectangle, Rh = rhombus, Sq = square,
    Tr = trapezium (exactly one pair of parallel sides), Ki = kite (two pairs of
    equal neighbouring sides, not a rhombus). Which of the six ALWAYS have the
    property?
    a) both pairs of opposite sides parallel
    b) exactly one pair of parallel sides
    c) both pairs of opposite sides equal
    d) all four sides equal

    Answers: a) Pa, Re, Rh, Sq   b) Tr   c) Pa, Re, Rh, Sq   d) Rh, Sq

             q) Sq   r) Pa, Re, Rh, Sq   s) Rh, Sq, Ki   t) Pa, Re, Rh, Sq
             u) Pa, Re, Rh, Sq, Tr, Ki   v) Rh, Sq, Ki

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: build the shapes from geostrips or straws and measure sides,
  angles and diagonals; fill in a big property table (rows: properties; columns:
  the six shapes) with ticks; learn the family tree; for angle sums always draw
  the triangles from one corner and write "(n - 2) x 180 degrees" before substituting;
  for regular polygons start from the exterior angle 360 degrees / n. Harder: prove
  that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other using congruent
  triangles (ASA); show the number of diagonals of an n-gon is n(n - 3)/2 (a
  hexagon has 9); find which pairs of regular polygons can tile together with a
  triangle; show that no polygon can have more than three acute interior angles;
  work out the interior angle sum of a star-shaped (concave) polygon.

================================================================================
TOPIC 6.23 - CIRCLES: CIRCUMFERENCE, AREA, pi
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - For EVERY circle, circumference / diameter is the same number, called pi
    ("pi"). pi = 3.14159... never ends and never repeats (it is irrational).
    Useful values: pi ~ 3.14 and pi ~ 22/7 (use 22/7 when the radius is a multiple
    of 7). Always say which value you used.
  - CIRCUMFERENCE (perimeter of a circle): C = pid = 2pir, because the diameter d
    is twice the radius r.
  - AREA: A = pir^2 (square the radius, NOT the diameter). Cutting a circle into
    thin sectors and rearranging them gives a near-rectangle pir long and r high.
  - EXACT answers are left "in terms of pi": r = 5 gives C = 10pi and A = 25pi.
    Backwards: r = C / 2pi; r^2 = A / pi, then take the square root.
  - SEMICIRCLE: curved part pir (half of 2pir), perimeter pir + 2r (do not forget
    the diameter), area pir^2/2. QUADRANT (quarter circle): arc pir/2, perimeter
    pir/2 + 2r, area pir^2/4.
  - RING (annulus) between radii R and r: area = piR^2 - pir^2 = pi(R^2 - r^2). SECTOR
    with angle theta: arc length = (theta/360) x 2pir, area = (theta/360) x pir^2.
  - WHEELS: in one revolution a wheel rolls one circumference. Distance = number
    of revolutions x circumference. Change km and m to cm (or the other way)
    before dividing.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Class 7 wraps a string round some round objects and measures the string (the
    circumference C) and the width across the middle (the diameter d). What do
    they notice?
       object     d (cm)    C (cm)    C / d
       bangle       7        22       3.14...
       plate       25        78.5     3.14
       coin         2.5       7.9     3.16
    Answer: C / d is always a little more than 3, about 3.14, whatever the size
    of the circle. This number is pi.
    Teacher explains: Work out each ratio: 22 / 7 ~ 3.14, 78.5 / 25 = 3.14,
    7.9 / 2.5 = 3.16. Small differences come from measuring. The TRUE value,
    found by mathematicians, is pi = 3.14159265..., a decimal that never ends and
    never repeats. Aryabhata (499 CE) gave 3.1416.
    So C = pi x d. Since d = 2r, also C = 2pir. For quick work we use pi ~ 3.14 or
    pi ~ 22/7 (22 / 7 = 3.142857...). Neither is exact. Common mistake: thinking
    pi = 22/7 exactly. Now you try: a bicycle wheel has d = 60 cm and C = 188 cm.
    Find C / d to 2 decimal places. (3.13)

D2. A circular park has radius 35 m. How long is the fence round it? Fencing
    costs ₹15 per metre. What is the cost? (Use pi = 22/7.)
    Answer: 220 m; ₹3300.
    Teacher explains:
       C = 2pir
         = 2 x 22/7 x 35     (35 / 7 = 5 first)
         = 2 x 22 x 5
         = 220 m
    Cancelling the 7 first keeps the numbers small: 35 / 7 = 5. Cost:
    220 x 15 = ₹3300. Choose 22/7 when the radius or diameter is a multiple of
    7. Common mistakes: using pir (half the circumference), or pir^2 (that is area,
    in m^2). Now you try: radius 21 m. (132 m)

D3. A pizza has diameter 30 cm. Find its circumference exactly (in terms of pi)
    and using pi = 3.14.
    Answer: C = 30pi cm ~ 94.2 cm.
    Teacher explains: With the diameter use C = pid directly: C = pi x 30 = 30pi
    cm. This is the EXACT answer. For a number: 30 x 3.14 = 94.2 cm. With the
    radius we would write C = 2 x pi x 15 = 30pi - the same.
    In exact form the number goes in front: write 30pi, not pi30. Leaving pi in the
    answer avoids rounding errors, so we use it in later working and only turn
    it into a decimal at the end. Now you try: diameter 12 cm. (12pi ~ 37.68 cm)

D4. Why is the area of a circle pir^2? Use the picture: the circle is cut into 16
    thin sectors, and they are arranged top-to-tail.
         /\/\/\/\/\/\/\/\
        /\/\/\/\/\/\/\/\/     height r
        <----- half of C = pir ----->
    Answer: The sectors make an almost-rectangle of length pir (half the
    circumference) and height r, so the area is pir x r = pir^2.
    Teacher explains: Half the sectors point up and half point down, so each
    long side uses half the curved edge: half of 2pir is pir. The height is the
    radius. The more sectors we cut, the straighter the edges and the closer the
    shape is to a rectangle, so A = pir x r = pir^2.
    Example: r = 7 cm, pi = 22/7: A = 22/7 x 7 x 7 = 22 x 7 = 154 cm^2. Area is in
    SQUARE units. Common mistake: squaring the diameter, or computing 2pir (the
    circumference). Now you try: r = 14 cm. (616 cm^2)

D5. A circular rangoli has radius 1.5 m. What area does it cover? (Use
    pi = 3.14.)
    Answer: 7.065 m^2 (exactly 2.25pi m^2).
    Teacher explains:
       A = pir^2
         = 3.14 x 1.5 x 1.5
         = 3.14 x 2.25
         = 7.065 m^2
    Square the radius FIRST: 1.5 x 1.5 = 2.25 (not 3). Then multiply by 3.14:
    3.14 x 2 = 6.28, 3.14 x 0.25 = 0.785, total 7.065. Count decimal places to
    check: 2 + 2 = 4 places in 7.0650. Estimate: 3 x 2 = 6, so about 7 is
    reasonable. Now you try: radius 2.5 m. (19.625 m^2)

D6. A wire 88 cm long is bent into a circle. Find the radius and the area
    enclosed. (pi = 22/7)
    Answer: r = 14 cm, area = 616 cm^2.
    Teacher explains: Work backwards from C = 2pir:
       2 x 22/7 x r = 88
            44/7 x r = 88
                  r = 88 x 7 / 44 = 14 cm
    Then A = 22/7 x 14 x 14 = 616 cm^2. If the same wire is bent into a square,
    each side is 88 / 4 = 22 cm and the area is 22 x 22 = 484 cm^2 - less. For a
    given perimeter, the circle encloses the most area. Common mistake: dividing
    88 by 22/7 and forgetting the 2. Now you try: a 44 cm wire. (r = 7 cm, area
    154 cm^2)

D7. A circular flower bed has area 154 m^2. Find its radius. (pi = 22/7) Also: a
    circle has area 36pi cm^2. What is its radius?
    Answer: r = 7 m; r = 6 cm.
    Teacher explains: A = pir^2, so r^2 = A / pi. First:
    r^2 = 154 / (22/7) = 154 x 7 / 22 = 49, and r = sqrt49 = 7 m. Second: 36pi = pir^2,
    so r^2 = 36 and r = 6 cm (pi cancels - another reason exact answers are nice).
    With 3.14: area 314 m^2 gives r^2 = 314 / 3.14 = 100, r = 10 m. Common
    mistake: stopping at r^2 (writing r = 49). Always finish with the square root
    and check: 22/7 x 7 x 7 = 154. Now you try: area 616 cm^2, pi = 22/7.
    (r = 14 cm)

D8. A protractor is a semicircle of diameter 14 cm. Find its perimeter and its
    area. (pi = 22/7)
    Answer: Perimeter 36 cm; area 77 cm^2.
    Teacher explains:
              . - ~ - .
          +-------+-------+
                14 cm
    Curved edge: half of the circumference, 1/2 x 22/7 x 14 = 22 cm. The
    perimeter goes all the way round, so ADD the straight edge (the diameter):
    22 + 14 = 36 cm. Area: half of pir^2 with r = 7: 1/2 x 22/7 x 7 x 7 = 77 cm^2.
    Common mistakes: forgetting the diameter in the perimeter, and using the
    diameter 14 in pir^2. Now you try: a semicircle of diameter 28 cm. (perimeter
    44 + 28 = 72 cm, area 308 cm^2)

D9. A flower bed in the corner of a lawn is a quadrant (quarter circle) of
    radius 14 m. Find the length of its edging (all round) and its area.
    (pi = 22/7)
    Answer: Perimeter 50 m; area 154 m^2.
    Teacher explains: A quadrant has ONE curved edge and TWO straight edges (two
    radii). Arc = 1/4 x 2 x 22/7 x 14 = 1/4 x 88 = 22 m.
    Perimeter = 22 + 14 + 14 = 50 m.
    Area = 1/4 x 22/7 x 14 x 14 = 1/4 x 616 = 154 m^2.
       shape        curved part     perimeter        area
       circle       2pir             2pir              pir^2
       semicircle   pir              pir + 2r          pir^2/2
       quadrant     pir/2            pir/2 + 2r        pir^2/4
    Now you try: a quadrant of radius 7 cm. (perimeter 25 cm, area 38.5 cm^2)

D10. A circular pond of radius 14 m has a path 7 m wide all round it. Find the
     area of the path. (pi = 22/7)
     Answer: 770 m^2.
     Teacher explains: The path is a RING (annulus): the big circle minus the
     small circle. Outer radius R = 14 + 7 = 21 m, inner radius r = 14 m.
        area = piR^2 - pir^2 = pi(R^2 - r^2)
             = 22/7 x (441 - 196)
             = 22/7 x 245
             = 770 m^2
     Common mistakes: using the width 7 as a radius (pi x 7^2 is a small circle,
     not the ring), and subtracting the radii before squaring (21 - 14 = 7). Now
     you try: radii 5 cm and 3 cm; give the area in terms of pi. (16pi cm^2)

D11. The minute hand of a clock tower is 21 cm long. How far does its tip travel
     in 15 minutes, and what area does the hand sweep? (pi = 22/7)
     Answer: Arc 33 cm; area 346.5 cm^2.
     Teacher explains: In 60 minutes the hand turns 360 degrees, so in 15 minutes it
     turns 90 degrees, a QUARTER of a turn. The tip moves along a quarter of the
     circle: arc = 90/360 x 2 x 22/7 x 21 = 1/4 x 132 = 33 cm. The swept region
     is a SECTOR: area = 90/360 x 22/7 x 21 x 21 = 1/4 x 1386 = 346.5 cm^2.
     General rule for angle theta: take the fraction theta/360 of the whole
     circumference (arc) or of the whole area (sector). Now you try: 20 minutes
     (120 degrees). (arc 44 cm, area 462 cm^2)

D12. A bicycle wheel has diameter 70 cm. How many complete turns does it make in
     travelling 1.1 km? (pi = 22/7)
     Answer: 500 revolutions.
     Teacher explains: In one revolution the wheel rolls forward exactly one
     circumference: C = 22/7 x 70 = 220 cm. Put the distance in the SAME unit:
     1.1 km = 1100 m = 110,000 cm. Number of revolutions = 110,000 / 220 = 500.
     The other direction: distance = revolutions x circumference, e.g. 250 turns
     cover 250 x 220 = 55,000 cm = 550 m. Common mistake: dividing km by cm
     without converting. Now you try: a wheel of radius 42 cm makes 1000
     revolutions. How far does it go? (264,000 cm = 2.64 km)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: measure real circles (bangles, plates, bottle tops) with string
  and find C / d many times; write "r or d?" next to every question and halve
  the diameter before using pir^2; keep the formula card C = 2pir, A = pir^2 on the
  desk; with pi = 22/7 always cancel the 7 first; draw semicircles and quadrants
  and trace the perimeter with a finger to see the straight edges. Harder: show
  that doubling the radius doubles the circumference but multiplies the area by
  4; find the area of the shaded region between a square of side 14 cm and its
  inscribed circle (196 - 154 = 42 cm^2); find how far the tip of a 7 cm hour
  hand travels in a day (88 cm); research Archimedes' method of trapping pi
  between polygons of 96 sides; estimate pi by dropping grains of rice on a
  square with a quadrant drawn in it.

================================================================================
TOPIC 6.24 - SURFACE AREA AND VOLUME: PRISMS, CYLINDERS, CONES, SPHERES,
             PYRAMIDS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - VOLUME = space inside (cm^3, m^3); SURFACE AREA = total area of all the faces
    or curved surfaces (cm^2, m^2). CURVED (or lateral) surface area leaves out
    the ends; TOTAL surface area includes them.
  - PRISM (same cross-section all along): V = area of cross-section x length.
    Cuboid: V = lbh, TSA = 2(lb + bh + lh), walls only = 2(l + b) x h. Cube:
    V = s^3, TSA = 6s^2. Triangular prism: V = 1/2 x base x height x length.
  - CYLINDER (a circular prism): V = pir^2h; curved surface CSA = 2pirh (the label
    unrolls to a rectangle 2pir by h); TSA = 2pirh + 2pir^2.
  - CONE: V = 1/3 x pir^2h (one third of the cylinder with the same base and
    height); slant height l = sqrt(r^2 + h^2); CSA = pirl; TSA = pirl + pir^2.
  - SPHERE: V = 4/3 x pir^3, SA = 4pir^2. HEMISPHERE: V = 2/3 x pir^3, curved surface
    2pir^2, total (with the flat circle) 3pir^2.
  - PYRAMID: V = 1/3 x base area x height. For a square pyramid the slant height
    of a face comes from Pythagoras, and TSA = base + 4 triangles.
  - UNITS: 1 cm^3 = 1 mL; 1000 cm^3 = 1 L; 1 m^3 = 1000 L = 1,000,000 cm^3;
    1 m^2 = 10,000 cm^2. Composite solids: add (or subtract) volumes; for surface
    area count only the surfaces on the outside.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A classroom is 5 m long, 4 m wide and 3 m high. Find the volume of air in it
    and the area of the four walls. Painting the walls and the ceiling costs ₹25
    per m^2. What is the cost?
    Answer: Volume 60 m^3; walls 54 m^2; walls + ceiling 74 m^2, cost ₹1850.
    Teacher explains: Volume: V = l x b x h = 5 x 4 x 3 = 60 m^3.
    Walls: two walls are 5 x 3 and two are 4 x 3. Quicker: walk round the room -
    the perimeter 2 x (5 + 4) = 18 m - and multiply by the height:
    18 x 3 = 54 m^2. This is the LATERAL surface area 2(l + b) x h. Ceiling:
    5 x 4 = 20 m^2. Total to paint: 54 + 20 = 74 m^2, cost 74 x 25 = ₹1850 (the
    floor is not painted).
    Common mistake: using the full TSA 2(lb + bh + lh) = 94 m^2, which includes
    the floor. Read what is to be covered. Now you try: a room 6 m x 4 m x 3 m.
    Area of the four walls? (60 m^2)

D2. A tent is a triangular prism. Its end is a triangle with base 3 m and height
    2 m, and the tent is 5 m long. Find its volume and its total surface area.
              /\
             /  \ 2.5 m       end: base 3 m, height 2 m
            / 2 m\            length 5 m
           /__|___\
             3 m
    Answer: V = 15 m^3; TSA = 46 m^2.
    Teacher explains: Volume of any prism = cross-section area x length.
    Cross-section: 1/2 x 3 x 2 = 3 m^2. V = 3 x 5 = 15 m^3.
    Surface: 2 triangles (2 x 3 = 6 m^2) and 3 rectangles. The sloping sides need
    Pythagoras: half the base is 1.5 m, so the slope is
    sqrt(1.5^2 + 2^2) = sqrt6.25 = 2.5 m. Rectangles: (2.5 + 2.5 + 3) x 5 = 40 m^2.
    TSA = 6 + 40 = 46 m^2. (Canvas without the floor: 46 - 15 = 31 m^2.) Tip: the
    rectangles together are perimeter of the triangle x length. Now you try: a
    prism whose end is a right-angled triangle with sides 6, 8, 10 cm, length
    12 cm. (V = 288 cm^3, TSA = 336 cm^2)

D3. A cylindrical water tank has radius 0.7 m and height 2 m. How many litres
    does it hold? (pi = 22/7)
    Answer: 3.08 m^3 = 3080 L.
    Teacher explains:
       V = pir^2h
         = 22/7 x 0.7 x 0.7 x 2
         = 22 x 0.1 x 0.7 x 2     (0.7 / 7 = 0.1)
         = 3.08 m^3
    A cylinder is a prism with a circular cross-section, so its volume is the
    area of the circle times the height: pir^2 x h. Then 1 m^3 = 1000 L, so
    3.08 m^3 = 3080 L.
    Common mistakes: using the diameter as r, and forgetting to square the
    radius. Now you try: radius 1.4 m, height 1 m. (6.16 m^3 = 6160 L)

D4. A tin can has radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. Find the area of the label round
    its side and the total area of metal. (pi = 22/7)
    Answer: Label (curved surface) 440 cm^2; total surface 748 cm^2.
    Teacher explains:
         ( top )
       +----------------------+
       |      label           | h = 10
       +----------------------+
            length 2pir = 44
         (bottom)
    Peel off the label: it is a RECTANGLE. Its length is the distance round the
    can, 2pir = 2 x 22/7 x 7 = 44 cm, and its width is the height 10 cm.
    CSA = 44 x 10 = 440 cm^2 (= 2pirh). The two ends are circles of area
    22/7 x 7 x 7 = 154 cm^2 each. TSA = 440 + 2 x 154 = 748 cm^2.
    An open tank or a pipe uses fewer ends: open at top, CSA + 1 circle; a pipe,
    CSA only. Now you try: radius 3.5 cm, height 10 cm. (CSA 220 cm^2, TSA
    297 cm^2)

D5. A birthday cap is a cone with radius 6 cm and height 8 cm. Find its slant
    height, the paper needed (curved surface) and the volume inside. Give exact
    answers and then use pi = 3.14.
    Answer: l = 10 cm; CSA = 60pi ~ 188.4 cm^2; V = 96pi ~ 301.44 cm^3.
    Teacher explains: The height, the radius and the slant height make a
    right-angled triangle inside the cone, with l as hypotenuse:
    l = sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt100 = 10 cm.
    Curved surface: CSA = pirl = pi x 6 x 10 = 60pi ~ 60 x 3.14 = 188.4 cm^2.
    Volume:
    V = 1/3 x pi x 6^2 x 8 = 1/3 x pi x 36 x 8 = 96pi ~ 96 x 3.14 = 301.44 cm^3. With
    a base the TSA would be 60pi + 36pi = 96pi cm^2.
    Common mistake: using the height h in pirl instead of the slant height l (and
    l in the volume instead of h). Now you try: r = 5 cm, h = 12 cm. (l = 13 cm,
    CSA 65pi cm^2, V 100pi cm^3)

D6. Why does a cone have 1/3 in its volume formula? A cone of ice cream has
    radius 7 cm and height 12 cm. Find its volume. (pi = 22/7)
    Answer: A cone holds exactly one third of the cylinder with the same base
    and height. V = 1/3 x 22/7 x 7 x 7 x 12 = 616 cm^3.
    Teacher explains: Experiment: fill a paper cone with rice and pour it into a
    cylinder with the same radius and height. It takes exactly THREE cones to
    fill the cylinder. So V(cone) = 1/3 x pir^2h. The same is true for a pyramid
    and the prism on the same base.
       cylinder: 22/7 x 7 x 7 x 12 = 1848 cm^3
       cone:     1848 / 3            = 616 cm^3
    Now you try: a cone with radius 7 cm and height 9 cm. (462 cm^3)

D7. A large decorative globe is a sphere of radius 21 cm. Find its surface area
    and volume. (pi = 22/7)
    Answer: SA = 5544 cm^2; V = 38,808 cm^3.
    Teacher explains:
    SA = 4pir^2 = 4 x 22/7 x 21 x 21 = 4 x 22 x 3 x 21 = 5544 cm^2.
    V = 4/3 x pir^3 = 4/3 x 22/7 x 21 x 21 x 21 = 38,808 cm^3 (cancel: 21 / 7 = 3
    and 21 / 3 = 7, then 4 x 22 x 3 x 7 x 21 = 38,808).
    Archimedes showed the surface of a sphere is exactly 4 times the area of its
    great circle (pir^2). In terms of pi, a ball of radius 3 has
    SA = 4 x pi x 9 = 36pi and V = 4/3 x pi x 27 = 36pi - the same number, but
    different units (cm^2 and cm^3). Common mistake: 4/3 x pir^2 (mixing the
    formulas). Now you try: radius 6 cm, in terms of pi. (SA 144pi cm^2, V 288pi
    cm^3)

D8. A steel bowl is a hemisphere of radius 7 cm. How much does it hold? What is
    the area of its curved surface? What is the total surface area of a SOLID
    hemisphere of the same radius? (pi = 22/7)
    Answer: V = 718 2/3 cm^3 (about 0.72 L); curved surface 308 cm^2; solid
    hemisphere TSA 462 cm^2.
    Teacher explains: A hemisphere is half a sphere, so
    V = 2/3 x pir^3 = 2/3 x 22/7 x 343 = 2156/3 = 718 2/3 cm^3. Curved
    surface = half of 4pir^2 = 2pir^2 = 2 x 22/7 x 49 = 308 cm^2.
    A solid hemisphere also has a flat circular face pir^2 = 154 cm^2, so its
    TSA = 2pir^2 + pir^2 = 3pir^2 = 462 cm^2. A bowl has no lid, so only the curved
    part counts. Now you try: a hemisphere of radius 21 cm. (curved surface
    2772 cm^2, V 19,404 cm^3)

D9. A square pyramid has base side 10 m and vertical height 12 m. Find its
    volume, the slant height of each triangular face, and its total surface
    area.
    Answer: V = 400 m^3; slant height 13 m; TSA = 360 m^2.
    Teacher explains: The base area is 10 x 10 = 100 m^2, so
    V = 1/3 x 100 x 12 = 400 m^3 (one third of base area x height).
    Slant height: from the top, drop straight down to the centre of the base,
    then go to the middle of one edge (half of 10 m is 5 m). The slant height is
    the hypotenuse: sqrt(12^2 + 5^2) = sqrt169 = 13 m.
    TSA = base + 4 triangles = 100 + 4 x 1/2 x 10 x 13 = 100 + 260 = 360 m^2.
    Common mistake: using the vertical height 12 as the height of the triangular
    faces. Now you try: base side 6 cm, height 4 cm. (V = 48 cm^3, slant height
    5 cm, TSA = 96 cm^2)

D10. A cylindrical jug has radius 7 cm and height 20 cm. How many litres does it
     hold, and how many 200 mL glasses can be filled from it? (pi = 22/7)
     Answer: 3080 cm^3 = 3.08 L; 15 full glasses (3080 / 200 = 15.4).
     Teacher explains: V = 22/7 x 7 x 7 x 20 = 154 x 20 = 3080 cm^3. Now convert:
        1 cm^3 = 1 mL          1000 cm^3 = 1 L
        1 m^3 = 1000 L          1 m^3 = 1,000,000 cm^3
        1 m^2 = 10,000 cm^2      1 cm^2 = 100 mm^2
     So 3080 cm^3 = 3080 mL = 3.08 L. Glasses: 3080 / 200 = 15.4, so 15 glasses
     can be FILLED (the 16th is less than half full). Why is
     1 m^3 = 1,000,000 cm^3 and not 100 cm^3? A cube of edge 1 m = 100 cm has
     volume 100 x 100 x 100 cm^3. Now you try: how many 250 mL glasses from the
     same jug? (12, since 3080 / 250 = 12.32)

D11. A toy is a cone of height 4 cm standing on a hemisphere of radius 3 cm
     (same radius). Find its volume and its surface area in terms of pi.
     Answer: V = 30pi cm^3; SA = 33pi cm^2.
     Teacher explains: Volume: add the parts. Hemisphere 2/3 x pi x 27 = 18pi;
     cone 1/3 x pi x 9 x 4 = 12pi. Total 18pi + 12pi = 30pi cm^3.
     Surface: only what you can touch from outside - the curved part of the
     hemisphere 2pi x 9 = 18pi and the curved part of the cone. Slant height
     l = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = 5, CSA = pi x 3 x 5 = 15pi. Total 18pi + 15pi = 33pi cm^2. The
     circle where they join is INSIDE, so it is not counted. Now you try: a
     capsule is a cylinder of radius 3 cm and length 10 cm with a hemisphere on
     each end. (V = 90pi + 36pi = 126pi cm^3, SA = 60pi + 36pi = 96pi cm^2)

D12. A cone, a sphere and a cylinder all have radius 3 cm, and the cone and
     cylinder have height 6 cm (the same as the sphere's diameter). Compare
     their volumes.
     Answer: Cone 18pi, sphere 36pi, cylinder 54pi cm^3: in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3.
     Teacher explains: Cone: 1/3 x pi x 9 x 6 = 18pi. Sphere: 4/3 x pi x 27 = 36pi.
     Cylinder: pi x 9 x 6 = 54pi. Divide by 18pi: 1 : 2 : 3.
     Archimedes was so proud of finding that the sphere is 2/3 of the cylinder
     around it that he asked for a sphere in a cylinder to be carved on his
     tomb. It is true for every radius: with height 2r, cone 2/3 x pir^3, sphere
     4/3 x pir^3, cylinder 2pir^3. Now you try: radius 6 cm, height 12 cm. (144pi,
     288pi, 432pi cm^3)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: handle real objects (a tin, a funnel, a ball, a box) and unroll or
  unfold them to see the net; list the parts of the surface before calculating;
  keep one formula card for each solid; always write the unit (cm^2 for area, cm^3
  for volume); with pi = 22/7 cancel the 7s first; check the answer with a rough
  estimate using pi ~ 3. Harder: find how the volume changes when the radius of a
  cylinder is doubled (x 4) and when its height is doubled (x 2); find the
  volume of metal in a pipe of outer radius 5 cm, inner radius 4 cm and length
  70 cm (pi(25 - 16) x 70 = 630pi cm^3); a sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and
  recast into a cylinder of radius 4 cm - find its height (288pi / 16pi = 18 cm);
  find the volume of a frustum (a cone with its top cut off).

================================================================================
TOPIC 6.25 - TRANSFORMATIONS: TRANSLATION, ROTATION, REFLECTION, DILATION
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A TRANSFORMATION moves every point of a shape (the OBJECT) to a new position
    (the IMAGE). Image points are named with a dash: A -> A'.
  - TRANSLATION (slide) by a vector: the column vector with top a and bottom b
    (written [a, b] in these notes) means a right (left if negative) and b up
    (down if negative): (x, y) -> (x + a, y + b).
  - REFLECTION in a mirror line: each image point is the same distance behind
    the mirror, on the perpendicular. Rules: x-axis (x, y) -> (x, -y); y-axis
    (x, y) -> (-x, y); line y = x (x, y) -> (y, x); line y = -x (x, y) -> (-y, -x);
    line x = k (x, y) -> (2k - x, y); line y = k (x, y) -> (x, 2k - y). Points on
    the mirror do not move.
  - ROTATION about a centre through an angle (anticlockwise unless we say
    clockwise). About the origin O: 90 degrees anticlockwise (x, y) -> (-y, x); 180 degrees
    (x, y) -> (-x, -y); 90 degrees clockwise = 270 degrees anticlockwise (x, y) -> (y, -x). For
    another centre, move the centre to O, rotate, and move back.
  - DILATION (enlargement) with centre O and scale factor k: (x, y) -> (kx, ky).
    k > 1 enlarges, 0 < k < 1 reduces; every length is multiplied by k, every
    area by k^2, and angles do not change.
  - To DESCRIBE a single transformation fully: translation - the vector;
    reflection - the mirror line; rotation - centre, angle and direction;
    dilation - centre and scale factor.
  - Translations, reflections and rotations keep size and shape (the image is
    CONGRUENT); a reflection reverses the order of the labels (clockwise becomes
    anticlockwise). A dilation keeps shape but not size (the image is SIMILAR).

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Triangle A(1, 2), B(4, 2), C(1, 5) is translated by the vector [5, -3] (5
    right, 3 down). Find the image.
    Answer: A'(6, -1), B'(9, -1), C'(6, 2).
    Teacher explains: A translation is a slide: every point moves the SAME way
    by the SAME amount. In a textbook the vector is written as a column:
          (  5 )     top: x-step (+ right, - left)
          ( -3 )     bottom: y-step (+ up, - down)
    Add the top number to every x and the bottom number to every y:
    A(1, 2) -> (1 + 5, 2 - 3) = (6, -1); B(4, 2) -> (9, -1); C(1, 5) -> (6, 2). The
    image has the same size, shape and direction, so a translation is described
    completely by its vector.
    Common mistake: adding the vector to x only, or mixing up the order (top is
    ALWAYS the x-step). Now you try: P(-2, 4) translated by [3, -6]. ((1, -2))

D2. The point P(-2, 3) is moved by a translation to P'(4, -1). What is the
    vector? Which vector moves P' back to P?
    Answer: [6, -4]; back: [-6, 4].
    Teacher explains: Vector = image - object, done separately for x and y:
    x-step 4 - (-2) = 6, y-step -1 - 3 = -4. So the vector is [6, -4]: 6 right,
    4 down. Check: (-2 + 6, 3 - 4) = (4, -1).
    To undo a translation, go the opposite way: change both signs, [-6, 4].
    Common mistake: object - image, which gives the reverse vector. Now you try:
    (5, 1) is translated to (2, 7). ([-3, 6])

D3. Reflect triangle A(2, 1), B(5, 1), C(5, 3) in the x-axis, and then
    (separately) in the y-axis.
    Answer: x-axis: (2, -1), (5, -1), (5, -3). y-axis: (-2, 1), (-5, 1),
    (-5, 3).
    Teacher explains:
              y
              |        + C(5, 3)
              |   A +--+ B
         -----+---------------- x     mirror: the x-axis
              |   A'+--+ B'
              |        + C'(5, -3)
    In the x-axis the mirror is horizontal: x stays the same and y changes sign,
    (x, y) -> (x, -y). A point 3 above the axis goes to 3 below it. In the y-axis
    the mirror is vertical: (x, y) -> (-x, y). A point ON the mirror, such as
    (4, 0) in the x-axis, does not move.
    The image is congruent but "flipped": going A -> B -> C was anticlockwise, and
    A' -> B' -> C' is clockwise. Common mistake: changing the wrong coordinate -
    remember "x-axis: change y". Now you try: reflect (-3, -7) in the y-axis.
    ((3, -7))

D4. Reflect the point (3, 1) in the line y = x and in the line y = -x.
    Answer: In y = x: (1, 3). In y = -x: (-1, -3).
    Teacher explains: The line y = x goes through (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2)... at
    45 degrees. Reflecting in it SWAPS the coordinates: (x, y) -> (y, x). Fold squared
    paper along y = x and the point (3, 1) lands exactly on (1, 3).
    The line y = -x goes through (1, -1), (2, -2)... Reflecting in it swaps AND
    changes both signs: (x, y) -> (-y, -x). So (3, 1) -> (-1, -3). Check: the
    midpoint of (3, 1) and (-1, -3) is (1, -1), which is on y = -x, as it must
    be.
    Common mistake: only swapping for y = -x. Now you try: reflect (-2, 5) in
    y = -x. ((-5, 2))

D5. Reflect the point (5, 1) in the line x = 2, and the point (3, 4) in the line
    y = -1.
    Answer: (-1, 1) and (3, -6).
    Teacher explains: x = 2 is a VERTICAL line through (2, 0). So y stays the
    same. The point is 5 - 2 = 3 units to the right of the mirror, so the image
    is 3 units to the left: x = 2 - 3 = -1. The image is (-1, 1). Formula: new
    x = 2k - x = 4 - 5 = -1.
    y = -1 is a HORIZONTAL line. Now x stays the same: the point is 4 - (-1) = 5
    units above the mirror, so the image is 5 below it: y = -1 - 5 = -6.
    Formula: new y = 2k - y = -2 - 4 = -6.
    Common mistake: x = 2 "looks like" it is about x, so pupils change y. Draw
    the line first! Now you try: reflect (-3, 4) in y = 1. ((-3, -2))

D6. Rotate the point (3, 1) through 90 degrees anticlockwise about the origin. Then
    rotate triangle (1, 1), (4, 1), (4, 3) in the same way.
    Answer: (3, 1) -> (-1, 3). Triangle: (-1, 1), (-1, 4), (-3, 4).
    Teacher explains: Use tracing paper: trace the axes and the point, put a
    pencil point on O, turn the paper a quarter turn anticlockwise (the traced
    x-axis now lies on the y-axis) and read where the point has gone: (-1, 3).
    The rule: (x, y) -> (-y, x). Swap the coordinates and change the sign of the
    NEW first one. For the triangle: (1, 1) -> (-1, 1), (4, 1) -> (-1, 4),
    (4, 3) -> (-3, 4). The distance from O stays the same, and the line from O to
    the point turns through 90 degrees.
    Common mistake: using (y, -x), which is the CLOCKWISE rule. Now you try:
    rotate (2, 5) through 90 degrees anticlockwise about O. ((-5, 2))

D7. Rotate (3, 1) about the origin through 180 degrees, and through 90 degrees clockwise. What
    is a rotation of 270 degrees anticlockwise?
    Answer: 180 degrees: (-3, -1). 90 degrees clockwise: (1, -3). 270 degrees anticlockwise is the
    same as 90 degrees clockwise.
    Teacher explains:
       rotation about O               rule
       90 degrees anticlockwise              (x, y) -> (-y, x)
       180 degrees (either direction)        (x, y) -> (-x, -y)
       90 degrees clockwise = 270 degrees anti.     (x, y) -> (y, -x)
    A half turn changes both signs; the image is directly opposite the point
    through O. Three quarter turns anticlockwise end in the same place as one
    quarter turn clockwise, because 270 degrees + 90 degrees = 360 degrees.
    Check a rule with an easy point: (1, 0) rotated 90 degrees clockwise must go to
    (0, -1); the rule (y, -x) gives (0, -1). Now you try: rotate (-4, 2) through
    90 degrees clockwise about O. ((2, 4))

D8. Rotate P(5, 2) through 90 degrees anticlockwise about the centre C(2, 1).
    Answer: P' = (1, 4).
    Teacher explains: The rules work only about the origin, so MOVE the centre
    to the origin first:
       step 1  P relative to C:  (5 - 2, 2 - 1) = (3, 1)
       step 2  rotate 90 degrees anti:  (3, 1) -> (-1, 3)
       step 3  move back:        (-1 + 2, 3 + 1) = (1, 4)
    Check: CP and CP' have the same length (both sqrt10), and the step from C to P,
    (3, 1), has turned into (-1, 3), a right-angle turn. Tracing paper with the
    pencil on C gives the same answer. Now you try: rotate (4, 3) through 180 degrees
    about (1, 1). ((-2, -1))

D9. Dilate triangle A(2, 1), B(4, 1), C(2, 4) with centre O and scale factor 3.
    Compare lengths, angles and area. What happens with scale factor 1/2 to the
    point (8, 6)?
    Answer: A'(6, 3), B'(12, 3), C'(6, 12). Lengths x 3, angles the same,
    area x 9. (8, 6) -> (4, 3).
    Teacher explains: Multiply both coordinates by k: (x, y) -> (3x, 3y). Each
    image point is on the line from O through the object point, 3 times as far
    from O.
    AB = 4 - 2 = 2 and A'B' = 12 - 6 = 6 (x 3); AC = 3 and A'C' = 9 (x 3). The
    angle at A is still 90 degrees. Area: 1/2 x 2 x 3 = 3 becomes 1/2 x 6 x 9 = 27,
    which is 9 = 3^2 times as big. With k = 1/2 the image is SMALLER:
    (8, 6) -> (4, 3). A scale factor between 0 and 1 still counts as a dilation
    ("enlargement").
    Now you try: dilate (6, -4) with centre O and scale factor 1/2. ((3, -2))

D10. A(2, 3) -> A'(6, 9) and B(4, 1) -> B'(12, 3) under a dilation. Find the scale
     factor and the centre.
     Answer: Scale factor 3, centre O(0, 0).
     Teacher explains: Every coordinate has been multiplied by 3: 2 x 3 = 6,
     3 x 3 = 9, 4 x 3 = 12, 1 x 3 = 3. That is the rule (x, y) -> (3x, 3y), a
     dilation with centre O and k = 3.
     Check with lengths: AB^2 = 2^2 + 2^2 = 8 and A'B'^2 = 6^2 + 6^2 = 72 = 9 x 8, so
     A'B' = 3 x AB. To find a centre in general, join A to A' and B to B' and
     extend the lines: they cross at the centre. Here both lines pass through O.
     Now you try: (4, 8) -> (1, 2) and (6, -2) -> (1.5, -0.5). Find k. (k = 1/4)

D11. Triangle P(1, 2), Q(3, 2), R(3, 5) is mapped to P'(-2, 1), Q'(-2, 3),
     R'(-5, 3). Describe the single transformation fully.
     Answer: A rotation of 90 degrees anticlockwise about the origin.
     Teacher explains: Step 1: same size? PQ = 2 and P'Q' = 2, QR = 3 and
     Q'R' = 3, so it is not a dilation. Step 2: test the rules on P(1, 2):
     (x, -y) gives (1, -2), (y, x) gives (2, 1), (-y, x) gives (-2, 1). The
     rotation rule fits. Step 3: test it on Q and R too: (3, 2) -> (-2, 3) and
     (3, 5) -> (-5, 3). All fit.
     A full description needs the centre (the origin), the angle (90 degrees) and the
     direction (anticlockwise). "It turned" is not enough. Now you try: (1, 2),
     (4, 2), (4, 6) -> (2, 1), (2, 4), (6, 4). (reflection in the line y = x)

D12. Which transformations keep the size of a shape? Which keep its shape? Which
     reverse the order of the labels?
     Answer: Translations, reflections and rotations keep size and shape
     (congruent images). Dilations keep shape only (similar images). Only
     reflections reverse the order of the labels.
     Teacher explains:
                       lengths   angles   area    label order
        translation     same      same     same    same
        reflection      same      same     same    reversed
        rotation        same      same     same    same
        dilation (k)    x k       same     x k^2    same
     Translations, reflections and rotations are called ISOMETRIES ("same
     measure"). A shape and its image under an isometry are congruent. Under a
     dilation the image is similar (topic 6.26). A reflection turns a left hand
     into a right hand - you cannot slide or turn a left glove to make a right
     glove. Now you try: a triangle of area 5 cm^2 is dilated with k = 2. What is
     the new area? (20 cm^2)

M11. Describe fully the single transformation that maps the first triangle onto
     the second.
     a) (1, 2), (3, 2), (3, 5) -> (-2, 1), (-2, 3), (-5, 3)
     b) (1, 2), (4, 2), (4, 6) -> (2, 1), (2, 4), (6, 4)
     c) (2, 1), (5, 1), (5, 3) -> (2, -1), (5, -1), (5, -3)
     d) (2, 1), (5, 1), (5, 3) -> (-2, 3), (1, 3), (1, 5)
     e) (1, 1), (3, 1), (1, 4) -> (3, 3), (9, 3), (3, 12)
     f) (2, 3), (4, 3), (4, 6) -> (-2, -3), (-4, -3), (-4, -6)
     g) (-3, 1), (-1, 1), (-1, 4) -> (3, 1), (1, 1), (1, 4)
     h) (1, 2), (2, 5), (4, 1) -> (2, -1), (5, -2), (1, -4)
     i) (1, 1), (2, 3), (4, 2) -> (9, 1), (8, 3), (6, 2)
     j) (4, 8), (8, 4), (8, 8) -> (1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 2)
     k) (2, 1), (3, 4), (5, 2) -> (-1, -2), (-4, -3), (-2, -5)
     l) (0, 1), (2, 2), (1, 4) -> (0, -5), (2, -6), (1, -8)
     Answers: a) rotation 90 degrees anticlockwise about O   b) reflection in y = x
              c) reflection in the x-axis   d) translation by [-4, 2]
              e) dilation, centre O, k = 3   f) rotation 180 degrees about O
              g) reflection in the y-axis   h) rotation 90 degrees clockwise about O
              i) reflection in x = 5   j) dilation, centre O, k = 1/4
              k) reflection in y = -x   l) reflection in y = -2

M12. In a) to l) apply the first transformation, then the second, and give the
     final point. In m) to r) name the single transformation equal to "first,
     then second".
     a) (3, 1): reflection in the x-axis, then reflection in the y-axis
     b) (3, 1): reflection in the y-axis, then reflection in the x-axis
     c) (2, 5): rotation 90 degrees anticlockwise about O, then rotation 90 degrees
        anticlockwise about O
     d) (4, -1): reflection in y = x, then reflection in the x-axis
     e) (-2, 3): translation by [2, 3], then translation by [-5, 1]
     f) (1, 4): rotation 90 degrees anticlockwise about O, then reflection in the
        x-axis
     g) (5, 2): reflection in x = 1, then reflection in x = 4
     h) (-3, -2): dilation, centre O, k = 2, then translation by [1, 1]
     i) (6, 0): rotation 90 degrees clockwise about O, then reflection in y = x
     j) (2, -4): dilation, centre O, k = 3, then dilation, centre O, k = 1/2
     k) (0, 7): reflection in y = -x, then reflection in y = x
     l) (-1, 6): reflection in y = 2, then reflection in y = -1
     m) reflection in the x-axis, then reflection in the y-axis
     n) rotation 90 degrees anticlockwise about O, then rotation 90 degrees anticlockwise
        about O
     o) reflection in y = x, then reflection in the x-axis
     p) translation by [2, 3], then translation by [-5, 1]
     q) reflection in x = 1, then reflection in x = 4
     r) dilation, centre O, k = 3, then dilation, centre O, k = 1/2
     Answers: a) (-3, -1)   b) (-3, -1)   c) (-2, -5)   d) (-1, -4)   e) (-5, 7)
              f) (-4, -1)   g) (11, 2)   h) (-5, -3)   i) (-6, 0)   j) (3, -6)
              k) (0, -7)   l) (-1, 0)   m) rotation 180 degrees about O
              n) rotation 180 degrees about O   o) rotation 90 degrees clockwise about O
              p) translation by [-3, 4]   q) translation by [6, 0]
              r) dilation, centre O, k = 1.5

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: use squared paper and tracing paper for every question; say the
  rule aloud before using it ("x-axis: change y"); draw the mirror line in
  colour before reflecting; for rotations turn the book itself; check every
  answer by plotting the object and the image; begin with points in the first
  quadrant, then use negatives. Harder: find the single transformation equal to
  two reflections in parallel lines (a translation by twice the gap) and in
  perpendicular lines (a half turn about the crossing point); find the centre of
  a rotation from a shape and its image using perpendicular bisectors; dilate
  with a negative scale factor (k = -2 sends (1, 3) to (-2, -6)); design a
  wallpaper pattern using translations and reflections.

================================================================================
TOPIC 6.26 - SIMILARITY AND SCALE DRAWINGS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - Two figures are SIMILAR (symbol ~) if one is an exact enlargement or
    reduction of the other: all corresponding ANGLES are equal AND all
    corresponding SIDES are in the same ratio. Congruent figures are similar
    with ratio 1.
  - SCALE FACTOR k = image length / object length (the same for every pair of
    corresponding sides). k > 1 enlarges, k < 1 reduces. Always match sides by
    their angles, not by their position on the page.
  - For TRIANGLES one condition is enough. AA: two pairs of equal angles (the
    third pair is then equal too). SSS: all three pairs of sides in the same
    ratio. SAS: two pairs of sides in the same ratio and the angles between them
    equal. For other polygons both angles and sides must be checked.
  - Missing sides: find k from a known pair, then multiply (or divide) the other
    side by k; or write a proportion x/6 = 10/4 and cross-multiply. A line
    parallel to one side of a triangle cuts off a small triangle similar to the
    whole one.
  - Shadows at the same time of day: sun rays are parallel, so objects and their
    shadows make similar right-angled triangles: height / shadow is the same for
    all.
  - SCALE DRAWINGS and MAPS: a scale 1 : n means 1 cm on the drawing represents
    n cm in real life. Real length = drawing x n; drawing = real / n; convert
    units last (100 cm = 1 m, 100,000 cm = 1 km, so 1 : 100,000 - one lakh -
    means 1 cm represents 1 km).
  - If lengths are multiplied by k, AREAS are multiplied by k^2 and VOLUMES by
    k^3.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A photo 4 cm by 6 cm is enlarged to 10 cm by 15 cm. Is the enlargement
    similar to the original? What about a print 8 cm by 10 cm?
    Answer: 10 x 15: yes, k = 2.5 for both sides. 8 x 10: no - 8 / 4 = 2 but
    10 / 6 ~ 1.67, so faces would look stretched.
    Teacher explains: Divide corresponding sides, short with short and long with
    long: 10 / 4 = 2.5 and 15 / 6 = 2.5. The same ratio, so every length is
    multiplied by the same scale factor k = 2.5, and all the angles are still
    90 degrees. The rectangles are similar.
    For 8 x 10: 8 / 4 = 2 but 10 / 6 = 1 2/3. Different ratios, so the shape has
    changed: NOT similar. A quick check: the long side / the short side must be
    the same: 6 / 4 = 1.5 = 15 / 10, but 10 / 8 = 1.25. Now you try: is a 6 x 9
    rectangle similar to a 4 x 6 rectangle? (yes, k = 1.5)

D2. A square of side 3 cm and a rhombus of side 5 cm with angles 60 degrees and 120 degrees
    have their sides in the same ratio. Are they similar? A 2 x 6 rectangle and
    a 4 x 4 square have equal angles. Are they similar?
    Answer: Neither pair is similar. The first pair has proportional sides but
    different angles; the second has equal angles but sides not in proportion.
    Teacher explains: For polygons with 4 or more sides, BOTH conditions are
    needed: equal angles AND sides in the same ratio. The square and the rhombus
    fail on angles (90 degrees against 60 degrees and 120 degrees): the rhombus is a "pushed over"
    square. The rectangle and the square fail on sides: 4 / 2 = 2 but
    4 / 6 = 2/3.
    Triangles are special: if the angles are equal, the sides are automatically
    in proportion, and the other way round. That is why AA or SSS alone is
    enough for triangles. Now you try: are all squares similar? Are all
    rectangles similar? (all squares yes; rectangles no)

D3. One triangle has angles 50 degrees and 60 degrees. Another has angles 60 degrees and 70 degrees. Are
    they similar?
    Answer: Yes. The third angles are 70 degrees and 50 degrees, so both triangles have angles
    50 degrees, 60 degrees, 70 degrees (AA).
    Teacher explains: Find the third angle of each: 180 degrees - (50 degrees + 60 degrees) = 70 degrees and
    180 degrees - (60 degrees + 70 degrees) = 50 degrees. Both triangles have exactly the angles 50 degrees, 60 degrees
    and 70 degrees, so they are similar. Two pairs of equal angles are always enough
    (AA), because the third angles must then be equal too.
    When you name them, keep the order of equal angles: if angle A = angle P, angle B = angle Q,
    angle C = angle R, write delta ABC ~ delta PQR. Then AB matches PQ, BC matches QR and CA matches
    RP. Now you try: angles 40 degrees and 85 degrees in one triangle, 55 degrees and 85 degrees in another.
    (similar: both are 40 degrees, 55 degrees, 85 degrees)

D4. delta ABC ~ delta PQR with AB = 6 cm, BC = 8 cm, AC = 9 cm and PQ = 9 cm. Find QR and
    PR.
    Answer: k = 1.5; QR = 12 cm, PR = 13.5 cm.
    Teacher explains:
       k = PQ / AB = 9 / 6 = 1.5
       QR = BC x k = 8 x 1.5 = 12 cm
       PR = AC x k = 9 x 1.5 = 13.5 cm
    Step 1: find a pair of corresponding sides where BOTH lengths are known (AB
    and PQ). Step 2: scale factor = new / old. Step 3: multiply every other side
    by k. Check the ratios: 12 / 8 = 1.5 and 13.5 / 9 = 1.5.
    The same with a proportion: QR/8 = 9/6, so QR = 8 x 9 / 6 = 12. Common
    mistake: adding (9 - 6 = 3, so QR = 8 + 3 = 11). Similar figures MULTIPLY,
    they do not add. Now you try: PQ = 12 cm. (QR = 16 cm, PR = 18 cm)

D5. In delta XYZ, XY = 15 cm, YZ = 12 cm and XZ = 9 cm. delta LMN is similar to it with
    angle L = angle X, angle M = angle Y, angle N = angle Z, and LM = 10 cm. Find MN and LN.
    Answer: k = 2/3; MN = 8 cm, LN = 6 cm.
    k = 10/15 = 2/3 (a reduction, because LMN is smaller).
    MN = 12 x 2/3 = 8 cm and LN = 9 x 2/3 = 6 cm. Check: 8 / 12 = 2/3 and
    6 / 9 = 2/3.
    Common mistake: matching sides by where they are drawn. Figures may be
    turned or flipped; always match through the angles. Now you try: LM = 5 cm.
    (MN = 4 cm, LN = 3 cm)

    DE = 5 cm. Find BC.
                  A
                 / \
              4 /   \
               D-----E      DE = 5
            6 /       \
             B---------C    BC = ?
    Answer: BC = 12.5 cm.
    shared. By AA, delta ADE ~ delta ABC. Match the WHOLE side AB with AD:
    AB = 4 + 6 = 10 cm, so k = 10 / 4 = 2.5 and BC = 5 x 2.5 = 12.5 cm.
    Common mistake: using DB instead of AB (6 / 4 = 1.5 gives 7.5 cm, wrong).
    The small triangle is ADE and the big one is ABC - their sides are AD and
    AB, not AD and DB. Now you try: AD = 3 cm, DB = 9 cm, DE = 4 cm.
    (BC = 16 cm)

D7. At 4 p.m. a 2 m pole casts a shadow 3 m long. At the same moment a tree
    casts a shadow 18 m long. How tall is the tree?
    Answer: 12 m.
    Teacher explains: The sun's rays are parallel, so the rays make the same
    angle with the ground everywhere. Pole + shadow and tree + shadow form two
    right-angled triangles with equal angles: similar (AA).
       height / shadow is the same:
       h / 18 = 2 / 3
            h = 18 x 2 / 3 = 12 m
    Or: the tree's shadow is 18 / 3 = 6 times as long, so the tree is 6 times as
    tall: 2 x 6 = 12 m. This is how Thales measured the height of a pyramid. Now
    you try: a girl 1.5 m tall has a shadow 2 m long; a building's shadow is
    40 m. How tall is the building? (30 m)

D8. To find the width AB of a pond, Arjun puts pegs so that AE and BD are
    and DE = 3 m. How wide is the pond?
         A ~~~~~~~ B      pond
           \       /
             \   /
               C
             /   \
           /       \
         D --------- E
    Answer: AB = 9 m.
    Teacher explains: The two triangles ABC and EDC make a "bow tie". The angles
    at C are vertically opposite, hence equal, and angle BAC = angle DEC (alternate
    So AB/ED = AC/EC: AB = 3 x 12 / 4 = 9 m. The big triangle is 3 times the
    small one (12 / 4 = 3), so AB = 3 x 3 = 9 m. Surveyors use such tricks to
    measure distances they cannot walk across. Now you try: AC = 15 m, CE = 5 m,
    DE = 2.4 m. (7.2 m)

D9. The plan of a classroom is drawn to the scale 1 : 50. On the plan the room
    is 16 cm by 12 cm. What are the real measurements? A cupboard is 4.5 m long.
    How long is it on the plan?
    Answer: The room is 8 m by 6 m. The cupboard is 9 cm long on the plan.
    Teacher explains: 1 : 50 means 1 cm on the plan represents 50 cm in the
    room. Real = plan x 50: 16 x 50 = 800 cm = 8 m and 12 x 50 = 600 cm = 6 m.
    Backwards, plan = real / 50, but change to cm FIRST: 4.5 m = 450 cm, and
    450 / 50 = 9 cm.
    Common mistake: dividing 4.5 by 50 and getting 0.09 cm - the units were
    mixed. Always write the unit at every step. A scale has no units: 1 : 50 is
    the same in cm, m or inches. Now you try: a plan at 1 : 100 shows a wall
    7.5 cm long. How long is the real wall? (7.5 m)

D10. A trekking map has scale 1 : 50,000. Two villages are 7.4 cm apart on the
     map. How far apart are they really? A road is 12 km long; how long is it on
     the map?
     Answer: 3.7 km; 24 cm.
     Teacher explains: 1 cm on the map represents 50,000 cm = 500 m = 0.5 km. So
     7.4 cm x 50,000 = 370,000 cm = 3.7 km. Or: 7.4 x 0.5 km = 3.7 km.
     Backwards: 12 km = 1,200,000 cm, and 1,200,000 / 50,000 = 24 cm.
        1 m  = 100 cm
        1 km = 1000 m = 100,000 cm   (one lakh centimetres)
        so 1 : 100,000 means 1 cm represents 1 km
     Common mistake: forgetting that 1 km is 100,000 cm, not 1000 cm. Now you
     try: on a 1 : 200,000 map two towns are 5.5 cm apart. (11 km)

D11. A photo 4 cm by 6 cm is enlarged with scale factor 3. How do the perimeter
     and the area change? A floor plan has scale 1 : 100; a room measures 5 cm
     by 4 cm on it. What is the real floor area?
     Answer: Perimeter x 3 (20 cm -> 60 cm); area x 9 (24 cm^2 -> 216 cm^2). The
     room is 20 m^2.
     Teacher explains: The new photo is 12 cm by 18 cm. Perimeter: 20 cm becomes
     60 cm, x 3 like every length. Area: 4 x 6 = 24 cm^2 becomes
     12 x 18 = 216 cm^2 = 9 x 24. Area is length x length, so it is multiplied by
     k x k = k^2 = 9. Draw it: the big photo holds 9 copies of the small one (3
     rows of 3).
     On the plan, 1 cm represents 100 cm = 1 m, so 1 cm^2 represents
     1 m x 1 m = 1 m^2. The room is 5 m x 4 m = 20 m^2 (plan area
     20 cm^2 x 100^2 = 200,000 cm^2 = 20 m^2). Now you try: on a 1 : 200 plan a room
     is 3 cm by 2 cm. Real floor area? (24 m^2)

D12. Two similar jars have heights 10 cm and 15 cm. The small one holds 400 mL.
     How much does the large one hold?
     Answer: 1350 mL. k = 1.5, volume factor 1.5^3 = 3.375, and
     400 x 3.375 = 1350.
     Teacher explains: Volume is length x length x length, so if every length is
     multiplied by k, the volume is multiplied by k^3. Here k = 15 / 10 = 1.5 and
     k^3 = 1.5 x 1.5 x 1.5 = 3.375. The large jar holds 400 x 3.375 = 1350 mL.
     Its label (surface area) is k^2 = 2.25 times as big.
        lengths x k      areas x k^2      volumes x k^3
        k = 2            x 4             x 8
        k = 3            x 9             x 27
        k = 1/2          x 1/4           x 1/8
     Common mistake: multiplying the volume by k only (600 mL). Now you try:
     cubes of edge 2 cm and 6 cm. How many times the volume is the big one? (27
     times)

PART B - MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------

             n) yes, k = 3/7   o) yes, k = 3/4   p) no

M2. The sides of two triangles are given, in matching order. Are the triangles

    i) 7, 8, 9 and 14, 16, 17      j) 3, 3, 3 and 7, 7, 7

    m) 9, 12, 15 and 3, 4, 5       n) 2, 4, 5 and 5, 10, 12

             j) yes, k = 7/3   k) yes, k = 1.5   l) no   m) yes, k = 1/3   n) no
             o) yes, k = 5/6   p) yes, k = 4

M3. Two angles of each of two triangles are given. Find the third angles and

    a) 50 degrees, 60 degrees and 60 degrees, 70 degrees    b) 40 degrees, 80 degrees and 80 degrees, 60 degrees

    Answers: a) yes (50 degrees, 60 degrees, 70 degrees)   b) yes (40 degrees, 60 degrees, 80 degrees)

M8. Shadows at the same time of day. In a) to h) a pole of height h_1 has shadow
    s_1; find the height of an object with shadow s_2. In i) to n) find the shadow
    of an object of height h_2 (all in m).
    a) h_1 = 2, s_1 = 3, s_2 = 18       b) h_1 = 1.5, s_1 = 2, s_2 = 40
    c) h_1 = 1, s_1 = 0.5, s_2 = 12     d) h_1 = 3, s_1 = 4, s_2 = 20
    e) h_1 = 1.8, s_1 = 2.4, s_2 = 16   f) h_1 = 5, s_1 = 2, s_2 = 9
    g) h_1 = 2.5, s_1 = 1, s_2 = 6      h) h_1 = 1.2, s_1 = 0.8, s_2 = 30
    i) h_1 = 2, s_1 = 3, h_2 = 10       j) h_1 = 1.5, s_1 = 2, h_2 = 45
    k) h_1 = 4, s_1 = 1, h_2 = 60       l) h_1 = 1, s_1 = 1.5, h_2 = 7
    m) h_1 = 6, s_1 = 9, h_2 = 14       n) h_1 = 2, s_1 = 5, h_2 = 3
    Answers: a) h_2 = 12   b) h_2 = 30   c) h_2 = 24   d) h_2 = 15   e) h_2 = 12
             f) h_2 = 22.5   g) h_2 = 15   h) h_2 = 45   i) s_2 = 15   j) s_2 = 60
             k) s_2 = 15   l) s_2 = 10.5   m) s_2 = 21   n) s_2 = 7.5
