TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: colour the matching parts of two triangles in the same colour and
  say the letters in order; for every congruence proof first list what is GIVEN,
  then look for a common side or vertically opposite angles; build triangles
  from straws or strips (three lengths fix the triangle; 3, 4, 8 will not
  close); for side-angle order, draw an arrow from each angle across the
  triangle to its opposite side. Harder: prove SSS from SAS (place the triangles
  back to back and use isosceles triangles); prove that the medians to the equal
  sides of an isosceles triangle are equal; show that a median is less than half
  the sum of the two sides next to it (AB + AC > 2AD); prove that the sum of the
  three medians is less than the perimeter; find all triangles with whole-number
  sides and perimeter 15.

================================================================================
TOPIC 7.22 - QUADRILATERALS: PARALLELOGRAM THEOREMS, MID-POINT THEOREM
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - ANGLE SUM: the angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360 degrees (a diagonal splits
    it into two triangles, 2 x 180 degrees).
  - A PARALLELOGRAM is a quadrilateral with BOTH pairs of opposite sides
    parallel. THEOREMS: a diagonal divides it into two CONGRUENT triangles
    (ASA); opposite sides are EQUAL; opposite angles are EQUAL; consecutive
    angles add up to 180 degrees; the diagonals BISECT each other.
  - CONVERSES (tests for a parallelogram): a quadrilateral is a parallelogram if
    (i) both pairs of opposite sides are equal, or (ii) both pairs of opposite
    angles are equal, or (iii) the diagonals bisect each other, or (iv) ONE pair
    of opposite sides is both EQUAL and PARALLEL.
  - SPECIAL PARALLELOGRAMS: a RECTANGLE has a right angle (then all four are
    right angles) and its diagonals are EQUAL; a RHOMBUS has equal adjacent
    sides (so all four sides are equal) and its diagonals bisect each other at
    RIGHT ANGLES; a SQUARE is both, with equal diagonals that are perpendicular
    bisectors of each other.
  - Tests: a parallelogram with equal diagonals is a rectangle; with
    perpendicular diagonals it is a rhombus; with equal AND perpendicular
    diagonals it is a square.
  - MID-POINT THEOREM: the segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a
    triangle is PARALLEL to the third side and HALF of it. If E, F are the
  - CONVERSE: the line through the mid-point of one side of a triangle, parallel
    to another side, BISECTS the third side.
  - Consequences: the three mid-points of a triangle's sides form a triangle
    with HALF the perimeter and a QUARTER of the area; the mid-points of the
    sides of ANY quadrilateral form a parallelogram whose perimeter equals the
    sum of the diagonals; the segment joining the mid-points of the legs of a
    trapezium is parallel to the parallel sides and equals half their sum.
  - INTERCEPT THEOREM: if three or more parallel lines cut off equal intercepts
    on one transversal, they cut off equal intercepts on every transversal.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prove that the angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360 degrees. The angles of a
    quadrilateral are in the ratio 3 : 5 : 9 : 13. Find them.
                 D ------------------ C
                 |  \                /
                 |       \         /
                 |            \   /
                 A ------------- B
            (diagonal BD splits ABCD into delta ABD and delta BCD)
    Answer: Each of the two triangles has angle sum 180 degrees, so the total is 360 degrees.
    The angles are 36 degrees, 60 degrees, 108 degrees and 156 degrees.
    Teacher explains: Draw the diagonal BD. It splits angle B into angle ABD + angle DBC and angle D
    into angle ADB + angle BDC.
            Statement                                 Reason
            angle A + angle ABD + angle ADB = 180 degrees                   angle sum of delta ABD
            angle C + angle DBC + angle BDC = 180 degrees                   angle sum of delta BCD
            angle A + (angle ABD + angle DBC) + angle C + (angle ADB + angle BDC) = 360 degrees    add
            angle A + angle B + angle C + angle D = 360 degrees                  the parts make angle B, angle D
    Ratio: 3 + 5 + 9 + 13 = 30 parts make 360 degrees, so one part is 12 degrees: the angles
    are 3 x 12 = 36 degrees, 5 x 12 = 60 degrees, 9 x 12 = 108 degrees and 13 x 12 = 156 degrees. Check:
    36 + 60 + 108 + 156 = 360. The proof works for every CONVEX quadrilateral
    (and, with the right diagonal, for a concave one too). Common mistake: using
    180 degrees for a quadrilateral. Now you try: three angles of a quadrilateral are
    75 degrees, 90 degrees and 110 degrees. Find the fourth. (85 degrees)

D2. ABCD is a parallelogram. Prove that the diagonal AC divides it into two
    congruent triangles, and deduce that AB = CD, AD = CB and angle B = angle D. If AB = 9
    cm, BC = 6 cm and angle B = 110 degrees, find CD, AD, angle D, angle A and angle C.
                D ----------------------- C
               /                 .-'     /
              /            .-'          /
             /       .-'               /
            /  .-'                    /
           A ----------------------- B
    AD = 6 cm, angle D = 110 degrees, angle A = angle C = 70 degrees.
    Teacher explains:
            Statement                   Reason
            AC = CA                     common side
            AB = CD, BC = DA, angle B = angle D   CPCT
    Using the other diagonal BD in the same way gives angle A = angle C. So in a
    parallelogram the opposite sides are equal and the opposite angles are
    CD = AB = 9 cm, AD = BC = 6 cm, angle D = angle B = 110 degrees, angle A = 180 degrees - 110 degrees = 70 degrees and
    angle C = angle A = 70 degrees. Check: 70 + 110 + 70 + 110 = 360. Take care with the letter
    parallelogram has one angle of 58 degrees. Find the others. (122 degrees, 58 degrees, 122 degrees)

D3. Prove the converse: if both pairs of opposite sides of a quadrilateral are
    equal, it is a parallelogram. Why does the ironing-board or "lazy tongs"
    mechanism keep its top parallel to the floor?
    mechanism with rods of fixed equal opposite lengths, the quadrilateral stays
    a parallelogram whatever the angle, so the top stays parallel to the bottom.
    Teacher explains: Draw the diagonal BD.
            Statement                   Reason
            AB = CD                     given
            AD = CB                     given
            BD = DB                     common side
            angle ABD = angle CDB                 CPCT
            angle ADB = angle CBD                 CPCT
    Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so ABCD is a parallelogram. A
    parallelogram with fixed side lengths is NOT rigid: its angles can change.
    But because opposite sides stay equal, the figure stays a parallelogram, and
    so one side always stays parallel to the opposite side. This is used in
    parallel rulers, car jacks, some desk lamps and folding gates. Common
    mistake: thinking ONE pair of equal opposite sides is enough; an isosceles
    trapezium has one pair of equal (non-parallel) sides but is not a
    parallelogram. Now you try: a quadrilateral has sides AB = 7, BC = 4,
    CD = 7, DA = 4 (in cm). Is it a parallelogram? (yes: both pairs of opposite
    sides equal)

D4. Prove that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, and state the
    converse. In parallelogram ABCD the diagonals meet at O with OA = (3x - 1)
    cm, OC = (x + 7) cm, OB = (2y) cm and OD = (y + 5) cm. Find x, y, AC and BD.
                D ----------------------- C
               /  `-.               .-'  /
              /      `-.       .-'      /
             /           ` O .         /
            /        .-'      `-.     /
           /    .-'              `-. /
          A ----------------------- B
    Answer: OA = OC and OB = OD. x = 4, y = 5, AC = 22 cm, BD = 20 cm. Converse:
    if the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other, it is a
    parallelogram.
    Teacher explains:
            Statement                   Reason
            AB = CD                     opposite sides of a parallelogram
            OA = OC, OB = OD            CPCT
    Numbers:
            3x - 1 = x + 7,  2x = 8,  x = 4:   OA = OC = 11, AC = 22 cm
            2y = y + 5,  y = 5:                OB = OD = 10, BD = 20 cm
    The converse is proved with vertically opposite angles: if OA = OC and
    EACH OTHER, but they are not equal to each other (except in a rectangle).
    Now you try: in a parallelogram AC = 18 cm; find OA. (9 cm)

D5. Prove that if one pair of opposite sides of a quadrilateral is equal AND
    parallel, it is a parallelogram. Use it: ABCD is a parallelogram and E, F
    are the mid-points of AB and CD. Show that AECF is a parallelogram.
                D ---------- F ---------- C
               /       .-'             .'/
              /   .-'              .-'  /
             /.-'              .-'     /
            A ---------- E ---------- B
            Statement                   Reason
            AB = CD                     given
            AC = CA                     common side
            angle BCA = angle DAC                 CPCT
    and AB = DC, so AE = FC (Axiom 7). One pair of opposite sides is equal and
    often the QUICKEST, because it needs only one pair of sides. Common mistake:
    "equal" alone or "parallel" alone is not enough (think of an isosceles
    trapezium, or any trapezium). Now you try: if AB = 10 cm in the figure, how
    long is EB? (5 cm)

D6. In parallelogram ABCD, angle A = (3x + 10) degrees and angle B = (5x - 30) degrees. Find all four
    angles. Then prove that the bisectors of angle A and angle B meet at a right angle.
    Answer: x = 25; angle A = angle C = 85 degrees, angle B = angle D = 95 degrees. If the bisectors meet at P,
    then angle PAB + angle PBA = 1/2(angle A + angle B) = 90 degrees, so angle APB = 90 degrees.
    Teacher explains: angle A and angle B are CONSECUTIVE angles, which are co-interior
    angles between the parallel sides AD and BC, so they add up to 180 degrees:
            (3x + 10) + (5x - 30) = 180
                         8x - 20 = 180
                              x = 25
            angle A = 3 x 25 + 10 = 85 degrees,  angle B = 5 x 25 - 30 = 95 degrees
    Opposite angles are equal: angle C = 85 degrees and angle D = 95 degrees. Check:
    85 + 95 + 85 + 95 = 360. For the bisectors, in delta APB:
            angle PAB + angle PBA = 1/2angle A + 1/2angle B = 1/2 x 180 degrees = 90 degrees
            angle APB = 180 degrees - 90 degrees = 90 degrees        (angle sum of delta APB)
    With the numbers: 42.5 degrees + 47.5 degrees = 90 degrees. Doing this at all four corners shows
    that the four angle bisectors of a parallelogram (not a rhombus) form a
    RECTANGLE. Common mistake: setting consecutive angles EQUAL (that would give
    x = 20 and angles of 70 degrees, which do not add up to 180 degrees). Now you try:
    angle A = (2x) degrees and angle C = (x + 40) degrees in a parallelogram. (opposite angles: x = 40,
    angle A = 80 degrees, angle B = 100 degrees)

D7. Prove that a parallelogram with one right angle is a rectangle, and that the
    diagonals of a rectangle are equal. Conversely, show that a parallelogram
    with equal diagonals is a rectangle. How does a carpenter use this to check
    a door frame?
            D ---------------------- C
            |                        |
            |                        |
            A ---------------------- B
    Answer: If angle A = 90 degrees then angle B = 180 degrees - 90 degrees = 90 degrees, angle C = angle A = 90 degrees,
    The carpenter measures both diagonals: if they are equal, the frame is
    rectangular.
    Teacher explains:
            Statement                   Reason
            AB = BA                     common side
            angle DAB = angle CBA = 90 degrees           angles of a rectangle
            AD = BC                     opposite sides of a parallelogram
            BD = AC                     CPCT
    AC = BD), so angle ABC = angle BAD. These are consecutive angles of a parallelogram,
    which add up to 180 degrees, so each is 90 degrees. A carpenter or mason cannot easily
    measure a 90 degrees angle on a big frame, but can measure two diagonals with a
    tape: equal diagonals (together with equal opposite sides) guarantee right
    angles. Common mistake: thinking ANY quadrilateral with equal diagonals is a
    rectangle; an isosceles trapezium also has equal diagonals. The
    quadrilateral must first be a parallelogram. Now you try: a rectangle has
    sides 6 cm and 8 cm. Find each diagonal. (sqrt(36 + 64) = 10 cm)

D8. Prove that the diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular bisectors of each
    other. A rhombus has diagonals 16 cm and 12 cm. Find its side. Which
    parallelograms are squares?
                      D
                    /   \
                  /       \
                A --- O --- C
                  \       /
                    \   /
                      B
    is 10 cm. A parallelogram is a square if its diagonals are equal AND
    perpendicular (or: it is both a rectangle and a rhombus).
    Teacher explains: A rhombus is a parallelogram, so its diagonals bisect each
    other: OA = OC and OB = OD.
            Statement                   Reason
            AB = CB                     sides of a rhombus
            OA = OC                     diagonals of a parallelogram bisect
            OB = OB                     common side
            angle AOB = angle COB                 CPCT
            angle AOB = angle COB = 90 degrees           linear pair of equal angles
    Numbers: OA = 16 / 2 = 8 cm and OB = 12 / 2 = 6 cm, and angle AOB = 90 degrees, so by
    Pythagoras AB = sqrt(8^2 + 6^2) = sqrt100 = 10 cm. The perimeter is 40 cm. Summary
    of the special parallelograms:
            rectangle:  equal diagonals
            rhombus:    perpendicular diagonals (they also bisect the angles)
            square:     equal AND perpendicular diagonals
    Common mistake: thinking the diagonals of a rhombus are equal; they are
    equal only in a square. Now you try: rhombus diagonals 10 cm and 24 cm.
    Side? (sqrt(25 + 144) = 13 cm)

D9. Prove the mid-point theorem: if E and F are the mid-points of sides AB and
                        A
                      /   \
                    /       \
                E /-----------\F
                /               \
              /                   \
            B-----------------------C
    Teacher explains: Through C draw a line parallel to BA, meeting EF produced
    at G.
            Statement                   Reason
            AF = CF                     F is the mid-point of AC
            angle AFE = angle CFG                 vertically opposite angles
            AE = CG, EF = FG            CPCT
            BE = AE = CG                E is the mid-point of AB
            EF = 1/2EG = 1/2BC              EF = FG
    all the earlier results: congruence, alternate angles and the parallelogram
    tests. It gives a quick way to measure a length you cannot reach: to find
    the width BC of a pond, measure the distance EF between the mid-points of AB
    and AC on dry land and double it. Common mistake: halving the wrong side; EF
    is half of the side it does NOT touch. Now you try: EF = 4.5 cm. Find BC. (9
    cm)

D10. Prove the converse of the mid-point theorem: the line through the mid-point
     of one side of a triangle parallel to another side bisects the third side.
     mid-point of AD and the line through E parallel to AB meets BC at F. Show
     that F is the mid-point of BC and find EF.
                    D --------- C
                   /             \
                E ------------------ F
                 /                   \
                A ------------------- B
     Answer: F is the mid-point of BC, and EF = (12 + 8)/2 = 10 cm.
     Teacher explains: CONVERSE. In delta ABC let E be the mid-point of AB and let
     the line through E parallel to BC meet AC at F. Let F' be the mid-point of
     parallel to BC (Playfair's axiom), so EF and EF' are the same line and
     F = F': F is the mid-point. TRAPEZIUM: draw the diagonal AC, meeting EF at
     G.
                      so G is the mid-point of AC and EG = 1/2DC = 4 cm
                      so F is the mid-point of CB and GF = 1/2AB = 6 cm
             EF = EG + GF = 4 + 6 = 10 cm = (AB + DC)/2
     The segment joining the mid-points of the non-parallel sides of a trapezium
     is parallel to the parallel sides and equals HALF THEIR SUM. It is the
     "average width" of the trapezium, which is why the area of a trapezium is
     (average of parallel sides) x height. Common mistake: taking EF = 1/2AB or
     1/2DC. Now you try: a trapezium has parallel sides 15 cm and 9 cm. Length of
     the mid-segment? (12 cm)

D11. (a) delta ABC has sides 8 cm, 10 cm and 12 cm. D, E, F are the mid-points of its
     sides. Find the sides and the perimeter of delta DEF, and compare the areas. (b)
     P, Q, R, S are the mid-points of the sides of a quadrilateral ABCD with
     diagonals AC = 9 cm and BD = 7 cm. What kind of figure is PQRS and what is
     its perimeter?
     Answer: (a) 4, 5 and 6 cm; perimeter 15 cm, half of 30 cm; area of delta DEF is
     a quarter of the area of delta ABC. (b) PQRS is a parallelogram with perimeter
     9 + 7 = 16 cm.
     Teacher explains: (a) Each side of delta DEF joins two mid-points, so it is HALF
     the side it does not touch:
             sides of delta ABC:   8     10     12     perimeter 30
             sides of delta DEF:   4      5      6     perimeter 15
     The three segments cut delta ABC into FOUR triangles; each is congruent to delta DEF
     (SSS: all have sides 4, 5, 6), so area(delta DEF) = 1/4 area(delta ABC). (b) In delta ABC, P
     parallel). This is VARIGNON'S theorem, true for EVERY quadrilateral.
             PQ = SR = 1/2 x 9 = 4.5,   QR = PS = 1/2 x 7 = 3.5
             perimeter = 2(4.5 + 3.5) = 16 = AC + BD
     If the diagonals are equal, PQRS is a rhombus; if they are perpendicular,
     it is a rectangle. Common mistake: expecting PQRS to have the same shape as
     ABCD. Now you try: the mid-points of the sides of a rectangle with
     diagonals 10 cm. What figure, and what perimeter? (a rhombus with side 5
     cm; perimeter 20 cm)

D12. State the intercept theorem. Three parallel lines l, m, n cut a transversal
     p at A, B, C with AB = BC = 3 cm, and another transversal q at D, E, F with
     DE = 4.5 cm. Find EF. How can ruled notebook paper be used to divide a
     strip of card into 5 equal parts?
             l  -----A--------D--------
                      \        \
             m  -------B--------E------
                        \        \
             n  ---------C--------F----
     Answer: If parallel lines make equal intercepts on one transversal, they
     make equal intercepts on every transversal; so EF = DE = 4.5 cm. Lay the
     strip across the notebook so that its ends are on two ruled lines 5 spaces
     apart; the lines in between cut it into 5 equal parts.
     Teacher explains: Proof: join A to F, meeting m at G.
                      so G is the mid-point of AF   (converse of the mid-point
                                                           theorem)
                      so E is the mid-point of FD, and DE = EF
     The notebook lines are parallel and EQUALLY spaced, so they make equal
     intercepts on a line perpendicular to them; by the theorem they make equal
     intercepts on ANY slanting line, including the strip of card. Tilt the
     strip until one end is on line 0 and the other on line 5: the lines 1, 2,
     3, 4 mark the division points. This is also the idea behind dividing a
     segment in a given ratio with ruler and compass (topic 7.28). Common
     mistake: using the theorem when the lines are NOT parallel, or when the
     intercepts on the first transversal are not equal. Now you try: four
     parallel lines cut p into three equal parts of 2 cm and cut q with the
     first part 3.2 cm. Length on q from the first to the fourth line?
     (3 x 3.2 = 9.6 cm)

M12. True or false?
     a) The angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360 degrees.
     b) A diagonal of a parallelogram divides it into two congruent triangles.
     c) The diagonals of a parallelogram are equal.
     d) The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
     e) Consecutive angles of a parallelogram are equal.
     f) Every rectangle is a parallelogram.
     g) Every rhombus is a square.
     h) Every square is a rhombus.
     i) The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular.
     j) The diagonals of a rectangle are perpendicular.
     k) A quadrilateral with equal diagonals is a rectangle.
     l) A parallelogram with equal diagonals is a rectangle.
     m) A quadrilateral with one pair of sides equal and parallel is a
        parallelogram.
     n) A trapezium has two pairs of parallel sides.
     o) The mid-point segment of a triangle is half the third side.
     p) The mid-point triangle has half the area of the triangle.
     q) Joining the mid-points of any quadrilateral gives a parallelogram.
     r) The mid-segment of a trapezium equals half the sum of the parallel
        sides.
     s) A parallelogram can have exactly three right angles.
     t) The bisectors of two consecutive angles of a parallelogram meet at 90 degrees.
     Answers: a) true   b) true   c) false   d) true   e) false   f) true
              g) false   h) true   i) true   j) false   k) false   l) true
              m) true   n) false   o) true   p) false (a quarter)   q) true
              r) true   s) false   t) true

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: make a family tree of quadrilaterals (quadrilateral -> trapezium ->
  parallelogram -> rectangle / rhombus -> square) and list the properties each
  inherits; build parallelograms from Meccano strips or straws and push them to
  see what changes and what stays the same; fold a paper triangle so that the
  apex touches the base to see the mid-point segment; for each proof, mark the
  parallel sides with arrows first. Harder: prove that the quadrilateral formed
  by the angle bisectors of a parallelogram is a rectangle; prove that the
  medians of a triangle meet at a point two-thirds of the way along each (use
  the mid-point theorem twice); show that the line joining the mid-points of the
  diagonals of a trapezium is parallel to the parallel sides and equals half
  their difference; explore Varignon's parallelogram in GeoGebra by dragging the
  vertices.

================================================================================
TOPIC 7.23 - AREAS OF PARALLELOGRAMS AND TRIANGLES ON SAME BASE
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - Two figures are ON THE SAME BASE AND BETWEEN THE SAME PARALLELS when they
    share a side (the base) and the vertices (or side) opposite the base lie on
    one line parallel to the base. We write ar(ABCD) for the area of ABCD.
  - THEOREM 1: parallelograms on the same base (or on equal bases) and between
    the same parallels are equal in area. Proof by congruent triangles: cut a
    triangle off one end and add a congruent triangle at the other end. So area
    of a parallelogram = base x height, for EITHER pair of sides:
    b_1 x h_1 = b_2 x h_2.
  - A diagonal divides a parallelogram into two congruent triangles. Hence if a
    triangle and a parallelogram are on the same base and between the same
    parallels, ar(triangle) = 1/2 x ar(parallelogram), which gives area of a
    triangle = 1/2 x base x height.
  - THEOREM 2: triangles on the same base (or equal bases) and between the same
    parallels are equal in area. CONVERSE: triangles on the same base and on the
    same side of it with equal areas lie between the same parallels (their
    heights are equal).
  - Triangles with the same height have areas in the ratio of their bases. A
    MEDIAN divides a triangle into two triangles of equal area; the two
    diagonals of a parallelogram divide it into four triangles of equal area; in
    ar(AOD) = ar(BOC), where O is the meeting point of the diagonals.
  - In proofs write each step with a reason (same base and same parallels,
    median, diagonal of a parallelogram, congruent triangles) and add or
    subtract areas of pieces.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prove that parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels
    are equal in area.
          \   /           \   /
            D---------------C
         parallelograms ABCD and EFCD on the same base DC
    ar(ABCD) = ar(ADE) + ar(EDCB) = ar(BCF) + ar(EDCB) = ar(EFCD).
    Teacher explains: Both parallelograms stand on DC and their top sides AB and
    EF lie on the same line AF, parallel to DC. Compare the two triangles at the
    ends:
       Statement                    Reason
       ar(ADE) = ar(BCF)            congruent figures, equal areas
    Now add the same piece EDCB to both:
    ar(ABCD) = ar(ADE) + ar(EDCB) = ar(BCF) + ar(EDCB) = ar(EFCD). The
    parallelogram has only been cut and re-glued: a triangle moved from one end
    to the other. So every parallelogram on base DC between these parallels has
    the same area as the RECTANGLE on DC between them, namely base x height.
    Common mistake: thinking the "slanting" parallelogram is bigger because its
    sides are longer. Its perimeter is bigger; its area is not. Now you try: a
    parallelogram and a rectangle stand on the same base 12 cm between the same
    parallels 5 cm apart. Area of each? (60 cm^2)

D2. In parallelogram ABCD, AB = 16 cm, the height AE onto DC is 8 cm and the
    height CF onto AD is 10 cm. Find AD.
    Answer: AD = 12.8 cm.
    Teacher explains: A parallelogram has TWO base-height pairs, one for each
    pair of sides, and both give the same area:
       area = DC x AE = 16 x 8 = 128 cm^2      (DC = AB = 16 cm)
       area = AD x CF = AD x 10
       AD x 10 = 128,  AD = 128 / 10 = 12.8 cm
    Rule: b_1 x h_1 = b_2 x h_2. The height must be PERPENDICULAR to the base it is
    paired with: AE goes with DC (or AB), CF goes with AD (or BC). Check: the
    longer side has the shorter height (16 > 12.8 and 8 < 10). Common mistake:
    multiplying AB by CF, which mixes a base with the wrong height. Now you try:
    AB = 12 cm, height onto AB is 7 cm, AD = 10 cm. Find the height onto AD.
    (8.4 cm)

D3. Prove that triangles on the same base and between the same parallels are
    equal in area. Then find the area of every triangle whose base is AB = 10 cm
    and whose third vertex lies on a line parallel to AB at a distance of 6 cm.
    Answer: Each such triangle is half of a parallelogram on AB between the same
    parallels, so all have the same area: 1/2 x 10 x 6 = 30 cm^2.
       Statement                          Reason
       ar(ABP) = ar(ABQ)                  halves of equal areas
    So sliding the top vertex along the parallel line never changes the area:
    the base and the height stay the same. With AB = 10 cm and height 6 cm:
    area = 1/2 x 10 x 6 = 30 cm^2 for every position. Common mistake: taking the
    slanting side AP as the height. The height is the perpendicular distance
    between the parallels. Now you try: base 9 cm, parallels 8 cm apart. Area of
    each triangle? (36 cm^2)

D4. ABCD is a parallelogram of area 84 cm^2 and P is any point on side CD. Find
    ar(APB) and ar(APD) + ar(BPC). Does the answer depend on where P is?
    Answer: ar(APB) = 42 cm^2 and ar(APD) + ar(BPC) = 42 cm^2, wherever P is on
    CD.
    Teacher explains: delta APB and parallelogram ABCD are on the same base AB and
    between the same parallels AB and DC. So
       ar(APB) = 1/2 x ar(ABCD) = 1/2 x 84 = 42 cm^2
       ar(APD) + ar(BPC) = ar(ABCD) - ar(APB) = 84 - 42 = 42 cm^2
    Why half? Area of the triangle = 1/2 x AB x h and area of the
    parallelogram = AB x h, with the SAME h. Moving P along CD changes the two
    side triangles (one grows while the other shrinks) but never their total.
    Common mistake: thinking P must be the midpoint of CD. It does not matter.
    Now you try: a parallelogram of area 50 cm^2, P on CD. ar(APB)? (25 cm^2)

D5. Prove that a median of a triangle divides it into two triangles of equal
    area. In delta ABC, AD is a median and E is the midpoint of AD. If
    ar(ABC) = 64 cm^2, find ar(BED).
    Answer: ar(ABD) = ar(ACD); ar(BED) = 1/4 x ar(ABC) = 16 cm^2.
    ar(ACD) = 1/2 x DC x AN. Since D is the midpoint of BC, BD = DC, so the two
    areas are equal: EQUAL BASES, SAME HEIGHT.
       ar(ABD) = 1/2 ar(ABC) = 1/2 x 64 = 32     (AD is a median)
       BE is a median of delta ABD                    (E is mid AD)
       ar(BED) = 1/2 ar(ABD) = 1/2 x 32 = 16 cm^2
    So ar(BED) = 1/2 x 1/2 x ar(ABC) = 1/4 x 64 = 16 cm^2. The same idea is used
    over and over: every time a median is drawn, the area is halved. Common
    mistake: halving the length but forgetting that the triangles must also have
    the same height (they do, because they share the vertex opposite the halved
    side). Now you try: ar(ABC) = 36 cm^2. Find ar(BED). (9 cm^2)

D6. Itwaari has a four-sided field ABCD. The panchayat asks him to give up the
    corner at D for a health centre and take equal land on the other side so
    that his field becomes a TRIANGLE of the same area. How can it be done? If
    ar(ABC) = 180 m^2 and ar(ACD) = 120 m^2, what is the area of the new
    triangular field?
    ar(ACD) = ar(ACE), so ar(ABE) = ar(ABCD) = 300 m^2.
    BC extended at E. Step 3: delta ACD and delta ACE are on the same base AC and between
    the same parallels AC and DE, so they have EQUAL areas. Hence
       ar(ABE) = ar(ABC) + ar(ACE)
               = ar(ABC) + ar(ACD) = ar(ABCD)
               = 180 + 120 = 300 m^2
    Itwaari gives up the corner piece near D and gains an equal piece near E;
    the total is unchanged. Common mistake: drawing DE parallel to a SIDE
    instead of the diagonal AC. Now you try: ar(ABC) = 250 m^2 and
    ar(ACD) = 170 m^2. Area of the new triangle? (420 m^2)

D7. Prove that the diagonals of a parallelogram divide it into four triangles of
    equal area. A tile ABCD in the shape of a parallelogram has area 96 cm^2. Its
    diagonals meet at O. Find ar(AOB) and ar(AOB) + ar(COD).
    Answer: Each of the four triangles has area 24 cm^2;
    ar(AOB) + ar(COD) = 48 cm^2.
    Teacher explains: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so O
    is the midpoint of AC and of BD.
       BO is a median of delta ABC  ->  ar(AOB) = ar(BOC)
       CO is a median of delta BCD  ->  ar(BOC) = ar(COD)
       DO is a median of delta CDA  ->  ar(COD) = ar(DOA)
    So all four are equal, each 1/4 of the parallelogram: 96 / 4 = 24 cm^2, and
    ar(AOB) + ar(COD) = 24 + 24 = 48 cm^2. Notice: the four triangles are NOT all
    congruent (AOB and BOC have different shapes unless ABCD is a rhombus), yet
    their areas are equal. Equal area does not mean congruent. Now you try: a
    parallelogram of area 70 cm^2. Area of delta BOC? (17.5 cm^2)

    that ar(AOD) = ar(BOC). If ar(ABC) = 40 cm^2 and ar(AOB) = 25 cm^2, find
    ar(AOD).
    Answer: ar(ABD) = ar(ABC) (same base AB, same parallels); subtracting
    ar(AOB) gives ar(AOD) = ar(BOC) = 40 - 25 = 15 cm^2.
    Teacher explains:
            A +---------+ B
             /  \     /  \
           /   /     \     \
        D +-----------------+ C
       Statement                          Reason
       ar(ABD) - ar(AOB)                  subtract the common
           = ar(ABC) - ar(AOB)            piece delta AOB
       ar(AOD) = ar(BOC)
    Numbers: ar(BOC) = ar(ABC) - ar(AOB) = 40 - 25 = 15 cm^2, and so
    ar(AOD) = 15 cm^2. The two side triangles of a trapezium are always equal in
    area, even when the trapezium is not isosceles. Common mistake: saying delta AOD
    ar(BDC) = 54 cm^2, ar(DOC) = 36 cm^2. Find ar(AOD). (18 cm^2)

D9. D and E are points on the sides AB and AC of delta ABC such that
    Answer: delta DBC and delta EBC are on the same base BC, on the same side, with equal
    Teacher explains: This is the CONVERSE of theorem 2. Proof: let the heights
    of D and E above BC be h_1 and h_2.
       1/2 x BC x h_1 = ar(DBC) = ar(EBC) = 1/2 x BC x h_2
       so h_1 = h_2
    D and E are on the same side of BC at the same distance from it, so the line
    DE is parallel to BC (two points at equal heights above a line lie on a
    parallel line). Converses need care: the triangles must be on the SAME side
    try: delta PQR and delta PQS are on the same side of PQ = 8 cm and both have area
    28 cm^2. What is the distance between the parallels PQ and RS? (7 cm)

D10. ABCD is a parallelogram of area 120 cm^2 and E is the midpoint of CD. Find
     ar(ABE), ar(ADE) and ar(BCE).
     Answer: ar(ABE) = 60 cm^2, ar(ADE) = 30 cm^2, ar(BCE) = 30 cm^2.
     Teacher explains:
          D +------E------+ C
           /  .       .  /
          /     .   .   /
       A +-------------+ B          E is the midpoint of DC
     ar(ABE) = 1/2 x 120 = 60 cm^2. The rest, 120 - 60 = 60 cm^2, is shared by
     delta ADE and delta BCE. They have equal bases DE = EC and the same height (the
     distance between AB and DC), so each is 60 / 2 = 30 cm^2.
     Another way: with base b and height h, bh = 120 and
     ar(ADE) = 1/2 x (b/2) x h = bh/4 = 30. Check: 60 + 30 + 30 = 120. Now you
     try: the area is 88 cm^2 and E is the midpoint of CD. ar(ADE)? (22 cm^2)

D11. Budhia wants to divide her triangular field ABC of area 1,350 m^2 equally
     among herself and her two sons, each piece being a triangle with a vertex
     at the well at A. How can she do it?
     Answer: Divide BC into three equal parts at D and E and join AD and AE.
     Each of delta ABD, delta ADE and delta AEC has area 1,350 / 3 = 450 m^2.
     Teacher explains: All three triangles have their vertex at A, so they have
     the SAME height h (the perpendicular from A to BC). Their bases BD, DE, EC
     are equal, so their areas 1/2 x base x h are equal.
                         A
                      / / \ \
                    /  /   \  \
                  /   /     \   \
                B----D-------E----C      BD = DE = EC
     General rule: triangles with the same height have areas in the ratio of
     their bases. If instead BD : DC = 2 : 3, then ar(ABD) : ar(ADC) = 2 : 3, so
     ar(ABD) = 2/5 x 1,350 = 540 m^2. Common mistake: dividing the ANGLE at A
     into three equal parts; equal angles do not give equal areas. Now you try:
     divide a triangle of area 1,000 m^2 into 4 equal parts from one vertex. Area
     of each? (250 m^2)

D12. P is any point inside parallelogram ABCD. Prove that
     ar(APB) + ar(PCD) = 1/2 ar(ABCD). If ar(ABCD) = 150 cm^2, ar(APB) = 40 cm^2
     and ar(APD) = 48 cm^2, find ar(PCD) and ar(PBC).
     Answer: ar(PCD) = 35 cm^2 and ar(PBC) = 27 cm^2.
     ABFE and EFCD are parallelograms.
        add:  ar(APB) + ar(PCD) = 1/2 [ar(ABFE) + ar(EFCD)]
                                = 1/2 ar(ABCD)
     The same argument with a line through P parallel to AD gives
     ar(APD) + ar(PBC) = 1/2 ar(ABCD). Numbers: half of 150 is 75, so
     ar(PCD) = 75 - 40 = 35 cm^2 and ar(PBC) = 75 - 48 = 27 cm^2. Check:
     40 + 35 + 48 + 27 = 150. Now you try: ar(ABCD) = 90 cm^2, ar(APB) = 20 cm^2.
     Find ar(PCD). (25 cm^2)

PART B - MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Area of a parallelogram A = b x h (lengths in cm, areas in cm^2). Find the

    a) b = 12, h = 7      b) b = 9, h = 8       c) b = 15, h = 6

    j) b = 0.8, h = 0.5   k) A = 96, b = 12     l) A = 150, b = 25
    m) A = 84, b = 7      n) A = 45, b = 6      o) A = 200, b = 16
    p) A = 63, b = 4.5    q) A = 1, b = 4       r) A = 96, h = 6
    s) A = 120, h = 15    t) A = 99, h = 11     u) A = 72, h = 9.6
    v) A = 30, h = 2.5    w) A = 144, h = 1.2   x) A = 17, h = 4
    Answers: a) A = 84   b) A = 72   c) A = 90   d) A = 70   e) A = 30
             f) A = 121   g) A = 300   h) A = 32   i) A = 117   j) A = 0.4
             k) h = 8   l) h = 6   m) h = 12   n) h = 7.5   o) h = 12.5
             p) h = 14   q) h = 0.25   r) b = 16   s) b = 8   t) b = 9
             u) b = 7.5   v) b = 12   w) b = 120   x) b = 4.25

M2. A parallelogram has sides b_1 and b_2 with the heights h_1 and h_2 onto them, so
    b_1 x h_1 = b_2 x h_2. Find the missing one.

M12. True or false? Correct the false ones.
     a) Parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels have
        equal areas.
     b) Parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels have
        equal perimeters.
     c) A triangle and a parallelogram on the same base and between the same
        parallels have equal areas.
     d) A median divides a triangle into two triangles of equal area.
     e) A median divides a triangle into two congruent triangles.
     f) The diagonals of a parallelogram divide it into four triangles of equal
        area.
     g) Triangles with equal areas are congruent.
     h) Congruent triangles have equal areas.
     k) Triangles with the same height have areas in the ratio of their bases.
     l) Two triangles on the same base with equal areas always lie between the
        same parallels.
     m) A rectangle and a parallelogram on the same base and between the same
        parallels have equal areas.
     n) Area of a parallelogram = product of two adjacent sides.
     o) The triangle formed by joining the midpoints of the sides of a triangle
        has 1/4 of its area.
     p) Joining the midpoints of the sides of a parallelogram gives a
        quadrilateral with 1/2 of its area.
     Answers: a) true   b) false (the slanting one has a longer perimeter)
              c) false (the triangle is half)   d) true
              e) false (equal area only, unless the triangle is isosceles with
                 the median from the apex)   f) true   g) false   h) true
              i) true   j) false (true only if AB = DC)   k) true
              l) false (they must be on the same side of the base)   m) true
              n) false (base x perpendicular height)   o) true   p) true

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: cut a paper parallelogram along a height and slide the triangle to
  the other end to make a rectangle; shade the pieces in colour; draw both
  parallel lines heavily and mark the height in every figure; for each new
  triangle say aloud "same base? same parallels? same height?"; use squared
  paper and count squares to see that sliding the top vertex keeps the area.
  Harder: prove that the four triangles cut off by the diagonals of a
  quadrilateral satisfy ar(AOB) x ar(COD) = ar(BOC) x ar(AOD); prove that
  joining the midpoints of any quadrilateral gives half its area; show how to
  turn any pentagon into a triangle of equal area by two parallel-line steps;
  and investigate with GeoGebra by dragging P along the top line and watching
  the area stay fixed.

================================================================================
TOPIC 7.24 - CIRCLE THEOREMS: CHORDS, ARCS, ANGLES SUBTENDED, CYCLIC
             QUADRILATERALS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - Words: a CHORD joins two points of the circle (a diameter is the longest
    chord); an ARC is a piece of the circle (minor arc less than a semicircle,
    major arc more); a SEGMENT is the region between a chord and an arc; the
    angle a chord SUBTENDS at a point is the angle between the lines from its
    ends to that point.
  - EQUAL CHORDS subtend EQUAL ANGLES at the centre (proof: SSS) and,
    conversely, chords that subtend equal angles at the centre are equal. Equal
    chords cut off equal arcs, and equal arcs have equal chords.
  - The PERPENDICULAR from the centre to a chord BISECTS the chord (proof: RHS),
    and the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to
    it. With radius r, chord c and distance d from the centre: r^2 = d^2 + (c/2)^2.
    Equal chords are EQUIDISTANT from the centre (and conversely); a longer
    chord is nearer to the centre.
  - There is exactly ONE circle through three non-collinear points: its centre
    is where the perpendicular bisectors of the joining segments meet. No circle
    passes through three collinear points.
  - ANGLE AT THE CENTRE = TWICE the angle at the circumference standing on the
    same arc. Hence ANGLES IN THE SAME SEGMENT are equal, and the ANGLE IN A
    SEMICIRCLE is 90 degrees. An angle standing on a major arc is acute; on a minor arc
    it is obtuse.
  - CYCLIC QUADRILATERAL (all four vertices on a circle): OPPOSITE angles add up
    to 180 degrees; conversely, if a pair of opposite angles adds up to 180 degrees, the
    quadrilateral is cyclic. An EXTERIOR angle equals the INTERIOR OPPOSITE
    angle. A cyclic parallelogram is a rectangle.
  - In angle chasing write a REASON for every step: radii equal (isosceles
    triangle), angle at centre, same segment, semicircle, cyclic quadrilateral,
    exterior angle, angle sum of a triangle.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prove that equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre. In a
    circle with centre O, AB = CD = 6 cm and angle AOB = 70 degrees. Find angle COD and angle OCD.
    angle OCD = (180 degrees - 70 degrees) / 2 = 55 degrees.
    Teacher explains:
       Statement                  Reason
       OA = OC                    radii
       OB = OD                    radii
       AB = CD                    given
       angle AOB = angle COD                CPCT
    Every chord together with the two radii to its ends makes an ISOSCELES
    triangle, because radii are equal. So in delta OCD the base angles are equal:
    angle OCD = angle ODC = (180 degrees - 70 degrees) / 2 = 55 degrees. The converse is proved the same way
    forgetting that the proof needs the SAME circle (or equal circles); a 6 cm
    chord in a bigger circle subtends a smaller angle. Now you try: equal chords
    PQ and RS, angle POQ = 84 degrees. Find angle ORS. (48 degrees)

D2. Prove that the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects
    the chord. A chord of a circle of radius 13 cm is 24 cm long. How far is it
    from the centre?
    Teacher explains:
                   O
            13 /   |d  \ 13
              /    |     \
            A------M------B
               12     12
       Statement                  Reason
       OA = OB                    radii (hypotenuses)
       OM = OM                    common
       AM = MB                    CPCT
    Now use Pythagoras in delta OMA: AM = 24 / 2 = 12 cm, so
    d^2 = 13^2 - 12^2 = 169 - 144 = 25 and d = 5 cm. The key triangle is always:
    radius as hypotenuse, HALF the chord and the distance as the legs,
    r^2 = d^2 + (c/2)^2. Common mistake: using the whole chord 24 instead of 12.
    Now you try: radius 10 cm, chord 6 cm from the centre. Length of the chord?
    (16 cm)

D3. Water flows in a pipe of inner diameter 52 cm. The water surface is 48 cm
    wide. How deep is the water?
    Answer: 16 cm deep if the pipe is less than half full (36 cm if it is more
    than half full).
    Teacher explains: Draw the cross-section: a circle of radius 26 cm, and the
    water surface is a chord of length 48 cm. The perpendicular from the centre
    bisects it, giving half-chord 24 cm.
       d^2 = 26^2 - 24^2 = 676 - 576 = 100,   d = 10 cm
       depth = r - d = 26 - 10 = 16 cm     (surface above the
                                            bottom, below centre)
       or depth = r + d = 26 + 10 = 36 cm  (surface above centre)
    The distance d is measured from the CENTRE, so to get the depth we must go
    from the surface down to the bottom of the pipe: r - d or r + d. Always ask
    which side of the centre the chord lies. Common mistake: giving d = 10 cm as
    the depth. Now you try: diameter 10 cm, surface width 8 cm, less than half
    full. Depth? (2 cm)

D4. AB and CD are parallel chords of a circle of radius 13 cm, with AB = 10 cm
    and CD = 24 cm. Find the distance between them when they are (a) on the same
    side of the centre, (b) on opposite sides.
    Answer: (a) 7 cm, (b) 17 cm.
    Teacher explains: Both chords are perpendicular to the same line through the
    centre, so their distances from O lie along one straight line.
       AB: d_1^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144,   d_1 = 12 cm
       CD: d_2^2 = 13^2 - 12^2 = 169 - 144 = 25,  d_2 = 5 cm
       same side:      12 - 5 = 7 cm
       opposite sides: 12 + 5 = 17 cm
    Notice the longer chord (24 cm) is NEARER the centre (5 cm) than the shorter
    one (12 cm). Draw both pictures; one problem has two answers unless the
    position is stated. Common mistake: halving the distance instead of the
    chord. Now you try: radius 5 cm, parallel chords 6 cm and 8 cm. Distance
    between them? (1 cm or 7 cm)

D5. Prove that equal chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre. In a
    circle of radius 17 cm, which is nearer to the centre: a chord of 30 cm or a
    chord of 16 cm?
    30 cm chord is 8 cm from the centre, the 16 cm chord 15 cm: the longer chord
    is nearer.
    Teacher explains: Let M and N be the feet of the perpendiculars from O to AB
    and CD. They bisect the chords, so AM = CN (halves of equal chords).
       Statement                  Reason
       angle OMA = angle ONC = 90 degrees          perpendiculars
       OA = OC                    radii
       AM = CN                    halves of equal chords
       OM = ON                    CPCT
    Numbers: 17^2 - 15^2 = 289 - 225 = 64, so the 30 cm chord is 8 cm away;
    17^2 - 8^2 = 289 - 64 = 225, so the 16 cm chord is 15 cm away. Since
    d^2 = r^2 - (c/2)^2, a bigger chord leaves a smaller d. The converse (chords
    equidistant from the centre are equal) also holds. Now you try: radius
    25 cm, chords of 48 cm and 14 cm. Distances? (7 cm and 24 cm)

D6. Prove that the angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle
    it subtends at any point on the remaining part of the circle. If
    angle AOB = 100 degrees, find angle ACB for C on the major arc and for C on the minor arc.
    Answer: angle AOB = 2angle ACB. For C on the major arc angle ACB = 50 degrees; on the minor arc
    angle ACB = 130 degrees.
    Teacher explains:
                     C
                   / | \
                 /   |   \         join CO and extend to D
               /     O     \
             /    /  |  \    \
            A  /     D     \  B
    Join CO and extend it to D. OA = OC (radii), so delta OAC is isosceles:
    angle OAC = angle OCA = x. The exterior angle angle AOD = x + x = 2x. In the same way
    angle BOD = 2y where y = angle OCB. Adding: angle AOB = 2x + 2y = 2(x + y) = 2angle ACB.
    Numbers: C on the major arc: angle ACB = 100 degrees / 2 = 50 degrees. C on the minor arc: that
    angle stands on the MAJOR arc, whose central angle is the reflex angle
    360 degrees - 100 degrees = 260 degrees, so angle ACB = 260 degrees / 2 = 130 degrees. Check: 50 degrees + 130 degrees = 180 degrees: the
    two angles are opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral. Common mistake:
    halving the wrong central angle. Always look at WHICH arc the angle stands
    on. Now you try: angle AOB = 140 degrees. Angle at a point on the major arc? (70 degrees)

D7. Explain why angles in the same segment are equal and why the angle in a
    semicircle is 90 degrees. A carpenter has a circular table top and a set square.
    How can she find a diameter? If AB is a diameter of length 10 cm and
    AC = 6 cm, find BC.
    Answer: Each angle in the segment is half the same central angle, so they
    are equal; for a semicircle the central angle is 180 degrees, so the angle is 90 degrees.
    BC = 8 cm.
    Teacher explains: Same segment: angle ACB and angle ADB both stand on arc AB, so each
    equals 1/2 angle AOB. They are equal. Semicircle: when AB is a diameter,
    angle AOB = 180 degrees (a straight angle), so angle ACB = 180 degrees / 2 = 90 degrees.
    Carpenter: put the right-angled corner of the set square ON the edge of the
    table; where its two arms cross the edge are the ends of a diameter (the
    converse: a chord subtending 90 degrees at the circle is a diameter). Do it twice;
    the diameters cross at the centre.
       angle ACB = 90 degrees  (angle in a semicircle)
       BC^2 = AB^2 - AC^2 = 10^2 - 6^2 = 100 - 36 = 64,   BC = 8 cm
    Common mistake: putting the right angle anywhere except ON the circle. Now
    you try: diameter 13 cm, one chord from its end is 5 cm. The other chord to
    the same point? (12 cm)

D8. Prove that the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180 degrees. In
    cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, angle A = (2x + 10) degrees and angle C = (3x - 5) degrees. Find the
    angles.
    Answer: x = 35, angle A = 80 degrees, angle C = 100 degrees.
    Teacher explains: Let O be the centre. angle BAD stands on arc BCD and angle BCD
    stands on arc BAD. The two central angles on these arcs together make a full
    turn:
       angle BAD = 1/2 x (central angle on arc BCD)
       angle BCD = 1/2 x (central angle on arc BAD)
       angle BAD + angle BCD = 1/2 x 360 degrees = 180 degrees
    In the same way angle B + angle D = 180 degrees (or: all four add up to 360 degrees).
       (2x + 10) + (3x - 5) = 180
                 5x + 5 = 180
                      x = 35
       angle A = 2 x 35 + 10 = 80 degrees,   angle C = 3 x 35 - 5 = 100 degrees
    Consequence: a cyclic parallelogram is a RECTANGLE, since its opposite
    angles are equal AND add up to 180 degrees, so each is 90 degrees. Common mistake: adding
    ADJACENT angles (angle A + angle B) to 180 degrees. That is true for a parallelogram, not for
    a cyclic quadrilateral. Now you try: angle B = (4y) degrees and angle D = (y + 30) degrees. Find angle B.
    (120 degrees)

D9. ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. AB is produced to E and angle CBE = 75 degrees. Find
    angle ADC, and give reasons. If also angle BAD = 95 degrees, find angle BCD.
    Answer: angle ADC = 75 degrees; angle BCD = 85 degrees.
    Teacher explains:
       Statement                  Reason
       angle ABC = 180 degrees - 75 degrees = 105 degrees   angles on a straight line
       angle ADC = 180 degrees - 105 degrees = 75 degrees   opposite angles, cyclic quad
       angle BCD = 180 degrees - 95 degrees = 85 degrees    opposite angles, cyclic quad
    So the EXTERIOR angle angle CBE equals the INTERIOR OPPOSITE angle angle ADC. This is
    always true: both equal 180 degrees - angle ABC. It is a quick shortcut in angle
    chasing, but in a proof write the two steps. Converse: if an exterior angle
    equals the interior opposite angle, the quadrilateral is cyclic. Common
    mistake: taking the interior angle NEXT to the exterior angle. Now you try:
    ABCD cyclic, DC produced to F, angle BCF = 68 degrees. Find angle BAD. (68 degrees)

D10. A, B, C and D lie on a circle; the chords AC and BD meet at E. If
     angle BEC = 130 degrees and angle ECD = 20 degrees, find angle BAC.
     Answer: angle BAC = 110 degrees.
     Teacher explains:
        Statement                  Reason
        angle BEC = angle EDC + angle ECD         exterior angle of delta CDE
        angle EDC = 130 degrees - 20 degrees = 110 degrees
        angle BDC = angle EDC = 110 degrees         (E lies on BD)
        angle BAC = angle BDC = 110 degrees         angles in the same segment
     Both angle BAC and angle BDC stand on chord BC, on the same side of it, so they are
     equal. Plan for angle chasing: mark every given angle, look for isosceles
     triangles (radii), same-segment pairs, cyclic quadrilaterals, and write one
     reason per line. Check: in delta CDE, 110 + 20 + 50 = 180, where
     angle CED = 180 - 130 = 50. Now you try: angle BEC = 120 degrees, angle ECD = 35 degrees. Find angle BAC.
     (85 degrees)

D11. Three villages A, B and C are not in a straight line. The panchayat wants a
     water tank equally far from all three. Where should it go? If the villages
     form a right-angled triangle with sides 6 km, 8 km and 10 km, how far is
     the tank from each village?
     Answer: At the meeting point of the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC
     (the circumcentre). For the right-angled triangle it is the midpoint of the
     10 km side, 5 km from each village.
     Teacher explains: Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is
     equally far from A and B. The perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC meet at
     one point O, which is then equally far from A, B and C: the centre of the
     ONLY circle through A, B and C. (If A, B, C were collinear the two
     bisectors would be parallel and never meet, so no circle exists.)
     Right-angled triangle: 6^2 + 8^2 = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10^2, so the angle opposite
     the 10 km side is 90 degrees. An angle of 90 degrees on a circle stands on a DIAMETER
     (converse of the semicircle theorem), so the 10 km side is a diameter and
     the centre is its midpoint: radius 10 / 2 = 5 km. Now you try: villages
     forming a 5-12-13 km triangle. Distance of the tank from each? (6.5 km)

D12. A chord of a circle is equal to the radius. Find the angle it subtends (a)
     at the centre, (b) at a point on the major arc, (c) at a point on the minor
     arc. Repeat for a chord of length rsqrt2.
     Answer: Chord = r: 60 degrees, 30 degrees, 150 degrees. Chord = rsqrt2: 90 degrees, 45 degrees, 135 degrees.
     Teacher explains: Chord AB = r: triangle OAB has OA = OB = AB = r, so it is
     EQUILATERAL and angle AOB = 60 degrees. On the major arc: 60 degrees / 2 = 30 degrees. On the minor
     arc: (360 degrees - 60 degrees) / 2 = 150 degrees, or 180 degrees - 30 degrees = 150 degrees (cyclic quadrilateral).
        chord rsqrt2:  OA^2 + OB^2 = r^2 + r^2 = 2r^2 = AB^2
        so angle AOB = 90 degrees (converse of Pythagoras)
        major arc: 90 degrees / 2 = 45 degrees,  minor arc: 180 degrees - 45 degrees = 135 degrees
     The two inscribed angles on opposite sides of a chord always add up to
     180 degrees, because together with the chord they form a cyclic quadrilateral. Now
     you try: a chord subtends 120 degrees at the centre. Angles at points on the major
     and minor arcs? (60 degrees and 120 degrees)

M12. True or false? Correct the false ones.
     a) Equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre.
     b) The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.
     c) A longer chord is farther from the centre.
     d) Through three collinear points there is exactly one circle.
     e) The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the
        same arc.
     f) Angles in the same segment are equal.
     g) The angle in a semicircle is 180 degrees.
     h) An angle in the minor segment is acute.
     i) Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are equal.
     j) The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior
        opposite angle.
     k) Every parallelogram is cyclic.
     l) An isosceles trapezium is cyclic.
     m) A rhombus that is not a square can be cyclic.
     n) Equal arcs of a circle have equal chords.
     o) If a chord subtends 90 degrees at a point of the circle, the chord is a
        diameter.
     p) The diameter is the longest chord.
     Answers: a) true   b) true   c) false (a longer chord is nearer)
              d) false (there is none)   e) true   f) true   g) false (90 degrees)
              h) false (it is obtuse; it stands on the major arc)
              i) false (they add up to 180 degrees)   j) true
              k) false (only rectangles)   l) true   m) false   n) true
              o) true   p) true

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw a big circle with a compass for every question and mark the
  centre; mark radii with ticks at once (every chord with two radii gives an
  isosceles triangle); for chord questions always draw the perpendicular from
  the centre and label r, d and HALF the chord; for angle questions shade the
  arc the angle stands on, then look for the angle at the centre on the same
  arc; cut out a cyclic quadrilateral and tear off opposite corners to see them
  make a straight angle. Harder: prove that the angle subtended by an arc at the
  centre is double the angle at the circumference when the centre lies OUTSIDE
  the angle; prove the converse of the cyclic quadrilateral theorem by
  contradiction; prove that the bisectors of the angles of any quadrilateral
  form a cyclic quadrilateral; find the radius of the circle through (0, 0),
  (8, 0) and (0, 6); and investigate with GeoGebra how angle ACB stays fixed as C
  moves on the arc.

================================================================================
TOPIC 7.25 - TANGENTS TO A CIRCLE; NUMBER OF TANGENTS FROM A POINT
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A TANGENT is a line that meets the circle at exactly ONE point, the POINT OF
    CONTACT. A SECANT meets it at two points. A line may also miss the circle
    altogether.
  - THEOREM: the tangent at any point of a circle is PERPENDICULAR to the radius
    through the point of contact (proof: the radius is the shortest distance
    from the centre to the tangent). Conversely, the line through the end of a
    radius perpendicular to it is a tangent.
  - NUMBER OF TANGENTS from a point P at distance d from the centre of a circle
    of radius r: none if P is inside (d < r), exactly one if P is on the circle
    (d = r), exactly two if P is outside (d > r).
  - THEOREM: the two tangents from an external point are EQUAL in length (proof:
    RHS). The centre lies on the bisector of the angle between them. Tangent
    length t = sqrt(d^2 - r^2), from the right angle between radius and tangent.
  - If PA and PB are the tangents, then angle APB + angle AOB = 180 degrees (quadrilateral OAPB
    has two right angles), angle OPA = 1/2 angle APB, and triangle PAB is isosceles.
    Tangents at the ends of a diameter are parallel.
  - A quadrilateral circumscribing a circle (all four sides tangents) has
    AB + CD = AD + BC. For the INCIRCLE of a triangle with sides a, b, c and
    semi-perimeter s, the tangent lengths from A, B, C are s - a, s - b, s - c;
    in a right triangle the inradius is r = (a + b - c)/2.
  - ALTERNATE SEGMENT THEOREM (introduction): the angle between a tangent and a
    chord through the point of contact equals the angle the chord subtends in
    the alternate (opposite) segment.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prove that the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the
    radius through the point of contact.
    Answer: Every point of the tangent other than P lies outside the circle, so
    OP is the shortest segment from O to the tangent, and the shortest segment
    Teacher explains:
                      O
                      |  \
                      |     \ R
                      |        \
       -------------- P -------- Q ------   tangent at P
    Take any point Q on the tangent other than P. If Q were inside or on the
    circle, the line would cut the circle again, and it would be a secant, not a
    tangent. So Q is OUTSIDE, and OQ is longer than the radius: OQ > OR = OP,
    where R is where OQ crosses the circle.
    So OP is shorter than every other segment from O to the line: it is the
    SHORTEST distance, and the shortest distance from a point to a line is along
    measuring one drawing. Now you try: the tangent at P has a point Q with
    PQ = 12 cm; the radius is 5 cm. Find OQ. (13 cm)

D2. A circle has radius 5 cm. How many tangents can be drawn to it from a point
    P at distance (a) 3 cm, (b) 5 cm, (c) 8 cm from the centre? Explain.
    Answer: (a) none, (b) exactly one, (c) exactly two.
    Teacher explains: (a) d = 3 < 5: P is INSIDE. Every line through P crosses
    the circle twice (it is a secant), so no tangent is possible.
    (b) d = 5 = r: P is ON the circle. There is exactly one line through P
    perpendicular to OP, and it is the only tangent at P.
    (c) d = 8 > 5: P is OUTSIDE. Imagine a line through P turning: it misses the
    circle, then just touches it, cuts it, and just touches it again on the
    other side. So there are exactly TWO tangents, symmetric about the line OP.
       position of P      d compared with r     tangents
       inside             d < r                 0
       on the circle      d = r                 1
       outside            d > r                 2
    Real life: a bicycle wheel standing on a flat road touches it at exactly one
    point; the road is a tangent and the spoke to that point is vertical. Now
    you try: r = 7 cm, d = 7.5 cm. How many tangents? (2)

D3. Prove that the lengths of the two tangents drawn from an external point to a
    circle are equal. Show also that the centre lies on the bisector of the
    angle between them.
    Teacher explains:
                 A
               /    \
               \    /
                 B
       Statement                     Reason
       OP = OP                       common hypotenuse
       OA = OB                       radii
       PA = PB                       CPCT
       angle OPA = angle OPB, angle AOP = angle BOP      CPCT
    So OP bisects both the angle between the tangents at P and the angle AOB
    between the radii. A kite OAPB is formed: two pairs of equal adjacent sides
    (OA = OB, PA = PB). This result is behind almost every tangent problem.
    Common mistake: using SAS; the right angle is NOT between the two known
    sides, so the correct test is RHS. Now you try: PA = 9 cm. Find PB. (9 cm)

D4. A point P is 13 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. Find the
    length of the tangent from P. Then: a person stands on a hill 0.5 km high.
    Taking the radius of the Earth as 6400 km, how far away is the horizon (the
    tangent length)?
    Answer: 12 cm; about 80.0 km.
    Teacher explains: The radius to the point of contact T is perpendicular to
    the tangent, so delta OTP has its right angle at T and OP is the hypotenuse:
       PT^2 = OP^2 - OT^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144,   PT = 12 cm
    For the hill: OP = 6400 + 0.5 = 6400.5 km and OT = 6400 km.
       PT^2 = 6400.5^2 - 6400^2
           = (6400.5 - 6400)(6400.5 + 6400)     (difference of squares)
           = 0.5 x 12800.5 = 6400.25
       PT = sqrt6400.25 ~ 80.0 km
    The difference of squares saves a lot of work with big numbers. Common
    mistake: adding the squares (d^2 + r^2). The DISTANCE to the centre is the
    hypotenuse, the longest side. Now you try: d = 25 cm, r = 7 cm. Tangent
    length? (24 cm)

D5. PA and PB are tangents from P to a circle with centre O, and angle APB = 80 degrees.
    Find angle AOB, angle OPA, angle PAB and angle OAB.
    Answer: angle AOB = 100 degrees, angle OPA = 40 degrees, angle PAB = 50 degrees, angle OAB = 40 degrees.
    Teacher explains:
       Statement                      Reason
       angle AOB = 360 degrees - 90 degrees - 90 degrees - 80 degrees  angle sum of quad OAPB
            = 100 degrees
       angle OPA = 80 degrees / 2 = 40 degrees           OP bisects angle APB
       angle PAB = (180 degrees - 80 degrees) / 2 = 50 degrees  PA = PB, isosceles delta PAB
       angle OAB = 90 degrees - 50 degrees = 40 degrees         angle OAP = 90 degrees
    Remember: angle APB + angle AOB = 180 degrees, because the other two angles of the
    quadrilateral OAPB are right angles. Notice angle OAB = angle OPA = 40 degrees and angle PAB = 1/2
    angle AOB = 50 degrees, the angle in the alternate segment. Common mistake: taking
    angle AOB = 80 degrees (the same as angle APB). Now you try: angle APB = 60 degrees. Find angle AOB. (120 degrees)

D6. Two concentric circles have radii 5 cm and 3 cm. Find the length of the
    chord of the larger circle that touches the smaller circle, and prove that
    it is bisected at the point of contact.
    Answer: 8 cm; the radius of the small circle to the point of contact is
    perpendicular to the chord, and a perpendicular from the centre bisects a
    chord.
    Teacher explains:
       AM^2 = OA^2 - OM^2 = 5^2 - 3^2 = 25 - 9 = 16,   AM = 4 cm
       AB = 2 x 4 = 8 cm
    Two theorems work together: the tangent-radius theorem for the SMALL circle
    and the perpendicular-bisector-of-a-chord theorem for the BIG circle. Every
    such chord has the same length, because it is always 3 cm from the centre.
    Common mistake: using the difference of radii 5 - 3 = 2. Now you try: radii
    13 cm and 5 cm. Length of the chord? (24 cm)

D7. A quadrilateral ABCD is drawn to circumscribe a circle (all four sides touch
    it). Prove that AB + CD = AD + BC. If AB = 6 cm, BC = 7 cm and CD = 4 cm,
    find AD.
    Answer: Adding equal tangent lengths gives AB + CD = AD + BC; AD = 3 cm.
    Teacher explains: Let the tangent lengths from A, B, C, D be a, b, c, d (the
    two tangents from each vertex are equal). Each side is made of two tangent
    pieces:
       AB = a + b      BC = b + c      CD = c + d      DA = d + a
       AB + CD = a + b + c + d = AD + BC
    So in every circumscribed quadrilateral the two pairs of OPPOSITE sides have
    equal sums. Numbers: 6 + 4 = AD + 7, so AD = 10 - 7 = 3 cm. Common mistake:
    adding ADJACENT sides. Now you try: AB = 9 cm, BC = 8 cm, CD = 5 cm. Find
    AD. (6 cm)

D8. Prove that a parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus.
    Answer: AB + CD = AD + BC, and in a parallelogram AB = CD and AD = BC, so
    2AB = 2BC, AB = BC: all four sides are equal.
    Teacher explains:
       AB + CD = AD + BC        circumscribed quadrilateral
       AB = CD, AD = BC         opposite sides of a parallelogram
       AB + AB = BC + BC        substitute
       AB = BC                  so all four sides are equal
    A parallelogram with all sides equal is a RHOMBUS. This is a typical short
    proof: combine a property of the circle (tangent lengths) with a property of
    the figure (opposite sides equal). The circle is then centred where the
    diagonals of the rhombus meet. Common mistake: starting from "a rhombus has
    equal sides" - that is what we must prove. Now you try: a rectangle
    circumscribes a circle. What kind of rectangle must it be? (a square)

D9. The incircle of delta ABC touches AB, BC, CA at P, Q, R. If AB = 12 cm, BC = 8 cm
    and CA = 10 cm, find the tangent lengths AP, BQ and CR.
    Answer: AP = 7 cm, BQ = 5 cm, CR = 3 cm.
    Teacher explains: Let AP = AR = x, BP = BQ = y, CQ = CR = z (equal
    tangents).
       x + y = 12      (AB)
       y + z = 8       (BC)
       z + x = 10      (CA)
       add: 2(x + y + z) = 30,   x + y + z = 15 = s
       x = 15 - 8 = 7,   y = 15 - 10 = 5,   z = 15 - 12 = 3
    The shortcut: the tangent length from a vertex is s - (the side OPPOSITE
    that vertex), where s is the semi-perimeter. Check: 7 + 5 = 12, 5 + 3 = 8,
    3 + 7 = 10. Common mistake: subtracting the side next to the vertex. Now you
    try: AB = 7 cm, BC = 5 cm, CA = 6 cm. Tangent length from A? (4 cm)

D10. A right-angled triangle has legs 5 cm and 12 cm. Find the radius of its
     incircle.
     Answer: r = 2 cm.
     Teacher explains: Hypotenuse: sqrt(5^2 + 12^2) = sqrt169 = 13 cm. Let the incircle
     angle C = 90 degrees, so OECF is a square: the tangent lengths from C are both r.
        tangents from A: 5 - r     tangents from B: 12 - r
        hypotenuse = (5 - r) + (12 - r) = 13
        17 - 2r = 13,   r = 2 cm
        formula: r = (a + b - c)/2 = (5 + 12 - 13)/2 = 2
     Check with areas: joining O to the vertices splits the triangle into three
     triangles of height r, so area = r x s. Area = 1/2 x 5 x 12 = 30 and
     s = (5 + 12 + 13)/2 = 15, so r = 30 / 15 = 2. Both methods agree. Now you
     try: legs 8 cm and 15 cm. Inradius? (3 cm)

D11. Prove that the tangents drawn at the ends of a diameter of a circle are
     parallel. A round table top of diameter 1.2 m is pushed between two
     parallel walls so that it touches both. How far apart are the walls?
     Answer: Both tangents are perpendicular to the same line AB, so they are
     parallel; the walls are 1.2 m apart.
     Teacher explains: Let AB be a diameter, with tangents l at A and m at B.
        OA and OB lie on AB        AB is a diameter
     The distance between the parallel tangents is the length of AB, the
     diameter. So the walls are 1.2 m apart. The converse also holds: if the
     tangents at A and B are parallel, then AB is a diameter. Common mistake:
     thinking any two tangents can be parallel; only those at the ends of a
     diameter are. Now you try: two parallel tangents of a circle are 14 cm
     apart. Radius? (7 cm)

D12. AT is the tangent at A to a circle with centre O, and AB is a chord with
     angle TAB = 65 degrees. C is a point on the major arc and D on the minor arc. Find
     angle ACB, angle AOB and angle ADB.
     Answer: angle ACB = 65 degrees, angle AOB = 130 degrees, angle ADB = 115 degrees.
     Teacher explains: ALTERNATE SEGMENT THEOREM: the angle between the tangent
     and the chord equals the angle in the alternate segment. Why? Draw the
     diameter AE.
        angle ABE = 90 degrees                     angle in a semicircle
        angle TAB = 90 degrees - angle EAB = angle AEB       angle sum of delta ABE
        angle AEB = angle ACB                    same segment
     Numbers: angle ACB = angle TAB = 65 degrees; angle AOB = 2 x 65 degrees = 130 degrees (angle at the centre);
     angle OAB = 90 degrees - 65 degrees = 25 degrees, and in isosceles delta OAB: 180 - 25 - 25 = 130. The
     same answer. Now you try: angle TAB = 50 degrees. Angle in the alternate segment? (50 degrees)

M9. Find the inradius. Right triangles: r = (a + b - c)/2. Other triangles:
    r = area / s, where s is the semi-perimeter.
    a) legs 3, 4, hypotenuse 5       b) legs 5, 12, hypotenuse 13

    e) legs 6, 8, hypotenuse 10      f) legs 20, 21, hypotenuse 29
    g) legs 9, 40, hypotenuse 41     h) legs 12, 16, hypotenuse 20
    i) legs 1.5, 2, hypotenuse 2.5   j) legs 12, 35, hypotenuse 37
    k) sides 13, 14, 15, area 84     l) sides 5, 5, 6, area 12
    m) sides 10, 10, 12, area 48     n) sides 13, 20, 21, area 126

M12. True or false? Correct the false ones.
     a) A tangent meets a circle at exactly one point.
     b) A secant meets a circle at exactly one point.
     c) The tangent at a point is perpendicular to the radius through it.
     d) From a point inside a circle, one tangent can be drawn.
     e) From a point on a circle, exactly one tangent can be drawn.
     f) From a point outside a circle, exactly two tangents can be drawn.
     g) The two tangents from an external point are equal in length.
     h) If PA and PB are tangents, angle APB = angle AOB.
     i) Tangents at the ends of a diameter are parallel.
     j) Tangents at the ends of any chord are parallel.
     k) For a circumscribed quadrilateral, AB + BC = CD + DA.
     l) A parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus.
     m) The tangent length from P is sqrt(d^2 + r^2).
     n) The centre lies on the bisector of the angle between the two tangents
        from a point.
     o) The inradius of a 3-4-5 triangle is 1.
     p) A line perpendicular to a radius at its outer end is a tangent.
     Answers: a) true   b) false (two points)   c) true   d) false (none)
              e) true   f) true   g) true   h) false (angle APB + angle AOB = 180 degrees)
              i) true   j) false (only for a diameter)
              k) false (AB + CD = BC + DA)   l) true   m) false (sqrt(d^2 - r^2))
              n) true   o) true   p) true

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: roll a coin along a ruler to see a tangent touch at one point;
  always draw the radius to the point of contact and mark the right angle first;
  mark equal tangent lengths with the same letter (x, y, z) from each vertex;
  for the tangent length say "distance to the centre is the hypotenuse, subtract
  the squares"; build the kite OAPB from straws. Harder: prove the alternate
  segment theorem fully; prove that angle APB = 2angle OAB for tangents PA and PB; given
  BD = 8, DC = 6 and inradius 4 in a triangle, find the other sides (13 cm and
  15 cm, using area = r x s); find the length of the common external tangent of
  two circles; and prove that the tangents at the ends of a chord meet on the
  perpendicular bisector of the chord.

================================================================================
TOPIC 7.26 - SIMILAR TRIANGLES: BASIC PROPORTIONALITY (THALES) THEOREM,
             AA/SSS/SAS SIMILARITY
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - Two triangles are SIMILAR (delta ABC ~ delta PQR) if their corresponding angles are
    equal AND their corresponding sides are in the same ratio:
    triangles are similar.
  - BASIC PROPORTIONALITY THEOREM (BPT, Thales): a line parallel to one side of
    a triangle, cutting the other two sides at D and E, divides them in the same
    ratio: AD/DB = AE/EC. Also AD/AB = AE/AC = DE/BC (delta ADE ~ delta ABC). Proof: by
    areas of triangles with the same height.
  - CONVERSE of BPT: if a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same
    ratio, it is parallel to the third side.
  - SIMILARITY CRITERIA. AAA (or AA): two pairs of equal angles (the third pair
    then follows from the angle sum). SSS: all three pairs of sides in the same
    ratio. SAS: one pair of equal angles and the sides INCLUDING those angles in
    the same ratio. (SSA is not a test.)
  - To match vertices: equal angles correspond; for SSS match smallest with
    smallest, middle with middle, largest with largest; the vertex shared by two
    matched sides corresponds.
  - Applications: heights from shadows (sun rays are parallel, so AA), lamp-post
    shadows, trapezium diagonals (AO/OC = BO/OD = AB/CD), and the altitude to
    the hypotenuse of a right triangle, which splits it into two triangles
    similar to the whole and to each other.

D6. Explain why two pairs of equal angles are enough for similarity. In delta ABC,
    angle A = 50 degrees and angle B = 70 degrees; in delta PQR, angle P = 60 degrees and angle Q = 50 degrees. Are the triangles
    similar? Write the correspondence and the equal ratios.
    AB/QR = BC/RP = CA/PQ.
    Teacher explains: If two angles match, the third angles match too, because
    each is 180 degrees minus the other two. Triangles with equal angles have the same
    shape (the AAA criterion); so AA is enough.
       delta ABC: angle A = 50 degrees, angle B = 70 degrees, angle C = 180 degrees - 50 degrees - 70 degrees = 60 degrees
       delta PQR: angle P = 60 degrees, angle Q = 50 degrees, angle R = 180 degrees - 60 degrees - 50 degrees = 70 degrees
    delta ABC ~ delta PQR just because the letters are in alphabetical order; that would
    pair A (50 degrees) with P (60 degrees). Now you try: angle D = 35 degrees, angle E = 95 degrees and angle X = 95 degrees,
    angle Y = 50 degrees. Correspondence? (delta DEF ~ delta ZXY)

       ratio: 6/4 = 1.5   9/6 = 1.5   12/8 = 1.5    all equal
    So the triangles are similar by SSS with scale factor 1.5 = 3/2. To name the
    Write delta ABC ~ delta RPQ. Common mistake: comparing sides in the order they happen
    to be listed (4 with 9, 6 with 12). Now you try: sides 3, 4, 6 and 4.5, 6,
    9. Similar? (yes, scale factor 1.5)
