TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw every figure and label r, h, l and theta on it; write the
  fraction theta/360 first and simplify it (90 degrees is 1/4, 60 degrees is 1/6, 120 degrees is 1/3);
  keep a formula card for sector, segment, cone, sphere and frustum; for
  combined solids colour the surfaces you can see and cross out the hidden ones;
  for recasting write "volume before = volume after" as the first line. Harder:
  show that sector area = 1/2 x arc x r; find the area of the Reuleaux triangle
  on side a (pi/2 - sqrt3/2)a^2; prove that the volume of a hemisphere, cone and
  cylinder of equal radius and height r are in the ratio 2 : 1 : 3; find the
  height of a frustum whose volume equals half the cone it was cut from; design
  a bucket that holds exactly 10 litres with R = 2r.

================================================================================
TOPIC 7.32 - TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS IN RIGHT TRIANGLES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - In a right-angled triangle, name the sides FROM THE ANGLE you are using: the
    HYPOTENUSE is opposite the right angle (always the longest side); the
    OPPOSITE side is across from the angle A; the ADJACENT side is next to A
    (and is not the hypotenuse). Change the angle and opposite and adjacent
    swap.
  - The six TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS of an acute angle A: sin A =
    opposite/hypotenuse, cos A = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan A = opposite/adjacent
    (memory aid SOH CAH TOA), and their reciprocals cosec A = 1/sin A = hyp/opp,
    sec A = 1/cos A = hyp/adj, cot A = 1/tan A = adj/opp.
  - QUOTIENT relations: tan A = sin A/cos A and cot A = cos A/sin A. "sin A" is
    ONE symbol (the sine of angle A), never "sin x A".
  - The ratios depend only on the ANGLE, not on the size of the triangle:
    triangles with the same angles are SIMILAR, so their side ratios are equal.
  - Because the hypotenuse is the longest side, 0 < sin A < 1 and 0 < cos A < 1
    for acute A, so cosec A > 1 and sec A > 1; tan A and cot A can be any
    positive number (tan A > 1 when A > 45 degrees).
  - Given ONE ratio, find the others: draw a right triangle, label the two known
    sides as multiples of k (sin A = 3/5: opposite 3k, hypotenuse 5k), find the
    third side by Pythagoras (4k), then read off every ratio. Given a ratio and
    a side, find the other sides by scaling.
  - COMPLEMENTARY ANGLES: in triangle ABC with angle B = 90 degrees, A + C = 90 degrees, and the
    side opposite A is adjacent to C. So sin(90 degrees - A) = cos A, cos(90 degrees - A) =
    sin A, tan(90 degrees - A) = cot A, cot(90 degrees - A) = tan A, sec(90 degrees - A) = cosec A,
    cosec(90 degrees - A) = sec A. Example: sin 72 degrees = cos 18 degrees, so sin 72 degrees/cos 18 degrees = 1.
  - Notation: sin^2A means (sin A)^2, not sin(A^2). Leave surd answers
    rationalised: 1/sqrt5 = sqrt5/5.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. In triangle ABC, angle B = 90 degrees, AB = 4 cm, BC = 3 cm and AC = 5 cm. Name the
    hypotenuse, the opposite side and the adjacent side for angle A, and again
    for angle C. Then write sin A and sin C.
    Answer: For A: hypotenuse AC = 5, opposite BC = 3, adjacent AB = 4, so
    sin A = 3/5. For C: hypotenuse AC = 5, opposite AB = 4, adjacent BC = 3, so
    sin C = 4/5.
    Teacher explains:
          A
          |\
        4 | \ 5          hypotenuse: opposite the right angle
          |  \           opposite:   across from the angle
          |_  \          adjacent:   touches the angle
          |_|__\
          B  3  C
    Stand at the angle you are working with and look across the triangle: the
    side you see is the OPPOSITE side. Of the two sides touching the angle, the
    longer one (across from the right angle) is the HYPOTENUSE and the other is
    ADJACENT. The hypotenuse never changes, but opposite and adjacent SWAP when
    we move from A to C. That is why sin A = 3/5 but sin C = 4/5. Common
    mistake: calling the hypotenuse the adjacent side because it touches the
    angle. Now you try: in the same triangle, write cos A and cos C.
    (cos A = 4/5, cos C = 3/5)

D2. In triangle ABC right-angled at B, AB = 12 cm, BC = 5 cm and AC = 13 cm.
    Write all six trigonometric ratios of angle A.
    Answer: sin A = 5/13, cos A = 12/13, tan A = 5/12, cosec A = 13/5,
    sec A = 13/12, cot A = 12/5.
    Teacher explains: For angle A: opposite = BC = 5, adjacent = AB = 12,
    hypotenuse = AC = 13. Check first that the sides fit Pythagoras:
    5^2 + 12^2 = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13^2. Then use SOH CAH TOA:
       sin A = opp/hyp = 5/13      cosec A = hyp/opp = 13/5
       cos A = adj/hyp = 12/13     sec A   = hyp/adj = 13/12
       tan A = opp/adj = 5/12      cot A   = adj/opp = 12/5
    The right-hand column is the left-hand column turned upside down: these are
    the RECIPROCAL ratios. Check a quotient relation: sin A /
    cos A = (5/13) / (12/13) = 5/12 = tan A. Common mistake: pairing cosec with
    cos and sec with sin - it is the other way round (each pair has exactly one
    "co"). Now you try: AB = 8, BC = 15, AC = 17. (sin A = 15/17, cos A = 8/17,
    tan A = 15/8, cosec A = 17/15, sec A = 17/8, cot A = 8/15)

D3. Two wheelchair ramps rise at the same angle A. Ramp P rises 0.5 m over a
    sloping length of 6 m; ramp Q is 9 m long. How high does Q rise? Explain why
    sin A is the same for both.
    Answer: Q rises 0.75 m; sin A = 0.5/6 = 0.75/9 = 1/12 for both.
    Teacher explains: Drop a vertical from the top of each ramp: each ramp is
    the hypotenuse of a right triangle with the same angle A. Two right
    triangles with an equal acute angle have all three angles equal, so they are
    SIMILAR (AA), and corresponding sides are in the same ratio. Hence
    rise/length is the same number for both - and that number is sin A. So
    sin A = 0.5/6 = 1/12, and for Q: height = 9 x sin A = 9 x 1/12 = 0.75 m.
    This is why a trigonometric ratio is a property of the ANGLE alone: we can
    build tables of sin, cos and tan and use them for any triangle. Common
    mistake: thinking a bigger triangle with the same angle has a bigger sine.
    Now you try: a 4 m ramp at the same angle; how high? (1/3 m ~ 0.33 m)

D4. If sin A = 3/5 (A acute), find the other five trigonometric ratios of A.
    Answer: cos A = 4/5, tan A = 3/4, cosec A = 5/3, sec A = 5/4, cot A = 4/3.
    Teacher explains: sin A = opp/hyp = 3/5 does NOT say that the sides are 3
    and 5, only that they are in the ratio 3 : 5. So take opposite = 3k and
    hypotenuse = 5k (k > 0). By Pythagoras:
       adjacent^2 = (5k)^2 - (3k)^2 = 25k^2 - 9k^2 = 16k^2
       adjacent  = 4k
    Now every ratio: cos A = 4k/5k = 4/5, tan A = 3k/4k = 3/4, and the
    reciprocals cosec A = 5/3, sec A = 5/4, cot A = 4/3. The k always cancels,
    which is the similar-triangles idea again. Common mistake: finding the third
    side as 5 - 3 = 2. Now you try: cos A = 12/13. (sin A = 5/13, tan A = 5/12,
    cosec A = 13/5, sec A = 13/12, cot A = 12/5)

D5. If cot theta = 7/8, evaluate (1 + sin theta)(1 - sin theta) / [(1 + cos theta)(1 - cos theta)].
    Answer: 49/64.
    Teacher explains: Take adjacent = 7k, opposite = 8k; hypotenuse =
    sqrt(49k^2 + 64k^2) = ksqrt113. So sin theta = 8/sqrt113 and cos theta = 7/sqrt113. Use
    (1 + x)(1 - x) = 1 - x^2 on top and bottom:
       top    = 1 - sin^2theta = 1 - 64/113 = 49/113
       bottom = 1 - cos^2theta = 1 - 49/113 = 64/113
       value  = (49/113) / (64/113) = 49/64
    Notice 49/64 = (7/8)^2 = cot^2theta. That is no accident: next topic we prove 1 -
    sin^2theta = cos^2theta, so the expression is cos^2theta/sin^2theta = cot^2theta. A surd hypotenuse
    such as sqrt113 is common; keep it exact. Now you try: if tan theta = 3/4, evaluate
    (1 - sin^2theta)/(1 - cos^2theta). (16/25 / 9/25 = 16/9)

D6. A ramp makes an angle A with the ground where sin A = 5/13. The top of the
    ramp is 1.5 m above the ground. How long is the ramp, and how far does it
    reach along the ground?
    Answer: Length 3.9 m; horizontal distance 3.6 m.
    Teacher explains: sin A = opposite/hypotenuse, and the opposite side
    (the height) is 1.5 m:
       1.5/L = 5/13   so   L = 1.5 x 13/5 = 3.9 m
       cos A = 12/13  (5-12-13 triangle)
       ground = L x cos A = 3.9 x 12/13 = 3.6 m
    Check with Pythagoras: 1.5^2 + 3.6^2 = 2.25 + 12.96 = 15.21 = 3.9^2. To find a
    side: write the ratio that contains the known side and the unknown side,
    then solve. Scale factor view: 5 parts = 1.5 m, so 1 part = 0.3 m, 13
    parts = 3.9 m, 12 parts = 3.6 m. Now you try: tan A = 3/4 and the ground
    distance is 20 m; find the height and the hypotenuse. (15 m, 25 m)

D7. A right triangle has legs 1 cm (opposite A) and 2 cm (adjacent to A). Find
    all six ratios of A, rationalising the denominators.
    Answer: sin A = sqrt5/5, cos A = 2sqrt5/5, tan A = 1/2, cosec A = sqrt5, sec A =
    sqrt5/2, cot A = 2.
    Teacher explains: Hypotenuse = sqrt(1^2 + 2^2) = sqrt5. Then sin A = 1/sqrt5 and
    cos A = 2/sqrt5. To RATIONALISE, multiply top and bottom by sqrt5:
       sin A = 1/sqrt5 = sqrt5/5         cosec A = sqrt5
       cos A = 2/sqrt5 = 2sqrt5/5        sec A   = sqrt5/2
       tan A = 1/2                 cot A   = 2
    Both forms are correct; the rationalised form is easier to compare and to
    add. Approximate check: sqrt5 ~ 2.236, so sin A ~ 0.447 and cos A ~ 0.894, both
    less than 1 as they must be. Now you try: legs 1 and 1. (sin = cos = sqrt2/2,
    tan = cot = 1, cosec = sec = sqrt2)

D8. Explain why tan A = sin A/cos A and why sec A x cos A = 1. If sin A = 0.6
    and cos A = 0.8, find the other four ratios.
    Answer: tan A = 0.75, cot A = 4/3, cosec A = 5/3, sec A = 1.25.
    Teacher explains: Write each ratio with its sides (o, a, h for opposite,
    adjacent, hypotenuse):
       sin A/cos A = (o/h) / (a/h) = o/h x h/a = o/a = tan A
       sec A x cos A = h/a x a/h = 1
    So we never need the sides once we know sin and cos: tan A = 0.6/0.8 = 0.75,
    cot A = 0.8/0.6 = 4/3, cosec A = 1/0.6 = 5/3, sec A = 1/0.8 = 1.25. Each
    ratio has a partner that multiplies with it to give 1: sin with cosec, cos
    with sec, tan with cot. Common mistake: thinking that 1/0.6 is 1.6
    (it is 1.666...). Now you try: sin A = 0.28 and cos A = 0.96. (tan A = 7/24,
    cot A = 24/7, cosec A = 25/7, sec A = 25/24)

D9. In triangle ABC with angle B = 90 degrees, show that sin C = cos A and tan C = cot A.
    Deduce the six complementary-angle rules.
    Answer: Since A + C = 90 degrees, C = 90 degrees - A, and sin(90 degrees - A) = cos A,
    cos(90 degrees - A) = sin A, tan(90 degrees - A) = cot A, cot(90 degrees - A) = tan A,
    sec(90 degrees - A) = cosec A, cosec(90 degrees - A) = sec A.
    Teacher explains: Angle sum: A + 90 degrees + C = 180 degrees, so C = 90 degrees - A: A and C are
    COMPLEMENTARY. The side BC is opposite A but adjacent to C; the side AB is
    adjacent to A but opposite C; AC is the hypotenuse for both.
       sin C = AB/AC = cos A      cos C = BC/AC = sin A
       tan C = AB/BC = cot A      cot C = BC/AB = tan A
       sec C = AC/BC = cosec A    cosec C = AC/AB = sec A
    Replace C by 90 degrees - A to get the rules. The names tell the story: "co-sine"
    is the sine of the COmplement. Examples: sin 70 degrees = cos 20 degrees, tan 65 degrees =
    cot 25 degrees, sec 80 degrees = cosec 10 degrees. Now you try: write cos 58 degrees and cot 85 degrees as
    ratios of the complementary angles. (sin 32 degrees, tan 5 degrees)

D10. Without tables, evaluate (a) sin 18 degrees/cos 72 degrees, (b) tan 26 degrees/cot 64 degrees, (c)
     cos 48 degrees - sin 42 degrees, (d) cosec 31 degrees - sec 59 degrees. Also write sin 67 degrees + cos 75 degrees
     using angles between 0 degrees and 45 degrees.
     Answer: (a) 1 (b) 1 (c) 0 (d) 0; sin 67 degrees + cos 75 degrees = cos 23 degrees + sin 15 degrees.
     Teacher explains: Look for two angles that add to 90 degrees, then change one
     ratio into its co-ratio:
        (a) cos 72 degrees = sin(90 degrees - 72 degrees) = sin 18 degrees, so the value is 1
        (b) cot 64 degrees = tan 26 degrees, so the value is 1
        (c) sin 42 degrees = cos 48 degrees, so the value is 0
        (d) sec 59 degrees = cosec 31 degrees, so the value is 0
     For the last part: 67 degrees = 90 degrees - 23 degrees, so sin 67 degrees = cos 23 degrees; 75 degrees = 90 degrees - 15 degrees,
     so cos 75 degrees = sin 15 degrees. A calculator check: sin 18 degrees ~ 0.3090 and
     cos 72 degrees ~ 0.3090. Common mistake: cancelling "sin" against "cos" or
     subtracting the angles. Now you try: tan 35 degrees x tan 55 degrees.
     (tan 35 degrees x cot 35 degrees = 1)

D11. Find the acute angle A if (a) tan 2A = cot(A - 18 degrees), (b) sec 4A =
     cosec(A - 20 degrees) where 4A is acute.
     Answer: (a) A = 36 degrees (b) A = 22 degrees.
     Teacher explains: Rewrite one side with the co-ratio and compare angles.
     (a) cot(A - 18 degrees) = tan(90 degrees - (A - 18 degrees)) = tan(108 degrees - A), so
        2A = 108 degrees - A   ->   3A = 108 degrees   ->   A = 36 degrees
     Check: 2A = 72 degrees and A - 18 degrees = 18 degrees, and tan 72 degrees = cot 18 degrees since
     72 degrees + 18 degrees = 90 degrees. (b) sec 4A = cosec(90 degrees - 4A), so 90 degrees - 4A = A - 20 degrees,
     giving 5A = 110 degrees and A = 22 degrees. Check: 4A = 88 degrees and A - 20 degrees = 2 degrees, which add
     to 90 degrees. Shortcut: if f(X) = co-f(Y) with X and Y acute, then X + Y = 90 degrees.
     Now you try: sin 3A = cos(A - 26 degrees). (A = 29 degrees)

D12. Which of these are possible for an acute angle A? (a) sin A = 4/3 (b)
     cos A = 0.99 (c) tan A = 7 (d) sec A = 0.5 (e) cosec A = 1.2. Give reasons.
     Also: if 3 cot A = 4, check that (1 - tan^2A)/(1 + tan^2A) = cos^2A - sin^2A.
     Answer: (a) no (b) yes (c) yes (d) no (e) yes. Both sides of the check
     equal 7/25.
     Teacher explains: sin A and cos A are "side / hypotenuse", and the
     hypotenuse is the LONGEST side, so they lie between 0 and 1: (a) 4/3 > 1 is
     impossible; (b) 0.99 is fine (a very small angle). tan A = opp/adj can be
     any positive number: (c) is fine (a steep angle). sec A = hyp/adj > 1
     always, so (d) 0.5 is impossible, and cosec A = 1.2 > 1 is possible. For
     the check: cot A = 4/3, so tan A = 3/4, and a 3-4-5 triangle gives
     sin A = 3/5, cos A = 4/5.
        (1 - 9/16)/(1 + 9/16) = (7/16)/(25/16) = 7/25
        cos^2A - sin^2A = 16/25 - 9/25 = 7/25
     Now you try: can cot A = 0.001? can cos A = 1.01? (yes; no)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: label the sides O, A, H from the angle before writing any ratio;
  keep a SOH CAH TOA card and a "reciprocal pairs" card (sin with cosec, cos
  with sec, tan with cot); always check the triangle with Pythagoras first; for
  complementary angles draw the triangle and look from the other acute angle;
  use only Pythagorean triples (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17) until the method is
  secure. Harder: show that sin A < A (in radians) < tan A using areas of a
  sector and two triangles; prove that sin A + cos A <= sqrt2; find sin 15 degrees using a
  30-60-90 triangle with a 15 degrees extension; if sin A = (p^2 - q^2)/(p^2 + q^2), find
  the other five ratios; explore with a spreadsheet how sin A and cos A change
  as A goes from 0 degrees to 90 degrees.

================================================================================
TOPIC 7.33 - TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS OF STANDARD ANGLES (0 degrees, 30 degrees, 45 degrees, 60 degrees, 90 degrees)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - The EXACT values below come from two triangles: the right isosceles triangle
    (45 degrees-45 degrees-90 degrees, sides 1, 1, sqrt2) and half of an equilateral triangle
    (30 degrees-60 degrees-90 degrees, sides 1, sqrt3, 2). Learn them; they are used in every later
    topic.
  - sin: 0, 1/2, 1/sqrt2, sqrt3/2, 1 for 0 degrees, 30 degrees, 45 degrees, 60 degrees, 90 degrees (pattern sqrt0/2, sqrt1/2,
    sqrt2/2, sqrt3/2, sqrt4/2). cos: the same list backwards. tan = sin/cos: 0, 1/sqrt3, 1,
    sqrt3, not defined. cosec, sec, cot are the reciprocals.
  - tan 90 degrees, sec 90 degrees, cot 0 degrees and cosec 0 degrees are NOT DEFINED (division by zero).
    Never write them as 0 or "infinity".
  - As A increases from 0 degrees to 90 degrees: sin A increases from 0 to 1, cos A decreases
    from 1 to 0, tan A increases from 0 without limit. sin A = cos A only at
    45 degrees.
  - EVALUATING: replace each ratio by its exact value in brackets, square where
    there is a ^2 (sin^260 degrees = (sqrt3/2)^2 = 3/4), then simplify fractions and surds.
    Rationalise at the end.
  - SOLVING: turn the value back into an angle using the table: sin 2theta = sqrt3/2
    with 2theta acute gives 2theta = 60 degrees, theta = 30 degrees. For two unknowns, e.g. sin(A + B) = 1
    and cos(A - B) = sqrt3/2, get A + B = 90 degrees and A - B = 30 degrees, then solve the pair
    of equations (A = 60 degrees, B = 30 degrees).
  - Ratios do NOT distribute: sin(A + B) != sin A + sin B and sin 2A != 2 sin A in
    general. Test claimed rules at standard angles; one failure disproves a
    rule.
  - Decimal values: sqrt2/2 ~ 0.707, sqrt3/2 ~ 0.866, sqrt3 ~ 1.732, sqrt3/3 ~ 0.577.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Use a right-angled isosceles triangle to find sin 45 degrees, cos 45 degrees and tan 45 degrees.
    Answer: sin 45 degrees = cos 45 degrees = 1/sqrt2 = sqrt2/2, tan 45 degrees = 1.
    Teacher explains:
          C
          |\
        a |  \  asqrt2      angle A = angle C = 45 degrees
          |_   \         AB = BC = a
          |_|____\        AC^2 = a^2 + a^2 = 2a^2
          B   a   A
    In triangle ABC with angle B = 90 degrees and AB = BC = a, the base angles are equal, so
    each is (180 degrees - 90 degrees)/2 = 45 degrees. Pythagoras: AC = sqrt(2a^2) = asqrt2. For angle A:
    opposite = BC = a, adjacent = AB = a, hypotenuse = asqrt2.
       sin 45 degrees = a/(asqrt2) = 1/sqrt2 = sqrt2/2
       cos 45 degrees = a/(asqrt2) = 1/sqrt2 = sqrt2/2
       tan 45 degrees = a/a = 1
    The a cancels: the size of the triangle does not matter. So cosec 45 degrees =
    sec 45 degrees = sqrt2 and cot 45 degrees = 1. Common mistake: writing 1/2 for sin 45 degrees
    (1/2 is sin 30 degrees). Now you try: check that sin^245 degrees + cos^245 degrees = 1.
    (1/2 + 1/2 = 1)

D2. Cut an equilateral triangle of side 2a in half to find the six ratios of 30 degrees
    and 60 degrees.
    Answer: sin 30 degrees = 1/2, cos 30 degrees = sqrt3/2, tan 30 degrees = 1/sqrt3 = sqrt3/3; sin 60 degrees =
    sqrt3/2, cos 60 degrees = 1/2, tan 60 degrees = sqrt3.
    Teacher explains:
              A
             /|\          all angles of ABC are 60 degrees
           /   |   \      BD = a,  angle BAD = 30 degrees
          /60 degrees |    \     AD^2 = (2a)^2 - a^2 = 3a^2, AD = asqrt3
         B-----D-----C
            a     a
    Triangle ABD has angles 30 degrees, 60 degrees, 90 degrees and sides BD = a, AD = asqrt3, AB = 2a
    (ratio 1 : sqrt3 : 2; the shortest side is opposite 30 degrees).
       angle 30 degrees (at A): opp = a, adj = asqrt3, hyp = 2a
          sin 30 degrees = 1/2, cos 30 degrees = sqrt3/2, tan 30 degrees = 1/sqrt3 = sqrt3/3
       angle 60 degrees (at B): opp = asqrt3, adj = a, hyp = 2a
          sin 60 degrees = sqrt3/2, cos 60 degrees = 1/2, tan 60 degrees = sqrt3
    Notice sin 30 degrees = cos 60 degrees and sin 60 degrees = cos 30 degrees, as the complementary rule
    says. Reciprocals: cosec 30 degrees = 2, sec 30 degrees = 2/sqrt3 = 2sqrt3/3, cot 30 degrees = sqrt3;
    cosec 60 degrees = 2sqrt3/3, sec 60 degrees = 2, cot 60 degrees = sqrt3/3. Now you try: find tan 30 degrees x
    tan 60 degrees. (1)

D3. Explain the values of the ratios at 0 degrees and 90 degrees, and why tan 90 degrees is not
    defined.
    Answer: sin 0 degrees = 0, cos 0 degrees = 1, tan 0 degrees = 0; sin 90 degrees = 1, cos 90 degrees = 0,
    tan 90 degrees is not defined (as are sec 90 degrees, cot 0 degrees and cosec 0 degrees).
    Teacher explains: Keep the hypotenuse at length 1 and let angle A shrink
    towards 0 degrees. The opposite side shrinks to 0 and the adjacent side stretches
    to 1, so sin A = opp/1 -> 0, cos A = adj/1 -> 1, tan A = opp/adj -> 0. We
    DEFINE sin 0 degrees = 0, cos 0 degrees = 1, tan 0 degrees = 0. Now let A grow towards 90 degrees: the
    opposite side approaches 1 and the adjacent side approaches 0, so
    sin 90 degrees = 1 and cos 90 degrees = 0. But tan 90 degrees = sin 90 degrees/cos 90 degrees = 1/0, and
    division by 0 has no answer: tan 90 degrees is NOT DEFINED. Likewise sec 90 degrees = 1/0,
    cosec 0 degrees = 1/0 and cot 0 degrees = 1/0 are not defined, while cot 90 degrees = 0/1 = 0. As
    A approaches 90 degrees, tan A grows without limit (tan 89 degrees ~ 57.29). Common
    mistake: writing tan 90 degrees = 0 or = 1. Now you try: find cosec 90 degrees and sec 0 degrees.
    (1 and 1)

D4. Give a quick way to remember the sin, cos and tan values of 0 degrees, 30 degrees, 45 degrees,
    60 degrees, 90 degrees, and write the full table.
    Answer: sin = sqrt0/2, sqrt1/2, sqrt2/2, sqrt3/2, sqrt4/2; cos is the same list reversed;
    tan = sin / cos. The table is below.
    Teacher explains: Write the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 under the angles, take
    square roots and divide by 2: this gives sin. Reverse the list for cos.
    Divide sin by cos for tan. Then turn each upside down for cosec, sec, cot.
       A       0 degrees       30 degrees      45 degrees      60 degrees      90 degrees
       sin A   0        1/2      sqrt2/2     sqrt3/2     1
       cos A   1        sqrt3/2     sqrt2/2     1/2      0
       tan A   0        sqrt3/3     1        sqrt3       n.d.
       cosec A n.d.     2        sqrt2       2sqrt3/3    1
       sec A   1        2sqrt3/3    sqrt2       2        n.d.
       cot A   n.d.     sqrt3       1        sqrt3/3     0
       (n.d. = not defined; 1/sqrt2 = sqrt2/2, 1/sqrt3 = sqrt3/3, 2/sqrt3 = 2sqrt3/3)
    Check the table with two facts: sin A = cos(90 degrees - A) (read the sin row
    backwards to get the cos row) and sin^2A + cos^2A = 1 in every column, e.g. at
    60 degrees: 3/4 + 1/4 = 1. Common mistake: swapping tan 30 degrees and tan 60 degrees - remember
    tan increases, so tan 30 degrees = sqrt3/3 ~ 0.577 is the smaller. Now you try: from
    memory, give cot 30 degrees, sec 45 degrees and cosec 60 degrees. (sqrt3, sqrt2, 2sqrt3/3)

D5. Evaluate 2 sin^230 degrees + tan^260 degrees - cos^245 degrees.
    Answer: 3.
    Teacher explains: Replace each ratio by its value IN BRACKETS, then square:
       2 sin^230 degrees + tan^260 degrees - cos^245 degrees
       = 2(1/2)^2 + (sqrt3)^2 - (1/sqrt2)^2
       = 2 x 1/4 + 3 - 1/2
       = 1/2 + 3 - 1/2 = 3
    sin^230 degrees means (sin 30 degrees)^2 = (1/2)^2 = 1/4, NOT sin(900 degrees) and not 2 x 1/2.
    Brackets make the squaring safe, especially with surds: (sqrt3)^2 = 3 and
    (1/sqrt2)^2 = 1/2. Common mistake: working out (2 x 1/2)^2 for 2 sin^230 degrees; the 2
    multiplies AFTER squaring. Now you try: sin^260 degrees + cos^260 degrees + tan^245 degrees.
    (3/4 + 1/4 + 1 = 2)

D6. Evaluate (5 cos^260 degrees + 4 sec^230 degrees - tan^245 degrees)/(sin^230 degrees + cos^230 degrees).
    Answer: 67/12.
    Teacher explains:
       top    = 5(1/2)^2 + 4(2/sqrt3)^2 - 1^2
              = 5/4 + 16/3 - 1 = 15/12 + 64/12 - 12/12 = 67/12
       bottom = (1/2)^2 + (sqrt3/2)^2 = 1/4 + 3/4 = 1
       value  = 67/12 / 1 = 67/12
    Work out the top and the bottom SEPARATELY, then divide. The bottom is
    sin^230 degrees + cos^230 degrees, which is always 1 (next topic proves sin^2A + cos^2A = 1
    for every A). (2/sqrt3)^2 = 4/3, so 4 sec^230 degrees = 16/3. Use a common denominator
    of 12 to add the fractions. Now you try: (sin 30 degrees + tan 45 degrees -
    cosec 60 degrees)/(sec 30 degrees + cos 60 degrees + cot 45 degrees). (value (3sqrt3 - 4)/(3sqrt3 + 4), which
    rationalises to (43 - 24sqrt3)/11)

D7. Solve for theta: (a) sin 2theta = sqrt3/2, (b) 2 cos 3theta = 1, (c) sqrt3 tan(theta - 15 degrees) = 1.
    In each case the angle inside the ratio is between 0 degrees and 90 degrees.
    Answer: (a) theta = 30 degrees (b) theta = 20 degrees (c) theta = 45 degrees.
    Teacher explains: First make the ratio stand alone, then read the angle from
    the table, then solve the simple equation:
       (a) sin 2theta = sqrt3/2          -> 2theta = 60 degrees          -> theta = 30 degrees
       (b) cos 3theta = 1/2           -> 3theta = 60 degrees          -> theta = 20 degrees
       (c) tan(theta - 15 degrees) = 1/sqrt3    -> theta - 15 degrees = 30 degrees     -> theta = 45 degrees
    Check (a): sin(2 x 30 degrees) = sin 60 degrees = sqrt3/2. The condition "between 0 degrees and 90 degrees"
    matters: in Stage 8 you will meet angles beyond 90 degrees and sin 120 degrees is also
    sqrt3/2, which would give a second answer theta = 60 degrees. Common mistake: dividing the
    VALUE by 2 (sin theta = sqrt3/4) instead of the ANGLE. Now you try: tan 2theta = sqrt3
    with 2theta acute. (theta = 30 degrees)

D8. Find A and B (0 degrees < B < A, A + B <= 90 degrees) if (a) sin(A + B) = 1 and
    cos(A - B) = sqrt3/2; (b) tan(A + B) = sqrt3 and tan(A - B) = 1/sqrt3.
    Answer: (a) A = 60 degrees, B = 30 degrees (b) A = 45 degrees, B = 15 degrees.
    Teacher explains: Turn each equation into an equation between angles, then
    solve the pair by adding and subtracting:
       (a) A + B = 90 degrees,  A - B = 30 degrees
           add: 2A = 120 degrees, A = 60 degrees;  then B = 90 degrees - 60 degrees = 30 degrees
       (b) A + B = 60 degrees,  A - B = 30 degrees
           add: 2A = 90 degrees,  A = 45 degrees;  then B = 60 degrees - 45 degrees = 15 degrees
    Check (b): tan(45 degrees + 15 degrees) = tan 60 degrees = sqrt3 and tan(45 degrees - 15 degrees) =
    tan 30 degrees = 1/sqrt3. This is a trigonometry question that becomes a pair of
    linear equations (topic 7.8). Now you try: cos(A - B) = 1 and sin(A + B) =
    sqrt3/2. (A - B = 0 degrees, A + B = 60 degrees: A = B = 30 degrees)

D9. Check at standard angles: (a) is sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A true for A = 30 degrees?
    (b) is sin(A + B) = sin A + sin B true for A = 30 degrees, B = 60 degrees? (c) is cos 2A =
    cos^2A - sin^2A true for A = 30 degrees and 45 degrees?
    Answer: (a) yes: both sides sqrt3/2. (b) no: 1 on the left, (1 + sqrt3)/2 on the
    right. (c) yes: 1/2 and 0 on both sides.
    Teacher explains:
       (a) sin 60 degrees = sqrt3/2;  2 x 1/2 x sqrt3/2 = sqrt3/2          equal
       (b) sin 90 degrees = 1;     sin 30 degrees + sin 60 degrees = 1/2 + sqrt3/2   not equal
       (c) A = 30 degrees: cos 60 degrees = 1/2; 3/4 - 1/4 = 1/2          equal
           A = 45 degrees: cos 90 degrees = 0;   1/2 - 1/2 = 0            equal
    A single counter-example PROVES that a rule is false, as in (b): sin does
    not "multiply out" over a sum. But agreement at a few angles does NOT prove
    a rule is true for all angles; (a) and (c) are true identities, proved in
    Stage 8. Checking at standard angles is still the best way to catch
    mistakes. Now you try: does cos(60 degrees - 30 degrees) equal cos 60 degrees - cos 30 degrees? (no:
    sqrt3/2 on the left, (1 - sqrt3)/2 on the right)

D10. A 6 m ladder leans against a wall making 60 degrees with the ground. How high up
     the wall does it reach and how far is its foot from the wall?
     Answer: Height 3sqrt3 ~ 5.20 m; foot 3 m from the wall.
     Teacher explains:
           |`-.
           |   `-.   6 m
         h |      `-.
           |_        `-.  60 degrees
           +---- d -------
     The ladder is the hypotenuse. Height h is OPPOSITE the 60 degrees angle, the
     distance d is ADJACENT:
        sin 60 degrees = h/6   ->  h = 6 x sqrt3/2 = 3sqrt3 ~ 5.196 ~ 5.20 m
        cos 60 degrees = d/6   ->  d = 6 x 1/2 = 3 m
     Check: 3^2 + (3sqrt3)^2 = 9 + 27 = 36 = 6^2. Choose the ratio that links the side
     you KNOW with the side you WANT. Now you try: the same ladder at 45 degrees.
     (height = foot distance = 3sqrt2 ~ 4.24 m)

D11. In triangle ABC, angle B = 90 degrees, BC = 5 cm and angle ACB = 30 degrees. Find AB and AC.
     Answer: AB = 5/sqrt3 = 5sqrt3/3 ~ 2.89 cm; AC = 10/sqrt3 = 10sqrt3/3 ~ 5.77 cm.
     Teacher explains: For the 30 degrees angle at C: AB is opposite, BC = 5 is
     adjacent, AC is the hypotenuse.
        tan 30 degrees = AB/BC  ->  AB = 5 x 1/sqrt3 = 5sqrt3/3
        cos 30 degrees = BC/AC  ->  AC = 5 / (sqrt3/2) = 10/sqrt3 = 10sqrt3/3
     Check with the 1 : sqrt3 : 2 pattern of a 30 degrees-60 degrees-90 degrees triangle: the side
     opposite 30 degrees is the shortest (AB = 5sqrt3/3), the hypotenuse is twice it
     (10sqrt3/3), and the side opposite 60 degrees is sqrt3 times it (5). Now you try:
     angle C = 60 degrees, BC = 4 cm. (AB = 4sqrt3 ~ 6.93 cm, AC = 8 cm)

D12. State whether true or false, with a reason: (a) sin A increases as A
     increases from 0 degrees to 90 degrees; (b) cos A increases in the same range; (c)
     sin theta = cos theta for all theta; (d) cot A is not defined at A = 0 degrees; (e) sin 30 degrees +
     sin 60 degrees = sin 90 degrees.
     Answer: (a) T (b) F (c) F (d) T (e) F.
     Teacher explains: Read along the rows of the table. (a) sin: 0, 0.5, 0.707,
     0.866, 1 - increasing. (b) cos: 1, 0.866, 0.707, 0.5, 0 - DECREASING. (c)
     Only at 45 degrees are they equal; at 30 degrees they are 1/2 and sqrt3/2. (d) cot 0 degrees =
     cos 0 degrees/sin 0 degrees = 1/0: not defined. (e) 1/2 + sqrt3/2 ~ 1.366, but sin 90 degrees = 1.
     For "true for all" statements one counter-example is enough to answer F.
     Common mistake: believing all ratios behave like sin. Now you try: true or
     false: tan A > sin A for 0 degrees < A < 90 degrees. (true: tan A = sin A/cos A and
     cos A < 1)

M12. Evaluate exactly. (In Stage 8 you will see that each is a single ratio of

     a) sin 30 degrees cos 60 degrees + cos 30 degrees sin 60 degrees

     f) (tan 45 degrees - tan 30 degrees)/(1 + tan 45 degrees tan 30 degrees)
     g) sin 45 degrees cos 30 degrees + cos 45 degrees sin 30 degrees
     h) cos 45 degrees cos 30 degrees + sin 45 degrees sin 30 degrees
     i) sin 60 degrees cos 45 degrees - cos 60 degrees sin 45 degrees
     j) cos 45 degrees cos 60 degrees - sin 45 degrees sin 60 degrees
     k) 3 sin 30 degrees - 4 sin^330 degrees
     l) 4 cos^330 degrees - 3 cos 30 degrees
     m) (1 - cos 60 degrees)/sin 60 degrees
     n) sin 60 degrees/(1 + cos 60 degrees)
     Answers: a) 1   b) 0   c) sqrt3/2   d) 1   e) sqrt3 + 2   f) 2 - sqrt3
              g) (sqrt2 + sqrt6)/4   h) (sqrt2 + sqrt6)/4   i) (sqrt6 - sqrt2)/4   j) (sqrt2 - sqrt6)/4
              k) 1   l) 0   m) sqrt3/3   n) sqrt3/3

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: build the table from the two triangles every day for a week until
  it can be written from memory in two minutes; always put values in brackets
  before squaring; practise rationalising 1/sqrt2 and 1/sqrt3 separately; use a
  calculator to check decimal values (sin 60 degrees ~ 0.866). Harder: find sin 15 degrees and
  cos 15 degrees exactly from the 45 degrees - 30 degrees values ((sqrt6 - sqrt2)/4, (sqrt6 + sqrt2)/4); find
  tan 22.5 degrees from a right isosceles triangle with an extended leg (sqrt2 - 1); prove
  that sin 18 degrees = (sqrt5 - 1)/4 using a 36 degrees-72 degrees-72 degrees golden triangle; show that
  sin theta + cos theta is largest at 45 degrees.

================================================================================
TOPIC 7.34 - TRIGONOMETRIC IDENTITIES (sin^2 + cos^2 = 1 ETC.)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - An IDENTITY is an equation that is true for EVERY value of the angle for
    which both sides are defined (an equation such as sin theta = 1/2 is true only
    for some angles).
  - The three Pythagorean identities: sin^2theta + cos^2theta = 1 (for all theta), 1 + tan^2theta =
    sec^2theta (0 degrees <= theta < 90 degrees), 1 + cot^2theta = cosec^2theta (0 degrees < theta <= 90 degrees). Divide the first
    by cos^2theta or by sin^2theta to get the other two.
  - Useful rearrangements: sin^2theta = 1 - cos^2theta = (1 - cos theta)(1 + cos theta);
    cos^2theta = 1 - sin^2theta; sec^2theta - tan^2theta = 1 = (sec theta - tan theta)(sec theta + tan theta);
    cosec^2theta - cot^2theta = 1.
  - Expressing in terms of one ratio (theta acute): cos theta = sqrt(1 - sin^2theta), tan theta =
    sin theta/sqrt(1 - sin^2theta), sec theta = sqrt(1 + tan^2theta), sin theta = tan theta/sqrt(1 + tan^2theta), and so
    on.
  - PROVING an identity: start from the MORE COMPLICATED side and change it step
    by step into the other side. Useful moves: write everything in sin and cos;
    combine fractions over a common denominator; factorise; multiply top and
    bottom by a conjugate such as (1 + cos theta); replace 1 by sin^2theta + cos^2theta. Never
    treat the identity as an equation to be "solved" by doing the same thing to
    both sides.
  - Algebra you need: (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2, (a - b)(a + b) = a^2 - b^2, a^3 -
    b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2), a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2), and the rules
    for fractions.
  - CHECKING: test a claimed identity at a few angles (30 degrees, 45 degrees, 60 degrees, or any
    angle on a calculator). If it fails at one angle, it is NOT an identity. If
    it passes, that is evidence, not a proof.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prove that sin^2A + cos^2A = 1 for every acute angle A, and check it at
    A = 30 degrees and A = 0 degrees.
    Answer: By Pythagoras (opp^2 + adj^2 = hyp^2), dividing by hyp^2 gives sin^2A +
    cos^2A = 1. At 30 degrees: 1/4 + 3/4 = 1; at 0 degrees: 0 + 1 = 1.
    Teacher explains:
          C
          |\          angle B = 90 degrees: opp = BC, adj = AB, hyp = AC
          | \         BC^2 + AB^2 = AC^2   (Pythagoras)
          |  \
          |_  \       divide every term by AC^2:
          |_|__A      (BC/AC)^2 + (AB/AC)^2 = 1
          B           sin^2A + cos^2A = 1
    This is Pythagoras' theorem written in trigonometry. The argument works for
    EVERY right triangle, so the identity holds for every acute A, and the table
    shows it also holds at 0 degrees and 90 degrees (0 + 1 and 1 + 0). sin^2A means (sin A)^2.
    Rearrangements used all the time: sin^2A = 1 - cos^2A and cos^2A = 1 - sin^2A.
    Common mistake: writing sin A + cos A = 1 (no squares); at 45 degrees that gives
    sqrt2/2 + sqrt2/2 = sqrt2, not 1. Now you try: check the identity at 60 degrees.
    (3/4 + 1/4 = 1)

D2. Derive 1 + tan^2A = sec^2A and 1 + cot^2A = cosec^2A from sin^2A + cos^2A = 1. For
    which angles in 0 degrees <= A <= 90 degrees are they true?
    Answer: Divide by cos^2A (allowed when A != 90 degrees) and by sin^2A (when A != 0 degrees).
    So 1 + tan^2A = sec^2A for 0 degrees <= A < 90 degrees and 1 + cot^2A = cosec^2A for 0 degrees <
    A <= 90 degrees.
    Teacher explains:
       sin^2A + cos^2A = 1         / cos^2A:
       sin^2A/cos^2A + 1 = 1/cos^2A  ->  tan^2A + 1 = sec^2A
       sin^2A + cos^2A = 1         / sin^2A:
       1 + cos^2A/sin^2A = 1/sin^2A  ->  1 + cot^2A = cosec^2A
    We may only divide by something that is NOT zero: cos 90 degrees = 0, so the first
    is not claimed at 90 degrees (and indeed tan 90 degrees and sec 90 degrees are not defined);
    sin 0 degrees = 0, so the second excludes 0 degrees. Check at 60 degrees: 1 + (sqrt3)^2 = 4 = 2^2 =
    sec^260 degrees. Rearranged forms: sec^2A - tan^2A = 1 and cosec^2A - cot^2A = 1. Now
    you try: check 1 + cot^2A = cosec^2A at 30 degrees. (1 + 3 = 4 = 2^2)

D3. Express cos A, tan A, cosec A, sec A and cot A in terms of sin A only
    (A acute).
    Answer: cos A = sqrt(1 - sin^2A), tan A = sin A/sqrt(1 - sin^2A), cosec A = 1/sin A,
    sec A = 1/sqrt(1 - sin^2A), cot A = sqrt(1 - sin^2A)/sin A.
    Teacher explains: Start from cos^2A = 1 - sin^2A. For acute A, cos A > 0, so
    take the positive root: cos A = sqrt(1 - sin^2A). Then every other ratio follows
    from the quotient and reciprocal relations:
       tan A   = sin A/cos A = sin A/sqrt(1 - sin^2A)
       cosec A = 1/sin A
       sec A   = 1/cos A = 1/sqrt(1 - sin^2A)
       cot A   = cos A/sin A = sqrt(1 - sin^2A)/sin A
    Test with sin A = 3/5: sqrt(1 - 9/25) = sqrt(16/25) = 4/5 = cos A, and
    tan A = (3/5)/(4/5) = 3/4 - the 3-4-5 triangle again. Common mistake:
    sqrt(1 - sin^2A) = 1 - sin A (the root does not split). Now you try: express
    sin A and sec A in terms of tan A. (sin A = tan A/sqrt(1 + tan^2A), sec A =
    sqrt(1 + tan^2A))

D4. If tan A = 1/sqrt7, find (cosec^2A - sec^2A)/(cosec^2A + sec^2A) using identities,
    without drawing a triangle.
    Answer: 3/4.
    Teacher explains: Use cosec^2A = 1 + cot^2A and sec^2A = 1 + tan^2A. With
    tan^2A = 1/7 and cot^2A = 7:
       cosec^2A = 1 + 7   = 8
       sec^2A   = 1 + 1/7 = 8/7
       value = (8 - 8/7)/(8 + 8/7) = (48/7)/(64/7) = 48/64 = 3/4
    Identities let us jump straight from tan to sec and cosec. Check with a
    triangle: opposite 1, adjacent sqrt7, hypotenuse sqrt8, so cosec^2A = 8 and
    sec^2A = 8/7 - the same. Common mistake: using cosec^2A = 1 + tan^2A (wrong
    pairing: cosec goes with cot). Now you try: if cot A = 2, find sec^2A.
    (tan^2A = 1/4, sec^2A = 5/4)

D5. Prove that (sec theta - tan theta)(sec theta + tan theta) = 1. Hence, if sec theta + tan theta = 3,
    find sec theta - tan theta, sec theta and tan theta.
    Answer: LHS = sec^2theta - tan^2theta = 1. If sec theta + tan theta = 3 then sec theta -
    tan theta = 1/3, sec theta = 5/3 and tan theta = 4/3.
    Teacher explains:
       LHS = (sec theta - tan theta)(sec theta + tan theta)
           = sec^2theta - tan^2theta          (difference of two squares)
           = 1                       (since 1 + tan^2theta = sec^2theta)
           = RHS
    So sec theta + tan theta and sec theta - tan theta are RECIPROCALS. With sum 3, the
    difference is 1/3. Adding the two equations: 2 sec theta = 3 + 1/3 = 10/3,
    sec theta = 5/3; subtracting: 2 tan theta = 3 - 1/3 = 8/3, tan theta = 4/3. Check:
    1 + 16/9 = 25/9 = (5/3)^2. Write proofs as a column starting with "LHS =" and
    ending with "= RHS", one step per line. Now you try: prove
    (cosec theta - cot theta)(cosec theta + cot theta) = 1. (cosec^2theta - cot^2theta = 1)

D6. Prove (sin theta + cos theta)^2 = 1 + 2 sin theta cos theta. If sin theta + cos theta = sqrt2, find
    sin theta cos theta and theta (acute).
    Answer: sin theta cos theta = 1/2 and theta = 45 degrees.
    Teacher explains:
       LHS = (sin theta + cos theta)^2
           = sin^2theta + 2 sin theta cos theta + cos^2theta
           = (sin^2theta + cos^2theta) + 2 sin theta cos theta
           = 1 + 2 sin theta cos theta = RHS
    Similarly (sin theta - cos theta)^2 = 1 - 2 sin theta cos theta. With sin theta + cos theta = sqrt2:
    2 = 1 + 2 sin theta cos theta, so sin theta cos theta = 1/2. Then
    (sin theta - cos theta)^2 = 1 - 1 = 0, so sin theta = cos theta and theta = 45 degrees. Common mistake:
    (sin theta + cos theta)^2 = sin^2theta + cos^2theta = 1 (the middle term is forgotten). Now you
    try: if sin theta + cos theta = 7/5, find sin theta cos theta. (49/25 = 1 + 2 sin theta cos theta,
    so 12/25)

D7. Prove that (1 - cos theta)/(1 + cos theta) = (cosec theta - cot theta)^2.
    Answer: Start from the right-hand side and write it in sin and cos.
    Teacher explains:
       RHS = (cosec theta - cot theta)^2
           = (1/sin theta - cos theta/sin theta)^2
           = (1 - cos theta)^2/sin^2theta
           = (1 - cos theta)^2/(1 - cos^2theta)
           = (1 - cos theta)^2/((1 - cos theta)(1 + cos theta))
           = (1 - cos theta)/(1 + cos theta) = LHS
    The RHS looked more complicated, so we started there. Key moves: change
    cosec and cot into sin and cos; replace sin^2theta by 1 - cos^2theta; factorise the
    difference of squares; cancel the common factor (1 - cos theta). Numeric check
    at theta = 60 degrees: LHS = (1/2)/(3/2) = 1/3; RHS = (2/sqrt3 - 1/sqrt3)^2 = (1/sqrt3)^2 = 1/3.
    Now you try: prove (1 + sin theta)/(1 - sin theta) = (sec theta + tan theta)^2. (same method,
    with cos^2theta = (1 - sin theta)(1 + sin theta))

D8. Prove that sin theta/(1 + cos theta) + (1 + cos theta)/sin theta = 2 cosec theta.
    Answer: Combine the two fractions over a common denominator.
    Teacher explains:
       LHS = [sin^2theta + (1 + cos theta)^2] / [(1 + cos theta) sin theta]
           = [sin^2theta + 1 + 2 cos theta + cos^2theta] / [(1 + cos theta) sin theta]
           = [2 + 2 cos theta] / [(1 + cos theta) sin theta]
           = 2(1 + cos theta) / [(1 + cos theta) sin theta]
           = 2/sin theta = 2 cosec theta = RHS
    The step "sin^2theta + cos^2theta = 1" turns 1 + 1 into 2. Then factorise 2 and cancel
    (1 + cos theta). Adding fractions is exactly as in algebra: a/b +
    c/d = (ad + bc)/(bd). Check at 90 degrees: 1/1 + 1/1 = 2 = 2 cosec 90 degrees. Common
    mistake: adding tops and bottoms separately. Now you try: prove
    cos theta/(1 - sin theta) + cos theta/(1 + sin theta) = 2 sec theta. (common denominator 1 -
    sin^2theta = cos^2theta)

D9. Prove that sqrt((1 + sin theta)/(1 - sin theta)) = sec theta + tan theta (theta acute).
    Answer: Multiply top and bottom inside the root by (1 + sin theta).
    Teacher explains:
       LHS = sqrt[(1 + sin theta)(1 + sin theta) / ((1 - sin theta)(1 + sin theta))]
           = sqrt[(1 + sin theta)^2 / (1 - sin^2theta)]
           = sqrt[(1 + sin theta)^2 / cos^2theta]
           = (1 + sin theta)/cos theta          (both positive for acute theta)
           = 1/cos theta + sin theta/cos theta = sec theta + tan theta = RHS
    Multiplying by the CONJUGATE (1 + sin theta) makes the denominator a perfect
    square cos^2theta, so the square root disappears. We need cos theta > 0 and 1 + sin theta
    > 0 to take the root, which is true for acute theta. Check at 30 degrees:
    sqrt((3/2)/(1/2)) = sqrt3 and sec 30 degrees + tan 30 degrees = 2/sqrt3 + 1/sqrt3 = 3/sqrt3 = sqrt3. Now you
    try: prove sqrt((1 - cos theta)/(1 + cos theta)) = cosec theta - cot theta.
    (multiply by 1 - cos theta)

D10. Prove that tan theta/(1 - cot theta) + cot theta/(1 - tan theta) = 1 + sec theta cosec theta.
     Answer: Write everything in sin theta and cos theta, then use the factorisation of
     a^3 - b^3.
     Teacher explains:
        LHS = sin^2theta/[cos theta(sin theta - cos theta)] - cos^2theta/[sin theta(sin theta - cos theta)]
            = (sin^3theta - cos^3theta)/[sin theta cos theta(sin theta - cos theta)]
            = (sin theta - cos theta)(sin^2theta + sin theta cos theta + cos^2theta)
              / [sin theta cos theta(sin theta - cos theta)]
            = (1 + sin theta cos theta)/(sin theta cos theta)
            = 1/(sin theta cos theta) + 1 = 1 + sec theta cosec theta = RHS
     First line: tan theta/(1 - cot theta) = (sin theta/cos theta) / ((sin theta - cos theta)/sin theta) =
     sin^2theta/(cos theta(sin theta - cos theta)); in the second fraction 1 -
     tan theta = (cos theta - sin theta)/cos theta = -(sin theta - cos theta)/cos theta, which makes the
     minus sign. The cube identity is the key algebraic step. Check at 30 degrees:
     LHS = (sqrt3/3)/(1 - sqrt3) + sqrt3/(1 - sqrt3/3) ~ -0.789 + 4.098 = 3.309;
     RHS = 1 + (2/sqrt3)(2) ~ 3.309. Now you try: check the identity at 60 degrees. (both
     sides 1 + 4/sqrt3 ~ 3.309)

D11. If sec theta + tan theta = p, show that sin theta = (p^2 - 1)/(p^2 + 1). Find sin theta when
     p = 2.
     Answer: sin theta = 3/5 when p = 2.
     Teacher explains: From D5, sec theta - tan theta = 1/p. Add and subtract:
        sec theta = (p + 1/p)/2 = (p^2 + 1)/(2p)
        tan theta = (p - 1/p)/2 = (p^2 - 1)/(2p)
        sin theta = tan theta/sec theta = (p^2 - 1)/(p^2 + 1)
     For p = 2: sin theta = (4 - 1)/(4 + 1) = 3/5, and sec theta = 5/4, tan theta = 3/4 -
     the 3-4-5 triangle. Notice sin theta = tan theta / sec theta because
     (sin theta/cos theta) / (1/cos theta) = sin theta. Common mistake: squaring sec theta + tan theta =
     p and forgetting the middle term. Now you try: p = 3. (sin theta = 8/10 = 4/5)

D12. Ravi claims sin theta + cos theta = 1 is an identity because it works at 0 degrees and
     90 degrees. Is he right? How should we test claimed identities?
     Answer: No. At 45 degrees, sin 45 degrees + cos 45 degrees = sqrt2 ~ 1.414, not 1, so it is not an
     identity. One counter-example disproves; agreement at a few angles only
     supports a claim and a proof is needed.
     Teacher explains: An identity must hold for EVERY angle. Test several
     angles, including "ordinary" ones like 30 degrees, 45 degrees, 60 degrees:
        theta       sin theta + cos theta          1 + tan^2theta    sec^2theta
        0 degrees      0 + 1 = 1              1            1
        30 degrees     (1 + sqrt3)/2 ~ 1.366     4/3          4/3
        45 degrees     sqrt2 ~ 1.414             2            2
        60 degrees     (sqrt3 + 1)/2 ~ 1.366     4            4
     The first column is not constant, so sin theta + cos theta = 1 is false in general
     (it is only an EQUATION with solutions 0 degrees and 90 degrees). The last two columns
     agree at every test angle, which supports 1 + tan^2theta = sec^2theta - and D2 proves
     it. A calculator at a strange angle like 37 degrees is a good extra test. Now you
     try: test (sin theta + cos theta)^2 = sin^2theta + cos^2theta at 30 degrees. (LHS = 1 + 2 x 1/2 x
     sqrt3/2 = 1 + sqrt3/2 ~ 1.866, RHS = 1: not an identity)

PART B - MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Simplify to a number or a single term.
    a) (1 - sin^2theta) sec^2theta
    b) (1 + tan^2theta) cos^2theta
    c) sin theta cot theta
    d) cos theta tan theta
    e) (sec^2theta - 1) cot^2theta
    f) (cosec^2theta - 1) tan^2theta
    g) sin^2theta + cos^2theta + tan^2theta
    h) 9 sec^2theta - 9 tan^2theta
    i) (1 + cos theta)(1 - cos theta)(1 + cot^2theta)
    j) sec theta (1 - sin theta)(sec theta + tan theta)
    k) tan theta/sec theta
    l) cot theta/cosec theta
    m) (sin theta + cos theta)^2 + (sin theta - cos theta)^2
    n) sin theta sec theta
    o) (1 - cos^2theta) cosec^2theta
    p) cot^2theta - cosec^2theta
    q) tan^2theta - sec^2theta
    r) (sec theta + tan theta)(1 - sin theta)
    s) cos theta cosec theta
    t) sin^4theta - cos^4theta + cos^2theta
    u) 1/(1 + sin theta) + 1/(1 - sin theta)
    v) (1 + tan^2theta)/(1 + cot^2theta)
    Answers: a) 1   b) 1   c) cos theta   d) sin theta   e) 1   f) 1   g) sec^2theta   h) 9
             i) 1   j) 1   k) sin theta   l) cos theta   m) 2   n) tan theta   o) 1   p) -1
             q) -1   r) cos theta   s) cot theta   t) sin^2theta   u) 2 sec^2theta   v) tan^2theta

M2. theta is acute. Express the first ratio in terms of the second only.
    a) cos theta in terms of sin theta     b) tan theta in terms of sin theta
    c) sec theta in terms of sin theta     d) cot theta in terms of sin theta
    e) sin theta in terms of cos theta     f) tan theta in terms of cos theta
    g) cosec theta in terms of cos theta   h) cot theta in terms of cos theta
    i) sec theta in terms of tan theta     j) cos theta in terms of tan theta
    k) sin theta in terms of tan theta     l) cosec theta in terms of tan theta
    m) sin theta in terms of cot theta     n) cos theta in terms of cot theta
    o) tan theta in terms of sec theta     p) sin theta in terms of sec theta
    q) cot theta in terms of cosec theta   r) cos theta in terms of cosec theta
    Answers: a) sqrt(1 - sin^2theta)   b) sin theta/sqrt(1 - sin^2theta)   c) 1/sqrt(1 - sin^2theta)
             d) sqrt(1 - sin^2theta)/sin theta   e) sqrt(1 - cos^2theta)   f) sqrt(1 - cos^2theta)/cos theta
             g) 1/sqrt(1 - cos^2theta)   h) cos theta/sqrt(1 - cos^2theta)   i) sqrt(1 + tan^2theta)
             j) 1/sqrt(1 + tan^2theta)   k) tan theta/sqrt(1 + tan^2theta)   l) sqrt(1 + tan^2theta)/tan theta
             m) 1/sqrt(1 + cot^2theta)   n) cot theta/sqrt(1 + cot^2theta)   o) sqrt(sec^2theta - 1)
             p) sqrt(sec^2theta - 1)/sec theta   q) sqrt(cosec^2theta - 1)
             r) sqrt(cosec^2theta - 1)/cosec theta

M3. theta is acute. Use the identities (not a triangle) to find sin theta, cos theta, tan theta
    (in this order).
    a) cos theta = 7/25      b) sin theta = 20/29
    c) sec theta = 13/12     d) cosec theta = 29/20
    e) tan theta = 2         f) cot theta = 3
    g) sin theta = 1/3       h) cos theta = 2/3
    i) sec theta = 3         j) tan theta = 1/2
    k) cosec theta = 5/4     l) cot theta = 1/4
    m) sin theta = 9/41      n) sec theta = 17/15
    o) tan theta = 5/2       p) cos theta = 1/4
    Answers: a) 24/25, 7/25, 24/7   b) 20/29, 21/29, 20/21
             c) 5/13, 12/13, 5/12   d) 20/29, 21/29, 20/21   e) 2sqrt5/5, sqrt5/5, 2
             f) sqrt10/10, 3sqrt10/10, 1/3   g) 1/3, 2sqrt2/3, sqrt2/4   h) sqrt5/3, 2/3, sqrt5/2
             i) 2sqrt2/3, 1/3, 2sqrt2   j) sqrt5/5, 2sqrt5/5, 1/2   k) 4/5, 3/5, 4/3
             l) 4sqrt17/17, sqrt17/17, 4   m) 9/41, 40/41, 9/40   n) 8/17, 15/17, 8/15
             o) 5sqrt29/29, 2sqrt29/29, 5/2   p) sqrt15/4, 1/4, sqrt15

M4. Evaluate without a calculator (use identities and complementary angles).
    a) sin^220 degrees + cos^220 degrees
    b) 9 sec^237 degrees - 9 tan^237 degrees
    c) (1 + tan^240 degrees) cos^240 degrees
    d) 5 cosec^212 degrees - 5 cot^212 degrees
    e) sin^263 degrees + sin^227 degrees
    f) cos^217 degrees + cos^273 degrees
    g) sec^250 degrees - cot^240 degrees
    h) 3 cosec^258 degrees - 3 tan^232 degrees
    i) (1 - sin^235 degrees) sec^235 degrees
    j) tan^225 degrees - sec^225 degrees
    k) cot^270 degrees - cosec^270 degrees
    l) sin 55 degrees sec 55 degrees cot 55 degrees
    m) 2(sin^244 degrees + sin^246 degrees)
    n) cos^215 degrees - sin^275 degrees
    o) (sec 10 degrees - tan 10 degrees)(sec 10 degrees + tan 10 degrees)
    p) sin^21 degrees + sin^289 degrees + tan 45 degrees
    Answers: a) 1   b) 9   c) 1   d) 5   e) 1   f) 1   g) 1   h) 3   i) 1
             j) -1   k) -1   l) 1   m) 2   n) 0   o) 1   p) 2

M5. Prove, starting from the left-hand side. Give each step (the answers show
    one correct chain).
    a) (sec theta - tan theta)(sec theta + tan theta) = 1
    b) (cosec theta - cot theta)(cosec theta + cot theta) = 1
    c) (sin theta + cos theta)^2 = 1 + 2 sin theta cos theta
    d) (sin theta - cos theta)^2 = 1 - 2 sin theta cos theta
    e) cos^2theta(1 + tan^2theta) = 1
    f) sin theta cot theta sec theta = 1
    g) tan theta + cot theta = sec theta cosec theta
    h) sin^4theta - cos^4theta = sin^2theta - cos^2theta
    i) sec^4theta - sec^2theta = tan^4theta + tan^2theta
    j) (1 - sin theta)(1 + sin theta) sec^2theta = 1
    k) cos theta/(1 - sin theta) = (1 + sin theta)/cos theta
    l) 1/(sec theta - tan theta) = sec theta + tan theta
    Answers:
      a) LHS = sec^2theta - tan^2theta
             = 1 = RHS
      b) LHS = cosec^2theta - cot^2theta
             = 1 = RHS
      c) LHS = sin^2theta + cos^2theta + 2 sin theta cos theta
             = 1 + 2 sin theta cos theta = RHS
      d) LHS = sin^2theta + cos^2theta - 2 sin theta cos theta
             = 1 - 2 sin theta cos theta = RHS
      e) LHS = cos^2theta sec^2theta
             = 1 = RHS
      f) LHS = sin theta x cos theta/sin theta x 1/cos theta
             = 1 = RHS
      g) LHS = sin theta/cos theta + cos theta/sin theta
             = (sin^2theta + cos^2theta)/(sin theta cos theta)
             = 1/(sin theta cos theta)
             = sec theta cosec theta = RHS
      h) LHS = (sin^2theta - cos^2theta)(sin^2theta + cos^2theta)
             = sin^2theta - cos^2theta = RHS
      i) LHS = sec^2theta(sec^2theta - 1)
             = (1 + tan^2theta) tan^2theta
             = tan^2theta + tan^4theta = RHS
      j) LHS = (1 - sin^2theta) sec^2theta
             = cos^2theta sec^2theta
             = 1 = RHS
      k) LHS = cos theta(1 + sin theta)/(1 - sin^2theta)
             = cos theta(1 + sin theta)/cos^2theta
             = (1 + sin theta)/cos theta = RHS
      l) LHS = (sec theta + tan theta)/(sec^2theta - tan^2theta)
             = sec theta + tan theta = RHS

M6. Prove (harder). Each answer shows one correct chain, starting from the side
    named.
    a) (1 + sin theta)/(1 - sin theta) = (sec theta + tan theta)^2
    b) cos theta/(1 - tan theta) + sin theta/(1 - cot theta) = sin theta + cos theta
    c) (cosec theta - sin theta)(sec theta - cos theta) = sin theta cos theta
    d) (1 + cot theta - cosec theta)(1 + tan theta + sec theta) = 2
    e) (sin theta - 2 sin^3theta)/(2 cos^3theta - cos theta) = tan theta
    f) (sin theta + cosec theta)^2 + (cos theta + sec theta)^2 = 7 + tan^2theta + cot^2theta
    g) (1 + sec theta)/sec theta = sin^2theta/(1 - cos theta)
    h) sin theta/(1 - cos theta) = cosec theta + cot theta
    i) 1/(cosec theta - cot theta) - 1/sin theta = 1/sin theta - 1/(cosec theta + cot theta)
    j) (cos theta - sin theta + 1)/(cos theta + sin theta - 1) = cosec theta + cot theta
    Answers:
      a) RHS = ((1 + sin theta)/cos theta)^2
             = (1 + sin theta)^2/cos^2theta
             = (1 + sin theta)^2/((1 - sin theta)(1 + sin theta))
             = (1 + sin theta)/(1 - sin theta) = LHS
      b) LHS = cos^2theta/(cos theta - sin theta) + sin^2theta/(sin theta - cos theta)
             = (cos^2theta - sin^2theta)/(cos theta - sin theta)
             = cos theta + sin theta = RHS
      c) LHS = ((1 - sin^2theta)/sin theta)((1 - cos^2theta)/cos theta)
             = (cos^2theta/sin theta)(sin^2theta/cos theta)
             = sin theta cos theta = RHS
      d) LHS = ((sin theta + cos theta - 1)/sin theta)((cos theta + sin theta + 1)/cos theta)
             = ((sin theta + cos theta)^2 - 1)/(sin theta cos theta)
             = (2 sin theta cos theta)/(sin theta cos theta)
             = 2 = RHS
      e) LHS = sin theta(1 - 2 sin^2theta)/(cos theta(2 cos^2theta - 1))
             = sin theta(1 - 2 sin^2theta)/(cos theta(2(1 - sin^2theta) - 1))
             = sin theta(1 - 2 sin^2theta)/(cos theta(1 - 2 sin^2theta))
             = tan theta = RHS
      f) LHS = sin^2theta + 2 + cosec^2theta + cos^2theta + 2 + sec^2theta
             = 5 + cosec^2theta + sec^2theta
             = 5 + (1 + cot^2theta) + (1 + tan^2theta)
             = 7 + tan^2theta + cot^2theta = RHS
      g) LHS = cos theta + 1
             = (1 - cos^2theta)/(1 - cos theta)
             = sin^2theta/(1 - cos theta) = RHS
      h) LHS = sin theta(1 + cos theta)/(1 - cos^2theta)
             = sin theta(1 + cos theta)/sin^2theta
             = (1 + cos theta)/sin theta
             = cosec theta + cot theta = RHS
      i) LHS = cosec theta + cot theta - cosec theta
             = cot theta
             = cosec theta - (cosec theta - cot theta)
             = 1/sin theta - 1/(cosec theta + cot theta) = RHS
      j) LHS = (cot theta - 1 + cosec theta)/(cot theta + 1 - cosec theta)
             = (cot theta + cosec theta - (cosec^2theta - cot^2theta))/(cot theta - cosec theta + 1)
             = (cosec theta + cot theta)(1 - cosec theta + cot theta)/(cot theta - cosec theta + 1)
             = cosec theta + cot theta = RHS

M7. Evaluate the left side and the right side at theta = 30 degrees, 45 degrees and 60 degrees
    (as "left, right"). Decide: identity (proved in this topic or Stage 8) or
    not an identity?
    a) sin theta + cos theta = 1
    b) 1 + tan^2theta = sec^2theta
    c) sin^2theta - cos^2theta = 1
    d) sec^2theta + cosec^2theta = sec^2theta cosec^2theta
    e) tan theta + cot theta = 2
    f) cos^2theta - sin^2theta = 1 - 2 sin^2theta
    g) (sin theta + cos theta)^2 = 1
    h) sin theta/cos theta = tan theta
    i) sec theta - cos theta = sin theta tan theta
    j) cosec theta - sin theta = cos theta cot theta
    k) sin 2theta = 2 sin theta
    l) tan^2theta - sin^2theta = tan^2theta sin^2theta
    Answers: a) 30 degrees: (sqrt3 + 1)/2, 1; 45 degrees: sqrt2, 1; 60 degrees: (sqrt3 + 1)/2, 1 -> not an
                identity
             b) 30 degrees: 4/3, 4/3; 45 degrees: 2, 2; 60 degrees: 4, 4 -> identity
             c) 30 degrees: -1/2, 1; 45 degrees: 0, 1; 60 degrees: 1/2, 1 -> not an identity
             d) 30 degrees: 16/3, 16/3; 45 degrees: 4, 4; 60 degrees: 16/3, 16/3 -> identity
             e) 30 degrees: 4sqrt3/3, 2; 45 degrees: 2, 2; 60 degrees: 4sqrt3/3, 2 -> not an identity
             f) 30 degrees: 1/2, 1/2; 45 degrees: 0, 0; 60 degrees: -1/2, -1/2 -> identity
             g) 30 degrees: (sqrt3 + 2)/2, 1; 45 degrees: 2, 1; 60 degrees: (sqrt3 + 2)/2, 1 -> not an
                identity
             h) 30 degrees: sqrt3/3, sqrt3/3; 45 degrees: 1, 1; 60 degrees: sqrt3, sqrt3 -> identity
             i) 30 degrees: sqrt3/6, sqrt3/6; 45 degrees: sqrt2/2, sqrt2/2; 60 degrees: 3/2, 3/2 -> identity
             j) 30 degrees: 3/2, 3/2; 45 degrees: sqrt2/2, sqrt2/2; 60 degrees: sqrt3/6, sqrt3/6 -> identity
             k) 30 degrees: sqrt3/2, 1; 45 degrees: 1, sqrt2; 60 degrees: sqrt3/2, sqrt3 -> not an identity
             l) 30 degrees: 1/12, 1/12; 45 degrees: 1/2, 1/2; 60 degrees: 9/4, 9/4 -> identity

M8. Find (i) the "other" expression (sec theta - tan theta or cosec theta - cot theta), (ii)
    sec theta, tan theta (or cosec theta, cot theta), (iii) sin theta (or cos theta). Answer in the form
    (i); (ii); (iii).
    a) sec theta + tan theta = 2     b) sec theta + tan theta = 3
    c) sec theta + tan theta = 5     d) sec theta + tan theta = 3/2
    e) sec theta + tan theta = 7     f) sec theta + tan theta = 4
    g) sec theta + tan theta = 5/3   h) sec theta + tan theta = 7/5
    i) cosec theta + cot theta = 3   j) cosec theta + cot theta = 2
    k) cosec theta + cot theta = 5
    Answers: a) 1/2; 5/4, 3/4; 3/5   b) 1/3; 5/3, 4/3; 4/5
             c) 1/5; 13/5, 12/5; 12/13   d) 2/3; 13/12, 5/12; 5/13
             e) 1/7; 25/7, 24/7; 24/25   f) 1/4; 17/8, 15/8; 15/17
             g) 3/5; 17/15, 8/15; 8/17   h) 5/7; 37/35, 12/35; 12/37
             i) 1/3; 5/3, 4/3; 4/5   j) 1/2; 5/4, 3/4; 3/5
             k) 1/5; 13/5, 12/5; 12/13

M9. Find sin theta cos theta, and then the square of the other combination:
    (sin theta - cos theta)^2 for the first six, (sin theta + cos theta)^2 for the rest. Answer:
    sin theta cos theta; square.
    a) sin theta + cos theta = sqrt2      b) sin theta + cos theta = 7/5
    c) sin theta + cos theta = 17/13   d) sin theta + cos theta = 4/3
    e) sin theta + cos theta = 1       f) sin theta + cos theta = 6/5
    g) sin theta - cos theta = 1/5     h) sin theta - cos theta = 7/13
    i) sin theta - cos theta = 0       j) tan theta + cot theta = 2
    k) tan theta + cot theta = 4       l) tan theta + cot theta = 25/12
    Answers: a) 1/2; 0   b) 12/25; 1/25   c) 60/169; 49/169   d) 7/18; 2/9
             e) 0; 1   f) 11/50; 14/25   g) 12/25; 49/25   h) 60/169; 289/169
             i) 1/2; 2   j) 1/2; 2   k) 1/4; 3/2   l) 12/25; 49/25

M10. Eliminate theta: find an equation connecting x and y.
     a) x = 3 cos theta, y = 3 sin theta
     b) x = 2 sec theta, y = 2 tan theta
     c) x = 4 cos theta, y = 3 sin theta
     d) x = sec theta + tan theta, y = sec theta - tan theta
     e) x = 5 cosec theta, y = 5 cot theta
     f) x = sin theta + cos theta, y = sin theta - cos theta
     g) x = tan theta, y = cot theta
     h) x = 3 tan theta, y = 4 sec theta
     i) x = cos theta, y = sec theta
     j) x = 2 sin theta, y = 5 cos theta
     k) x = cosec theta + cot theta, y = cosec theta - cot theta
     l) x = 1 + sin theta, y = cos theta
     Answers: a) x^2 + y^2 = 9   b) x^2 - y^2 = 4   c) x^2/16 + y^2/9 = 1   d) xy = 1
              e) x^2 - y^2 = 25   f) x^2 + y^2 = 2   g) xy = 1   h) y^2/16 - x^2/9 = 1
              i) xy = 1   j) x^2/4 + y^2/25 = 1   k) xy = 1   l) (x - 1)^2 + y^2 = 1

M11. Write in terms of sin theta and cos theta, then simplify to one or two terms.
     a) sec theta - cos theta
     b) cosec theta - sin theta
     c) tan theta + cot theta
     d) sin theta/(1 + cos theta) + (1 + cos theta)/sin theta
     e) cos theta/(1 - sin theta) + cos theta/(1 + sin theta)
     f) (sin^3theta + cos^3theta)/(sin theta + cos theta)
     g) (sin^3theta - cos^3theta)/(sin theta - cos theta)
     h) (1 - cos theta)(1 + cos theta)/sin theta
     i) sec^2theta cosec^2theta - sec^2theta
     j) 1/(1 + cos theta) + 1/(1 - cos theta)
     k) tan theta sin theta + cos theta
     l) cot theta cos theta + sin theta
     m) (1 - sin^2theta)/(1 - cos^2theta)
     n) sec^4theta - tan^4theta
     Answers: a) sin theta tan theta   b) cos theta cot theta   c) sec theta cosec theta   d) 2 cosec theta
              e) 2 sec theta   f) 1 - sin theta cos theta   g) 1 + sin theta cos theta   h) sin theta
              i) cosec^2theta   j) 2 cosec^2theta   k) sec theta   l) cosec theta   m) cot^2theta
              n) sec^2theta + tan^2theta

M12. True (T) or false (F) for all acute theta? (Spot the mistake: a false one fails
     at theta = 45 degrees or 30 degrees.)
     a) sin^2theta + cos^2theta = 1
     b) 1 + tan^2theta = cosec^2theta
     c) sec^2theta - 1 = tan^2theta
     d) cosec^2theta + cot^2theta = 1
     e) sin theta + cos theta = 1
     f) (sin theta + cos theta)^2 = 1 + 2 sin theta cos theta
     g) tan theta cot theta = 1
     h) sec theta = 1/sin theta
     i) (1 - sin theta)(1 + sin theta) = cos^2theta
     j) sec^2theta + tan^2theta = 1
     k) cosec^2theta - cot^2theta = 1
     l) tan^2theta = sec^2theta + 1
     m) cos^2theta - sin^2theta = 1
     n) sin theta cosec theta = 1
     o) 1 - cos^2theta = sin^2theta
     p) sqrt(sin^2theta + cos^2theta) = sin theta + cos theta
     Answers: a) T   b) F   c) T   d) F   e) F   f) T   g) T   h) F   i) T
              j) F   k) T   l) F   m) F   n) T   o) T   p) F

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep the three identities and their rearrangements on a card; in
  every proof first rewrite tan, cot, sec and cosec in sin and cos; practise the
  algebra (common denominators, difference of squares) with x and y before using
  sin and cos; after each proof check it at 30 degrees with the table. Harder: prove
  (1 + cot theta - cosec theta)(1 + tan theta + sec theta) = 2 in two different ways; show that
  sin^6theta + cos^6theta = 1 - 3 sin^2theta cos^2theta; if cos theta + sin theta = sqrt2 cos theta, prove cos theta -
  sin theta = sqrt2 sin theta; find the minimum value of sin^2theta + cosec^2theta
  (answer 2, at theta = 90 degrees) and of 4 sin^2theta + cosec^2theta; show that sec^2theta + cosec^2theta >=
  4.

================================================================================
TOPIC 7.35 - HEIGHTS AND DISTANCES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - The LINE OF SIGHT joins the observer's eye to the object. The ANGLE OF
    ELEVATION is the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when we
    look UP; the ANGLE OF DEPRESSION is the angle between the horizontal and the
    line of sight when we look DOWN. Both are measured from the HORIZONTAL,
    never from the vertical.
  - The angle of depression of B seen from A equals the angle of elevation of A
    seen from B (alternate angles between parallel horizontal lines).
  - Method: (1) draw a clear diagram with the horizontal, the vertical object
    and the right angle; (2) mark the angle and the known length; (3) choose the
    ratio linking the known side and the wanted side - usually tan theta =
    height/horizontal distance (use sin or cos when the sloping length is
    involved); (4) solve and give the exact answer, then a decimal.
  - Standard values: tan 30 degrees = 1/sqrt3, tan 45 degrees = 1, tan 60 degrees = sqrt3; sin 30 degrees = 1/2,
    sin 60 degrees = sqrt3/2. Use sqrt3 ~ 1.732 and sqrt2 ~ 1.414 for decimals.
  - TWO OBSERVATION POINTS on the same side at distance d apart with angles alpha
    (far) and beta (near): h cot alpha - h cot beta = d, so h = d/(cot alpha - cot beta). On
    OPPOSITE sides: h cot alpha + h cot beta = d.
  - OBSERVER ABOVE THE GROUND (building, cliff, lighthouse): draw the horizontal
    through the eye; add the observer's height at the end. Flagstaff on a
    building: find the horizontal distance from the building first, then the
    full height, then subtract.
  - Moving objects: distance travelled = difference of the two horizontal
    distances; speed = distance / time.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Explain angle of elevation and angle of depression with a picture. Riya
    stands on a balcony and sees her friend Sam on the ground at an angle of
    depression of 30 degrees. At what angle of elevation does Sam see Riya?
    Answer: 30 degrees. The angle of depression from Riya equals the angle of elevation
    from Sam.
    Teacher explains:
       R ------------------------ horizontal through Riya's eye
       |`-.   30 degrees = angle of depression
       |   `-.
       |      `-.     line of sight
       |         `-.
       |            `-.   30 degrees = angle of elevation
       +---------------`- S    ground (horizontal)
    Both angles are measured from a HORIZONTAL line: elevation when you look up
    from the lower point, depression when you look down from the higher point.
    The two horizontal lines are parallel and the line of sight cuts both, so
    the angles are ALTERNATE ANGLES and are equal. Common mistakes: measuring
    the depression from the vertical wall (that gives 60 degrees, the complement), and
    putting the depression angle at the bottom of the diagram. Now you try: from
    the top of a cliff the angle of depression of a boat is 45 degrees. What is the
    angle of elevation of the cliff top from the boat? (45 degrees)

D2. From a point on the ground 30 m from the foot of a tower, the angle of
    elevation of the top is 60 degrees. Find the height of the tower.
    Answer: h = 30sqrt3 ~ 51.96 m.
    Teacher explains:
         T
         |`-.
         |   `-.
       h |      `-.
         |_        `-.  60 degrees
         B----- 30 ----- P
    We know the side ADJACENT to 60 degrees (30 m) and want the OPPOSITE side (h), so
    use tan:
       tan 60 degrees = h/30
       h = 30 x tan 60 degrees = 30sqrt3 ~ 30 x 1.732 = 51.96 m
    Always write the exact answer first (30sqrt3 m), then the decimal. Estimate:
    tan 60 degrees is about 1.7, so the tower is a little less than twice the distance.
    Common mistake: using sin 60 degrees = h/30 - but 30 m is not the hypotenuse. Now
    you try: distance 50 m, elevation 30 degrees. (50/sqrt3 = 50sqrt3/3 ~ 28.87 m)

D3. A kite is flying on a string 80 m long. The string is straight and makes 60 degrees
    with the ground. How high is the kite? How far along the ground is it from
    the person?
    Answer: Height 40sqrt3 ~ 69.28 m; horizontal distance 40 m.
    Teacher explains: The string is the HYPOTENUSE, so use sin for the height
    and cos for the horizontal distance:
       sin 60 degrees = h/80   ->  h = 80 x sqrt3/2 = 40sqrt3 ~ 69.28 m
       cos 60 degrees = d/80   ->  d = 80 x 1/2 = 40 m
    Check with Pythagoras: 40^2 + (40sqrt3)^2 = 1600 + 4800 = 6400 = 80^2. Real kites
    fly higher when the string is steeper: at 30 degrees the same string gives only
    80 x 1/2 = 40 m. Now you try: a 12 m ladder reaches a window when it makes
    60 degrees with the ground. How high is the window? (6sqrt3 ~ 10.39 m)

D4. From the top of a lighthouse 75 m above the sea, the angle of depression of
    a boat is 30 degrees. How far is the boat from the foot of the lighthouse?
    Answer: 75sqrt3 ~ 129.90 m.
    Teacher explains:
       L ------------------ horizontal
       |`-.  30 degrees
       |    `-.
    75 |       `-.
       |          `-.
       |_         30 degrees `-.
       F-------- d ------- B
    The angle of depression at L equals the angle of elevation at B
    (alternate angles), so the triangle has 30 degrees at B. Opposite = 75, adjacent =
    d:
       tan 30 degrees = 75/d
       d = 75/tan 30 degrees = 75sqrt3 ~ 75 x 1.732 = 129.9 m
    Dividing by tan 30 degrees = 1/sqrt3 is the same as multiplying by sqrt3. Common mistake:
    putting the 30 degrees at the top between the vertical and the line of sight. Now
    you try: height 50 m, depression 45 degrees. (50 m)

D5. The shadow of a tower is 40 m longer when the sun's altitude is 30 degrees than
    when it is 60 degrees. Find the height of the tower.
    Answer: h = 20sqrt3 ~ 34.64 m.
    Teacher explains:
         T
         |\ `-.
       h | \    `-.
         |  \      `-.
         |_  \ 60 degrees     `-. 30 degrees
         B----C------------D
           x        40
    Let x be the shorter shadow. From the two right triangles:
       tan 60 degrees = h/x          ->  x = h/sqrt3
       tan 30 degrees = h/(x + 40)   ->  x + 40 = hsqrt3
       subtract: 40 = hsqrt3 - h/sqrt3 = 2h/sqrt3
       h = 20sqrt3 ~ 34.64 m,   x = 20 m
    The sun's altitude is its angle of elevation. The lower the sun, the longer
    the shadow. Eliminating x is the key step: write BOTH horizontal distances
    in terms of h. Now you try: the shadow of a pole is sqrt3 times its height.
    Find the sun's altitude. (tan theta = 1/sqrt3, theta = 30 degrees)

D6. From a point P on level ground, the angle of elevation of the top of a tower
    is 30 degrees. On walking 20 m towards the tower, it becomes 60 degrees. Find the height
    of the tower and the distance of the second point from the tower.
    Answer: h = 10sqrt3 ~ 17.32 m; the second point is 10 m from the tower.
    Teacher explains: Let the second point Q be x m from the foot B. Then:
       from Q: h = x tan 60 degrees = xsqrt3
       from P: h = (x + 20) tan 30 degrees = (x + 20)/sqrt3
       xsqrt3 = (x + 20)/sqrt3   ->  3x = x + 20  ->  x = 10
       h = 10sqrt3 ~ 17.32 m
    Two unknowns (h and x) need two equations - one from each viewpoint. Notice
    triangle PQT is isosceles: its angle at P is 30 degrees and the exterior angle at Q
    is 60 degrees, so angle PTQ = 30 degrees and QT = PQ = 20 m; then h = 20 sin 60 degrees = 10sqrt3. Common
    mistake: using 20 as the distance from P to the tower. Now you try: angles
    45 degrees and 60 degrees, walk 30 m. (h = 15(3 + sqrt3) ~ 70.98 m)

D7. A flagstaff stands on top of a building 20 m high. From a point on the
    ground, the angles of elevation of the bottom and the top of the flagstaff
    are 45 degrees and 60 degrees. Find the length of the flagstaff.
    Answer: 20(sqrt3 - 1) ~ 14.64 m.
    Teacher explains:
            F  (top of flagstaff)
            |
            T  (top of building)
            |
         20 |       angles at P: 45 degrees to T, 60 degrees to F
            |_
            B-------- d -------- P
    First find the distance d from the 45 degrees triangle BTP: tan 45 degrees = 20/d, so
    d = 20 m. Then the full height BF from the 60 degrees triangle:
       tan 60 degrees = BF/20   ->  BF = 20sqrt3
       flagstaff = BF - BT = 20sqrt3 - 20 = 20(sqrt3 - 1)
                 ~ 20 x 0.732 = 14.64 m
    Two triangles share the SAME horizontal distance d - that is the link.
    Common mistake: using tan(60 degrees - 45 degrees) for the flagstaff alone; angles cannot
    be subtracted like that. Now you try: building 10 m, angles 30 degrees and 60 degrees.
    (d = 10sqrt3, flagstaff = 30 - 10 = 20 m)

D8. From the top of a 7 m high building, the angle of elevation of the top of a
    cable tower is 60 degrees and the angle of depression of its foot is 45 degrees. Find the
    height of the tower.
    Answer: 7(1 + sqrt3) ~ 19.12 m.
    Teacher explains:
                            C
                            |
       A ------ d --------- E       AE horizontal
       |  `-. 45 degrees           |       angle CAE = 60 degrees, angle EAD = 45 degrees
     7 |      `-.           | 7
       |_         `-.       |
       B-------- d -------- D
    Draw the horizontal AE through the observer. Depression 45 degrees to the foot D:
    tan 45 degrees = 7/d, so d = 7 m. Elevation 60 degrees to the top C: CE = d tan 60 degrees = 7sqrt3.
    Tower height = CE + ED = 7sqrt3 + 7 = 7(sqrt3 + 1) ~ 7 x 2.732 ~ 19.12 m. The part
    of the tower BELOW the observer's eye is equal to the building's height. Now
    you try: building 10 m, elevation 30 degrees, depression 45 degrees. (d = 10,
    tower = 10 + 10/sqrt3 ~ 15.77 m)

D9. A man on the top of a lighthouse 100 m high sees a ship sailing straight
    towards it. The angle of depression of the ship changes from 30 degrees to 45 degrees. How
    far did the ship travel? If this took 2 minutes, find its speed.
    Answer: 100(sqrt3 - 1) ~ 73.20 m; speed ~ 36.6 m per minute.
    Teacher explains:
       first distance  = 100/tan 30 degrees = 100sqrt3
       second distance = 100/tan 45 degrees = 100
       travelled = 100sqrt3 - 100 = 100(sqrt3 - 1) ~ 73.20 m
       speed ~ 73.2 / 2 = 36.6 m per minute
    As the ship comes closer, the angle of depression INCREASES. Work out each
    horizontal distance separately and subtract. Using sqrt3 ~ 1.732:
    100 x 0.732 = 73.2 m. Common mistake: thinking the distance is proportional
    to the angle (it is not; tan is not linear). Now you try: cliff 60 m,
    depression 45 degrees then 60 degrees. (60 - 20sqrt3 ~ 25.36 m)

D10. An aeroplane flies horizontally at a height of 1500sqrt3 m. From a point on
     the ground the angle of elevation changes from 60 degrees to 30 degrees in 15 seconds.
     Find its speed in km/h.
     Answer: 3000 m in 15 s = 200 m/s = 720 km/h.
     Teacher explains:
        A1 ----------------------- A2    plane, height 1500sqrt3 m
        |                           |
        B1 ------------------------ B2   ground points below A1, A2
        observer P is on the line B1B2, before B1:
        PB1 = x1 (elevation 60 degrees),  PB2 = x2 (elevation 30 degrees)
        x1 = 1500sqrt3/tan 60 degrees = 1500sqrt3/sqrt3 = 1500 m
        x2 = 1500sqrt3/tan 30 degrees = 1500sqrt3 x sqrt3 = 4500 m
        distance flown = 4500 - 1500 = 3000 m
        speed = 3000 / 15 = 200 m/s;  200 x 3.6 = 720 km/h
     The height is chosen so the surds cancel. To change m/s to km/h multiply by
     3.6 (3600 seconds per hour, 1000 m per km). Common mistake: giving the
     answer in m/s when km/h is asked. Now you try: height 1000 m, elevation
     changes from 45 degrees to 30 degrees in 10 s. (1000(sqrt3 - 1) ~ 732 m,
     73.2 m/s ~ 263.52 km/h)

D11. Two poles of equal height stand on opposite sides of a road 80 m wide. From
     a point between them on the road, the angles of elevation of their tops are
     60 degrees and 30 degrees. Find the height of the poles and the position of the point.
     Answer: Height 20sqrt3 ~ 34.64 m; the point is 20 m from the first pole and
     60 m from the second.
     Teacher explains:
        A                              C
        |`-.                        .-'|
        |   `-.                  .-'   |
      h |      `-.  60 degrees  30 degrees .-'       | h
        |_________`-.___.-'____________|
        B      x      P       80 - x   D
        h = x tan 60 degrees = xsqrt3
        h = (80 - x) tan 30 degrees = (80 - x)/sqrt3
        3x = 80 - x  ->  x = 20,  h = 20sqrt3 ~ 34.64 m
     On OPPOSITE sides the two horizontal distances ADD to the width of the
     road; on the same side they SUBTRACT. The steeper angle (60 degrees) belongs to
     the nearer pole. Now you try: road 100 m, both angles 45 degrees. (point in the
     middle, h = 50 m)

D12. From a point 60 m above a still lake, the angle of elevation of a cloud is
     30 degrees and the angle of depression of its reflection in the lake is 60 degrees. Find
     the height of the cloud above the lake.
     Answer: 120 m.
     Teacher explains: The reflection is as far BELOW the water as the cloud is
     ABOVE it. Let the cloud be H m above the lake and x m away horizontally
     from the observer:
        cloud:      tan 30 degrees = (H - 60)/x   ->  x = sqrt3(H - 60)
        reflection: tan 60 degrees = (H + 60)/x   ->  x = (H + 60)/sqrt3
        sqrt3(H - 60) = (H + 60)/sqrt3
        3H - 180 = H + 60  ->  2H = 240  ->  H = 120 m
     The observer is 60 m up, so the cloud is H - 60 above eye level and the
     reflection is H + 60 below eye level. Setting the two expressions for x
     equal eliminates it. Now you try: observer 20 m above the lake, angles 30 degrees
     and 60 degrees. (H = 40 m)

PART B - MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. A point on level ground is d m from the foot of a vertical tower; the angle
    of elevation of the top is theta. Find the height (exact, then with sqrt3 ~ 1.732;
    metres).
    a) d = 30 m, theta = 60 degrees    b) d = 50 m, theta = 30 degrees    c) d = 20 m, theta = 45 degrees
    d) d = 100 m, theta = 60 degrees   e) d = 15 m, theta = 30 degrees    f) d = 40 m, theta = 45 degrees
    g) d = 12 m, theta = 60 degrees    h) d = 9 m, theta = 30 degrees     i) d = 25 m, theta = 60 degrees
    j) d = 60 m, theta = 30 degrees    k) d = 7 m, theta = 45 degrees     l) d = 10 m, theta = 60 degrees
    m) d = 18 m, theta = 30 degrees    n) d = 45 m, theta = 60 degrees    o) d = 33 m, theta = 45 degrees

    Answers: a) 30sqrt3 ~ 51.96   b) 50sqrt3/3 ~ 28.87   c) 20   d) 100sqrt3 ~ 173.20
