TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: insist on FACTORISING first, every time; draw the asymptotes as
  dashed lines before plotting any points; for the sign chart put the factors in
  rows and the intervals in columns; test one number in every interval; for
  inequalities say aloud 'one side, one fraction, compare with zero'. Harder:
  find the hole and the oblique asymptote of y = (x^3 + 1)/(x^2 - 1) (hole
  (-1, -3/2), asymptote y = x, since y = x + 1/(x - 1)); prove that
  y = (ax + b)/(cx + d) with c != 0 is its own inverse exactly when a + d = 0;
  show that (x^2 - 3x + 4)/(x^2 + 3x + 4) always lies between 1/7 and 7; sketch
  y = x + 1/x and prove |x + 1/x| >= 2.

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.5 - MATHEMATICAL LOGIC: PROPOSITIONS, CONNECTIVES, QUANTIFIERS, TRUTH
            TABLES

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A STATEMENT (proposition) is a sentence that is either true or false, not
    both. Questions, commands, exclamations, opinions and open sentences such as
    x + 3 = 7 (true for some x, false for others) are not statements. A
    statement may be true even if nobody yet knows its truth value (Goldbach's
    conjecture).
    are false); conditional p -> q (if p then q: FALSE ONLY when p is true and q
    the same truth value).
  - TRUTH TABLES list every combination of truth values: 2^n rows for n simple
    statements. Standard row order for p, q: TT, TF, FT, FF. Precedence: ~
    they have identical truth-table columns.
  - For p -> q: CONVERSE q -> p, INVERSE ~p -> ~q, CONTRAPOSITIVE ~q -> ~p. Only the
    contrapositive is equivalent to the original; the converse and the inverse
    are equivalent to each other. 'p only if q' means p -> q; 'p is sufficient
    for q' means p -> q; 'q is necessary for p' means p -> q.
  - An ARGUMENT is VALID when the conclusion is true in every row where all the

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Which of these are statements? Give the truth value of each statement. (a)
    New Delhi is the capital of India. (b) x + 3 = 7. (c) Please close the door.
    (d) Every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes. (e) This
    sentence is false. (f) sqrt2 is a rational number. (g) Maths is the most
    beautiful subject. (h) 2^6 - 1 is prime.
    Answer: Statements: (a) true, (d) (truth value unknown so far, but it is
    either true or false), (f) false, (h) false (63 = 7 x 9). Not statements:
    (b), (c), (e), (g).
    Teacher explains: Test each sentence with the question 'Is it definitely
    either true or false?'
       (b) open sentence: true for x = 4, false otherwise
       (c) a command: neither true nor false
       (e) a paradox: if it is true it is false, and vice versa
       (g) an opinion: depends on the person
    (d) is Goldbach's conjecture (1742): nobody has proved or disproved it, but
    it IS a statement, because it is certainly either true or false. (h)
    2^6 - 1 = 63 = 7 x 9 is not prime, so (h) is a FALSE statement: a false
    sentence is still a statement. Note: (b) becomes a statement if we add a
    quantifier: 'there is a real x with x + 3 = 7' (true). Common mistake:
    thinking only true sentences are statements. Now you try: is 'x^2 >= 0 for
    every real x' a statement? Is 'Is 7 prime?'? (yes, true; no, a question)

D2. Write the negation of each statement in clear English: (a) 7 is a prime
    number. (b) All students of the class passed. (c) Some rivers of India flow
    east. (d) There is no rational number x with x^2 = 2. (e) Rahul is tall and
    Rahul is strong.
    Answer: (a) 7 is not a prime number. (b) At least one student of the class
    did not pass. (c) No river of India flows east. (d) There is a rational
    number x with x^2 = 2. (e) Rahul is not tall or Rahul is not strong.
    Teacher explains: The negation ~p must be true exactly when p is false. It
    is NOT the 'opposite extreme':
       p: All students passed.
       wrong ~p: All students failed.      (too strong)
       right ~p: Some student did not pass (at least one failed).
    If one student fails and the rest pass, both p and 'all failed' are false,
    so 'all failed' cannot be the negation. Similarly the negation of 'some
    rivers flow east' is 'no river flows east'. For (e), De Morgan: not (tall
    and strong) = not tall OR not strong. Truth values: (a) is true, so its
    negation is false; (d) is true (sqrt2 is irrational), so its negation is false.
    Common mistake: negating 'and' by 'and'. Now you try: negate 'Every square
    is a rectangle' and 'Ravi or Sita will come'. (Some square is not a
    rectangle; Ravi will not come and Sita will not come)

D3. Let p: 'It is raining' and q: 'The school is closed'. Write in words ~p,
    raining but the school is open' and 'The school is closed only if it is
    raining'.
    is raining, then the school is closed. q -> p: If the school is closed, then
    q -> p.
    Teacher explains: 'but' is logically the same as 'and' (it only adds a sense
    means p -> q: 'the school is closed only if it is raining' says: whenever the
    school is closed, it is raining: q -> p. Ways of saying p -> q:
       if p then q;  p implies q;  p only if q;  q if p;
       p is sufficient for q;  q is necessary for p;  q whenever p
    Common mistake: translating 'q if p' as q -> p. Now you try: write 'You can
    vote only if you are 18 or older' in symbols, with v: you can vote, e: you
    are 18 or older. (v -> e)

D4. Write the truth table of p -> q. Explain with a promise why p -> q is true
    when p is false.
    Answer: p -> q is false only in the row p = T, q = F:
       p    q    p -> q
       T    T    T
       T    F    F
       F    T    T
       F    F    T
    Teacher explains: Think of a promise by a parent: 'If you score 90% (p), I
    will buy you a cycle (q).' The promise is BROKEN only in one case: you score
    90% and do not get the cycle (p true, q false). If you do not score 90% (p
    false), the promise is not broken whatever happens, so p -> q counts as TRUE
    in the last two rows. Such a conditional is called 'vacuously true'. So 'If
    2 + 2 = 5 then the Moon is a cheese' is TRUE. Also p -> q does NOT claim that
    p causes q; it only rules out 'p true and q false'. Common mistake: thinking
    p -> q is false when p is false. Now you try: truth values of 'If 3 is even,
    then 4 is odd' and 'If 3 is odd, then 4 is odd'. (T, since 3 is not even; F)

    Answer: The columns are identical in both cases (TFFT and FTTT).
    Teacher explains: Build the table column by column, from the inside out:
       T    T    T      T      T            T
       T    F    F      T      F            F
       F    T    T      F      F            F
       F    F    T      T      T            T
    The last two columns agree in every row, so the statements are equivalent:
    'p if and only if q' means 'p -> q AND q -> p'. For De Morgan:
       T    T    T      F         F    F    F
       T    F    F      T         F    T    T
       F    T    F      T         T    F    T
       F    F    F      T         T    T    T
    gives T on the left and F on the right). Now you try: check with a table

D6. For the statement 'If a number is divisible by 6, then it is divisible by
    3', write the converse, the inverse and the contrapositive, and give the
    truth value of each.
    Answer: Original: true. Converse: 'If a number is divisible by 3, then it is
    divisible by 6' - false (9). Inverse: 'If a number is not divisible by 6,
    then it is not divisible by 3' - false (9). Contrapositive: 'If a number is
    not divisible by 3, then it is not divisible by 6' - true.
    Teacher explains: With p: divisible by 6 and q: divisible by 3:
       original        p -> q        true (6k = 3(2k))
       converse        q -> p        false: 9 is divisible by 3, not by 6
       inverse        ~p -> ~q       false: 9 again
       contrapositive ~q -> ~p       true
    The contrapositive ALWAYS has the same truth value as the original
    contrapositives of each other). This is why a proof 'by contrapositive' is
    legitimate. A single number such as 9 is a counterexample that makes the
    converse false. Common mistake: believing that a true statement has a true
    converse ('all squares are rectangles' does not give 'all rectangles are
    squares'). Now you try: contrapositive of 'If x = 2 then x^2 = 4', and is the
    converse true? (If x^2 != 4 then x != 2; converse false, x = -2)

    Answer: The last column is all T, so it is a tautology (modus ponens).
    Teacher explains: Build the table column by column:
       T    T    T      T            T
       T    F    F      F            T
       F    T    T      F            T
       F    F    T      F            T
    In words: 'if p is true, and p implies q, then q is true' - the basic rule
    of every mathematical proof. A tautology is true because of its FORM alone,
    when p is F it is T, so it is neither: a contingency (it is equivalent to
    p -> q). Common mistake: calling a statement a tautology because it is true
    in the rows you happened to check; ALL rows must be T. Now you try: is
    chain rule, hypothetical syllogism)

    Teacher explains: p -> q is false only when p is T and q is F, and so is
    Negating with De Morgan:
    So the negation of a conditional is NOT another conditional: 'It is not true
    that if it rains the match is cancelled' means 'It rains and the match is
    not cancelled'. Now simplify:

    Answer: (a) T (b) F (c) F (d) T (e) F (f) T.
       (a) squares of reals are never negative              T
       (b) x = -2 is not a natural number                   F
       (c) counterexample x = 1/2: 1/4 > 1/2 is false       F
       (d) for each x choose y = -x                         T
       (e) one y would have to work for EVERY x:
           x = 0 forces y = 0, then x = 1 gives 1 != 0       F
       (f) x = sqrt2                                           T
    (d) and (e) use the same words in a different ORDER. In (d) y may depend on
    x (a different y for each x); in (e) a single y must serve all x. Everyday

     true. (d) There are real x and y with x < y and x^2 >= y^2 - negation true
     (x = -3, y = 1).
     negate the inside:

D11. Decide whether each argument is valid: (a) If it rains, the match is
     cancelled. It rains. So the match is cancelled. (b) If it rains, the match
     is cancelled. The match is cancelled. So it rained. (c) If Anu studies, she
     passes. Anu did not pass. So she did not study. (d) If it rains, the match
     is cancelled. It did not rain. So the match was not cancelled.
     Answer: (a) valid (modus ponens); (b) invalid (affirming the consequent);
     (c) valid (modus tollens); (d) invalid (denying the antecedent).
     Teacher explains: Let p: it rains, q: the match is cancelled. An argument
     is valid when NO row makes all premises true and the conclusion false.
        p    q    p -> q
        T    T    T
        T    F    F
        F    T    T
        F    F    T
        (a) premises p -> q, p:  only row 1; there q = T        valid
        (b) premises p -> q, q:  rows 1 and 3; row 3 has p = F  invalid
        (c) premises p -> q, ~q: only row 4; there ~p = T       valid
        (d) premises p -> q, ~p: rows 3 and 4; row 3 has q = T  invalid
     Row 3 is the trouble-maker in (b) and (d): the match may be cancelled for
     another reason (bad light) without rain. Validity is about FORM: a valid
     argument with a false premise may give a false conclusion, but a valid
     argument with true premises always gives a true conclusion. Common mistake:
     judging an argument by whether its conclusion happens to be true. Now you
     try: 'All mangoes are fruits; this is a fruit; so it is a mango.' (invalid,
     affirming the consequent)

     an island every person is a knight (always tells the truth) or a knave
     (always lies). A says 'B is a knave.' B says 'A and I are of the same
     type.' What are A and B?
     Answer: (a) Proof below. (b) A is a knight and B is a knave.
     Teacher explains: (a) The contrapositive of 'n^2 even -> n even' is 'n
     odd -> n^2 odd', which is easy: n = 2k + 1 gives
     n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1, odd. Since a statement and its
     contrapositive are equivalent, the original is proved. (A direct proof
     would need to 'take a square root', which is awkward.) (b) Let a: 'A is a
     knight', b: 'B is a knight'. A knight's statement is true and a knave's is
     false, so each person's statement is EQUIVALENT to his being a knight:
        T  T   F      F        T         T
        T  F   T      T        F         T
        F  T   F      T        F         F
        F  F   T      F        T         F
     Only row 2 makes both equivalences hold: A is a knight, B a knave. Check: A
     truthfully says B is a knave; B (a knave) falsely claims they are the same
     type. Common mistake: in (a) proving the CONVERSE (n even -> n^2 even)
     instead. Now you try: C says 'At least one of us is a knave' about C and D.
     What are C and D? (C knight, D knave)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always write the four-row (or eight-row) table in the standard
  order and fill it column by column; for p -> q remember the one 'broken
  promise' row; to negate, first say 'it is not true that ...' and then simplify
  to prove. Harder: show that every truth function of p and q can be written
  (2^(2^n): 16 for n = 2); on the knights-and-knaves island, A says 'I am a knave
  of a limit and its negation.

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.6 - PRINCIPLE OF MATHEMATICAL INDUCTION
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - PRINCIPLE OF MATHEMATICAL INDUCTION (PMI): let P(n) be a statement about the
    natural number n. If (1) BASE CASE: P(1) is true, and (2) INDUCTIVE STEP:
    natural number n. Picture an endless row of dominoes: the first falls, and
    each one knocks over the next.
  - The assumption 'P(k) is true' is the INDUCTIVE HYPOTHESIS. In the step you
    must USE it: write P(k + 1), find P(k) inside it, replace that part using
    the hypothesis, and simplify to the required form.
  - BOTH parts are essential. Without the base case: 'n^2 + n is odd' has a valid
    inductive step but is false for every n. Without a proof of the step:
    n^2 + n + 41 is prime for n = 1, 2, ..., 39 but not for n = 40. Checking many
    cases is NOT a proof.
  - SUMS: 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2; 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + n^2 = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6;
    1^3 + 2^3 + ... + n^3 = [n(n + 1)/2]^2; 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n - 1) = n^2;
    a + ar + ... + ar^n^-^1 = a(r^n - 1)/(r - 1), r != 1. To prove a sum formula, ADD
    the next term (the (k + 1)th term) to both sides of P(k).
  - DIVISIBILITY: to show d divides f(n), write f(k) = dm (m an integer), then
    split f(k + 1) into a multiple of f(k) plus something visibly divisible by
  - INEQUALITIES: the base case may be n = n_0 > 1 (n! > 2^n holds from n = 4). In
    the step, use the hypothesis and then a simple estimate:
  - STRONG INDUCTION: assume P(1), P(2), ..., P(k) are all true and prove
    P(k + 1). Useful when P(k + 1) depends on earlier cases, not just the
    previous one (prime factorisation, Fibonacci numbers, coin problems).
    Several base cases may be needed.
  - Common errors: proving P(k) instead of P(k + 1); writing P(k + 1) by adding
    1 to the whole formula instead of replacing n by k + 1; assuming what is to
    be proved; forgetting the last term of the sum; an inductive step that
    silently fails for the smallest k (the 'all horses have the same colour'
    fallacy).

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Explain the principle of mathematical induction and use it to prove that
    1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2 for every natural number n.
    Answer: Base case and inductive step both hold (below), so the formula is
    Teacher explains: Let P(n): 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2.
       Base case  n = 1:   LHS = 1,   RHS = 1 x 2/2 = 1.   P(1) true.
       Inductive hypothesis: assume P(k): 1 + 2 + ... + k = k(k + 1)/2.
       To prove P(k + 1):  1 + 2 + ... + k + (k + 1) = (k + 1)(k + 2)/2.
       LHS = [1 + 2 + ... + k] + (k + 1)
           = k(k + 1)/2 + (k + 1)          (by the hypothesis)
           = (k + 1)(k/2 + 1)
           = (k + 1)(k + 2)/2 = RHS
    true; the step with k = 1 gives P(2); with k = 2 it gives P(3); and so on -
    like dominoes, every n is reached. Write P(k + 1) by REPLACING n by k + 1
    everywhere, and write down clearly what you are aiming for before starting.
    Common mistake: 'proving' P(k + 1) by substituting numbers. Now you try:
    prove 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n - 1) = n^2. (step: k^2 + (2k + 1) = (k + 1)^2)

D2. Prove by induction that 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + n^2 = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6. Then use it
    to find 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + 20^2 and 11^2 + 12^2 + ... + 20^2.
    Answer: Proof below; 2,870 and 2,485.
    assume 1^2 + ... + k^2 = k(k + 1)(2k + 1)/6. Aim: sum to (k + 1)^2 equals
    (k + 1)(k + 2)(2k + 3)/6.
       LHS = k(k + 1)(2k + 1)/6 + (k + 1)^2
           = (k + 1)[k(2k + 1) + 6(k + 1)]/6       (take out (k + 1)/6)
           = (k + 1)(2k^2 + 7k + 6)/6
           = (k + 1)(k + 2)(2k + 3)/6 = RHS
    The key move is to take out the COMMON FACTOR (k + 1) instead of multiplying
    everything out; then factorise 2k^2 + 7k + 6 = (k + 2)(2k + 3), which you can
    check by expanding. Numbers: n = 20 gives 20 x 21 x 41/6 = 2,870. For 11^2 to
    20^2, subtract the first ten: 2,870 - 10 x 11 x 21/6 = 2,870 - 385 = 2,485.
    Common mistake: adding k^2 instead of (k + 1)^2 as the new term. Now you try:
    1^2 + 2^2 + ... + 30^2. (30 x 31 x 61/6 = 9,455)

D3. Prove that 1^3 + 2^3 + ... + n^3 = [n(n + 1)/2]^2, and deduce that the sum of
    the first n cubes is the square of the sum of the first n numbers.
    Answer: Proof below. Since 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2, the sum of cubes is
    (1 + 2 + ... + n)^2. Example: 1^3 + 2^3 + 3^3 + 4^3 = 100 = 10^2.
    formula for k.
       1^3 + ... + k^3 + (k + 1)^3 = k^2(k + 1)^2/4 + (k + 1)^3
                                = (k + 1)^2[k^2 + 4(k + 1)]/4
                                = (k + 1)^2(k + 2)^2/4
    Again take out the common factor (k + 1)^2/4 first; then
    k^2 + 4k + 4 = (k + 2)^2 is a perfect square. Check n = 3:
    Aryabhata (499 CE), who stated the formulas for sum k^2 and sum k^3. Common mistake:
    expanding (k + 1)^3 and k^2(k + 1)^2 fully and getting lost in a quartic. Now
    you try: find 1^3 + 2^3 + ... + 10^3. (55^2 = 3,025)

D10. Spot the mistake. (a) 'P(n): n^2 + n is odd. If k^2 + k is odd, then
     (k + 1)^2 + (k + 1) = (k^2 + k) + 2(k + 1) is odd + even = odd. So P(n) is
     true for all n.' (b) 'n^2 + n + 41 is prime for n = 1, 2, ..., 10, so it is
     prime for all n.' (c) 'All horses have the same colour: one horse is one
     colour; if any k horses have one colour, then for k + 1 horses, the first k
     have one colour and the last k have one colour, and they overlap, so all
     k + 1 have one colour.'
     Answer: (a) The base case is false (1 + 1 = 2 is even); in fact n^2 + n is
     always even. (b) No inductive step: n = 40 gives 1681 = 41^2. (c) The step
     fails from k = 1 to k = 2: the two groups of 1 horse do not overlap.
     Teacher explains: Induction needs BOTH parts, and the step must work for
     EVERY k from the base case upward.
        (a) step valid, base false         conclusion false for all n
        (b) many base cases, no step       fails at n = 40 (and n = 41)
        (c) base true, step invalid at k = 1
     In (b), n^2 + n + 41 is prime for n = 0, 1, ..., 39 (Euler's polynomial),
     yet 40^2 + 40 + 41 = 1600 + 81 = 1681 = 41 x 41. In (c) the argument 'the
     first k and the last k overlap' needs k + 1 >= 3; with 2 horses the first
     group is {horse 1} and the last is {horse 2}, and nothing links them.
     Common mistake: believing a pattern because it holds for the first ten
     k = k + 1 then k + 1 = k + 2'? (the base case 1 = 2 is false)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: use the same four-line layout every time: 'Let P(n): ...', 'Base
  case', 'Assume P(k)', 'To prove P(k + 1)'; write the target P(k + 1) in full
  BEFORE starting the algebra; in sums, underline the part that equals the
  hypothesis; test every statement numerically for n = 1, 2, 3 first. Harder:
  prove that every n >= 1 can be written as a sum of distinct powers of 2 (binary
  by induction on k (Cauchy's forward-backward method); prove that n lines in
  general position divide the plane into (n^2 + n + 2)/2 regions (7 for n = 3);

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.7 - RADIAN MEASURE; TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS OF ANY ANGLE; UNIT CIRCLE
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - ONE RADIAN is the angle at the centre of a circle subtended by an arc equal
    in length to the radius. A full turn is 2pi radians, so pi rad = 180 degrees, 1
    Degrees -> radians: multiply by pi/180; radians -> degrees: multiply by 180/pi.
    From now on an angle with no unit is in RADIANS.
  - ARC LENGTH s = rtheta and SECTOR AREA A = 1/2r^2theta = 1/2rs, with theta in radians (these
    simple formulas are the reason radians are used). The perimeter of a sector
    is 2r + rtheta.
  - UNIT CIRCLE definition: rotate the point (1, 0) anticlockwise through theta
    (clockwise if theta < 0) to P(theta) on x^2 + y^2 = 1. Then cos theta = x-coordinate,
    sin theta = y-coordinate, tan theta = y/x (x != 0), and cosec theta = 1/y, sec theta = 1/x,
    cot theta = x/y. For a point (x, y) at distance r from O on the terminal side:
    sin theta = y/r, cos theta = x/r, tan theta = y/x.
  - QUADRANTAL angles: P(0) = (1, 0), P(pi/2) = (0, 1), P(pi) = (-1, 0),
    P(3pi/2) = (0, -1). So sin 0 = 0, cos pi/2 = 0, sin pi = 0, cos pi = -1,
    sin 3pi/2 = -1; tan pi/2 and tan 3pi/2 are NOT DEFINED (x = 0).
  - SIGNS (ASTC, 'All Students Take Coffee'): Quadrant I all positive; II only
    sin (and cosec) positive; III only tan (and cot); IV only cos (and sec).
    -1 <= sin theta <= 1, -1 <= cos theta <= 1, and sin^2theta + cos^2theta = 1 for every theta.
  - REFERENCE ANGLE alpha: the acute angle between the terminal side and the x-axis
    (pi - theta in II, theta - pi in III, 2pi - theta in IV). The value of a ratio of theta is +/-
    the same ratio of alpha, with the sign from ASTC: sin 210 degrees = -sin 30 degrees = -1/2,
    cos 3pi/4 = -cos pi/4 = -sqrt2/2.
  - PERIODICITY and NEGATIVE angles: sin(theta + 2npi) = sin theta, cos(theta + 2npi) = cos theta,
    tan(theta + npi) = tan theta; sin(-theta) = -sin theta, cos(-theta) = cos theta, tan(-theta) = -tan theta.
    Reduce any angle into [0, 2pi) (or [0 degrees, 360 degrees)) first.
  - ALLIED ANGLES: sin(pi - theta) = sin theta, cos(pi - theta) = -cos theta; sin(pi + theta) = -sin theta,
    cos(pi + theta) = -cos theta; sin(2pi - theta) = -sin theta, cos(2pi - theta) = cos theta; sin(pi/2 +/-
    theta) = cos theta, cos(pi/2 + theta) = -sin theta, cos(pi/2 - theta) = sin theta. Rule: with pi or 2pi
    the function stays the same, with pi/2 or 3pi/2 it changes to its co-function;
    the sign is the sign of the ORIGINAL function in the quadrant where the
    angle lies (taking theta acute).

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Define one radian. Show that pi radians = 180 degrees, and convert 30 degrees, 45 degrees, 135 degrees,
    210 degrees and 1 degrees to radians. How many degrees is 1 radian?
    Answer: 30 degrees = pi/6, 45 degrees = pi/4, 135 degrees = 3pi/4, 210 degrees = 7pi/6, 1 degrees = pi/180 ~ 0.01745
    Teacher explains: Draw a circle of radius r and mark an arc of length r: the
    angle it makes at the centre is ONE RADIAN, whatever the size of the circle.
    The whole circumference is 2pir, that is 2pi arcs of length r, so a full turn
    is 2pi radians = 360 degrees, and pi rad = 180 degrees.
       degrees -> radians: multiply by pi/180
           30 degrees  = 30 x pi/180  = pi/6          45 degrees  = pi/4
           135 degrees = 135pi/180    = 3pi/4         210 degrees = 210pi/180 = 7pi/6
       radians -> degrees: multiply by 180/pi
    Keep pi in the answer (exact) unless a decimal is asked for. Since 1
    rad ~ 57 degrees, an angle of 2 rad is a little under 115 degrees and 3 rad is just under
    180 degrees. Common mistake: thinking 1 rad = 1 degrees, or writing pi = 180 (pi is a
    NUMBER ~ 3.14; pi RADIANS is 180 degrees). Now you try: convert 240 degrees and 330 degrees to
    radians and 5pi/12 to degrees. (4pi/3; 11pi/6; 75 degrees)

D2. Convert to degrees: 5pi/6, 7pi/4, -pi/3, 11pi/5, 2.5 rad (in degrees and
    minutes, using pi ~ 3.1416).
    Teacher explains: Replace pi by 180 degrees and simplify:
       5pi/6   = 5 x 180 degrees/6  = 150 degrees
       7pi/4   = 7 x 180 degrees/4  = 315 degrees
       -pi/3   = -180 degrees/3     = -60 degrees
       11pi/5  = 11 x 180 degrees/5 = 396 degrees   (more than one full turn)
       2.5    = 2.5 x 180 degrees/pi ~ 450 degrees/3.1416 ~ 143.239 degrees
    A radian measure WITHOUT pi (like 2.5) is still a radian measure: multiply by
    180/pi. Negative angles are measured CLOCKWISE. Common mistake: multiplying
    2.5 by 180 and forgetting to divide by pi. Now you try: 3pi/8 and 4 rad in

D3. (a) The minute hand of a clock is 14 cm long. How far does its tip move in
    20 minutes? (b) A pendulum 75 cm long swings through an arc of 21 cm.
    Through what angle does it swing (in radians and degrees)?
    Teacher explains: Use s = rtheta with theta in RADIANS.
       (a) 20 minutes = 1/3 of a turn: theta = 2pi/3
           s = rtheta = 14 x 2pi/3 = 28pi/3 ~ 29.32 cm
       (b) theta = s/r = 21/75 = 0.28 rad
           0.28 x 180 degrees/pi ~ 16.04 degrees
    Why s = rtheta: the arc is the fraction theta/(2pi) of the whole circumference, so
    s = (theta/2pi) x 2pir = rtheta. In degrees the formula would be s = pirtheta/180, which is
    why radians are simpler. With pi ~ 22/7, (a) gives 29.33 cm. Common mistake:
    using theta = 120 in s = rtheta (that would give 1,680 cm!). Now you try: a wheel of
    radius 35 cm turns through 3 radians. How far does a point on the rim
    travel? (105 cm)

D4. (a) Find the area of a sector of radius 21 cm with angle 120 degrees. (b) A train
    runs on a circular curve of radius 1.5 km at 54 km/h. Through what angle
    does it turn in 10 seconds?
    Answer: (a) 147pi cm^2 ~ 461.8 cm^2 (arc 14pi ~ 43.98 cm). (b) 0.1 rad ~ 5.73 degrees.
    Teacher explains: (a) 120 degrees = 2pi/3 rad.
       A = 1/2r^2theta = 1/2 x 21^2 x 2pi/3 = 441pi/3 = 147pi ~ 461.8 cm^2
    The sector is the fraction theta/(2pi) of the disc: (theta/2pi) x pir^2 = 1/2r^2theta. The arc
    is 21 x 2pi/3 = 14pi ~ 43.98 cm, and the perimeter of the sector is
    42 + 14pi ~ 85.98 cm. (b) 54 km/h = 54,000 m / 3,600 s = 15 m/s, so in 10 s
    the train covers s = 150 m of track. theta = s/r = 150/1500 = 0.1 rad ~ 5.73 degrees.
    Railway engineers describe curves by exactly this kind of calculation.
    Common mistake: mixing units (1.5 km with metres). Now you try: a sector has
    radius 10 cm and area 40 cm^2. Find its angle and arc length.
    (theta = 2A/r^2 = 0.8 rad; s = 8 cm)

D5. Define sin theta and cos theta for ANY angle using the unit circle. Find sin, cos
    and tan of 0, pi/2, pi, 3pi/2 and 2pi, and explain why -1 <= sin theta <= 1.
    Answer: P(theta) = (cos theta, sin theta). Values:
       theta        0      pi/2     pi      3pi/2    2pi
       sin theta    0      1       0      -1      0
       cos theta    1      0       -1     0       1
       tan theta    0      n.d.    0      n.d.    0     (n.d. = not defined)
    Teacher explains: Start at (1, 0) on the circle x^2 + y^2 = 1 and turn through
    theta (anticlockwise for positive theta). The point reached is P(theta); its
    x-coordinate is cos theta and its y-coordinate is sin theta:
                                y
                                | P(pi/2) = (0, 1)
                           .  ' * '  .
                       .'       |       '.        P(theta) = (cos theta, sin theta)
             II      .          |      *   .
          sin +     :           |     /|    :      I   all +
                   :            |   /  |sin theta:
       (-1, 0) ----*------------+--/---+-----*---- x
          P(pi)     :            O  theta  cos theta  :  (1, 0) = P(0)
          III       :           |           :      IV
          tan +      '.         |         .'       cos +
                       '.       |       .'
                           '  . * .  '
                                | P(3pi/2) = (0, -1)
    For an acute theta this agrees with the right-triangle definitions: the
    hypotenuse OP is 1, so opposite = sin theta and adjacent = cos theta. Because P lies
    on the unit circle, cos^2theta + sin^2theta = 1 for EVERY theta, and both coordinates lie
    between -1 and 1. tan theta = sin theta/cos theta fails exactly when cos theta = 0, i.e. at
    cos, tan of -pi/2 and of 5pi/2. (-1, 0, n.d.; 1, 0, n.d.)

D6. Explain the sign rule ASTC and use it to give the sign of sin 200 degrees,
    cos 300 degrees, tan 100 degrees, sec 250 degrees, cosec(-100 degrees) and cot 5pi/3.
    Answer: sin 200 degrees -, cos 300 degrees +, tan 100 degrees -, sec 250 degrees -, cosec(-100 degrees) -,
    cot 5pi/3 -.
    Teacher explains: The signs of x and y in each quadrant decide the signs:
           II (90 degrees-180 degrees)          I (0 degrees-90 degrees)
           x < 0, y > 0           x > 0, y > 0
           Sin (cosec) +          All +
          ------------------+------------------
           III (180 degrees-270 degrees)        IV (270 degrees-360 degrees)
           x < 0, y < 0           x > 0, y < 0
           Tan (cot) +            Cos (sec) +
       200 degrees: III, only tan +       sin 200 degrees < 0
       300 degrees: IV, only cos +        cos 300 degrees > 0
       100 degrees: II, only sin +        tan 100 degrees < 0
       250 degrees: III                   sec 250 degrees = 1/cos 250 degrees < 0
       -100 degrees = 260 degrees (III)          cosec(-100 degrees) < 0
       5pi/3 = 300 degrees (IV)            cot 5pi/3 < 0
    A reciprocal has the same sign as the function it comes from. Memory aid:
    'All Students Take Coffee', going anticlockwise from quadrant I. Common
    mistake: placing -100 degrees in quadrant II (turn CLOCKWISE 100 degrees from the positive
    x-axis: you land in III). Now you try: signs of sin 3 and cos 3 (3 radians).
    (3 rad ~ 172 degrees, quadrant II: sin +, cos -)

D7. Find the exact values of sin 150 degrees, cos 225 degrees, tan 300 degrees, sin(7pi/6), cos(11pi/6)
    and tan(2pi/3) using reference angles.
    Answer: 1/2, -sqrt2/2, -sqrt3, -1/2, sqrt3/2, -sqrt3.
    Teacher explains: Find the quadrant, the reference angle alpha (the acute angle
    to the x-axis), then attach the ASTC sign:
       angle   quadrant   alpha      value
       150 degrees    II         30 degrees    sin 150 degrees = +sin 30 degrees = 1/2
       225 degrees    III        45 degrees    cos 225 degrees = -cos 45 degrees = -sqrt2/2
       300 degrees    IV         60 degrees    tan 300 degrees = -tan 60 degrees = -sqrt3
       7pi/6    III        pi/6    sin 7pi/6 = -sin pi/6 = -1/2
       11pi/6   IV         pi/6    cos 11pi/6 = +cos pi/6 = sqrt3/2
       2pi/3    II         pi/3    tan 2pi/3 = -tan pi/3 = -sqrt3
    Why it works: P(theta) and P(alpha) are mirror images of each other in an axis or in
    the origin, so their coordinates have the same SIZE and differ only in sign.
    Reference angle: 180 degrees - theta (II), theta - 180 degrees (III), 360 degrees - theta (IV). Common
    mistake: using the reference angle 90 degrees - theta (measure to the x-axis, never the
    y-axis). Now you try: sin 240 degrees, cos 5pi/4, tan 330 degrees. (-sqrt3/2; -sqrt2/2; -sqrt3/3)

D8. Use the unit circle to prove sin(pi - theta) = sin theta, cos(pi - theta) = -cos theta,
    sin(pi + theta) = -sin theta and cos(pi/2 - theta) = sin theta. Hence simplify
    sin(pi - theta) cos(pi/2 + theta) + cos(pi + theta) sin(pi/2 + theta).
    Answer: Proofs below; the expression equals -1.
    Teacher explains: P(pi - theta) is the reflection of P(theta) in the y-axis; P(pi + theta)
    is its reflection in the origin; P(pi/2 - theta) is its reflection in the line
    y = x:
       P(theta)        = (cos theta, sin theta)
    Also cos(pi/2 + theta) = -sin theta and sin(pi/2 + theta) = cos theta. So
       sin(pi - theta) cos(pi/2 + theta) + cos(pi + theta) sin(pi/2 + theta)
         = sin theta(-sin theta) + (-cos theta)(cos theta) = -(sin^2theta + cos^2theta) = -1
    Rule of thumb: with pi and 2pi the function name stays; with pi/2 and 3pi/2 it
    ORIGINAL function in the quadrant of the angle, pretending theta is acute. Check
    with theta = 30 degrees: sin 150 degrees cos 120 degrees + cos 210 degrees sin 120 degrees
    tan(pi + theta) cot(3pi/2 - theta). (tan theta x tan theta = tan^2theta)

D9. Find sin 765 degrees, cos(-1110 degrees), tan(17pi/4) and sin(-11pi/6).
    Answer: sqrt2/2, sqrt3/2, 1, 1/2.
    Teacher explains: Remove whole turns (360 degrees or 2pi) first; tan repeats every
    180 degrees (pi):
       765 degrees   = 2 x 360 degrees + 45 degrees        sin 765 degrees = sin 45 degrees = sqrt2/2
       -1110 degrees = -3 x 360 degrees - 30 degrees       cos(-1110 degrees) = cos(-30 degrees) = cos 30 degrees = sqrt3/2
       17pi/4  = 4pi + pi/4              tan(17pi/4) = tan(pi/4) = 1
       -11pi/6 = -2pi + pi/6             sin(-11pi/6) = sin(pi/6) = 1/2
    For negative angles you may also use sin(-theta) = -sin theta, cos(-theta) = cos theta:
    sin(-11pi/6) = -sin(11pi/6) = -(-1/2) = 1/2, the same. cos is EVEN and sin,
    tan are ODD functions. Common mistake: dividing the angle by 360 and using
    the decimal part wrongly; subtract multiples of 360 degrees instead. Now you try:
    cos 1485 degrees and tan(-585 degrees). (1485 degrees = 4 x 360 degrees + 45 degrees: sqrt2/2;
    -585 degrees = -720 degrees + 135 degrees: tan 135 degrees = -1)

D10. (a) sin theta = 3/5 and theta lies in the second quadrant. Find the other five
     trigonometric ratios. (b) tan x = -5/12 with 3pi/2 < x < 2pi. Find sin x and
     cos x.
     Answer: (a) cos theta = -4/5, tan theta = -3/4, cosec theta = 5/3, sec theta = -5/4,
     cot theta = -4/3. (b) sin x = -5/13, cos x = 12/13.
     Teacher explains: Draw a reference triangle with the known sides, find the
     third side by Pythagoras, then give each ratio its ASTC sign.
            quadrant II: x < 0, y > 0, so cos theta = -4/5
            tan theta = sin theta/cos theta = (3/5)/(-4/5) = -3/4
            quadrant IV: sin < 0, cos > 0
     Or algebraically: cos^2theta = 1 - sin^2theta = 16/25, cos theta = +/-4/5, and the quadrant
     picks the minus sign. The magnitudes come from the triangle, the SIGNS from
     ratios positive. Now you try: cos theta = -12/13, pi < theta < 3pi/2: find sin theta and
     tan theta. (-5/13; 5/12)

D11. Prove that cos 570 degrees sin 510 degrees + sin(-330 degrees) cos(-390 degrees) = 0, and evaluate
     sin^2(pi/6) + cos^2(pi/3) - tan^2(3pi/4) + sec(5pi/3).
     Answer: The first expression is 0 (below). The second equals 3/2.
     Teacher explains: Reduce each angle, then use reference angles:
        cos 570 degrees = cos 210 degrees = -cos 30 degrees = -sqrt3/2
        sin 510 degrees = sin 150 degrees = sin 30 degrees = 1/2
        sin(-330 degrees) = -sin 330 degrees = -(-1/2) = 1/2
        cos(-390 degrees) = cos 390 degrees = cos 30 degrees = sqrt3/2
        total: (-sqrt3/2)(1/2) + (1/2)(sqrt3/2) = -sqrt3/4 + sqrt3/4 = 0
     For the second:
        sin^2(pi/6) = 1/4,  cos^2(pi/3) = 1/4,  tan^2(3pi/4) = (-1)^2 = 1,
        sec(5pi/3) = 1/cos(5pi/3) = 1/(1/2) = 2
        1/4 + 1/4 - 1 + 2 = 3/2
     Squares remove signs, but single ratios keep them: work out each factor
     completely before multiplying. Common mistake: cos(-390 degrees) = -cos 390 degrees (cos
     is even). Now you try: evaluate tan 225 degrees cot 405 degrees + tan 765 degrees cot 675 degrees.
     (1 x 1 + 1 x (-1) = 0)

D12. Write the coordinates of P(theta) on the unit circle for every multiple of pi/6
     and pi/4 from 0 to 2pi, and describe the patterns.
     Answer: See the table.
        theta      P(theta)                 theta       P(theta)
        0      (1, 0)               pi       (-1, 0)
        pi/6    (sqrt3/2, 1/2)          7pi/6    (-sqrt3/2, -1/2)
        pi/4    (sqrt2/2, sqrt2/2)         5pi/4    (-sqrt2/2, -sqrt2/2)
        pi/3    (1/2, sqrt3/2)          4pi/3    (-1/2, -sqrt3/2)
        pi/2    (0, 1)               3pi/2    (0, -1)
        2pi/3   (-1/2, sqrt3/2)         5pi/3    (1/2, -sqrt3/2)
        3pi/4   (-sqrt2/2, sqrt2/2)        7pi/4    (sqrt2/2, -sqrt2/2)
        5pi/6   (-sqrt3/2, 1/2)         11pi/6   (sqrt3/2, -1/2)
     Teacher explains: Only THREE non-trivial numbers appear: 1/2, sqrt2/2 and sqrt3/2
     (and 0, 1). Each point in the first quadrant is copied into the other
     quadrants by reflection; only the signs change (ASTC). Multiples of pi/4
     have equal coordinates in size; multiples of pi/6 and pi/3 swap 1/2 and sqrt3/2.
     Pattern check: the right column is the left column with both signs changed
     (P(theta + pi) = -P(theta), point reflection in O). Every entry satisfies
     x^2 + y^2 = 1, e.g. 1/4 + 3/4 = 1. Common mistake: mixing up which coordinate
     is sin (it is the SECOND one, y). Now you try: P(-pi/4) and P(13pi/6).
     ((sqrt2/2, -sqrt2/2); (sqrt3/2, 1/2))

     n) sin 10 degrees + sin 20 degrees + sin 190 degrees + sin 200 degrees
     o) cos 1 degrees + cos 2 degrees + ... + cos 180 degrees
     p) sin^2(pi/8) + sin^2(3pi/8) + sin^2(5pi/8) + sin^2(7pi/8)
     Answers:
       a) 1
       b) 3/2
       c) 0
       d) 0
       e) -1
       f) 10
       g) 6
       h) -1
       i) 4
       j) 1
       k) 0
       l) 0
       m) 0
       n) 0
       o) -1
       p) 2

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw the unit circle for every question and mark the angle; learn
  the first-quadrant values only and get all others by reference angle + ASTC
  sign; for conversions write 'pi rad = 180 degrees' and multiply by the right fraction;
  keep a clock face in mind: each hour mark is 30 degrees = pi/6. Harder: show that the
  area of the segment cut off by a chord subtending theta is 1/2r^2(theta - sin theta); find
  the angle between the hands of a clock at 4:20 (10 degrees = pi/18); prove that
  sin 1 > cos 1 and decide which is larger, sin 2 or sin 3
  (sin 2 ~ 0.909 > sin 3 ~ 0.141); show that
  sin^2theta + sin^2(theta + 2pi/3) + sin^2(theta + 4pi/3) = 3/2 for all theta.

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.8 - GRAPHS OF TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS; PERIODICITY
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - y = sin x: domain R, range [-1, 1], period 2pi, ODD (symmetric about O);
    zeros at x = npi; maximum 1 at pi/2 + 2npi, minimum -1 at 3pi/2 + 2npi.
    y = cos x: domain R, range [-1, 1], period 2pi, EVEN (symmetric in the
    y-axis); zeros at pi/2 + npi; cos x = sin(x + pi/2), so its graph is the sine
    curve shifted pi/2 to the left.
  - y = tan x: domain R - {pi/2 + npi} (vertical asymptotes there), range R,
    period pi, odd, zeros at npi, increasing on each branch. y = cot x: asymptotes
    at x = npi, period pi, decreasing branches.
  - y = cosec x = 1/sin x and y = sec x = 1/cos x: period 2pi, range
    the U-shaped branches touch the sine or cosine curve at its maxima and
    minima.
  - A function f is PERIODIC with period T > 0 if f(x + T) = f(x) for all x; the
    smallest such T is THE period. For y = A sin(bx + c) + d (and the same with
    cos): AMPLITUDE |A|, PERIOD 2pi/|b|, PHASE SHIFT -c/b (to the right if
    positive), MIDLINE y = d, range [d - |A|, d + |A|]. For A tan(bx + c) + d
    the period is pi/|b|.
  - To sketch y = A sin(bx + c) + d: write it as A sin(b(x + c/b)) + d; one
    cycle starts where bx + c = 0 and ends where bx + c = 2pi; split the cycle
    into four equal parts and plot midline, max, midline, min, midline (reversed
    if A < 0).
  - PERIODS OF COMBINATIONS: sin 2x + cos 3x has period LCM(pi, 2pi/3) = 2pi (LCM
    of fractions = LCM of numerators / HCF of denominators). |sin x|, sin^2x and
    |cos x| have period pi; |sin x| + |cos x| has period pi/2.
    sin x + cos x = sqrt2 sin(x + pi/4) still has period 2pi.
  - TRANSFORMATIONS: y = f(x) + d moves up d; y = f(x - h) moves right h;
    y = af(x) stretches vertically by a (reflects in the x-axis if a < 0);
    y = f(bx) compresses horizontally by b; y = |f(x)| reflects the negative
    parts upwards; y = f(|x|) mirrors the right half to the left.
  - The NUMBER OF SOLUTIONS of an equation such as sin x = x/10 equals the
    number of intersection points of the two graphs; sketch both carefully (mark
    where the line leaves the band -1 <= y <= 1).

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Make a table of values of y = sin x for 0 <= x <= 2pi in steps of pi/6, sketch
    the graph for -2pi <= x <= 2pi, and list its main properties.
    Answer: Domain R, range [-1, 1], period 2pi, odd function; zeros at x = npi;
    maximum 1 at x = pi/2 + 2npi, minimum -1 at x = 3pi/2 + 2npi.
    Teacher explains: The table (sqrt3/2 ~ 0.87):
       x      0    pi/6   pi/3    pi/2   2pi/3   5pi/6    pi
       sin x  0    0.5   0.87   1     0.87   0.5     0
       x      7pi/6   4pi/3    3pi/2   5pi/3    11pi/6   2pi
       sin x  -0.5   -0.87   -1     -0.87   -0.5    0
    Plot and join SMOOTHLY (a wave, not straight lines):
                                          |
        1     *********                   |   *********
            ***       ***                 | ***       ***
           **           **                |**           **
        0 **-------------***-------------***-------------***-------------**
                           **           **|                **           **
                            ***       *** |                 ***       ***
       -1                     *********   |                   *********
                                          |
         -2pi             -pi               0               pi              2pi
    From the unit circle, sin x is the height of P(x): it climbs from 0 to 1 in
    the first quarter turn, falls to 0, to -1, and back to 0; then it repeats,
    because P(x + 2pi) = P(x). So the period is 2pi. It is ODD (sin(-x) = -sin x):
    the graph has rotational symmetry about the origin. Near 0, sin x ~ x (the
    curve leaves O at 45 degrees). Common mistake: drawing pointed tops like a zig-zag;
    the curve is flat at every maximum and minimum. Now you try: for which x in
    [0, 2pi] is sin x > 1/2? (pi/6 < x < 5pi/6)

D2. Sketch y = cos x for -2pi <= x <= 2pi. Compare it with y = sin x and explain why
    cos x = sin(x + pi/2).
    Answer: The cosine curve is the sine curve shifted pi/2 to the LEFT. Domain
    R, range [-1, 1], period 2pi, even; zeros at pi/2 + npi; maximum 1 at 2npi,
    minimum -1 at (2n + 1)pi.
    Teacher explains:
                                          |
        1 *****                       *********                       *****
              ***                   ***   |   ***                   ***
                **                 **     |     **                 **
        0 -------***-------------***------+------***-------------***-------
                   **           **        |        **           **
                    ***       ***         |         ***       ***
       -1             *********           |           *********
                                          |
         -2pi             -pi               0               pi              2pi
    cos x is the x-coordinate of P(x): it starts at 1, falls to 0 at pi/2, to -1
    at pi, and returns. Using allied angles, sin(x + pi/2) = cos x, so every point
    of y = sin x moved pi/2 to the left lands on y = cos x. The graph is
    symmetric in the y-axis (cos(-x) = cos x): cos is an EVEN function. Common
    mistake: shifting the wrong way: y = sin(x + pi/2) moves LEFT (x must be
    smaller by pi/2 to give the same inside value). Now you try: where in [0, 2pi]
    is cos x < 0? (pi/2 < x < 3pi/2)

D3. Sketch y = tan x for -3pi/2 < x < 3pi/2. State its domain, range, period and
    asymptotes.
    Answer: Domain: all x except pi/2 + npi; range R; period pi; vertical
    asymptotes x = pi/2 + npi; zeros at x = npi; odd.
    Teacher explains: tan x = sin x/cos x is undefined where cos x = 0. Near
    x = pi/2 from the left, sin x ~ 1 and cos x is small and positive, so
          :                 * :         |       * :                ** :
          :                ** :         |      ** :                *  :
        2 :                *  :         |      *  :               **  :
          :               **  :         |     **  :              **   :
          :             ***   :         |   ***   :             **    :
          :           ***     :         | ***     :          ****     :
        0 :--------****-------:-------*****-------:-------****--------:
          :     ****          :     *** |         :     ***           :
          :    **             :   ***   |         :   ***             :
          :   **              :  **     |         :  **               :
       -2 :  **               :  *      |         :  *                :
          :  *                : **      |         : **                :
          : **                : *       |         : *                 :
                   -pi       -pi/2        0        pi/2        pi
        (: marks the asymptotes x = +/-pi/2, +/-3pi/2)
    Each branch is the same, so the period is pi, not 2pi: tan(x + pi) = tan x
    because both sin and cos change sign. Key points on the middle branch:
    (-pi/4, -1), (0, 0), (pi/4, 1). Common mistake: drawing tan x with period 2pi,
    or joining branches across an asymptote. Now you try: period and asymptotes
    of y = tan 2x. (period pi/2; x = pi/4 + npi/2)

D4. Sketch y = sec x using the graph of y = cos x, and state the domains and
    ranges of sec x, cosec x and cot x.
    domain R - {npi}, same range. cot x: domain R - {npi}, range R, period pi.
    Teacher explains: sec x = 1/cos x. Where cos x = +/-1, sec x = +/-1 (the curves
    touch); where |cos x| is small, |sec x| is large; where cos x = 0 there is
    an asymptote. The cosine curve is drawn with dots, sec x with stars:
                    : *       |       * :                   : *
                    : *       |       * :                   : *
                    : **      |      ** :                   : **
                    :  **     |     **  :                   :  **
        1 . . . . . : . ******.****** . : . . . . . . . . . : . ******.
                    : ................. :                   : .........
        0 --------.....-------+-------.....---------------.....--------
          ......... :         |         : ................. :
       -1 .****** . : . . . . | . . . . : . ******.****** . : . . . . .
                **  :         |         :  **           **  :
                 ** :         |         : **             ** :
                  * :         |         : *               * :
                  * :         |         : *               * :
         -pi       -pi/2        0        pi/2        pi       3pi/2       2pi
    Since |cos x| <= 1, |sec x| = 1/|cos x| >= 1: no value between -1 and 1 is
    ever taken. The branches are U-shaped, opening up where cos x > 0 and down
    where cos x < 0. cosec x is the same picture built on sin x (asymptotes at
    x = npi). cot x = cos x/sin x: asymptotes at npi, period pi, decreasing
    branches through (pi/2, 0). Common mistake: giving the range of sec x as
    [-1, 1]. Now you try: at which x in [0, 2pi] does cosec x = -1? (x = 3pi/2)

D5. Find the amplitude and period of y = 3 sin 2x, y = -2 cos(x/2) and
    y = (1/2) sin 3x, and describe each as a transformation of the basic curve.
    Answer: 3 sin 2x: amplitude 3, period pi. -2 cos(x/2): amplitude 2, period 4pi
    (reflected in the x-axis). (1/2) sin 3x: amplitude 1/2, period 2pi/3.
    Teacher explains: For y = A sin bx or A cos bx: amplitude |A| (half the
    distance from the lowest to the highest point) and period 2pi/|b| (one full
    cycle of the inside bx needs bx to run through 2pi):
       y = 3 sin 2x:      |A| = 3,    period 2pi/2 = pi
       y = -2 cos(x/2):   |A| = 2,    period 2pi/(1/2) = 4pi
       y = (1/2) sin 3x:  |A| = 1/2,  period 2pi/3
    A stretches the curve vertically (range [-|A|, |A|]); b squeezes it
    horizontally (b = 2 fits two waves into 2pi). The minus in -2 cos(x/2) flips
    it: it starts at -2 at x = 0. The amplitude is always POSITIVE. Common
    mistake: period = 2pi x b (for sin 2x that gives 4pi; in fact the wave is
    faster, so the period is SHORTER). Now you try: amplitude and period of
    y = 5 cos(pix). (5; 2)

D6. For y = 3 sin(2x - pi/3) + 1, find the amplitude, period, phase shift,
    midline and range, and plot one full cycle.
    Answer: Amplitude 3, period pi, phase shift pi/6 to the right, midline y = 1,
    range [-2, 4]. One cycle: (pi/6, 1), (5pi/12, 4), (2pi/3, 1), (11pi/12, -2),
    (7pi/6, 1).
    Teacher explains: Factor out b inside: 3 sin(2(x - pi/6)) + 1. So the basic
    sine wave is stretched by 3, squeezed to period pi, moved pi/6 right and 1 up.
    One cycle runs where 0 <= 2x - pi/3 <= 2pi, i.e. pi/6 <= x <= 7pi/6; divide it into
    four quarters of length pi/4:
       2x - pi/3    0       pi/2      pi       3pi/2      2pi
       x           pi/6     5pi/12    2pi/3    11pi/12    7pi/6
       y           1       4        1       -2        1
                   |
         4         |              ********
                   |            ***      ***
                   |          ***          **
                   |         **             ***
                   |        **                **
                   |       **                  **
         1 . . . . | . . *** . . . . . . . . . .** . . . . . . . . . .**
                   |    **                       **                  **
         0 --------+---**-------------------------**----------------**--
                   |  **                           ***             **
                   |***                              **          ***
           *      ***                                 ***      ***
        -2 ********|                                    ********
                   |
                   0     pi/6       5pi/12       2pi/3      11pi/12      7pi/6
         (dotted row: the midline y = 1)
    The range is [1 - 3, 1 + 3] = [-2, 4]. The phase shift is
    -c/b = (pi/3)/2 = pi/6, NOT pi/3: a common mistake is to read the shift before
    factoring out the 2. Check: at x = 0,
    y = 3 sin(-pi/3) + 1 = 1 - 3sqrt3/2 ~ -1.60, which fits the curve. Now you try:
    amplitude, period, phase shift and range of y = 2 cos(3x + pi) - 1. (2; 2pi/3;
    pi/3 to the left; [-3, 1])

D7. At a harbour the water depth h (metres) t hours after midnight is modelled
    by h = 3 + 2 sin(pit/6). Find the period, the high and low water levels and
    when they first occur, and the depth at 1 a.m. Then find a function of the
    form y = A sin(bx) + d whose graph has maximum 5 at x = pi/4 and minimum -1
    at x = 3pi/4.
    Answer: Period 12 h; high water 5 m at 3 a.m., low water 1 m at 9 a.m.;
    depth at 1 a.m. is 4 m. Second function: y = 3 sin 2x + 2.
    Teacher explains: Period = 2pi/(pi/6) = 12 hours (two tides a day, roughly).
    The sine part lies between -1 and 1, so h lies between 3 - 2 = 1 m and
    3 + 2 = 5 m. The first maximum is where pit/6 = pi/2, t = 3; the first minimum
    where pit/6 = 3pi/2, t = 9. At t = 1: h = 3 + 2 sin(pi/6) = 3 + 1 = 4 m. For
    the second part:
       midline d = (5 + (-1))/2 = 2      amplitude A = (5 - (-1))/2 = 3
       max to min is half a period: 3pi/4 - pi/4 = pi/2, so period = pi, b = 2
    Common mistake: using the difference max - min as the amplitude (it is TWICE
    the amplitude). Now you try: a Ferris wheel of radius 10 m has its centre 12
    m above the ground and turns once every 4 minutes. Write the height if you
    start at the level of the centre, going up. (h = 12 + 10 sin(pit/2), t in
    minutes)

D8. Find the period of (a) sin 2x + cos 3x, (b) |sin x|, (c) sin^2x, (d) sin x
    cos x, (e) tan 3x + sin 2x, (f) sin x + cos x, (g) |sin x| + |cos x|.
    Answer: (a) 2pi (b) pi (c) pi (d) pi (e) pi (f) 2pi (g) pi/2.
    Teacher explains: (a) sin 2x has period pi, cos 3x has period 2pi/3. The sum
    repeats when BOTH parts repeat: the least common multiple.
    (b) |sin(x + pi)| = |-sin x| = |sin x|, and nothing smaller works: pi. (c)
    sin^2x = (1 - cos 2x)/2 has the period of cos 2x: pi. (d) sin x
    cos x = (1/2) sin 2x: period pi. (e) tan 3x has period pi/3, sin 2x has period
    pi; LCM = pi. (f) sin x + cos x = sqrt2 sin(x + pi/4): period 2pi (adding does not
    always reduce the period). (g) Replacing x by x + pi/2 turns |sin x| into
    |cos x| and |cos x| into |sin x|, so the sum is unchanged: period pi/2,
    though each part has period pi. Common mistake: multiplying the periods ((a)
    would give 2pi^2/3). Now you try: period of sin 4x + cos 6x.
    (LCM(pi/2, pi/3) = pi)

D9. Decide whether each function is even, odd or neither: x sin x, x + sin x,
    sin x + cos x, sin^2x, x^2 tan x, cos x + x^2, sin|x|.
    Answer: Even: x sin x, sin^2x, cos x + x^2, sin|x|. Odd: x + sin x, x^2 tan x.
    Neither: sin x + cos x.
    Teacher explains: Replace x by -x and use sin(-x) = -sin x, cos(-x) = cos x,
    tan(-x) = -tan x:
       (-x) sin(-x) = (-x)(-sin x) = x sin x            even
       -x + sin(-x) = -(x + sin x)                      odd
       sin(-x) + cos(-x) = -sin x + cos x               neither
       sin^2(-x) = (-sin x)^2 = sin^2x                     even
       (-x)^2 tan(-x) = -x^2 tan x                        odd
       cos(-x) + (-x)^2 = cos x + x^2                     even
       sin|-x| = sin|x|                                 even
    Products follow sign rules: odd x odd = even, odd x even = odd. Even graphs
    are symmetric in the y-axis, odd graphs about the origin. Common mistake:
    calling sin x + cos x odd because sin x is odd; a sum of an odd and an even
    function (both non-zero) is neither. Now you try: x cos x and tan^2x. (odd;
    even)

D10. Use graphs to find the number of real solutions of (a) sin x = x/10,
     (b) cos x = x, (c) 2 sin x = 1 on [0, 2pi].
     Answer: (a) 7 (b) 1 (c) 2.
     Teacher explains: (a) Draw y = sin x (stars) and the line y = x/10 (o's).
     The line stays inside the band -1 <= y <= 1 only for -10 <= x <= 10, so all
     intersections lie there:
                                            |
         1 **                ***            |  ****               **** ooooooo
            ***            *** **           | **  **           ooooooooo
              **          **    **          |**    **   oooooooo**    **
               *          *      **         **  ooooooooo      **      **
         0 ----**--------**-------**----ooooooooo----**-------**--------**----
                **      **      ooooooooo  **         **      *          *
                 **    **oooooooo   **    **|          **    **          **
                 ooooooooo           **  ** |           ** ***            ***
        -1 ooooooo ****               ****  |            ***                **
                                            |
             -10        -2pi                 0                 2pi         10
     For x > 0: the line crosses the arches of sin x on (0, pi) [at x = 0 itself
     and once more, near 2.85], on (2pi, 3pi) twice (3pi ~ 9.42 < 10) and misses
     the negative arches because the line is positive there: positive solutions:
     1 + 2 = 3. By symmetry (both are odd) there are 3 negative ones, plus
     x = 0: 7 in total. (b) y = cos x decreases from 1 at 0 to 0 at pi/2 while
     y = x rises; they cross exactly once, near 0.739; for x > 1 the line is
     above 1 and for x < 0 cos x > 0 > x. (c) sin x = 1/2 at x = pi/6 and 5pi/6: 2
     solutions. Common mistake in (a): forgetting x = 0 or the negative side.
     Now you try: number of solutions of sin x = x/5. (3)

D11. Starting from y = sin x, describe how to obtain y = sin(x - pi/4),
     y = sin x + 2, y = -sin x, y = 2 sin x, y = sin 2x, y = |sin x| and
     y = sin|x|.
     Answer: Right pi/4; up 2; reflect in the x-axis; vertical stretch x2;
     horizontal squeeze by 2 (period pi); reflect the negative arches upwards;
     keep x >= 0 and mirror it in the y-axis.
     Teacher explains: Changes OUTSIDE the function act on y (vertical, and as
     expected); changes INSIDE act on x (horizontal, and the 'opposite' way):
        y = sin(x - pi/4)   shift right pi/4    (zeros at pi/4 + npi)
        y = sin x + 2      shift up 2         (range [1, 3])
        y = -sin x         reflect in x-axis  (also = sin(-x))
        y = 2 sin x        stretch x2 in y    (range [-2, 2])
        y = sin 2x         squeeze x1/2 in x  (period pi)
        y = |sin x|        flip the parts below the axis up (period pi)
        y = sin|x|         mirror the right half onto the left (not periodic)
     sin|x| is even but NOT periodic: for x >= 0 it is sin x and for x < 0 it is
     sin(-x) = -sin x, so it has a sharp corner at x = 0 (like |x|) and nowhere
     else; a periodic graph would repeat that corner. Common mistake:
     y = sin(x - pi/4) moved LEFT. Now you try: describe y = 3 - sin(x + pi/2).
     (shift left pi/2 (giving cos x), reflect, then up 3: y = 3 - cos x, range
     [2, 4])

D12. Find the range of (a) y = 3 - 2 cos x, (b) y = 1/(2 + sin x), (c)
     y = sin x + cos x, (d) y = sin^2x - sin x, and the domain of (e)
     y = sqrt(sin x).
     Answer: (a) [1, 5] (b) [1/3, 1] (c) [-sqrt2, sqrt2] (d) [-1/4, 2] (e) the
     Teacher explains: Start from -1 <= sin x <= 1 (or cos x) and build up:
        (c) sin x + cos x = sqrt2 (sin x cos(pi/4) + cos x sin(pi/4))
            least -1/4 at s = 1/2; greatest 2 at s = -1
        (e) need sin x >= 0: the upper arches, [0, pi], [2pi, 3pi], ...
     In (d) the maximum 2 comes from the END point s = -1, not from the vertex;
     always check the ends of the allowed interval. Common mistake: in (c)
     adding the ranges to get [-2, 2]; sin x and cos x are never both 1 at the
     same x. Now you try: range of 4 sin x - 3 cos x. ([-5, 5], since
     sqrt(16 + 9) = 5)

PART B - MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. State the amplitude and the period (tan has no amplitude).
    a) y = 3 sin 2x                b) y = -2 cos(x/2)

    e) y = sin 4x                  f) y = -cos 3x
    g) y = 4 sin(2x/3)             h) y = 2 tan 3x

      m) 3; pi

      p) 4; pi

      s) 1; 2pi/3

M2. State the phase shift, the midline and the range.
    a) y = 3 sin(2x - pi/3) + 1
    b) y = 2 cos(3x + pi) - 1
    c) y = sin(x - pi/4)
    d) y = 4 cos(2x + pi/2) + 3
    e) y = -2 sin(x/2 + pi/6) + 1
    f) y = 5 cos(x - pi/3) - 2
    g) y = sin(3x + pi/2) + 2
    h) y = -3 cos(4x - pi)
    i) y = 2 sin(pix - pi/2) + 5
    j) y = 6 cos(x/3) - 6
    k) y = tan(2x - pi/2) + 1
    l) y = (1/2) cos(2x + pi/3) + 1/2
    m) y = cos(x + pi/6)
    n) y = 2 sin(2x + pi)
    o) y = 3 cos(x/2 - pi/4) + 2
    p) y = -sin(2x - pi/2) - 3
    q) y = 4 sin x - 1
    r) y = (5/2) cos 2x + 3/2
    s) y = sin(6x + pi)
    t) y = -4 cos(3x - pi/2) + 4
    Answers:
      a) pi/6 right; y = 1; [-2, 4]
      b) pi/3 left; y = -1; [-3, 1]
      c) pi/4 right; y = 0; [-1, 1]
      d) pi/4 left; y = 3; [-1, 7]
      e) pi/3 left; y = 1; [-1, 3]
      f) pi/3 right; y = -2; [-7, 3]
      g) pi/6 left; y = 2; [1, 3]
      h) pi/4 right; y = 0; [-3, 3]
      i) 1/2 right; y = 5; [3, 7]

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: plot from a table of values at multiples of pi/6 before sketching;
  always mark the midline, the maximum and the minimum first; for
  y = A sin(bx + c) + d find the start of a cycle by solving bx + c = 0 and the
  length by 2pi/b, then divide into four equal steps; check a sketch with one
  calculator value. Harder: prove that sin x is not periodic with any period
  smaller than 2pi; show that sin(x^2) and sin|x| are not periodic; find the
  period of sin x + sin(sqrt2 x) (it is not periodic: sqrt2 is irrational); show that
  the equation sin x = x/100 has 63 solutions.

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.9 - COMPOUND, MULTIPLE AND SUB-MULTIPLE ANGLE FORMULAS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - COMPOUND ANGLES: sin(A +/- B) = sin A cos B +/- cos A sin B; cos(A +/-
    not only acute ones.
  - EXACT VALUES of 15 degrees, 75 degrees, 105 degrees, 165 degrees ... come from 45 degrees +/- 30 degrees, 60 degrees +/- 45 degrees and
    so on: sin 15 degrees = (sqrt6 - sqrt2)/4, cos 15 degrees = (sqrt6 + sqrt2)/4, tan 15 degrees = 2 - sqrt3,
    tan 75 degrees = 2 + sqrt3.
  - DOUBLE ANGLE: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A; cos 2A = cos^2A - sin^2A = 2cos^2A - 1
    = 1 - 2sin^2A; tan 2A = 2 tan A/(1 - tan^2A). Also
    sin 2A = 2 tan A/(1 + tan^2A) and cos 2A = (1 - tan^2A)/(1 + tan^2A).
  - TRIPLE ANGLE: sin 3A = 3 sin A - 4 sin^3A; cos 3A = 4cos^3A - 3 cos A;
    tan 3A = (3 tan A - tan^3A)/(1 - 3tan^2A).
  - HALF ANGLE (SUB-MULTIPLE): cos^2(A/2) = (1 + cos A)/2,
    sin^2(A/2) = (1 - cos A)/2, tan(A/2) = sin A/(1 + cos A) = (1 - cos A)/sin A.
    The SIGN of sin(A/2), cos(A/2) is decided by the quadrant of A/2, not of A.
  - SUM TO PRODUCT: sin C + sin D = 2 sin((C + D)/2) cos((C - D)/2);
    sin C - sin D = 2 cos((C + D)/2) sin((C - D)/2); cos C + cos D
    = 2 cos((C + D)/2) cos((C - D)/2); cos C - cos D
    = -2 sin((C + D)/2) sin((C - D)/2).
  - PRODUCT TO SUM: 2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A - B);
    2 cos A sin B = sin(A + B) - sin(A - B);
    2 cos A cos B = cos(A - B) + cos(A + B);
    2 sin A sin B = cos(A - B) - cos(A + B).
  - a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + alpha) with R = sqrt(a^2 + b^2), cos alpha = a/R,
    sin alpha = b/R. Hence its MAXIMUM is R and MINIMUM is -R. Used for maxima, for
    solving a sin x + b cos x = c and in physics (adding waves).
  - PROVING IDENTITIES: work on one side; choose the formula that makes angles
    match; check the identity NUMERICALLY at two or three angles first (a check
    is evidence, not a proof). In a triangle, A + B + C = 180 degrees gives extra facts
    such as sin(A + B) = sin C.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Find the exact values of sin 15 degrees, cos 15 degrees and tan 15 degrees. Explain why sin 15 degrees
    is NOT sin 45 degrees - sin 30 degrees.
    Answer: sin 15 degrees = (sqrt6 - sqrt2)/4, cos 15 degrees = (sqrt6 + sqrt2)/4, tan 15 degrees = 2 - sqrt3.
    Teacher explains: Write 15 degrees = 45 degrees - 30 degrees, two angles whose ratios we know.
       sin(45 degrees - 30 degrees) = sin 45 degrees cos 30 degrees - cos 45 degrees sin 30 degrees
                      = (sqrt2/2)(sqrt3/2) - (sqrt2/2)(1/2) = (sqrt6 - sqrt2)/4
       cos(45 degrees - 30 degrees) = cos 45 degrees cos 30 degrees + sin 45 degrees sin 30 degrees
                      = (sqrt2/2)(sqrt3/2) + (sqrt2/2)(1/2) = (sqrt6 + sqrt2)/4
       tan(45 degrees - 30 degrees) = (1 - 1/sqrt3)/(1 + 1/sqrt3) = (sqrt3 - 1)/(sqrt3 + 1)
                      = (sqrt3 - 1)^2/(3 - 1) = (4 - 2sqrt3)/2 = 2 - sqrt3
    Check with a calculator: (sqrt6 - sqrt2)/4 ~ (2.449 - 1.414)/4 ~ 0.2588 = sin 15 degrees.
    The function sin is NOT linear: sin 45 degrees - sin 30 degrees ~ 0.707 - 0.5 = 0.207,
    which is wrong. Common mistakes: writing sin(A - B) = sin A - sin B; and in
    cos(A - B) using a minus sign (cos of a DIFFERENCE has a PLUS). Now you try:
    find sin 75 degrees and tan 75 degrees from 45 degrees + 30 degrees. ((sqrt6 + sqrt2)/4; 2 + sqrt3)

D2. Given sin A = 3/5 with A in the second quadrant and cos B = 5/13 with B in
    the fourth quadrant, find sin(A + B), cos(A + B) and tan(A + B). In which
    quadrant is A + B?
    Answer: sin(A + B) = 63/65, cos(A + B) = 16/65, tan(A + B) = 63/16; A + B is
    in the first quadrant.
    Teacher explains: Step 1: complete each triangle and fix the SIGNS by the
    quadrant. A in QII: cos A = -sqrt(1 - 9/25) = -4/5. B in QIV:
    sin B = -sqrt(1 - 25/169) = -12/13.
       sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B
                  = (3/5)(5/13) + (-4/5)(-12/13) = 15/65 + 48/65 = 63/65
       cos(A + B) = cos A cos B - sin A sin B
                  = (-4/5)(5/13) - (3/5)(-12/13) = -20/65 + 36/65 = 16/65
       tan(A + B) = sin/cos = 63/16
    Both sine and cosine are positive, so A + B is in the FIRST quadrant (for
    example A ~ 143.13 degrees and B ~ -67.38 degrees give A + B ~ 75.75 degrees). Common mistake:
    taking cos A = +4/5 and sin B = +12/13; a sign slip there gives 16/65 and
    -63/65, a completely different angle. ALWAYS fix the signs from the
    quadrants first. Now you try: with the same A and B, find sin(A - B) and
    cos(A - B). (sin(A - B) = -33/65; cos(A - B) = -56/65)

D3. Prove that cos(A + B) cos(A - B) = cos^2A - sin^2B, and check it numerically
    at A = 50 degrees, B = 20 degrees. Use it to find cos 75 degrees cos 15 degrees.
    Answer: Proof below; at A = 50 degrees, B = 20 degrees both sides are 0.2962 (4 d.p.);
    cos 75 degrees cos 15 degrees = 1/4.
    Teacher explains: Expand both brackets:
       (cos A cos B - sin A sin B)(cos A cos B + sin A sin B)
       = cos^2A cos^2B - sin^2A sin^2B                  (difference of squares)
       = cos^2A (1 - sin^2B) - (1 - cos^2A) sin^2B
       = cos^2A - cos^2A sin^2B - sin^2B + cos^2A sin^2B = cos^2A - sin^2B
    The key move is to write everything in cos A and sin B, the letters in the
    answer. Numerical check: cos 70 degrees cos 30 degrees = 0.3420 x 0.8660 = 0.2962 and
    cos^250 degrees - sin^220 degrees = 0.4132 - 0.1170 = 0.2962. For cos 75 degrees cos 15 degrees take
    A = 45 degrees, B = 30 degrees: cos^245 degrees - sin^230 degrees = 1/2 - 1/4 = 1/4. Similarly
    sin(A + B) sin(A - B) = sin^2A - sin^2B. Common mistake: "cancelling" the
    middle terms before multiplying out. Now you try: find sin 75 degrees sin 15 degrees with
    the companion identity. (sin^245 degrees - sin^230 degrees = 1/4)

D4. If tan theta = 3/4 and theta lies in the third quadrant, find sin 2theta, cos 2theta and
    tan 2theta. In which quadrant is 2theta?
    Answer: sin 2theta = 24/25, cos 2theta = 7/25, tan 2theta = 24/7; 2theta is in the first
    quadrant (going round the circle once more).
    Teacher explains: In QIII both sin and cos are negative: sin theta = -3/5,
    cos theta = -4/5.
       sin 2theta = 2 sin theta cos theta = 2(-3/5)(-4/5) = 24/25
       cos 2theta = cos^2theta - sin^2theta = 16/25 - 9/25 = 7/25
       tan 2theta = 2 tan theta/(1 - tan^2theta) = (3/2)/(1 - 9/16) = (3/2)/(7/16) = 24/7
    The tan formula gives a check: (24/25) / (7/25) = 24/7. theta is between 180 degrees
    and 270 degrees (theta ~ 216.87 degrees), so 2theta ~ 433.74 degrees, which is 73.74 degrees after a full turn:
    first quadrant, as the signs show. Quicker route: sin 2theta
    = 2 tan theta/(1 + tan^2theta) = (3/2)/(25/16) = 24/25 without finding sin theta at all.
    Common mistake: saying sin theta = 3/5 because tan is positive (forgetting
    QIII). Now you try: cos theta = -5/13, theta in QII; find sin 2theta and cos 2theta.
    (-120/169; -119/169)

D5. Prove sin 3theta = 3 sin theta - 4 sin^3theta. Then show that sin 18 degrees = (sqrt5 - 1)/4 using
    2 x 18 degrees = 90 degrees - 3 x 18 degrees.
    Answer: Proof below; sin 18 degrees = (sqrt5 - 1)/4 ~ 0.3090.
    Teacher explains: sin 3theta = sin(2theta + theta) = sin 2theta cos theta + cos 2theta
    sin theta = 2 sin theta cos^2theta + (1 - 2 sin^2theta) sin theta = 2 sin theta
    (1 - sin^2theta) + sin theta - 2 sin^3theta = 3 sin theta - 4 sin^3theta. Now let theta = 18 degrees, so
    5theta = 90 degrees and 2theta = 90 degrees - 3theta. Take sines: sin 2theta = cos 3theta, i.e. 2 sin theta
    cos theta = 4cos^3theta - 3 cos theta. Divide by cos theta (!= 0): 2 sin theta = 4cos^2theta - 3
    = 4(1 - sin^2theta) - 3 = 1 - 4 sin^2theta. Put s = sin theta:
       4s^2 + 2s - 1 = 0   ->   s = (-2 +/- sqrt(4 + 16))/8 = (-1 +/- sqrt5)/4
    sin 18 degrees > 0, so s = (sqrt5 - 1)/4 ~ 0.3090 (calculator: sin 18 degrees = 0.30902).
    Then cos 36 degrees = 1 - 2 sin^218 degrees = (1 + sqrt5)/4, which is half the golden ratio.
    Common mistake: keeping the negative root. Now you try: prove
    cos 3theta = 4cos^3theta - 3 cos theta and use it to check cos 3theta at theta = 20 degrees.
    (4(0.9397)^3 - 3(0.9397) = 0.5000 = cos 60 degrees)

D6. Find the exact values of cos 22.5 degrees, sin 22.5 degrees and tan 22.5 degrees. Then show
    tan(theta/2) = (1 - cos theta)/sin theta.
    Answer: cos 22.5 degrees = sqrt(2 + sqrt2)/2, sin 22.5 degrees = sqrt(2 - sqrt2)/2,
    tan 22.5 degrees = sqrt2 - 1.
    Teacher explains: 22.5 degrees is half of 45 degrees. From cos 2A = 2cos^2A - 1:
    cos^2A = (1 + cos 2A)/2.
       cos^222.5 degrees = (1 + sqrt2/2)/2 = (2 + sqrt2)/4   ->   cos 22.5 degrees = sqrt(2 + sqrt2)/2
       sin^222.5 degrees = (1 - sqrt2/2)/2 = (2 - sqrt2)/4   ->   sin 22.5 degrees = sqrt(2 - sqrt2)/2
    Both are positive because 22.5 degrees is in QI. For tan use the neat form:
    tan(theta/2) = sin(theta/2)/cos(theta/2) = [2 sin(theta/2) sin(theta/2)]/[2 sin(theta/2) cos(theta/2)]
    = (1 - cos theta)/sin theta. With theta = 45 degrees: (1 - sqrt2/2)/(sqrt2/2) = sqrt2 - 1 ~ 0.4142
    (calculator: tan 22.5 degrees = 0.41421). Similarly tan(theta/2) = sin theta/(1 + cos theta).
    Common mistake: choosing the sign of sin(A/2) from the quadrant of A. If
    A = 300 degrees (QIV), A/2 = 150 degrees is in QII, so sin(A/2) > 0 and cos(A/2) < 0. Now
    you try: find tan 67.5 degrees exactly. (sqrt2 + 1)

D7. Express sin 5x + sin 3x and cos 7x - cos 3x as products. Hence prove
    (sin 5x + sin 3x)/(cos 5x + cos 3x) = tan 4x, and evaluate
    sin 75 degrees + sin 15 degrees.
    Answer: sin 5x + sin 3x = 2 sin 4x cos x;
    cos 7x - cos 3x = -2 sin 5x sin 2x; sin 75 degrees + sin 15 degrees = sqrt6/2.
    Teacher explains: Sum to product takes HALF the sum and HALF the difference
    of the angles:
       sin 5x + sin 3x = 2 sin((5x + 3x)/2) cos((5x - 3x)/2) = 2 sin 4x cos x
       cos 5x + cos 3x = 2 cos 4x cos x
       cos 7x - cos 3x = -2 sin 5x sin 2x
    So (sin 5x + sin 3x)/(cos 5x + cos 3x) = (2 sin 4x cos x)/(2 cos 4x cos x)
    = tan 4x (where cos x != 0 and cos 4x != 0). Check at x = 10 degrees:
    (sin 50 degrees + sin 30 degrees)/(cos 50 degrees + cos 30 degrees) = 1.2660/1.5088 = 0.8391 = tan 40 degrees.
    And sin 75 degrees + sin 15 degrees = 2 sin 45 degrees cos 30 degrees = 2(sqrt2/2)(sqrt3/2) = sqrt6/2 ~ 1.2247.
    Common mistake: forgetting the minus sign in cos C - cos D. Now you try:
    evaluate cos 75 degrees + cos 15 degrees and sin 75 degrees - sin 15 degrees. (sqrt6/2; sqrt2/2)

D8. Use product-to-sum formulas to show cos 20 degrees cos 40 degrees cos 80 degrees = 1/8 and write
    2 sin 3x cos x as a sum.
    Answer: 2 sin 3x cos x = sin 4x + sin 2x; cos 20 degrees cos 40 degrees cos 80 degrees = 1/8.
    Teacher explains: 2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A - B), so
    2 sin 3x cos x = sin 4x + sin 2x. For the product of three cosines, a
    cleverer route uses sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A repeatedly. Multiply and divide
    by 8 sin 20 degrees:
       8 sin 20 degrees cos 20 degrees cos 40 degrees cos 80 degrees = 4 sin 40 degrees cos 40 degrees cos 80 degrees
                                        = 2 sin 80 degrees cos 80 degrees = sin 160 degrees
    Since sin 160 degrees = sin 20 degrees, the product is sin 20 degrees/(8 sin 20 degrees) = 1/8. By
    product-to-sum instead: cos 20 degrees cos 40 degrees = (cos 20 degrees + cos 60 degrees)/2; times
    cos 80 degrees: (cos 20 degrees cos 80 degrees + (1/2) cos 80 degrees)/2
    = ((cos 100 degrees + cos 60 degrees)/2 + cos 80 degrees/2)/2
    = (1/2)(1/2)(cos 100 degrees + cos 80 degrees + 1/2) = 1/8 because cos 100 degrees = -cos 80 degrees.
    Calculator: 0.9397 x 0.7660 x 0.1736 = 0.1250. Now you try: show sin 20 degrees
    sin 40 degrees sin 80 degrees = sqrt3/8. (~ 0.2165)

D9. Write 3 sin x + 4 cos x in the form R sin(x + alpha). Hence find its greatest
    and least values and the value of x in [0 degrees, 360 degrees) where the greatest value
    occurs.
    Answer: 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 53.13 degrees); greatest 5 at x = 36.87 degrees,
    least -5 (at x = 216.87 degrees).
    Teacher explains: Expand R sin(x + alpha) = R sin x cos alpha + R cos x sin alpha and
    compare: R cos alpha = 3, R sin alpha = 4. Square and add: R^2 = 9 + 16 = 25, R = 5.
    Divide: tan alpha = 4/3 with cos alpha and sin alpha both positive, so
    alpha = tan^-^1(4/3) ~ 53.13 degrees. Since -1 <= sin(x + alpha) <= 1, the expression lies
    between -5 and 5. Maximum when x + 53.13 degrees = 90 degrees, x ~ 36.87 degrees; minimum when
    x + 53.13 degrees = 270 degrees, x ~ 216.87 degrees. Check: 3 sin 36.87 degrees + 4 cos 36.87 degrees
    = 3(0.6) + 4(0.8) = 5. In general a sin x + b cos x has range [-sqrt(a^2 + b^2),
    sqrt(a^2 + b^2)]. Common mistake: taking R = a + b = 7. Now you try: greatest
    value of sin x + sqrt3 cos x and where it occurs. (2 sin(x + 60 degrees): max 2 at
    x = 30 degrees)

D10. Prove that tan 3A tan 2A tan A = tan 3A - tan 2A - tan A (whenever all the
     tangents are defined). Check at A = 10 degrees.
     Answer: Proof from tan 3A = tan(2A + A). At A = 10 degrees both sides ~ 0.0371.
     Teacher explains: tan 3A = (tan 2A + tan A)/(1 - tan 2A tan A).
     Cross-multiply:
        tan 3A - tan 3A tan 2A tan A = tan 2A + tan A
        tan 3A - tan 2A - tan A = tan 3A tan 2A tan A
     Check at A = 10 degrees: tan 30 degrees tan 20 degrees tan 10 degrees = 0.57735 x 0.36397 x 0.17633
     = 0.03705 and tan 30 degrees - tan 20 degrees - tan 10 degrees = 0.57735 - 0.36397 - 0.17633
     = 0.03705. Keep 5 d.p. in such checks: rounding to 3 d.p. too early can
     make a true identity look false. The trick "write the biggest angle as a
     sum and cross-multiply" proves many such identities. Now you try: prove
     tan 50 degrees = tan 40 degrees + 2 tan 10 degrees. (use tan 10 degrees = tan(50 degrees - 40 degrees) and tan 50 degrees
     tan 40 degrees = 1)

D11. In a triangle ABC (A + B + C = 180 degrees), prove sin 2A + sin 2B + sin 2C
     = 4 sin A sin B sin C. Check it for the triangle with A = 50 degrees, B = 60 degrees,
     C = 70 degrees.
     Answer: Proof below; both sides ~ 2.4936 for the 50 degrees, 60 degrees, 70 degrees triangle.
     Teacher explains: sin 2A + sin 2B = 2 sin(A + B) cos(A - B)
     = 2 sin C cos(A - B), because A + B = 180 degrees - C. And sin 2C = 2 sin C cos C
     = -2 sin C cos(A + B), because cos C = -cos(A + B). So the left side
        = 2 sin C [cos(A - B) - cos(A + B)] = 2 sin C x 2 sin A sin B
        = 4 sin A sin B sin C
     Check: sin 100 degrees + sin 120 degrees + sin 140 degrees = 0.98481 + 0.86603 + 0.64279
     = 2.49362 and 4 sin 50 degrees sin 60 degrees sin 70 degrees = 4 x 0.76604 x 0.86603 x 0.93969
     = 2.49362. In triangle identities replace A + B by 180 degrees - C to bring in the
     third angle. Now you try: prove cos 2A + cos 2B + cos 2C
     = -1 - 4 cos A cos B cos C. (similar steps; check with 50 degrees, 60 degrees, 70 degrees:
     both ~ -1.4397)

D12. A flagpole 6 m tall stands on top of a building 10 m tall. A student stands
     8 m from the foot of the building. Find the exact value of tan theta where theta is
     the angle the flagpole subtends at the student's eye (take the eye at
     ground level), and theta in degrees.
     Answer: tan theta = 3/14, theta ~ 12.09 degrees.
     Teacher explains: Let alpha be the angle of elevation of the top of the
     building and beta that of the top of the flagpole: tan alpha = 10/8 = 5/4,
     tan beta = 16/8 = 2, and theta = beta - alpha.
        tan theta = (tan beta - tan alpha)/(1 + tan beta tan alpha) = (2 - 5/4)/(1 + 5/2)
              = (3/4)/(7/2) = 3/14
     theta = tan^-^1(3/14) ~ 12.09 degrees. Check: beta = tan^-^1 2 ~ 63.43 degrees, alpha ~ 51.34 degrees,
     difference 12.09 degrees. The compound-angle formula gives the answer exactly
     without rounding the two angles first. At what distance d is the flagpole
     seen at its LARGEST angle? tan theta = 6d/(d^2 + 160) is greatest when
     d = sqrt160 ~ 12.65 m (AM-GM on d + 160/d). Now you try: with the student at
     20 m, find tan theta. (tan theta = 6 x 20/(400 + 160) = 3/14 as well: the same
     angle at d = 8 and d = 20, since 8 x 20 = 160)

M12. True (T) for all angles where defined, or false (F)? Test a false one at a
     simple angle such as A = 30 degrees, B = 60 degrees.
     a) sin(A + B) = sin A + sin B
     b) cos(A - B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B
     c) tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 + tan A tan B)
     d) sin 2A = 2 sin A
     e) cos 2A = 1 - 2sin^2A
     f) cos 2A = 2cos^2A + 1
     g) sin 3A = 3 sin A - 4 sin^3A
     h) cos 3A = 3 cos A - 4 cos^3A
     i) 1 + cos 2A = 2cos^2A
     j) 1 - cos 2A = 2 sin^2A
     k) sin 2A/(1 + cos 2A) = tan A
     l) (1 - cos 2A)/sin 2A = cot A
     m) sin A + sin B = 2 sin((A + B)/2) cos((A - B)/2)
     n) cos A - cos B = 2 sin((A + B)/2) sin((A - B)/2)
     o) 2 sin A sin B = cos(A - B) - cos(A + B)
     p) 2 cos A sin B = sin(A + B) + sin(A - B)
     q) cos^4A - sin^4A = cos 2A
     r) (sin A + cos A)^2 = 1 + sin 2A
     s) tan A + cot A = 2/sin 2A
     t) cot A - tan A = 2 cot 2A
     u) sin(A + B) sin(A - B) = sin^2A - sin^2B
     v) cos(A + B) + cos(A - B) = 2 sin A sin B
     w) sin 4A = 4 sin A cos A cos 2A
     x) tan 2A = 2 tan A/(1 + tan^2A)

              j) T   k) T   l) F   m) T   n) F   o) T   p) F   q) T   r) T
