TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep a formula card with the six compound-angle formulas and
  colour the signs (cos of a sum has a MINUS); derive the double-angle formulas
  by putting B = A, so there is less to memorise; before proving any identity,
  test it at 30 degrees or 45 degrees with a calculator; draw the quadrant diagram (All, Sin,
  Tan, Cos) every time signs matter. Harder: prove that
  cos(pi/7) cos(2pi/7) cos(4pi/7) = -1/8 (multiply by sin(pi/7)); show that
  tan A tan(60 degrees - A) tan(60 degrees + A) = tan 3A and hence find tan 20 degrees tan 40 degrees
  tan 80 degrees (sqrt3); find the maximum of 5 sin x + 12 cos x + 7 (20); if A + B = 45 degrees,
  show (1 + tan A)(1 + tan B) = 2 and deduce tan 22.5 degrees = sqrt2 - 1; express cos^4x
  as a sum of cosines of multiples of x ((3 + 4 cos 2x + cos 4x)/8).

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.10 - TRIGONOMETRIC EQUATIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A trigonometric EQUATION is true only for some angles. Because the functions
    are periodic, a solvable equation has INFINITELY many solutions. PRINCIPAL
    SOLUTIONS are those in 0 <= x < 2pi (some books: the principal value only);
  - sin x = k and cos x = k have solutions only when -1 <= k <= 1; tan x = k has
    solutions for every real k. For a non-standard k use alpha = sin^-^1k, cos^-^1k or
    tan^-^1k (calculator, radians or degrees).
  - MULTIPLE ANGLES: solve for the whole angle first (sin 2x = 1/2 gives
    2x = ...), then divide; a range 0 <= x < 2pi becomes 0 <= 2x < 4pi, so there are
    TWICE as many solutions.
  - METHODS: (1) reduce to one function, often a QUADRATIC in sin x, cos x or
    tan x (use sin^2 + cos^2 = 1, cos 2x = 1 - 2sin^2x ...), and reject values
    outside [-1, 1]; (2) FACTORISE (never divide by sin x or cos x: you lose
    solutions); (3) sum-to-product to make a product equal to 0; (4)
    a cos x + b sin x = c: write as R cos(x - alpha) = c with R = sqrt(a^2 + b^2);
    solutions exist only if |c| <= R.
  - CHECK every solution in the ORIGINAL equation: squaring and multiplying by a
    function can create EXTRA roots, and tan, sec must be defined. Count
    solutions in an interval with a quick graph.
  - Degrees or radians: answer in the unit of the question; general solutions in
    degrees use 180 degreesn and 360 degreesn.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Find the principal solutions (0 <= x < 2pi) and the general solution of
    sin x = 1/2.
    Answer: Principal solutions x = pi/6 and x = 5pi/6. General solution
    Teacher explains: On the unit circle, sin x is the y-coordinate. The line
    y = 1/2 cuts the circle twice: at pi/6 (QI) and at pi - pi/6 = 5pi/6 (QII),
    where sine is also positive.
                y
        5pi/6  * | *  pi/6          line y = 1/2
           *    |    *
        --*-----+-----*-- x
           *    |    *
              * | *
    Adding any multiple of 2pi gives more solutions: pi/6 + 2npi and 5pi/6 + 2npi.
    The single formula x = npi + (-1)^npi/6 contains both: n = 0 gives pi/6, n = 1
    gives pi - pi/6 = 5pi/6, n = 2 gives 2pi + pi/6, n = -1 gives -pi - pi/6 = -7pi/6
    (which is 5pi/6 - 2pi). Common mistake: writing only x = pi/6 (the calculator
    gives just one value). Now you try: general solution of sin x = -sqrt3/2.
    (x = npi + (-1)^n(-pi/3), i.e. npi - (-1)^npi/3; principal 4pi/3, 5pi/3)

D2. Solve cos x = -sqrt3/2 (principal and general solutions).
    Answer: Principal solutions 5pi/6 and 7pi/6; general solution x = 2npi +/- 5pi/6.
    Teacher explains: The reference angle is pi/6 (cos(pi/6) = sqrt3/2). Cosine is
    negative in QII and QIII, so x = pi - pi/6 = 5pi/6 or x = pi + pi/6 = 7pi/6. For
    value alpha = 5pi/6: 2npi + 5pi/6 gives 5pi/6, 17pi/6, ...; 2npi - 5pi/6 gives -5pi/6,
    7pi/6 (n = 1), ... . Why +/-? Cosine is the x-coordinate, and the angles alpha and
    -alpha have the same x-coordinate (reflection in the x-axis). Check:
    cos(7pi/6) = -cos(pi/6) = -sqrt3/2. Common mistake: writing 2npi +/- 7pi/6 AND 2npi +/-
    5pi/6 (the same set twice), or 2npi +/- pi/6 (that is cos x = +sqrt3/2). Now you
    try: general solution of cos x = 0. (x = (2n + 1)pi/2 = npi + pi/2)

D3. Solve tan x = -sqrt3 and sec x = sqrt2 (general solutions and solutions in [0,
    2pi)).
    Answer: tan x = -sqrt3: x = npi - pi/3; in [0, 2pi): 2pi/3, 5pi/3. sec x = sqrt2:
    cos x = sqrt2/2, x = 2npi +/- pi/4; in [0, 2pi): pi/4, 7pi/4.
    Teacher explains: tan has period pi, so ONE value in each interval of length
    pi is enough: tan(-pi/3) = -sqrt3, hence x = npi + (-pi/3). Taking n = 1, 2: 2pi/3,
    tan(2pi/3) = sin/cos = (sqrt3/2)/(-1/2) = -sqrt3. Common mistake: using x = 2npi + alpha
    for tan and so losing half the solutions. Now you try: cot x = 1 and
    cosec x = -2. (x = npi + pi/4; x = npi + (-1)^n(-pi/6), principal 7pi/6, 11pi/6)

D4. Solve sin 2x = sqrt3/2 for 0 <= x < 2pi.
    Answer: x = pi/6, pi/3, 7pi/6, 4pi/3.
    Teacher explains: Put u = 2x. When 0 <= x < 2pi, 0 <= u < 4pi: TWO turns of the
    circle, so expect twice as many solutions.
       sin u = sqrt3/2:  u = pi/3, 2pi/3          (first turn)
                      u = 7pi/3, 8pi/3        (add 2pi)
       x = u/2:       x = pi/6, pi/3, 7pi/6, 4pi/3
    Or from the general solution: 2x = npi + (-1)^npi/3, x = npi/2 + (-1)^npi/6;
    n = 0, 1, 2, 3 give pi/6, pi/3, 7pi/6, 4pi/3, and n = 4 gives 2pi + pi/6, too big.
    Check x = 7pi/6: sin(7pi/3) = sin(pi/3) = sqrt3/2. Common mistake: dividing the
    range too: solving sin u = sqrt3/2 only in [0, 2pi) and getting just two
    answers. Now you try: solve cos 3x = 0 for 0 <= x < pi. (pi/6, pi/2, 5pi/6)

D5. Solve 2cos^2x + 3 sin x = 0, giving the general solution and the solutions in
    [0, 2pi).
    Answer: sin x = -1/2: x = npi + (-1)^n(-pi/6); in [0, 2pi): 7pi/6, 11pi/6.
    Teacher explains: Two different functions: change cos^2x into sin x, since
    sin x also appears.
       2(1 - sin^2x) + 3 sin x = 0
       2 sin^2x - 3 sin x - 2 = 0
       (2 sin x + 1)(sin x - 2) = 0
       sin x = -1/2   or   sin x = 2 (impossible: |sin x| <= 1)
    Reference angle pi/6; sine negative in QIII and QIV: x = pi + pi/6 = 7pi/6 and
    2pi - pi/6 = 11pi/6. General: x = npi + (-1)^n(-pi/6) = npi - (-1)^npi/6. Check 7pi/6:
    cos^2(7pi/6) = 3/4, so 2(3/4) + 3(-1/2) = 3/2 - 3/2 = 0. Common mistake:
    forgetting to reject sin x = 2, or writing it as "x = sin^-^12". Now you try:
    solve 2 sin^2x + cos x - 1 = 0 in [0, 2pi). (cos x = 1 or -1/2: 0, 2pi/3, 4pi/3)

D6. Solve sin x + sqrt3 cos x = sqrt2. Show also that 3 cos x + 4 sin x = 6 has no
    solution.
    Answer: x = npi + (-1)^npi/4 - pi/3; in [0, 2pi): 5pi/12 and 23pi/12. The second
    equation has no solution because 6 > 5 = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2).
    Teacher explains: Write the left side as R sin(x + alpha): R = sqrt(1 + 3) = 2,
    cos alpha = 1/2, sin alpha = sqrt3/2, alpha = pi/3.
       2 sin(x + pi/3) = sqrt2   ->   sin(x + pi/3) = sqrt2/2
       x + pi/3 = npi + (-1)^npi/4   ->   x = npi + (-1)^npi/4 - pi/3
    In [0, 2pi): x + pi/3 lies in [pi/3, 7pi/3); there sin = sqrt2/2 at 3pi/4 and 9pi/4,
    so x = 3pi/4 - pi/3 = 5pi/12 and x = 9pi/4 - pi/3 = 23pi/12. Check x = 5pi/12
    (75 degrees): sin 75 degrees + sqrt3 cos 75 degrees = 0.9659 + 0.4483 = 1.4142 = sqrt2. For
    3 cos x + 4 sin x the largest possible value is sqrt(9 + 16) = 5, so it can
    Common mistake: dividing by cos x to get a "tan" equation (that loses
    x = pi/2 type roots). Now you try: solve cos x - sin x = 1 in [0, 2pi).
    (sqrt2 cos(x + pi/4) = 1: x = 0, 3pi/2)

D7. Solve (i) cos 3x = cos x and (ii) sin 2x = cos x (general solutions).
    Answer: (i) x = npi/2. (ii) x = (2n + 1)pi/2 or x = npi + (-1)^npi/6.
    x = npi, or 3x = 2npi - x, giving x = npi/2. The first set is inside the second
    (npi = 2npi/2), so the answer is x = npi/2. Check x = pi/2:
    cos(3pi/2) = 0 = cos(pi/2). (ii) Do NOT divide by cos x. Write
    2 sin x cos x - cos x = 0, cos x (2 sin x - 1) = 0: cos x = 0 gives
    x = (2n + 1)pi/2; sin x = 1/2 gives x = npi + (-1)^npi/6. In [0, 2pi): pi/6, pi/2,
    5pi/6, 3pi/2 (four solutions). Dividing by cos x would give only pi/6 and 5pi/6.
    Common mistake: "cancelling" a trig factor. Now you try: solve
    sin 3x = sin x in [0, pi]. (3x = x + 2npi or 3x = pi - x + 2npi: 0, pi/4, 3pi/4,
    pi)

D8. Solve sin x + sin 3x + sin 5x = 0.
    Teacher explains: Pair the outer terms with sum-to-product:
    sin 5x + sin x = 2 sin 3x cos 2x. The equation becomes
       2 sin 3x cos 2x + sin 3x = 0   ->   sin 3x (2 cos 2x + 1) = 0
    sin 3x = 0 gives 3x = npi, x = npi/3. cos 2x = -1/2 gives 2x = 2npi +/- 2pi/3,
    x = npi +/- pi/3. But npi +/- pi/3 = (3n +/- 1)pi/3 is already of the form kpi/3! So the
    second family adds nothing new, and the complete answer is x = npi/3. In [0,
    2pi): 0, pi/3, 2pi/3, pi, 4pi/3, 5pi/3. Check x = pi/3:
    sin 60 degrees + sin 180 degrees + sin 300 degrees = sqrt3/2 + 0 - sqrt3/2 = 0. Lesson: after finding
    several families, check whether one contains another. Now you try: solve
    cos x + cos 3x = 0. (2 cos 2x cos x = 0: x = (2n + 1)pi/4 or x = (2n + 1)pi/2)

D9. How many solutions does 2 sin^2x - sin x = 0 have in [0, 2pi]? How many
    solutions does sin x = x/10 have (all real x)?
    Answer: 5 solutions: 0, pi/6, 5pi/6, pi, 2pi. The equation sin x = x/10 has 7
    solutions.
    Teacher explains: Factorise: sin x (2 sin x - 1) = 0. sin x = 0: x = 0, pi,
    2pi (the interval is CLOSED, so 2pi counts). sin x = 1/2: pi/6, 5pi/6. Total 5.
    For sin x = x/10 no algebra works; count intersections of the graphs
    y = sin x and y = x/10. The line leaves the band -1 <= y <= 1 when x is beyond
    +/-10, so only -10 <= x <= 10 matters. Look at x > 0 arch by arch:
       interval        sin x      line x/10       crossings
       (0, pi)          positive   0 to 0.31       1 (near 2.85)
       (pi, 2pi)         negative   positive        0
       (2pi, 3pi)        positive   0.63 to 0.94    2 (near 7.07, 8.42)
       (3pi, 10]        negative   positive        0
    So 3 positive roots. By symmetry (both sides are odd functions) there are 3
    negative roots, plus x = 0: 7 in all. Now you try: how many solutions has
    cos x = x/5? (3)

D10. Solve tan x + sec x = sqrt3 and explain why one "solution" must be rejected.
     Answer: x = 2npi + pi/6.
     Teacher explains: Multiply by cos x (allowed only where cos x != 0):
     sin x + 1 = sqrt3 cos x, so sqrt3 cos x - sin x = 1, i.e. 2 cos(x + pi/6) = 1.
        x + pi/6 = 2npi +/- pi/3
        x = 2npi + pi/6    or    x = 2npi - pi/2
     For x = -pi/2 (and 3pi/2 ...) cos x = 0, so tan x and sec x are NOT DEFINED:
     these are EXTRANEOUS roots created when we multiplied by cos x. Check
     x = pi/6: tan 30 degrees + sec 30 degrees = 1/sqrt3 + 2/sqrt3 = 3/sqrt3 = sqrt3. Squaring also creates
     extra roots: from sin x + cos x = 1, squaring gives sin 2x = 0, x = npi/2,
     but x = pi and x = 3pi/2 give -1, not 1. Always check in the ORIGINAL
     equation. Now you try: solve sin x + cos x = 1 in [0, 2pi). (0, pi/2)

D11. A giant wheel at a Dussehra mela has its lowest point 5 m above the ground;
     a seat's height is h = 20 - 15 cos(pit/10) metres, t minutes after it passes
     the bottom. When, during the first 20 minutes, is the seat 27.5 m high? For
     how long in each turn is it above 27.5 m?
     Answer: At t = 20/3 ~ 6.67 min and t = 40/3 ~ 13.33 min; above 27.5 m for
     20/3 ~ 6.67 minutes per turn.
     Teacher explains: 20 - 15 cos(pit/10) = 27.5 gives
     cos(pit/10) = -7.5/15 = -1/2. One turn takes 20 min (period 2pi / pi/10 = 20),
     so 0 <= pit/10 < 2pi:
        pit/10 = 2pi/3   ->   t = 20/3 ~ 6.67 min
        pit/10 = 4pi/3   ->   t = 40/3 ~ 13.33 min
     Between these times cos(pit/10) < -1/2, so h > 27.5: for 40/3 - 20/3 = 20/3
     min, one third of each turn. Check t = 10 (the top): h = 20 + 15 = 35 m.
     Real problems: set up the model, find the range of the angle from the range
     of t, then solve. Now you try: when is h = 12.5 m in the first turn?
     (cos = 1/2: t = 10/3 and 50/3 min)

D12. Solve sin x + sin 2x + sin 3x = cos x + cos 2x + cos 3x.
     Answer: x = 2npi +/- 2pi/3 or x = npi/2 + pi/8.
     Teacher explains: Group the outer terms on each side:
        sin 3x + sin x = 2 sin 2x cos x,   cos 3x + cos x = 2 cos 2x cos x
        sin 2x (2 cos x + 1) = cos 2x (2 cos x + 1)
        (2 cos x + 1)(sin 2x - cos 2x) = 0
     Either cos x = -1/2: x = 2npi +/- 2pi/3; or sin 2x = cos 2x, tan 2x = 1
     (cos 2x = 0 would force sin 2x = 0 too, impossible), 2x = npi + pi/4,
     x = npi/2 + pi/8. Check x = pi/8: sin 22.5 degrees + sin 45 degrees + sin 67.5 degrees
     = 0.3827 + 0.7071 + 0.9239 = 2.0137 and cos 22.5 degrees + cos 45 degrees + cos 67.5 degrees
     = 0.9239 + 0.7071 + 0.3827 = 2.0137. Common mistake: cancelling
     (2 cos x + 1) and losing a family. Now you try: solve sin^4x + cos^4x = 5/8.
     (1 - (1/2)sin^22x = 5/8, cos 4x = -1/2: x = npi/2 +/- pi/6)

PART B - MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Find all solutions with 0 <= x < 2pi.
    a) sin x = 0       b) sin x = 1/2     c) sin x = sqrt2/2    d) sin x = sqrt3/2
    e) sin x = 1       f) sin x = -1/2    g) sin x = -sqrt2/2   h) sin x = -sqrt3/2
    i) sin x = -1      j) sin x = 2       k) cos x = 0       l) cos x = 1/2
    m) cos x = sqrt2/2    n) cos x = sqrt3/2    o) cos x = 1       p) cos x = -1/2
    q) cos x = -sqrt2/2   r) cos x = -sqrt3/2   s) cos x = -1      t) cos x = 2
    Answers: a) 0, pi   b) pi/6, 5pi/6   c) pi/4, 3pi/4   d) pi/3, 2pi/3   e) pi/2
             f) 7pi/6, 11pi/6   g) 5pi/4, 7pi/4   h) 4pi/3, 5pi/3   i) 3pi/2
             j) no solution   k) pi/2, 3pi/2   l) pi/3, 5pi/3   m) pi/4, 7pi/4
             n) pi/6, 11pi/6   o) 0   p) 2pi/3, 4pi/3   q) 3pi/4, 5pi/4
             r) 5pi/6, 7pi/6   s) pi   t) no solution

M2. Find all solutions with 0 <= x < 2pi.
    a) tan x = 0       b) tan x = 1      c) tan x = sqrt3
    d) tan x = sqrt3/3    e) tan x = -1     f) tan x = -sqrt3
    g) tan x = -sqrt3/3   h) cot x = sqrt3     i) cot x = -1
    j) cot x = 0       k) sec x = 2      l) sec x = -sqrt2
    m) sec x = 1       n) cosec x = -2   o) cosec x = 2sqrt3/3
    p) cosec x = 1     q) sec x = 1/2    r) cosec x = -sqrt2
    Answers: a) 0, pi   b) pi/4, 5pi/4   c) pi/3, 4pi/3   d) pi/6, 7pi/6
             e) 3pi/4, 7pi/4   f) 2pi/3, 5pi/3   g) 5pi/6, 11pi/6   h) pi/6, 7pi/6
             i) 3pi/4, 7pi/4   j) pi/2, 3pi/2   k) pi/3, 5pi/3   l) 3pi/4, 5pi/4   m) 0
             n) 7pi/6, 11pi/6   o) pi/3, 2pi/3   p) pi/2   q) no solution
             r) 5pi/4, 7pi/4

    a) sin x = sqrt3/2   b) sin x = -1/2
    c) sin x = sqrt2/2   d) sin x = -sqrt2/2
    e) sin x = 0      f) sin x = 1
    g) sin x = -1     h) sin x = 1/3
    i) cos x = 1/2    j) cos x = -1/2
    k) cos x = sqrt2/2   l) cos x = -sqrt2/2
    m) cos x = sqrt3/2   n) cos x = 0
    o) cos x = 1      p) cos x = -1
    q) cos x = 3/4    r) cos x = -2/5
    s) sin^2x = 1/4    t) cos^2x = 1/2
    Answers:
      a) x = npi + (-1)^npi/3
      b) x = npi - (-1)^npi/6
      c) x = npi + (-1)^npi/4
      d) x = npi - (-1)^npi/4
      e) x = npi

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw the unit circle (or the graph) for EVERY equation and mark
  the reference angle in each quadrant; practise the four-quadrant rule "All,
  Sin, Tan, Cos"; for multiple angles always write the new range of 2x or 3x
  first; check each answer by substitution on a calculator. Harder: solve
  sin x + sin 2x + sin 3x + sin 4x = 0 (write it as
  4 sin(5x/2) cos x cos(x/2) = 0: x = 2npi/5, (2n + 1)pi/2 or (2n + 1)pi); find all
  x in [0, 2pi) with sin^8x + cos^8x = 17/32 (x = npi/4 + pi/8, eight values); for
  which k does sin x + cos x = k have exactly two solutions in [0, 2pi)?
  (-sqrt2 < k < sqrt2); prove that sin x = x has only the solution x = 0
  (|sin x| < |x| for x != 0).

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.11 - INVERSE TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
    sin^-^1x (also written arcsin x) is the unique angle in [-pi/2, pi/2] whose sine
    is x. sin^-^1x does NOT mean 1/sin x.
  - PRINCIPAL BRANCHES (domain -> range): sin^-^1: [-1, 1] -> [-pi/2, pi/2]; cos^-^1:
    or x >= 1 -> [0, pi] except pi/2; cosec^-^1: x <= -1 or x >= 1 -> [-pi/2, pi/2] except
    0.
  - NEGATIVE ARGUMENTS: sin^-^1(-x) = -sin^-^1x, tan^-^1(-x) = -tan^-^1x,
    cosec^-^1(-x) = -cosec^-^1x (odd); cos^-^1(-x) = pi - cos^-^1x,
    cot^-^1(-x) = pi - cot^-^1x, sec^-^1(-x) = pi - sec^-^1x.
  - RECIPROCALS AND COMPLEMENTS: cosec^-^1x = sin^-^1(1/x), sec^-^1x = cos^-^1(1/x);
    cot^-^1x = tan^-^1(1/x) for x > 0 (pi + tan^-^1(1/x) for x < 0).
    sin^-^1x + cos^-^1x = pi/2 (|x| <= 1), tan^-^1x + cot^-^1x = pi/2,
    sec^-^1x + cosec^-^1x = pi/2 (|x| >= 1).
  - SUM FORMULA: tan^-^1x + tan^-^1y = tan^-^1((x + y)/(1 - xy)) if
    xy < 1; = pi + tan^-^1((x + y)/(1 - xy)) if x > 0, y > 0, xy > 1; = pi/2 if x,
    y > 0 and xy = 1. tan^-^1x - tan^-^1y = tan^-^1((x - y)/(1 + xy)) if xy > -1. Also
    2 tan^-^1x = sin^-^1(2x/(1 + x^2)) (|x| <= 1) = cos^-^1((1 - x^2)/(1 + x^2))
    (x >= 0) = tan^-^1(2x/(1 - x^2)) (|x| < 1).
  - COMPOSITIONS: sin(sin^-^1x) = x for every x in [-1, 1], but sin^-^1(sin theta) = theta
    ONLY when theta is in [-pi/2, pi/2]; otherwise find the angle in the principal
    range with the same sine (sin^-^1(sin(2pi/3)) = pi/3). To find sin(cos^-^1(3/5))
    draw a right triangle.
  - GRAPHS: the graph of sin^-^1x is the reflection of the restricted sine graph
    in the line y = x; sin^-^1 and tan^-^1 increase, cos^-^1 and cot^-^1 decrease;
    tan^-^1x has horizontal asymptotes y = +/-pi/2.
  - Convention: answers in RADIANS unless degrees are asked for.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Find the principal values of sin^-^1(1/2), cos^-^1(-1/2) and tan^-^1(-1). Why must
    we restrict the domain of sin x before inverting it?
    Answer: sin^-^1(1/2) = pi/6, cos^-^1(-1/2) = 2pi/3, tan^-^1(-1) = -pi/4.
    Teacher explains: Infinitely many angles have sine 1/2 (pi/6, 5pi/6, 13pi/6,
    ...), so a FUNCTION must pick one. On [-pi/2, pi/2] sine is increasing, takes
    every value in [-1, 1] exactly once, and so has an inverse. sin^-^1(1/2): the
    angle in [-pi/2, pi/2] with sine 1/2 is pi/6. cos^-^1(-1/2): the angle in [0, pi]
    with cosine -1/2 is pi - pi/3 = 2pi/3 (NOT -pi/3, which is outside [0, pi]).
    tan^-^1(-1): the angle in (-pi/2, pi/2) with tangent -1 is -pi/4 (NOT 3pi/4). Rule
    of thumb: sin^-^1 and tan^-^1 of a negative number are NEGATIVE angles; cos^-^1 of
    a negative number is an OBTUSE angle. Common mistake: reading sin^-^1x as
    1/sin x; sin^-^1(1/2) is an angle, (sin(1/2))^-^1 ~ 2.09 is a number. Now you
    try: sin^-^1(-sqrt3/2), cos^-^1(-sqrt2/2), cot^-^1(-1). (-pi/3; 3pi/4; 3pi/4)

D2. Find the domain of f(x) = sin^-^1(2x - 1) and of g(x) = cos^-^1(x^2 - 1). What is
    the range of h(x) = 3 - 2 cos^-^1x?
    Answer: f: 0 <= x <= 1. g: -sqrt2 <= x <= sqrt2. h: -2pi + 3 <= h <= 3, i.e. [3 - 2pi, 3].
    Teacher explains: The input of sin^-^1 and cos^-^1 must lie in [-1, 1].
       -1 <= 2x - 1 <= 1   ->   0 <= 2x <= 2   ->   0 <= x <= 1
       -1 <= x^2 - 1 <= 1   ->   0 <= x^2 <= 2   ->   -sqrt2 <= x <= sqrt2
    For the range: 0 <= cos^-^1x <= pi, so -2pi <= -2 cos^-^1x <= 0 (multiplying by -2
    REVERSES the inequalities) and 3 - 2pi <= h <= 3. h(1) = 3 and
    h(-1) = 3 - 2pi ~ -3.28. Common mistakes: solving only 2x - 1 <= 1; forgetting
    to flip the signs when multiplying by a negative number. Now you try: domain
    of sin^-^1(x/3) + cos^-^1(x - 1). (-3 <= x <= 3 and 0 <= x <= 2 together: 0 <= x <= 2)

D3. Evaluate sin(cos^-^1(3/5)), tan(sin^-^1(-5/13)) and write cos(tan^-^1x) in terms
    of x.
    Answer: 4/5; -5/12; 1/sqrt(1 + x^2).
    Teacher explains: Let theta = cos^-^1(3/5): cos theta = 3/5 and theta is in [0, pi], where
    sine is never negative. Draw a right triangle with adjacent 3, hypotenuse 5:
          /|
       5 / |  4        sin theta = 4/5
        /  |
       /theta__|
         3
    For alpha = sin^-^1(-5/13), alpha is in [-pi/2, 0): cos alpha = +12/13 (cosine is positive
    cos(tan^-^1x) = 1/sqrt(1 + x^2) for every x. Check x = 1: cos(pi/4) = 1/sqrt2. Common
    mistake: forgetting the sign (tan(sin^-^1(-5/13)) is negative). Now you try:
    sec(tan^-^1(-3/4)) and sin(cot^-^1x) for x > 0. (5/4; 1/sqrt(1 + x^2))

D4. Find sin^-^1(sin(2pi/3)), cos^-^1(cos(7pi/6)), tan^-^1(tan(3pi/4)) and sin^-^1(sin 2).
    Answer: pi/3, 5pi/6, -pi/4 and pi - 2.
    Teacher explains: sin^-^1(sin theta) = theta only when theta is already in [-pi/2, pi/2].
    Otherwise look for the angle IN the principal range with the same ratio:
       sin(2pi/3) = sin(pi - 2pi/3) = sin(pi/3),  pi/3 in [-pi/2, pi/2]   -> pi/3
       cos(7pi/6) = cos(2pi - 7pi/6) = cos(5pi/6), 5pi/6 in [0, pi]     -> 5pi/6
       tan(3pi/4) = tan(3pi/4 - pi) = tan(-pi/4), -pi/4 in (-pi/2, pi/2) -> -pi/4
       sin 2 = sin(pi - 2), pi - 2 ~ 1.14 in [-pi/2, pi/2]            -> pi - 2
    (Here 2 is in radians, about 114.6 degrees, which is outside [-pi/2, pi/2].) The
    graph of y = sin^-^1(sin x) is a zigzag: y = x on [-pi/2, pi/2], y = pi - x on
    [pi/2, 3pi/2], y = x - 2pi on [3pi/2, 5pi/2], and so on. Common mistake:
    answering 2pi/3 "because sin^-^1 undoes sin". Now you try: cos^-^1(cos(-pi/3)) and
    tan^-^1(tan 2). (pi/3; 2 - pi)

D5. Prove that sin^-^1x + cos^-^1x = pi/2 for -1 <= x <= 1. Hence evaluate
    sin^-^1(1/3) + cos^-^1(1/3) and solve sin^-^1x = 2 cos^-^1x.
    Answer: pi/2; x = sqrt3/2.
    Teacher explains: Let theta = sin^-^1x, so sin theta = x and -pi/2 <= theta <= pi/2. Then
    cos(pi/2 - theta) = sin theta = x, and pi/2 - theta lies in [0, pi], the range of cos^-^1. So
    cos^-^1x = pi/2 - theta, i.e. sin^-^1x + cos^-^1x = pi/2. (Both conditions matter: the
    ratio must match AND the angle must be in the principal range.) The sum is
    pi/2 whatever x is, so sin^-^1(1/3) + cos^-^1(1/3) = pi/2 without knowing either
    angle. For the equation put cos^-^1x = pi/2 - sin^-^1x:
       sin^-^1x = 2(pi/2 - sin^-^1x)   ->   3 sin^-^1x = pi   ->   sin^-^1x = pi/3
    so x = sin(pi/3) = sqrt3/2. Check: sin^-^1(sqrt3/2) = pi/3 and
    2 cos^-^1(sqrt3/2) = 2(pi/6) = pi/3. Similarly tan^-^1x + cot^-^1x = pi/2. Now you try:
    solve tan^-^1x + 2 cot^-^1x = 2pi/3. (pi/2 + cot^-^1x = 2pi/3, cot^-^1x = pi/6, x = sqrt3)

D6. Show that tan^-^1(1/2) + tan^-^1(1/3) = pi/4 and find tan^-^12 + tan^-^13.
    Answer: pi/4; 3pi/4.
    Teacher explains: Use tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 - tan A tan B). With
    A = tan^-^1(1/2), B = tan^-^1(1/3):
       tan(A + B) = (1/2 + 1/3)/(1 - 1/6) = (5/6)/(5/6) = 1
    A and B are both in (0, pi/4), so A + B is in (0, pi/2), and the angle there
    with tangent 1 is pi/4. For tan^-^12 + tan^-^13: (2 + 3)/(1 - 6) = -1, but here
    xy = 6 > 1: both angles are between pi/4 and pi/2, so the sum lies between pi/2
    and pi, and the angle there with tangent -1 is 3pi/4 (NOT -pi/4). This is why
    the formula needs "+ pi" when x, y > 0 and xy > 1. Numerically:
    1.1071 + 1.2490 = 2.3562 = 3pi/4. A lovely consequence:
    tan^-^11 + tan^-^12 + tan^-^13 = pi/4 + 3pi/4 = pi. Now you try:
    tan^-^1(1/4) + tan^-^1(3/5). (pi/4)

D7. Prove 2 tan^-^1(1/3) + tan^-^1(1/7) = pi/4.
    Answer: Proof below.
    Teacher explains: First the double: 2 tan^-^1(1/3) = tan^-^1((2/3)/(1 - 1/9))
    = tan^-^1((2/3)/(8/9)) = tan^-^1(3/4) (valid as |1/3| < 1). Then add:
       tan^-^1(3/4) + tan^-^1(1/7) = tan^-^1((3/4 + 1/7)/(1 - 3/28))
                               = tan^-^1((25/28)/(25/28)) = tan^-^11 = pi/4
    (xy = 3/28 < 1, so no pi is added). Numerical check:
    2(0.32175) + 0.14190 = 0.78540 = pi/4. Formulas of this kind (Machin's
    pi/4 = 4 tan^-^1(1/5) - tan^-^1(1/239)) were used to calculate pi to hundreds of
    digits by hand. Now you try: show
    tan^-^1(1/2) + tan^-^1(1/5) + tan^-^1(1/8) = pi/4. (first two give tan^-^1(7/9); then
    (7/9 + 1/8)/(1 - 7/72) = 1)

D8. Evaluate cos(2 sin^-^1(1/3)), sin(2 tan^-^1(1/2)) and tan(1/2 cos^-^1(3/5)).
    Answer: 7/9; 4/5; 1/2.
    Teacher explains: Name the angle, then use a double- or half-angle formula.
       theta = sin^-^1(1/3):  cos 2theta = 1 - 2 sin^2theta = 1 - 2/9 = 7/9
    Calculator check: cos(2 x 0.33984) = 0.77778 = 7/9. Now you try:
    sin(2 cos^-^1(-3/5)). (2(4/5)(-3/5) = -24/25)

D9. Solve tan^-^1(2x) + tan^-^1(3x) = pi/4.
    Answer: x = 1/6.
    Teacher explains: Take tan of both sides: (2x + 3x)/(1 - 6x^2) = 1, so
    5x = 1 - 6x^2, 6x^2 + 5x - 1 = 0, (6x - 1)(x + 1) = 0: x = 1/6 or x = -1.
    CHECK both in the original equation: x = 1/6: tan^-^1(1/3) + tan^-^1(1/2) = pi/4
    (D6). x = -1: tan^-^1(-2) + tan^-^1(-3) = -3pi/4, not pi/4, because both terms are
    negative. Taking tan of both sides loses the information about WHICH angle,
    so extra roots can appear; x = -1 is rejected. Now you try: solve
    tan^-^1(x + 1) + tan^-^1(x - 1) = tan^-^1(8/31). (4x^2 + 31x - 8 = 0: x = 1/4;
    x = -8 is rejected)

D10. Sketch the graphs of y = sin^-^1x, y = cos^-^1x and y = tan^-^1x, stating domain,
     range, and whether each increases or decreases.
     Answer: See the table and description; sin^-^1 and tan^-^1 increase,
     cos^-^1 decreases.
     Teacher explains: Each graph is the reflection in y = x of the restricted
     graph:
        x         -1      -1/2     0      1/2      1
        sin^-^1x    -pi/2    -pi/6     0      pi/6      pi/2
        cos^-^1x     pi      2pi/3    pi/2     pi/3      0
        x         -10     -1       0       1       10
        tan^-^1x   -1.47   -pi/4      0      pi/4      1.47
     Plot these points and join them smoothly: sin^-^1 rises from (-1, -pi/2) to
     (1, pi/2), steep at the ends; cos^-^1 falls from (-1, pi) to (1, 0); tan^-^1 is
     an S-shaped curve squeezed between the lines y = -pi/2 and y = pi/2. sin^-^1x:
     domain [-1, 1], range [-pi/2, pi/2], passes through (0, 0), odd, increasing.
     cos^-^1x: domain [-1, 1], range [0, pi], through (0, pi/2), decreasing,
     asymptotes y = +/-pi/2 (never reached). Note that cos^-^1x = pi/2 - sin^-^1x, so
     its graph is the sin^-^1 graph turned upside down and moved up by pi/2. Now
     you try: state the domain and range of y = sin^-^1x + cos^-^1x. ([-1, 1]; the
     single value pi/2: the graph is a horizontal segment)

D11. Prove that tan^-^1(cos x/(1 - sin x)) = pi/4 + x/2 for -pi/2 < x < pi/2, and
     check at x = pi/6.
     Answer: Proof below; at x = pi/6 both sides equal pi/3.
     Teacher explains: Use half angles: cos x = cos^2(x/2) - sin^2(x/2) and
     1 - sin x = cos^2(x/2) + sin^2(x/2) - 2 sin(x/2) cos(x/2)
     = (cos(x/2) - sin(x/2))^2.
        cos x/(1 - sin x) = (c - s)(c + s)/(c - s)^2  = (c + s)/(c - s)
                          = (1 + tan(x/2))/(1 - tan(x/2)) = tan(pi/4 + x/2)
     (c = cos(x/2), s = sin(x/2), and c - s != 0 in this range.) Since
     -pi/2 < x < pi/2, the angle pi/4 + x/2 lies in (0, pi/2), inside the range of
     tan^-^1, so tan^-^1(tan(pi/4 + x/2)) = pi/4 + x/2. Check x = pi/6:
     cos(pi/6)/(1 - 1/2) = sqrt3, tan^-^1sqrt3 = pi/3 = pi/4 + pi/12. The RANGE condition is
     what makes the last step valid. Now you try: show
     tan^-^1(sqrt(1 + x^2) - 1)/x = (1/2) tan^-^1x for x != 0 (put x = tan theta).
     (sqrt(1 + tan^2theta) - 1)/tan theta = (1 - cos theta)/sin theta = tan(theta/2))

D12. In a cinema the screen is 3 m tall and its bottom edge is 2 m above a
     viewer's eye level. A viewer sits x m from the wall. Write the viewing
     angle theta with inverse tangents, simplify it to one inverse tangent, and find
     where theta is greatest.
     Answer: theta = tan^-^1(5/x) - tan^-^1(2/x) = tan^-^1(3x/(x^2 + 10)); greatest when
     x = sqrt10 ~ 3.16 m, theta = tan^-^1(3/(2sqrt10)) ~ 25.38 degrees.
     Teacher explains: The top edge is 5 m above the eye, the bottom 2 m. The
     angles of elevation are tan^-^1(5/x) and tan^-^1(2/x); theta is their difference.
     With the subtraction formula (xy = 10/x^2 > -1):
        theta = tan^-^1((5/x - 2/x)/(1 + 10/x^2)) = tan^-^1(3x/(x^2 + 10))
     tan^-^1 is increasing, so theta is greatest when 3x/(x^2 + 10) = 3/(x + 10/x) is
     greatest, i.e. when x + 10/x is least. By AM-GM, x + 10/x >= 2sqrt10, with
     equality at x = sqrt10. Then 3/(2sqrt10) ~ 0.4743 and theta ~ 0.4429 rad ~ 25.38 degrees.
     Check at x = 2: tan^-^12.5 - tan^-^11 = 68.20 degrees - 45 degrees = 23.20 degrees, smaller. Sitting
     too close or too far both shrink the angle. Now you try: find theta when x = 5.
     (tan^-^1(15/35) = tan^-^1(3/7) ~ 23.20 degrees, the same as at x = 2, because
     2 x 5 = 10)

  Struggling: draw the three principal ranges as arcs on the unit circle
  (sin^-^1 and tan^-^1 on the right half, cos^-^1 on the upper half) and check every
  answer lands on its arc; for sin(cos^-^1x) always draw the triangle; for
  sin^-^1(sin theta) sketch the zigzag graph. Harder: prove Machin's formula
  pi/4 = 4 tan^-^1(1/5) - tan^-^1(1/239); show that
  = tan^-^1(n + 1) - pi/4 (telescoping: each term is tan^-^1(k + 1) - tan^-^1k), and
  find the sum to infinity (pi/4); solve sin^-^1x + sin^-^1(2x) = pi/3 (x = sqrt21/14);
  sketch y = sin^-^1(sin x) and y = cos^-^1(cos x) for -2pi <= x <= 2pi.

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.12 - SINE RULE, COSINE RULE; SOLUTION OF TRIANGLES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - NOTATION: in triangle ABC the side a = BC is opposite angle A, b = CA
    opposite B, c = AB opposite C; A + B + C = 180 degrees. The largest side is
    opposite the largest angle.
  - SINE RULE: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C = 2R, where R is the radius of the
    circumcircle. Use it when you know a side and its OPPOSITE angle (AAS, ASA
    after finding the third angle, SSA).
  - COSINE RULE: a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos A (and the two cyclic versions); for an
    angle: cos A = (b^2 + c^2 - a^2)/(2bc). Use it for SAS (two sides and the
    included angle) and SSS. If A = 90 degrees it is Pythagoras; cos A < 0 (A obtuse)
    exactly when a^2 > b^2 + c^2.
  - AREA: delta  = 1/2ab sin C = 1/2bc sin A = 1/2ca sin B; Heron:
    delta  = sqrt(s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)) with s = (a + b + c)/2; also R = abc/(4delta ) and
    inradius r = delta /s.
  - PROJECTION FORMULAS: a = b cos C + c cos B, b = c cos A + a cos C,
    c = a cos B + b cos A.
  - AMBIGUOUS CASE (SSA: given a, b and angle A): let h = b sin A. If A is
    acute: a < h no triangle; a = h one (right-angled at B); h < a < b TWO
    triangles (B and 180 degrees - B); a >= b one. If A is right or obtuse: a <= b none,
    a > b one. With the sine rule, sin B > 1 means no triangle; always test
    whether 180 degrees - B also works.
  - SOLVING A TRIANGLE means finding all three sides and all three angles. Keep
    full calculator accuracy in the middle of a calculation and round only the
    final answers (sides and angles to 2 d.p.); give exact values (surds) when
    the data allow it.
  - APPLICATIONS: bearings (measured clockwise from north, three figures: 060 degrees),
    heights and distances with two observation points, surveying plots of land.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. In triangle ABC, A = 40 degrees, B = 65 degrees and a = 12 cm. Solve the triangle.
    Answer: C = 75 degrees, b ~ 16.92 cm, c ~ 18.03 cm.
    Teacher explains: A side and its opposite angle are known (a and A), so the
    sine rule works. First the third angle: C = 180 degrees - 40 degrees - 65 degrees = 75 degrees.
       b = a sin B/sin A = 12 x sin 65 degrees/sin 40 degrees = 12 x 0.90631/0.64279 = 16.92
       c = a sin C/sin A = 12 x sin 75 degrees/sin 40 degrees = 12 x 0.96593/0.64279 = 18.03
    Check the order: the angles 40 degrees < 65 degrees < 75 degrees and the sides 12 < 16.92 < 18.03
    match (largest side opposite largest angle). Also 2R = a/sin A = 18.67, so
    R ~ 9.33 cm. Common mistake: using the calculator in radian mode (sin 40 in
    radians is 0.745, giving nonsense). Now you try: A = 50 degrees, C = 70 degrees, c = 20;
    find a and b. (B = 60 degrees; a ~ 16.30, b ~ 18.43)

D2. Two sides of a triangle are b = 7 cm and c = 5 cm and the angle between them
    is A = 60 degrees. Find a, the other angles and the area.
    Answer: a = sqrt39 ~ 6.24 cm, B ~ 76.10 degrees, C ~ 43.90 degrees, area = 35sqrt3/4 ~ 15.16
    cm^2.
    Teacher explains: SAS: use the cosine rule for the third side.
       a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos A = 49 + 25 - 2(7)(5)(1/2) = 74 - 35 = 39
       a = sqrt39 ~ 6.245
    Now find the SMALLER unknown angle with the sine rule (it cannot be obtuse),
    or use the cosine rule for either angle (the cosine rule is never
    ambiguous):
       cos C = (a^2 + b^2 - c^2)/(2ab) = (39 + 49 - 25)/(2 x 7 x sqrt39) = 0.72058
       C = 43.90 degrees,   B = 180 degrees - 60 degrees - 43.90 degrees = 76.10 degrees
    Area = 1/2bc sin A = 1/2 x 7 x 5 x sqrt3/2 = 35sqrt3/4 ~ 15.16 cm^2. Common mistake:
    finding the LARGEST angle with the sine rule, sin B = 0.9707, then taking
    B = 76.10 degrees without asking whether 103.90 degrees is possible (it is not here,
    because 60 degrees + 103.90 degrees + 43.90 degrees != 180 degrees, but the cosine rule avoids the
    worry). Now you try: b = 5, c = 8, A = 60 degrees: find a. (a = 7 exactly)

D3. Find the angles of the triangle with sides 7, 8 and 9 cm, and its area.
    Answer: Angles 48.19 degrees, 58.41 degrees, 73.40 degrees; area 12sqrt5 ~ 26.83 cm^2.
    Teacher explains: SSS: cosine rule in the form cos A = (b^2 + c^2 - a^2)/(2bc).
    Let a = 7, b = 8, c = 9.
       cos A = (64 + 81 - 49)/(2 x 8 x 9) = 96/144 = 2/3     A = 48.19 degrees
       cos B = (49 + 81 - 64)/(2 x 7 x 9) = 66/126 = 11/21   B = 58.41 degrees
       C = 180 degrees - 48.19 degrees - 58.41 degrees = 73.40 degrees
    (check with the rule: cos C = (49 + 64 - 81)/112 = 2/7, C = 73.40 degrees.) Area by
    Heron: s = 12, delta  = sqrt(12 x 5 x 4 x 3) = sqrt720 = 12sqrt5 ~ 26.83. Or delta  = 1/2bc
    sin A = 1/2 x 8 x 9 x sqrt5/3 = 12sqrt5, since sin A = sqrt(1 - 4/9) = sqrt5/3. Common
    mistake: in cos A = (b^2 + c^2 - a^2)/(2bc) putting the wrong side on the
    minus: the side OPPOSITE the angle is the one subtracted. Now you try:
    angles of the triangle with sides 3, 5, 7. (the largest angle is 120 degrees
    exactly; the others 21.79 degrees and 38.21 degrees)

D4. In triangle ABC, A = 30 degrees, a = 6 cm and b = 10 cm. Show that there are two
    possible triangles and solve both.
    Answer: Triangle 1: B ~ 56.44 degrees, C ~ 93.56 degrees, c ~ 11.98 cm. Triangle 2:
    B ~ 123.56 degrees, C ~ 26.44 degrees, c ~ 5.34 cm.
    Teacher explains: The height from C to the line AB is
    h = b sin A = 10 x 0.5 = 5. Since 5 < 6 < 10 (h < a < b), the side a can
    reach the line AB in TWO places:
                    C
                  / /|\
             10 /  / | \  6
              /  6/  |5 \
            /30 degrees /   |   \
          A-----B2---+----B1       AB2 = 5.34, AB1 = 11.98
    Sine rule: sin B = b sin A/a = 10 x 0.5/6 = 5/6. B = sin^-^1(5/6) = 56.44 degrees OR
    B = 180 degrees - 56.44 degrees = 123.56 degrees; both leave room for C (A + B < 180 degrees).
       B1 = 56.44 degrees:  C = 93.56 degrees,  c = a sin C/sin A = 6 x 0.99807/0.5 = 11.98
       B2 = 123.56 degrees: C = 26.44 degrees,  c = 6 x 0.44530/0.5 = 5.34
    Check: the two values of c add to 2b cos A = 20 x 0.8660 = 17.32 (they are
    the roots of c^2 - 2bc cos A + b^2 - a^2 = 0, which is the cosine rule written
    as a quadratic in c). Common mistake: giving only the calculator value
    56.44 degrees. Now you try: A = 30 degrees, b = 10: how many triangles when a = 4, 5, 8,
    12? (0; 1, right-angled; 2; 1)

D5. Explain all the cases of SSA (angle A, sides a and b given) when A is acute,
    using h = b sin A. Then decide the number of triangles for A = 40 degrees, b = 12
    and a = 7, 12 sin 40 degrees, 9, 15.
    Answer: a < h: none; a = h: one; h < a < b: two; a >= b: one. For the data
    (h = 7.71): a = 7: none; a = h: one; a = 9: two; a = 15: one.
    Teacher explains: Swing the side a like a door hinged at C: it must reach
    the ray from A.
       a < h           a = h            h < a < b          a >= b
       too short       touches once     cuts the ray       cuts once (the other
                       (right angle)    twice              point is behind A)
    With A = 40 degrees, b = 12: h = 12 x sin 40 degrees = 7.713. a = 7 < h: no triangle (sine
    rule would give sin B = 12 sin 40 degrees/7 = 1.1019 > 1, impossible). a = h:
    B = 90 degrees exactly, one triangle. a = 9: 7.71 < 9 < 12, two triangles,
    sin B = 0.8571, B = 58.99 degrees or 121.01 degrees. a = 15 >= 12: one triangle, B = 30.95 degrees
    (the value 149.05 degrees is impossible because then A + B > 180 degrees). If A is obtuse
    or right: one triangle when a > b, none otherwise. Now you try: A = 120 degrees,
    b = 5: how many triangles for a = 4 and a = 7? (none; one)

D6. Find the area of triangle PQR with PQ = 9 cm, PR = 14 cm and angle P = 40 degrees. If
    instead the area is 42 cm^2 with the same two sides, find angle P.
    Answer: Area ~ 40.50 cm^2. angle P ~ 41.81 degrees or 138.19 degrees.
    Teacher explains: With two sides and the INCLUDED angle: area
    = 1/2 x PQ x PR x sin P = 1/2 x 9 x 14 x sin 40 degrees = 63 x 0.64279 = 40.50 cm^2.
    Why: the height from Q to PR is 9 sin P, and area = 1/2 x base x height. For
    the reverse problem: 42 = 63 sin P, sin P = 2/3, P = 41.81 degrees or
    180 degrees - 41.81 degrees = 138.19 degrees. BOTH give the same area, because
    sin P = sin(180 degrees - P): two different triangles (one acute at P, one obtuse).
    Common mistake: using a side and an angle that are not included, such as
    1/2 x PQ x QR x sin P. Now you try: area of a triangle with sides 5 and 8 and
    included angle 150 degrees. (1/2 x 5 x 8 x 1/2 = 10)

D7. Prove the sine rule in the form a/sin A = 2R, and prove the projection
    formula a = b cos C + c cos B. Deduce the cosine rule.
    Answer: Proofs below.
    Teacher explains: Sine rule: draw the circumcircle (centre O, radius R) and
    the diameter BD. The angle BDC equals A (angles in the same segment; if A is
    obtuse, BDC = 180 degrees - A, and sin is the same). Angle BCD = 90 degrees (angle in a
    semicircle). In the right triangle BCD: BC = BD sin(BDC), i.e. a = 2R sin A.
    The same for b and c gives a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C = 2R. Projection:
    drop the perpendicular from A to BC at D. If B and C are acute, BD = c cos B
    and DC = b cos C, so a = BD + DC = b cos C + c cos B (the formula stays true
    when an angle is obtuse, because then the cosine is negative). Cosine rule:
    write the three projection formulas, multiply them by a, -b, -c and add:
       a^2 - b^2 - c^2 = ab cos C + ac cos B - bc cos A - ba cos C - ca cos B
                     - cb cos A = -2bc cos A
    so a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos A. Check with a = 7, b = 8, c = 9 (D3):
    cos C = 2/7 and cos B = 11/21, so b cos C + c cos B = 16/7 + 33/7 = 49/7 = 7
    = a. Now you try: verify c = a cos B + b cos A for the 7, 8, 9 triangle.
    (7 x 11/21 + 8 x 2/3 = 11/3 + 16/3 = 9)

D8. A ship leaves port P and sails 40 km on a bearing of 060 degrees to Q, then 25 km
    on a bearing of 130 degrees to R. Find the distance PR and the bearing of R from P.
    Answer: PR ~ 53.94 km on a bearing of about 085.82 degrees.
    Teacher explains: Draw north lines at P and Q. At Q the direction back to P
    is the bearing 240 degrees (060 degrees + 180 degrees), and QR is on 130 degrees, so the angle
    PQR = 240 degrees - 130 degrees = 110 degrees.
        N           N
        |           |   Q
        |        .  +-----.  130 degrees
        |     .   110 degrees      .
        |  .  40              . 25
        P  060 degrees                  R
    Cosine rule: PR^2 = 40^2 + 25^2 - 2 x 40 x 25 x cos 110 degrees. Since
    2000 x cos 110 degrees = -684.04, PR^2 = 1600 + 625 + 684.04 = 2909.04 and
    PR = 53.94 km. Then the angle QPR from the sine rule:
    sin QPR = 25 sin 110 degrees/53.94 = 0.43556, QPR = 25.82 degrees, and the bearing of R is
    060 degrees + 25.82 degrees = 085.82 degrees. Common mistake: using the angle 130 degrees - 60 degrees = 70 degrees as
    the angle inside the triangle; draw the north lines! Now you try: find the
    bearing of P from R. (085.82 degrees + 180 degrees = 265.82 degrees)

D9. From a point A on level ground the angle of elevation of the top T of a
    tower is 30 degrees. After walking 20 m towards the tower, to B, it is 45 degrees. Find
    the height of the tower exactly and to 2 d.p.
    Answer: Height = 10(sqrt3 + 1) ~ 27.32 m.
    Teacher explains: In triangle ABT: angle A = 30 degrees, angle
    ABT = 180 degrees - 45 degrees = 135 degrees, so angle ATB = 180 degrees - 30 degrees - 135 degrees = 15 degrees. Sine rule
    for BT:
       BT/sin 30 degrees = AB/sin 15 degrees   ->   BT = 20 x (1/2)/sin 15 degrees = 10/sin 15 degrees
    Height h = BT sin 45 degrees = 10 sin 45 degrees/sin 15 degrees. With sin 15 degrees = (sqrt6 - sqrt2)/4
    (topic 8.9):
       h = 10 x (sqrt2/2) x 4/(sqrt6 - sqrt2) = 20sqrt2/(sqrt6 - sqrt2) = 20/(sqrt3 - 1)
         = 20(sqrt3 + 1)/2 = 10(sqrt3 + 1) ~ 27.32 m
    Check with right triangles: h = x tan 45 degrees = (x + 20) tan 30 degrees gives
    x = (x + 20)/sqrt3, x(sqrt3 - 1) = 20, x = 10(sqrt3 + 1), the same. The sine-rule
    method also works when the ground is sloping or the tower leans, where right
    triangles fail. Now you try: with angles 30 degrees and 60 degrees and AB = 30 m, find the
    height. (15sqrt3 ~ 25.98 m)

D10. Prove that in any triangle (b^2 - c^2)/a^2 = sin(B - C)/sin A. Check it for
     the triangle A = 50 degrees, B = 70 degrees, C = 60 degrees.
     Answer: Proof below; both sides ~ 0.2267 for that triangle.
     Teacher explains: By the sine rule a = 2R sin A etc., so
        (b^2 - c^2)/a^2 = (sin^2B - sin^2C)/sin^2A
     From topic 8.9, sin^2B - sin^2C = sin(B + C) sin(B - C), and
     sin(B + C) = sin(180 degrees - A) = sin A. So the right side is
     sin A sin(B - C)/sin^2A = sin(B - C)/sin A. Check:
     sin 10 degrees/sin 50 degrees = 0.17365/0.76604 = 0.22668; with 2R = 1, b^2 - c^2
     = sin^270 degrees - sin^260 degrees = 0.88302 - 0.75 = 0.13302 and a^2 = sin^250 degrees = 0.58682,
     ratio 0.22668. The method "replace sides by 2R sin" turns side identities
     into angle identities. Now you try: prove a cos A + b cos B = c cos(A - B).
     (the left side is R(sin 2A + sin 2B) = 2R sin(A + B) cos(A - B)
     = c cos(A - B))

D11. For the triangle with sides a = 13, b = 14, c = 15 find the area, the
     circumradius R, the inradius r and the length of the median from A.
     Answer: Area 84; R = 65/8 = 8.125; r = 4; median m_a = sqrt(673)/2 ~ 12.97.
     Teacher explains: s = (13 + 14 + 15)/2 = 21; Heron:
     delta  = sqrt(21 x 8 x 7 x 6) = sqrt7056 = 84.
        R = abc/(4delta ) = 13 x 14 x 15/336 = 2730/336 = 65/8
        r = delta /s = 84/21 = 4
     For the median AM (M the midpoint of BC, BM = 6.5) use the cosine rule in
     triangles ABM and ABC with the common angle B: cos B = (a^2 + c^2 - b^2)/(2ac)
     = (169 + 225 - 196)/390 = 198/390 = 33/65, then AM^2
     = c^2 + (a/2)^2 - 2c(a/2) cos B = 225 + 42.25 - 195 x 33/65 = 267.25 - 99
     = 168.25, AM = sqrt168.25 = sqrt673/2 ~ 12.97. General formula (Apollonius): m_a^2
     = (2b^2 + 2c^2 - a^2)/4 = (392 + 450 - 169)/4 = 673/4. The 13-14-15 triangle
     is famous because its area and its altitude to side 14 (12) are whole
     numbers. Now you try: find R and r for the triangle with sides 3, 4, 5.
     (R = 5/2, r = 1)

D12. A farmer's field ABCD has sides AB = 40 m, BC = 55 m, CD = 35 m, DA = 50 m,
     and the diagonal AC = 60 m (measured with a chain). Find the area of the
     field in m^2 and in hectares, and the angles ABC and ADC.
     Answer: Area ~ 1944.18 m^2 ~ 0.19 hectare; angle ABC ~ 76.53 degrees, angle ADC ~ 87.95 degrees.
     Teacher explains: A surveyor splits the field along the diagonal into two
     triangles whose three sides are known, then uses Heron's formula for each.
        delta ABC: s = (40 + 55 + 60)/2 = 77.5
              area = sqrt(77.5 x 37.5 x 22.5 x 17.5) = 1069.74 m^2
        delta ACD: s = (35 + 50 + 60)/2 = 72.5
              area = sqrt(72.5 x 37.5 x 22.5 x 12.5) = 874.44 m^2
     Total 1944.18 m^2; 1 hectare = 10,000 m^2, so about 0.19 ha. Angles by the
     cosine rule: cos ABC = (40^2 + 55^2 - 60^2)/(2 x 40 x 55) = 1025/4400
     = 41/176, angle ABC = 76.53 degrees; cos ADC = (35^2 + 50^2 - 60^2)/(2 x 35 x 50)
     = 125/3500 = 1/28, angle ADC = 87.95 degrees. The four sides alone do NOT fix the shape
     of a quadrilateral (it can flex), which is why the diagonal is measured.
     Common mistake: using Heron's formula on all four sides at once
     (Brahmagupta's formula works only for cyclic quadrilaterals). Now you try:
     a triangular plot has sides 30 m, 40 m and 50 m. Find its area. (600 m^2; it
     is right-angled)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always draw and label the triangle, putting each side opposite its
  angle; decide first which rule fits (a side with its opposite angle known:
  sine rule; otherwise cosine rule); keep the calculator in DEGREE mode; store
  intermediate values in memory instead of retyping rounded numbers; in SSA
  problems always test 180 degrees - B. Harder: prove Heron's formula from the cosine
  rule and 1/2bc sin A; show that r = 4R sin(A/2) sin(B/2) sin(C/2) and check it
  for the 13-14-15 triangle; for which values of a does A = 35 degrees, b = 20 give
  exactly one triangle? (a = 20 sin 35 degrees ~ 11.47 or a >= 20); a triangle has sides
  x, x + 1, x + 2 and its largest angle is twice its smallest: find x (x = 4,
  sides 4, 5, 6).

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.13 - COMPLEX NUMBERS: ALGEBRA, ARGAND PLANE, MODULUS-ARGUMENT FORM
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - i is a number with i^2 = -1. A COMPLEX NUMBER is z = a + bi with a, b real:
    a = Re z (real part), b = Im z (imaginary part, a REAL number). Two complex
    numbers are equal only if their real parts are equal AND their imaginary
    parts are equal.
  - POWERS OF i repeat with period 4: i^1 = i, i^2 = -1, i^3 = -i, i^4 = 1; so i^n
    depends on the remainder of n / 4. Also 1/i = -i.
  - ARITHMETIC: add and multiply like algebra, replacing i^2 by -1. Divide by
    multiplying top and bottom by the CONJUGATE of the denominator:
    (a + bi)(a - bi) = a^2 + b^2.
    conjugate of a sum/product/quotient is the sum/product/quotient of the
  - ARGAND PLANE: z = a + bi is the point (a, b). MODULUS |z| = sqrt(a^2 + b^2)
    (distance from 0); |z_1 - z_2| is the distance between the points.
    |z_1z_2| = |z_1||z_2|, |z_1/z_2| = |z_1|/|z_2|, |z_1 + z_2| <= |z_1| + |z_2| (triangle
    inequality).
  - ARGUMENT: the angle theta from the positive real axis to the point. The
    PRINCIPAL argument satisfies -pi < theta <= pi. Find the reference angle tan^-^1|b/a|
    and place it in the right quadrant (QII: pi - alpha, QIII: -pi + alpha, QIV: -alpha).
    arg 0 is not defined.
  - MODULUS-ARGUMENT (POLAR) FORM: z = r(cos theta + i sin theta) = re^(itheta) (Euler).
    Multiplying MULTIPLIES moduli and ADDS arguments; dividing divides moduli
    and subtracts arguments (adjust by 2pi to stay in (-pi, pi]). Multiplying by i
    rotates a point by 90 degrees anticlockwise.
  - LOCI: |z - z_0| = r is a circle, centre z_0, radius r; |z - z_1| = |z - z_2| is
    the perpendicular bisector of z_1z_2; arg(z - z_0) = theta is a half-line from z_0
    (z_0 excluded). Replace z by x + iy to get the Cartesian equation.
  - SQUARE ROOTS of a + bi: put (x + iy)^2 = a + bi, so x^2 - y^2 = a, 2xy = b, and
    use x^2 + y^2 = sqrt(a^2 + b^2). There are always exactly two roots, negatives of
    each other.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Simplify i^5, i^1^0, i^2^0^2^6, i^-^3 and 1 + i + i^2 + ... + i^1^0^0.
    Answer: i^5 = i, i^1^0 = -1, i^2^0^2^6 = -1, i^-^3 = i, and the sum is 1.
    Teacher explains: The powers cycle every 4:
       n mod 4      0     1     2     3
       i^n           1     i    -1    -i
    i^5: 5 = 4 + 1, so i^5 = i. i^1^0: 10 = 8 + 2, so -1. i^2^0^2^6: 2026 = 4 x 506 + 2,
    so -1. i^-^3 = 1/i^3 = 1/(-i) = i (or: -3 = -4 + 1, remainder 1). The sum has
    101 terms; each block of four consecutive powers adds to 1 + i - 1 - i = 0,
    and 101 = 4 x 25 + 1, so after 25 zero blocks only the last term i^1^0^0 = 1
    remains. (Or use the geometric series:
    (1 - i^1^0^1)/(1 - i) = (1 - i)/(1 - i) = 1.) Common mistake:
    sqrt(-4) x sqrt(-9) = sqrt36 = 6. Wrong! sqrt(-4) = 2i and sqrt(-9) = 3i, and
    2i x 3i = 6i^2 = -6: the rule sqrta sqrtb = sqrt(ab) holds only for a, b >= 0. Now you
    try: i^9^9 and i^-^1. (-i; -i)

D2. Write (3 + 4i)(2 - i) and (3 + 4i)/(1 - 2i) in the form a + bi.
    Answer: 10 + 5i and -1 + 2i.
    Teacher explains: Multiply like brackets (FOIL), then use i^2 = -1:
       (3 + 4i)(2 - i) = 6 - 3i + 8i - 4i^2 = 6 + 5i + 4 = 10 + 5i
    For division, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom,
    1 + 2i, which makes the bottom REAL:
       (3 + 4i)(1 + 2i)   3 + 6i + 4i + 8i^2   -5 + 10i
       ---------------- = ----------------- = -------- = -1 + 2i
       (1 - 2i)(1 + 2i)        1 - 4i^2            5
    Check by multiplying back: (-1 + 2i)(1 - 2i) = -1 + 2i + 2i - 4i^2 = 3 + 4i.
    The denominator is always a^2 + b^2 = 1 + 4 = 5. Common mistake: dividing real
    parts and imaginary parts separately: 3/1 + (4/-2)i = 3 - 2i is wrong. Now
    you try: (2 + i)^2 and 1/(1 + i). (3 + 4i; 1/2 - i/2)

    real and non-negative.
       x + iy + 2(x - iy) = 6 - i   ->   3x - iy = 6 - i
    Equate REAL parts: 3x = 6, x = 2. Equate IMAGINARY parts: -y = -1, y = 1. So
    z = 2 + i. Check: 2 + i + 2(2 - i) = 6 - i. In general
    (a + bi)(a - bi) = a^2 - (bi)^2 = a^2 + b^2, which is real and >= 0, and equals 0
    only when z = 0. This is why multiplying by the conjugate clears i from a
    z = 3 + 2i)

D4. Find the modulus and principal argument of z_1 = 1 + isqrt3, z_2 = -1 + i,
    z_3 = -sqrt3 - i and z_4 = 2 - 2i. Mark them on an Argand diagram.
    Answer: |z_1| = 2, arg pi/3; |z_2| = sqrt2, arg 3pi/4; |z_3| = 2, arg -5pi/6;
    |z_4| = 2sqrt2, arg -pi/4.
    Teacher explains: Plot each point first, THEN find the angle:
                       Im
         z_2 (-1, 1) *   |   * z_1 (1, sqrt3)
                        |
         ---------------+--------------- Re
       z_3 (-sqrt3, -1) *   |
                        |   * z_4 (2, -2)
    Reference angle alpha = tan^-^1|b/a|: for z_1, tan^-^1sqrt3 = pi/3, QI, so arg = pi/3. z_2:
    alpha = pi/4, QII, arg = pi - pi/4 = 3pi/4. z_3: alpha = tan^-^1(1/sqrt3) = pi/6, QIII,
    arg = -pi + pi/6 = -5pi/6 (principal: between -pi and pi, so NOT 7pi/6). z_4:
    alpha = pi/4, QIV, arg = -pi/4. Moduli: |z_1| = sqrt(1 + 3) = 2, |z_2| = sqrt2, |z_3| = 2,
    |z_4| = sqrt8 = 2sqrt2. Common mistake: calculator tan^-^1(b/a) for z_3 gives
    tan^-^1(-1/-sqrt3) = pi/6, which is the wrong quadrant. Now you try: modulus and
    argument of -4 and -3i. (4, pi; 3, -pi/2)

D5. Write z = -2 + 2i in modulus-argument form and in exponential form. Write
    w = 4(cos(2pi/3) + i sin(2pi/3)) in the form a + bi.
    Answer: z = 2sqrt2(cos(3pi/4) + i sin(3pi/4)) = 2sqrt2 e^(3ipi/4); w = -2 + 2sqrt3 i.
    Teacher explains: |z| = sqrt(4 + 4) = 2sqrt2; z is in QII with reference angle
    pi/4, so arg z = 3pi/4. Polar form r(cos theta + i sin theta), exponential form
    re^(itheta) (Euler's formula e^(itheta) = cos theta + i sin theta). For w: cos(2pi/3) = -1/2
    and sin(2pi/3) = sqrt3/2, so w = 4(-1/2) + 4(sqrt3/2)i = -2 + 2sqrt3 i. Check:
    |w|^2 = 4 + 12 = 16. Polar form is often written r cis theta. Special case:
    e^(ipi) = -1, so e^(ipi) + 1 = 0 (Euler's identity, linking five famous
    numbers). Common mistake: writing 2sqrt2(cos(-pi/4) + i sin(-pi/4)), the angle
    from tan^-^1(2/(-2)) = -pi/4, which is the point 2 - 2i. Now you try: write -5i
    and 3e^(-ipi/6) in the other form. (5(cos(-pi/2) + i sin(-pi/2)); 3sqrt3/2 - 3i/2)

D6. If z_1 = 2(cos(pi/3) + i sin(pi/3)) and z_2 = 3(cos(pi/4) + i sin(pi/4)), find
    z_1z_2 and z_1/z_2 in polar form. What does multiplication by i do to a point?
    Answer: z_1z_2 = 6(cos(7pi/12) + i sin(7pi/12));
    z_1/z_2 = (2/3)(cos(pi/12) + i sin(pi/12)). Multiplying by i rotates by 90 degrees
    anticlockwise.
    Teacher explains: Expand (cos A + i sin A)(cos B + i sin B)
    = (cos A cos B - sin A sin B) + i(sin A cos B + cos A sin B)
    = cos(A + B) + i sin(A + B), by the compound-angle formulas (8.9). So moduli
    MULTIPLY and arguments ADD:
       z_1z_2:  r = 2 x 3 = 6,    theta = pi/3 + pi/4 = 7pi/12
       z_1/z_2: r = 2/3,          theta = pi/3 - pi/4 = pi/12
    Since i = 1(cos(pi/2) + i sin(pi/2)), multiplying by i keeps the modulus and
    adds pi/2 to the argument: a quarter turn anticlockwise. Example:
    i(3 + i) = -1 + 3i; the point (3, 1) moves to (-1, 3). As a check in
    Cartesian form: z_1 = 1 + sqrt3 i, z_2 = (3sqrt2/2)(1 + i), z_1z_2
    = (3sqrt2/2)(1 - sqrt3 + i(1 + sqrt3)) ~ -1.553 + 5.796i, and 6 cos(105 degrees) = -1.553,
    6 sin(105 degrees) = 5.796. Now you try: find (1 + i)(sqrt3 + i) in polar form.
    (2sqrt2(cos(5pi/12) + i sin(5pi/12)))

D7. Describe the locus of z when (i) |z - (1 + 2i)| = 3, (ii) |z - 1| = |z + i|.
    Give Cartesian equations.
    Answer: (i) The circle centre (1, 2), radius 3: (x - 1)^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 9.
    (ii) The perpendicular bisector of the points 1 and -i: the line y = -x.
    Teacher explains: |z - w| is the DISTANCE between the points z and w. (i)
    All points at distance 3 from 1 + 2i: a circle. Algebra:
    z - (1 + 2i) = (x - 1) + (y - 2)i, so its modulus squared is
    (x - 1)^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 9. (ii) Points equally far from 1 and from -i: the
    perpendicular bisector of the segment from (1, 0) to (0, -1). Algebra:
    (x - 1)^2 + y^2 = x^2 + (y + 1)^2, so -2x + 1 = 2y + 1, y = -x. Check:
    z = 2 - 2i gives |1 - 2i| = sqrt5 and |2 - i| = sqrt5. Common mistake: reading
    |z + i| as distance from +i (it is distance from -i, since
    z + i = z - (-i)). Now you try: the locus |z + 2| = 2|z - 1|.
    ((x + 2)^2 + y^2 = 4((x - 1)^2 + y^2): x^2 + y^2 - 4x = 0, circle centre (2, 0),
    radius 2)

D8. Find the square roots of 5 + 12i and of -8 - 6i.
    Answer: +/-(3 + 2i) and +/-(1 - 3i).
    Teacher explains: Let (x + iy)^2 = 5 + 12i. Then x^2 - y^2 + 2ixy = 5 + 12i:
       x^2 - y^2 = 5,   2xy = 12,   and   x^2 + y^2 = |5 + 12i| = 13
    Adding: 2x^2 = 18, x = +/-3; subtracting: 2y^2 = 8, y = +/-2. Since xy = 6 > 0, x
    and y have the SAME sign: 3 + 2i or -3 - 2i. Check:
    (3 + 2i)^2 = 9 + 12i - 4 = 5 + 12i. For -8 - 6i: x^2 - y^2 = -8, 2xy = -6,
    x^2 + y^2 = 10, so x^2 = 1, y^2 = 9, and xy = -3 < 0 means opposite signs:
    1 - 3i or -1 + 3i. The third equation (from the moduli) avoids a quartic.
    Common mistake: forgetting to use the sign of xy and listing four "roots".
    Now you try: square roots of -3 + 4i and of 2i. (+/-(1 + 2i); +/-(1 + i))

D9. Find real numbers x and y such that (x + iy)(2 - 3i) = 4 + i.
    Answer: x = 5/13, y = 14/13.
    Teacher explains: Method 1: divide. x + iy = (4 + i)/(2 - 3i)
    = (4 + i)(2 + 3i)/13 = (8 + 12i + 2i + 3i^2)/13 = (5 + 14i)/13. Method 2:
    expand and equate parts: (2x + 3y) + (2y - 3x)i = 4 + i, so
       2x + 3y = 4
       -3x + 2y = 1     ->   x = 5/13,  y = 14/13
    (multiply the first by 3, the second by 2 and add: 13y = 14). Both give the
    same answer. Equating real and imaginary parts turns ONE complex equation
    into TWO real equations; this is the key idea for solving equations in
    complex numbers. Now you try: find real x, y with
    (x - 2y) + (2x + y)i = 1 + 7i. (x = 3, y = 1)

D10. Prove that |z_1z_2| = |z_1||z_2| and that |z_1 + z_2| <= |z_1| + |z_2|. When is
     there equality in the second? Check with z_1 = 3 + 4i, z_2 = 5 - 12i.
     Answer: Proofs below; |z_1z_2| = 65 = 5 x 13 and
     |z_1 + z_2| = sqrt128 ~ 11.31 <= 18. Equality holds when one number is a
     non-negative real multiple of the other.
                   <= |z_1|^2 + |z_2|^2 + 2|z_1||z_2| = (|z_1| + |z_2|)^2
     triangle is shorter than the sum of the other two. Check:
     z_1z_2 = 15 - 36i + 20i - 48i^2 = 63 - 16i, |63 - 16i| = sqrt(3969 + 256) = sqrt4225
     = 65 = 5 x 13. z_1 + z_2 = 8 - 8i, |8 - 8i| = 8sqrt2 ~ 11.31 < 5 + 13 = 18. Now
     you try: show |z_1 - z_2| >= ||z_1| - |z_2|| for the same numbers.
     (|-2 + 16i| = sqrt260 ~ 16.12 >= 8)

D11. If |z - 3 - 4i| = 2, find the greatest and least values of |z|. Describe
     the region |z - 3i| < |z + 3i| and the half-line arg(z - 1) = pi/4.
     Answer: Greatest |z| = 7, least 3. |z - 3i| < |z + 3i| is the upper
     half-plane y > 0. arg(z - 1) = pi/4 is the half-line y = x - 1 with x > 1.
     Teacher explains: z lies on the circle with centre 3 + 4i and radius 2. The
     centre is at distance |3 + 4i| = 5 from the origin. The line from 0 through
     the centre meets the circle at distances 5 - 2 = 3 and 5 + 2 = 7: these are
     the least and greatest values of |z| (triangle inequality:
     5 - 2 <= |z| <= 5 + 2). The nearest point is (3/5)(3 + 4i) = 1.8 + 2.4i, the
     farthest (7/5)(3 + 4i) = 4.2 + 5.6i. For the region: points nearer to 3i
     than to -3i; the perpendicular bisector of these two points is the real
     axis, so the region is Im z > 0 (strict, so the axis is excluded). For
     arg(z - 1) = pi/4: the vector from 1 to z makes 45 degrees with the real axis, so
     z = 1 + t + ti with t > 0, i.e. y = x - 1, x > 1 (the point 1 itself has no
     argument). Now you try: least and greatest |z + 1| when |z - 2i| = 1.
     (sqrt5 - 1; sqrt5 + 1)

D12. In AC circuits engineers use complex impedances (and write j for i). Two
     branches with impedances Z_1 = 3 + 4j ohms and Z_2 = 6 - 8j ohms are joined
     in parallel. Find the total impedance Z = Z_1Z_2/(Z_1 + Z_2) and its modulus.
     Answer: Z = (450 + 200j)/97 ~ 4.64 + 2.06j ohms; |Z| = 50/sqrt97 ~ 5.08 ohms.
     Teacher explains: Numerator: (3 + 4j)(6 - 8j) = 18 - 24j + 24j - 32j^2
     = 18 + 32 = 50. Denominator: Z_1 + Z_2 = 9 - 4j. So
        Z = 50/(9 - 4j) = 50(9 + 4j)/(81 + 16) = (450 + 200j)/97
          ~ 4.639 + 2.062j
        |Z| = 50/|9 - 4j| = 50/sqrt97 ~ 5.077
     the division. Notice |Z_1| = 5 and |Z_2| = 10, yet |Z| ~ 5.08 is NOT
     (5 x 10)/(5 + 10) = 3.33: moduli do not add. Now you try: find Z_1 + Z_2 and
     Z_1Z_2 for Z_1 = 2 + j, Z_2 = 1 - 3j. (3 - 2j; 5 - 5j)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw EVERY complex number as a point on squared paper before
  finding its argument; make a table of the four quadrant rules for the
  principal argument; practise i-powers with the cycle i, -1, -i, 1; when
  dividing, write the conjugate step in full; for loci, first say it in words
  ("distance from 2 equals 1"). Harder: prove that if |z| = 1 then
  (z - 1)/(z + 1) is purely imaginary (z != -1); find the complex numbers with
  equilateral triangle when z_1^2 + z_2^2 + z_3^2 = z_1z_2 + z_2z_3 + z_3z_1 and test it
  segment).

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.14 - DE MOIVRE'S THEOREM; ROOTS OF UNITY
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - DE MOIVRE'S THEOREM: (cos theta + i sin theta)^n = cos ntheta + i sin ntheta for every
    integer n (proved by induction for n >= 1, and for negative n using
    1/(cos theta + i sin theta) = cos theta - i sin theta). In exponential form:
    (e^(itheta))^n = e^(intheta).
  - POWERS: to find (a + bi)^n write a + bi = r(cos theta + i sin theta); then
    (a + bi)^n = r^n(cos ntheta + i sin ntheta). Much faster than the binomial expansion:
    (1 + i)^1^0 = (sqrt2)^1^0(cos(10pi/4) + i sin(10pi/4)) = 32i.
  - nth ROOTS OF UNITY: the solutions of z^n = 1 are
    z = cos(2kpi/n) + i sin(2kpi/n) = e^(2kpii/n), k = 0, 1, ..., n - 1. They are
    the vertices of a regular n-gon on the unit circle, one vertex at 1. If
    alpha = e^(2pii/n), the roots are 1, alpha, alpha^2, ..., alpha^n^-^1.
  - SUM AND PRODUCT: for n >= 2 the n roots add to 0
    sum of their m-th powers is n if n divides m, otherwise 0.
  - nth ROOTS OF ANY z = r(cos theta + i sin theta): w_k
    = r^(1/n)(cos((theta + 2kpi)/n) + i sin((theta + 2kpi)/n)), k = 0, ..., n - 1: n
    equally spaced points on the circle of radius r^(1/n).
  - TRIGONOMETRY FROM DE MOIVRE: expand (cos theta + i sin theta)^n by the binomial
    theorem and compare real and imaginary parts to get cos ntheta, sin ntheta in powers
    of cos theta, sin theta. Conversely, with z = e^(itheta): z + 1/z = 2 cos theta,
    z - 1/z = 2i sin theta, z^n + z^-^n = 2 cos ntheta, which turns powers such as cos^4theta
    into sums of multiple angles.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. State De Moivre's theorem and prove it for positive integers n by induction.
    Show that it also holds for n = -1.
    Answer: (cos theta + i sin theta)^n = cos ntheta + i sin ntheta; proof below.
    Teacher explains: Let P(n) be the statement. P(1) is obvious. Assume P(k):
         = (cos ktheta cos theta - sin ktheta sin theta) + i(sin ktheta cos theta + cos ktheta sin theta)
         = cos(k + 1)theta + i sin(k + 1)theta          (compound angles, 8.9)
    so P(k + 1) is true, and by induction (8.6) P(n) holds for all n >= 1. For
    n = -1: 1/(cos theta + i sin theta) = (cos theta - i sin theta)/(cos^2theta + sin^2theta)
    = cos theta - i sin theta = cos(-theta) + i sin(-theta). Applying this to the positive case
    gives every negative n; n = 0 gives 1 = 1. In words: to raise a number of
    modulus 1 to the power n, multiply its angle by n. Check theta = pi/2, n = 2:
    i^2 = cos pi + i sin pi = -1. Now you try: simplify (cos(pi/9) + i sin(pi/9))^6.
    (cos(2pi/3) + i sin(2pi/3) = -1/2 + sqrt3 i/2)

D2. Find (1 + i)^1^0 and (1 + i)^-^4.
    Answer: (1 + i)^1^0 = 32i; (1 + i)^-^4 = -1/4.
    Teacher explains: Change to polar form: |1 + i| = sqrt2, arg = pi/4, so
    1 + i = sqrt2(cos(pi/4) + i sin(pi/4)).
     (1 + i)^1^0 = (sqrt2)^1^0(cos(10pi/4) + i sin(10pi/4)) = 32(cos(5pi/2) + i sin(5pi/2))
              = 32(0 + i) = 32i
     (1 + i)^-^4 = (sqrt2)^-^4(cos(-pi) + i sin(-pi)) = (1/4)(-1) = -1/4
    Quick check for the first: (1 + i)^2 = 2i, so (1 + i)^1^0 = (2i)^5 = 32i^5 = 32i.
    The binomial theorem would need eleven terms. Common mistake: raising the
    modulus to the power but forgetting to multiply the ANGLE (writing
    32(cos(pi/4) + i sin(pi/4))). Now you try: (1 - i)^8 and (1 + i)^5. (16;
    -4 - 4i)

D3. Find (sqrt3 + i)^6 and (1 - sqrt3 i)^5 in the form a + bi.
    Answer: (sqrt3 + i)^6 = -64; (1 - sqrt3 i)^5 = 16 + 16sqrt3 i.
    Teacher explains: sqrt3 + i = 2(cos(pi/6) + i sin(pi/6)), so (sqrt3 + i)^6
    = 2^6(cos pi + i sin pi) = 64(-1) = -64. 1 - sqrt3 i = 2(cos(-pi/3) + i sin(-pi/3))
    (QIV), so
       (1 - sqrt3 i)^5 = 32(cos(-5pi/3) + i sin(-5pi/3))
                  = 32(cos(pi/3) + i sin(pi/3)) = 32(1/2 + (sqrt3/2)i)
                  = 16 + 16sqrt3 i
    (-5pi/3 and pi/3 differ by 2pi.) Reality check with moduli:
    |16 + 16sqrt3 i| = 16 x 2 = 32 = 2^5. Common mistake: taking arg(1 - sqrt3 i) = pi/3
    (wrong quadrant). Now you try: (-1 + i)^4 and (sqrt3 - i)^3. (-4; -8i)

    z^2 + z + 1 = 0, whose roots are z = (-1 +/- sqrt(1 - 4))/2 = (-1 +/- isqrt3)/2. By De
    roots of z^3 - 1 = 0 is 0). On the Argand diagram the three roots are the
    vertices of an equilateral triangle inscribed in the unit circle.

D6. Find the sixth roots of unity, mark them, and check that their sum is 0 and
    their product is -1.
    Answer: 1, 1/2 + sqrt3 i/2, -1/2 + sqrt3 i/2, -1, -1/2 - sqrt3 i/2, 1/2 - sqrt3 i/2.
    Teacher explains: z = cos(2kpi/6) + i sin(2kpi/6) = cos(kpi/3) + i sin(kpi/3),
    k = 0, ..., 5:
       k      0     1          2           3     4           5
       angle  0     pi/3        2pi/3        pi     4pi/3        5pi/3
       z      1   1/2+sqrt3i/2  -1/2+sqrt3i/2   -1   -1/2-sqrt3i/2   1/2-sqrt3i/2
    They form a regular hexagon with side 1. Sum: the real parts
    1 + 1/2 - 1/2 - 1 - 1/2 + 1/2 = 0 and the imaginary parts cancel in pairs.
    Product: the roots pair into conjugates (product |z|^2 = 1) except 1 and -1,
    the cube roots (k even) and the square roots +/-1 (k = 0, 3). Now you try:
    list the 4th roots of unity and their product. (1, i, -1, -i; -1)

D7. Prove that for n >= 2 the n-th roots of unity add to 0 and multiply to
    squares of the 4th roots of unity.
    Answer: Proof below; the first sum is 0; the sum of squares is 0.
    Teacher explains: The roots are the n roots of z^n - 1 = 0, a polynomial with
    no z^n^-^1 term and constant term -1. By the relations between roots and
    coefficients (sum of roots = -(coefficient of z^n^-^1),
    Alternatively with alpha = e^(2pii/n): 1 + alpha + ... + alpha^n^-^1 = (alpha^n - 1)/(alpha - 1) = 0
    since alpha^n = 1 and alpha != 1. For n = 5 the sum is 0. Squares of 1, i, -1, -i:
    1 - 1 + 1 - 1 = 0. In general the sum of the m-th powers is n when n divides
    m (every term is 1) and 0 otherwise (it is a geometric series with ratio
    try: product of the 5th roots of unity and sum of their cubes. (1; 0)

D8. Find the cube roots of 8i and show them on an Argand diagram.
    Answer: sqrt3 + i, -sqrt3 + i, -2i.
    Teacher explains: 8i = 8(cos(pi/2) + i sin(pi/2)). A cube root has modulus
       k = 0:  2(cos(pi/6) + i sin(pi/6))   = sqrt3 + i
       k = 1:  2(cos(5pi/6) + i sin(5pi/6)) = -sqrt3 + i
       k = 2:  2(cos(3pi/2) + i sin(3pi/2)) = -2i
    They lie on the circle of radius 2, 120 degrees apart (an equilateral triangle).
    the + 2kpi, which gives just one root. Now you try: the cube roots of -27.
    (3/2 + 3sqrt3 i/2, -3, 3/2 - 3sqrt3 i/2)

D9. Solve z^4 = -16 and write the roots in the form a + bi. Hence factorise
    z^4 + 16 into two real quadratic factors.
    Answer: z = +/-sqrt2 +/- sqrt2 i (all four sign choices);
    z^4 + 16 = (z^2 - 2sqrt2 z + 4)(z^2 + 2sqrt2 z + 4).
    Teacher explains: -16 = 16(cos pi + i sin pi); roots have modulus 16^(1/4) = 2
    and arguments (pi + 2kpi)/4 = pi/4, 3pi/4, 5pi/4, 7pi/4:
       2 cis(pi/4) = sqrt2 + sqrt2 i      2 cis(3pi/4) = -sqrt2 + sqrt2 i
       2 cis(5pi/4) = -sqrt2 - sqrt2 i    2 cis(7pi/4) = sqrt2 - sqrt2 i
    (cis theta is short for cos theta + i sin theta.) Pair each root with its conjugate:
    (z - (sqrt2 + sqrt2 i))(z - (sqrt2 - sqrt2 i)) = z^2 - 2sqrt2 z + 4, and similarly
    z^2 + 2sqrt2 z + 4. Multiply out to check: (z^2 + 4)^2 - 8z^2 = z^4 + 8z^2 + 16 - 8z^2
    = z^4 + 16. Real polynomials always factor into real linear and quadratic
    factors this way. Now you try: solve z^4 = -4. (+/-1 +/- i)

D10. Use De Moivre's theorem to express cos 3theta and sin 3theta in powers of cos theta and
     sin theta, and deduce a formula for tan 3theta.
     Answer: cos 3theta = 4cos^3theta - 3 cos theta; sin 3theta = 3 sin theta - 4 sin^3theta;
     tan 3theta = (3t - t^3)/(1 - 3t^2) with t = tan theta.
     Teacher explains: Write c = cos theta, s = sin theta. By De Moivre and the binomial
     theorem:
        cos 3theta + i sin 3theta = (c + is)^3 = c^3 + 3c^2(is) + 3c(is)^2 + (is)^3
                          = (c^3 - 3cs^2) + i(3c^2s - s^3)
     Equate real parts: cos 3theta = c^3 - 3c(1 - c^2) = 4c^3 - 3c. Imaginary parts:
     sin 3theta = 3(1 - s^2)s - s^3 = 3s - 4s^3. Divide the two expressions by c^3:
     tan 3theta = (3c^2s - s^3)/(c^3 - 3cs^2) = (3t - t^3)/(1 - 3t^2). Check at theta = 20 degrees:
     4(0.93969)^3 - 3(0.93969) = 0.5 = cos 60 degrees. This is quicker than repeated
     compound-angle formulas, especially for 5theta. Now you try: express cos 4theta in
     powers of cos theta. (8cos^4theta - 8cos^2theta + 1)

D11. Let z = cos theta + i sin theta. Show that z^n + 1/z^n = 2 cos ntheta and use it to write
     cos^4theta in terms of cos 4theta and cos 2theta. Hence find the exact value of
     cos^4(pi/8) + cos^4(3pi/8).
     Answer: cos^4theta = (cos 4theta + 4 cos 2theta + 3)/8; the value is 3/4.
     Teacher explains: By De Moivre z^n = cos ntheta + i sin ntheta and
     z^-^n = cos ntheta - i sin ntheta; adding, z^n + z^-^n = 2 cos ntheta. So 2 cos theta = z + 1/z
     and
        16cos^4theta = (z + 1/z)^4 = z^4 + 4z^2 + 6 + 4/z^2 + 1/z^4
                = (z^4 + 1/z^4) + 4(z^2 + 1/z^2) + 6 = 2 cos 4theta + 8 cos 2theta + 6
     so cos^4theta = (cos 4theta + 4 cos 2theta + 3)/8. At theta = pi/8: cos(pi/2) = 0,
     cos(pi/4) = sqrt2/2, giving (2sqrt2 + 3)/8; at theta = 3pi/8: cos(3pi/2) = 0,
     cos(3pi/4) = -sqrt2/2, giving (3 - 2sqrt2)/8. Sum: 6/8 = 3/4. Numerically
     0.72855 + 0.02145 = 0.75. Such "linearised" forms are exactly what is
     needed to integrate cos^4theta (8.44). Now you try: write sin^3theta in terms of
     sin 3theta and sin theta. ((3 sin theta - sin 3theta)/4)

D12. Using the fifth roots of unity, prove that cos(2pi/5) = (sqrt5 - 1)/4.
     Answer: Proof below.
     Teacher explains: Let z = e^(2pii/5) != 1. From
     z^5 - 1 = (z - 1)(z^4 + z^3 + z^2 + z + 1) = 0 we get z^4 + z^3 + z^2 + z + 1 = 0.
     Divide by z^2:
        (z^2 + 1/z^2) + (z + 1/z) + 1 = 0
     Put w = z + 1/z = 2 cos(2pi/5); then z^2 + 1/z^2 = w^2 - 2, so w^2 + w - 1 = 0
     and w = (-1 +/- sqrt5)/2. Since 2pi/5 = 72 degrees is acute, w > 0, so w = (sqrt5 - 1)/2
     and cos 72 degrees = (sqrt5 - 1)/4 ~ 0.30902 (calculator: cos 72 degrees = 0.30902). The
     other root (-1 - sqrt5)/2 = 2 cos(4pi/5) gives cos 144 degrees = -(1 + sqrt5)/4. This
     links roots of unity with the regular pentagon, which Gauss extended to
     construct the regular 17-gon with ruler and compasses. Now you try: use the
     same method with z = e^(2pii/7) to show
     cos(2pi/7) + cos(4pi/7) + cos(6pi/7) = -1/2. (the sum of the six non-real
     roots is -1)
