              o) yes (3 and 2)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw a quick sketch for every question (a line with a positive
  slope rises to the right; intercepts are where it crosses the axes); always
  convert to Ax + By + C = 0 before using distance, foot or image formulas;
  check an equation by substituting the given points; for "parallel" keep A and
  B, for "perpendicular" swap them and change one sign. Harder: find the
  equations of the lines through (1, 2) making 60 degrees with x + sqrt3y = 0; show that
  the bisectors of the angles between two lines are (a_1x + b_1y + c_1)/sqrt(a_1^2 +
  b_1^2) = +/-(a_2x + b_2y + c_2)/sqrt(a_2^2 + b_2^2) and find the incentre of a triangle with
  them; prove that the medians, altitudes and perpendicular bisectors of a
  triangle are each concurrent (centroid, orthocentre, circumcentre) and that
  these three points are collinear (the Euler line).

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.25 - CONIC SECTIONS: CIRCLE, PARABOLA, ELLIPSE, HYPERBOLA
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A CONIC is the curve cut from a double cone by a plane. Focus-directrix
    definition: a conic is the locus of P with PS = e x PM, where S is the
    FOCUS, PM the distance from P to the DIRECTRIX and e the ECCENTRICITY.
    e = 1: parabola; 0 < e < 1: ellipse; e > 1: hyperbola; a circle is the limit
    e = 0.
  - CIRCLE with centre (h, k) and radius r: (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2. GENERAL
    FORM x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (-g, -f) and radius
    sqrt(g^2 + f^2 - c): a real circle if g^2 + f^2 - c > 0, a point circle if it is 0,
    no real locus if it is negative. Divide first if x^2 and y^2 have a common
    coefficient other than 1. Circle on the DIAMETER from (x_1, y_1) to (x_2, y_2):
    (x - x_1)(x - x_2) + (y - y_1)(y - y_2) = 0. Circle through three points: put
    each point into the general form and solve for g, f, c.
  - PARABOLA (vertex at the origin, a > 0). y^2 = 4ax: focus (a, 0), directrix
    x = -a, axis y = 0, opens right. y^2 = -4ax: focus (-a, 0), directrix x = a,
    opens left. x^2 = 4ay: focus (0, a), directrix y = -a, opens up. x^2 = -4ay:
    focus (0, -a), directrix y = a, opens down. In every case the LATUS RECTUM
    (the focal chord perpendicular to the axis) has length 4a; for y^2 = 4ax its
    ends are (a, +/-2a).
  - SHIFTED PARABOLA: (y - k)^2 = 4a(x - h) has vertex (h, k), focus (h + a, k),
    directrix x = h - a, axis y = k (a may be negative: then it opens left).
    (x - h)^2 = 4a(y - k): vertex (h, k), focus (h, k + a), directrix y = k - a,
    axis x = h. Complete the square to reach these forms.
  - ELLIPSE x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 with a > b > 0: c^2 = a^2 - b^2, e = c/a < 1, foci
    (+/-c, 0) = (+/-ae, 0), vertices (+/-a, 0), ends of the minor axis (0, +/-b),
    directrices x = +/-a/e, latus rectum 2b^2/a. Major axis 2a, minor axis 2b. For
    every point P on it, PS + PS' = 2a. If the bigger number is under y^2 the
    major axis is vertical: foci (0, +/-c), directrices y = +/-a/e.
  - HYPERBOLA x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1: c^2 = a^2 + b^2, e = c/a > 1, foci (+/-c, 0),
    vertices (+/-a, 0), directrices x = +/-a/e, latus rectum 2b^2/a, ASYMPTOTES
    y = +/-(b/a)x, and |PS - PS'| = 2a. y^2/a^2 - x^2/b^2 = 1 opens up and down: foci
    (0, +/-c), asymptotes y = +/-(a/b)x. RECTANGULAR hyperbola: a = b, e = sqrt2
    (x^2 - y^2 = a^2, or xy = c^2 after a 45 degrees turn).
  - SHIFTED ellipse or hyperbola: complete the square to reach (x - h)^2/A +/-
    (y - k)^2/B = 1; the centre is (h, k) and everything else moves with it (foci
    (h +/- c, k) for a horizontal major or transverse axis).
  - IDENTIFYING Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0: with no xy term, A = C gives
    a circle, AC = 0 a parabola, AC > 0 an ellipse, AC < 0 a hyperbola; in
    general B^2 - 4AC < 0 ellipse (or circle), = 0 parabola, > 0 hyperbola.
    Degenerate cases (a point, a pair of lines, no real points) show up when
    completing the square.
  - TANGENT at (x_1, y_1) on the curve: replace x^2 by xx_1, y^2 by yy_1, x by
    (x + x_1)/2, y by (y + y_1)/2, xy by (xy_1 + x_1y)/2. So x^2 + y^2 = r^2 gives
    xx_1 + yy_1 = r^2, y^2 = 4ax gives yy_1 = 2a(x + x_1), and x^2/a^2 +/- y^2/b^2 = 1 gives
    xx_1/a^2 +/- yy_1/b^2 = 1. The line y = mx + c touches x^2 + y^2 = r^2 when
    c^2 = r^2(1 + m^2), y^2 = 4ax when c = a/m, x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 when
    c^2 = a^2m^2 + b^2.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A garden sprinkler at the point (2, -3) (units: metres) waters every point
    within 5 m of it. Write the equation of the boundary circle in centre-radius
    form and in general form. Is the tap at (5, 1) on the boundary, inside or
    outside? The bench at (6, 1)? The flower bed at (3, -1)?
    Answer: (x - 2)^2 + (y + 3)^2 = 25, i.e. x^2 + y^2 - 4x + 6y - 12 = 0. The tap
    is ON the circle, the bench is outside and the flower bed is inside.
    Teacher explains: A circle is the set of points at distance r from the
    centre (h, k). By the distance formula sqrt((x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2) = r, and
    squaring gives (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2. Here h = 2, k = -3, r = 5:
       (x - 2)^2 + (y - (-3))^2 = 5^2
       (x - 2)^2 + (y + 3)^2 = 25
       x^2 - 4x + 4 + y^2 + 6y + 9 = 25
       x^2 + y^2 - 4x + 6y - 12 = 0
    To test a point, work out (x - 2)^2 + (y + 3)^2 and compare it with 25:
       tap (5, 1):         3^2 + 4^2 = 25      = 25, on the circle
       bench (6, 1):       4^2 + 4^2 = 32      > 25, outside
       flower bed (3, -1): 1^2 + 2^2 = 5       < 25, inside
    In general form the same test is the sign of S = x^2 + y^2 - 4x + 6y - 12 at
    the point: S = 0 on, S > 0 outside, S < 0 inside. Common mistake: writing
    (y - 3)^2 for the centre (2, -3); the sign inside the bracket is the opposite
    of the coordinate. Another: forgetting to square the radius. Now you try:
    the circle with centre (-1, 4) and radius 3, in general form.
    (x^2 + y^2 + 2x - 8y + 8 = 0)

D2. Find the centre and radius of x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 4y - 12 = 0, first by
    completing the square and then by the formula. What do
    x^2 + y^2 + 2x + 4y + 5 = 0 and x^2 + y^2 + 2x + 4y + 6 = 0 represent?
    Answer: Centre (3, -2), radius 5. The second is the single point (-1, -2) (a
    point circle); the third has no real points.
    Teacher explains: Group the x terms and the y terms and complete each
    square:
       (x^2 - 6x + 9) + (y^2 + 4y + 4) = 12 + 9 + 4
       (x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 25
    so the centre is (3, -2) and r = 5. FORMULA: compare with
    x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0: 2g = -6, 2f = 4, c = -12, so g = -3, f = 2. The
    centre is (-g, -f) = (3, -2) and r = sqrt(g^2 + f^2 - c) = sqrt(9 + 4 + 12) = sqrt25
    = 5. For x^2 + y^2 + 2x + 4y + 5 = 0: g = 1, f = 2, c = 5 and g^2 + f^2 - c = 0,
    so the 'circle' has radius 0: only the point (-1, -2) satisfies it, since
    (x + 1)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 0 forces both squares to be 0. With c = 6,
    g^2 + f^2 - c = -1 < 0: a sum of squares cannot be negative, so there are no
    real points at all. If the equation is 2x^2 + 2y^2 - 8x + 12y - 6 = 0, DIVIDE
    by 2 first: the formula needs the coefficient of x^2 and y^2 to be 1. Now you
    try: centre and radius of x^2 + y^2 + 8x - 2y + 8 = 0. ((-4, 1), 3)

D3. Find the circle through A(5, 3), B(-1, 3) and C(-3, -1). Also find the
    circle that has the points (1, 2) and (5, 6) as the ends of a diameter.
    Answer: x^2 + y^2 - 4x + 2y - 20 = 0 (centre (2, -1), radius 5);
    x^2 + y^2 - 6x - 8y + 17 = 0 (centre (3, 4), radius 2sqrt2).
    Teacher explains: Let the circle be x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 and
    substitute each point:
       A(5, 3):    25 + 9 + 10g + 6f + c = 0     10g + 6f + c = -34
       B(-1, 3):   1 + 9 - 2g + 6f + c = 0       -2g + 6f + c = -10
       C(-3, -1):  9 + 1 - 6g - 2f + c = 0       -6g - 2f + c = -10
    Subtract to remove c: (A) - (B) gives 12g = -24, so g = -2; (B) - (C) gives
    4g + 8f = 0, so f = 1. Then c = -10 + 2g - 6f = -10 - 4 - 6 = -20. The
    circle is x^2 + y^2 - 4x + 2y - 20 = 0, centre (2, -1), r = sqrt(4 + 1 + 20) = 5.
    CHECK every point: for C, 9 + 1 + 12 - 2 - 20 = 0. Geometric idea: the
    centre is where the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC meet (AB is
    horizontal, so its bisector is x = 2 at once). DIAMETER FORM: P(x, y) is on
    the circle exactly when the angle in the semicircle is 90 degrees, i.e. the slopes
    from P to the two ends multiply to -1: (x - 1)(x - 5) + (y - 2)(y - 6) = 0,
    giving x^2 + y^2 - 6x - 8y + 17 = 0; centre = midpoint (3, 4),
    r = sqrt(9 + 16 - 17) = sqrt8. Now you try: the circle through (0, 0), (8, 0) and
    (0, 6). (x^2 + y^2 - 8x - 6y = 0; centre (4, 3), r = 5)

D4. A satellite dish is a paraboloid: its cross-section is the parabola y^2 = 4ax
    with the vertex at the bottom of the dish. The dish is 1.2 m across and
    0.15 m deep. Where must the receiver go? Then write down the focus,
    directrix, axis and latus rectum of y^2 = 12x.
    Answer: At the focus, 0.6 m from the vertex along the axis. For y^2 = 12x:
    focus (3, 0), directrix x = -3, axis y = 0, latus rectum 12 with ends
    (3, +/-6).
    Teacher explains: Put the vertex of the dish at O with the axis along the
    x-axis. The rim is 0.6 m from the axis (half of 1.2 m) and 0.15 m along it,
    so (0.15, 0.6) is on y^2 = 4ax: 0.36 = 4a x 0.15 = 0.6a, a = 0.6. The focus
    is (a, 0) = (0.6, 0). Every ray parallel to the axis reflects through the
    focus - this is why dishes, car headlights and solar cookers are parabolic.
    For y^2 = 12x: 4a = 12, a = 3.
       focus (a, 0) = (3, 0)        directrix x = -a, i.e. x = -3
       axis y = 0 (the x-axis)      vertex (0, 0)
       latus rectum 4a = 12, ends (a, +/-2a) = (3, +/-6)
    Check with the definition PS = PM for the point (3, 6): PS = 6 (straight up
    from the focus) and PM = 3 - (-3) = 6. Common mistake: taking a = 12 (the
    number in the equation is 4a). Now you try: focus, directrix and latus
    rectum of y^2 = 20x. ((5, 0), x = -5, 20)

D5. Find the focus, directrix, axis and length of the latus rectum of (a)
    y^2 = -8x, (b) x^2 = 16y, (c) x^2 = -6y. Sketch which way each opens.
    Answer: (a) (-2, 0), x = 2, y = 0, 8; opens left. (b) (0, 4), y = -4, x = 0,
    16; opens up. (c) (0, -3/2), y = 3/2, x = 0, 6; opens down.
    Teacher explains: Match each equation to one of the four standard forms
    (a > 0):
       equation    focus      directrix   axis    opens
       y^2 = 4ax    (a, 0)     x = -a      y = 0   right
       y^2 = -4ax   (-a, 0)    x = a       y = 0   left
       x^2 = 4ay    (0, a)     y = -a      x = 0   up
       x^2 = -4ay   (0, -a)    y = a       x = 0   down
    The SQUARED variable tells you the axis is the OTHER one: y^2 goes with the
    x-axis. The sign on the other side tells you the direction. (a) 4a = 8,
    a = 2: focus (-2, 0), directrix x = 2. (b) 4a = 16, a = 4: focus (0, 4),
    directrix y = -4. (c) 4a = 6, a = 3/2: focus (0, -3/2), directrix y = 3/2.
    The focus is always INSIDE the curve and the directrix outside, the same
    distance a from the vertex. The latus rectum is 4a in each case: 8, 16, 6.
    Now you try: x^2 = -12y. ((0, -3), y = 3, LR 12)

D6. Find the vertex, focus, directrix and axis of y^2 - 4y - 8x + 28 = 0. Then
    find the parabola with focus (2, 3) and directrix y = -1.
    Answer: Vertex (3, 2), focus (5, 2), directrix x = 1, axis y = 2.
    (x - 2)^2 = 8(y - 1), i.e. x^2 - 4x - 8y + 12 = 0.
    Teacher explains: Complete the square in the variable that is squared:
       y^2 - 4y = 8x - 28
       y^2 - 4y + 4 = 8x - 24
       (y - 2)^2 = 8(x - 3)
    Compare with (y - k)^2 = 4a(x - h): vertex (3, 2) and 4a = 8, a = 2.
    Everything shifts with the vertex: focus (3 + 2, 2) = (5, 2), directrix
    x = 3 - 2 = 1, axis y = 2. For the second part use the DEFINITION: P(x, y)
    is as far from the focus as from the directrix:
    sqrt((x - 2)^2 + (y - 3)^2) = |y + 1|. Square:
    (x - 2)^2 + y^2 - 6y + 9 = y^2 + 2y + 1, so (x - 2)^2 = 8y - 8 = 8(y - 1).
    Check: the vertex is halfway between focus and directrix, (2, 1), and a = 2
    (focus 2 above the vertex). Common mistake: writing (y - 2)^2 = 8x - 3
    (forgetting to take out the factor 8). Now you try: vertex and focus of
    x^2 + 6x - 4y + 1 = 0. (V(-3, -2), F(-3, -1))

D7. For the ellipse x^2/25 + y^2/9 = 1 find a, b, c, e, the foci, vertices,
    directrices and latus rectum. Prove that PS + PS' = 2a for every point P on
    it, and check at P(0, 3).
    Answer: a = 5, b = 3, c = 4, e = 4/5; foci (+/-4, 0); vertices (+/-5, 0);
    directrices x = +/-25/4; latus rectum 18/5.
    Teacher explains: a^2 = 25 and b^2 = 9 (the bigger number is under x^2, so the
    major axis is along the x-axis).
       c^2 = a^2 - b^2 = 25 - 9 = 16,  c = 4        e = c/a = 4/5
       foci (+/-c, 0) = (+/-4, 0)                  vertices (+/-5, 0), (0, +/-3)
       directrices x = +/-a/e = +/-25/4            latus rectum 2b^2/a = 18/5
    PROOF: for P(x, y) on the ellipse, y^2 = b^2(1 - x^2/a^2) and b^2 = a^2 - c^2, so
    PS^2 = (x - c)^2 + y^2 = x^2 - 2cx + c^2 + b^2 - b^2x^2/a^2 = a^2 - 2cx + c^2x^2/a^2
    = (a - ex)^2. Since |x| <= a and e < 1, a - ex > 0, so PS = a - ex; in the
    same way PS' = a + ex. Adding: PS + PS' = 2a, whatever P is. At P(0, 3):
    PS = sqrt(16 + 9) = 5 and PS' = 5, sum 10 = 2a. This is the 'pins and string'
    construction: fix a string of length 2a at the two foci and trace. Now you
    try: e and the foci of x^2/100 + y^2/36 = 1. (e = 4/5, (+/-8, 0))

D8. An elliptical 'whispering gallery' is 20 m long and 12 m wide. A whisper at
    one focus is heard clearly at the other. How far from the centre are the
    foci? Then find the ellipse with foci (0, +/-3) and major axis 10.
    Answer: 8 m from the centre on the long axis. x^2/16 + y^2/25 = 1.
    Teacher explains: Put the centre at O with the long axis on the x-axis:
    2a = 20, 2b = 12, so a = 10, b = 6 and c = sqrt(a^2 - b^2) = sqrt(100 - 36) = 8. The
    foci are (+/-8, 0): 8 m either side of the centre (sound from one focus
    reflects off the wall to the other focus, and all paths have the same length
    2a, so the sound arrives together). Second part: the foci are on the y-axis,
    so the major axis is VERTICAL and the form is x^2/b^2 + y^2/a^2 = 1 with a > b.
    2a = 10 gives a = 5, c = 3, b^2 = a^2 - c^2 = 25 - 9 = 16:
       x^2/16 + y^2/25 = 1        (vertices (0, +/-5), e = 3/5)
    Common mistake: writing x^2/25 + y^2/16 = 1, which has its foci on the x-axis.
    Now you try: the ellipse with vertices (+/-6, 0) and e = 2/3.
    (x^2/36 + y^2/20 = 1)

D9. For the hyperbola 9x^2 - 16y^2 = 144 find a, b, c, e, the foci, vertices,
    directrices, latus rectum and asymptotes. Check |PS - PS'| = 2a at the end
    of a latus rectum.
    Answer: x^2/16 - y^2/9 = 1: a = 4, b = 3, c = 5, e = 5/4; foci (+/-5, 0);
    vertices (+/-4, 0); directrices x = +/-16/5; latus rectum 9/2; asymptotes
    y = +/-(3/4)x.
    Teacher explains: Divide by 144 to get 1 on the right: x^2/16 - y^2/9 = 1, so
    a^2 = 16, b^2 = 9. For a HYPERBOLA the squares ADD: c^2 = a^2 + b^2 = 25, c = 5
    and e = c/a = 5/4 > 1.
       foci (+/-5, 0)       vertices (+/-4, 0)     directrices x = +/-a/e = +/-16/5
       latus rectum 2b^2/a = 18/4 = 9/2        asymptotes y = +/-(b/a)x = +/-(3/4)x
    The asymptotes come from x^2/16 - y^2/9 = 0: for large x the curve hugs these
    lines. At x = 5, y^2 = 9(25/16 - 1) = 81/16, so P(5, 9/4) is an end of the
    latus rectum. PS = 9/4 (straight up from S(5, 0)) and
    PS' = sqrt(10^2 + (9/4)^2) = sqrt(1681/16) = 41/4. PS' - PS = 32/4 = 8 = 2a. Common
    mistake: c^2 = a^2 - b^2 (that is the ellipse). Now you try: e and the
    asymptotes of x^2/4 - y^2/5 = 1. (e = 3/2, y = +/-(sqrt5/2)x)

D10. Reduce 4x^2 + 9y^2 - 16x + 18y - 11 = 0 to standard form and find its centre,
     vertices, foci and eccentricity. Then do the same for
     9x^2 - 4y^2 - 36x - 8y - 4 = 0.
     Answer: (x - 2)^2/9 + (y + 1)^2/4 = 1: centre (2, -1), vertices (5, -1) and
     (-1, -1), foci (2 +/- sqrt5, -1), e = sqrt5/3. Second: (x - 2)^2/4 - (y + 1)^2/9 = 1:
     centre (2, -1), vertices (4, -1) and (0, -1), foci (2 +/- sqrt13, -1),
     e = sqrt13/2.
     Teacher explains: Take out the coefficient of x^2 and of y^2 BEFORE
     completing the square:
        4(x^2 - 4x) + 9(y^2 + 2y) = 11
        4(x^2 - 4x + 4) + 9(y^2 + 2y + 1) = 11 + 16 + 9 = 36
        4(x - 2)^2 + 9(y + 1)^2 = 36
        (x - 2)^2/9 + (y + 1)^2/4 = 1
     So the centre is (2, -1), a = 3 (along x), b = 2, c = sqrt(9 - 4) = sqrt5 and
     e = sqrt5/3. Vertices (2 +/- 3, -1) = (5, -1), (-1, -1); foci (2 +/- sqrt5, -1). Note
     we added 4 x 4 = 16 and 9 x 1 = 9 to the right side, not just 4 and 1: that
     is the most common mistake. Second curve:
     9(x - 2)^2 - 4(y + 1)^2 = 4 + 36 - 4 = 36, so (x - 2)^2/4 - (y + 1)^2/9 = 1,
     a = 2, b = 3, c = sqrt13, e = sqrt13/2. Now you try: x^2 + 4y^2 - 2x - 3 = 0.
     ((x - 1)^2/4 + y^2 = 1, centre (1, 0), e = sqrt3/2)

D11. Name the conic: (a) x^2 + y^2 - 4x = 5, (b) y^2 - 4x + 2y = 0, (c)
     4x^2 + 9y^2 - 8x = 32, (d) x^2 - 4y^2 + 2x = 3, (e) x^2 - y^2 = 0. Then find the
     locus of a point whose distance from (3, 0) is half its distance from the
     line x = 12.
     Answer: (a) circle (b) parabola (c) ellipse (d) hyperbola (e) a pair of
     lines y = +/-x. The locus is the ellipse x^2/36 + y^2/27 = 1.
     Teacher explains: With no xy term, look at the coefficients A of x^2 and C
     of y^2:
        A = C (same sign)   circle        A or C = 0    parabola
        AC > 0              ellipse       AC < 0        hyperbola
     (a) A = C = 1: circle ((x - 2)^2 + y^2 = 9). (b) no x^2 term: parabola. (c)
     AC = 36 > 0: ellipse. (d) AC = -4 < 0: hyperbola. (e) looks like a
     hyperbola but factorises: (x - y)(x + y) = 0, two lines - a DEGENERATE
     conic, the plane passing through the vertex of the cone. Always complete
     the square before trusting the name. For the locus use PS = e x PM with
     e = 1/2: sqrt((x - 3)^2 + y^2) = (1/2)|x - 12|; square and multiply by 4:
     4x^2 - 24x + 36 + 4y^2 = x^2 - 24x + 144, so 3x^2 + 4y^2 = 108,
     x^2/36 + y^2/27 = 1. Check: a = 6, e = 1/2, so c = ae = 3 (the focus) and
     a/e = 12 (the directrix). Now you try: name 2x^2 + 2y^2 - 3x = 0 and
     3x^2 - y^2 = 3. (circle; hyperbola)

D12. Find the tangent to x^2 + y^2 = 25 at (3, 4), to y^2 = 8x at (2, 4) and to
     x^2/25 + y^2/9 = 1 at (4, 9/5). Find the tangents to x^2/16 + y^2/9 = 1 with
     slope 1.
     Answer: 3x + 4y = 25; y = x + 2; 4x + 5y = 25; y = x +/- 5.
     Teacher explains: Rule for the tangent at a point (x_1, y_1) ON the curve: x^2
     -> xx_1, y^2 -> yy_1, x -> (x + x_1)/2, y -> (y + y_1)/2.
        x^2 + y^2 = 25 at (3, 4):         3x + 4y = 25
        y^2 = 8x at (2, 4):              4y = 4(x + 2), so y = x + 2
        x^2/25 + y^2/9 = 1 at (4, 9/5):   4x/25 + y/5 = 1, so 4x + 5y = 25
     For the circle the tangent is perpendicular to the radius: the radius to
     (3, 4) has slope 4/3 and the tangent slope -3/4. Slope form: the line
     y = mx + c meets x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 in points given by a quadratic in x; it
     TOUCHES when the discriminant is zero, which simplifies to c^2 = a^2m^2 + b^2.
     With m = 1: c^2 = 16 + 9 = 25, c = +/-5, giving y = x + 5 and y = x - 5 (an
     ellipse has two parallel tangents of every slope). Check y = x + 2 with
     y^2 = 8x: (x + 2)^2 = 8x gives x^2 - 4x + 4 = 0, (x - 2)^2 = 0, a double root,
     so it touches at x = 2. Now you try: the tangent to x^2/16 - y^2/9 = 1 at
     (5, 9/4). (5x - 4y = 16)

       g) (x + 1)^2/9 - (y - 2)^2/16 = 1; C(-1, 2); e = 5/3; foci (4, 2) and

       h) (y - 1)^2/16 - (x - 3)^2/9 = 1; C(3, 1); e = 5/4; foci (3, 6) and
          (3, -4)
       i) (x - 1)^2 - (y - 1)^2/3 = 1; C(1, 1); e = 2; foci (3, 1) and (-1, 1)
       j) (x + 1)^2/3 + (y + 1)^2/2 = 1; C(-1, -1); e = sqrt3/3; foci (0, -1) and
          (-2, -1)
       k) (y - 2)^2/4 - x^2/12 = 1; C(0, 2); e = 2; foci (0, 6) and (0, -2)
       l) (x - 4)^2/100 + (y + 3)^2/64 = 1; C(4, -3); e = 3/5; foci (10, -3) and
          (-2, -3)

M12. Name the conic (parts a to n), or find the tangent at the given point
     (parts o to x; write it as ax + by = c).
     a) name: x^2 + y^2 - 4x = 5
     b) name: y^2 - 4x + 2y = 0
     c) name: 4x^2 + 9y^2 - 8x = 32
     d) name: x^2 - 4y^2 + 2x = 3
     e) name: x^2 + y^2 + 2x + 2y + 2 = 0
     f) name: x^2 - y^2 = 0
     g) name: xy = 4
     h) name: x^2 + 2xy + y^2 - 4x + 4y = 0
     i) name: 3x^2 + 3y^2 - 6x + 12y = 0
     j) name: x^2 + xy + y^2 = 3
     k) name: x = 3y^2 - 2y
     l) name: 5x^2 - 5y^2 = 20
     m) name: x^2 + y^2 + 6x - 8y + 30 = 0
     n) name: 2x^2 + y^2 - 4x + 2y = 5
     o) tangent: x^2 + y^2 = 25 at (3, 4)
     p) tangent: x^2 + y^2 - 4x + 2y - 20 = 0 at (5, 3)
     q) tangent: y^2 = 8x at (2, 4)
     r) tangent: x^2 = 12y at (6, 3)
     s) tangent: x^2/16 + y^2/9 = 1 at (0, 3)
     t) tangent: x^2/25 + y^2/9 = 1 at (4, 9/5)
     u) tangent: x^2/16 - y^2/9 = 1 at (5, 9/4)
     v) tangent: x^2 - y^2 = 9 at (5, 4)
     w) tangent: xy = 4 at (2, 2)
     x) tangent: y^2 = -4x at (-1, 2)
     Answers:
       a) circle
       b) parabola
       c) ellipse
       d) hyperbola
       e) a single point
       f) a pair of lines
       g) hyperbola
       h) parabola
       i) circle
       j) ellipse
       k) parabola
       l) hyperbola
       m) no real points
       n) ellipse
       o) 3x + 4y = 25
       p) 3x + 4y = 27
       q) x - y = -2
       r) x - y = 3
       s) y = 3
       t) 4x + 5y = 25
       u) 5x - 4y = 16
       v) 5x - 4y = 9
       w) x + y = 4
       x) x + y = 1

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw every conic on squared paper and mark the focus, directrix
  and vertices before writing formulas; keep a one-page table of the four
  parabolas and of ellipse versus hyperbola (c^2 = a^2 - b^2 against c^2 = a^2 + b^2);
  always divide to get 1 on the right side; complete the square slowly, writing
  the numbers added to BOTH sides; check every answer by substituting a vertex
  or a latus-rectum end. Harder: prove the reflection property of the parabola
  (the tangent at P makes equal angles with PS and with the line through P
  parallel to the axis); show that the product of the distances from the foci of
  an ellipse to any tangent is b^2; find the locus of the midpoints of focal
  chords of y^2 = 4ax (y^2 = 2a(x - a)); show that the tangents at the ends of a
  focal chord of a parabola meet at right angles on the directrix; find the
  equation of the director circle x^2 + y^2 = a^2 + b^2 of an ellipse.

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.26 - INTRODUCTION TO 3D COORDINATE GEOMETRY
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - Three mutually perpendicular axes OX, OY, OZ through the origin O form a
    RIGHT-HANDED system: curl the fingers of the right hand from OX to OY and
    the thumb points along OZ. They fix three COORDINATE PLANES: the xy-plane
    (z = 0), the yz-plane (x = 0) and the zx-plane (y = 0).
  - A point P(x, y, z): x is its signed distance from the yz-plane, y from the
    zx-plane, z from the xy-plane. Points on the x-axis are (x, 0, 0), on the
    y-axis (0, y, 0), on the z-axis (0, 0, z); points on the xy-plane are
    (x, y, 0), and so on.
  - The three planes cut space into 8 OCTANTS, named by the signs of (x, y, z):
    I (+, +, +), II (-, +, +), III (-, -, +), IV (+, -, +), V (+, +, -), VI
    (-, +, -), VII (-, -, -), VIII (+, -, -). A point with a zero coordinate
    lies on a coordinate plane and is in no octant.
  - FEET and DISTANCES from P(x, y, z): the foot on the xy-plane is (x, y, 0)
    and the distance is |z|; the foot on the x-axis is (x, 0, 0) and the
    distance is sqrt(y^2 + z^2); the distance from O is sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2).
  - DISTANCE FORMULA: PQ = sqrt((x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2) (Pythagoras
    twice). Use it to test right-angled, isosceles and equilateral triangles,
    parallelograms, and to find loci (points equidistant from A and B form a
    plane).
  - SECTION FORMULA: the point dividing PQ internally in the ratio m : n is
    ((mx_2 + nx_1)/(m + n), (my_2 + ny_1)/(m + n), (mz_2 + nz_1)/(m + n)); externally,
    replace n by -n: ((mx_2 - nx_1)/(m - n), ...). MIDPOINT: m = n = 1. To find
    the ratio in which a plane (e.g. the yz-plane) cuts PQ, take the ratio k : 1
    and set that coordinate equal to 0 (k > 0 internal, k < 0 external).
  - CENTROID of the triangle ABC: ((x_1 + x_2 + x_3)/3, (y_1 + y_2 + y_3)/3,
    (z_1 + z_2 + z_3)/3); of a tetrahedron: the average of the four vertices.
    Fourth vertex of the parallelogram ABCD: D = A + C - B (coordinate by
    coordinate).
  - COLLINEAR points: A, B, C lie on one line when one distance is the sum of
    the other two (AB + BC = AC), or when the differences B - A and C - A are
    proportional.
    P(x, y, z) and r = OP: l = x/r, m = y/r, n = z/r. DIRECTION RATIOS are any
    numbers a, b, c proportional to l, m, n; the line through (x_1, y_1, z_1) and
    (x_2, y_2, z_2) has direction ratios x_2 - x_1, y_2 - y_1, z_2 - z_1 and
    l = +/-a/sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2) etc.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A drone takes off from the corner O of a school ground. Take x metres east,
    y metres north and z metres up. It hovers at P(12, -4, 3). In which octant
    is it? Where is the point on the ground directly below it, how high is it,
    and how far is it from O? How far is it from the east-west boundary line
    (the x-axis)?
    Answer: Octant IV (+, -, +). The point below it is (12, -4, 0); it is 3 m
    high, 13 m from O, and 5 m from the x-axis.
    Teacher explains: Read the coordinates as three moves from O: 12 m east, 4 m
    SOUTH (y is negative), 3 m up. The signs (+, -, +) give octant IV. The
    ground is the xy-plane (z = 0), so the point straight below is (12, -4, 0)
    and the height is |z| = 3 m.
       OP^2 = 12^2 + (-4)^2 + 3^2 = 144 + 16 + 9 = 169,  OP = 13 m
    Why: O to the foot F(12, -4, 0) is a flat distance sqrt(144 + 16) = sqrt160; then
    F to P is 3 m straight up, at right angles, so OP^2 = 160 + 9 = 169. The
    distance from the x-axis: the foot on the x-axis is (12, 0, 0), and from
    there P is 4 m across and 3 m up: sqrt(4^2 + 3^2) = 5 m. In general the distance
    of (x, y, z) from the x-axis is sqrt(y^2 + z^2) - leave out the coordinate of
    THAT axis. Common mistake: answering |x| = 12 (that is the distance from the
    yz-plane). Now you try: P(-6, 2, -3): octant, distance from O, distance from
    the z-axis. (VI; 7; 2sqrt10)

D2. The three coordinate planes cut space into eight octants. List the sign
    pattern of every octant, and place (-3, 1, -2), (2, -5, -1), (-4, -4, 9) and
    (0, 3, -4).
    Answer: VI, VIII, III; (0, 3, -4) lies on the yz-plane (in no octant).
    Teacher explains: The numbering goes round the top four first (z > 0),
    anticlockwise from the +x, +y quarter, then the same four underneath
    (z < 0):
       octant    I   II   III   IV     V   VI   VII   VIII
       x         +   -    -     +      +   -    -     +
       y         +   +    -     -      +   +    -     -
       z         +   +    +     +      -   -    -     -
    (-3, 1, -2) is (-, +, -): VI. (2, -5, -1) is (+, -, -): VIII. (-4, -4, 9) is
    (-, -, +): III. (0, 3, -4) has x = 0, so it is ON the yz-plane, the wall
    between octants; a point with two zero coordinates is on an axis, e.g.
    (0, 0, -6) is on the z-axis. Only the SIGNS matter, not the sizes:
    (-0.001, 500, -2) is in VI as well. Common mistake: numbering V to VIII in a
    different order - memorise that V to VIII are I to IV with z made negative.
    Now you try: (5, -1, 7), (-2, -2, -2), (4, 0, 0). (IV; VII; on the x-axis)

D3. Derive the distance formula in three dimensions and find the distance
    between A(1, -2, 3) and B(4, 2, 15).
    Answer: AB = sqrt((x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2); here AB = 13.
    Teacher explains: Draw the box (cuboid) with A and B at opposite corners and
    edges parallel to the axes. Its edges are |x_2 - x_1|, |y_2 - y_1| and
    |z_2 - z_1|. Let C be the corner level with A and directly below B. In the
    bottom face, Pythagoras gives AC^2 = (x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2. CB is vertical,
    so the angle ACB is 90 degrees and AB^2 = AC^2 + CB^2
    = (x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2.
       AB^2 = (4 - 1)^2 + (2 - (-2))^2 + (15 - 3)^2
           = 9 + 16 + 144 = 169,   AB = 13
    Setting A = O gives OP = sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2). Squares make the order of
    subtraction irrelevant, but watch double negatives: 2 - (-2) = 4. Common
    mistake: forgetting one of the three squares. Now you try: the distance
    between (2, -1, 3) and (-2, 1, 3). (2sqrt5)

D4. Show that A(0, 7, 10), B(-1, 6, 6) and C(-4, 9, 6) are the vertices of a
    right-angled isosceles triangle. Where is the right angle?
    Answer: AB = BC = 3sqrt2 and AB^2 + BC^2 = CA^2 = 36; the right angle is at B.
    Teacher explains: Work with SQUARED lengths to avoid roots:
       AB^2 = (-1 - 0)^2 + (6 - 7)^2 + (6 - 10)^2 = 1 + 1 + 16 = 18
       BC^2 = (-4 + 1)^2 + (9 - 6)^2 + (6 - 6)^2 = 9 + 9 + 0 = 18
       CA^2 = (0 + 4)^2 + (7 - 9)^2 + (10 - 6)^2 = 16 + 4 + 16 = 36
    AB = BC, so the triangle is isosceles; 18 + 18 = 36 means AB^2 + BC^2 = CA^2,
    so by the converse of Pythagoras the angle opposite CA, the angle at B, is
    90 degrees. Test checklist for three points: all three sides equal (equilateral),
    two equal (isosceles), the biggest square equal to the sum of the other two
    (right-angled), the biggest length equal to the sum of the other two
    (collinear - not a triangle at all). Now you try: show that (1, 0, 0),
    (0, 1, 0) and (0, 0, 1) form an equilateral triangle. (each side sqrt2)

D5. Find the locus of points equidistant from A(1, 2, 3) and B(3, 2, -1). Then
    find the point on the y-axis equidistant from (3, 1, 2) and (5, 5, 2).
    Answer: The plane x = 2z (x - 2z = 0). The point (0, 5, 0).
    Teacher explains: Let P(x, y, z) with PA^2 = PB^2:
       (x - 1)^2 + (y - 2)^2 + (z - 3)^2 = (x - 3)^2 + (y - 2)^2 + (z + 1)^2
       -2x + 1 - 6z + 9 = -6x + 9 + 2z + 1
       4x - 8z = 0,   so x = 2z
    The x^2, y^2, z^2 terms cancel, so the locus is a PLANE (the perpendicular
    bisector plane of AB: in 3D the 'perpendicular bisector' is a plane, not a
    line). Check the midpoint (2, 2, 1): x = 2 = 2 x 1. For the second part a
    point on the y-axis is (0, y, 0):
       9 + (y - 1)^2 + 4 = 25 + (y - 5)^2 + 4
       y^2 - 2y + 14 = y^2 - 10y + 54,  8y = 40,  y = 5
    Check: the distances are sqrt(9 + 16 + 4) = sqrt29 and sqrt(25 + 0 + 4) = sqrt29. Common
    mistake: writing a general point on the y-axis as (y, 0, 0). Now you try:
    the point on the x-axis equidistant from (1, 2, 3) and (3, 4, 1).
    ((3, 0, 0))

D6. Find the point R that divides the join of P(2, -3, 4) and Q(8, 0, 10) in the
    ratio 1 : 2 internally. Explain the section formula.
    Answer: R(4, -2, 6).
    Teacher explains: R divides PQ in the ratio m : n when PR : RQ = m : n. Drop
    perpendiculars from P, R, Q to the xy-plane: the feet lie on a line and the
    similar-triangle argument of 2D works for each coordinate separately, so
       R = ((mx_2 + nx_1)/(m + n), (my_2 + ny_1)/(m + n), (mz_2 + nz_1)/(m + n))
    With m = 1 (next to Q) and n = 2 (next to P):
       x = (1 x 8 + 2 x 2)/3 = 12/3 = 4
       y = (1 x 0 + 2 x (-3))/3 = -6/3 = -2
       z = (1 x 10 + 2 x 4)/3 = 18/3 = 6
    Check: R is one third of the way from P to Q: P + (1/3)(Q - P) = (2 + 2,
    -3 + 1, 4 + 2) = (4, -2, 6). Memory trick: CROSS multiply - m goes with the
    FAR point Q. Common mistake: (mx_1 + nx_2)/(m + n), which gives the point 1/3
    of the way from Q instead. Now you try: the point dividing (1, 2, 3) and
    (4, 5, 6) in the ratio 2 : 1. ((3, 4, 5))

D7. Find the point dividing P(1, -2, 3) and Q(3, 4, -5) externally in the ratio
    2 : 3. In what ratio does the yz-plane divide the join of A(-2, 4, 7) and
    B(3, -5, 8), and at which point?
    Answer: (-3, -14, 19). The yz-plane divides AB internally in the ratio 2 : 3
    at (0, 2/5, 37/5).
    Teacher explains: EXTERNAL division: the point is outside the segment, and
    the formula is the internal one with n replaced by -n:
       x = (2 x 3 - 3 x 1)/(2 - 3) = 3/(-1) = -3
       y = (2 x 4 - 3 x (-2))/(2 - 3) = 14/(-1) = -14
       z = (2 x (-5) - 3 x 3)/(2 - 3) = -19/(-1) = 19
    For the ratio, let the point divide AB in k : 1. Its x-coordinate is
    (3k - 2)/(k + 1), and on the yz-plane x = 0, so 3k - 2 = 0 and k = 2/3. The
    ratio is 2/3 : 1 = 2 : 3, positive, so INTERNAL. The point:
       y = (2 x (-5) + 3 x 4)/5 = 2/5,   z = (2 x 8 + 3 x 7)/5 = 37/5
    A negative k would mean external division (the plane misses the segment).
    Tip: A and B have x-coordinates of opposite signs, so the yz-plane must
    cross between them. Now you try: the ratio in which the xy-plane divides the
    join of (1, 2, -3) and (4, -1, 6). (1 : 2 internally, at (2, 1, 0))

D8. A(1, 2, 3), B(-2, 0, 5) and C(4, -5, 1) are three vertices of a
    parallelogram ABCD. Find the centroid of the triangle ABC and the fourth
    vertex D. If the centroid of a triangle is (1, 1, 1) and two vertices are
    (3, -5, 7) and (-1, 7, -6), find the third vertex.
    Answer: Centroid (1, -1, 3); D(7, -3, -1); third vertex (1, 1, 2).
    Teacher explains: The centroid is the average of the three vertices:
       G = ((1 - 2 + 4)/3, (2 + 0 - 5)/3, (3 + 5 + 1)/3) = (1, -1, 3)
    In a parallelogram the diagonals bisect each other, so the midpoints of AC
    and BD are the same: A + C = B + D, so D = A + C - B:
       D = (1 + 4 + 2, 2 - 5 - 0, 3 + 1 - 5) = (7, -3, -1)
    Check: the midpoint of AC is (2.5, -1.5, 2) and of BD is ((-2 + 7)/2,
    (0 - 3)/2, (5 - 1)/2) = (2.5, -1.5, 2). For the third vertex:
    A + B + C = 3G, so C = 3G - A - B = (3 - 3 + 1, 3 + 5 - 7,
    3 - 7 + 6) = (1, 1, 2). Common mistake: D = A + B - C (that is the
    parallelogram ABDC in a different order). Now you try: the centroid of the
    tetrahedron with vertices (0, 0, 0), (4, 0, 0), (0, 8, 0) and (0, 0, 12).
    ((1, 2, 3))

D9. Show that A(2, 3, 4), B(-1, -2, 1) and C(5, 8, 7) are collinear. Which point
    is between the other two?
    Answer: BA = AC = sqrt43 and BC = 2sqrt43 = BA + AC, so they are collinear, with A
    in the middle (A is the midpoint of BC).
    Teacher explains: Method 1 (distances):
       AB^2 = 9 + 25 + 9 = 43        AB = sqrt43
       AC^2 = 9 + 25 + 9 = 43        AC = sqrt43
       BC^2 = 36 + 100 + 36 = 172    BC = sqrt172 = 2sqrt43
    BC = AB + AC exactly, so the 'triangle' is flat: the three points are on one
    line, A between B and C. Method 2 (proportional differences):
    B - A = (-3, -5, -3) and C - A = (3, 5, 3) = -(B - A); the same direction
    (reversed), so the points are collinear, and the factor -1 says A is halfway
    between. Method 2 avoids square roots and is quicker. Common mistake with
    method 1: rounded decimals (6.56 + 6.56 and 13.11) only suggest equality;
    keep the surds exact. Now you try: are (1, 2, 3), (3, 5, 7) and (5, 8, 10)
    collinear? (no: the differences (2, 3, 4) and (4, 6, 7) are not
    proportional)

D10. Find the direction cosines of OP, where P is (2, -3, 6), and the angles OP
     makes with the axes. Prove that l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1 for every line.
     Teacher explains: Let r = OP = sqrt(4 + 9 + 36) = 7. Drop a perpendicular from
     P to the x-axis; it meets it at (2, 0, 0), and in the right triangle
        l = 2/7,   m = -3/7,   n = 6/7
        alpha = arccos(2/7) ~ 73.4 degrees,  beta = arccos(-3/7) ~ 115.4 degrees,
     A negative cosine means an obtuse angle (P is on the -y side). PROOF:
     l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = (x^2 + y^2 + z^2)/r^2 = r^2/r^2 = 1. So the three angles cannot be
     4/49 + 9/49 + 36/49 = 49/49 = 1. Common mistake: using the angles with the
     coordinate PLANES instead of the axes. Now you try: the direction cosines
     of OP for P(1, 2, 2). ((1/3, 2/3, 2/3))

D11. Find the direction ratios and direction cosines of the line through
     A(1, 2, -1) and B(3, -4, 2). Can a line make angles 45 degrees, 60 degrees, 60 degrees with the
     axes? 45 degrees, 45 degrees, 45 degrees? Find the direction cosines of a line equally inclined
     to the three axes.
     Answer: Direction ratios 2, -6, 3; direction cosines +/-(2/7, -6/7, 3/7).
     Yes; no; +/-(1/sqrt3, 1/sqrt3, 1/sqrt3).
     Teacher explains: Direction ratios of AB are the differences
     B - A = (2, -6, 3) (any multiple, e.g. -4, 12, -6, is also a set of
     direction ratios). To get direction cosines divide by
     sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2) = sqrt(4 + 36 + 9) = 7. A line has TWO directions, so the
     signs can all be reversed: +/-(2/7, -6/7, 3/7). For the angles test
     l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1:
        45 degrees, 60 degrees, 60 degrees:  1/2 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 1     possible
        45 degrees, 45 degrees, 45 degrees:  1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 3/2   impossible
     Equally inclined: l = m = n, so 3l^2 = 1 and l = +/-1/sqrt3 = +/-sqrt3/3 (each angle
     about 54.7 degrees, the direction of the diagonal of a cube). Direction ratios are
     NOT unique, direction cosines are unique up to sign. Common mistake:
     calling 2, -6, 3 the direction cosines (their squares add to 49, not 1).
     Now you try: a line makes 90 degrees with the x-axis and 60 degrees with the y-axis; find
     its angle with the z-axis. (30 degrees or 150 degrees)

D12. A classroom is a cuboid 5 m long, 4 m wide and 3 m high. Put one corner of
     the floor at O with the edges along the axes. Find the length of the
     longest rod that fits in the room, the centre of the room, and how far the
     far top corner is from the vertical edge through O and from the floor.
     Answer: The longest rod is the space diagonal 5sqrt2 ~ 7.07 m; the centre is
     (2.5, 2, 1.5); the far top corner (5, 4, 3) is sqrt41 ~ 6.40 m from the
     vertical edge (the z-axis) and 3 m from the floor.
     Teacher explains: The far top corner is P(5, 4, 3). The longest straight
     rod joins O and P:
        OP = sqrt(5^2 + 4^2 + 3^2) = sqrt50 = 5sqrt2 ~ 7.07 m
     (longer than the floor diagonal sqrt41 ~ 6.40 m). The centre of the room is
     the midpoint of OP: (2.5, 2, 1.5). The vertical edge through O is the
     z-axis, so the distance from it ignores z:
     sqrt(x^2 + y^2) = sqrt(25 + 16) = sqrt41 ~ 6.40 m; the distance from the floor (the
     xy-plane) is |z| = 3 m. Summary for a point (x, y, z):
        from the x-axis sqrt(y^2 + z^2)     from the yz-plane |x|
        from the y-axis sqrt(z^2 + x^2)     from the zx-plane |y|
        from the z-axis sqrt(x^2 + y^2)     from the xy-plane |z|
     Common mistake: mixing up 'distance from the x-axis' with 'distance from
     the yz-plane'. Now you try: for P(3, 4, 12), find OP and the distance from
     each axis. (13; 4sqrt10, 3sqrt17, 5)

PART B - MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Name the octant (I to VIII), or say which plane or axis the point lies on.
    a) (2, 3, 5)        b) (-2, 3, 5)       c) (-2, -3, 5)
    d) (2, -3, 5)       e) (2, 3, -5)       f) (-2, 3, -5)
    g) (-2, -3, -5)     h) (2, -3, -5)      i) (-1, 4, -7)
    j) (6, -2, 3)       k) (-3, -3, 8)      l) (5, 1, -1)
    m) (0, 2, 3)        n) (4, 0, -1)       o) (1, -1, 0)
    p) (0, 0, -6)       q) (7, 0, 0)        r) (0, -2, 0)
    s) (0, 0, 0)        t) (-1/2, 2, -3)    u) (1/2, -1/3, -4)
    v) (-sqrt2, -sqrt3, -1)   w) (-10, 20, -30)   x) (3, -7, 1/10)
    Answers: a) I   b) II   c) III   d) IV   e) V   f) VI   g) VII   h) VIII
             i) VI   j) IV   k) III   l) V   m) on the yz-plane
             n) on the zx-plane   o) on the xy-plane   p) on the z-axis
             q) on the x-axis   r) on the y-axis   s) the origin   t) VI
             u) VIII   v) VII   w) VI   x) IV

M2. Find the foot of the perpendicular from the point to the given plane or
    axis.
    a) (3, -4, 5), xy-plane     b) (3, -4, 5), yz-plane

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: build a model: the corner of a room (two walls and the floor) is
  the three coordinate planes; stand pencils along the edges as axes and point
  to (2, 3, 1) with a finger; draw the cuboid with the two points as opposite
  corners before using the distance formula; say 'leave out that axis's
  coordinate' for the distance from an axis; keep a sign table of the octants on
  the desk. Harder: prove that the centroid of a tetrahedron divides each line
  joining a vertex to the centroid of the opposite face in the ratio 3 : 1; show
  that the points (0, 0, 0), (a, 0, 0), (0, a, 0), (0, 0, a) and (a, a, a) are
  not all at the same distance from any point (or find the sphere through the
  first four); find the equation of the sphere with centre (1, -2, 3) and radius
  4; show that the angle theta between lines with direction cosines (l_1, m_1, n_1) and
  (l_2, m_2, n_2) satisfies cos theta = l_1l_2 + m_1m_2 + n_1n_2.

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.27 - POLAR COORDINATES AND PARAMETRIC EQUATIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - POLAR COORDINATES (r, theta): r is the distance from the POLE O and theta the angle
    from the INITIAL LINE (the positive x-axis), anticlockwise positive, in
    RADIANS. Convention in this topic: the PRINCIPAL form has r > 0 and
    -pi < theta <= pi; the pole is r = 0 with any theta.
  - CONVERSION: x = r cos theta, y = r sin theta; r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2), and theta is the angle
    with cos theta = x/r and sin theta = y/r. tan theta = y/x alone is NOT enough: draw the
    point and choose the quadrant ((-1, -1) has theta = -3pi/4, not pi/4).
    Non-standard angles are written with arctan: (3, 4) is (5, arctan(4/3)).
  - One point has infinitely many polar names: (r, theta) = (r, theta + 2npi) = (-r,
    theta + pi). A NEGATIVE r means: face the direction theta and walk backwards.
  - CONVERTING EQUATIONS: polar to Cartesian - replace r cos theta by x, r sin theta by
    y and r^2 by x^2 + y^2 (multiply by r first if needed: r = 2a cos theta gives
    r^2 = 2ar cos theta, i.e. x^2 + y^2 = 2ax, a circle of centre (a, 0) and radius a).
    Cartesian to polar - substitute x = r cos theta, y = r sin theta and simplify.
  - STANDARD POLAR CURVES: r = a (circle, centre O); theta = alpha (line through O);
    r cos theta = a (line x = a); r = 2a cos theta, r = 2a sin theta (circles through O);
    r = a(1 +/- cos theta), a(1 +/- sin theta) (CARDIOIDS); r = a cos ntheta or a sin ntheta (ROSES:
    inner loop when b > a); r = atheta (Archimedean SPIRAL); r^2 = a^2 cos 2theta
    (LEMNISCATE); r = l/(1 + e cos theta) (a conic with focus O and eccentricity e).
  - DISTANCE between (r_1, theta_1) and (r_2, theta_2): sqrt(r_1^2 + r_2^2 - 2r_1r_2 cos(theta_1 - theta_2))
    (cosine rule); area of the triangle they make with the pole:
    (1/2)r_1r_2|sin(theta_1 - theta_2)|.
  - PARAMETRIC EQUATIONS x = f(t), y = g(t): as the parameter t runs, the point
    traces the curve in a definite direction (t is often time). Standard forms:
    line x = x_1 + at, y = y_1 + bt (direction (a, b)); circle x = h + r cos t,
    y = k + r sin t; ellipse x = a cos t, y = b sin t; parabola x = at^2,
    y = 2at; hyperbola x = a sec t, y = b tan t; rectangular hyperbola x = ct,
    y = c/t.
  - ELIMINATING THE PARAMETER: make t the subject of one equation and
    substitute, or use an identity (cos^2t + sin^2t = 1, sec^2t - tan^2t = 1,
    cos 2t = 1 - 2sin^2t). Always state RESTRICTIONS: x = t^2, y = t^2 gives only
    the half-line y = x, x >= 0. (Derivatives of parametric curves come in topic
    8.36.)

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A radar at O reports a ship at distance 10 km in the direction theta = pi/3 from
    due east (the initial line), and a fishing boat at (4, 3pi/4). Find their
    Cartesian coordinates (x east, y north, in km).
    Answer: Ship (5, 5sqrt3) ~ (5, 8.66); boat (-2sqrt2, 2sqrt2) ~ (-2.83, 2.83).
    Teacher explains: Drop a perpendicular from the point to the initial line:
    the right triangle has hypotenuse r and angle theta at O, so
       x = r cos theta,     y = r sin theta
       ship: x = 10 cos(pi/3) = 10 x 1/2 = 5,  y = 10 sin(pi/3) = 5sqrt3
       boat: x = 4 cos(3pi/4) = -2sqrt2,          y = 4 sin(3pi/4) = 2sqrt2
    The formulas work in every quadrant because cos and sin carry the signs:
    3pi/4 is in the second quadrant, so x < 0 and y > 0. Check with Pythagoras:
    5^2 + (5sqrt3)^2 = 25 + 75 = 100 = 10^2. Radar screens, the positions of fielders
    round a cricket pitch and the rotation of a ceiling fan are naturally polar.
    Common mistake: using degrees mode on the calculator with a radian angle.
    Now you try: (6, -pi/6) and (2, pi). ((3sqrt3, -3); (-2, 0))

D2. Convert to polar form (r > 0, -pi < theta <= pi): (-2, 2), (-sqrt3, -1), (3, -3sqrt3),
    (0, -5) and (3, 4).
    Answer: (2sqrt2, 3pi/4), (2, -5pi/6), (6, -pi/3), (5, -pi/2), (5, arctan(4/3)) with
    arctan(4/3) ~ 0.927.
    Teacher explains: Step 1: r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2). Step 2: find the reference angle
       point       r     reference   quadrant   theta
       (-2, 2)     2sqrt2   pi/4         II         pi - pi/4 = 3pi/4
       (-sqrt3, -1)   2     pi/6         III        -pi + pi/6 = -5pi/6
       (3, -3sqrt3)   6     pi/3         IV         -pi/3
       (0, -5)     5     on an axis  -y-axis    -pi/2
       (3, 4)      5     arctan(4/3) I          arctan(4/3) ~ 0.927
    Common mistake: a calculator gives arctan(-1/-sqrt3) = arctan(1/sqrt3) = pi/6 for
    (-sqrt3, -1), which is the first-quadrant point (sqrt3, 1). Always sketch. Check
    (-sqrt3, -1): 2 cos(-5pi/6) = -sqrt3 and 2 sin(-5pi/6) = -1. Now you try: (-1, sqrt3)
    and (4, -4). ((2, 2pi/3); (4sqrt2, -pi/4))

D3. Show that (3, pi/6), (3, 13pi/6), (3, -11pi/6), (-3, 7pi/6) and (-3, -5pi/6) are
    all the same point. Why is the pole special?
    Answer: All give (x, y) = (3sqrt3/2, 3/2).
    Teacher explains: Adding 2pi to theta turns a full circle and lands in the same
    place, so (3, pi/6) = (3, 13pi/6) = (3, -11pi/6). A NEGATIVE r means: face
    along theta and walk backwards r units, which is the same as walking forwards in
    the direction theta + pi (or theta - pi). So (-3, 7pi/6) is the point at distance 3 in
    the direction 7pi/6 - pi = pi/6, the same point again, and so is (-3, -5pi/6).
    Check one with the formulas: x = -3 cos(7pi/6) = -3 x (-sqrt3/2) = 3sqrt3/2 and
    y = -3 sin(7pi/6) = -3 x (-1/2) = 3/2. The pole O is r = 0 and ANY theta, so
    (0, 1) and (0, 2) in polar form are both the origin. This is why we fix the
    PRINCIPAL form r > 0, -pi < theta <= pi for answers. Now you try: write (2, -3pi/4)
    with theta in [0, 2pi) and also with a negative r. ((2, 5pi/4); (-2, pi/4))

D4. Convert to Cartesian form and describe: r = 4, theta = pi/4, r = 6 cos theta,
    r sin theta = 3 and r = 4 sin theta.
    Answer: x^2 + y^2 = 16 (circle, centre O, radius 4); y = x (line through O);
    x^2 + y^2 = 6x, i.e. (x - 3)^2 + y^2 = 9 (circle, centre (3, 0), radius 3);
    y = 3 (horizontal line); x^2 + y^2 = 4y, i.e. x^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 4 (circle,
    centre (0, 2), radius 2).
    Teacher explains: The dictionary is x = r cos theta, y = r sin theta, r^2 = x^2 + y^2.
    r = 4: square, r^2 = 16, so x^2 + y^2 = 16. theta = pi/4: tan theta = y/x = 1 so y = x
    (negative r gives the other half of the line). r = 6 cos theta: multiply by r to
    make recognisable pieces:
       r^2 = 6r cos theta   ->   x^2 + y^2 = 6x   ->   (x - 3)^2 + y^2 = 9
    a circle through the pole with centre (3, 0). r sin theta = 3 is just y = 3.
    r = 4 sin theta: r^2 = 4r sin theta, x^2 + y^2 = 4y, x^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 4. In general
    r = 2a cos theta and r = 2a sin theta are circles of radius |a| through O, centred
    on the x-axis and y-axis. Common mistake: turning r = 6 cos theta into
    sqrt(x^2 + y^2) = 6x/sqrt(x^2 + y^2) and giving up; multiply by r first. Now you try:
    r = -8 cos theta and r cos theta = -2. (x^2 + y^2 + 8x = 0, circle centre (-4, 0),
    radius 4; x = -2)

D5. Convert to polar form: x^2 + y^2 = 9, x = 5, x^2 + y^2 - 4x = 0, y = x^2,
    x^2 - y^2 = 1, xy = 4 and x + y = 2.
    Answer: r = 3; r = 5 sec theta; r = 4 cos theta; r = tan theta sec theta; r^2 cos 2theta = 1;
    r^2 sin 2theta = 8; r(cos theta + sin theta) = 2.
    Teacher explains: Substitute x = r cos theta, y = r sin theta and simplify with
    identities:
       x^2 + y^2 = 9:      r^2 = 9, r = 3
       x = 5:            r cos theta = 5, r = 5 sec theta
       x^2 + y^2 = 4x:     r^2 = 4r cos theta, r = 4 cos theta (r = 0 is included)
       y = x^2:           r sin theta = r^2 cos^2theta, r = sin theta/cos^2theta = tan theta sec theta
       x^2 - y^2 = 1:      r^2(cos^2theta - sin^2theta) = 1, r^2 cos 2theta = 1
       xy = 4:           r^2 sin theta cos theta = 4, r^2 sin 2theta = 8
       x + y = 2:        r(cos theta + sin theta) = 2
    When we divide by r we lose the pole, so check whether r = 0 is on the curve
    (for x^2 + y^2 = 4x it is, and r = 4 cos theta gives r = 0 at theta = pi/2, so nothing
    is lost). Polar form is best for curves with circular symmetry about O;
    Cartesian form is best for lines not through O. Now you try: polar form of
    x^2 + y^2 + 6y = 0 and of y = -2. (r = -6 sin theta; r = -2 cosec theta)

D6. Sketch the cardioid r = 2(1 + cos theta) from a table of values, and describe
    its shape and symmetry.
    Answer: r = 4, 3, 2, 1, 0 at theta = 0, pi/3, pi/2, 2pi/3, pi; a heart-shaped curve,
    symmetric about the initial line, with a cusp at the pole.
    Teacher explains: Make a table (cos is known exactly at these angles):
       theta            0     pi/3    pi/2    2pi/3    pi
       cos theta        1     1/2    0      -1/2    -1
       r            4     3      2      1       0
    Plot each point at distance r in direction theta: (4, 0), (3, pi/3), (2, pi/2),
    (1, 2pi/3) and the pole at theta = pi. SYMMETRY TEST: replacing theta by -theta does not
    change cos theta, so the lower half is the mirror image of the upper half in the
    initial line. The curve passes through the pole with a sharp point (a cusp)
    when theta = pi. Its widest point is (4, 0), and it crosses the y-axis at
    (0, +/-2). Cardioid means 'heart-shaped'; the cross-section of a coffee cup
    caustic and the pickup pattern of some microphones are cardioids. Now you
    try: the values of r = 3(1 - sin theta) at theta = 0, pi/2, pi and -pi/2. (3, 0, 3, 6)

D7. How many petals do the roses r = 3 cos 2theta and r = 3 sin 3theta have, and how
    long is each petal? What do r = 1 + 2 cos theta, r = theta (theta >= 0) and r^2 = 4 cos 2theta
    look like?
    Answer: r = 3 cos 2theta: 4 petals; r = 3 sin 3theta: 3 petals; each petal has
    Archimedean spiral; r^2 = 4 cos 2theta a lemniscate (figure of eight) with loops
    of length 2.
    Teacher explains: For r = a cos ntheta or a sin ntheta each petal reaches the
    maximum r = |a|. RULE: n odd gives n petals, n even gives 2n petals. Why:
    when n is odd, the negative values of r retrace the same petals (the curve
    repeats after theta = pi); when n is even they draw new petals. For r = 3 cos 2theta
    the petals point along theta = 0, pi/2, pi, 3pi/2 (where cos 2theta = +/-1). For
    r = a + b cos theta: b > a gives an inner loop (r becomes negative for some theta;
    here when cos theta < -1/2), b = a is the cardioid, b < a a dimpled or oval
    shape. SPIRAL r = theta: r grows steadily, so each turn is 2pi further out.
    LEMNISCATE r^2 = 4 cos 2theta exists only where cos 2theta >= 0, that is
    -pi/4 <= theta <= pi/4 and 3pi/4 <= theta <= 5pi/4, giving two loops of length 2 through O.
    Now you try: petals of r = 2 sin 4theta and of r = cos 5theta. (8; 5)

D8. Find the distance between A(3, pi/6) and B(4, 2pi/3), and the area of the
    triangle OAB. Then find the distance between (2, pi/3) and (4, 0).
    Answer: AB = 5, area 6; the second distance is 2sqrt3.
    Teacher explains: In triangle OAB, OA = r_1, OB = r_2 and the angle
    AOB = |theta_1 - theta_2|, so the COSINE RULE gives
       AB^2 = r_1^2 + r_2^2 - 2r_1r_2 cos(theta_1 - theta_2)
       area = (1/2) r_1 r_2 |sin(theta_1 - theta_2)|
    Here theta_2 - theta_1 = 2pi/3 - pi/6 = pi/2, so cos = 0 and sin = 1:
       AB^2 = 9 + 16 - 0 = 25, AB = 5;   area = (1/2)(3)(4)(1) = 6
    Second: AB^2 = 4 + 16 - 2(2)(4) cos(pi/3) = 20 - 8 = 12, AB = 2sqrt3. Check by
    converting: (2, pi/3) = (1, sqrt3) and (4, 0) = (4, 0), distance
    sqrt(9 + 3) = sqrt12 = 2sqrt3. The formula saves converting and is exact. Common
    mistake: subtracting r values or forgetting the factor 2 in the cosine rule.
    Now you try: the distance between (1, pi/3) and (2, -pi/3). (sqrt7)

D9. An ant walks in a straight line so that at time t seconds it is at
    x = 1 + 3t, y = 2 - 4t (in cm). Where is it at t = 0 and t = 2? How fast
    does it move? Find the Cartesian equation of its path and where it crosses
    the x-axis.
    Answer: (1, 2) and (7, -6); 5 cm/s; 4x + 3y = 10; it crosses the x-axis at
    (5/2, 0) when t = 1/2.
    Teacher explains: Substitute t: at t = 0, (1, 2); at t = 2, (1 + 6,
    2 - 8) = (7, -6). Each second x grows by 3 and y falls by 4, so the
    direction vector is (3, -4) and the speed is sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = 5 cm/s. Eliminate
    t:
       t = (x - 1)/3   ->   y = 2 - 4(x - 1)/3   ->   3y = 6 - 4x + 4
       4x + 3y = 10
    On the x-axis y = 0: 2 - 4t = 0, t = 1/2, x = 1 + 3/2 = 5/2. In general
    x = x_1 + at, y = y_1 + bt is the line through (x_1, y_1) with direction (a, b);
    the parametric form also tells us WHEN the ant is where, which the Cartesian
    equation does not. Now you try: the line through (2, -1) and (5, 3) in
    parametric form, and its Cartesian equation. (x = 2 + 3t, y = -1 + 4t;
    4x - 3y = 11)

D10. Eliminate the parameter: (a) x = 2 + 5 cos t, y = -1 + 5 sin t; (b)
     x = 4 cos t, y = 3 sin t. Which way does each point move as t increases,
     and what part is traced for 0 <= t <= pi?
     Answer: (a) (x - 2)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 25, a circle; (b) x^2/16 + y^2/9 = 1, an
     ellipse. Both are traced anticlockwise; for 0 <= t <= pi we get the upper half
     of each.
     Teacher explains: Isolate cos t and sin t and use cos^2t + sin^2t = 1:
        (a) cos t = (x - 2)/5, sin t = (y + 1)/5
            (x - 2)^2/25 + (y + 1)^2/25 = 1, (x - 2)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 25
        (b) cos t = x/4, sin t = y/3,  x^2/16 + y^2/9 = 1
     At t = 0 the points are (7, -1) and (4, 0); at t = pi/2 they are (2, 4) and
     (0, 3): moving anticlockwise. For 0 <= t <= pi, sin t >= 0, so y >= -1 in (a)
     and y >= 0 in (b): the upper halves. For the ellipse, t is NOT the polar
     angle of the point (it is the 'eccentric angle'): at t = pi/4 the point is
     (2sqrt2, 3sqrt2/2), whose polar angle is arctan(3/4), not pi/4. Common mistake:
     squaring and adding without dividing first, getting x^2 + y^2 = ... for (b).
     Now you try: eliminate t from x = 1 + 2 cos t, y = 3 + 2 sin t.
     ((x - 1)^2 + (y - 3)^2 = 4)

D11. A batter hits a cricket ball from ground level. With g = 10 m/s^2 its
     position after t seconds is x = 15t, y = 20t - 5t^2 (metres). Find the
     Cartesian equation of the path, when and where it lands, and its greatest
     height. Also show that x = at^2, y = 2at is the parabola y^2 = 4ax.
     Answer: y = (4/3)x - x^2/45; it lands after 4 s, 60 m away; greatest height
     20 m (at t = 2 s, x = 30 m).
     Teacher explains: From x = 15t, t = x/15. Substitute:
        y = 20(x/15) - 5(x/15)^2 = (4/3)x - x^2/45
     a parabola opening downwards, as a thrown ball should. It lands when y = 0:
     5t(4 - t) = 0, so t = 0 (the hit) or t = 4 s, and then x = 15 x 4 = 60 m.
     By symmetry the top is halfway in time, t = 2: y = 40 - 20 = 20 m at
     x = 30 m. Check with the Cartesian form: (4/3)(30) - 900/45 = 40 - 20 = 20.
     For the standard parabola: from y = 2at, t = y/(2a), so
     x = a x y^2/(4a^2) = y^2/(4a), that is y^2 = 4ax. Every point (at^2, 2at) is on
     y^2 = 4ax, which is why this is the standard parametric form (used in topic
     8.25). Common mistake: squaring (x/15) as x^2/15. Now you try: eliminate t
     from x = 3t^2, y = 6t. (y^2 = 12x)

D12. Eliminate the parameter, stating any restriction: (a) x = t^2, y = t^2; (b)
     x = cos 2t, y = sin t; (c) x = sec t, y = tan t; (d) x = t + 1/t,
     y = t - 1/t.
     Answer: (a) y = x with x >= 0 (a half-line); (b) x = 1 - 2y^2, -1 <= y <= 1;
     (c) x^2 - y^2 = 1; (d) x^2 - y^2 = 4.
     Teacher explains: (a) y = x, but x = t^2 can never be negative, so only the
     half-line from O is traced (twice: t and -t give the same point). (b)
     Use cos 2t = 1 - 2sin^2t: x = 1 - 2y^2. Since y = sin t, -1 <= y <= 1, so only
     the arc of this parabola from (-1, -1) to (-1, 1) is traced. (c)
     sec^2t - tan^2t = 1 gives x^2 - y^2 = 1, a rectangular hyperbola. (d) Square
     and subtract:
        x^2 = t^2 + 2 + 1/t^2,   y^2 = t^2 - 2 + 1/t^2,   x^2 - y^2 = 4
     Also |x| = |t + 1/t| >= 2, which the hyperbola x^2 - y^2 = 4 satisfies
     automatically. A famous parametric curve with no simple Cartesian equation
     is the CYCLOID x = a(t - sin t), y = a(1 - cos t): the path of a mark on a
     rolling bicycle wheel of radius a. Now you try: eliminate t from x = cos t,
     y = cos 2t. (y = 2x^2 - 1, -1 <= x <= 1)

M6. Find the distance d between the polar points and the area of the triangle
    they form with the pole.
    a) (3, pi/6), (4, 2pi/3)   b) (2, pi/3), (4, 0)
    c) (1, 0), (1, pi/2)      d) (6, pi/2), (6, -pi/6)
    e) (2, pi), (2, 0)        f) (2, 5pi/6), (2sqrt3, pi/3)
    g) (7, pi/3), (8, 0)      h) (5, 0), (3, pi)
    i) (1, pi/3), (2, -pi/3)   j) (-2, pi/6), (2, pi/6)
    k) (4, pi/4), (4, 3pi/4)   l) (3, -pi/2), (5, pi/6)
    Answers:
      a) d = 5, area 6

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: use polar graph paper (circles and rays) and plot points by
  turning then walking; ALWAYS sketch the point before choosing theta; keep the
  conversion dictionary x = r cos theta, y = r sin theta, r^2 = x^2 + y^2 on the board; for
  parametric curves make a table of t, x, y and plot the points in order with
  arrows; check every elimination by substituting one value of t. Harder: find
  the area enclosed by the cardioid r = a(1 + cos theta) using (1/2)integral r^2 dtheta (3pia^2/2);
  show that the polar equation of a conic with focus at O and directrix x = -d
  is r = ed/(1 - e cos theta); find the Cartesian equation of the curve traced by
  the midpoint of a ladder sliding down a wall (a quarter circle); investigate
  the curves x = sin at, y = sin bt (Lissajous figures) with a graphing tool.

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.28 - VECTORS: ADDITION, SCALAR MULTIPLE, COMPONENTS, POSITION VECTORS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A VECTOR has magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force); a
    SCALAR has magnitude only. AB is the vector from A to B, |AB| its length.
    Special vectors: the ZERO vector 0; a UNIT vector (length 1); EQUAL vectors
    (same length and direction, anywhere in space); the NEGATIVE -a; COLLINEAR
    (parallel) vectors, which lie along parallel lines.
  - COMPONENTS: with unit vectors i, j, k along the x-, y- and z-axes,
    a = a_1i + a_2j + a_3k, also written (a_1, a_2, a_3). |a| = sqrt(a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2) and
  - ADDITION: TRIANGLE law AB + BC = AC; PARALLELOGRAM law (the sum of two
    vectors from one point is the diagonal); POLYGON law AB + BC + CD = AD. In
    components, add (or subtract) coordinate by coordinate. Addition is
    commutative and associative; a + 0 = a and a + (-a) = 0; |a + b| <= |a| + |b|
    (triangle inequality).
  - SCALAR MULTIPLE: lambdaa has length |lambda||a|, the same direction as a if lambda > 0 and
    the opposite direction if lambda < 0. a and b (b != 0) are PARALLEL exactly when
    a = lambdab, i.e. when their components are proportional: a_1/b_1 = a_2/b_2 = a_3/b_3.
  - POSITION VECTORS: the position vector of P(x, y, z) is OP = xi + yj + zk.
    For any two points AB = b - a ('end minus start') and |AB| is the distance
    AB.
  - SECTION FORMULA: R dividing AB internally in the ratio m : n has
    r = (mb + na)/(m + n); externally r = (mb - na)/(m - n). Midpoint (a + b)/2;
    centroid of a triangle (a + b + c)/3.
  - COLLINEAR POINTS: A, B, C are collinear exactly when AB = lambdaAC for some
    scalar lambda (the vectors are parallel AND share the point A).
  - LINEAR COMBINATIONS: any vector in the plane is xa + yb for two non-parallel
    vectors a, b; any vector in space is xa + yb + zc for three non-coplanar a,
    b, c. Find x, y, z by equating components.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A delivery drone starts at the point (1, 1, 0) (metres) and flies with the
    constant velocity v = 6i + 2j + 3k m/s. What is its speed? Where is it after
    5 s? How far has it travelled?
    Answer: Speed 7 m/s; it reaches (31, 11, 15); it has travelled 35 m.
    Teacher explains: The components say how fast the drone moves in each axis
    direction: 6 m/s east, 2 m/s north and 3 m/s up. The SPEED is the magnitude
    of the velocity:
       |v| = sqrt(6^2 + 2^2 + 3^2) = sqrt(36 + 4 + 9) = sqrt49 = 7 m/s
    In 5 s the displacement is 5v = 30i + 10j + 15k, so the new position vector
    is
       (i + j) + (30i + 10j + 15k) = 31i + 11j + 15k,  the point (31, 11, 15)
    The distance travelled is |5v| = 5 x 7 = 35 m (for a straight flight at
    constant velocity, distance = speed x time). Velocity is a vector; speed is
    its magnitude, a scalar. Common mistake: adding the components,
    6 + 2 + 3 = 11 m/s, as the speed. Now you try: the speed for
    v = 2i - 3j + 6k km/h, and the position after 2 h from the origin. (7 km/h;
    (4, -6, 12))

    1.
    Teacher explains: Magnitude by Pythagoras in three dimensions:
       |a| = sqrt(2^2 + (-3)^2 + 6^2) = sqrt(4 + 9 + 36) = sqrt49 = 7
    Divide every component by the length:
       check: 4/49 + 9/49 + 36/49 = 49/49 = 1
    DIRECTION COSINES of a (the cosines of the angles with the axes). Only the
    zero vector has no unit vector. Common mistake: dividing by 2 - 3 + 6 = 5.
    Now you try: the unit vector along i + j + k. ((1/sqrt3)(i + j + k), i.e.
    (sqrt3/3)(i + j + k))

D3. a = i + 2j - 3k and b = 2i - j + 5k. Find a + b, a - b and |a + b|, and
    check the triangle inequality. Explain the triangle, parallelogram and
    polygon laws.
    Answer: a + b = 3i + j + 2k, a - b = -i + 3j - 8k, |a + b| = sqrt14 ~ 3.74,
    which is less than |a| + |b| = sqrt14 + sqrt30 ~ 9.22.
    Teacher explains: Add and subtract component by component:
       a + b = (1 + 2)i + (2 - 1)j + (-3 + 5)k = 3i + j + 2k
       a - b = (1 - 2)i + (2 + 1)j + (-3 - 5)k = -i + 3j - 8k
       |a + b| = sqrt(9 + 1 + 4) = sqrt14;  |a| = sqrt14, |b| = sqrt30
    TRIANGLE LAW: place b with its tail at the head of a; a + b goes from the
    first tail to the last head (AB + BC = AC). PARALLELOGRAM LAW: with a and b
    from the same point, a + b is the diagonal (and a - b is the other diagonal,
    from the head of b to the head of a). POLYGON LAW: AB + BC + CD + DE = AE,
    and a closed polygon gives 0. The triangle inequality |a + b| <= |a| + |b|
    says one side of a triangle is at most the sum of the other two; equality
    only when a and b point the same way. Now you try: |a - b| for these
    vectors. (sqrt74)

D4. Show that a = 2i - 3j + k and b = -6i + 9j - 3k are parallel. Find lambda so that
    lambdai + 6j - 4k is parallel to 3i - 9j + 6k. Are 2i + 4j - k and 3i + 6j + 2k
    parallel?
    Answer: b = -3a (parallel, opposite directions). lambda = -2. No.
    Teacher explains: Two vectors are parallel when one is a scalar multiple of
    the other, i.e. the ratios of corresponding components are equal:
       -6/2 = 9/(-3) = -3/1 = -3    so b = -3a
    The negative factor means b points the opposite way, and |b| = 3|a|. For lambda:
       lambda/3 = 6/(-9) = -4/6,  all equal to -2/3,  so lambda = -2
    (check the two known ratios agree first: 6/(-9) = -2/3 = -4/6). For the last
    pair: 3/2 = 6/4 = 1.5 but 2/(-1) = -2, so they are NOT parallel. With a zero
    component, compare directly: 2i + 0j is parallel to 5i + 0j but not to
    5i + j. Common mistake: checking only two of the three ratios. Now you try:
    find p and q if 2i + pj + 3k is parallel to 4i - 6j + qk. (p = -3, q = 6)

D5. A is (1, 2, -3) and B is (4, -2, 9). Find AB, the distance AB and the unit
    vector in the direction of AB.
    Answer: AB = 3i - 4j + 12k, |AB| = 13, unit vector
    (3/13)i - (4/13)j + (12/13)k.
    Teacher explains: Let a = i + 2j - 3k and b = 4i - 2j + 9k be the position
    vectors. Going from A to B by way of O: AB = AO + OB = -a + b, so
       AB = b - a = (4 - 1)i + (-2 - 2)j + (9 + 3)k = 3i - 4j + 12k
       |AB| = sqrt(9 + 16 + 144) = sqrt169 = 13
       unit vector = AB/13 = (3/13)i - (4/13)j + (12/13)k
    'End minus start' gives AB; start minus end gives BA = -AB. The length of AB
    is the distance formula of topic 8.26 in vector dress. Common mistake:
    AB = a - b. Now you try: P(2, 0, -1), Q(0, 3, 5): find PQ and |PQ|.
    (-2i + 3j + 6k; 7)

D6. Prove the section formula r = (mb + na)/(m + n). Use it to find the point
    dividing A(1, 2, 3) and B(7, -4, 9) internally in the ratio 1 : 2, and the
    point dividing them externally in the ratio 2 : 1.
    Answer: Internal: 3i + 5k, the point (3, 0, 5). External: 13i - 10j + 15k,
    the point (13, -10, 15).
    Teacher explains: R lies on AB with AR : RB = m : n, so n AR = m RB:
       n(r - a) = m(b - r)   ->   nr + mr = mb + na   ->   r = (mb + na)/(m + n)
    Internal 1 : 2 (m = 1, n = 2):
       r = (b + 2a)/3 = ((7 + 2)i + (-4 + 4)j + (9 + 6)k)/3 = 3i + 0j + 5k
    External 2 : 1: R is outside, AR : RB = 2 : 1 with R beyond B, and the
    formula becomes r = (mb - na)/(m - n):
       r = (2b - a)/1 = (14 - 1)i + (-8 - 2)j + (18 - 3)k = 13i - 10j + 15k
    Check the external point: B is the midpoint of A and R: ((1 + 13)/2,
    (2 - 10)/2, (3 + 15)/2) = (7, -4, 9). Correct, since AR = 2RB means RB = AB.
    Common mistake: attaching m to a. Now you try: the point dividing a = 2i - j
    and b = 5i + 8j in the ratio 2 : 1 internally. (4i + 5j)

D7. Prove that the medians of a triangle meet at the point with position vector
    g = (a + b + c)/3, and find it for A(1, 2, 3), B(3, -1, 4) and C(-1, 5, 5).
    Answer: g = i + 2j + 4k, the point (1, 2, 4).
    Teacher explains: The midpoint D of BC has position vector d = (b + c)/2.
    The point dividing the median AD in the ratio 2 : 1 is
       (2d + 1a)/3 = (b + c + a)/3
    This expression is SYMMETRIC in a, b, c, so the point dividing BE in the
    ratio 2 : 1 (E the midpoint of CA) and the one dividing CF in 2 : 1 give the
    same vector: all three medians pass through G, with AG : GD = 2 : 1. For the
    triangle:
       g = ((1 + 3 - 1)i + (2 - 1 + 5)j + (3 + 4 + 5)k)/3
         = (3i + 6j + 12k)/3 = i + 2j + 4k
    Check with the median from A: d = (b + c)/2 = i + 2j + 4.5k, and (2d + a)/3
    = ((2 + 1)i + (4 + 2)j + (9 + 3)k)/3 = i + 2j + 4k. The vector proof is
    shorter than any coordinate-geometry proof. Common mistake: dividing by 2
    instead of 3. Now you try: the centroid of A(2, 0, 0), B(0, 3, 0),
    C(0, 0, 6). ((2/3)i + j + 2k)

D8. Show that A(1, -2, -8), B(5, 0, -2) and C(11, 3, 7) are collinear and find
    the ratio in which B divides AC. Find k if P(1, 2, 3), Q(2, k, 5) and
    R(4, 8, 9) are collinear.
    Answer: BC = (3/2)AB, so they are collinear and B divides AC in the ratio
    2 : 3. k = 4.
    Teacher explains: Compute two vectors that share a point:
       AB = 4i + 2j + 6k,   BC = 6i + 3j + 9k = (3/2)(4i + 2j + 6k)
    AB and BC are parallel and share B, so A, B, C lie on one line. Since
    BC = (3/2)AB, AB : BC = 2 : 3 (both in the same direction, so B is between A
    and C). For k: PQ = i + (k - 2)j + 2k and PR = 3i + 6j + 6k. Collinear means
    PR = lambdaPQ: from i and k components lambda = 3 and lambda = 3, so 6 = 3(k - 2) and
    k = 4. Check: PQ = i + 2j + 2k and PR = 3PQ. Note the clash of letters: k is
    both the unknown and the unit vector, so write the components in brackets
    enough for LINES in general; here the shared point B makes it work. Now you
    try: are (0, 1, 2), (1, 3, 5) and (3, 7, 11) collinear? (yes: the second
    difference is twice the first)

D9. Find the direction cosines of a = i - j + sqrt2 k and the angles it makes with
    the axes. Find the vectors of magnitude 2sqrt3 that are equally inclined to the
    three axes.
    Answer: 1/2, -1/2, sqrt2/2; angles 60 degrees, 120 degrees, 45 degrees. +/-(2i + 2j + 2k).
    Check: 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/2 = 1. Equally inclined
    2sqrt3 is 2sqrt3 x (+/-1/sqrt3)(i + j + k) = +/-(2i + 2j + 2k); check
    |2i + 2j + 2k| = sqrt12 = 2sqrt3. Common mistake: taking direction cosines of a
    vector as its components before dividing by |a|. Now you try: the angles

D10. Find the vector of magnitude 9 in the direction of a = 2i - j + 2k, the
     vector of magnitude 5 opposite to 3i + 4k, and the vector of magnitude 14
     along a + b, where b = i + 3j + 4k.
     Answer: 6i - 3j + 6k; -3i - 4k; 6i + 4j + 12k.
     Teacher explains: The recipe is (required length) x (unit vector in the
     required direction):
        |3i + 4k| = 5,  opposite unit vector -(3i + 4k)/5,  5 x it = -3i - 4k
        a + b = 3i + 2j + 6k,  |a + b| = sqrt(9 + 4 + 36) = 7
        14 x (3i + 2j + 6k)/7 = 6i + 4j + 12k
     Check the first: |6i - 3j + 6k| = sqrt(36 + 9 + 36) = sqrt81 = 9. 'Opposite to'
     means multiply by -1. Common mistake: multiplying a itself by 9 (giving
     length 27). Now you try: the vector of length 4 in the direction of i - j.
     (2sqrt2 i - 2sqrt2 j)

D11. Use vectors to prove the midpoint theorem: the segment joining the
     midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half
     as long. Then show that the midpoints of the sides of ANY quadrilateral
     form a parallelogram.
     Answer: If M, N are the midpoints of AB, AC then MN = (1/2)BC. For a
     quadrilateral ABCD with midpoints P, Q, R, S of AB, BC, CD, DA:
     PQ = SR = (1/2)AC.
     Teacher explains: Use position vectors a, b, c. The midpoints are
     m = (a + b)/2 and n = (a + c)/2, so
        MN = n - m = (a + c)/2 - (a + b)/2 = (c - b)/2 = (1/2)BC
     A vector equal to (1/2)BC is parallel to BC and has half its length: that
     is the whole theorem in one line. Quadrilateral (Varignon's theorem):
        PQ = (b + c)/2 - (a + b)/2 = (c - a)/2 = (1/2)AC
        SR = (c + d)/2 - (d + a)/2 = (c - a)/2 = (1/2)AC
     PQ = SR, so one pair of opposite sides of PQRS is equal and parallel, and
     PQRS is a parallelogram, even if ABCD is not convex or not flat! Check with
     numbers: A(0, 0, 0), B(4, 0, 0), C(6, 4, 2), D(0, 2, 4): P(2, 0, 0),
     Q(5, 2, 1), R(3, 3, 3), S(0, 1, 2); PQ = (3, 2, 1) = SR. Now you try: show
     that the diagonals of a parallelogram OACB (OA = a, OB = b) bisect each
     other. (both midpoints are (a + b)/2)

D12. Three ropes pull on a hot-air balloon with forces F_1 = 2i + 3j - k,
     F_2 = -i + 2j + 4k and F_3 = 3i - j + 2k (in kN). Find the resultant force
     and its size. What single extra force would keep the balloon in
     equilibrium?
     Answer: R = 4i + 4j + 5k, |R| = sqrt57 ~ 7.55 kN; the extra force is
     -4i - 4j - 5k.
     Teacher explains: Forces are vectors, so they add component by component
     (polygon law):
        i:  2 - 1 + 3 = 4
        j:  3 + 2 - 1 = 4
        k: -1 + 4 + 2 = 5          R = 4i + 4j + 5k
        |R| = sqrt(16 + 16 + 25) = sqrt57 ~ 7.55 kN
     EQUILIBRIUM means the total force is the zero vector, so the extra force
     must be -R = -4i - 4j - 5k, the same size sqrt57 kN in the opposite direction.
     Its direction cosines are -4/sqrt57, -4/sqrt57, -5/sqrt57. Adding magnitudes
     (|F_1| + |F_2| + |F_3| = sqrt14 + sqrt21 + sqrt14 ~ 12.07) gives a wrong answer unless
     all the forces point the same way. Now you try: forces 3i - j and
     -i + 4j + 2k; the force needed for equilibrium. (-2i - 3j - 2k)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw arrows for every sum and difference before computing; say
  'end minus start' for AB; line up components in columns (i, j, k) when adding;
  always divide by the MAGNITUDE (not the sum of components) for a unit vector;
  check parallel vectors by writing all three ratios. Harder: prove with vectors
  that the midpoints of the sides of any quadrilateral form a parallelogram
  (Varignon); show that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other;
  where the line joining a vertex of a tetrahedron to the centroid of the
  opposite face meets the other such lines.

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.29 - DOT PRODUCT AND CROSS PRODUCT; SCALAR TRIPLE PRODUCT
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
    perpendicular to a and b given by the RIGHT-HAND RULE. In components it is
    the determinant with rows (i, j, k), (a_1, a_2, a_3), (b_1, b_2, b_3): a x b
    = (a_2b_3 - a_3b_2)i - (a_1b_3 - a_3b_1)j + (a_1b_2 - a_2b_1)k.
  - i x j = k, j x k = i, k x i = j (cyclic), and reversing the order changes
    the sign: b x a = -(a x b). a x a = 0; a x b = 0 exactly when a and b are
    parallel (or one is 0). The cross product is distributive but NOT
    commutative and NOT associative.
  - |a x b| = area of the PARALLELOGRAM with sides a, b; the triangle ABC has
    area (1/2)|AB x AC|. Unit vectors perpendicular to both a and b:
    components of a, b, c (rows in that order). It is unchanged by a CYCLIC
    change, [a b c] = [b c a] = [c a b], and changes sign when two vectors are
  - |[a b c]| = VOLUME of the parallelepiped with edges a, b, c; the tetrahedron
    ABCD has volume (1/6)|[AB AC AD]|. a, b, c are COPLANAR exactly when
    [a b c] = 0; four points A, B, C, D are coplanar exactly when
    [AB AC AD] = 0.

D2. Find the angle between a = i + j and b = j + k, and between a = 2i - j + 2k
    and c = i + 2j - 2k.
    Answer: 60 degrees; arccos(-4/9) ~ 116.4 degrees (obtuse).
       theta = arccos(-4/9) ~ 116.4 degrees
    A negative dot product always means an obtuse angle. Geometric check of the
    first answer: the points O, P(1, 1, 0) and Q(0, 1, 1) form a triangle with
    OP = OQ = sqrt2 and PQ = sqrt(1 + 0 + 1) = sqrt2, an equilateral triangle, so the
    angle at O is 60 degrees. The angle between two vectors is always between 0 and pi
    (0 degrees and 180 degrees). Common mistake: forgetting to divide by BOTH magnitudes. Now
    you try: the angle between i + 2j + 2k and 2i + j - 2k. (arccos(0) = 90 degrees)
