       scalar projection = 10/sqrt6 = 10sqrt6/6 = 5sqrt6/3
                         = (5/3)i + (10/3)j + (5/3)k
    Check: the remainder a - (5/3)(i + 2j + k) = (1/3)i - (1/3)j + (1/3)k is
    perpendicular to b: 1/3 - 2/3 + 1/3 = 0. So a splits into a part along b and
    a part perpendicular to b, which is how forces are resolved on a slope. A
    negative scalar projection means the shadow points opposite to b. Common
    mistake: dividing by |a| instead of |b|. Now you try: the scalar projection
    of i - j + k on 2i + j + 2k. (1)

    are found by SQUARING (dot a vector with itself):
    (This is the cosine rule in vector form: |a - b| is the third side of the
    triangle with sides 3, 4 and angle 60 degrees.) If |a + b| = |a - b|, subtracting
    with equal diagonals is a rectangle. Common mistake: |a + b| = |a| + |b| = 7
    |2a + b|. (sqrt29)

D6. Find a x b for a = 2i + j - k and b = i - j + 2k. Check that it is
    perpendicular to both a and b, and find b x a.
    Answer: a x b = i - 5j - 3k; b x a = -i + 5j + 3k.
    Teacher explains: Write the determinant with i, j, k on top and expand along
    the first row:
               | i   j   k |
       a x b = | 2   1  -1 |
               | 1  -1   2 |
       = (1 x 2 - (-1)(-1))i - (2 x 2 - (-1) x 1)j + (2 x (-1) - 1 x 1)k
       = (2 - 1)i - (4 + 1)j + (-2 - 1)k = i - 5j - 3k
    Swapping the rows of a determinant changes its sign, so b x a = -(a x b).
    The cyclic table i x j = k, j x k = i, k x i = j (and j x i = -k, etc.)
    gives the same result term by term. Now you try: (i + 2j + 3k) x (i - j).
    (3i + 3j - 3k)

D7. Find the area of the triangle with vertices A(1, 1, 1), B(2, 3, 4) and
    C(4, 3, 2), and the area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides
    a = 3i + j + 4k and b = i - j + k.
    Answer: Triangle: 2sqrt6 ~ 4.90; parallelogram: sqrt42 ~ 6.48.
    Teacher explains: |a x b| = |a||b| sin theta = base x height of the
    parallelogram on a and b. The triangle is half of the parallelogram on AB
    and AC:
       AB = i + 2j + 3k,  AC = 3i + 2j + k
       AB x AC = (2 - 6)i - (1 - 9)j + (2 - 6)k = -4i + 8j - 4k
       |AB x AC| = sqrt(16 + 64 + 16) = sqrt96 = 4sqrt6,  area = 2sqrt6
    For the parallelogram:
       a x b = (1 x 1 - 4 x (-1))i - (3 x 1 - 4 x 1)j + (3 x (-1) - 1 x 1)k
             = 5i + j - 4k,   area = sqrt(25 + 1 + 16) = sqrt42
    If the area comes out 0 the points are collinear (or the vectors parallel).
    Common mistake: forgetting the 1/2 for a triangle, or using AB x BC with a
    wrong sign (the magnitude is the same either way). Now you try: the area of
    the triangle with vertices (0, 0, 0), (1, 2, 3), (2, 3, 1). (5sqrt3/2, since
    the cross product is -7i + 5j - k)

D8. Find the unit vectors perpendicular to both a = 3i + 2j + 2k and
    these vectors.
    Answer: +/-(1/3)(-2i + 2j + k).
    Teacher explains: a x b is perpendicular to both; divide by its length:
       a x b = (2(-2) - 2 x 2)i - (3(-2) - 2 x 1)j + (3 x 2 - 2 x 1)k
             = -8i + 8j + 4k,   |a x b| = sqrt(64 + 64 + 16) = 12
       unit vectors: +/-(-8i + 8j + 4k)/12 = +/-(-(2/3)i + (2/3)j + (1/3)k)
    There are TWO answers (up and down). Lagrange: |a|^2 = 17, |b|^2 = 9,
    just sin^2theta + cos^2theta = 1 multiplied by |a|^2|b|^2, and it gives a quick check on
    a cross product. Common mistake: giving only one of the two unit vectors.
    Now you try: a unit vector perpendicular to i + j and j + k.
    (+/-(1/sqrt3)(i - j + k))

D9. A mechanic pulls on a spanner. The force F = 2i + 3j - k newtons acts at the
    point with position vector r = i - 2j + 3k metres relative to the bolt. Find
    the moment (torque) of F about the bolt and its magnitude.
         = (2 - 9)i - (-1 - 6)j + (3 + 4)k = -7i + 7j + 7k
    of the force): a longer spanner gives more turning effect. Pushing along the
    r = 2i. (2k)

D10. Find [a b c] for a = 2i - 3j + 4k, b = i + 2j - k, c = 3i - j + 2k, and the
     volume of the parallelepiped with edges a, b, c. Check that [b c a] gives
     the same number and [b a c] its negative.
     Answer: [a b c] = -7; the volume is 7 cubic units; [b c a] = -7,
     [b a c] = 7.
        | 2  -3   4 |
        | 1   2  -1 |  = 2(4 - 1) + 3(2 + 3) + 4(-1 - 6)
        | 3  -1   2 |  = 6 + 15 - 28 = -7
     b x c is perpendicular to the base parallelogram with area |b x c|, and
     7. A cyclic shift of the rows (a b c -> b c a) is two row swaps, so the
     determinant is unchanged; one swap (b a c) changes the sign. The sign of
     [a b c] tells whether a, b, c form a right-handed (positive) or left-handed
     (negative) set. Common mistake: giving the volume as -7. Now you try:
     [i + j, j + k, k + i]. (2)

D11. Find lambda so that 2i - j + k, i + 2j - 3k and 3i + lambdaj + 5k are coplanar. Show
     that A(4, 5, 1), B(0, -1, -1), C(3, 9, 4) and D(-4, 4, 4) are coplanar.
     Answer: lambda = -4. [AB AC AD] = 0, so the points are coplanar.
     Teacher explains: Three vectors are coplanar exactly when the
     parallelepiped they make is flat, i.e. [a b c] = 0:
        | 2  -1   1 |
        | 1   2  -3 |  = 2(10 + 3lambda) + 1(5 + 9) + 1(lambda - 6) = 7lambda + 28
        | 3   lambda   5 |
     7lambda + 28 = 0 gives lambda = -4. For four points, use the three edges from A:
        AB = -4i - 6j - 2k,  AC = -i + 4j + 3k,  AD = -8i - j + 3k
        [AB AC AD] = -4(12 + 3) + 6(-3 + 24) - 2(1 + 32)
                   = -60 + 126 - 66 = 0
     so D lies in the plane of A, B, C. Common mistake: using the position
     vectors a, b, c, d directly - [a b c] = 0 says O, A, B, C are coplanar,
     which is a different question. Now you try: are i + j, j + k and i - k
     coplanar? (yes: the determinant is 0, since i - k = (i + j) - (j + k))

D12. Find the volume of the tetrahedron with vertices A(1, 1, 1), B(2, 1, 3),
     C(3, 2, 2) and D(3, 3, 4). Then, with a = i + j, b = j + k, c = k + i,
     Answer: Volume 5/6. a x (b x c) = -i + j; (a x b) x c = -i + k.
     Teacher explains: A tetrahedron is 1/6 of the parallelepiped on the same
     three edges:
        AB = i + 2k,  AC = 2i + j + k,  AD = 2i + 2j + 3k
        [AB AC AD] = 1(3 - 2) - 0(6 - 2) + 2(4 - 2) = 1 + 4 = 5
        volume = (1/6) x 5 = 5/6
     (1/3 x base x height, where the base triangle is half a parallelogram:
     (1/3)(1/2) = 1/6.) Triple products:
        b x c = (1 - 0)i - (0 - 1)j + (0 - 1)k = i + j - k
        a x (b x c) = (1(-1) - 0 x 1)i - (1(-1) - 0 x 1)j + (1 - 1)k = -i + j
        a x b = i - j + k,   (a x b) x c = (-1 - 0)i - (1 - 1)j + (0 + 1)k
              = -i + k
     So the brackets matter: the cross product is not associative. Memory aid
     try: the volume of the tetrahedron O(0, 0, 0), (2, 0, 0), (0, 3, 0),
     (0, 0, 4). (4)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: say 'dot gives a number, cross gives a vector' aloud before each
  question; write vectors in a column layout before multiplying; for cross
  products always write the 3 x 3 determinant and circle the minus sign on j;
  check every cross product by dotting it with both factors (you must get 0);
  use a real box to see why |[a b c]| is a volume. Harder: prove the sine rule
  for a triangle using a x b = b x c = c x a when a + b + c = 0; prove that
  c x a] = [a b c]^2; find the shortest distance from a point to a line using
  |AP x u|/|u| (used in topic 8.30); prove the cosine rule
  c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab cos C with dot products.

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.30 - LINES AND PLANES IN 3D; ANGLES AND DISTANCES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - LINE through the point A (position vector a) with direction b: VECTOR form
    r = a + lambdab (lambda any real number). CARTESIAN (symmetric) form through
    (x_1, y_1, z_1) with direction ratios a, b, c:
    (x - x_1)/a = (y - y_1)/b = (z - z_1)/c. Through two points use the direction
    ratios x_2 - x_1, y_2 - y_1, z_2 - z_1. A 0 in a denominator means that coordinate
    is constant along the line.
  - Two lines in space either INTERSECT, are PARALLEL, or are SKEW (neither:
    they do not meet and are not parallel). To decide, solve the equations of
    the general points; to find the intersection, put lambda and mu back.
  - SHORTEST DISTANCE between skew lines r = a_1 + lambdab_1 and r = a_2 + mub_2:
    PARALLEL lines r = a_1 + lambdab, r = a_2 + mub: d = |(a_2 - a_1) x b|/|b|. From a
    point P to the line r = a + lambdab: |(p - a) x b|/|b|.
    a(x - x_1) + b(y - y_1) + c(z - z_1) = 0, i.e. ax + by + cz = d, whose normal
    with (l, m, n) the unit normal and p >= 0 the distance from O. INTERCEPT form
    x/a + y/b + z/c = 1. Through three points A, B, C: use n = AB x AC.
  - INTERSECTION of a line and a plane: substitute the general point of the line
    into the plane and solve for lambda.
  - DISTANCE from (x_1, y_1, z_1) to the plane ax + by + cz + d = 0:
    |ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 + d|/sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2). Between PARALLEL planes
    ax + by + cz + d_1 = 0 and ax + by + cz + d_2 = 0 (same a, b, c!):
    |d_1 - d_2|/sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2). The FOOT of the perpendicular and the IMAGE of a
    point come from the line through the point along n.
  - COPLANAR LINES: r = a_1 + lambdab_1 and r = a_2 + mub_2 lie in one plane exactly when

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A laser beam starts at A(1, 2, 3) and travels in the direction 2i - j + 4k.
    Write the equation of the beam in vector and Cartesian form. Does it hit a
    sensor at (5, 0, 11)? At (3, 1, 6)?
    Answer: r = (i + 2j + 3k) + lambda(2i - j + 4k);
    (x - 1)/2 = (y - 2)/(-1) = (z - 3)/4. (5, 0, 11) is on it (lambda = 2); (3, 1, 6)
    is not.
    Teacher explains: Every point of the line is 'start + lambda x direction':
       r = (i + 2j + 3k) + lambda(2i - j + 4k)
       x = 1 + 2lambda,  y = 2 - lambda,  z = 3 + 4lambda
    Making lambda the subject of each equation and equating gives the Cartesian form
    (x - 1)/2 = (y - 2)/(-1) = (z - 3)/4. To test a point, find lambda from one
    coordinate and check the others: for (5, 0, 11), lambda = 2 from x, and then
    y = 2 - 2 = 0 and z = 3 + 8 = 11, all agree: ON the beam (for lambda >= 0, the ray
    itself). For (3, 1, 6), x gives lambda = 1, y gives lambda = 1, but z gives lambda = 3/4:
    NOT on it. Common mistake: writing (x + 1)/2 for the point (1, 2, 3) (the
    sign in the bracket is the opposite of the coordinate), or putting the
    point's coordinates in the denominators. Now you try: the line through
    (-2, 4, -5) parallel to 3i + 5j + 6k. ((x + 2)/3 = (y - 4)/5 = (z + 5)/6)

D2. Find the Cartesian equation of the line through (-1, 0, 2) and (3, 4, 6),
    and of the line through (3, -2, -5) and (3, -2, 6). Write
    (4 - x)/2 = (y + 1)/3 = z/(-1) in vector form.
    Answer: (x + 1)/1 = y/1 = (z - 2)/1 (i.e. x + 1 = y = z - 2); x = 3, y = -2
    (the line parallel to the z-axis); r = (4i - j) + lambda(-2i + 3j - k).
    Teacher explains: Direction ratios from the two points: (3 + 1, 4 - 0,
    6 - 2) = (4, 4, 4), which we may scale to (1, 1, 1). So
    (x + 1)/1 = (y - 0)/1 = (z - 2)/1. For (3, -2, -5) and (3, -2, 6) the
    direction ratios are (0, 0, 11): x and y never change, so the line is x = 3,
    y = -2 (some books write (x - 3)/0 = (y + 2)/0 = (z + 5)/11, meaning the
    numerators are 0). For the last one, first make the coefficient of x equal
    to +1:
       (4 - x)/2 = (x - 4)/(-2)
    so the point is (4, -1, 0) and the direction ratios are (-2, 3, -1):
    r = (4i - j + 0k) + lambda(-2i + 3j - k). Common mistake: reading the direction
    as (2, 3, -1) from (4 - x)/2. Now you try: the line through (1, 2, 3) and
    (4, 2, -1). ((x - 1)/3 = (z - 3)/(-4), y = 2)

D3. Find the angle between the lines (x - 2)/2 = (y - 1)/5 = (z + 3)/(-3) and
    (x + 2)/(-1) = (y - 4)/8 = (z - 5)/4. Are the lines
    (x - 5)/7 = (y + 2)/(-5) = z/1 and x/1 = y/2 = z/3 perpendicular?
    Answer: theta = arccos(26/(9sqrt38)) ~ 62.1 degrees. Yes, they are perpendicular.
    Teacher explains: Only the DIRECTIONS matter (the points do not):
    b_1 = (2, 5, -3), b_2 = (-1, 8, 4).
       |b_1| = sqrt(4 + 25 + 9) = sqrt38,   |b_2| = sqrt(1 + 64 + 16) = 9
       cos theta = 26/(9sqrt38) ~ 0.4686,   theta ~ 62.1 degrees
    they are perpendicular - even though they may not meet (skew lines can be
    perpendicular). Common mistake: using the points instead of the direction
    ratios. Now you try: the angle between x/2 = y/2 = z/1 and
    (x - 5)/4 = (y - 2)/1 = (z - 3)/8. (arccos(2/3) ~ 48.2 degrees)

D4. Show that the lines (x - 1)/1 = (y - 2)/(-1) = (z - 3)/2 and
    (x - 2)/1 = (y + 2)/2 = (z - 9)/(-2) intersect, and find the point.
    Answer: They meet at (3, 0, 7).
    Teacher explains: Write the general points: (1 + lambda, 2 - lambda, 3 + 2lambda) and
    (2 + mu, -2 + 2mu, 9 - 2mu). They meet when all three coordinates agree:
       x:  1 + lambda = 2 + mu         lambda - mu = 1
       y:  2 - lambda = -2 + 2mu       lambda + 2mu = 4
       z:  3 + 2lambda = 9 - 2mu       (the check equation)
    From the first two, 3mu = 3, mu = 1, lambda = 2. Check z: 3 + 4 = 7 and 9 - 2 = 7,
    equal, so the lines really meet; the point is (1 + 2, 2 - 2,
    3 + 4) = (3, 0, 7). If the third equation had failed, the lines would be
    SKEW (not parallel, since (1, -1, 2) and (1, 2, -2) are not proportional).
    Always use DIFFERENT parameters lambda and mu for the two lines. Common mistake:
    using lambda for both lines, which only finds points reached at the same
    parameter value. Now you try: do x = y = z and (x - 1)/1 = y/2 = (z + 1)/3
    meet? (yes, at (2, 2, 2))

D5. Find the shortest distance between the skew lines
    r = (i + j) + lambda(2i - j + k) and r = (2i + j - k) + mu(3i - 5j + 2k), and
    explain the formula.
    Answer: d = 10/sqrt59 = 10sqrt59/59 ~ 1.30.
    Teacher explains: The shortest segment between two skew lines is
    perpendicular to BOTH, so it is parallel to b_1 x b_2. Its length is the
    projection of any joining vector a_2 - a_1 on that common normal:
       b_1 x b_2 = (-2 + 5)i - (4 - 3)j + (-10 + 3)k = 3i - j - 7k
       |b_1 x b_2| = sqrt(9 + 1 + 49) = sqrt59
       a_2 - a_1 = (2i + j - k) - (i + j) = i - k
    being parallel) they intersect. If b_1 x b_2 = 0 the lines are parallel and a
    different formula is needed (D6). Common mistake: forgetting the absolute
    value, or dividing by |a_2 - a_1|. Now you try: the shortest distance between
    r = i + lambdaj and r = k + mui. (1)

D6. Find the distance between the parallel lines
    r = (i + 2j - 4k) + lambda(2i + 3j + 6k) and
    r = (3i + 3j - 5k) + mu(2i + 3j + 6k). Find also the distance of the point
    P(1, 2, 3) from the line r = lambda(i + j + k).
    Answer: sqrt293/7 ~ 2.45; sqrt2 ~ 1.41.
    Teacher explains: For parallel lines the joining vector a_2 - a_1 and the
    common direction b make a parallelogram whose height is the distance:
       a_2 - a_1 = 2i + j - k,   b = 2i + 3j + 6k,  |b| = 7
       (a_2 - a_1) x b = (6 + 3)i - (12 + 2)j + (6 - 2)k = 9i - 14j + 4k
       d = sqrt(81 + 196 + 16)/7 = sqrt293/7
    The same idea gives the distance from a point: the line passes through O
    with b = i + j + k, and OP = i + 2j + 3k:
       OP x b = (2 - 3)i - (1 - 3)j + (1 - 2)k = -i + 2j - k
       d = sqrt6/sqrt3 = sqrt2
    Check the second by the foot of the perpendicular: the foot is (2, 2, 2)
    (lambda = (1 + 2 + 3)/3 = 2), and P to (2, 2, 2) is sqrt(1 + 0 + 1) = sqrt2. Now you
    try: the distance of (0, 0, 0) from the line r = i + lambdaj. (1)

D7. Reduce 2x - 3y + 6z + 14 = 0 to normal form and find the distance of the
    plane from O and the direction cosines of its normal. Find the plane through
    (1, -1, 2) with normal 2i + 3j - k.
    Answer: -(2/7)x + (3/7)y - (6/7)z = 2: distance 2, direction cosines
    (-2/7, 3/7, -6/7). 2x + 3y - z + 3 = 0.
    Teacher explains: In normal form lx + my + nz = p, (l, m, n) is a UNIT
    normal and p >= 0. Here |n| = sqrt(4 + 9 + 36) = 7. Move the constant:
    2x - 3y + 6z = -14. The right side must be positive, so divide by -7:
       -(2/7)x + (3/7)y - (6/7)z = 2
    The distance from O is 2, and the unit normal pointing from O towards the
    plane is (-2/7, 3/7, -6/7). A plane through a point with a given normal:
       2(x - 1) + 3(y + 1) - (z - 2) = 0,   2x + 3y - z + 3 = 0
    Check: 2 - 3 - 2 + 3 = 0. Common mistake: dividing by 7 and keeping -2 on
    the right (p must be non-negative). Now you try: the distance from O to
    x + 2y - 2z = 9. (3)

D8. Find the plane through A(1, 1, 0), B(1, 2, 1) and C(-2, 2, -1), and write it
    in intercept form. Find the plane with intercepts 2, -3 and 4 on the axes.
    Answer: 2x + 3y - 3z = 5, i.e. x/(5/2) + y/(5/3) + z/(-5/3) = 1.
    6x - 4y + 3z = 12.
    Teacher explains: The normal is perpendicular to AB and AC, so take their
    cross product:
       AB = j + k,  AC = -3i + j - k
       n = AB x AC = (-1 - 1)i - (0 + 3)j + (0 + 3)k = -2i - 3j + 3k
       -2(x - 1) - 3(y - 1) + 3(z - 0) = 0,   2x + 3y - 3z = 5
    Check B: 2 + 6 - 3 = 5 and C: -4 + 6 + 3 = 5. For intercept form divide by
    the constant: x/(5/2) + y/(5/3) - z/(5/3) = 1; the plane meets the axes at
    x = 5/2, y = 5/3, z = -5/3. The plane with intercepts 2, -3, 4 is
    x/2 + y/(-3) + z/4 = 1; multiply by 12: 6x - 4y + 3z = 12. If the three
    points are collinear, AB x AC = 0 and there is no unique plane. Now you try:
    the plane through (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1). (x + y + z = 1)

D9. Find the angle between the planes 2x + y - 2z = 5 and 3x - 6y - 2z = 7. Find

    instead of cos (sin is for a line and a plane, D10). Now you try: the angle

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: model lines with pencils and planes with books or a sheet of card;
  always write a line as 'point + lambda x direction' and read the point and the
  direction off separately; underline the normal (a, b, c) of every plane; for
  any distance question first ask 'point, line or plane?' and choose the formula
  from a table; check intersection points in BOTH equations. Harder: find the
  equation of the plane through the intersection of x + y + z = 6 and
  2x + 3y + 4z + 5 = 0 passing through (1, 1, 1) (20x + 23y + 26z = 69); find
  the image of a line in a plane; find the equations of the common perpendicular
  of two skew lines and its feet; show that the locus of points equidistant from
  two parallel planes is the plane midway between them; find the volume of the
  tetrahedron cut from the first octant by x/a + y/b + z/c = 1 (abc/6).

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.31 - LIMITS: INTUITION, ALGEBRA OF LIMITS, STANDARD LIMITS (sin x / x)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - MEANING: lim (x -> a) f(x) = L means f(x) can be made as close to L as we
    like by taking x close enough to a, but NOT equal to a. The value f(a) (or
  - ONE-SIDED LIMITS: the left-hand limit (x -> a^-, x < a) and the right-hand
    limits exist and are EQUAL.
  - ALGEBRA OF LIMITS: if lim f = L and lim g = M then lim (f +/- g) = L +/- M, lim
    kf = kL, lim fg = LM, lim f/g = L/M (M != 0), lim f^n = L^n, lim ^nsqrtf = ^nsqrtL
    (L >= 0 for even n). So for polynomials, and rational functions with non-zero
    denominator, just SUBSTITUTE x = a.
  - INDETERMINATE FORM 0/0: substitution gives no answer. Remove the common
    factor (x - a) by FACTORISING, by RATIONALISING (multiply by the conjugate
    of the surd expression), or by using a STANDARD LIMIT.
  - STANDARD LIMITS (x in RADIANS): (x^n - a^n)/(x - a) -> na^n^-^1 as x -> a; sin x/x
    -> 1, tan x/x -> 1 and (1 - cos x)/x^2 -> 1/2 as x -> 0; (e^x - 1)/x -> 1,
    (a^x - 1)/x -> ln a and ln(1 + x)/x -> 1 as x -> 0; (1 + x)^(1/x) -> e as x -> 0
  - LIMITS AT INFINITY: 1/x^n -> 0 (n > 0). For a rational function divide top and
    bottom by the highest power of x in the DENOMINATOR: degree of
    numerator < degree of denominator gives 0; equal degrees give the ratio of
    the leading coefficients; a higher numerator degree gives no finite limit
  - A LIMIT FAILS TO EXIST when the one-sided limits differ (a jump, as for
    infinity', not a real number limit), or when f oscillates (sin(1/x) at 0).
  - SANDWICH (SQUEEZE) THEOREM: if g(x) <= f(x) <= h(x) near a and g, h -> L, then
    f -> L. It proves sin x/x -> 1 and x sin(1/x) -> 0.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A ball is dropped from a tower; after t seconds it has fallen s = 5t^2
    metres. Find its average speed between t = 2 and t = 2 + h, and use a table
    to guess its speed at the instant t = 2. Also guess lim (x -> 2)
    (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2) from a table.
    Answer: Average speed 20 + 5h m/s, which tends to 20 m/s as h -> 0; the limit
    is 4.
    Teacher explains: Average speed = distance/time:
       (5(2 + h)^2 - 5 x 4)/h = (20 + 20h + 5h^2 - 20)/h = 20 + 5h   (h != 0)
       h         1      0.1     0.01     -0.01    -0.1
       speed     25     20.5    20.05    19.95    19.5
    As h -> 0 from either side the average speed approaches 20 m/s: the speed at
    the instant t = 2 is the LIMIT, 20 m/s. At h = 0 the formula is 0/0,
    meaningless, which is why we need limits. Similarly for
    g(x) = (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2):
       x       1.9    1.99    1.999    2.001    2.01    2.1
       g(x)    3.9    3.99    3.999    4.001    4.01    4.1
    g(2) is not defined, but g(x) = x + 2 for x != 2, so the graph is the line
    y = x + 2 with a HOLE at (2, 4), and the limit is 4. The limit is about what
    happens NEAR x = 2, not AT x = 2. Now you try: guess lim (x -> 1)
    (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) from x = 0.9, 0.99, 1.01, 1.1. (1.9, 1.99, 2.01, 2.1: the
    limit is 2)

D2. Find lim (x -> 2) (x^3 - 2x + 5) and lim (x -> 1) (x^2 + 1)/(x + 3). If lim
    f(x) = 3 and lim g(x) = -2 as x -> a, find the limits of 2f - 3g, fg, f/g and
    sqrt(f + 6).
    Answer: 9; 1/2; 12, -6, -3/2, 3.
    Teacher explains: Polynomials: the limit is the value, because limits
    respect sums, products and constant multiples:
       lim (x^3 - 2x + 5) = 8 - 4 + 5 = 9
    Quotients: allowed when the denominator's limit is not 0:
       lim (x^2 + 1)/(x + 3) = (1 + 1)/(1 + 3) = 2/4 = 1/2
    With the given limits, apply the rules one at a time:
       lim (2f - 3g) = 2(3) - 3(-2) = 12
       lim fg = 3 x (-2) = -6,        lim f/g = 3/(-2) = -3/2
       lim sqrt(f + 6) = sqrt(3 + 6) = 3
    The quotient rule FAILS if lim g = 0; then we must simplify first (D3, D4).
    Common mistake: 'substituting' into a 0/0 expression and writing 0/0 = 1 or
    0. Now you try: lim (x -> -1) (x^2 + 3x)/(x - 1). (1)

D3. Find lim (x -> 2) (x^3 - 8)/(x^2 - 4) and lim (x -> 3) (x^2 - 5x + 6)/(x^2 - 9).
    Answer: 3; 1/6.
    Teacher explains: Substitution gives 0/0, so (x - 2) is a factor of BOTH
    numerator and denominator (factor theorem). Factorise and cancel (allowed,
    since x != 2 in a limit):
       (x^3 - 8)/(x^2 - 4) = (x - 2)(x^2 + 2x + 4)/((x - 2)(x + 2))
                         = (x^2 + 2x + 4)/(x + 2) -> (4 + 4 + 4)/4 = 3
       (x^2 - 5x + 6)/(x^2 - 9) = (x - 2)(x - 3)/((x - 3)(x + 3))
                              = (x - 2)/(x + 3) -> 1/6
    If after cancelling you still get 0/0, cancel again; if you get
    (non-zero)/0, the limit does not exist (the function blows up). Common
    mistake: cancelling terms instead of factors, e.g. x^2/x^2 in
    (x^2 - 5x + 6)/(x^2 - 9). Now you try: lim (x -> 1) (x^2 - 1)/(x^2 + x - 2).
    (2/3)

D4. Find lim (x -> 0) (sqrt(x + 4) - 2)/x and lim (x -> 0) (sqrt(1 + x) - sqrt(1 - x))/x.
    Answer: 1/4; 1.
    Teacher explains: With a surd, multiply top and bottom by the CONJUGATE, so
    that (sqrtA - B)(sqrtA + B) = A - B^2 removes the root:
       (sqrt(x + 4) - 2)/x x (sqrt(x + 4) + 2)/(sqrt(x + 4) + 2)
       = (x + 4 - 4)/(x(sqrt(x + 4) + 2)) = 1/(sqrt(x + 4) + 2) -> 1/(2 + 2) = 1/4
       (sqrt(1 + x) - sqrt(1 - x))/x = ((1 + x) - (1 - x))/(x(sqrt(1 + x) + sqrt(1 - x)))
       = 2/(sqrt(1 + x) + sqrt(1 - x)) -> 2/2 = 1
    Check the first with a calculator: x = 0.001 gives
    (sqrt4.001 - 2)/0.001 ~ 0.24998. Do NOT expand the denominator after
    multiplying: the x must stay as a factor so that it cancels. Now you try:
    lim (x -> 9) (sqrtx - 3)/(x - 9). (1/6)

D5. Prove that lim (x -> 0) sin x/x = 1 (x in radians). What happens if x is in
    degrees?
    Answer: The limit is 1; in degrees sin(x degrees)/x -> pi/180 ~ 0.01745.
    Teacher explains: Draw the unit circle with centre O, A = (1, 0),
    P = (cos x, sin x) with 0 < x < pi/2, and let the tangent at A meet OP at T,
    so AT = tan x. Compare three areas:
       triangle OAP   <   sector OAP   <   triangle OAT
       (1/2) sin x    <   (1/2) x      <   (1/2) tan x
    Divide by (1/2) sin x (positive) and take reciprocals:
       1 < x/sin x < 1/cos x,   so   cos x < sin x/x < 1
    since sin(-x)/(-x) = sin x/x, the left-hand limit is the same. Table
    (radians): x = 0.1 gives 0.99833, x = 0.01 gives 0.99998. In degrees,
    x degrees = pix/180 radians, so sin(x degrees)/x = (pi/180) x sin(pix/180)/(pix/180) -> pi/180:
    this is why calculus always uses radians. Now you try: lim (x -> 0) tan x/x.
    (1, since tan x/x = (sin x/x)(1/cos x))

D6. Find lim (x -> 0) sin 5x/(3x), lim (x -> 0) tan 2x/sin 3x and
    lim (x -> 0) sin(x^2)/x.
    Answer: 5/3; 2/3; 0.
    Teacher explains: Make the ANGLE and the DENOMINATOR match, then use sin theta/theta
    -> 1 with theta -> 0:
       sin 5x/(3x) = (5/3) x sin 5x/(5x) -> (5/3) x 1 = 5/3
       tan 2x/sin 3x = (tan 2x/(2x)) x (3x/sin 3x) x (2x/(3x)) -> 1 x 1 x 2/3
       sin(x^2)/x = (sin(x^2)/x^2) x x -> 1 x 0 = 0
    General results: sin ax/x -> a, sin ax/sin bx -> a/b, tan ax/tan bx -> a/b.
    Common mistake: 'cancelling' the x in sin 5x/(3x) to get sin 5/3 - sin 5x is
    NOT sin x 5x. Another: using sin 5x/(3x) -> 5x/(3x) without justifying it
    (the matching step IS the justification). Now you try:
    lim (x -> 0) sin 3x/sin 7x. (3/7)

D7. Show that lim (x -> 0) (1 - cos x)/x^2 = 1/2, and find lim (x -> 0)
    (1 - cos 4x)/x^2 and lim (x -> 0) (tan x - sin x)/x^3.
    Answer: 1/2; 8; 1/2.
    Teacher explains: Use 1 - cos x = 2 sin^2(x/2):
       (1 - cos x)/x^2 = 2 sin^2(x/2)/x^2 = (1/2) x (sin(x/2)/(x/2))^2 -> 1/2
    For 1 - cos 4x = 2 sin^2 2x:
       2 sin^2 2x/x^2 = 2 x 4 x (sin 2x/(2x))^2 -> 8
    (or: (1 - cos kx)/x^2 -> k^2/2 = 16/2). For the third, factor out tan x:
       tan x - sin x = tan x (1 - cos x)
       (tan x - sin x)/x^3 = (tan x/x) x (1 - cos x)/x^2 -> 1 x 1/2 = 1/2
    Check numerically: x = 0.01 gives (1 - cos 0.01)/0.0001 ~ 0.499996. Common

D8. A bank pays 100% interest per year, compounded n times a year, on ₹1.

    Then find lim (x -> 0) (1 + 3x)^(1/x), lim (x -> 0) (e^(2x) - 1)/x and
    lim (x -> 0) (2^x - 1)/x.
    Answer: ₹2, ₹2.25, ₹2.6130, ₹2.7146 -> e ~ 2.71828; e^3; 2; ln 2 ~ 0.693.
    Teacher explains: Each period multiplies the money by (1 + 1/n), and there
    are n periods:
       (1 + 1/n)^n   2      2.25    2.6130    2.7146    -> e = 2.71828...
    With x = 1/n this is (1 + x)^(1/x) -> e as x -> 0. Then
       (1 + 3x)^(1/x) = ((1 + 3x)^(1/(3x)))^3 -> e^3
       (e^(2x) - 1)/x = 2 x (e^(2x) - 1)/(2x) -> 2 x 1 = 2

D9. Prove that lim (x -> a) (x^n - a^n)/(x - a) = na^n^-^1 for a positive integer n,
    and find lim (x -> 2) (x^5 - 32)/(x - 2) and lim (x -> 8)
    (x^(1/3) - 2)/(x - 8). If lim (x -> 2) (x^n - 2^n)/(x - 2) = 80, find n.
    Answer: 80; 1/12; n = 5.
    Teacher explains: Factorise (check by multiplying out, all middle terms
    cancel):
       x^n - a^n = (x - a)(x^n^-^1 + x^n^-^2a + x^n^-^3a^2 + ... + a^n^-^1)
    Cancel (x - a); the bracket has n terms, each -> a^n^-^1 as x -> a, so the limit
    is na^n^-^1. (The result also holds for rational n and a > 0.) Now:
       (x^5 - 32)/(x - 2) = (x^5 - 2^5)/(x - 2) -> 5 x 2^4 = 80
       (x^(1/3) - 8^(1/3))/(x - 8) -> (1/3) x 8^(-2/3) = (1/3)(1/4) = 1/12
    For n: n x 2^n^-^1 = 80; try n = 5: 5 x 16 = 80. (n x 2^n^-^1 increases with n, so
    n = 5 is the only answer.) Common mistake: writing 32 as 2^4. Now you try:
    lim (x -> 1) (x^1^0 - 1)/(x - 1) and lim (x -> 1) (x^5 - 1)/(x^3 - 1). (10; 5/3)

D12. Explain why lim (x -> 0) 1/x, lim (x -> 0) 1/x^2 and lim (x -> 0) sin(1/x) do
     that lim (x -> 3) (2x + 1) = 7.
     sin(1/x): oscillates between -1 and 1; x sin(1/x) -> 0 by the sandwich
     Teacher explains: Three ways a limit can fail:
        1/x        x = +/-0.001 gives +/-1000: the two sides go opposite ways
        sin(1/x)   takes every value from -1 to 1 infinitely often near 0
     For sin(1/x): at x = 1/(npi) it is 0 and at x = 2/((4n + 1)pi) it is 1, and
     both kinds of point come arbitrarily close to 0. But
     -|x| <= x sin(1/x) <= |x| and both bounds -> 0, so x sin(1/x) -> 0 (sandwich).
     within 0.01 of 7 it suffices to be within 0.005 of 3. Now you try: does
     lim (x -> 0) x^2 sin(1/x) exist? (yes, 0, since -x^2 <= x^2 sin(1/x) <= x^2)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always try substitution first and write down what you get (a
  number, 0/0, or non-zero/0); make tables of values on a calculator in RADIAN
  mode; draw the graph with an open circle for the hole; keep a card with the
  standard limits and practise 'matching' the angle and the denominator; for
  one-sided limits test x = a - 0.001 and a + 0.001. Harder: prove lim (x -> 0)
  by showing the sequence is increasing and bounded by 3; investigate

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.32 - CONTINUITY
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - f is CONTINUOUS at x = a when three things hold: (1) f(a) is defined; (2)
    lim (x -> a) f(x) exists (left- and right-hand limits equal); (3) the limit
    equals f(a). In short lim (x -> a) f(x) = f(a). f is LEFT-continuous at a if
  - f is continuous on an open interval if it is continuous at every point; on
    [a, b] it must also be right-continuous at a and left-continuous at b.
    Informally: the graph can be drawn without lifting the pen. Continuity is
    only asked at points of the DOMAIN.
  - STANDARD CONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS (on their domains): polynomials, rational
    functions (except where the denominator is 0), sin x, cos x, e^x, a^x, |x|
    (everywhere), tan x (except x = pi/2 + npi), ln x (x > 0), sqrtx (x >= 0,
    right-continuous at 0). Sums, differences, products, quotients
    (denominator != 0) and COMPOSITIONS of continuous functions are continuous.
  - TYPES OF DISCONTINUITY at a: REMOVABLE - the limit exists but is not f(a),
    or f(a) is undefined (redefine f(a) = the limit to repair it); JUMP - both
    one-sided limits are finite but different (jump = RHL - LHL); INFINITE - f ->
    oscillating, as sin(1/x) at 0.
    at 0; |x| is continuous everywhere (it has a corner at 0, which affects
    differentiability, not continuity).
  - FINDING CONSTANTS in a piecewise function: at each joining point, set
    LHL = RHL = f(a) and solve (one equation per join for one unknown, two
    equations when there are two unknowns).
  - INTERMEDIATE VALUE THEOREM (IVT): if f is continuous on [a, b] and k lies
    between f(a) and f(b), then f(c) = k for some c in (a, b). In particular, if
    f(a) and f(b) have OPPOSITE SIGNS, f has a root in (a, b). Halving the
    interval each time (BISECTION) traps the root. The IVT needs continuity on
    the WHOLE closed interval, and it proves existence only (it does not say how
    many roots, or where exactly).

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Let f(x) = (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3) for x != 3. Is f continuous at 3 if (a) f(3) = 6,
    (b) f(3) = 5, (c) f(3) is not defined? Check the three conditions each time.
    Answer: (a) continuous; (b) not continuous (removable discontinuity); (c)
    not continuous at 3 (3 is not in the domain; the discontinuity is
    removable).
    Teacher explains: For x != 3, (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3) = (x - 3)(x + 3)/(x - 3)
    = x + 3, so lim (x -> 3) f(x) = 6 in every case. Now check the three
    conditions:
               f(3) defined?   limit exists?   limit = f(3)?
       (a)     yes (6)         yes (6)         yes          continuous
       (b)     yes (5)         yes (6)         no           not continuous
       (c)     no              yes (6)         -            not continuous
    The graph is the line y = x + 3 with the point at x = 3 either filled in the
    right place (a), lifted to height 5 (b), or missing (c). In (b) and (c) the
    defect is REMOVABLE: define f(3) = 6 and the function becomes continuous.
    Common mistake: stopping after condition (2) - a limit can exist and still
    differ from the value. Now you try: is g(x) = (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) (x != 1),
    g(1) = 2 continuous at 1? (yes: the limit is 2 = g(1))

D2. Where is each function continuous: (a) (x^2 + 1)/(x^2 - 5x + 6), (b) tan x,
    (c) sqrt(x - 1) + ln(4 - x), (d) sin(x^2) + e^(cos x), (e) |x - 2|?
    Answer: (a) all x except 2 and 3; (b) all x except pi/2 + npi; (c) 1 <= x < 4
    (right-continuous at 1); (d) all real x; (e) all real x.
    Teacher explains: Use the building blocks and the rules. (a) A rational
    function is continuous wherever its denominator is not 0:
    x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3), so it fails only at 2 and 3 (not in the
    domain). (b) tan x = sin x/cos x fails where cos x = 0, i.e. x = pi/2 + npi.
    (c) sqrt(x - 1) needs x >= 1 and ln(4 - x) needs x < 4; each piece is continuous
    on its domain, so the sum is continuous on [1, 4), right-continuous at the
    end point 1. (d) x^2 and sin are continuous, so sin(x^2) is (composition);
    cos x and e^x are continuous, so e^(cos x) is; their sum is continuous
    everywhere. (e) x - 2 and |u| are continuous, so |x - 2| is continuous
    everywhere, even at the corner x = 2. Common mistake: calling a function
    'discontinuous at 2' when 2 is not in its domain and then forgetting to say
    so. Now you try: where is 1/(e^x - 1) continuous? (all x != 0)

D3. An electricity board charges B(u) = 5u rupees for u <= 100 units and
    B(u) = 7u + c for u > 100. Find c so that the bill is continuous at
    100 units. Find k so that f(x) = kx + 1 (x <= 2), f(x) = 3x - 1 (x > 2) is
    continuous.
    Answer: c = -200; k = 2.
    Teacher explains: At a joining point, the left piece, the right piece and
    the value must agree:
       B(100) = 5 x 100 = 500 = LHL
       700 + c = 500   ->   c = -200
    With c = -200 there is no sudden jump in the bill when a family uses one
    unit more than 100: a fair tariff. For f: LHL = f(2) = 2k + 1 and
    RHL = 3(2) - 1 = 5, so 2k + 1 = 5 and k = 2. Check: the pieces 2x + 1 and
    3x - 1 both give 5 at x = 2. Common mistake: using the wrong piece for f(2)
    (check where the '=' sign is). Now you try: k if f(x) = x^2 + k (x < 3),
    f(x) = 4x (x >= 3) is continuous. (k = 3)

D4. Find k so that each function is continuous at 0: (a) f(x) = sin 3x/x
    (x != 0), f(0) = k; (b) g(x) = (1 - cos 4x)/x^2 (x != 0), g(0) = k; (c)
    h(x) = (e^x - 1)/x (x != 0), h(0) = k.
    Answer: (a) k = 3; (b) k = 8; (c) k = 1.
    Teacher explains: The value must equal the limit, which we find with the
    standard limits of topic 8.31:
       sin 3x/x = 3 x sin 3x/(3x) -> 3
       (1 - cos 4x)/x^2 = 2 sin^2 2x/x^2 = 8 (sin 2x/(2x))^2 -> 8
       (e^x - 1)/x -> 1
    So k = 3, 8 and 1. These are REMOVABLE discontinuities repaired by the right
    choice of value. Check (a) numerically: x = 0.001
    gives sin 0.003/0.001 ~ 2.9999955. Common mistake: putting x = 0
    into sin 3x/x and deciding k = 0 (0/0 is not 0). Now you try: k if
    f(x) = tan 2x/x (x != 0), f(0) = k is continuous. (k = 2)

D5. Find a and b so that f is continuous at x = 1, where f(x) = ax + 1 for
    x < 1, f(1) = 3 and f(x) = bx^2 - 1 for x > 1. Then find a and b so that
    g(x) = x^2 (x <= 1), ax + b (1 < x < 3), 2x + 5 (x >= 3) is continuous
    everywhere.
    Answer: a = 2, b = 4. For g: a = 5, b = -4.
    Teacher explains: At x = 1 all three must equal 3:
       LHL = a + 1 = 3        ->   a = 2
       RHL = b - 1 = 3        ->   b = 4
    For g there are TWO joins, giving two equations:
       x = 1:  1^2 = a + b             a + b = 1
       x = 3:  3a + b = 2(3) + 5      3a + b = 11
    Subtract: 2a = 10, a = 5, b = -4. Check: the middle piece 5x - 4 gives 1 at
    x = 1 and 11 at x = 3, matching both neighbours. Each piece is a polynomial,
    so continuity can fail only at the joins. Now you try: a and b if
    f(x) = x + a (x < 0), f(0) = b, f(x) = x^2 + 2 (x > 0). (a = 2, b = 2)

D6. Classify the discontinuity: (a) (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) at 1, (b) |x|/x at 0, (c)
    1/(x - 2) at 2, (d) sin(1/x) at 0, (e) f(x) = x + 1 (x < 1), f(x) = 5 - x
    (x >= 1) at 1.
    Answer: (a) removable; (b) jump; (c) infinite; (d) oscillating; (e) jump of
    2.
    Teacher explains: Find the one-sided limits and compare:
       function            LHL      RHL      type
       (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1)    2        2        removable (f(1) undefined)
       |x|/x               -1       1        jump (size 2)
       sin(1/x)            none     none     oscillating
       piecewise (e)       2        4        jump (size 2)
    Only a REMOVABLE discontinuity can be repaired by changing one value. A jump
    cannot: no value at 1 can equal both 2 and 4. Infinite and oscillating
    discontinuities have no finite one-sided limits at all. Note: for (b), 0 is
    not in the domain of |x|/x, but it is still a jump point of the graph. Now

D7. A car park charges ₹30 for each hour or part of an hour. Sketch the charge

D9. State the Intermediate Value Theorem. Show that x^3 - x - 1 = 0 has a root
    between 1 and 2, and use bisection twice to narrow it down.
    Answer: f(1) = -1 < 0 < 5 = f(2), so a root lies in (1, 2); after two
    bisections it lies in (1.25, 1.5), and a third gives (1.25, 1.375). (The
    root is ~ 1.3247.)
    Teacher explains: IVT: if f is continuous on [a, b] and k is between f(a)
    and f(b), then f(c) = k for at least one c in (a, b). f is a polynomial,
    hence continuous, and it changes sign on [1, 2], so it must cross 0 there.
    BISECTION: test the midpoint and keep the half where the sign changes:
       interval        midpoint m    f(m)                      new interval
       (1, 2)          1.5           3.375 - 1.5 - 1 = 0.875   (1, 1.5)
       (1, 1.5)        1.25          1.953 - 1.25 - 1 = -0.297 (1.25, 1.5)
       (1.25, 1.5)     1.375         2.600 - 1.375 - 1 = 0.225 (1.25, 1.375)
    Each step halves the width (1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, ...), so ten steps give the
    root to within about 0.001. The IVT promises at least one root; here the
    graph rises steadily for x > 1, so there is exactly one. Now you try: show
    that x^3 + 2x - 5 = 0 has a root between 1 and 2. (f(1) = -2, f(2) = 7)

D10. Show that cos x = x has a solution between 0 and pi/2. A hiker leaves the
     foot of a hill at 6 a.m., reaches the top at 6 p.m., sleeps, and walks down
     the same path next day from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. Show there is a place where
     she was at the same time of day on both days.
     Answer: g(x) = cos x - x has g(0) = 1 > 0 and g(pi/2) = -pi/2 < 0, so
     g(c) = 0 for some c. For the hiker, apply the IVT to the difference of her
     two heights.
     Teacher explains: Rearrange as g(x) = 0 with g(x) = cos x - x, continuous
     (difference of continuous functions):
        g(0) = cos 0 - 0 = 1 > 0
        g(pi/2) = cos(pi/2) - pi/2 = -pi/2 < 0
     So some c in (0, pi/2) has cos c = c (c ~ 0.739). Hiker: let U(t) be her
     height at time t on day 1 and D(t) on day 2; both are continuous. The
     difference h(t) = U(t) - D(t) is (0 - top) < 0 at 6 a.m. and (top - 0) > 0
     at 6 p.m., so h(t) = 0 at some time: same height, same time, hence the same
     place on the path. The IVT gives existence with no formula for the answer.
     Now you try: show that e^x = 3 - x has a solution in (0, 1).
     (g(x) = e^x + x - 3: g(0) = -2, g(1) = e - 2 > 0)

D11. Find and classify all the discontinuities of f(x) = (x^2 - 1)/(x^2 - 3x + 2),
     and redefine f where possible to remove them.
     Answer: x = 1: removable (limit -2), define f(1) = -2; x = 2: infinite
     (cannot be removed).
     Teacher explains: Factorise: f(x) = (x - 1)(x + 1)/((x - 1)(x - 2)). f is
     continuous except where the denominator is 0, at x = 1 and x = 2.
        at 1: cancel (x - 1): f(x) = (x + 1)/(x - 2) -> 2/(-1) = -2
     At x = 1 the limit exists, so defining f(1) = -2 makes f continuous there
     (removable). At x = 2 there is a vertical asymptote: an infinite
     discontinuity, which no value can repair. Rule for rational functions: a
     zero of the denominator that cancels completely with the numerator is a
     hole (removable); one that does not cancel is an asymptote. Now you try:
     find and classify the discontinuities of (x^2 - 4)/(x^2 - x - 2). (x = 2
     removable, limit 4/3; x = -1 infinite)

D12. Explain why the IVT fails for f(x) = 1/x on [-1, 1], and why its converse
     is false. Prove that every continuous f: [0, 1] -> [0, 1] has a FIXED POINT
     (f(c) = c).
     Answer: 1/x is not continuous on [-1, 1] (undefined at 0), so although
     f(-1) = -1 < 0 < 1 = f(1) there is no root. Converse: x^2 takes the value 0
     in (-1, 1) without a sign change. Fixed point: apply the IVT to
     g(x) = f(x) - x.
     Teacher explains: The IVT needs continuity on the WHOLE closed interval.
     contradiction, because the hypothesis fails. The converse ('if there is a
     root then f changes sign') is false: f(x) = x^2 has f(-1) = f(1) = 1 > 0 but
     f(0) = 0. FIXED POINT: let g(x) = f(x) - x, continuous on [0, 1]. Since
     0 <= f(x) <= 1:
        g(0) = f(0) - 0 >= 0,      g(1) = f(1) - 1 <= 0
     If g(0) = 0 or g(1) = 0 we are done; otherwise g(0) > 0 > g(1) and the IVT
     gives c in (0, 1) with g(c) = 0, i.e. f(c) = c. Example: f(x) = cos x on
     [0, 1] maps into [0, 1] and has the fixed point c ~ 0.739. The same idea
     proves that every polynomial of ODD degree has a real root (it is negative
     for large negative x and positive for large positive x, or the other way).
     Now you try: show that x^5 - 3x + 1 = 0 has a root in (0, 1). (f(0) = 1,
     f(1) = -1)

      l) LHL 0, RHL -1, f(a) = -1; not continuous

M9. The function is not defined at the given point. What value f(a) makes it
    continuous there (or say why this is impossible)?
    a) (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2) at x = 2
    b) sin 2x/x at x = 0
    c) (sqrt(x + 1) - 1)/x at x = 0
    d) (e^x - 1)/x at x = 0
    e) x sin(1/x) at x = 0
    f) (1 - cos x)/x^2 at x = 0
    g) (x^3 - 27)/(x - 3) at x = 3
    h) |x|/x at x = 0
    i) 1/x at x = 0
    j) tan 3x/sin x at x = 0
    k) (x^2 + x - 2)/(x^2 - 1) at x = 1
    l) ln(1 + x)/x at x = 0
    m) (x - 1)/(sqrtx - 1) at x = 1
    n) sin(1/x) at x = 0
    o) (1 + x)^(2/x) at x = 0
    p) (x^2 - 2x)/(x^2 - 4) at x = -2
    Answers:
      a) f(2) = 4
      b) f(0) = 2
      c) f(0) = 1/2
      d) f(0) = 1
      e) f(0) = 0
      f) f(0) = 1/2
      g) f(3) = 27
      h) impossible (jump: LHL -1, RHL 1)
      i) impossible (infinite)
      j) f(0) = 3
      k) f(1) = 3/2
      l) f(0) = 1
      m) f(1) = 2
      n) impossible (oscillating)
      o) f(0) = e^2
      p) impossible (infinite)

M10. Show that f(x) = 0 has a root in the interval: give f at the end points (f
     is continuous there).
     a) x^3 - x - 1 on [1, 2]
     b) x^3 + 2x - 5 on [1, 2]
     c) x^5 - 3x + 1 on [0, 1]
     d) x^2 - 2 on [1, 2]
     e) cos x - x on [0, pi/2]
     f) e^x + x - 3 on [0, 1]
     g) x^3 - 4x + 1 on [0, 1]
     h) x^4 - x - 10 on [1, 2]
     i) 2^x - 3x on [0, 1]
     j) ln x + x - 2 on [1, 2]
     k) x^3 + x^2 - 1 on [0, 1]
     l) sin x - x/2 on [pi/2, pi]
     m) x^3 - 3x + 1 on [1, 2]
     n) x - e^-^x on [0, 1]
     o) x^4 - 5x + 2 on [0, 1]
     p) tan x - 1 - x on [1, 3/2]
     Answers:
       a) f(1) = -1, f(2) = 5; sign change, so a root
       b) f(1) = -2, f(2) = 7; sign change, so a root
       c) f(0) = 1, f(1) = -1; sign change, so a root
       d) f(1) = -1, f(2) = 2; sign change, so a root
       e) f(0) = 1, f(pi/2) = -pi/2; sign change, so a root
       f) f(0) = -2, f(1) = e - 2 ~ 0.718; sign change, so a root
       g) f(0) = 1, f(1) = -2; sign change, so a root
       h) f(1) = -10, f(2) = 4; sign change, so a root
       i) f(0) = 1, f(1) = -1; sign change, so a root
       j) f(1) = -1, f(2) = ln 2 ~ 0.693; sign change, so a root
       k) f(0) = -1, f(1) = 1; sign change, so a root
       l) f(pi/2) = 1 - pi/4 ~ 0.215, f(pi) = -pi/2; sign change, so a root
       m) f(1) = -1, f(2) = 3; sign change, so a root
       n) f(0) = -1, f(1) = 1 - 1/e ~ 0.632; sign change, so a root
       o) f(0) = 2, f(1) = -2; sign change, so a root
       p) f(1) = tan 1 - 2 ~ -0.443, f(3/2) = tan(3/2) - 5/2 ~ 11.601; sign
          change, so a root

M11. Find consecutive integers n, n + 1 between which the LARGEST real root
     lies, then do two steps of bisection.
     a) x^3 - x - 1 = 0
     b) x^3 + 2x - 5 = 0
     c) x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0
     d) x^3 + x - 1 = 0
     e) x^3 - 6x + 2 = 0
     f) x^4 - 2x - 1 = 0
     g) x^3 - 9 = 0
     h) x^2 - 7 = 0
     i) x^3 - 3x^2 + 1 = 0
     j) x^3 + 3x - 6 = 0

       d) (0, 1); (0.5, 1); (0.5, 0.75)
       e) (2, 3); (2, 2.5); (2.25, 2.5)
       f) (1, 2); (1, 1.5); (1.25, 1.5)
       g) (2, 3); (2, 2.5); (2, 2.25)
       h) (2, 3); (2.5, 3); (2.5, 2.75)

M12. True or false? Give a reason or a counterexample for 'false'.
     a) Every polynomial is continuous at every real number.
     b) If lim (x -> a) f(x) exists, then f is continuous at a.
     c) If f is continuous at a, then lim (x -> a) f(x) = f(a).
     d) |x| is continuous at 0.
     f) tan x is continuous on (-pi/2, pi/2).
     g) 1/x is continuous on its domain.
     h) If f and g are continuous at a, so is f/g.
     i) If f is continuous and f(1) < 0 < f(2), then f has a root in (1, 2).
     j) If f has a root in (a, b), then f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs.
     k) A jump discontinuity can be removed by redefining f at one point.
     l) The sum of two discontinuous functions is always discontinuous.
     m) sin(1/x), with f(0) = 0, is continuous at 0.
     n) x sin(1/x), with f(0) = 0, is continuous at 0.
     o) Every odd-degree polynomial has at least one real root.
     p) If f is continuous on [0, 1] with values in [0, 1], then f(c) = c for
        some c.
     Answers:
       a) true
       b) false (e.g. f(a) may differ or be undefined)
       c) true
       d) true
       e) false (jump from 1 to 2)
       f) true
       g) true (0 is not in the domain)
       h) false (only if g(a) != 0)
       i) true (IVT)
       j) false (x^2 on [-1, 1])
       k) false (LHL != RHL, so no value equals both)
       m) false (oscillates)
       n) true
       o) true (IVT)
       p) true (fixed point)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw the graph of every piecewise function before deciding; fill
  in a three-column table (f(a), LHL, RHL) for each joining point; say 'no
  lifting of the pen' as the first test; for the IVT always write 'f is
  continuous on [a, b] because ...' before quoting signs. Harder: prove that if
  f is continuous and f(x) = 0 only at x = 1 and x = 3 then f has constant sign
  on (1, 3); show that x = cos x has exactly one solution; prove that a
  continuous function on [0, 2] with f(0) = f(2) takes equal values at two
  points 1 apart (apply the IVT to f(x + 1) - f(x)); study the Dirichlet
  function (1 for rational x, 0 for irrational x), discontinuous everywhere, and
  x times it, continuous only at 0.

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.33 - DERIVATIVE: DEFINITION FROM FIRST PRINCIPLES; GEOMETRIC MEANING
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - AVERAGE RATE OF CHANGE of y = f(x) from x = a to x = a + h is
    (f(a + h) - f(a))/h. On the graph it is the SLOPE OF THE SECANT (chord)
    joining (a, f(a)) and (a + h, f(a + h)).
  - The DERIVATIVE of f at a is f'(a) = lim h->0 (f(a + h) - f(a))/h, when this
    limit exists (as a finite number). Equivalent form: f'(a) = lim x->a
    (f(x) - f(a))/(x - a). Notation: f'(x), dy/dx, y', d/dx (f(x)), Df(x).
    Finding it straight from the limit is called differentiating FROM FIRST
    PRINCIPLES (ab initio).
  - GEOMETRIC MEANING: f'(a) is the slope of the TANGENT to y = f(x) at (a,
    f(a)); the tangent is the limiting position of the secants. Its equation is
    y - f(a) = f'(a)(x - a). PHYSICAL MEANING: the INSTANTANEOUS rate of change
    of y with respect to x (velocity = ds/dt, marginal cost, rate of growth).
  - Standard first-principles results: d/dx (c) = 0; d/dx (x^n) = nx^n^-^1 (binomial
    expansion of (x + h)^n); d/dx (ax^2 + bx + c) = 2ax + b; d/dx (1/x) = -1/x^2;
    d/dx (sqrtx) = 1/(2sqrtx) (rationalise the numerator); d/dx (sin x) = cos x and
    d/dx (cos x) = -sin x (x in RADIANS, using lim h->0 sin h/h = 1 and lim h->0
  - LEFT and RIGHT derivatives: Lf'(a) = lim h->0^- (f(a + h) - f(a))/h,
    both exist and are equal.
    f(a + h) - f(a) = [(f(a + h) - f(a))/h] x h -> f'(a) x 0 = 0). The converse
    is FALSE: |x| is continuous at 0 but has a CORNER there (Lf'(0) = -1,
  - NUMERICAL DERIVATIVES: the difference quotients for h = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001
    approach f'(a); the central difference (f(a + h) - f(a - h))/(2h) approaches
    much faster.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A stone is dropped from a bridge; after t seconds it has fallen s = 5t^2
    metres. Find its average speed from t = 2 to t = 2 + h for h = 1, 0.1, 0.01,
    0.001, and hence its speed at the instant t = 2.
    Answer: Average speed = 20 + 5h m/s: 25, 20.5, 20.05, 20.005. The
    instantaneous speed at t = 2 is 20 m/s.
    Teacher explains: Average speed = distance / time over the small interval:
       (s(2 + h) - s(2))/h = (5(4 + 4h + h^2) - 20)/h = (20h + 5h^2)/h = 20 + 5h
            h       average speed (m/s)
            1       25
            0.1     20.5
            0.01    20.05
            0.001   20.005
    As h shrinks the averages close in on 20, so the speed AT t = 2 is lim h->0
    (20 + 5h) = 20 m/s. This limit is exactly the derivative ds/dt at t = 2. We
    may cancel h because h != 0 while we compute the quotient; only then do we
    let h -> 0. Common mistake: putting h = 0 straight into (s(2 + h) - s(2))/h,
    which gives the meaningless 0/0. Now you try: find the speed at t = 3. (30
    m/s)

D2. Find the derivatives of x^2 and x^3 from first principles. Then prove d/dx
    (x^n) = nx^n^-^1 for every positive integer n.
    Answer: d/dx (x^2) = 2x, d/dx (x^3) = 3x^2, and in general nx^n^-^1.
    Teacher explains: Always write the definition first, then expand, cancel h,
    take the limit:
       f(x) = x^2:  (f(x + h) - f(x))/h = (x^2 + 2xh + h^2 - x^2)/h = 2x + h -> 2x
       f(x) = x^3:  ((x + h)^3 - x^3)/h = (3x^2h + 3xh^2 + h^3)/h
                                    = 3x^2 + 3xh + h^2 -> 3x^2
    For x^n use the binomial theorem (topic 8.18):
       (x + h)^n = x^n + nx^n^-^1h + C(n, 2)x^n^-^2h^2 + ... + h^n
       ((x + h)^n - x^n)/h = nx^n^-^1 + C(n, 2)x^n^-^2h + ... + h^n^-^1 -> nx^n^-^1
    Every term after the first still contains h, so it tends to 0. The rule
    "bring the power down, reduce the power by 1" is called the POWER RULE; it
    also holds for negative and fractional powers (see D4, D5 and topic 8.34).
    Common mistake: forgetting the middle terms, as in (x + h)^2 = x^2 + h^2. Now
    you try: find d/dx (x^4) from first principles. (4x^3)

D3. Find from first principles the derivative of f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c, and use it
    to find the derivative of 3x^2 - 5x + 2 and its value at x = 1.
    Answer: f'(x) = 2ax + b. For 3x^2 - 5x + 2 the derivative is 6x - 5, and at
    x = 1 it equals 1.
    Teacher explains: Work out f(x + h) - f(x) first, so the x^2 and x and c
    parts cancel:
       f(x + h) = a(x + h)^2 + b(x + h) + c = ax^2 + 2axh + ah^2 + bx + bh + c
       f(x + h) - f(x) = 2axh + ah^2 + bh
       (f(x + h) - f(x))/h = 2ax + ah + b  ->  2ax + b   as h -> 0
    The constant c disappears: a constant does not change, so its rate of change
    is 0. With a = 3, b = -5, c = 2: f'(x) = 6x - 5 and f'(1) = 1. This also
    shows that differentiation is LINEAR: the derivative of a sum is the sum of
    the derivatives and constants multiply through. Common mistake: writing the
    derivative of -5x as -5x or 5. Now you try: 4x^2 + 7x - 9. (8x + 7)

D4. Using the definition, show that d/dx (1/x) = -1/x^2 (x != 0), and find the
    slope of the curve y = 1/x at (2, 1/2).
    Answer: The derivative is -1/x^2; the slope at (2, 1/2) is -1/4.
    Teacher explains: Combine the two fractions over a common denominator before
    dividing by h:
       1/(x + h) - 1/x = (x - (x + h))/(x(x + h)) = -h/(x(x + h))
       (1/(x + h) - 1/x)/h = -1/(x(x + h))  ->  -1/x^2   as h -> 0
    This agrees with the power rule for n = -1: d/dx (x^-^1) = -x^-^2. At x = 2 the
    slope is -1/4. The slope is negative everywhere, so y = 1/x is falling on
    each branch. Common mistake: writing 1/(x + h) = 1/x + 1/h (false!). Now you
    try: d/dx (1/x^2) from first principles. (-2/x^3)

D5. Find d/dx (sqrtx) from first principles (x > 0) and hence the slope of y = sqrtx
    at x = 4.
    Answer: d/dx (sqrtx) = 1/(2sqrtx); at x = 4 the slope is 1/4.
    Teacher explains: A difference of square roots over h gives 0/0; RATIONALISE
    the numerator by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate sqrt(x + h) + sqrtx:
       (sqrt(x + h) - sqrtx)/h x (sqrt(x + h) + sqrtx)/(sqrt(x + h) + sqrtx)
         = ((x + h) - x)/(h(sqrt(x + h) + sqrtx))
         = 1/(sqrt(x + h) + sqrtx)  ->  1/(2sqrtx)   as h -> 0
    Power-rule check: sqrtx = x^(1/2), so the derivative is
    vertical tangent there and is NOT differentiable at 0. Common mistake:
    "multiplying out" the numerator only and leaving h in the denominator. Now
    you try: find d/dx (sqrt(x + 5)) from first principles. (1/(2sqrt(x + 5)))

D6. Prove that d/dx (sin x) = cos x, x in radians. Why must x be in radians?
    Answer: The difference quotient equals cos(x + h/2) x sin(h/2)/(h/2), which
    tends to cos x x 1 = cos x.
    Teacher explains: Use the formula sin C - sin D = 2 cos((C + D)/2)
    sin((C - D)/2):
       sin(x + h) - sin x = 2 cos(x + h/2) sin(h/2)
       (sin(x + h) - sin x)/h = cos(x + h/2) x sin(h/2)/(h/2)
    As h -> 0, cos(x + h/2) -> cos x (cosine is continuous) and sin(h/2)/(h/2) -> 1
    (standard limit, topic 8.31). So the limit is cos x. The standard limit
    lim theta->0 sin theta/theta = 1 is TRUE ONLY IN RADIANS; in degrees it would be pi/180,
    and every trig derivative would carry an extra factor pi/180. Check the
    geometry: at x = 0 the slope of y = sin x is cos 0 = 1, so the graph leaves
    the origin along y = x. Common mistake: expanding
    sin(x + h) = sin x + sin h. Now you try: prove d/dx (cos x) = -sin x using
    cos C - cos D = -2 sin((C + D)/2) sin((C - D)/2). (the quotient is
    -sin(x + h/2) x sin(h/2)/(h/2) -> -sin x)

    numerically for h = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001.
    1.051709, 1.005017, 1.000500, approaching 1.
    Teacher explains: Factor out e^x, which does not depend on h:
            0.1      1.051709
            0.01     1.005017
            0.001    1.000500
    So e^x is its own derivative: at every point the slope of y = e^x equals its
    so d/dx (a^x) = a^x ln a (topic 8.35). Common mistake: writing d/dx
    (e^x) = xe^x^-^1 (the power rule is for x^n with a FIXED power, not for a
    variable power). Now you try: find d/dx (e^3^x) from first principles, using

D8. Find the slope and the equation of the tangent to y = x^2 at (3, 9). Show
    that the secant from (3, 9) to (3 + h, (3 + h)^2) has slope 6 + h and explain
    how the tangent is the limit of the secants.
    Answer: Slope 6; tangent y = 6x - 9.
    Teacher explains: Secant slope = ((3 + h)^2 - 9)/h = (6h + h^2)/h = 6 + h. For
    h = 1, 0.5, 0.1 the secants have slopes 7, 6.5, 6.1: they swing round and
    settle on the tangent of slope 6.
       y |        /  secant, h = 1 (slope 7)
         +----------------- x
    Point-slope form: y - 9 = 6(x - 3), so y = 6x - 9. Check: the line meets the
    parabola where x^2 = 6x - 9, (x - 3)^2 = 0 - a DOUBLE root, the algebraic sign
    of touching. Common mistake: using the slope formula 2x without putting
    x = 3, and writing "y - 9 = 2x(x - 3)", which is not a line. Now you try:
    the tangent to y = x^3 at (1, 1). (slope 3; y = 3x - 2)

D9. The radius of a circular ripple is r cm. (i) Find the rate of change of its
    area A = pir^2 with respect to r when r = 5. (ii) Show that dA/dr equals the
    circumference. (iii) A cube of side x has volume V = x^3; find dV/dx at x = 4
    and interpret it.
    Answer: (i) 10pi ~ 31.42 cm^2 per cm; (ii) dA/dr = 2pir = circumference; (iii)
    dV/dx = 3x^2 = 48 cm^3 per cm at x = 4.
    Teacher explains: By the power rule dA/dr = pi x 2r = 2pir; at r = 5,
    cube, dV/dx = 3x^2 = 3 x 16 = 48 at x = 4: the extra volume when the side
    rate is (unit of y) per (unit of x). Common mistake: giving the area at
    r = 5 (25pi) instead of its rate of change. Now you try: V = (4/3)pir^3 for a
    sphere: find dV/dr at r = 3. (4pir^2 = 36pi ~ 113.10 cm^3 per cm, the surface
    area)

D10. Show that f(x) = |x| is continuous but not differentiable at x = 0. Then
     prove: if f is differentiable at a, it is continuous at a.
     Answer: Lf'(0) = -1 and Rf'(0) = 1 are different, so f'(0) does not exist,
     while lim x->0 |x| = 0 = f(0). Proof of the theorem below.
     Teacher explains: For |x| at 0 the difference quotient is |h|/h:
        h > 0:  |h|/h = h/h = 1       so  Rf'(0) = 1
        h < 0:  |h|/h = -h/h = -1     so  Lf'(0) = -1
     The graph is a V with a CORNER at the origin: the slope jumps from -1 to 1,
     so there is no single tangent. Yet |x| -> 0 = |0| as x -> 0, so it is
     continuous. Theorem: if f'(a) exists, then for h != 0
        f(a + h) - f(a) = [(f(a + h) - f(a))/h] x h  ->  f'(a) x 0 = 0
     so f(a + h) -> f(a): f is continuous at a. The contrapositive is useful: a
     function that is NOT continuous at a (a jump, a hole) cannot be
     differentiable there. The converse fails, as |x| shows. Other failures:
     mistake: thinking "no formula for the whole line" means "not
     differentiable". Now you try: is f(x) = x|x| differentiable at 0? (yes: the
     quotient is h|h|/h = |h| -> 0, so f'(0) = 0)

D11. Find a and b so that f(x) = x^2 for x <= 1, f(x) = ax + b for x > 1 is
     differentiable at x = 1. Then decide whether g(x) = x^2 + 1 for x < 1,
     g(x) = 2x for x >= 1 is differentiable at 1.
     Answer: a = 2, b = -1. g is differentiable at 1 with g'(1) = 2.
     Teacher explains: Two conditions: CONTINUITY (the pieces meet) and EQUAL
     one-sided slopes.
        continuity at 1:   1^2 = a(1) + b          a + b = 1
        left slope:  Lf'(1) = 2x at x = 1 = 2
        right slope: Rf'(1) = a                    a = 2, so b = -1
     So f(x) = 2x - 1 for x > 1: this is exactly the tangent to y = x^2 at
     (1, 1), which is why the join is smooth. For g: left value 1^2 + 1 = 2 and
     right value 2(1) = 2, so g is continuous; Lg'(1) = 2(1) = 2 and Rg'(1) = 2,
     equal, so g'(1) = 2. Common mistake: checking only the slopes. If the
     pieces do not meet, the one-sided difference quotient (f(1 + h) - f(1))/h
     blows up and f is not differentiable, whatever the slopes are. Now you try:
     find k so that f(x) = x^3 (x < 2), kx - 16 (x >= 2) is differentiable at 2,
     and check continuity. (k = 12; 8 = 24 - 16)

D12. For f(x) = x^3 at x = 2, compute the forward difference quotients
     (f(2 + h) - f(2))/h and the central differences (f(2 + h) - f(2 - h))/(2h)
     for h = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001. Which approaches f'(2) = 12 faster, and why?
     Answer: Forward: 12.61, 12.0601, 12.006001. Central: 12.01, 12.0001,
     12.000001. The central difference is far more accurate.
     Teacher explains: Algebra explains the table:
        forward: ((2 + h)^3 - 8)/h = 12 + 6h + h^2      error ~ 6h
        central: ((2 + h)^3 - (2 - h)^3)/(2h) = 12 + h^2  error = h^2
             h        forward       central
             0.1      12.610000     12.010000
             0.01     12.060100     12.000100
             0.001    12.006001     12.000001
     Each time h is divided by 10, the forward error drops about 10 times but
     the central error drops 100 times, because the h terms cancel in the
     symmetric quotient. Calculators and computers use such quotients. Warning:
     for tiny h (say 10^-^1^2) rounding errors in f(2 + h) - f(2) take over, so h
     cannot be made as small as we like on a machine. Common mistake: forgetting
     to divide by 2h in the central difference. Now you try: compute
     sin(0.1)/0.1, the forward quotient of sin x at 0 with h = 0.1. (0.998334,
     close to cos 0 = 1)

PART B - MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Find the average rate of change (the slope of the secant) of f over the
    given interval.
    a) x^2; [1, 3]      b) x^2; [-2, 0]        c) x^3; [0, 2]
    d) x^3; [1, 1.1]    e) 3x + 7; [-5, 4]    f) x^2 - 4x; [0, 4]
    g) 1/x; [1, 4]     h) 1/x; [-2, -1]      i) sqrtx; [4, 9]
    j) sqrtx; [0, 1]      k) 2x^2 + x; [1, 2]    l) 5 - x^2; [-1, 3]
    m) x^4; [-1, 1]     n) x^4; [1, 2]         o) sin x; [0, pi/2]
    p) cos x; [0, pi]   q) e^x; [0, 1]         r) ln x; [1, e]
    s) 2^x; [0, 3]      t) x^3 - 3x; [-2, 2]
    Answers: a) 4   b) -2   c) 4   d) 3.31   e) 3   f) 0   g) -1/4   h) -1/2
             i) 1/5   j) 1   k) 7   l) -2   m) 0   n) 15   o) 2/pi ~ 0.6366
             p) -2/pi ~ -0.6366   q) e - 1 ~ 1.7183   r) 1/(e - 1) ~ 0.5820
             s) 7/3   t) 1

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: Start every first-principles question by writing the definition in
  full, then do the algebra in three visible steps: expand or combine, cancel h,
  let h -> 0. Use numbers first (x = 3) before letters. Draw a secant and slide
  the second point towards the first; a table of difference quotients (D1, D12)
  makes the limit concrete. For the corner of |x|, draw the V and put a ruler on
  each arm. Harder: Prove d/dx (tan x) = sec^2x and d/dx (ln x) = 1/x from first
  principles (use lim (ln(1 + u))/u = 1). Show f(x) = x^2 sin(1/x), f(0) = 0 is
  differentiable at 0 but f' is not continuous there. If f(x + y) = f(x)f(y) for
  all x, y and f'(0) = 2, f(0) = 1, show f'(x) = 2f(x). Where is
  f(x) = |x^2 - 4x + 3| not differentiable? (x = 1 and x = 3.)

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.34 - DIFFERENTIATION RULES: PRODUCT, QUOTIENT, CHAIN RULE
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - POWER RULE: d/dx (x^n) = nx^n^-^1 for EVERY real n (whole, negative,
    xsqrtx = x^(3/2). d/dx (c) = 0 for a constant c.
  - LINEARITY: (cf)' = cf' and (f +/- g)' = f' +/- g'. So a polynomial is
    differentiated term by term. Simplify a quotient with a ONE-TERM denominator
    by splitting it before differentiating: (x^2 + 3x)/x = x + 3.
  - PRODUCT RULE: (uv)' = u'v + uv'. For three factors
    (uvw)' = u'vw + uv'w + uvw'. The derivative of a product is NOT the product
    of the derivatives.
  - QUOTIENT RULE: (u/v)' = (u'v - uv')/v^2 (v != 0): "low d-high minus high
    d-low, over low squared". The order in the numerator matters. Special case:
    (1/v)' = -v'/v^2.
  - CHAIN RULE: if y = f(u) and u = g(x), then dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx), i.e.
    (f(g(x)))' = f'(g(x)) x g'(x): differentiate the OUTSIDE function, keep the
    inside unchanged, then multiply by the derivative of the INSIDE. GENERAL
    POWER RULE: d/dx [g(x)]^n = n[g(x)]^n^-^1 g'(x); e.g. d/dx (3x^2 + 1)^5
    = 5(3x^2 + 1)^4 x 6x = 30x(3x^2 + 1)^4.
  - Useful chain results: d/dx sqrtg = g'/(2sqrtg); d/dx (1/g) = -g'/g^2; d/dx
    (ax + b)^n = na(ax + b)^n^-^1.
  - COMBINING RULES: decide the LAST operation (product, quotient or function of
    a function) and apply that rule first; use the others inside. Take out
    common factors to present answers neatly, e.g. x(x + 1)^5 gives
    (x + 1)^4(6x + 1).
  - Rules work with tables of values too: (fg)'(a) = f'(a)g(a) + f(a)g'(a),

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
    6/x^(2/3). Explain why rewriting as a power comes first.
    (vi) -4/x^(5/3).
    Teacher explains: The power rule only works on the form x^n, so rewrite every
    root and every reciprocal as a power, differentiate, then tidy up:
       (i)   x^7            ->  7x^6
       (ii)  1/x^3 = x^-^3     ->  -3x^-^4 = -3/x^4
       (iii) sqrtx = x^(1/2)   ->  (1/2)x^(-1/2) = 1/(2sqrtx)
       (v)   x^2sqrtx = x^(5/2) -> (5/2)x^(3/2) = (5/2)xsqrtx
       (vi)  6x^(-2/3)      ->  6 x (-2/3)x^(-5/3) = -4/x^(5/3)
    Subtracting 1 from a negative power makes it MORE negative: -3 - 1 = -4,
    -1/3 - 1 = -4/3. Common mistakes: d/dx (1/x^3) = 1/(3x^2) (differentiating the

D2. A small factory's cost of making x bicycles a day is
    C(x) = 0.01x^3 - 0.6x^2 + 15x + 2,000 rupees. Find the marginal cost C'(x) and
    its value when x = 20 and x = 40. What does it mean?
    Answer: C'(x) = 0.03x^2 - 1.2x + 15; C'(20) = ₹3 and C'(40) = ₹15 per
    bicycle.
    Teacher explains: Differentiate term by term (sum rule) and keep constants
    as multipliers (constant multiple rule); the fixed cost 2,000 has derivative
    0:
       C'(x) = 0.01 x 3x^2 - 0.6 x 2x + 15 + 0 = 0.03x^2 - 1.2x + 15
       C'(20) = 0.03 x 400 - 24 + 15 = 12 - 24 + 15 = 3
       C'(40) = 0.03 x 1,600 - 48 + 15 = 48 - 48 + 15 = 15
    Meaning: at 20 bicycles a day, making one more costs about ₹3 extra; at 40 a
    day, about ₹15 extra (the machines are overloaded). Check with actual costs:
    C(21) - C(20) = 2,143.01 - 2,140 = 3.01 ~ 3. The fixed cost does not affect
    the marginal cost. Common mistake: forgetting that the derivative of the
    constant 2,000 is 0, not 2,000. Now you try: R(x) = 50x - 0.5x^2; find
    R'(30). (R'(x) = 50 - x, R'(30) = 20)

D3. Prove the product rule (uv)' = u'v + uv', and use it to differentiate
    y = (x^2 + 1)(x^3 - 2x). Check by expanding first.
    Answer: y' = 5x^4 - 3x^2 - 2.
    Teacher explains: Add and subtract u(x + h)v(x) in the difference quotient:
       u(x + h)v(x + h) - u(x)v(x)
         = u(x + h)[v(x + h) - v(x)] + v(x)[u(x + h) - u(x)]
    Divide by h and let h -> 0: u(x + h) -> u(x) (differentiable, hence
    continuous), so the limit is uv' + vu'. Now the example, with u = x^2 + 1 and
    v = x^3 - 2x:
       u' = 2x,   v' = 3x^2 - 2
       y' = 2x(x^3 - 2x) + (x^2 + 1)(3x^2 - 2)
          = 2x^4 - 4x^2 + 3x^4 + x^2 - 2 = 5x^4 - 3x^2 - 2
    Check: y = x^5 - x^3 - 2x, so y' = 5x^4 - 3x^2 - 2. Same. Common mistake:
    (uv)' = u'v', which here gives 2x(3x^2 - 2) = 6x^3 - 4x, wrong. Now you try:
    (2x - 1)(x^2 + 3) by the product rule. (6x^2 - 2x + 6)

D4. Differentiate y = (2x + 1)/(x - 3) and y = x^2/(x + 1) with the quotient
    rule. Where are these derivatives defined?
    Answer: y' = -7/(x - 3)^2 (x != 3); y' = (x^2 + 2x)/(x + 1)^2 (x != -1).
    Teacher explains: Write u (top), v (bottom), u', v' in a small table first:
       u = 2x + 1   u' = 2      v = x - 3   v' = 1
       y' = (u'v - uv')/v^2 = (2(x - 3) - (2x + 1)(1))/(x - 3)^2
          = (2x - 6 - 2x - 1)/(x - 3)^2 = -7/(x - 3)^2
       u = x^2   u' = 2x         v = x + 1   v' = 1
       y' = (2x(x + 1) - x^2)/(x + 1)^2 = (x^2 + 2x)/(x + 1)^2 = x(x + 2)/(x + 1)^2
    The derivative -7/(x - 3)^2 is always negative: the graph of the first
    function falls on each side of x = 3. Common mistakes: reversing the
    numerator (uv' - u'v gives the wrong sign), forgetting to square v, and
    dropping brackets so that -(2x + 1) becomes -2x + 1. Now you try:
    (3x - 2)/(x + 4). (14/(x + 4)^2)

D5. Differentiate y = (3x^2 + 1)^5 using the chain rule. Explain the rule with
    u = 3x^2 + 1, and explain "rates multiply" with a simple example.
    Answer: dy/dx = 30x(3x^2 + 1)^4.
    Teacher explains: Let u = 3x^2 + 1, so y = u^5:
       dy/du = 5u^4,   du/dx = 6x
       dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx) = 5u^4 x 6x = 30x(3x^2 + 1)^4
    In words: bring down the power, keep the bracket as it is, lower the power
    by 1, then MULTIPLY BY THE DERIVATIVE OF THE BRACKET. Why rates multiply: if
    a cyclist's gear makes the wheel turn 3 times per pedal turn (du/dx = 3) and
    each wheel turn moves the bike 2 m (dy/du = 2), the bike moves 6 m per pedal
    turn (dy/dx = 2 x 3). Expanding (3x^2 + 1)^5 first would take 6 terms and much
    longer. Common mistake: 5(3x^2 + 1)^4 with the factor 6x missing. Now you try:
    (1 - 4x)^6 and (x^2 + 5x)^3. (-24(1 - 4x)^5; 3(2x + 5)(x^2 + 5x)^2)

D6. Differentiate y = sqrt(1 + x^3) and y = 1/(2x - 5)^2.
    Answer: y' = 3x^2/(2sqrt(1 + x^3)); y' = -4/(2x - 5)^3.
    Teacher explains: Write as powers, then use the general power rule:
       y = (1 + x^3)^(1/2)
       y' = (1/2)(1 + x^3)^(-1/2) x 3x^2 = 3x^2/(2sqrt(1 + x^3))
       y = (2x - 5)^-^2
       y' = -2(2x - 5)^-^3 x 2 = -4/(2x - 5)^3
    Memorise d/dx sqrtg = g'/(2sqrtg): "derivative of the inside over twice the root".
    The first derivative exists for 1 + x^3 > 0, i.e. x > -1; the second for
    x != 5/2. Common mistakes: writing 1/(2sqrt(1 + x^3)) (no chain factor), and
    treating 1/(2x - 5)^2 with the quotient rule and losing a sign (possible, but

D7. Differentiate y = x^2sqrt(1 - x^2) and simplify to a single fraction.
    Answer: y' = (2x - 3x^3)/sqrt(1 - x^2) = x(2 - 3x^2)/sqrt(1 - x^2), for -1 < x < 1.
    Teacher explains: The LAST operation is a product, so the product rule comes
    first and the chain rule is used inside it:
       u = x^2          u' = 2x
       v = sqrt(1 - x^2)   v' = -2x/(2sqrt(1 - x^2)) = -x/sqrt(1 - x^2)
       y' = 2xsqrt(1 - x^2) + x^2 x (-x/sqrt(1 - x^2))
          = (2x(1 - x^2) - x^3)/sqrt(1 - x^2)          (common denominator)
          = (2x - 3x^3)/sqrt(1 - x^2)
    To combine, multiply the first term top and bottom by sqrt(1 - x^2):
    sqrt(1 - x^2) x sqrt(1 - x^2) = 1 - x^2. Check at x = 0: y' = 0, and indeed y >= 0
    with y(0) = 0, a minimum. Common mistake: forgetting the chain factor -2x.
    Now you try: x(2x + 1)^3 and factorise. (y' = (2x + 1)^3 + 6x(2x + 1)^2
    = (2x + 1)^2(8x + 1))

D8. Differentiate y = x/sqrt(x^2 + 1) and y = (x + 1)^2/(x - 1), simplifying fully.
    Answer: y' = 1/(x^2 + 1)^(3/2); y' = (x + 1)(x - 3)/(x - 1)^2.
    Teacher explains: Quotient rule outside, chain rule inside:
       u = x, u' = 1;  v = sqrt(x^2 + 1), v' = x/sqrt(x^2 + 1)
       y' = (sqrt(x^2 + 1) - x x x/sqrt(x^2 + 1))/(x^2 + 1)
          = ((x^2 + 1) - x^2)/((x^2 + 1)sqrt(x^2 + 1)) = 1/(x^2 + 1)^(3/2)
    For the second: u = (x + 1)^2, u' = 2(x + 1); v = x - 1, v' = 1:
       y' = (2(x + 1)(x - 1) - (x + 1)^2)/(x - 1)^2
          = (x + 1)(2x - 2 - x - 1)/(x - 1)^2 = (x + 1)(x - 3)/(x - 1)^2
    Take out the common factor (x + 1) BEFORE expanding: it saves work and shows
    at once that y' = 0 at x = -1 and x = 3. Common mistake: cancelling (x + 1)
    against the denominator (it is not a factor of (x - 1)^2). Now you try:
    x/(x^2 + 4). ((4 - x^2)/(x^2 + 4)^2)

D9. The table gives values of f, g and their derivatives.
        x    f(x)   f'(x)   g(x)   g'(x)
        1     3      2       2      -1
        2     5      4       1       3
    Answer: 1, 7/4, -4, 6, -3.
    Teacher explains: Use the rules with numbers, reading carefully WHERE each
    derivative is evaluated:
       (fg)'(1) = f'(1)g(1) + f(1)g'(1) = 2 x 2 + 3 x (-1) = 1
       (f/g)'(1) = (f'(1)g(1) - f(1)g'(1))/g(1)^2 = (4 + 3)/4 = 7/4
    In the chain rule the OUTER derivative is taken at the INNER value g(a), not
    g'(3), which is not in the table)

D10. Show that (1/v)' = -v'/v^2, and use it with the product rule to derive the
     quotient rule. Hence prove the power rule for negative integers.
     Answer: (1/v)' = -v'/v^2 by the chain rule; then
     (u/v)' = (u x v^-^1)' = (u'v - uv')/v^2; and (x^-^n)' = -nx^-^n^-^1.
     Teacher explains: Write 1/v = v^-^1 and use the chain rule (outer function
     t^-^1, inner v):
        (v^-^1)' = -v^-^2 x v' = -v'/v^2
        (u/v)' = (u x v^-^1)' = u'v^-^1 + u(-v'/v^2)
               = u'/v - uv'/v^2 = (u'v - uv')/v^2
     For n a positive integer, x^-^n = 1/x^n, so (x^-^n)' = -nx^n^-^1/x^2^n = -nx^-^n^-^1,
     which is the power rule with power -n. So one rule covers all integer
     powers. Common mistake: (1/v)' = 1/v' (for v = x^2 that would give 1/(2x)
     instead of -2/x^3). Now you try: use (1/v)' to differentiate 1/(x^2 + 1).
     (-2x/(x^2 + 1)^2)

D11. A spherical balloon is inflated so that its radius after t seconds is
     r = 2t + 1 cm. Find the rate at which its volume V = (4/3)pir^3 is increasing
     when t = 2.
     Answer: dV/dt = 200pi ~ 628.32 cm^3/s.
     Teacher explains: V depends on r and r depends on t, so use the chain rule:
        dV/dr = 4pir^2,   dr/dt = 2
        dV/dt = (dV/dr)(dr/dt) = 4pir^2 x 2 = 8pir^2
        at t = 2:  r = 5,  dV/dt = 8pi x 25 = 200pi ~ 628.32 cm^3/s
     Units: (cm^3 per cm) x (cm per s) = cm^3 per s - the "cm" cancels just like
     du in dy/du x du/dx. The rate is not constant: it grows with r^2 because a
     bigger balloon has a bigger surface to push out. Common mistake: using
     t = 2 in place of r (dV/dr at r = 2 gives 16pi, the wrong quantity). Now you
     try: a circular stain has radius r = 3t cm; find dA/dt at t = 2 for
     A = pir^2. (dA/dt = 2pir x 3 = 36pi ~ 113.10 cm^2/s)

D12. Spot and correct each mistake: (a) d/dx (x^2 x x^3) = 2x x 3x^2 = 6x^3; (b)
     d/dx (2x + 1)^4 = 4(2x + 1)^3; (c) d/dx (5/x^2) = 5/(2x); (d)
     d/dx sqrt(x^2 + 9) = 1/(2sqrt(x^2 + 9)); (e) d/dx
     (x/(x + 1)) = (x - (x + 1))/(x + 1)^2.
     Answer: (a) 5x^4; (b) 8(2x + 1)^3; (c) -10/x^3; (d) x/sqrt(x^2 + 9); (e)
     1/(x + 1)^2.
     Teacher explains: Name the rule each student broke:
        (a) product of derivatives used. x^2 x x^3 = x^5, so 5x^4
            (or product rule: 2x x x^3 + x^2 x 3x^2 = 5x^4)
        (b) chain factor missing: 4(2x + 1)^3 x 2 = 8(2x + 1)^3
        (c) differentiated the denominator: 5x^-^2 -> -10x^-^3 = -10/x^3
        (d) chain factor missing: (2x)/(2sqrt(x^2 + 9)) = x/sqrt(x^2 + 9)
        (e) numerator reversed: (1 x (x + 1) - x x 1)/(x + 1)^2 = 1/(x + 1)^2
     Build the habit of a quick CHECK: plug in a number and compare with the
     difference quotient on a calculator, or differentiate in two ways (expand
     first, then use the rule). Now you try: find the error in d/dx
     (x/(x + 1)) = ((x + 1) - x)/(x + 1). (the denominator must be squared:
     1/(x + 1)^2)
