TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: Make a three-line checklist for every question - continuous on
  [a, b]? differentiable on (a, b)? f(a) = f(b)? - and tick it before solving.
  Draw the graph and the chord; slide a ruler parallel to the chord until it
  just touches the curve. Always test each c against a < c < b. Harder: Prove
  Cauchy's MVT: (f(b) - f(a))g'(c) = (g(b) - g(a))f'(c), using h(x)
  = (f(b) - f(a))g(x) - (g(b) - g(a))f(x). Show that if f'' > 0 on (a, b) the
  MVT point is unique. Prove e^x >= 1 + x for all x and |tan a - tan b| >= |a - b|
  on (-pi/2, pi/2). If f(0) = 0 and |f'(x)| <= |f(x)| on [0, 1], show f = 0 there.

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.41 - APPLICATIONS OF DERIVATIVES: RATE OF CHANGE, TANGENTS AND NORMALS,
             INCREASING AND DECREASING FUNCTIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - RATE OF CHANGE: dy/dx is the rate at which y changes per unit change in x;
    its units are (units of y) per (unit of x). dA/dr = 2pir for a circle,
    dV/dr = 4pir^2 for a sphere. Radians are used throughout.
  - RELATED RATES: when several quantities change with time t, write the
    EQUATION linking them first (Pythagoras, similar triangles, volume formula),
    differentiate BOTH sides with respect to t using the chain rule
    (d/dt(r^3) = 3r^2 dr/dt), and only THEN substitute the values at the instant
    asked. A decreasing quantity has a negative rate.
    NORMAL (perpendicular to the tangent): slope -1/m, so
    y - y_1 = -(1/m)(x - x_1). If m = 0 the tangent is y = y_1 and the normal is
    x = x_1; if dy/dx is infinite the tangent is vertical, x = x_1.
  - For IMPLICIT curves find dy/dx by implicit differentiation (circle:
    dy/dx = -x/y). For PARAMETRIC curves x = x(t), y = y(t):
    dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), evaluated at the given t. Useful results: the
    tangent to x^2 + y^2 = a^2 at (x_1, y_1) is xx_1 + yy_1 = a^2, and to
    x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 it is xx_1/a^2 + yy_1/b^2 = 1.
    undefined) and points outside the domain on a number line, test the sign of
    endpoints where f is continuous may also be included.
    approximate the extra cost / revenue of producing one more unit; profit
    P(x) = R(x) - C(x).

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Find the rate of change of the area A of a circle with respect to its radius
    r when r = 5 cm, and of the volume V of a sphere with respect to its radius
    when r = 3 cm. Then: for y = 7x - x^3, x increases at 4 units per second; how
    fast is the SLOPE of the curve changing when x = 2?
    Answer: dA/dr = 10pi ~ 31.42 cm^2 per cm; dV/dr = 36pi ~ 113.10 cm^3 per cm; the
    slope decreases at 48 units per second (dm/dt = -48).
    Teacher explains: "Rate of change of A with respect to r" means dA/dr: how
    many cm^2 the area gains per extra cm of radius at that moment.
        A = pir^2          dA/dr = 2pir     at r = 5:  2pi x 5 = 10pi
        V = (4/3)pir^3     dV/dr = 4pir^2    at r = 3:  4pi x 9 = 36pi
    Note that dA/dr = 2pir is the circumference: a thin ring of width dr adds
    area ~ 2pir dr. For the last part the slope is m = dy/dx = 7 - 3x^2, which
    itself changes with time. By the chain rule
    dm/dt = (dm/dx)(dx/dt) = -6x x 4 = -24x, and at x = 2 this is -48. Common
    mistakes: substituting r = 5 BEFORE differentiating (you get 25pi, a
    constant, whose derivative is 0), and forgetting units. Now you try: the
    rate of change of the surface area S = 6a^2 of a cube with respect to its
    edge a when a = 4 cm. (dS/da = 12a = 48 cm^2 per cm)

D2. Air is pumped into a spherical balloon at 100 cm^3 per second. How fast is
    the radius increasing when the radius is 10 cm? How fast is the surface area
    increasing at that instant?
    Answer: dr/dt = 1/(4pi) ~ 0.0796 cm/s; dS/dt = 20 cm^2/s.
    Teacher explains: Step 1: name the variables and write what is given and
    wanted: dV/dt = 100, want dr/dt when r = 10. Step 2: the equation linking V
    and r is V = (4/3)pir^3. Step 3: differentiate with respect to t (chain rule):
        dV/dt = 4pir^2 x dr/dt
          100 = 4pi(10)^2 x dr/dt = 400pi x dr/dt
        dr/dt = 100/(400pi) = 1/(4pi) ~ 0.0796 cm/s
        S = 4pir^2   so   dS/dt = 8pir x dr/dt = 8pi x 10 x 1/(4pi) = 20
    Notice that dr/dt gets SMALLER as the balloon grows: the same 100 cm^3
    spreads over a bigger surface, which is why a balloon seems to inflate
    quickly at first and then slowly. Common mistake: writing dV/dt = 4pir^2
    (forgetting the factor dr/dt). Now you try: a spherical soap bubble has
    radius increasing at 0.2 cm/s; find dV/dt when r = 5 cm.
    (dV/dt = 4pi x 25 x 0.2 = 20pi ~ 62.83 cm^3/s)

D3. A 13 m ladder leans against a vertical wall. Its foot is pulled away from
    the wall along the ground at 0.5 m/s. How fast is the top sliding down the
    wall when the foot is 5 m from the wall? How fast is the angle between the
    ladder and the ground changing then?
    Answer: The top slides down at 5/24 m/s ~ 0.208 m/s (dy/dt = -5/24); the
    angle decreases at 1/24 rad/s ~ 0.0417 rad/s.
    Teacher explains: Draw the right triangle: x = distance of the foot from the
    wall, y = height of the top. Pythagoras holds at EVERY instant:
        x^2 + y^2 = 169
        2x dx/dt + 2y dy/dt = 0      (differentiate w.r.t. t)
        at x = 5:  y = sqrt(169 - 25) = 12
        5 x 0.5 + 12 x dy/dt = 0
        dy/dt = -2.5/12 = -5/24 m/s
    The minus sign says y is DECREASING. For the angle theta with the ground,
    cos theta = x/13, so -sin theta dtheta/dt = (1/13) dx/dt. With sin theta = 12/13: dtheta/dt
    = -(0.5/13) / (12/13) = -0.5/12 = -1/24 rad/s. Common mistake: putting x = 5
    into x^2 + y^2 = 169 before differentiating, which makes x a constant and
    gives nonsense. Now you try: a 10 m ladder, foot moving away at 1.5 m/s; how
    fast does the top fall when the foot is 6 m from the wall? (y = 8,
    dy/dt = -6 x 1.5/8 = -9/8 = -1.125 m/s)

D4. Water is poured at 8 m^3 per minute into a conical tank with its vertex
    pointing down. The tank is 12 m deep and its top has radius 6 m. How fast is
    the water level rising when the water is 4 m deep?
    Answer: dh/dt = 2/pi ~ 0.637 m per minute.
    Teacher explains: The water forms a smaller cone with radius r and depth h.
    By similar triangles r/h = 6/12, so r = h/2. Replace r BEFORE
    differentiating so that only one changing variable is left:
        V = (1/3)pir^2h = (1/3)pi(h/2)^2h = pih^3/12
        dV/dt = (pih^2/4) x dh/dt
            8 = (pi x 16/4) x dh/dt = 4pi x dh/dt
        dh/dt = 8/(4pi) = 2/pi ~ 0.637 m/min
    As the water gets deeper the surface is wider, so the level rises more
    slowly. Common mistakes: using the tank's fixed radius 6 as r (r changes
    with h), and differentiating V = (1/3)pir^2h treating r as a constant. Now you
    try: same tank, find how fast the water SURFACE radius grows when h = 4 m.
    (r = h/2, dr/dt = (1/2)(2/pi) = 1/pi ~ 0.318 m/min)

D5. A man 1.8 m tall walks away from a lamp post 6 m high at 1.4 m/s. How fast
    is his shadow lengthening? How fast is the tip of the shadow moving?
    Answer: The shadow lengthens at 0.6 m/s; the tip moves at 2 m/s.
    Teacher explains: Let x = distance of the man from the post and s = length
    of his shadow. The light ray from the lamp top to the shadow tip makes two
    similar triangles:
           lamp
            |\
          6 |  \
            |    \  man
            |     |\
            |  1.8| \
            +-----+--+
               x    s
        6/(x + s) = 1.8/s  ->  6s = 1.8x + 1.8s  ->  4.2s = 1.8x
        s = (3/7)x          ds/dt = (3/7) x 1.4 = 0.6 m/s
        tip at x + s:       d(x + s)/dt = 1.4 + 0.6 = 2 m/s
    The answer does not depend on how far away he is: the shadow grows at a
    constant rate. Common mistake: answering 0.6 m/s for the TIP; the tip moves
    with the man AND runs ahead of him. Now you try: a girl 1.5 m tall walks
    away from a 4.5 m lamp at 1.2 m/s. (4.5s = 1.5x + 1.5s, s = x/2: shadow
    grows at 0.6 m/s, tip moves at 1.8 m/s)

D6. Find the equations of the tangent and the normal to y = x^3 - 2x + 1 at the
    point where x = 2. Where does the normal meet the x-axis?
    Answer: Tangent y = 10x - 15; normal x + 10y = 52; the normal meets the
    x-axis at (52, 0).
    Teacher explains: Three things are needed: the point, the slope of the
    tangent, and the point-slope formula.
        point:    y(2) = 8 - 4 + 1 = 5, so (2, 5)
        slope:    dy/dx = 3x^2 - 2, at x = 2: 12 - 2 = 10
        tangent:  y - 5 = 10(x - 2)       ->  y = 10x - 15
        normal:   slope -1/10
                  y - 5 = -(1/10)(x - 2)  ->  10y - 50 = -x + 2
                                          ->  x + 10y = 52
    Check: (2, 5) lies on both lines (10 x 2 - 15 = 5 and 2 + 50 = 52), and the
    slopes multiply to 10 x (-1/10) = -1. Putting y = 0 in the normal gives
    x = 52. Common mistakes: using the slope 10 for the normal too; writing the
    normal slope as +1/10 or -10. Now you try: tangent and normal to
    y = x^2 - 3x + 2 at x = 3. (point (3, 2), slope 3: tangent y = 3x - 7, normal
    x + 3y = 9)

D7. On the curve y = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5 find the points where the tangent is (a)
    parallel to the x-axis, (b) parallel to the line y = 15x + 2, (c)
    perpendicular to the line x + 15y = 4.
    Answer: (a) (-1, 10) and (3, -22); (b) (-2, 3) and (4, -15); (c) the same
    two points as (b).
    Teacher explains: Parallel lines have EQUAL slopes; a line parallel to the
    x-axis has slope 0. So set dy/dx equal to the required slope and solve for
    x, then find y from the CURVE (not from the line).
        dy/dx = 3x^2 - 6x - 9 = 3(x - 3)(x + 1)
        (a) 3(x - 3)(x + 1) = 0    ->  x = 3 or -1
            y(3) = 27 - 27 - 27 + 5 = -22,   y(-1) = -1 - 3 + 9 + 5 = 10
        (b) 3x^2 - 6x - 9 = 15      ->  x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0  ->  x = 4 or -2
            y(4) = 64 - 48 - 36 + 5 = -15,   y(-2) = -8 - 12 + 18 + 5 = 3
    (c) The line x + 15y = 4 has slope -1/15; a perpendicular line has slope 15
    (product -1), so this is the same as (b). Common mistake: substituting x
    into dy/dx instead of y to get the y-coordinate. Now you try: the point on
    y = x^2 - 4x + 1 where the tangent is parallel to y = 2x + 3. (2x - 4 = 2,
    x = 3: the point (3, -2))

D8. Find the tangent and normal to the circle x^2 + y^2 = 25 at (3, 4), and the
    tangent to the ellipse x^2/16 + y^2/9 = 1 at (16/5, 9/5). Show that every
    normal to a circle passes through its centre.
    Answer: Circle: tangent 3x + 4y = 25, normal 4x - 3y = 0 (through O).
    Ellipse: tangent x + y = 5.
    Teacher explains: Differentiate implicitly, remembering that y is a function
    of x, so d/dx(y^2) = 2y dy/dx:
        2x + 2y dy/dx = 0   ->   dy/dx = -x/y = -3/4 at (3, 4)
        tangent:  y - 4 = -(3/4)(x - 3)  ->  4y - 16 = -3x + 9
                                         ->  3x + 4y = 25
        normal:   y - 4 = (4/3)(x - 3)   ->  4x - 3y = 0
    The normal passes through (0, 0). In general the normal at (x_1, y_1) has
    slope y_1/x_1, so it is y = (y_1/x_1)x, a line through the centre: the radius is
    perpendicular to the tangent (as in topic 7.25). For the ellipse,
    (2x/16) + (2y/9) dy/dx = 0 gives dy/dx = -9x/(16y) = -(9 x 16/5)/(16 x 9/5)
    = -1, so y - 9/5 = -(x - 16/5), x + y = 5. This agrees with the formula
    xx_1/16 + yy_1/9 = 1: x/5 + y/5 = 1. Common mistake: writing d/dx(y^2) = 2y.
    Now you try: the tangent to x^2 + y^2 = 169 at (5, -12). (5x - 12y = 169)

D9. A curve is given by x = t^2, y = t^3. Find the tangent and the normal at the
    point where t = 2. Where is the tangent horizontal or vertical?
    Answer: At t = 2 the point is (4, 8), dy/dx = 3; tangent y = 3x - 4, normal
    x + 3y = 28. At t = 0, both dx/dt and dy/dt vanish: the curve has a cusp at
    the origin (it touches the x-axis there); it has no other horizontal or
    vertical tangents.
    Teacher explains: For a parametric curve, find dx/dt and dy/dt separately
    and divide:
        dx/dt = 2t,  dy/dt = 3t^2,  dy/dx = 3t^2/(2t) = 3t/2   (t != 0)
        t = 2:  point (4, 8),  slope 3
        tangent:  y - 8 = 3(x - 4)         ->  y = 3x - 4
        normal:   y - 8 = -(1/3)(x - 4)    ->  x + 3y = 28
    A horizontal tangent needs dy/dt = 0 with dx/dt != 0; a vertical one needs
    dx/dt = 0 with dy/dt != 0. Here both vanish only at t = 0; the slope 3t/2 -> 0
    as t -> 0, so the curve (y^2 = x^3, the semicubical parabola) meets the origin
    with a cusp touching the x-axis. Common mistake: computing (dx/dt)/(dy/dt),
    which is dx/dy. Now you try: x = t^2, y = 2t at t = 2. (point (4, 4),
    dy/dx = 1/t = 1/2: tangent x - 2y + 4 = 0, normal 2x + y = 12)

D10. Find the intervals in which f(x) = 2x^3 - 9x^2 + 12x + 1 is strictly
     increasing and strictly decreasing. Use a sign chart.
     Teacher explains: Factorise the derivative completely, then test each piece
     of the number line cut by its zeros:
                     x < 1      1 < x < 2      x > 2
         x - 1         -            +            +
         x - 2         -            -            +
         f           rises        falls        rises
               ------------(1)-----------(2)------------
     the graph rises to 6, falls to 5, then rises for ever. Common mistakes:
     factor sign when a factor is (2 - x). Now you try: f(x) = x^3 - 12x.
     (-2, 2))

D12. A factory's total cost of making x toys is
     C(x) = 0.005x^3 - 0.02x^2 + 30x + 5,000 rupees, and its revenue from selling
     x toys is R(x) = 3x^2 + 36x + 5 rupees. Find the marginal cost when x = 3

     costs about ₹30; selling the 6th toy brings about ₹66 more.

     The exact extra revenue from the 6th toy is R(6) - R(5) = 329 - 260 = 69,

PART B - MATHEMATICAL ONLY

M1. Find the rate of change (exact values).
    a) A = pir^2, dA/dr at r = 3
    b) A = pir^2, dA/dr at r = 7/2
    c) C = 2pir, dC/dr at r = 10
    d) V = (4/3)pir^3, dV/dr at r = 2
    e) V = (4/3)pir^3, dV/dr at r = 6
    f) S = 4pir^2, dS/dr at r = 5
    g) V = a^3 (cube), dV/da at a = 4
    h) S = 6a^2 (cube), dS/da at a = 2.5
    i) A = (sqrt3/4)a^2, dA/da at a = 6
    j) V = pir^2(10) (cylinder, h = 10), dV/dr at r = 3
    k) V = (1/3)pih^3 (cone with r = h), dV/dh at h = 3
    l) y = x^3 - 5x, dy/dx at x = 2
    m) y = x^2 + 1/x, dy/dx at x = 1
    n) y = sqrtx, dy/dx at x = 9
    o) s = 16t^2 (m, t in s), velocity at t = 3
    p) s = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t, velocity at t = 4
    q) s = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t, acceleration at t = 4
    r) y = sin x, dy/dx at x = pi/3
    s) y = e^x, dy/dx at x = ln 5
    t) y = ln x, dy/dx at x = 1/4
    Answers: a) 6pi   b) 7pi   c) 2pi   d) 16pi   e) 144pi   f) 40pi   g) 48   h) 30
             i) 3sqrt3   j) 60pi   k) 9pi   l) 7   m) 1   n) 1/6   o) 96   p) 9
             q) 12   r) 1/2   s) 5   t) 4

M2. Related rates: t is time. Differentiate with respect to t and find the rate
    asked.
    a) y = x^2, dx/dt = 3; find dy/dt at x = 4
    b) y = x^3, dx/dt = 2; find dy/dt at x = -1
    c) y = 5x - x^2, dx/dt = 4; find dy/dt at x = 2
    d) y = sqrtx, dx/dt = 6; find dy/dt at x = 9
    e) y = 1/x, dx/dt = -2; find dy/dt at x = 2
    f) y = ln x, dx/dt = 5; find dy/dt at x = 10

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always draw the diagram for a related-rates problem and label the
  CHANGING lengths with letters, fixed ones with numbers; write "given / wanted"
  before any calculus; differentiate first and substitute last. For tangents,
  write three lines every time: point, slope, equation. For monotonicity,
  tangent to xy = c^2 at (ct, c/t) cuts off a triangle of constant area 2c^2 with
  the axes; find the angle between y = x^2 and y = sqrtx at (1, 1) (tan theta = 3/4,
  theta ~ 36.87 degrees); do x^2 = 4y and 4y + x^2 = 8 cut orthogonally? (they meet at
  (+/-2, 1) with slopes 1 and -1: yes); a street light 6 m high, a man 2 m tall
  walking towards it at 1.5 m/s: how fast does the shadow shrink? (0.75 m/s);
  prove that f(x) = x/sin x increases on (0, pi/2).

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.42 - MAXIMA AND MINIMA; OPTIMISATION PROBLEMS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - f has a LOCAL MAXIMUM at c if f(c) >= f(x) for all x near c, and a LOCAL
    MINIMUM if f(c) <= f(x) near c. The ABSOLUTE (global) maximum is the largest
    value on the whole domain or interval.
    not exist. (Fermat) A local extremum at an interior point where f is
    +, local min; no change of sign, neither (a point of inflection with
    horizontal tangent, as for x^3).
    go back to the first derivative test.
  - ABSOLUTE EXTREMA on a closed interval [a, b] (they exist when f is
    continuous: Extreme Value Theorem): list f at the critical points inside
    (a, b) and at the ENDPOINTS a and b; the largest is the absolute max, the
    smallest the absolute min.
  - OPTIMISATION: 1) draw and name variables; 2) write the quantity to be
    maximised or minimised; 3) use the constraint to reduce it to ONE variable;
    4) state the domain; 5) differentiate, solve, and JUSTIFY (sign change,
    second derivative, or endpoint comparison); 6) answer the question asked,
    with units.
  - Classic results: fixed perimeter -> the square has the largest area; closed
    can of fixed volume with least surface area has h = 2r; box from an a x a
    sheet has largest volume when squares of side a/6 are cut; profit is
    greatest where MR = MC; maximising a distance d is the same as maximising d^2
    (easier: no square root).

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Find the critical points of f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x + 1 and use the first
    derivative test to classify them.
    Answer: Local maximum f(1) = 5; local minimum f(3) = 1.
    here).
                    x < 1      1 < x < 3      x > 3
        f           rises   max  falls   min   rises
        f(1) = 1 - 6 + 9 + 1 = 5      f(3) = 27 - 54 + 27 + 1 = 1
    At x = 1 the graph stops rising and starts falling (+ to -): a peak. At
    x = 3 it changes from - to +: a valley. These are LOCAL: f(5) = 21 is bigger
    Common mistake: giving only the x-values; a maximum or minimum VALUE is
    f(-1) = 4, local min f(1) = 0)

D2. Use the second derivative test to find the local extrema of
    f(x) = x^4 - 8x^2 + 3. Then explain what the test says about x^4, -x^4 and x^3 at
    x = 0.
    Answer: Local maxima: f(0) = 3; local minima: f(-2) = f(2) = -13. At 0 the
    neither.
    NOTHING. The first derivative test decides: 4x^3 goes from - to +, so x^4 has

D3. Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of f(x) = 2x^3 - 15x^2 + 36x + 1
    on the interval [1, 5].
    Answer: Absolute maximum 56 at x = 5; absolute minimum 24 at x = 1.
    Teacher explains: On a closed interval the extreme values occur either at a
    critical point inside, or at an ENDPOINT. So make a table of candidates:
        x        1     2     3     5
        f(x)    24    29    28    56
               min               max
    The local max f(2) = 29 and local min f(3) = 28 are NOT the absolute ones:
    the endpoints win here. Common mistakes: forgetting the endpoints, and
    including critical points that lie OUTSIDE the interval. Now you try:
    f(pi/4) = sqrt2, f(pi) = -1: max sqrt2, min -1)

D4. An open box is made from a square sheet of tin of side 18 cm by cutting
    equal squares from the four corners and folding up the sides. What size of
    square should be cut to make the volume as large as possible? What is that
    volume?
    Answer: Cut squares of side 3 cm; the greatest volume is 432 cm^3.
    Teacher explains: Let the cut squares have side x cm. The base is (18 - 2x)
    by (18 - 2x) and the height is x, so V(x) = x(18 - 2x)^2, with domain
    0 < x < 9.
              = (18 - 2x)(18 - 2x - 4x) = (18 - 2x)(18 - 6x)
        V(3) = 3 x 12 x 12 = 432 cm^3
    Check the ends: V -> 0 as x -> 0 or x -> 9, so the only critical point in the
    domain must give the maximum. In general for a sheet of side a the best cut
    is a/6. Common mistake: using 18 - x for the base (a square is cut from BOTH
    ends of each side). Now you try: a 24 cm square sheet. (x = 4 cm,
    V = 4 x 16^2 = 1,024 cm^3)

D5. A farmer has 200 m of fencing to enclose a rectangular field along a
    straight river; no fence is needed along the river. Find the dimensions of
    the largest field. Compare with a field fenced on all four sides.
    Answer: 50 m (perpendicular to the river) by 100 m (along it): area
    5,000 m^2. With four sides fenced, the best is a 50 m square: only 2,500 m^2.
    Teacher explains: Let x be each side perpendicular to the river; the side
    parallel to the river is 200 - 2x.
        A(x) = x(200 - 2x) = 200x - 2x^2,    0 < x < 100
        A(50) = 50 x 100 = 5,000 m^2
    Four sides: 2x + 2y = 200 gives A = x(100 - x), maximum at x = 50: a square
    of area 2,500 m^2. The river saves a whole side, so the area doubles. Common
    mistake: using 2x + 2y = 200 when one side is free. Now you try: 600 m of
    fencing, three sides of a rectangle, the fourth is a wall. (150 m by 300 m,
    area 45,000 m^2)

D6. A closed cylindrical can must hold 1,000 cm^3 (1 litre). Find the radius and
    height that use the least metal (least total surface area).
    area ~ 553.58 cm^2.
    Teacher explains: The constraint is the volume; the quantity to minimise is
    the area.
        pir^2h = 1,000   ->   h = 1,000/(pir^2)
        S = 2pir^2 + 2pirh = 2pir^2 + 2,000/r,     r > 0
        h = 1,000/(pir^2) = 2 x (500/pi)/r^2 = 2r^3/r^2 = 2r
    So the best can has height equal to its DIAMETER (h = 2r). Area: S
    = 2pir^2 + 2pir(2r) = 6pir^2 ~ 6pi x 29.37 ~ 553.58 cm^2. Real cans are often
    taller because of other costs (sealing, labels). Common mistake: minimising
    the volume instead of the area, or forgetting the two circular ends. Now you
    try: an OPEN-top cylinder holding 1,000 cm^3. (S = pir^2 + 2,000/r,
    r^3 = 1,000/pi, r ~ 6.83 cm, h = r)

D7. Find the points on the parabola y = x^2 nearest to the point (0, 2), and the
    least distance.
    Answer: (+/-sqrt6/2, 3/2), that is (+/-1.22, 1.5); least distance sqrt7/2 ~ 1.32.
    Teacher explains: A point on the curve is (x, x^2). Minimise the SQUARE of
    the distance (same minimum point, no square root):
        D(x) = d^2 = (x - 0)^2 + (x^2 - 2)^2 = x^4 - 3x^2 + 4
        D(0) = 4 (d = 2)     D(+/-sqrt(3/2)) = 9/4 - 9/2 + 4 = 7/4
    So the nearest points are (+/-sqrt(3/2), 3/2) = (+/-sqrt6/2, 3/2) and the least
    distance is sqrt(7/4) = sqrt7/2. The vertex (0, 0), which many students guess, is
    at distance 2: farther! Check: the normal to the parabola at the nearest
    point passes through (0, 2). Common mistake: differentiating sqrt(...) directly
    and making algebra slips; use d^2. Now you try: the point on the line
    2x + y = 5 nearest to the origin. (D = x^2 + (5 - 2x)^2, x = 2: (2, 1),
    distance sqrt5)

D8. A sweet shop finds that it can sell x boxes of barfi a week when the price
    is p = 120 - 0.5x rupees per box. The weekly cost of making x boxes is
    C(x) = 20x + 1,000 rupees. How many boxes should it make, and at what price,
    for the greatest profit?
    Answer: 100 boxes at ₹70 each; greatest weekly profit ₹4,000.
    Teacher explains: Profit = revenue - cost, and revenue = price x quantity.
        R(x) = x(120 - 0.5x) = 120x - 0.5x^2
        P(x) = R(x) - C(x) = 100x - 0.5x^2 - 1,000
        price p = 120 - 50 = ₹70;   P(100) = 10,000 - 5,000 - 1,000 = 4,000
    Economists say "produce until marginal revenue equals marginal cost":
    than 100 boxes needs a lower price that loses more than it gains. Common
    mistake: maximising the revenue (x = 120, price ₹60) instead of the profit.
    Now you try: p = 50 - x/10 and C = 10x + 500. (P = 40x - x^2/10 - 500,
    x = 200, p = ₹30, profit ₹3,500)

D9. A window is a rectangle topped by a semicircle (a Norman window). Its total
    perimeter (including the curved part) is 10 m. Find the dimensions that let
    in the most light (greatest area).
    Answer: Radius r = 10/(4 + pi) ~ 1.40 m, so the width 2r ~ 2.80 m; the
    rectangle's height h = r ~ 1.40 m; greatest area 50/(4 + pi) ~ 7.00 m^2.
    Teacher explains: Let the semicircle have radius r, so the rectangle is 2r
    wide and h high. The perimeter is two sides, the bottom and the arc:
        2h + 2r + pir = 10   ->   h = (10 - 2r - pir)/2
        A = 2rh + (1/2)pir^2 = r(10 - 2r - pir) + (1/2)pir^2
          = 10r - 2r^2 - (pi/2)r^2
    Then h = (10 - (2 + pi)r)/2 = (10 x 2/(4 + pi))/2 = 10/(4 + pi) = r: the
    rectangle is exactly half as tall as it is wide. Area = 10r - ((4 + pi)/2)r^2
    = 100/(4 + pi) - 50/(4 + pi) = 50/(4 + pi) ~ 7.00 m^2. Common mistakes: counting
    the base of the semicircle in the perimeter (it is inside the window), and
    using pir instead of (1/2)pir^2 for the semicircle's area. Now you try: a plain
    rectangular window of perimeter 10 m. (a square 2.5 m by 2.5 m, area
    6.25 m^2, less than the 7.00 m^2 of the Norman window)

D10. Find the rectangle of largest area that can be inscribed in a circle of
     radius 5 cm. Then find the cylinder of largest volume that fits inside a
     sphere of radius 6 cm.
     Answer: The square of side 5sqrt2 ~ 7.07 cm, area 50 cm^2. The cylinder has
     height 4sqrt3 ~ 6.93 cm, radius 2sqrt6 ~ 4.90 cm and volume 96pisqrt3 ~ 522.37 cm^3.
     Teacher explains: Rectangle: put the centre at O and a corner at (x, y) on
     the circle, so the rectangle is 2x by 2y with x^2 + y^2 = 25.
         A = 4xy = 4xsqrt(25 - x^2);  maximise A^2 = 16x^2(25 - x^2) = 16(25x^2 - x^4)
         d(A^2)/dx = 16(50x - 4x^3) = 0  ->  x^2 = 25/2,  x = 5/sqrt2 = y
         A = 4 x 25/2 = 50 cm^2  (a square of side 2x = 5sqrt2)
     Cylinder of height h in a sphere of radius 6: the radius r satisfies
     r^2 + (h/2)^2 = 36 (right triangle from the centre).
     = -3pih/2 < 0, a maximum. Common mistake: writing r^2 + h^2 = 36 (it is HALF
     the height that reaches the centre). Now you try: the largest rectangle in
     a semicircle of radius 4 (base on the diameter). (2x by y,
     A = 2xsqrt(16 - x^2), x = 2sqrt2: 4sqrt2 by 2sqrt2, area 16)

D11. Two positive numbers x and y have sum 15. Find them if x^2y^3 is as large as
     possible. Also find the number that exceeds its square by the greatest
     amount.
     Answer: x = 6, y = 9 (x^2y^3 = 26,244). The number is 1/2 (it exceeds its
     square by 1/4).
     Teacher explains: Use the sum to write everything in terms of x:
     y = 15 - x, and f(x) = x^2(15 - x)^3 with 0 < x < 15.
               = x(15 - x)^2[2(15 - x) - 3x] = x(15 - x)^2(30 - 5x)
         x = 6, y = 9,  x^2y^3 = 36 x 729 = 26,244
     ratio m : n (here 2 : 3 of 15). For the second part, g(x) = x - x^2,
     first. Now you try: two positive numbers with product 64 and least sum. (8
     and 8, sum 16)

D12. A fisherman is in a boat 4 km from the nearest point P of a straight shore.
     His village is 6 km along the shore from P. He rows at 3 km/h and walks at
     5 km/h. Where should he land to reach the village as quickly as possible?
     Answer: Land 3 km from P (3 km short of the village); the least time is
     34/15 h = 2 h 16 min.
     Teacher explains: Let him land x km from P (0 <= x <= 6). He rows sqrt(16 + x^2)
     km and walks 6 - x km. Time = distance / speed:
         T(x) = sqrt(16 + x^2)/3 + (6 - x)/5
         5x = 3sqrt(16 + x^2)  ->  25x^2 = 9x^2 + 144  ->  x^2 = 9  ->  x = 3
         T(3) = 5/3 + 3/5 = 34/15 h ~ 2.267 h
         T(0) = 4/3 + 6/5 = 38/15 ~ 2.533 h,   T(6) = sqrt52/3 ~ 2.404 h
     This is a CLOSED interval, so compare the critical point with both
     endpoints: x = 3 is the smallest, so it is the absolute minimum. Rowing
     straight to the village (x = 6) or straight to shore (x = 0) are both
     slower. (The same calculation gives Snell's law for light.) Common mistake:
     squaring 5x = 3sqrt(16 + x^2) wrongly as 25x^2 = 9 x 16 + x^2. Now you try: same,
     but walking at 5 km/h and rowing at 4 km/h. (x/(4sqrt(16 + x^2)) = 1/5,
     9x^2 = 256, x = 16/3 ~ 5.33 km)

M11. Economics (money in rupees; x = number of units).
     a) p = 120 - 0.5x, C = 20x + 1,000: best x, price, profit
     b) p = 50 - x/10, C = 10x + 500: best x, price, profit
     c) p = 200 - 2x, C = 40x + 1,200: best x, price, profit
     d) p = 80 - x, C = x^2 + 20x: best x, price, profit
     e) p = 300 - 4x, C = 60x + 2,000: best x, price, profit
     f) p = 100 - x/2, C = x^2/2 + 10x + 50: best x, price, profit
     g) R = 60x - x^2: x for maximum revenue
     h) R = x(400 - 5x): maximum revenue
     i) Average cost A = x/100 + 5 + 400/x: least
     j) Average cost A = 2x + 50 + 800/x: least
     k) Cinema: 500 tickets at ₹100; each ₹5 rise loses 20 sales. Best price
     l) Tour bus: 40 people pay ₹60 each; each extra person reduces every fare
        by ₹1. Best group size
     Answers: a) x = 100, p = ₹70, profit ₹4,000
              b) x = 200, p = ₹30, profit ₹3,500
              c) x = 40, p = ₹120, profit ₹2,000
              d) x = 15, p = ₹65, profit ₹450
              e) x = 30, p = ₹180, profit ₹1,600
              f) x = 45, p = ₹77.50, profit ₹1,975   g) x = 30, value 900
              h) x = 40, value 8,000   i) x = 200, value 9
              j) x = 20, value 130   k) ₹112.50 (2.5 rises), revenue ₹50,625
              l) 50 people at ₹50, revenue ₹2,500

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: insist on a written plan: variables, the formula to optimise, the
  constraint, one-variable function, domain. Draw the figure with the unknown
  marked. Keep a table of "candidates" for closed intervals. For the second
  point. Harder: prove that among all rectangles inscribed in a circle the
  square has the largest area, without calculus (AM-GM, topic 8.61); find the
  shortest ladder that reaches over a 2 m wall to a building 1 m behind it
  ((2^(2/3) + 1)^(3/2) ~ 4.16 m); show that the semi-vertical angle of the cone
  of greatest volume with given slant height is tan^-^1sqrt2; a right circular cone
  of greatest volume inscribed in a sphere of radius R has height 4R/3 and
  volume 8/27 of the sphere's; find the point on y^2 = 4x nearest to (2, 1)
  (d^2 = (y^2/4 - 2)^2 + (y - 1)^2 has derivative y^3/4 - 2, zero at y = 2: the point
  (1, 2), distance sqrt2).

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.43 - CURVE SKETCHING
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A good sketch shows the SHAPE and the KEY POINTS, not a plotted table. Work
    through the checklist: 1) domain; 2) intercepts (x = 0 and y = 0); 3)
    symmetry (even: f(-x) = f(x), symmetric in the y-axis; odd: f(-x) = -f(x),
    table of key points; 8) draw.
    denominator that is not cancelled); HORIZONTAL y = L where f(x) -> L as
    with degree of top = degree of bottom + 1, divide:
    x^2/(x - 1) = x + 1 + 1/(x - 1), asymptote y = x + 1).
    behaves like the ratio of its leading terms for large |x|.
  - Features of cubics: every cubic has exactly one inflection point, and the
    graph is symmetric about it; it has two turning points or none. A repeated
    root (x - a)^2 means the graph TOUCHES the x-axis at a; a triple root
    (x - a)^3 means it crosses with a horizontal tangent.
  - Sketches are also used to COUNT real roots: the number of solutions of
    f(x) = k is the number of times the horizontal line y = k meets the graph of
    f.
    marks the curve, | and - the axes; always label the key points and
    asymptotes in a table beside it.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Sketch y = x^3 - 3x^2 + 4, showing intercepts, turning points and the point of
    inflection.
    Answer: x-intercepts -1 and 2 (touching at 2), y-intercept 4; local max
    (0, 4), local min (2, 0); inflection (1, 2); concave down for x < 1, up for
    polynomial).
        intercepts: y(0) = 4;  x^3 - 3x^2 + 4 = (x + 1)(x - 2)^2 = 0
                    -> x = -1 (crosses), x = 2 (double root: touches)
                    -> max (0, 4), min (2, 0)
        x      -1    0     1     2     3
        y       0    4     2     0     4
             crosses max  infl  min
                        |                              *
                        |                             **
                    **********                        *
                  ***   |    ***                     *
                 **     |      ***                  *
                **      |         ***              *
               **       |           ***          **
              **        |             ****     ***
        ------*---------+----------------******-----------
             *          |
            **          |
            *           |
    The inflection point (1, 2) is exactly halfway between the turning points,
    and the cubic is symmetric about it: this is true for every cubic. Common
    mistake: thinking the graph crosses the axis at x = 2; at a double root it
    only touches. Now you try: sketch y = x^3 - 3x. (odd; intercepts 0, +/-sqrt3; max
    (-1, 2), min (1, -2); inflection (0, 0))

D2. Sketch y = x^4 - 4x^3. Explain why the origin is a point of inflection with a
    horizontal tangent, and not a turning point.
    Answer: Intercepts (0, 0) and (4, 0); only one turning point: minimum
    (3, -27); inflection points (0, 0) (horizontal tangent) and (2, -16);
    concave up for x < 0 and x > 2, down on (0, 2).
    Teacher explains:
        y = x^3(x - 4):  x-intercepts 0 (triple root) and 4
                sign: - for x < 0, - on (0, 3), + for x > 3
                -> minimum at x = 3: y = 81 - 108 = -27
                sign: + for x < 0, - on (0, 2), + for x > 2
                -> inflections at x = 0 (y = 0) and x = 2 (y = 16 - 32 = -16)
        x      -1     0     2     3     4
        y       5     0   -16   -27     0
    but it changes from concave up to concave down, and the tangent there is
    horizontal (y = 0). This happens because 0 is a TRIPLE root: near 0,
    y ~ -4x^3, which looks like an upside-down x^3. Common mistake: marking every
    stationary point as a max or a min. Now you try: y = 3x^4 - 4x^3. (min
    (1, -1); horizontal inflection (0, 0); inflection (2/3, -16/27))

D3. Test each function for symmetry: f(x) = x^4 - 2x^2, g(x) = x^3 - 3x,
    h(x) = x^3 + x^2, k(x) = x sin x, m(x) = e^x. Then use symmetry to sketch
    y = x^4 - 2x^2 with half the work.
    Answer: f even, g odd, h neither, k even, m neither. y = x^4 - 2x^2:
    intercepts 0, +/-sqrt2; max (0, 0), minima (+/-1, -1); inflections
    (+/-1/sqrt3, -5/9) ~ (+/-0.58, -0.56); a "W" shape.
    Teacher explains: Replace x by -x and compare:
        f(-x) = x^4 - 2x^2 = f(x)             even: mirror in the y-axis
        g(-x) = -x^3 + 3x = -g(x)            odd: half-turn about O
        h(-x) = -x^3 + x^2  (neither +/-h(x))   neither
        k(-x) = (-x)sin(-x) = x sin x      even (odd x odd = even)
        m(-x) = e^(-x)                      neither
          *                   |                   *
          *                   |                   *
          *                   |                   *
           *                  |                  *
           **                 |                 **
            *                 |                 *
        -----*-----------***********-----------*-----
              **      ****    |    ****      **
               ********       |       ********
                              |
    For the even function, study x >= 0 only and reflect.
    y = 1/9 - 2/3 = -5/9. Reflecting gives the W with the second minimum at
    (-1, -1); (0, 0) is a local max. Common mistake: "a function is either even
    or odd"; most are neither (h and m). Now you try: is f(x) = x/(x^2 + 1) even,
    odd or neither? (odd)

D4. Sketch y = x/(x^2 + 1): find the asymptote, the extreme values and the three
    points of inflection.
    Answer: Odd function through O; horizontal asymptote y = 0; max (1, 1/2),
    min (-1, -1/2); inflections at x = 0, +/-sqrt3, i.e. (0, 0) and
    (+/-sqrt3, +/-sqrt3/4) ~ (+/-1.73, +/-0.43).
    Teacher explains:
                + on (-1, 1), - outside -> max f(1) = 1/2, min f(-1) = -1/2
                zero at x = 0, +/-sqrt3 with sign changes -> three inflections
        f(sqrt3) = sqrt3/4 ~ 0.433
                                 |
                                 | **********
                                 |**        ***********
                                 |*                   *****
        -------------------------*-------------------------
        *****                   *|
            ***********        **|
                      ********** |
                                 |
    The curve starts just below the axis on the far left, falls to -1/2, rises
    through the origin to 1/2 and then sinks back towards the axis from above. A
    horizontal asymptote CAN be crossed (here at O), unlike a vertical one.
    try: y = 4x/(x^2 + 4). (max (2, 1), min (-2, -1), asymptote y = 0)

D5. Sketch y = x^2/(x - 1). Find its vertical and oblique asymptotes and its
    turning points.
    Answer: Vertical asymptote x = 1; oblique asymptote y = x + 1; local max
    (0, 0), local min (2, 4); concave down for x < 1, up for x > 1; no
    inflection.
    Teacher explains: Divide first: it shows the oblique asymptote at once.
        x^2/(x - 1) = x + 1 + 1/(x - 1)     (x^2 = (x - 1)(x + 1) + 1)
                -> max (0, 0), min (2, 4)
    There is no inflection point: the concavity changes at x = 1, but x = 1 is
    not in the domain. The left branch is an upside-down "U" with top (0, 0);
    the right branch is a "U" with bottom (2, 4), both hugging the two
    asymptotes. Note the local max 0 is LESS than the local min 4: on different
    branches this is allowed. Common mistake: finding a horizontal asymptote
    (there is none, degree 2 over 1). Now you try: y = (x^2 + 3)/(x - 1).
    (x + 1 + 4/(x - 1): asymptotes x = 1, y = x + 1; max (-1, -2), min (3, 6))

D6. Sketch y = 2x^2/(x^2 - 1). Use symmetry, asymptotes, the first and second
    derivatives.
    Answer: Even; vertical asymptotes x = +/-1; horizontal asymptote y = 2; local
    max (0, 0); increasing for x < 0, decreasing for x > 0 (x != +/-1); concave up
    for |x| > 1, down for |x| < 1; no inflection. The outer branches lie above
    y = 2.
    Teacher explains:
        even: f(-x) = f(x);  only intercept (0, 0)
        x      0     0.5     2     3
        y      0   -2/3    8/3   9/4
    Is y above or below the asymptote y = 2? y - 2 = 2/(x^2 - 1) > 0 for |x| > 1,
    middle branch is a cap between the two vertical asymptotes with top (0, 0).
    Common mistake: joining the branches across x = +/-1. Now you try:
    y = 1/(x^2 - 4). (even, x = +/-2, y = 0, max (0, -1/4) on the middle branch)

D7. Sketch y = x e^x.
    (-2, -2/e^2) ~ (-2, -0.27).
    Teacher explains:
                -> minimum f(-1) = -1/e
                -> inflection f(-2) = -2/e^2

    (x + 2). The graph creeps along just below the negative x-axis, dips to its

    try: y = x e^(-x). (max (1, 1/e), inflection (2, 2/e^2), asymptote y = 0 as

D8. Sketch y = ln x/x and deduce which is larger, e^pi or pi^e.
    3/(2e^(3/2))) ~ (4.48, 0.33). Since pi > e, ln pi/pi < 1/e = ln e/e, which
    gives e^pi > pi^e.
    Teacher explains:
                -> maximum f(e) = 1/e ~ 0.368
    Because f is decreasing for x > e and pi > e: ln pi/pi < ln e/e. Multiply by epi
    (positive): e ln pi < pi ln e = pi, so ln(pi^e) < ln(e^pi) and pi^e < e^pi
    (numerically 22.46 < 23.14). Common mistake: forgetting the domain
    restriction x > 0 and drawing a left half. Now you try: which is larger, 3^4
    or 4^3? (4 > 3 > e and f decreases there, so ln 4/4 < ln 3/3,
    3 ln 4 < 4 ln 3: 4^3 = 64 < 81 = 3^4)

D9. Sketch y = x^2 e^(-x).

    (2, 4/e^2) ~ (2, 0.54); inflections at x = 2 +/- sqrt2 ~ 0.59 and 3.41 (y ~ 0.19

                - for x < 0, + on (0, 2), - for x > 2

    (3.41, 0.38) inflection. The graph falls from very high on the left, touches
    O, rises to a hump at x = 2 and then decays towards the axis. Common
    mistake: product rule slips: d/dx(e^(-x)) = -e^(-x). Now you try:

D10. Sketch the "bell curve" y = e^(-x^2) and explain where it is steepest.
     Answer: Even; always positive; maximum (0, 1); inflections
     Teacher explains:
         f(+/-1/sqrt2) = e^(-1/2) = 1/sqrte ~ 0.607

                            ***   |   ***

                        ***       |       ***
                     ***          |          ***

     steepest points of any smooth curve are its inflection points. This curve

     y = 1/(1 + x^2). (max (0, 1); inflections (+/-1/sqrt3, 3/4); asymptote y = 0)

     x = -2; no extremum at x = 1 (horizontal inflection); inflection points at

                 - for x < -2, + for x > -2 (0 at x = 1, no change)
                 + for x < -1, - on (-1, 1), + for x > 1
                 -> concavity changes at x = -1 and x = 1
     So the graph falls to a minimum at x = -2, rises, bends from concave up to
     concave down at x = -1, flattens to a horizontal tangent at x = 1 (still
     EVEN power gives no sign change (no extremum); an ODD power gives one.
     Common mistake: listing x = 1 as a max or min. Now you try:

             l) max (e, 1/e); infl. (e^(3/2), 3e^(-3/2)/2)   m) min (1/e, -1/e)
             n) min (-1, -1/2); max (1, 1/2); infl. (-sqrt3, -sqrt3/4); infl. (0, 0);
                infl. (sqrt3, sqrt3/4)

M7. Rational functions: vertical asymptotes (VA), horizontal (HA) or oblique
    (OA) asymptote, and turning points.
    a) y = (x + 1)/(x - 1)
    b) y = 1/(x^2 - 1)
    c) y = x/(x^2 - 1)
    d) y = (x^2 - 4)/(x^2 - 1)
    e) y = x^2/(x^2 - 4)
    f) y = (x - 1)^2/x
    g) y = x + 4/x
    h) y = x^2/(x + 1)
    i) y = (x^2 + 1)/x
    j) y = (x^2 - 3)/(x - 2)
    k) y = 4x/(x^2 + 4)
    l) y = (x^2 + 4)/(x^2 - 4)
    Answers: a) VA x = 1; HA y = 1; no turning points
             b) VA x = -1, x = 1; HA y = 0; max (0, -1)
             c) VA x = -1, x = 1; HA y = 0; no turning points
             d) VA x = -1, x = 1; HA y = 1; min (0, 4)
             e) VA x = -2, x = 2; HA y = 1; max (0, 0)
             f) VA x = 0; OA y = x - 2; max (-1, -4); min (1, 0)
             g) VA x = 0; OA y = x; max (-2, -4); min (2, 4)
             h) VA x = -1; OA y = x - 1; max (-2, -4); min (0, 0)
             i) VA x = 0; OA y = x; max (-1, -2); min (1, 2)
             j) VA x = 2; OA y = x + 2; max (1, 2); min (3, 6)
             k) no VA; HA y = 0; min (-2, -1); max (2, 1)
             l) VA x = -2, x = 2; HA y = 1; max (0, -1)

M8. Find the turning points (x and y exactly).
    a) y = x e^(-x)
    b) y = x^2 e^x
    c) y = e^x/x
    d) y = e^(-x) sin x on [0, 2pi]
    e) y = x - e^x
    f) y = e^x - 2x
    g) y = x ln x
    h) y = x^2 ln x
    i) y = x - ln x
    j) y = ln x - x/e
    k) y = (ln x)^2
    l) y = x/ln x
    Answers: a) max at x = 1, y = 1/e
             b) max at x = -2, y = 4/e^2; min at x = 0, y = 0
             c) min at x = 1, y = e
             d) max at x = pi/4, y = sqrt2 e^(-pi/4)/2; min at x = 5pi/4,
                y = -sqrt2 e^(-5pi/4)/2   e) max at x = 0, y = -1
             f) min at x = ln 2, y = 2 - 2 ln 2   g) min at x = 1/e, y = -1/e
             h) min at x = e^(-1/2), y = -1/(2e)   i) min at x = 1, y = 1
             j) max at x = e, y = 0   k) min at x = 1, y = 0
             l) min at x = e, y = e

M9. True or false? Give a reason or counterexample where false.
    a) the graph of an odd function passes through the origin (if f(0) is
       defined)
    b) a cubic always has exactly one inflection point
    c) a cubic always has two turning points
    e) a graph can cross its horizontal asymptote
    f) a graph can cross its vertical asymptote
    g) y = x^2/(x - 1) has a horizontal asymptote
    h) at a double root the graph touches the x-axis
    i) a local maximum is always greater than a local minimum
    j) e^x is concave up everywhere
    k) ln x is concave down everywhere on its domain
    m) the inflection point of a cubic is midway between its turning points
    n) a rational function with degree of top < degree of bottom has y = 0 as an
       asymptote
    o) the number of real roots of f(x) = k equals the number of intersections
       of y = f(x) and y = k
    Answers: a) true   b) true   c) false (x^3 has none)   d) false (x^4 at 0)
             e) true (x/(x^2 + 1))   f) false   g) false (oblique y = x + 1)
             h) true   i) false (x^2/(x - 1): max 0 < min 4)   j) true   k) true
             l) true   m) true   n) true   o) true   p) true

     Answers: a) max at 0; min at 2   b) max at -1; min at 3
              c) no max; min at 1   d) no max; min at -1   e) max at 0; min at 2
              f) max at -2; min at 1   g) max at 4; min at 1
              h) no max; min at 0   i) no max; no min   j) max at 2; min at 1, 3
              k) no max; min at 1   l) max at 1; no min   m) no max; min at 1
              n) max at 1; min at 3   o) max at -1; min at 1
              p) no max; min at 1

M11. Find the constants, and write the function.
     a) y = x^3 + bx^2 + cx: turning points at x = 1 and x = 3
     b) y = x^3 + ax^2 + b: local min at (2, -1)
     c) y = ax^3 + bx^2: inflection at (1, 2)
     d) y = x^3 + ax^2 + bx + c: inflection (1, 1) with horizontal tangent
     e) y = ax^2 + bx + c: vertex (2, 5), through (0, 1)
     f) y = ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d: max (-1, 4), min (1, 0)
     g) y = x^4 + ax^2 + b: minima at x = +/-2, min value -10
     h) y = a/x + bx: turning point at (2, 8)
     i) y = (ax + b)/(x - c): asymptotes x = 2, y = 3, through (0, 1)
     j) y = (x^2 + a)/(x + b): VA x = -1, turning point at x = 1
     Answers: a) y = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x   b) y = x^3 - 3x^2 + 3   c) y = -x^3 + 3x^2
              d) y = x^3 - 3x^2 + 3x   e) y = -x^2 + 4x + 1   f) y = x^3 - 3x + 2
              g) y = x^4 - 8x^2 + 6   h) y = 2x + 8/x   i) y = (3x - 2)/(x - 2)
              j) y = (x^2 + 3)/(x + 1)

M12. Use a sketch of the left-hand side to find the number of real roots for
     each value of k.
     a) x^3 - 3x = k
     b) x^3 - 12x = k
     c) x^3 - 3x^2 = k
     d) 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 12x = k
     e) x^4 - 2x^2 = k
     f) x^4 - 8x^2 = k
     g) x e^x = k
     h) x e^(-x) = k
     i) ln x/x = k
     j) x/(x^2 + 1) = k
     k) For which k does x^3 - 3x + k = 0 have exactly one real root?
     l) Show that x^5 + x - 1 = 0 has exactly one real root
     Answers: a) three for -2 < k < 2; two for k = +/-2; one for |k| > 2
              b) three for -16 < k < 16; two for k = +/-16; one for |k| > 16
              c) three for -4 < k < 0; two for k = 0 or -4; one otherwise
              d) three for -20 < k < 7; two for k = -20 or 7; one otherwise
              e) four for -1 < k < 0; three for k = 0; two for k = -1 or k > 0;
                 none for k < -1
              f) four for -16 < k < 0; three for k = 0; two for k = -16 or
                 k > 0; none for k < -16
              g) two for -1/e < k < 0; one for k = -1/e or k >= 0; none for
                 k < -1/e
              h) two for 0 < k < 1/e; one for k = 1/e or k <= 0; none for k > 1/e
              i) two for 0 < k < 1/e; one for k = 1/e or k <= 0; none for k > 1/e
              j) two for 0 < |k| < 1/2; one for k = 0 or |k| = 1/2; none for
                 |k| > 1/2   k) k < -2 or k > 2

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: use the same eight-step checklist every time and fill in a printed
  points / sketch. Check the sketch on Desmos or GeoGebra afterwards and find
  what was missed. Start with cubics, then quartics, then rationals, then e^x and
  sketch y = (x^2 - 1)/(x^2 - 4) and find where it crosses its horizontal
  asymptote (never: y - 1 = 3/(x^2 - 4) != 0); sketch y = sin x + sin 2x on [0,
  2pi]; show that the curve y = (x - 1)/(x^2 + 1) has three collinear inflection
  points; sketch the curve y^2 = x^2(1 - x) (a loop) using y = +/-xsqrt(1 - x).

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.44 - INDEFINITE INTEGRALS; INTEGRATION BY SUBSTITUTION, BY PARTS,
             PARTIAL FRACTIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
    constant, so integral f(x) dx = F(x) + C. Always write + C, and CHECK every answer
    by differentiating it.
    integral e^x dx = e^x; integral a^x dx = a^x/ln a; integral sin x dx = -cos x; integral cos x dx = sin x;
    integral sec^2x dx = tan x; integral cosec^2x dx = -cot x; integral sec x tan x dx = sec x;
    integral cosec x cot x dx = -cosec x; integral 1/(1 + x^2) dx = tan^-^1x;
    integral 1/sqrt(1 - x^2) dx = sin^-^1x (all + C). Linear inside:
    integral f(ax + b) dx = (1/a)F(ax + b).
    integral sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x|, integral cosec x dx = ln|cosec x - cot x|.
  - TRIG POWERS: even powers use sin^2x = (1 - cos 2x)/2, cos^2x = (1 + cos 2x)/2;
    odd powers keep one factor and use sin^2x + cos^2x = 1 (integral cos^3x dx: put
    u = sin x); products use 2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A - B) etc.;
    tan^2x = sec^2x - 1.
  - BY PARTS: integral u dv = uv - integral v du, from the product rule. Choose u by LIATE
    (Logarithm, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential: the earlier one is
    u). Repeat for x^2e^x; for e^x sin x the integral comes back: solve for it.
  - PARTIAL FRACTIONS (proper fractions only; if degree top >= degree bottom,
    divide first): distinct linear factors A/(x - a) + B/(x - b); repeated
    (x - a)^2 gives A/(x - a) + B/(x - a)^2; an irreducible quadratic x^2 + px + q
    gives (Bx + C)/(x^2 + px + q). Find constants by the cover-up rule or by
    comparing coefficients.
  - SPECIAL FORMS (a > 0): integral 1/(x^2 + a^2) dx = (1/a)tan^-^1(x/a);
    integral 1/sqrt(a^2 - x^2) dx = sin^-^1(x/a); integral 1/(x^2 - a^2) dx
    = (1/(2a))ln|(x - a)/(x + a)|; integral sqrt(a^2 - x^2) dx
    = (x/2)sqrt(a^2 - x^2) + (a^2/2)sin^-^1(x/a). Complete the square first for
    x^2 + bx + c.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Find integral (3x^2 - 4x + 5) dx, integral (sqrtx + 1/x) dx and integral (e^x + sec^2x) dx. Why do we add
    a constant C, and how can you check an answer?
    Answer: x^3 - 2x^2 + 5x + C; (2/3)x^(3/2) + ln|x| + C; e^x + tan x + C. C is
    there because every function F + C has the same derivative; check by
    differentiating.
    Teacher explains: Integration reverses differentiation. For powers: add 1 to
    the power and divide by the new power.
        integral (3x^2 - 4x + 5) dx = 3 x x^3/3 - 4 x x^2/2 + 5x + C
                           = x^3 - 2x^2 + 5x + C
        integral (x^(1/2) + 1/x) dx = x^(3/2)/(3/2) + ln|x| + C
                           = (2/3)x^(3/2) + ln|x| + C
        check: d/dx[(2/3)x^(3/2)] = (2/3)(3/2)x^(1/2) = sqrtx, correct
    The derivative of any constant is 0, so x^3 - 2x^2 + 5x + 7 and
    x^3 - 2x^2 + 5x - 100 are both answers: + C stands for ALL of them (a family
    of parallel curves). Why ln|x| and not ln x? For x < 0, d/dx
    ln(-x) = (-1)/(-x) = 1/x as well, so ln|x| works on both sides of 0. The
    power rule fails for n = -1 (it would divide by 0): that is the case
    integral 1/x dx. Common mistakes: forgetting + C; writing integral x^2 dx = x^3 (forgot to
    divide by 3); integrating a product term by term. Now you try:
    integral (x^2 - 1)/sqrtx dx. (split: x^(3/2) - x^(-1/2); answer 2x^(5/2)/5 - 2sqrtx + C)

D2. Use the table of standard integrals: find
    integral (2 sin x - 3 cos x + 4/(1 + x^2)) dx and integral (2^x + 5/sqrt(1 - x^2)) dx. Then find
    integral (sin 3x + e^(2x)) dx and integral (2x + 1)^4 dx.
    Answer: -2 cos x - 3 sin x + 4 tan^-^1x + C; 2^x/ln 2 + 5 sin^-^1x + C;
    -(1/3)cos 3x + (1/2)e^(2x) + C; (2x + 1)^5/10 + C.
    Teacher explains: Read the table backwards from the derivatives you know:
        d/dx(-cos x) = sin x          so integral sin x dx = -cos x + C
        d/dx(tan^-^1x) = 1/(1 + x^2)     so integral 1/(1 + x^2) dx = tan^-^1x + C
        d/dx(2^x) = 2^x ln 2             so integral 2^x dx = 2^x/ln 2 + C
        d/dx(sin^-^1x) = 1/sqrt(1 - x^2)    so integral 1/sqrt(1 - x^2) dx = sin^-^1x + C
    For a LINEAR inside, ax + b, integrate as usual and divide by a (the chain
    rule would multiply by a when differentiating back):
    integral sin 3x dx = -(cos 3x)/3, integral e^(2x) dx = e^(2x)/2,
    integral (2x + 1)^4 dx = (2x + 1)^5/(5 x 2). This shortcut is ONLY for linear insides:
    integral (x^2 + 1)^4 dx is NOT (x^2 + 1)^5/(10x). Common mistake: the sign of integral sin x dx
    (it is -cos x). Now you try: integral (cos 4x - 1/(3x + 2)) dx.
    ((1/4)sin 4x - (1/3)ln|3x + 2| + C)

D3. Integrate by substitution: integral 2x(x^2 + 1)^5 dx, integral xsqrt(x^2 + 4) dx and
    integral x e^(-x^2) dx.
    Answer: (x^2 + 1)^6/6 + C; (1/3)(x^2 + 4)^(3/2) + C; -(1/2)e^(-x^2) + C.
    present (up to a constant factor). Put u = g(x):
        u = x^2 + 1,  du = 2x dx:   integral u^5 du = u^6/6 = (x^2 + 1)^6/6 + C
        u = x^2 + 4,  du = 2x dx, so x dx = du/2:
             integral sqrtu (du/2) = (1/2)(2/3)u^(3/2) = (1/3)(x^2 + 4)^(3/2) + C
        u = -x^2,     du = -2x dx, so x dx = -du/2:
    Every dx must be replaced: after substituting, NO x may remain. If you are
    left with an x you cannot express in u, the substitution is wrong. Check the
    second answer: d/dx[(1/3)(x^2 + 4)^(3/2)]
    = (1/3)(3/2)(x^2 + 4)^(1/2)(2x) = xsqrt(x^2 + 4), as required. Common mistakes:
    forgetting to change dx; forgetting to substitute back. Now you try:
    integral sin^3x cos x dx. (u = sin x: sin^4x/4 + C)

    integral (2x + 3)/(x^2 + 3x + 5) dx, integral e^x/(1 + e^x) dx and integral sec x dx.
    Answer: ln|sec x| + C (= -ln|cos x| + C); ln(x^2 + 3x + 5) + C;
    ln(1 + e^x) + C; ln|sec x + tan x| + C.
    integral du/u = ln|u| + C = ln|f(x)| + C. So whenever the TOP is the derivative of
    the BOTTOM, the answer is ln|bottom|.
        tan x = sin x/cos x = -(-sin x)/cos x
        integral tan x dx = -ln|cos x| + C = ln|sec x| + C
        d/dx(x^2 + 3x + 5) = 2x + 3:   ln|x^2 + 3x + 5| + C
        (x^2 + 3x + 5 > 0 always, so the modulus can be dropped)
        sec x = sec x(sec x + tan x)/(sec x + tan x)
              top = sec^2x + sec x tan x = d/dx(sec x + tan x)
        integral sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x| + C
    The sec x result is a clever trick (multiply top and bottom by
    sec x + tan x); learn the answer. Common mistake: integral tan x dx = sec^2x (that is
    the DERIVATIVE of tan x). Now you try: integral 1/(x ln x) dx and integral cot x dx.
    (ln|ln x| + C; ln|sin x| + C)

D5. Find integral sin^2x dx, integral cos^3x dx, integral tan^2x dx and integral sin 3x cos 2x dx.
    Answer: x/2 - (sin 2x)/4 + C; sin x - (sin^3x)/3 + C; tan x - x + C;
    -(cos 5x)/10 - (cos x)/2 + C.
    Teacher explains: There is no rule for integral sin^2x directly: rewrite the
    integrand first.
        sin^2x = (1 - cos 2x)/2:   integral  = x/2 - (sin 2x)/4 + C
        cos^3x = cos^2x cos x = (1 - sin^2x)cos x;  u = sin x, du = cos x dx
                integral (1 - u^2) du = u - u^3/3 = sin x - sin^3x/3 + C
        tan^2x = sec^2x - 1:        integral  = tan x - x + C
        2 sin 3x cos 2x = sin 5x + sin x
                integral  = (1/2)(-cos 5x/5 - cos x) = -cos 5x/10 - cos x/2 + C
    Rule of thumb: EVEN powers of sin or cos: double-angle formulas; an ODD
    power: save one factor for du and turn the rest into the other function with
    sin^2 + cos^2 = 1; products of different angles: product-to-sum. Common
    mistake: integral sin^2x dx = sin^3x/3 (the chain rule would need a cos x). Now you
    try: integral cos^2x dx and integral sin^3x dx. (x/2 + sin 2x/4 + C; -cos x + cos^3x/3 + C)

D6. Derive the formula for integration by parts and use it for integral x e^x dx and
    integral x cos x dx. How do you decide which factor is u?
    Answer: integral u dv = uv - integral v du. integral x e^x dx = x e^x - e^x + C = (x - 1)e^x + C;
    integral x cos x dx = x sin x + cos x + C.
    Teacher explains: Product rule: d(uv)/dx = u dv/dx + v du/dx. Integrate both
    sides: uv = integral u dv + integral v du, so integral u dv = uv - integral v du. Choose u so that du is
    SIMPLER, and dv so that you can integrate it.
        integral x e^x dx:   u = x,  dv = e^x dx,  du = dx,  v = e^x
                  = x e^x - integral e^x dx = x e^x - e^x + C
        integral x cos x dx:  u = x,  dv = cos x dx,  du = dx,  v = sin x
                  = x sin x - integral sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + C
    LIATE gives the order of preference for u: Logarithms, Inverse trig,
    Algebraic (powers of x), Trig, Exponentials. With u = e^x and dv = x dx
    instead, you would get (x^2/2)e^x - integral (x^2/2)e^x dx: worse! Check:
    d/dx[x e^x - e^x] = e^x + x e^x - e^x = x e^x, as required. Now you try:
    integral x sin x dx. (-x cos x + sin x + C)

D7. Find integral ln x dx, integral tan^-^1x dx and integral x^2 e^x dx.
    Answer: x ln x - x + C; x tan^-^1x - (1/2)ln(1 + x^2) + C; e^x(x^2 - 2x + 2) + C.
    Teacher explains: For integral ln x dx there is only ONE factor: take dv = dx (so
    v = x).
        integral ln x dx:  u = ln x, dv = dx, du = dx/x, v = x
                 = x ln x - integral x x (1/x) dx = x ln x - x + C
        integral tan^-^1x dx:  u = tan^-^1x, dv = dx, du = dx/(1 + x^2), v = x
                 = x tan^-^1x - integral x/(1 + x^2) dx = x tan^-^1x - (1/2)ln(1 + x^2) + C
        integral x^2 e^x dx:  u = x^2, v = e^x:  = x^2 e^x - integral 2x e^x dx
                 = x^2 e^x - 2(x e^x - e^x) = e^x(x^2 - 2x + 2) + C
    For x^2 e^x, parts is used TWICE; each time the power of x drops by 1. A quick
    table method (tabular integration) does the same: derivatives x^2, 2x, 2, 0
    against integrals e^x, e^x, e^x, with signs +, -, +. Common mistake: losing the
    minus sign in the second round (-2(x e^x - e^x) = -2x e^x + 2e^x). Now you try:
    integral x ln x dx. (u = ln x: (x^2/2)ln x - x^2/4 + C)

    to find integral e^x(1/x - 1/x^2) dx.
    Answer: I = (e^x/2)(sin x - cos x) + C; integral e^x(1/x - 1/x^2) dx = e^x/x + C.
    Teacher explains: Parts twice brings the ORIGINAL integral back; then solve
    for it like an equation.
        I = integral e^x sin x dx:  u = sin x, dv = e^x dx
          = e^x sin x - integral e^x cos x dx
          = e^x sin x - [e^x cos x - integral e^x(-sin x) dx]     (u = cos x again)
          = e^x sin x - e^x cos x - I
        2I = e^x(sin x - cos x)   ->   I = (e^x/2)(sin x - cos x) + C
    Keep the SAME type of choice in both rounds (u = trig both times); switching
    to u = e^x in the second round just undoes the first. For the second part:
    mistake: writing 2I = ... and forgetting to halve. Now you try: integral e^x
    cos x dx. ((e^x/2)(sin x + cos x) + C)

D9. Find integral (x + 5)/((x - 1)(x + 2)) dx using partial fractions. Then find
    integral x^2/(x^2 - 1) dx (divide first).
    Answer: 2 ln|x - 1| - ln|x + 2| + C = ln|(x - 1)^2/(x + 2)| + C;
    x + (1/2)ln|(x - 1)/(x + 1)| + C.
    Teacher explains: Write the fraction as a sum of simpler fractions, one for
    each linear factor:
        (x + 5)/((x - 1)(x + 2)) = A/(x - 1) + B/(x + 2)
        x + 5 = A(x + 2) + B(x - 1)
        x = 1:   6 = 3A   ->  A = 2
        x = -2:  3 = -3B  ->  B = -1
        integral [2/(x - 1) - 1/(x + 2)] dx = 2 ln|x - 1| - ln|x + 2| + C
    Putting x = 1 and x = -2 kills one bracket each time: this is the "cover-up"
    rule (cover the factor x - 1 in the original and put x = 1: 6/3 = 2). For
    x^2/(x^2 - 1) the top has the SAME degree as the bottom, so divide first:
    x^2/(x^2 - 1) = 1 + 1/(x^2 - 1), and 1/((x - 1)(x + 1))
    = (1/2)/(x - 1) - (1/2)/(x + 1). Common mistake: using partial fractions on
    an improper fraction without dividing. Now you try:
    integral (3x + 1)/(x^2 - x - 2) dx. ((3x + 1)/((x - 2)(x + 1))
    = (7/3)/(x - 2) + (2/3)/(x + 1): (7/3)ln|x - 2| + (2/3)ln|x + 1| + C)

D10. Find integral (3x + 1)/(x - 1)^2 dx and integral 1/(x(x - 1)^2) dx (repeated linear factors).
     Answer: 3 ln|x - 1| - 4/(x - 1) + C; ln|x| - ln|x - 1| - 1/(x - 1) + C.
     Teacher explains: A repeated factor (x - 1)^2 needs TWO fractions:
     A/(x - 1) + B/(x - 1)^2.
         (3x + 1)/(x - 1)^2: write 3x + 1 = 3(x - 1) + 4
             = 3/(x - 1) + 4/(x - 1)^2
             integral  = 3 ln|x - 1| + 4 x (x - 1)^(-1)/(-1)
               = 3 ln|x - 1| - 4/(x - 1) + C
         1/(x(x - 1)^2) = A/x + B/(x - 1) + C_1/(x - 1)^2
         1 = A(x - 1)^2 + Bx(x - 1) + C_1x
         x = 0: A = 1;   x = 1: C_1 = 1;   x^2 terms: 0 = A + B -> B = -1
     So integral  = ln|x| - ln|x - 1| - 1/(x - 1) + C. The cover-up rule gives A and C_1
     but NOT B: for B compare coefficients (or put another value such as x = 2:
     1 = A + 2B + 2C_1). Note integral 1/(x - 1)^2 dx = -1/(x - 1): a power, not a
     logarithm. Common mistake: writing only A/x + B/(x - 1)^2 (missing
     B/(x - 1)). Now you try: integral (x + 2)/(x + 1)^2 dx. (1/(x + 1) + 1/(x + 1)^2:
     ln|x + 1| - 1/(x + 1) + C)

D11. Find integral 1/((x + 1)(x^2 + 1)) dx (an irreducible quadratic factor).
     Answer: (1/2)ln|x + 1| - (1/4)ln(x^2 + 1) + (1/2)tan^-^1x + C.
     Teacher explains: x^2 + 1 cannot be factorised over the reals, so its
     fraction has a LINEAR top Bx + C:
         1/((x + 1)(x^2 + 1)) = A/(x + 1) + (Bx + C)/(x^2 + 1)
         1 = A(x^2 + 1) + (Bx + C)(x + 1)
         x = -1:          1 = 2A          ->  A = 1/2
         x^2 terms:        0 = A + B       ->  B = -1/2
         constant terms:  1 = A + C       ->  C = 1/2
         integral  = (1/2)ln|x + 1| + integral (-x/2 + 1/2)/(x^2 + 1) dx
           = (1/2)ln|x + 1| - (1/4)ln(x^2 + 1) + (1/2)tan^-^1x + C
     constant over x^2 + 1, which gives tan^-^1. Check by differentiating:
     1/(2(x + 1)) - x/(2(x^2 + 1)) + 1/(2(1 + x^2)) combines to
     1/((x + 1)(x^2 + 1)). Common mistake: using a constant top C/(x^2 + 1) for a
     quadratic factor. Now you try: integral 2/(x(x^2 + 1)) dx. (2/x - 2x/(x^2 + 1):
     2 ln|x| - ln(x^2 + 1) + C)

D12. Find integral 1/(x^2 + 9) dx, integral 1/sqrt(4 - x^2) dx, integral sqrt(9 - x^2) dx and
     integral 1/(x^2 + 4x + 13) dx.
     Answer: (1/3)tan^-^1(x/3) + C; sin^-^1(x/2) + C;
     (x/2)sqrt(9 - x^2) + (9/2)sin^-^1(x/3) + C; (1/3)tan^-^1((x + 2)/3) + C.
     Teacher explains: The first two come from the table with x/a in place of x:
         integral 1/(x^2 + a^2) dx = (1/a)tan^-^1(x/a) + C        (a = 3)
         integral 1/sqrt(a^2 - x^2) dx = sin^-^1(x/a) + C           (a = 2)
         integral sqrt(9 - x^2) dx:  x = 3 sin theta, dx = 3 cos theta dtheta, sqrt(9 - x^2) = 3 cos theta
            = integral 9cos^2theta dtheta = (9/2)(theta + sin theta cos theta)
            = (9/2)sin^-^1(x/3) + (9/2)(x/3)(sqrt(9 - x^2)/3)
            = (x/2)sqrt(9 - x^2) + (9/2)sin^-^1(x/3) + C
         x^2 + 4x + 13 = (x + 2)^2 + 9:  (1/3)tan^-^1((x + 2)/3) + C
     The substitution x = a sin theta turns sqrt(a^2 - x^2) into a cos theta (a TRIGONOMETRIC
     SUBSTITUTION); return to x with sin theta = x/a, cos theta = sqrt(a^2 - x^2)/a. For a
     quadratic with no real roots, complete the square and use the tan^-^1 form
     with u = x + 2. Common mistake: integral 1/(x^2 + 9) dx = tan^-^1(x/3) (the factor 1/3
     is missing). Now you try: integral 1/sqrt(3 + 2x - x^2) dx.
     (3 + 2x - x^2 = 4 - (x - 1)^2: sin^-^1((x - 1)/2) + C)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep a one-page table of standard integrals and derivatives side
  by side; ALWAYS differentiate the answer to check it. Before integrating,
  of different types (parts)? rational (partial fractions)? sqrt(a^2 - x^2) (trig
  substitution)? Practise 10 mixed integrals a day, labelled with the method
  first. Harder: find integral 1/(1 + e^x) dx (x - ln(1 + e^x) + C); integral sqrt(tan x) dx via
  u^2 = tan x (hard, JEE Advanced); integral dx/(a + b cos x) with t = tan(x/2);
  integral sec^3x dx = (1/2)(sec x tan x + ln|sec x + tan x|) + C by parts; derive a
  why integral e^(-x^2) dx has no elementary antiderivative, yet we can still compute
  areas under it numerically.

================================================================================
TOPIC 8.45 - DEFINITE INTEGRALS AS THE LIMIT OF A SUM; FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF
             CALCULUS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - RIEMANN SUMS: split [a, b] into n equal strips of width h = (b - a)/n, with
  - Sums needed: 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2; 1^2 + 2^2 +
    ... + n^2 = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6; 1^3 + ... + n^3 = (n(n + 1)/2)^2; a geometric
    sum r + r^2 + ... + r^n = r(r^n - 1)/(r - 1); and lim (h -> 0) (e^h - 1)/h = 1.
  - Reading a limit as an integral: lim (1/n) sum  f(i/n) = integral _0^1 f(x) dx (i from 1
  - SUBSTITUTION in a definite integral: change the limits to the new variable
    v du.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Estimate integral _0^2 x^2 dx using 4 strips, first with right endpoints and then with
    left endpoints. Compare with the exact value 8/3.
    Answer: R_4 = 3.75, L_4 = 1.75; the exact value 8/3 ~ 2.667 lies between them.
    Teacher explains: Width h = (2 - 0)/4 = 0.5. The strip heights are the
    function values at the chosen endpoints:
        x          0     0.5     1     1.5     2
        x^2         0    0.25     1    2.25     4
        R_4 = 0.5 x (0.25 + 1 + 2.25 + 4) = 0.5 x 7.5 = 3.75
        L_4 = 0.5 x (0 + 0.25 + 1 + 2.25) = 0.5 x 3.5 = 1.75
            |               *
            |           +---+
            |          *|   |    right-endpoint rectangles
            |       +---+   |    stick out above the rising
            |     * |   |   |    curve (overestimate)
            |  +--*-+   |   |
            +**+----+---+---+---
            0 0.5   1  1.5  2
    x^2 is increasing on [0, 2], so right endpoints overestimate and left
    endpoints underestimate. With more strips both approach 8/3: this limit IS
    the definite integral. The average (R_4 + L_4)/2 = 2.75 is the trapezium rule.
    Common mistake: using 5 heights (both ends) in one sum. Now you try: R_4 and
    L_4 for integral _0^4 x dx. (h = 1: R_4 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, L_4 = 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6;
    exact 8)

D2. Evaluate integral _1^3 (2x + 1) dx as the limit of a sum, and check with the area of a
    trapezium.
    Answer: 10.
        R_n = sum  (i = 1 to n) (2/n)(3 + 4i/n)
           = (2/n)[3n + (4/n)(1 + 2 + ... + n)]
           = (2/n)[3n + (4/n) x n(n + 1)/2]
           = (2/n)[3n + 2(n + 1)] = (2/n)(5n + 2) = 10 + 4/n
    Check: the region under y = 2x + 1 from x = 1 to 3 is a trapezium with
    parallel sides f(1) = 3 and f(3) = 7 and width 2: area = (3 + 7)/2 x 2 = 10.
    And by the Fundamental Theorem: [x^2 + x]_1^3 = 12 - 2 = 10. Common mistake:
    writing sum  3 = 3 instead of 3n (the constant is added n times). Now you try:
    integral _1^3 x dx as a limit. (h = 2/n, R_n = (2/n)(n + (2/n)n(n + 1)/2)
    = 4 + 2/n -> 4)

    Answer: R_n = (n + 1)(2n + 1)/(6n^2) -> 2/6 = 1/3. For [0, b]:
    R_n = b^3(n + 1)(2n + 1)/(6n^2) -> b^3/3.
    Teacher explains:
        R_n = sum  (1/n)(i^2/n^2) = (1/n^3)(1^2 + 2^2 + ... + n^2)
           = (1/n^3) x n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6
           = (n + 1)(2n + 1)/(6n^2) = (1 + 1/n)(2 + 1/n)/6
        on [0, b]:  h = b/n,  R_n = (b/n) sum  (bi/n)^2
                                  = b^3(n + 1)(2n + 1)/(6n^2) -> b^3/3
    Archimedes found this area (the parabolic segment) 2,000 years before
    calculus by a similar limiting argument. Divide top and bottom by n^2 to see
    the limit clearly. The result matches the antiderivative x^3/3, as the
    Fundamental Theorem promises. Common mistake: using the formula for sum  i
    instead of sum  i^2. Now you try: integral _0^2 x^3 dx from the definition. (R_n
    = (2/n)sum (2i/n)^3 = (16/n^4)(n(n + 1)/2)^2 = 4(n + 1)^2/n^2 -> 4)

D4. Evaluate integral _0^1 e^x dx as the limit of a sum.
    Answer: e - 1 ~ 1.718.
    Teacher explains: The heights form a GEOMETRIC progression: use its sum
    formula.
        h = 1/n:  R_n = h(e^h + e^(2h) + ... + e^(nh))
                  = h x e^h(e^(nh) - 1)/(e^h - 1)
                  = (e - 1) x e^h x h/(e^h - 1)          (nh = 1)
        so R_n -> e - 1
    The key standard limit is (e^h - 1)/h -> 1 as h -> 0 (topic 8.31): it is the
    statement that the slope of e^x at 0 is 1. Check with the antiderivative:
    [e^x]_0^1 = e - 1. Common mistake: summing a geometric series with the wrong
    number of terms: from e^h to e^(nh) there are n terms. Now you try:
    integral _0^2 e^x dx as a limit. (h = 2/n: (e^2 - 1) x e^h h/(e^h - 1) -> e^2 - 1 ~ 6.389)

D5. State the second part of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and use it to
    find integral _1^4 (3sqrtx - 1/x^2) dx and integral _0^(pi/2) cos x dx. Why is no + C needed?
    53/4 = 13.25 and 1.
    Teacher explains: Find ANY antiderivative, then subtract its values at the
    two limits:
        integral _1^4 (3x^(1/2) - x^(-2)) dx = [2x^(3/2) + 1/x]_1^4
           = (2 x 8 + 1/4) - (2 x 1 + 1) = 16.25 - 3 = 13.25
        integral _0^(pi/2) cos x dx = [sin x]_0^(pi/2) = sin(pi/2) - sin 0 = 1 - 0 = 1
    If we used F + C instead: (F(b) + C) - (F(a) + C) = F(b) - F(a); the C
    cancels, so we leave it out. Write the square-bracket step: it avoids sign
    errors when subtracting F(a), especially when F(a) is negative. Here
    4^(3/2) = (sqrt4)^3 = 8. Common mistakes: computing F(a) - F(b); forgetting to
    evaluate at the lower limit because "it is zero" (only sometimes!). Now you
    try: integral _1^2 (x^2 + 1/x) dx. ([x^3/3 + ln x]_1^2 = 7/3 + ln 2 ~ 3.026)

D6. Find (a) d/dx integral _0^x sqrt(1 + t^3) dt, (b) d/dx integral _1^(x^2) ln t dt, (c) d/dx
    Answer: (a) sqrt(1 + x^3); (b) 2x ln(x^2) = 4x ln x (x > 0); (c)
    2x e^(x^4) - e^(x^2); (d) -sin x/x.
    Teacher explains: FTC part 1: the derivative of an integral with respect to
    its upper limit is the integrand evaluated there. With a function g(x) as
        (a) f(t) = sqrt(1 + t^3):             sqrt(1 + x^3)
        (b) upper limit x^2, derivative 2x:   ln(x^2) x 2x = 4x ln x
        (d) x is the LOWER limit:            -sin x/x
    Note that we never need to find the integral itself; in (a) there is no
    elementary antiderivative at all. Common mistakes: forgetting the factor
    d/dx integral _0^(sin x) sqrt(1 - t^2) dt for 0 < x < pi/2. (sqrt(1 - sin^2x) x cos x = cos^2x)

    Answer: F(x + h) - F(x) is the area of a thin strip ~ f(x) x h, so the
    difference quotient tends to f(x). Part 2 follows because F and any
    antiderivative G differ by a constant.
    Teacher explains:
        if m and M are the least and greatest values of f on [x, x + h]:
            m <= (F(x + h) - F(x))/h <= M
        as h -> 0, m and M both -> f(x) (f is continuous)
    f = F(b) = F(b) - F(a) (as F(a) = 0) = (G(b) + K) - (G(a) + K)
    = G(b) - G(a). This theorem joins the two halves of calculus: areas (limits
    of sums) are computed by antiderivatives. Common mistake: thinking FTC needs
    the integrand to be a polynomial; it needs continuity. Now you try: if

D8. Evaluate integral _0^2 x(x^2 + 1)^3 dx, integral _0^(pi/2) sin^3x cos x dx and integral _1^e (ln x)^2/x dx by
    substitution, changing the limits.
    Answer: 78; 1/4; 1/3.
    Teacher explains: When you substitute in a definite integral, convert the
    LIMITS too; then there is no need to go back to x.
        u = x^2 + 1, du = 2x dx:   x = 0 -> u = 1,  x = 2 -> u = 5
           integral _1^5 u^3 (du/2) = (1/2)[u^4/4]_1^5 = (625 - 1)/8 = 78
        u = sin x, du = cos x dx:  x = 0 -> u = 0,  x = pi/2 -> u = 1
           integral _0^1 u^3 du = [u^4/4]_0^1 = 1/4
        u = ln x, du = dx/x:       x = 1 -> u = 0,  x = e -> u = 1
           integral _0^1 u^2 du = [u^3/3]_0^1 = 1/3
    Common mistake: changing the variable but keeping the old limits, e.g.
    (1/2)[u^4/4]_0^2 = 2 for the first one (wrong). If you prefer, find the
    antiderivative in x first ((x^2 + 1)^4/8) and use the ORIGINAL limits:
    (625 - 1)/8 = 78, the same. Now you try: integral _0^1 x e^(x^2) dx. (u = x^2:

D9. Evaluate integral _0^1 x e^x dx, integral _1^e ln x dx and integral _0^pi x sin x dx by parts.
    Answer: 1; 1; pi.
        integral _0^1 x e^x dx = [x e^x]_0^1 - integral _0^1 e^x dx = e - (e - 1) = 1
        integral _1^e ln x dx = [x ln x]_1^e - integral _1^e 1 dx = (e - 0) - (e - 1) = 1
        integral _0^pi x sin x dx = [-x cos x]_0^pi + integral _0^pi cos x dx
                        = (-pi x (-1) - 0) + [sin x]_0^pi = pi + 0 = pi
    Remember cos pi = -1 and ln 1 = 0, ln e = 1. It is often safer to find the
    whole antiderivative first (for x e^x: (x - 1)e^x) and then substitute:
    [(x - 1)e^x]_0^1 = 0 - (-1) = 1. Common mistake: evaluating uv but forgetting
    to put the limits into the second integral. Now you try: integral _0^(pi/2)
    x cos x dx. ([x sin x + cos x]_0^(pi/2) = pi/2 - 1 ~ 0.571)

D10. Evaluate integral _2^3 1/(x^2 - 1) dx, integral _0^1 1/(1 + x^2) dx and integral _0^1 1/sqrt(4 - x^2) dx. Give
     exact values and decimals.
     Answer: (1/2)ln(3/2) ~ 0.203; pi/4 ~ 0.785; pi/6 ~ 0.524.
     Teacher explains:
         1/(x^2 - 1) = (1/2)[1/(x - 1) - 1/(x + 1)]
         integral _2^3 = (1/2)[ln|(x - 1)/(x + 1)|]_2^3 = (1/2)(ln(2/4) - ln(1/3))
             = (1/2)ln((1/2) x 3) = (1/2)ln(3/2)
         integral _0^1 1/(1 + x^2) dx = [tan^-^1x]_0^1 = pi/4 - 0 = pi/4
         integral _0^1 1/sqrt(4 - x^2) dx = [sin^-^1(x/2)]_0^1 = sin^-^1(1/2) = pi/6
     Inverse trig values must be PRINCIPAL values in radians: tan^-^11 = pi/4, not
     45 and not 5pi/4. The second result gives a famous formula: pi = 4integral _0^1
     1/(1 + x^2) dx, which can be used to compute pi numerically. Use the log laws
     to tidy the first: ln a - ln b = ln(a/b). Common mistake:
     ln|(x - 1)/(x + 1)| at x = 2 is ln(1/3), not ln 3. Now you try: integral _0^1
     1/((x + 1)(x + 2)) dx. ([ln((x + 1)/(x + 2))]_0^1 = ln(2/3) - ln(1/2)
     = ln(4/3) ~ 0.288)

D11. Explain why integral _0^(2pi) sin x dx = 0, although the region between y = sin x and
     Answer: The integral counts area below the axis as negative: +2 - 2 = 0;
     the total area is 2 + 2 = 4. The second calculation is invalid: 1/x^2 is not
     continuous (not even defined) at 0; in fact the area is infinite.
     Teacher explains:
         integral _0^pi sin x dx = [-cos x]_0^pi = 1 + 1 = 2        (above the axis)
         integral _pi^(2pi) sin x dx = [-cos x]_pi^(2pi) = -1 - 1 = -2   (below)
         signed total:  2 + (-2) = 0;   area:  2 + |-2| = 4
     A definite integral is a SIGNED area. For a geometric area, split the
     interval at the zeros of f and add absolute values (topic 8.47). For the
     second: the FTC needs f continuous on the WHOLE of [a, b]. 1/x^2 is positive
     everywhere, so its integral can never be negative: the answer -2 is
     (x - 1) dx and the area between y = x - 1 and the x-axis on [0, 3]. (3/2;
     area 1/2 + 2 = 5/2)

D12. A particle moves along a line with velocity v(t) = 3t^2 - 12t + 9 m/s. Find
     its displacement and the total distance travelled from t = 0 to t = 4 s.
     Answer: Displacement 4 m; distance 12 m.
     Teacher explains: Displacement is the integral of velocity; distance is the
     integral of SPEED |v|, so split where v changes sign.
         s(t) = integral v dt = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t   (antiderivative)
         displacement = [s]_0^4 = 64 - 96 + 36 - 0 = 4 m
         v = 3(t - 1)(t - 3): v > 0 on (0, 1), v < 0 on (1, 3), v > 0 on (3, 4)
         s(0) = 0,  s(1) = 4,  s(3) = 0,  s(4) = 4
         distance = |4 - 0| + |0 - 4| + |4 - 0| = 12 m
     The particle goes forward 4 m, comes back 4 m to the start, then goes
     forward 4 m again. The same idea gives total water flow from a rate, total
     cost from marginal cost, and so on: "the integral of a rate of change is
     the total change" (net change theorem). Common mistake: answering 4 m for
     the distance. Now you try: v(t) = t - 2 on [0, 5]. (displacement 5/2 m;
     distance 2 + 9/2 = 13/2 m)
