Scoring guide (out of 80):
  68-80  Ready for Stage 9 (university mathematics).
  52-67  Nearly there - practise the topics of the missed questions for
         two weeks, then try those questions again.
  0-51   Keep working through Stage 8 (revise Stage 7 if needed); test
         again in a month.
  Questions 38-40 and 78-80 come from the optional olympiad track; do not
  count them against a student who has not studied topics 8.59-8.64.
  Compare the two parts: strong in B but weak in A means the student needs
  more practice with applications, derivations and proofs; strong in A
  but weak in B means more drill practice for speed and accuracy.

================================================================================
END OF STAGE 8 - READINESS CHECKLIST FOR STAGE 9
================================================================================
The student is ready for Stage 9 (university Year 1) when they can
usually:
  [ ] Use set notation, Venn diagrams and inclusion-exclusion
  [ ] Classify relations and functions; compose and invert functions
  [ ] Work with modulus, floor, signum, piecewise and rational functions
  [ ] Use truth tables, quantifiers and negations
  [ ] Prove statements by mathematical induction
  [ ] Use radians; find trig values of any angle; sketch trig graphs
  [ ] Use compound, double and half-angle formulas; solve trig equations
      in general and in intervals
  [ ] Use inverse trig functions with principal values
  [ ] Solve triangles with the sine and cosine rules, including the
      ambiguous case
  [ ] Calculate with complex numbers in Cartesian and polar form; use De
      Moivre's theorem and roots of unity
  [ ] Count with permutations and combinations; expand binomials and find
      particular terms
  [ ] Sum GP, AGP and special series; use AM >= GM >= HM
  [ ] Solve exponential and logarithmic equations
  [ ] Multiply matrices, find determinants and inverses, and solve linear
      systems by the matrix method and Cramer's rule
  [ ] Use all forms of straight lines and the properties of the four conics
  [ ] Work in 3D coordinates and with vectors: dot, cross and triple
      products; lines and planes; angles and distances
  [ ] Convert between polar/parametric and Cartesian forms
  [ ] Evaluate limits (including L'Hopital) and test continuity
  [ ] Differentiate every standard function by every rule, including
      implicit, parametric and logarithmic differentiation
  [ ] Apply derivatives: rates, tangents, monotonicity, extrema,
      optimisation, curve sketching, approximations, Newton-Raphson,
      Rolle and the Mean Value Theorem
  [ ] Integrate by substitution, parts and partial fractions; evaluate
      definite integrals using their properties
  [ ] Find areas between curves, volumes of revolution and arc lengths
  [ ] Write Taylor polynomials and test simple series for convergence
  [ ] Solve separable, homogeneous and linear first-order differential
      equations
  [ ] Compute variance, correlation and regression lines
  [ ] Use conditional probability, independence and Bayes' theorem
  [ ] Work with discrete random variables and the binomial, Poisson and
      normal distributions
  [ ] Solve linear programming problems graphically
  [ ] (Optional) Solve introductory olympiad problems in number theory,
      combinatorics, inequalities, geometry and algebra

Rigorous proof, real analysis, linear algebra, multivariable calculus and
discrete mathematics are the main new work of Stage 9.
================================================================================

================================================================================
  STAGE 9: UNDERGRADUATE - YEAR 1 (Bachelor's) - QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS
  Rigour and foundations
================================================================================

How to use this file (note for the parent / teacher)
----------------------------------------------------
- There are 25 topics (9.1 to 9.25, the same as in topic.txt), in six
  strands: Foundations and proof (9.1-9.4), Analysis and calculus
  (9.5-9.12), Linear algebra (9.13-9.18), Differential equations (9.19),
  Discrete mathematics, graphs, number theory and probability (9.20-9.23)
  and Tools of the working mathematician (9.24-9.25).
  Each topic has:
    * WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN   the checklist of definitions, theorems
                                  and methods in that topic
    * PART A - DESCRIPTIVE        12 questions (D1-D12): proofs,
                                  explanations, derivations and worked
                                  numerical problems, each with the answer
                                  and "Teacher explains" (the method step
                                  by step as a teacher shows it on the
                                  board, common mistakes, and a "Now you
                                  try" question)
    * PART B - MATHEMATICAL ONLY  12 questions (M1-M12): pure drills with
                                  answers. Most have many parts (a, b,
                                  c ...) so that EVERY case of the topic is
                                  practised - every convergence test, every
                                  kind of integral and coordinate change,
                                  every matrix size and method, every type
                                  of differential equation and recurrence -
                                  not just one example.
    * TEACHING TIPS               what to do if the student struggles, and
                                  how to make it harder
- In total: 300 descriptive + 300 mathematical questions, then a mixed
  revision test (equal descriptive and mathematical parts) and a readiness
  checklist for Stage 10.
- Level: first-year university mathematics (a Bachelor's in mathematics,
  physics, engineering or computer science): "Introduction to proof",
  Calculus I-III / Analysis I, Linear Algebra I, first ODE course,
  Discrete Mathematics, Probability I.
- What is new in Stage 9: RIGOUR. Definitions are exact, every claim needs
  a proof, and "it looks true" is not enough. The student learns to write
  proofs (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, induction, construction,
  counterexample), meets infinity properly (countable and uncountable
  studies convergence of sequences and series, extends calculus to several
  variables and vector fields, and learns linear algebra as the study of
  vector spaces and linear maps rather than only of matrices.
- Conventions: N = {1, 2, 3, ...} unless 0 is stated; log means the
  natural logarithm ln; vectors in R^n are columns unless written as rows;
  proof; angles are in radians; exact answers first, decimals with ~.
- Method: read the definition, write out an example and a non-example,
  then prove the theorem yourself before reading the proof. For every
  computation, know which theorem justifies it and check its hypotheses.
  Use Python/SageMath (topic 9.24) to CHECK calculations and to explore,
  and write solutions in LaTeX (topic 9.25) from the first week.
- Do 90-120 minutes a day: 2 descriptive questions (write the full proof
  or solution) and 2 drills per session, plus weekly mixed revision.
- Revise Stage 8 (A8.txt) whenever the student finds something difficult;
  especially 8.1-8.6 (sets, functions, logic, induction) before 9.1-9.4,
  and 8.31-8.50 (calculus) before 9.5-9.12.

================================================================================
TOPIC 9.1 - PROOF WRITING AND MATHEMATICAL LANGUAGE (QUANTIFIERS, NEGATION,
SETS, FUNCTIONS)

D2. For integers n consider S: 'If n^2 is even, then n is even.' Write its
    converse, inverse and contrapositive and decide which are true. Do the
    same for T: 'If x > 2 then x^2 > 4' (x real), and rewrite T using
    'sufficient', 'necessary' and 'only if'.
    Answer: For S all four statements are true. For T: statement true,
    'x^2 > 4 is necessary for x > 2'; 'x > 2 only if x^2 > 4'.
    The statement and its contrapositive always have the same truth value;
    the converse and the inverse always have the same truth value (the
    is easy: n = 2k + 1 gives n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1; that proves
    and only if'. For T the converse fails with ONE counterexample: x = -3
    for Q, and Q is NECESSARY (cannot be avoided) for P. 'P only if Q' means
    mistake: reading 'only if' as 'if'. Now you try: is the converse of 'if
    f is differentiable at a then f is continuous at a' true? (No: f(x) = |x|
    is continuous but not differentiable at 0.)

D5. Prove: (a) if m and n are odd integers then m + n is even and mn is odd;
    (b) if n^2 is even then n is even (by contrapositive); (c) for every integer
    n, n^2 + n is even (by cases); (d) for all real x, y,
    max(x, y) = (x + y + |x - y|)/2.
    Answer: Proofs below.
    Teacher explains: (a) DIRECT. Use different letters for the two numbers:
       m + n = 2k + 2l + 2 = 2(k + l + 1)                 even
       mn = 4kl + 2k + 2l + 1 = 2(2kl + k + l) + 1        odd
    Writing m = n = 2k + 1 would prove the result only for m = n.
    (b) CONTRAPOSITIVE: the direct route (n^2 = 2j, so n = sqrt(2j) ...) goes
    n^2 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1, odd. Since the contrapositive is equivalent, the
    statement is proved. (c) CASES: every integer is even or odd.
       n = 2k:      n^2 + n = 4k^2 + 2k = 2(2k^2 + k)             even
       n = 2k + 1:  n^2 + n = (2k + 1)(2k + 2) = 2(2k + 1)(k + 1) even
    (Quicker: n^2 + n = n(n + 1), a product of two consecutive integers, one
    of which is even.) (d) CASES on the sign of x - y:
       x >= y:  |x - y| = x - y,  (x + y + x - y)/2 = x = max(x, y)
       x < y:  |x - y| = y - x,  (x + y + y - x)/2 = y = max(x, y)
    Common mistakes: checking a few values of n instead of all; forgetting a
    case (for example x = y). Now you try: prove that if 3 does not divide n,
    then 3 divides n^2 - 1. (n = 3k +/- 1 gives n^2 - 1 = 9k^2 +/- 6k = 3(3k^2 +/- 2k))

    the formula for n (the induction hypothesis) and add (n + 1)^2:
       n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 + (n + 1)^2

    2^n > n^2 with n >= 5. Then
    using n^2 >= 3n (as n >= 3) and 3n > 2n + 1 (as n > 1). (c) STRONG
    induction: check four bases, then step back by 4:
    For n >= 16, n - 4 >= 12, so by hypothesis n - 4 = 4a + 5b, and then

D10. Decide which of these functions are injective, surjective or bijective,
     and find the inverse of each bijection:
     (a) f : R -> R, f(x) = 3x - 7      (b) g : R -> R, g(x) = x^2
     Answer: (a) bijective, f^-^1(y) = (y + 7)/3. (b) neither. (c) injective,
     not surjective. (d) surjective, not injective. (e) bijective,
     Teacher explains: INJECTIVE: start from f(x) = f(y) and deduce x = y.
     SURJECTIVE: start from an arbitrary b in the CODOMAIN and solve f(a) = b
     Lesson: a formula alone is not a function; the properties depend on the
     domain and the codomain. Common mistakes: testing surjectivity against
     the domain instead of the codomain; 'proving' injectivity from
     f : N -> N, f(n) = n + 1, injective? surjective? (Injective; not
     surjective, since 1 is not a value.)

     then g is surjective. (d) With f, g : N -> N, f(n) = n + 1, g(1) = 1 and
     These differ (at x = 1: 9 and 3), so composition is not commutative.
     (b) Let g(f(x)) = g(f(y)). g injective gives f(x) = f(y); f injective
     gives x = y. (c) If f(x) = f(y) then g(f(x)) = g(f(y)), and injectivity
     gives a with g(f(a)) = c, so b = f(a) satisfies g(b) = c. (d) g(f(n)) =
        f(g(1)) = f(1) = 2 != 1
     so g is only a LEFT inverse of f. Consistent with (c): f is injective
     (not surjective), g is surjective (not injective, since g(1) = g(2) = 1).
     A TWO-sided inverse exists exactly when f is bijective. Common mistakes:

D12. Let f : R -> R, f(x) = x^2. Find f([-1, 2]), f^-^1([1, 4]), f^-^1([-3, -1]),
     f^-^1((-1, 4)) and f^-^1(f([0, 1])). With A = [-2, -1] and B = [1, 2]
     every function, with equality when f is injective. Finally count the
     functions, injections and surjections from a 3-element set to a
     4-element set, and from the 4-element set to the 3-element set.
     injections, 0 surjections. 4 -> 3: 81 functions, 0 injections, 36
     surjections.
     Teacher explains: f(S) is 'where S goes'; f^-^1(T) is 'what lands in T'.
     No inverse function is needed for f^-^1(T).
        f([-1, 2]):  x^2 runs over [0, 1] on [-1, 0] and [0, 4] on [0, 2]
                     -> [0, 4]     (NOT [1, 4]: 0 is a value)
        f^-^1((-1, 4)): x^2 < 4 (x^2 > -1 always) -> (-2, 2)
        functions      4^3 = 64          (each of 3 inputs: 4 choices)
        surjections    0                (3 inputs cannot cover 4 outputs)
     and from the 4-set to the 3-set: 3^4 = 81 functions, no injections, and
     by inclusion-exclusion (remove the maps missing some value)
     Common mistakes: f^-^1([1, 4]) = [1, 2] (forgetting negatives); counting
     twice). Now you try: how many surjections are there from a 4-element set
     onto a 2-element set? (2^4 - 2 = 14)

M5. For each statement give the truth value of (S) the statement, (C) its
    converse, (P) its contrapositive. x, y are real, n is an integer.
    a) If x = 2 then x^2 = 4.
    b) If 6 divides n then 3 divides n.
    c) If x > 0 then x^3 > 0.
    d) If n^2 is odd then n is odd.
    e) If x^2 < 1 then x < 1.
    f) If a triangle is equilateral then it is isosceles.
    g) If xy = 0 then x = 0.
    h) If n is prime then n is odd.
    i) If x is rational then x^2 is rational.
    j) If x + y is irrational then x or y is irrational.
    k) If f is differentiable at a then f is continuous at a.
    l) If a sequence converges then it is bounded.
    m) If n is divisible by 4 then n is even.
    n) If x^2 = x then x = 1.
    Answers (S, C, P):
      a) T, F (x = -2), T      b) T, F (n = 3), T      c) T, T, T
      d) T, T, T               e) T, F (x = -2), T     f) T, F, T
      g) F (x = 1, y = 0), T, F                       h) F (n = 2), F (n = 9), F
      i) T, F (x = sqrt2), T      j) T, F (sqrt2 + (-sqrt2) = 0), T
      k) T, F (|x| at 0), T    l) T, F ((-1)^n), T      m) T, F (n = 2), T
      n) F (x = 0), T, F
      (S and P always agree: a statement and its contrapositive are
      equivalent.)

M6. Prove (proof sketches given).
    a) The product of two odd integers is odd.
    b) If n is even then 4 divides n^2.
    c) If 3n + 2 is odd then n is odd.
    d) If 3 divides n^2 then 3 divides n.
    e) sqrt3 is irrational.
    f) For every integer n, 6 divides n^3 - n.
    g) For all real x, x^2 - 6x + 10 > 0.
    h) If x > 0 then x + 1/x >= 2.
    i) There is no smallest positive rational number.
    j) For integers a, b, a^2 - 4b != 2.
    k) For every integer n, n^2 leaves remainder 0 or 1 on division by 4.
    l) If a | b and b | c then a | c.
    m) The sum of a rational and an irrational number is irrational.
    n) min(x, y) = (x + y - |x - y|)/2.
    o) log_2 5 is irrational.
    p) Among any three integers, two have an even sum.
    Answers:
      a) (2k + 1)(2l + 1) = 2(2kl + k + l) + 1.
         contradiction.
      f) n^3 - n = (n - 1)n(n + 1): among three consecutive integers one is
         even and one is a multiple of 3.
      g) x^2 - 6x + 10 = (x - 3)^2 + 1 >= 1 > 0.
      h) x + 1/x - 2 = (x - 1)^2/x >= 0 for x > 0.
      i) If r > 0 were the smallest, r/2 is a smaller positive rational.
      k) Cases n = 2k: n^2 = 4k^2; n = 2k + 1: n^2 = 4(k^2 + k) + 1.
      n) Cases x <= y: right side = (x + y - (y - x))/2 = x; x > y gives y.
      p) Only two parities exist, so two of the three share a parity

    a) 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n - 1) = n^2
    b) 1^3 + 2^3 + ... + n^3 = (n(n + 1)/2)^2
    d) 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^n^-^1 = 2^n - 1
    f) 3 divides 4^n - 1
    g) 5 divides n^5 - n
    h) 7 divides 3^2^n - 2^n
    i) n! > 2^n for n >= 4
    j) (1 + x)^n >= 1 + nx for x >= -1 (Bernoulli)
    l) F_n < 2^n (strong induction)
    m) Every n >= 8 is 3a + 5b with a, b >= 0 (strong induction)
    n) d/dx x^n = nx^n^-^1 (using the product rule)
    o) Find the error: 'all horses have the same colour' (step from a set of
       n horses to n + 1 by removing one horse at a time).
    Answers:
      a) Base 1 = 1. Step: n^2 + (2n + 1) = (n + 1)^2.
      b) Base 1 = 1. Step: n^2(n + 1)^2/4 + (n + 1)^3 = (n + 1)^2(n^2 + 4n + 4)/4
         = ((n + 1)(n + 2)/2)^2.
      c) Base 1 = 2! - 1. Step: (n + 1)! - 1 + (n + 1)(n + 1)!
         = (n + 2)(n + 1)! - 1 = (n + 2)! - 1.
         = (n + 1)(n + 2)(n + 3)/3.
      g) Base 0. Step: (n + 1)^5 - (n + 1) = (n^5 - n) + 5(n^4 + 2n^3 + 2n^2 + n).
         = 1 + (n + 1)x + nx^2 >= 1 + (n + 1)x (uses 1 + x >= 0).
         3a + 5b, so n = 3(a + 1) + 5b.
      o) The step fails from n = 1 to n = 2: the two sets of n = 1 horses
         (all but the first, all but the last) do not overlap, so nothing
         links the colours.

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: insist on a truth table whenever an implication feels odd, and
  read every quantified statement as a game ('you pick, I answer'); negate by
  the three rules only, one symbol at a time, writing each line; before any
  proof write 'Assume ...' and 'Want: ...' on two lines, and for functions
  always write the domain and codomain before deciding anything. Draw the
  graph of x^2 to answer image and preimage questions. Harder: prove that
  inverse iff it is surjective (this uses the axiom of choice); show that
  f(f^-^1(T)) = T for all T iff f is surjective and f^-^1(f(S)) = S for all S
  holds; show that the number of surjections from an n-set onto a k-set is

================================================================================
TOPIC 9.2 - NAIVE SET THEORY: CARDINALITY, COUNTABLE/UNCOUNTABLE SETS,
CANTOR'S DIAGONAL
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - Two sets have the SAME CARDINALITY, |A| = |B| (A and B are EQUINUMEROUS),
    when there is a BIJECTION A -> B. |A| <= |B| when there is an INJECTION
    |A| <= |B| but |A| != |B|. For finite sets this is ordinary counting; the
    PIGEONHOLE principle says there is no injection from an (n + 1)-set into
    an n-set.
  - A set is FINITE if it is equinumerous with {1, ..., n} for some n >= 0,
    COUNTABLE if finite or countably infinite (its elements can be LISTED
    a_1, a_2, a_3, ...), and UNCOUNTABLE otherwise. An infinite set can be
    A finite set never can.
  - Standard countable sets: N, Z (0, 1, -1, 2, -2, ...), N x N (Cantor's
    pairing pi(m, n) = (m + n)(m + n + 1)/2 + n is a bijection N_0 x N_0 -> N_0,
    alphabet, polynomials with integer or rational coefficients, ALGEBRAIC
    numbers.
  - Closure rules: a subset of a countable set is countable; the image of a
    countable set under any function is countable; a finite product of
    countable sets is countable; a COUNTABLE UNION of countable sets is
    countable (list them in a grid and use the pairing; this uses the axiom
    of choice to pick the listings). To prove A countable it is enough to
    find an injection A -> N or a surjection N -> A.
  - CANTOR'S DIAGONAL ARGUMENT: given any list r_1, r_2, ... of numbers in

    function. A finite hotel: an injection {1, ..., n + 1} -> {1, ..., n}

    guests' into N:

D3. Cantor's pairing function on N_0 x N_0 is pi(m, n) = (m + n)(m + n + 1)/2 + n.
    Compute pi(0, 0), pi(2, 3), pi(4, 1) and find the pair with pi(m, n) = 25.
    Explain why pi is a bijection and deduce that N x N is countable. Give
    also a simpler injection N x N -> N.
    Answer: pi(0, 0) = 0, pi(2, 3) = 18, pi(4, 1) = 16; pi^-^1(25) = (2, 4). An
    Teacher explains: pi walks through the grid along the anti-diagonals
    m + n = w = 0, 1, 2, ...:
          n=0 n=1 n=2 n=3
    m=0    0   2   5   9
    m=1    1   4   8
    m=2    3   7
    m=3    6
    The diagonals with w = 0, 1, ..., w - 1 contain 1 + 2 + ... + w =
    w(w + 1)/2 points, so the point (m, n) on diagonal w is number
    w(w + 1)/2 + n (counting from 0). Examples:
       pi(2, 3):  w = 5,  15 + 3 = 18        pi(4, 1):  w = 5,  15 + 1 = 16
    To invert z = 25: find the largest w with w(w + 1)/2 <= 25: 21 <= 25 < 28,
    so w = 6. Then n = 25 - 21 = 4 and m = w - n = 2. Check pi(2, 4) =
    factorisation (not surjective: 5 is missed), which is also enough: an
    injection into N proves countability. Common mistake: listing row by row
    (0,0), (0,1), (0,2), ...: you never reach row 1. Now you try: pi(3, 3)
    and pi^-^1(10). (24; (4, 0))

D4. Prove that Q is countable. List the positive rationals p/q (in lowest
    terms) of 'height' p + q <= 5, and count those of height 7.
    Answer: Heights 2 to 5 give 1/1; 1/2, 2/1; 1/3, 3/1; 1/4, 2/3, 3/2, 4/1
    (9 numbers). Height 7 gives 6 numbers.
    Teacher explains: Method 1 (injection): write each rational uniquely as
    This is injective and Z x N is countable (Z and N are countable, a
    product of two countable sets is countable), so Q is countable. Method 2
    (listing): for each height h = |p| + q there are only finitely many
    rationals, so list height 2, then height 3, and so on; every rational
    appears at some finite stage:
       h = 2:  1/1                         h = 3:  1/2, 2/1
       h = 4:  1/3, 3/1   (2/2 = 1/1 skip) h = 5:  1/4, 2/3, 3/2, 4/1
    For height h, p/q with p + q = h is in lowest terms exactly when
    5/2, 6/1. Putting 0 first and each -r after r gives a list of all of Q.
    The surprise: Q is dense (between any two reals there is a rational) but
    no bigger than N. Common mistake: listing 1/1, 1/2, 1/3, ... first and
    'then' 2/1, 2/2, ...: the first row never ends. Now you try: how many
    7/3, 9/1)

D5. Prove that a countable union of countable sets is countable. Deduce that

    algebraic numbers is countable.
    Answer: Proof below; 2 + 4 + 8 = 14 non-empty strings of length <= 3.
    Teacher explains: Let A_1, A_2, ... be countable. List each one (this is
    where the axiom of choice quietly picks a listing for every i):
       A_1:  a_1_1  a_1_2  a_1_3  ...
       A_2:  a_2_1  a_2_2  a_2_3  ...
       A_3:  a_3_1  a_3_2  a_3_3  ...
    so the union is countable (repeats and finite sets do no harm: skip
    finite; a countable union of finite sets is countable. Length <= 3:
    2 + 4 + 8 = 14 (15 with the empty string). (b) Polynomials of degree
    countable set; take the union over n. (c) Each non-zero polynomial has
    polynomials) (finite root sets): countable. Consequence: since R is
    uncountable (D6), most real numbers are TRANSCENDENTAL. Common mistakes:
    'each S_n is finite so S is finite'; forgetting that a countable union of
    FINITE sets can be infinite. Now you try: how many strings of length
    exactly 4 are there over the 26-letter alphabet? (26^4 = 456976)

     b) Every infinite set has a countably infinite subset.

     d) The intersection of two uncountable sets is uncountable.
     e) If A is uncountable and B is countable then A - B is uncountable.
     f) There is a surjection N -> R.
     g) There is an injection Q -> N.
     h) There is a bijection R -> P(N).
     i) For some non-empty set A there is a surjection A -> P(A).
     j) Q is dense in R, so |Q| = |R|.
     k) |(0, 1)| = |R|
     l) The set of irrational numbers is countable.
     m) If there is a surjection A -> B then |B| <= |A|.
     n) A set equinumerous with one of its proper subsets is infinite.
     o) Every infinite set is equinumerous with a proper subset of itself.
     p) The set of all finite subsets of R is countable.
     q) The Cantor set has the same cardinality as R.
     r) The continuum hypothesis has been proved from the ZFC axioms.
     s) |N x N| = |N|
     t) There is a largest cardinal number.
     u) There is a set of all sets.
     v) Some set is equinumerous with its power set.
     w) A countable union of countable sets is countable (with choice).
              g) T   h) T   i) F   j) F   k) T   l) F   m) T   n) T   o) T
              p) F (it has cardinality c)   q) T   r) F (independent)   s) T
              t) F   u) F (Russell)   v) F (Cantor)   w) T   x) T

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep coming back to one picture, pairing off two sets with
  arrows; say 'same size = there is a bijection' until it is automatic; act
  out Hilbert's Hotel with room numbers; draw the grid for N x N and walk the
  diagonals; for the diagonal argument write out a list of five decimals and
  build the new number digit by digit in a different colour. Emphasise that
  to show 'countable' it is enough to INJECT into N. Harder: prove
  |R^N| = c but |R^R| = 2^c; show that every uncountable closed set in R has
  cardinality c (Cantor-Bendixson); prove that the set of all subsets of N
  that are either finite or cofinite is countable while the set of
  'eventually periodic' 0-1 sequences is countable; show that any countable
  dense linear order without end points is order-isomorphic to Q (Cantor's
  back-and-forth argument); and read about Cohen's proof that the continuum
  hypothesis cannot be proved.

  - An EQUIVALENCE RELATION (~) is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. The

  - A PARTITION of A is a collection of non-empty, pairwise disjoint subsets

    equivalence relation form a partition, and every partition comes from
  - Standard examples: congruence mod n on Z (n classes [0], ..., [n - 1],
    parallel lines; similar triangles.
  - COUNTING on an n-element set: 2^(n^2) relations; 2^(n^2 - n) reflexive;
    2^(n(n + 1)/2) symmetric; 2^(n(n - 1)/2) reflexive and symmetric;
    BELL number B_n: 1, 1, 2, 5, 15, 52, 203, 877, 4140 (n = 0 to 8), with

  - A PARTIAL ORDER (<=, a POSET) is reflexive, ANTISYMMETRIC and transitive:
    STRICT order < is irreflexive and transitive. a and b are COMPARABLE if
    a <= b or b <= a; a TOTAL (linear) order makes every pair comparable. The
    HASSE DIAGRAM draws only the covering relations (a < b with nothing in
    between), larger elements higher.
  - SPECIAL ELEMENTS of a poset: m is MAXIMAL if nothing is strictly above it,
    GREATEST (maximum) if it is above everything; a greatest element is
    unique and is the only maximal one, but maximal elements need not be
    greatest (there may be several, or none). Similarly minimal/least. For
    INFIMUM (glb). In (N, |): sup{a, b} = lcm(a, b), inf = gcd(a, b); in
    inf is a LATTICE.
  - A WELL-ORDER is a total order in which every non-empty subset has a least
    well-ordering of N is equivalent to induction. The LEXICOGRAPHIC order
    on N x N ((a, b) < (c, d) if a < c, or a = c and b < d) is a well-order;
    the PRODUCT order (a <= c and b <= d) is only partial.
  - CHAINS (totally ordered subsets), ANTICHAINS (pairwise incomparable) and
    LINEAR EXTENSIONS (total orders containing <=; 'topological sorting'):
    every finite poset has one. In P({1, ..., n}) the largest antichain has

D1. On A = {1, 2, 3, 4} decide whether each relation is reflexive (R),
    symmetric (S), antisymmetric (A) or transitive (T). Which are equivalence
    relations, which partial orders? Give the classes of any equivalence.
      R_1 = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4), (1,2), (2,1)}
      R_2 = {(1,2), (2,3), (1,3)}
      R_3 = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4), (1,2), (2,3)}
      R_4 = {(1,2), (2,1), (1,1)}
    Answer: R_1: R, S, T (equivalence; classes {1, 2}, {3}, {4}). R_2: A, T
    (a strict order, not reflexive). R_3: R, A, not T. R_4: S only. R_5: S, A, T
    (not R).
    Teacher explains: Check each property against its definition, hunting
    for ONE failure:
       reflexive:     are all four loops (1,1), ..., (4,4) present?
       symmetric:     for each (a, b), is (b, a) there?
       antisymmetric: is there a pair (a, b), (b, a) with a != b?
       transitive:    for each 'path' (a, b), (b, c), is (a, c) there?
    R_3 fails transitivity: (1, 2) and (2, 3) are present but (1, 3) is not.
    R_4: (2, 1) and (1, 2) force (2, 2) for transitivity, and (2, 2) is
    missing; it is not reflexive either. R_2 has no pair to contradict
    satisfies every 'if ... then' property VACUOUSLY (there is no pair to
    test) but fails reflexivity, which demands loops. A relation that is
    both symmetric and antisymmetric can only contain loops. Common
    mistakes: calling R_4 antisymmetric because (1,1) is there; thinking a
    relation must be either symmetric or antisymmetric. Now you try: the
    identity relation {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4)}. (R, S, A, T: it is both
    an equivalence relation, with classes {1}, {2}, {3}, {4}, and a partial
    order)

D2. Decide which properties hold and identify the equivalence relations and
    partial orders: (a) on Z, a ~ b iff a - b is even; (b) on N, a | b; (c) on
    Z, a | b; (d) on R, x R y iff |x - y| <= 1; (e) on R, x R y iff xy > 0;
    Answer: (a) equivalence (2 classes: evens, odds). (b) partial order.
    (c) reflexive, transitive, not symmetric, not antisymmetric. (d)
    reflexive, symmetric, not transitive. (e) symmetric, transitive, not
    (f) equivalence (uncountably many classes x + Q).
    Teacher explains: (a) a - a = 0 is even; if a - b = 2k then
    b - a = 2(-k); if a - b = 2k and b - c = 2l then a - c = 2(k + l). (b)
    a | a; a | b and b | a with a, b >= 1 force a = b; a | b, b | c give
    2 != -2; symmetry fails: 2 | 4 but not 4 | 2. (d) The 'close to' relation:
       0 R 1  (|0 - 1| = 1)   and   1 R 2   but   |0 - 2| = 2 > 1
    0 is not > 0, so 0 is related to nothing and reflexivity fails; drop 0
    and the relation becomes 'same sign', an equivalence with two classes.
    Each class x + Q is countable, so there must be uncountably many classes
    (choosing one element from each gives the famous non-measurable Vitali
    set). Common mistake: calling (d) an equivalence because it 'looks like'
    equality. Now you try: on R, x ~ y iff x^2 = y^2. (Equivalence;
    [x] = {x, -x}, [0] = {0})

D4. Prove that the equivalence classes of ~ on A form a partition of A, and
    conversely that a partition defines an equivalence relation. For the
    partition {1, 4, 7}, {2, 5, 8}, {3, 6} of {1, ..., 8}, name the relation
    and count its ordered pairs.
    Answer: Proofs below; it is congruence mod 3 restricted to {1, ..., 8};
    it contains 3^2 + 3^2 + 2^2 = 22 pairs.
    Teacher explains: Three things make the classes a partition:
       cover A:    every a lies in its own class [a]
    Conversely, given a partition, define x ~ y iff x and y are in the same
    block. Every x is in some block (reflexive); 'same block' is symmetric;
    constructions are inverse to each other. Counting pairs: inside a block
    of size k every ordered pair (x, y) is related, k^2 pairs, and there are
    no pairs across blocks:
       {1, 4, 7}: 9     {2, 5, 8}: 9     {3, 6}: 4      total 22
    Common mistakes: counting k(k - 1)/2 (unordered, without loops) instead of
    k^2; forgetting to prove 'non-empty'. Now you try: how many ordered pairs
    are in the equivalence relation with blocks {a, b, c, d}, {e}, {f, g}?
    (16 + 1 + 4 = 21)

D8. List all partitions of {1, 2, 3}. Define the Stirling number S(n, k) and
    the Bell number B_n, prove S(n, k) = kS(n - 1, k) + S(n - 1, k - 1), and
    compute S(4, 2), B_4, S(5, 3) and B_5. How many equivalence relations does
    a 5-element set carry, and how many surjections are there from a 5-set
    onto a 3-set?
    Answer: 5 partitions: {1,2,3}; {1,2}{3}; {1,3}{2}; {2,3}{1}; {1}{2}{3}.
    S(4, 2) = 7, B_4 = 15, S(5, 3) = 25, B_5 = 52. 52 equivalence relations;
    Teacher explains: S(n, k) = number of partitions of an n-set into k
    the recurrence, look at the element n:
       n alone in a block:  partition the other n - 1 into k - 1 blocks:
                            S(n - 1, k - 1) ways
       n with others:       partition the other n - 1 into k blocks and put
    Build the triangle row by row (S(n, 1) = S(n, n) = 1):
       n = 1:   1                               B_1 = 1
       n = 2:   1   1                           B_2 = 2

D9. On a set with n elements count the relations that are (a) arbitrary;
    (b) reflexive; (c) symmetric; (d) reflexive and symmetric;
    (e) antisymmetric. Evaluate for n = 3.
    Answer: (a) 2^(n^2) = 512; (b) 2^(n^2 - n) = 64; (c) 2^(n(n + 1)/2) = 64;
    Teacher explains: A relation is a choice, for each of the n^2 cells of the
    n x n matrix, of 'in' or 'out'. Split the cells into the n DIAGONAL cells
    (a, a) and the n(n - 1)/2 OFF-DIAGONAL PAIRS {(a, b), (b, a)}:
       (a) every cell free                       2^(n^2)       = 2^9 = 512
       (b) diagonal forced in, rest free         2^(n^2 - n)   = 2^6 = 64
       (c) diagonal free (2^n), each pair both
           in or both out (2 per pair)           2^(n + n(n - 1)/2) = 2^6 = 64
       (d) diagonal forced, pairs as in (c)      2^(n(n - 1)/2) = 2^3 = 8
       (e) diagonal free, each pair: neither,
    Transitivity has no such simple formula: there are 13 transitive
    relations on 2 elements and 171 on 3, and the counts of partial orders
    are 3, 19, 219 for n = 2, 3, 4; only computer searches give large n.
    Common mistake in (e): allowing 4 choices per pair (both in is
    forbidden). Now you try: for n = 4, how many reflexive and how many
    symmetric relations are there? (2^1^2 = 4096; 2^1^0 = 1024)

D10. Draw the Hasse diagram of the divisors of 12 under divisibility. In the
     poset P = {2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12} under | find the minimal, maximal, least
     and greatest elements. In the divisors of 12 find the upper bounds and
     the least upper bound of {2, 3}, and the greatest lower bound of {4, 6}.
     Answer: Hasse diagram below. In P: minimal 2 and 3, maximal 8 and 12,
     no least and no greatest element. Upper bounds of {2, 3}: 6 and 12,
     lub 6 = lcm(2, 3); glb{4, 6} = 2 = gcd(4, 6).
     Teacher explains: Draw an edge from a up to b only when b COVERS a (a | b
     and nothing lies strictly between):
                  12
                /    \
               4      6
                \   /   \
                  2      3
                    \   /
                      1
     The covers are 1-2, 1-3, 2-4, 2-6, 3-6, 4-12, 6-12 (7 edges); 1-4 is
     NOT an edge because 2 lies between. Transitivity is read off as upward
     paths. In P = {2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12} (no 1, and 8 added): nothing in P
     divides 2 or 3 except themselves, so both are minimal, and since neither
     divides the other there is no least element. Nothing in P is a multiple of
     8 or of 12 except themselves: both maximal, no greatest. In (N, |) sup =
     lcm and inf = gcd, so the divisors of 12 form a LATTICE. Common mistakes:
     calling 12 the greatest element of P (8 does not divide 12); drawing all
     comparabilities instead of covers. Now you try: for the divisors of 30,
     describe the Hasse diagram and find lub and glb of {6, 10}. (A cube with 8
     vertices and 12 edges; lub 30, glb 2)

D11. (a) Show that the lexicographic order on R^2 ((a, b) < (c, d) iff a < c,
     or a = c and b < d) is a total order, and compare (1, 5) with (2, -3)
     and (2, 1) with (2, 4). (b) Show that the product order ((a, b) <= (c, d)
     iff a <= c and b <= d) is a partial order but not total. (c) Which of N,
     by the usual <=? (d) Prove that N x N with the lexicographic order is well
     ordered. (e) Prove that the well-ordering of N implies induction.
     Answer: (a) (1, 5) < (2, -3); (2, 1) < (2, 4). (b) (1, 5) and (2, -3)
     (0, 1] are not. (d), (e) below.
     Teacher explains: (a) LEXICOGRAPHIC = dictionary order: compare first
     letters, and only on a tie compare second letters. Given (a, b), (c, d):
     either a < c, or c < a, or a = c and then b < d, d < b or b = d. So any
     two are comparable: TOTAL. (1, 5) < (2, -3) because 1 < 2; the second
     coordinates are never looked at. (b) Reflexive, antisymmetric and
     transitive follow coordinatewise from <= on R, but 1 < 2 while 5 > -3, so
     neither (1, 5) <= (2, -3) nor the reverse. (c) WELL ORDERED: every
     non-empty subset has a LEAST element.
        N              yes (the well-ordering principle)
        Z              no: Z itself has no least element
        (0, 1]         no: (0, 1] itself has no least element
        S              yes: 0, 1/2, 2/3, ..., then 1 at the top
     P fails somewhere. The set of failures has a least element m; m != 1, so
     contradiction. Common mistakes: thinking 'has a least element' is
     enough for the set itself only (it is needed for every subset); calling
     <=? By >=? (No: no least element; yes: under >= it is 1, 1/2, 1/3, ... like
     N)

     maximal, least and greatest elements, a longest chain and a largest
     antichain. (b) Tasks a, b, c, d must be done one at a time, with a and
     b both before c (d is free). In how many orders can they be done? And
     if instead a comes before b and c, which both come before d? (c) Find
     and say whether they are attained.
     Answer: (a) Minimal: {1}, {2}, {3}; maximal: {1, 2}, {1, 3}, {2, 3}; no
     largest antichain e.g. the three singletons (3 elements). (b) 8 orders;
     2 orders. (c) sup S = 1 (not attained), inf S = 0 = min S; sup T = 3/2
     = max T, inf T = -1 (not attained).
     Teacher explains: (a) Draw the Hasse diagram: three singletons on the
     bottom row, three pairs on the top row, each singleton joined to the two
     pairs containing it (a hexagon). Nothing lies below a singleton inside
     incomparable, none is LEAST. Likewise the pairs are maximal but none is
     order of tasks is a LINEAR EXTENSION of the poset. First case: order a,
     b, c with c last among them: 2 ways (a b c, b a c); then insert d into
     any of the 4 gaps: 2 x 4 = 8. Second case (a 'diamond'): a first, d
     last, b and c in either order: a b c d, a c b d: 2. (c) The supremum is
     the LEAST upper bound, which need not belong to the set:
        S:  0, 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, ...    increasing to 1      sup 1, inf 0
        T:  n = 1: 0,  n = 2: 3/2,  n = 3: -2/3,  n = 4: 5/4, ...
            odd n:  -1 + 1/n > -1, approaching -1       inf -1
            even n: 1 + 1/n <= 3/2                       sup 3/2 at n = 2
     To prove sup S = 1: 1 is an upper bound, and for any c < 1 some
     1 - 1/n > c (Archimedes), so no smaller upper bound exists. Common
     mistakes: calling a maximal element 'the maximum'; claiming sup S = 1
     attained; 1/2, attained at n = 1)

M12. Prove (sketches).
     a) Congruence mod n is an equivalence relation on Z.
     b) Two equivalence classes are equal or disjoint.
     c) A partition defines an equivalence relation.
     d) (a, b) ~ (c, d) iff ad = bc is transitive on Z x (Z - {0}).
     e) Addition on Z/n is well defined.
     f) x ~ y iff f(x) = f(y) is an equivalence relation.
     h) Divisibility is a partial order on N but not on Z.
     i) The intersection of two equivalence relations on A is an equivalence
        relation; the union need not be.
     j) A non-empty finite poset has a minimal element.
     k) A greatest element, if it exists, is unique and is the only maximal
        element.
     l) Every finite poset has a linear extension.
     m) The lexicographic order on N x N is a well-order.
     n) If <= is a partial order then >= (a >= b iff b <= a) is a partial order,
        and a < b iff (a <= b and a != b) is irreflexive and transitive.
     Answers:
       f) Inherited from reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity of '='.
       g) {(1, 1)} on {1, 2} is symmetric and transitive, not reflexive (2 is
          related to nothing).
          2 | -2 and -2 | 2 but 2 != -2.
       j) Start anywhere and step down while possible; no infinite descent in
          a finite set (or take an element with fewest elements below it).
          m <= g forces m = g.
       l) Induction on |P|: remove a minimal element m (j), extend the rest,
          put m first.
       n) Reflexivity, antisymmetry, transitivity read backwards;
          contradiction.

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw every small relation as arrows between dots (loops for
  reflexive, two-way arrows for symmetric, 'shortcuts' for transitive) and
  look for the missing arrow; colour the blocks of a partition and point
  out that an equivalence relation is just 'same colour'; practise
  well-definedness with fractions (1/2 = 2/4) before quotient groups; for
  posets always draw the Hasse diagram before naming maximal or greatest
  elements. Harder: prove that the equivalence relations on A, ordered by
  inclusion, form a lattice isomorphic (reversed) to the partitions ordered
  Dilworth's theorem for finite posets (the least number of chains covering
  P equals the largest antichain) and Sperner's theorem; show that every
  partial order on a finite set is the intersection of its linear
  extensions; and prove that a total order is a well-order iff it has no
  strictly decreasing infinite sequence.

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - PEANO AXIOMS for N = {0, 1, 2, ...}: there is an element 0 and a SUCCESSOR
    map S : N -> N such that (i) S is one-one, (ii) 0 is not a successor, (iii)
    INDUCTION: any subset of N containing 0 and closed under S is all of N.
    Write 1 = S(0), 2 = S(1), .... Addition and multiplication are defined by
    law (associative, commutative, distributive, cancellation) is then PROVED by
    [(a, b)] stands for 'a - b'. Operations: [(a, b)] + [(c, d)] =
    exactly one representative of the form (n, 0) or (0, n).
    [(ac, bd)], [(a, b)]^-^1 = [(b, a)] for a != 0. Q is an ORDERED FIELD: a/b > 0
  - WELL-DEFINEDNESS: an operation on classes is defined through
    representatives, so you MUST prove the answer does not depend on the
    representatives chosen. Transitivity of ~ and well-definedness use
    cancellation in the previous system (in N for Z; in Z, with b != 0, for Q).
    non-empty and bounded above in Q but has NO least upper bound in Q (for any
    rational p > 0, q = (2p + 2)/(p + 2) lies strictly between p and sqrt2 and has
    q^2 - 2 = 2(p^2 - 2)/(p + 2)^2, the same sign as p^2 - 2).
  - SUPREMUM: s = sup A when s is an upper bound of A and no smaller number is;
    COMPLETENESS (least-upper-bound property): every non-empty subset of R that
    is bounded above has a supremum in R. R is the unique complete ordered field
    (up to isomorphism). Infima: inf A = -sup(-A).
    r > 0}. The supremum of a bounded set of cuts is their UNION, which is
    exactly why R is complete.
    converge in Q (1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, ...). R = (Cauchy sequences in Q)/~
    POSITIVE when x_n >= c for all large n, for some rational c > 0. Every
    Cauchy sequence is bounded; that is what makes the product well defined.
    nx > y; so 1/n -> 0); DENSITY (between any two reals lies a rational: take
    NESTED INTERVALS; every real has a decimal expansion, with 0.999... = 1
    because the sequences (0.9, 0.99, ...) and (1, 1, ...) are equivalent.
    downward closed); an intersection of cuts need not be a cut; 'Cauchy' and
    'convergent' agree in R but not in Q; N and Z do have the least-upper-bound
    property (a bounded set of integers has a maximum) but are not fields.

D1. Using only the Peano axioms and the recursive definitions a + 0 = a,
    S(n) = 0 because axiom (ii) says 0 is not a successor.
    Teacher explains: The numbers are NAMES: 1 = S(0), 2 = S(1), 3 = S(2),
    4 = S(3). Addition is defined by recursion on the SECOND argument, so we
    peel one S off the right each step:
       2 + 2 = 2 + S(1)      = S(2 + 1)
             = S(2 + S(0))   = S(S(2 + 0))
             = S(S(2))       = S(3) = 4
    = 2 is NOT a definition (the definition is a + 0 = a); it needs its own
    little induction (0 + 0 = 0; if 0 + b = b then 0 + S(b) = S(0 + b) = S(b)).
    Then
    The point of the construction: nothing about numbers is assumed; every fact
    comes from the axioms. Common mistakes: using 'a + 1 = S(a)' before proving
    it (it is a + S(0) = S(a + 0) = S(a), one line, but it must be said); using
    commutativity before it has been proved. Now you try: show 3 + 1 = 4 and

D12. In the Cauchy-sequence construction, prove (a) that ~ (x_n - y_n -> 0) is an
     equivalence relation, (b) that every Cauchy sequence is bounded, and use

        |x_n| <= max(|x_1|, |x_2|, ..., |x_{N-1}|, |x_N| + 1) = M
     (finitely many terms, then a band of width 2 around x_N).
     product sequence is itself Cauchy by the same splitting with m and n.
     two sequences are equivalent and name the same real. Common mistakes:
     thinking 0.999... is 'just less than 1' (there is no real strictly
     between them: their difference is smaller than every 10^-^n); forgetting
     boundedness in the product proof. Now you try: which real is the class of
     equivalent)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: build each system as a 'repair' of the previous one: Z repairs
  subtraction (pairs = debts), Q repairs division (pairs = fractions), R
  repairs gaps (cuts = left halves of the line, or Cauchy sequences = better
  and better approximations); always check an operation on classes with two
  different representatives before trusting it; draw the lattice of pairs
  (a, b) with the diagonals that form each integer; compute the Babylonian
  iterates by hand to feel a Cauchy sequence that has no rational limit.
  Harder: prove that any two complete ordered fields are isomorphic (map
  each rational to itself and extend by suprema); define multiplication of
  arbitrary cuts via signs and prove the distributive law; show the Cauchy and
  Dedekind constructions give isomorphic fields; prove that every ordered field
  with the least-upper-bound property is Archimedean, and give a non-Archimedean
  ordered field (rational functions R(x) ordered by leading coefficient, where
  x is 'infinitely large').

    L' (true only for continuous f); 'strict inequality passes to the limit'

TOPIC 9.6 - SEQUENCES AND SERIES OF REAL NUMBERS; CONVERGENCE TESTS

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
    with a_n > M for n >= N. Limit laws (sum, product, quotient), the ORDER law
  - MONOTONE CONVERGENCE THEOREM: a monotone bounded sequence converges (to
    and monotone by induction, THEN solve L = g(L). Examples:
  - SUBSEQUENCES: if a_n -> L every subsequence -> L (so two subsequences with
    different limits prove divergence). Every sequence has a MONOTONE
    subsequence; BOLZANO-WEIERSTRASS: every bounded sequence has a convergent
    subsequence. limsup a_n (liminf a_n) is the largest (smallest) subsequential
    H_2_n - H_n >= 1/2.
  - TESTS FOR a_n >= 0: COMPARISON (0 <= a_n <= b_n); LIMIT COMPARISON (a_n/b_n -> c,
    -> L, same conclusions. Ratio suits factorials and powers; root suits nth
    powers.
    series may be rearranged freely; a conditionally convergent one can be
    rearranged to any sum (RIEMANN REARRANGEMENT THEOREM).
    tests on series with terms of both signs without absolute values;
    'ratio = 1 so it diverges'; confusing the SEQUENCE of terms with the
    SEQUENCE of partial sums; forgetting that the Leibniz test needs b_n
    decreasing to 0.

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always write out the first five terms (of the sequence AND of the
  partial sums) before choosing a method; keep the test checklist in order:
  (1) nth-term test, (2) geometric / p-series / telescoping, (3) comparison or
  limit comparison with the dominant term, (4) ratio for factorials and
  powers, root for nth powers, (5) integral test or condensation for logs,
  (6) alternating series test, then check absolute convergence; say aloud
  'terms -> 0 is necessary, never sufficient'. Harder: prove Riemann's
  (so the root test is stronger); show e is irrational using

================================================================================
TOPIC 9.7 - TAYLOR AND MACLAURIN SERIES; POWER SERIES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
    ABSOLUTELY for |x - a| < R and DIVERGES for |x - a| > R. At the two end
    points x = a +/- R anything can happen, and each end point must be tested
    separately (p-series, alternating series test, nth-term test).
    test / CAUCHY-HADAMARD, 1/R = limsup |a_n|^(1/n), which always works. For
    series in x^2 or x^3 (gaps), apply the ratio test to the TERMS, not to the
    every |x| < |x_0| (compare with a geometric series). This is why the set of
    convergence is an interval centred at a.
  - Inside (a - R, a + R) a power series can be DIFFERENTIATED and INTEGRATED
    term by term, and the new series have the SAME radius R (end-point
    behaviour may change). The sum is infinitely differentiable there and
    MACLAURIN means a = 0. TAYLOR'S THEOREM (Lagrange remainder):
    the first omitted term.
  - The TAYLOR SERIES of f converges to f(x) exactly when R_n(x) -> 0. A smooth
    function need NOT equal its Taylor series: f(x) = e^(-1/x^2) (f(0) = 0) has
    every derivative 0 at 0, so its Maclaurin series is 0. Functions equal to
    their Taylor series near each point are called ANALYTIC.
    arctan x = x - x^3/3 + x^5/5 - ... (|x| <= 1); sinh x, cosh x (odd and even
    C(alpha, n) = alpha(alpha - 1)...(alpha - n + 1)/n!, valid for |x| < 1.
  - BUILD new series from old ones by substitution (e^(-x^2)), multiplication
    (e^x sin x), division (tan x = sin x/cos x), differentiation and
    integration; never by computing 10 derivatives by hand if avoidable.
  - USES: limits of 0/0 forms ((x - sin x)/x^3 -> 1/6), approximations with a
    guaranteed error, integrals with no elementary antiderivative
  - TRAPS: forgetting to test end points; using the ratio test on a series
    with missing powers; writing a Taylor series about a in powers of x
    instead of (x - a); assuming the Taylor series converges to f; treating
    the Lagrange c as a known number (it is only known to lie between a
    and x).

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Derive the Maclaurin series of e^x, sin x and cos x from the formula
    of x cos x, and check formally that e^(ix) = cos x + i sin x.
    Answer: e^x = 1 + x + x^2/2! + x^3/3! + ...; sin x = x - x^3/3! + x^5/5! - ...;
    x cos x = x - x^3/2! + x^5/4! - ...; e^(ix) = cos x + i sin x.
    Teacher explains: A Maclaurin series needs only the values of the
    derivatives at 0. Make a table:
       e^x      e^x      e^x      e^x      e^x           1, 1, 1, 1, 1, ...
       sin x   cos x   -sin x  -cos x  sin x        0, 1, 0, -1, 0, ...
       cos x   -sin x  -cos x  sin x   cos x        1, 0, -1, 0, 1, ...
    So a_n = 1/n! for e^x; for sin x only ODD powers survive with signs
    +, -, +, ...; for cos x only EVEN powers. Once we have a series we get
    others by SUBSTITUTION and MULTIPLICATION, not by differentiating again:
       e^(2x) = 1 + 2x + (2x)^2/2! + (2x)^3/3! + ... = 1 + 2x + 2x^2 + 4x^3/3 + ...
       x cos x = x(1 - x^2/2 + x^4/24 - ...) = x - x^3/2 + x^5/24 - ...
    Put x -> ix in e^x and group the real and imaginary terms (i^2 = -1, i^3 = -i,
    i^4 = 1):
       e^(ix) = 1 + ix - x^2/2! - ix^3/3! + x^4/4! + ix^5/5! - ...
              = (1 - x^2/2! + x^4/4! - ...) + i(x - x^3/3! + x^5/5! - ...)
    which is cos x + i sin x (Euler). Note sin is odd and cos is even, and the
    series show it: only odd, or only even, powers. Common mistakes: writing
    x^3/3 instead of x^3/3! = x^3/6; forgetting the alternating signs. Now you try:
    derive the Maclaurin series of cosh x = (e^x + e^(-x))/2.

D2. Find the Taylor polynomial of degree 4 of ln x about a = 1, and use it to
    estimate ln 1.1. Compare with the true value 0.0953102.
    Answer: P_4(x) = (x - 1) - (x - 1)^2/2 + (x - 1)^3/3 - (x - 1)^4/4;
    ln 1.1 ~ 0.0953083.
    Teacher explains: Differentiate and evaluate at a = 1:
       f(x) = ln x        f(1) = 0
    polynomial is in powers of (x - 1), NOT of x. At x = 1.1, x - 1 = 0.1:
       P_4(1.1) = 0.1 - 0.005 + 0.000333 - 0.000025 = 0.0953083
    The true value is 0.0953102, an error of about 2 x 10^-^6, which is less
    than the next term 0.1^5/5 = 2 x 10^-^6 (alternating series). The expansion
    is the familiar ln(1 + h) = h - h^2/2 + h^3/3 - ... with h = x - 1. Common
    mistakes: expanding about 0 (ln 0 does not exist); writing the terms as
    Now you try: the Taylor polynomial of degree 2 of sqrtx about 4, and the
    estimate of sqrt4.1. (2 + (x - 4)/4 - (x - 4)^2/64; 2.0248438)

    Teacher explains: THEOREM: inside the interval of convergence a power

D12. (a) Evaluate integral _0^1 e^(-x^2) dx correct to 3 decimal places using series.
     (b) Find the Taylor series of f(x) = 1/x about a = 2 and its interval of
     convergence; explain why R = 2.
     Teacher explains: (a) e^(-x^2) has no elementary antiderivative, but its
        integral _0^1 e^(-x^2) dx = integral _0^1 (1 - x^2 + x^4/2! - x^6/3! + ...) dx
                       = 1 - 1/3 + 1/10 - 1/42 + 1/216 - 1/1320 + 1/9360 - ...
     The series alternates with decreasing terms, so the error is less than
     the first omitted term. Adding up to -1/1320:
        1 - 0.333333 + 0.1 - 0.023810 + 0.004630 - 0.000758 = 0.746729
     with error less than 1/9360 < 0.00011, so the integral lies between
     0.74673 and 0.74684, and to 3 decimal places it is 0.747 (true value
     0.746824).
     (b) Write x = 2 + (x - 2) and use the geometric series:
     valid for |x - 2| < 2, i.e. 0 < x < 4; at x = 0 and x = 4 the terms have
     modulus 1/2 and do not tend to 0. The radius 2 is the DISTANCE FROM THE
     CENTRE 2 TO THE SINGULARITY at 0: a power series cannot converge across
     the point where f blows up. (Likewise 1/(1 + x^2) has R = 1 about 0
     because of the complex singularities +/-i, even though it is smooth on R.)
     Common mistakes in (a): rounding each term to 3 places before adding;
     stopping when the terms 'look small' without an error bound. Now you
     try: integral _0^1 sin(x^2) dx to 4 decimal places. (1/3 - 1/42 + 1/1320 - 1/75600
     = 0.31027 to 5 places, so 0.3103)

M12. Prove (proof sketches).
     a) (d/dx)e^x = e^x, using the series.
     b) (d/dx) sin x = cos x, using the series.
     d) If f is even, its Maclaurin series has only even powers.
     g) e^a e^b = e^(a+b), using the Cauchy product.
     h) e is irrational.
     i) The Maclaurin series of cos x converges to cos x for every x.
     k) The Maclaurin series of ln(1 + x) converges to ln(1 + x) at x = 1.
     l) A power series cannot converge at x = 3 and diverge at x = -2.
     Answers:
       c) Ratio of terms |x|/(n + 1) -> 0 < 1 for every fixed x.
       e) limsup |n a_n|^(1/n) = limsup |a_n|^(1/n) because n^(1/n) -> 1; the
          extra factor x^-^1 does not change convergence for x != 0.
          by x and let x -> 0 (continuity of power series) to get a_1 = b_1,
          and so on by induction.
       g) Both series converge absolutely, so the Cauchy product converges to
          the binomial theorem.
          equals 1/(q + 1) + 1/((q + 1)(q + 2)) + ... < 1/q <= 1,
          a contradiction.
       j) Differentiate term by term n times and put x = 0: every term with
          the remainder is at most integral _0^1 t^n dt = 1/(n + 1) -> 0.
       l) Convergence at 3 forces absolute convergence for |x| < 3 (Abel's
          lemma), including x = -2.

TEACHING TIPS
  the six standard series by heart and practise getting new ones by
  substitution only (e^(-x^2), 1/(1 + x^2), cos 3x); for R use the ratio test
  on the terms and then say aloud 'now the end points'; check a series
  numerically at a small x (x = 0.1) against a calculator. Harder: prove
  Abel's theorem on continuity at an end point and use it to justify
  ln 2 = 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - ...; show that the Taylor series of 1/(1 + x^2) about
  a = 1 has R = sqrt2 (distance to +/-i); derive Stirling-free bounds such as
  (n/e)^n < n! from e^n > n^n/n!; find the power series solution of
  short proof that pi is irrational as a research-style follow-up.

    Teacher explains: An improper integral is a LIMIT of ordinary integrals.
    In (a) the region under y = 1/x^2 has finite AREA although it is
    infinitely long; in (b) it does not. It is not enough for the integrand
    to tend to 0; it must tend to 0 FAST enough. 1/x^2 shrinks fast enough,
    1/x only just fails: the area from 1 to 10^n is n ln 10, which grows
    without bound, only slowly. Write the limit every time: the notation
    and calling it a number; concluding convergence from 1/x -> 0. Now you

     Teacher explains: First, CONVERGENCE: e^(-x^2) <= e^(-|x|) for |x| >= 1, so
     both halves converge; call the value I. There is no elementary
     antiderivative, so we use a famous trick: square it and pass to two
     dimensions.
     In polar coordinates x^2 + y^2 = r^2, dx dy = r dr dtheta:
     so I = sqrtpi (I > 0). The factor r from the Jacobian is exactly what makes
     the inner integral elementary. (Rigour: the integral over the square
     [-R, R]^2 lies between the integrals over the discs of radius R and
     Rsqrt2, which are pi(1 - e^(-R^2)) and pi(1 - e^(-2R^2)); both tend to pi.)
     SCALING: put x = u/sqrta:
        integral  e^(-ax^2) dx = (1/sqrta) integral  e^(-u^2) du = sqrt(pi/a)
     MOMENT: by parts with u = x, dv = x e^(-x^2) dx:
                          = 0 + (1/2)(sqrtpi/2) = sqrtpi/4
     This is why the normal density (1/sqrt(2pi)) e^(-x^2/2) has total area 1 and
     variance 1. Common mistake: dx dy = dr dtheta (forgetting the r). Now you

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A function f : R^n -> R (such as z = f(x, y)) has a GRAPH (a surface in R^3
    when n = 2) and LEVEL SETS f = c (level curves, contour lines; level
    path. Two paths with different limits prove that no limit exists;
    polar coordinates plus a squeeze (|f - L| <= g(r) -> 0) prove existence.
    equal there. Without continuity they can differ:
    partial and directional derivatives exist. Partials existing does NOT
    imply continuity (xy/(x^2 + y^2) at 0). If the partials are CONTINUOUS
    near the point (f is C^1), f is differentiable.
    m(dx/x) + n(dy/y).
  - CHAIN RULE: if z = f(x, y) with x = x(t), y = y(t), then
    u = v/|v|.
    (implicit function theorem).
    as x^2 - y^2, e^x sin y, ln(x^2 + y^2)); Euler: if f is homogeneous of degree n,
    limit on straight lines only (x^2y/(x^4 + y^2) -> 0 on every line but is 1/2
    on y = x^2); treating the other variable as a function when it is held

D1. Decide whether each limit exists as (x, y) -> (0, 0), and find it if it
    does: (a) xy/(x^2 + y^2), (b) x^2y/(x^2 + y^2), (c) (x^2 - y^2)/(x^2 + y^2),
    (d) sin(x^2 + y^2)/(x^2 + y^2).
    Answer: (a) does not exist. (b) 0. (c) does not exist. (d) 1.
    Teacher explains: In two variables (x, y) can approach (0, 0) along
    infinitely many paths, and the limit must be the same along all of them.
    To DISPROVE a limit, find two paths with different limits:
           m = 0 gives 0, m = 1 gives 1/2: NO limit
       (c) along y = 0: 1;  along x = 0: -1: NO limit
    To PROVE a limit, a few paths are never enough; bound |f - L| by
    something that depends only on r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2) and tends to 0. Polar
    coordinates x = r cos theta, y = r sin theta are convenient:
       (b) |x^2y/(x^2 + y^2)| = |r^3cos^2theta sin theta|/r^2 <= r  ->  0
    sin u/u -> 1, so the limit is 1. Common mistakes: 'along y = mx the limit
    is 0 for every m, so the limit is 0' (see D12, where the curve y = x^2
    gives a different answer); plugging in (0, 0) and writing 0/0 = 0. Now

D12. Let f(x, y) = x^2y/(x^4 + y^2) for (x, y) != (0, 0), f(0, 0) = 0. Show that
     Teacher explains: From the definition, with u = (a, b), a^2 + b^2 = 1:
        f(ta, tb)/t = t^3a^2b/(t(t^4a^4 + t^2b^2)) = a^2b/(t^2a^4 + b^2)
     If b != 0 this tends to a^2b/b^2 = a^2/b as t -> 0. If b = 0 then f(ta, 0) = 0

     so f has no limit at the origin: it is not continuous, hence not
     DIFFERENTIABILITY, not just the existence of all directional
     derivatives. Existence of all directional derivatives says nothing
     about approach along curves. Common mistake: concluding continuity from
     'the limit is 0 along every line'. Now you try: for f = xy/(x^2 + y^2)

M12. Prove (proof sketches).
     a) If f is differentiable at p, then f is continuous at p.
     f) f = xy/(x^2 + y^2), f(0, 0) = 0, has partial derivatives at 0 but is
        not continuous there.
     k) lim x^2y/(x^2 + y^2) = 0 as (x, y) -> (0, 0).
     Answers:
       b) f(a + h, b + k) - f(a, b) = [f(a + h, b + k) - f(a, b + k)] +
          tend to 0, which gives the o(sqrt(h^2 + k^2)) error.
       h) Differentiate f(tx, ty) = t^nf(x, y) with respect to t and put
          t = 1.
       j) Apply the one-variable product rule to each partial derivative.
       k) |x^2y/(x^2 + y^2)| <= |y| (since x^2 <= x^2 + y^2) -> 0.

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: say 'freeze the other variables' aloud before every partial
  derivative, and circle the frozen letters; draw the contour map of
  x^2 + 2y^2 with gradient arrows crossing the ellipses at right angles;
  always write u = v/|v| on its own line before a directional derivative;
  for the chain rule draw the tree and multiply along each branch; for
  limits, try y = 0, x = 0, y = mx and y = x^2 first, and switch to polar
  theorem in full; find all points where the tangent plane to z = x^3 - 3xy
  + y^3 is horizontal ((0, 0) and (1, 1)) as a bridge to optimisation;
  open set is constant; show that the steepest-descent paths of
  f = x^2 + 2y^2 are the curves y = Cx^2 (they are orthogonal to the ellipses);
  study the Jacobian matrix of a map R^2 -> R^2 as the multivariable
  derivative.

TOPIC 9.10 - MULTIPLE INTEGRALS; CHANGE OF VARIABLES; JACOBIANS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - DOUBLE INTEGRAL over a rectangle R = [a, b] x [c, d]: cut R into small
    rectangles of area delta A, pick a sample point in each and form the RIEMANN SUM
    continuous f (and for bounded f whose discontinuities lie on finitely many
    AREA of R.
    = integral _c^d (integral _a^b f dx) dy: an ITERATED integral, inner one first, the other
    variable held constant. If f(x, y) = g(x)h(y) on a rectangle the integral
    can disagree.
  - GENERAL REGIONS. Type I: D = {a <= x <= b, g_1(x) <= y <= g_2(x)}, so
    h_1(y) <= x <= h_2(y)}. Inner limits may depend on the outer variable; OUTER
    limits must be constants. Always SKETCH the region first.
  - REVERSING THE ORDER of integration: draw the region from the given limits,
    then describe the same region the other way. Used when the inner integral
    has no elementary antiderivative (e^{y^2}, sin y / y, sin(x^3), ...).
  - POLAR COORDINATES x = r cos theta, y = r sin theta: dA = r dr dtheta (never forget the
    extra r). Discs, annuli, sectors, cardioids and anything with x^2 + y^2 become
    easy. Area inside r = f(theta) is 1/2 integral  f(theta)^2 dtheta. The Gaussian integral
  - CHANGE OF VARIABLES: if T(u, v) = (x(u, v), y(u, v)) is a C^1 one-to-one map
    |J| is the factor by which T stretches small areas (volumes).
    reciprocal; no need to solve for x and y. Chain rule: J of a composite map
    is the product of the Jacobians.
  - Choose substitutions from the SHAPE of the region (lines x + y = const,
    INTEGRAND (a combination such as (x - y)/(x + y)).
    instead of |J|; outer limits depending on a variable; wrong limits after a

D10. State the change of variables formula for double integrals. Derive the
     where T is the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1).
     polar Jacobian is r; the integral is (sin 1)/2.
     Teacher explains: The Jacobian is the determinant of the matrix of
     partial derivatives:
                          | sin theta    r cos theta |
     Why the determinant: a tiny rectangle du x dv is mapped to (nearly) a
     parallelogram spanned by T_u du and T_v dv, whose area is
     |det(T_u, T_v)| du dv. For the triangle use u = x + y, v = x - y (the
     integrand is a function of these). The sides become:
        x + y = 1  ->  u = 1;   y = 0  ->  v = u;   x = 0  ->  v = -u
        | 1   1 |
     Common mistakes: using -2 or 2 instead of 1/2 (upside down); forgetting
     ((e - e^{-1})/4 = (sinh 1)/2)

  integral _0^1 integral _0^1 (x^2 - y^2)/(x^2 + y^2)^2 dy dx = pi/4 but the other order gives -pi/4, and
  explain why Fubini does not apply; show that integral _0^1integral _0^1 1/(1 - xy) dx dy = pi^2/6
  using u = (x + y)/2, v = (y - x)/2 (or by expanding a geometric series);
  compute the volume of the unit ball in R^n from integral  e^{-|x|^2} = pi^{n/2} and show
  = area x distance travelled by the centroid) and use it on a torus

================================================================================
TOPIC 9.11 - VECTOR CALCULUS: LINE INTEGRALS, SURFACE INTEGRALS, DIVERGENCE,
             CURL
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A VECTOR FIELD on a region of R^2 or R^3 assigns a vector F(x, y, z)
    = (P, Q, R) to each point (velocity of a fluid, a force, an electric
  - MEANING: div F at a point is the net outflow per unit volume (a SOURCE if
    positive, a SINK if negative; INCOMPRESSIBLE if div F = 0). curl F is
    twice the local angular velocity of the fluid; its component along a unit
    means curl F = 0. In the plane the 'scalar curl' is Q_x - P_y.
    div(r^n r) = (n + 3) r^n.
  - SCALAR LINE INTEGRAL along a curve C: r(t), a <= t <= b:
    density it is the MASS of a wire. It does NOT depend on the direction of
    travel or on the parametrisation.
    parametrisation but CHANGES SIGN when the orientation is reversed:
    closed curve.
    SIMPLY CONNECTED domain (no holes; e.g. all of R^3, a ball, a half-plane)
    circle. FIND f by integrating P in x, then fixing the 'constant' g(y, z)
    with Q and R.
    NORMAL N = r_u x r_v; area element dS = |r_u x r_v| du dv; AREA
    (upward) and dS = sqrt(1 + g_x^2 + g_y^2) dA. Sphere of radius a:
    outward unit normal n = r/a.
    of a shell, averages, centroids). FLUX of F through an ORIENTED surface:
    whether r_u x r_v points the chosen way (for closed surfaces: OUTWARD).
    Flux is the volume of fluid crossing S per unit time.
    to substitute the curve into F before integrating; a zero curl does not
    make F conservative on a region with a hole; N = r_u x r_v may point the
    wrong way (then change the sign); on a closed surface add the flux through
    EVERY piece (side, top, bottom).

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Find the divergence and curl of F = (xy, yz, zx) and of
    G = (x^2y, -2xz, 2yz). Verify that div(curl G) = 0.
    Answer: div F = x + y + z, curl F = (-y, -z, -x); div G = 2y(x + 1),
    curl G = (2x + 2z, 0, -x^2 - 2z), and div(curl G) = 2 + 0 - 2 = 0.
    Teacher explains: Divergence: differentiate each component with respect to
    ITS OWN variable and add:
    Curl: expand the determinant along the top row:
               |  i      j      k   |
               |  xy     yz     zx  |
             = i(0 - y) - j(z - 0) + k(0 - x) = (-y, -z, -x)
    For G: div G = 2xy + 0 + 2y = 2y(x + 1), and
              = (2z + 2x, 0 - 0, -2z - x^2)
    Common mistakes: forgetting the minus sign on the j-component; writing
    div F as a vector. Div eats a vector and gives a scalar; curl eats a
    vector and gives a vector. Now you try: div and curl of (yz, xz, xy).

    r = (x, y, z) and r = |r| (r != 0).
    Answer: Proofs below; each rests on the equality of mixed partial
    derivatives (Clairaut/Schwarz) or on the product rule.
    because mixed partials of a C^2 function are equal. (b) With F = (P, Q, R):
                  = R_yx - Q_zx + P_zy - R_xy + Q_xz - P_yz = 0
    (the six terms cancel in pairs). (c) Product rule in each component:
    = n r^n^-^2 r, and div r = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3:
    Special case n = -3: the inverse-square field r/r^3 has ZERO divergence
    away from O. Common mistake: treating r as a constant when

    writing ds = dt (you would get 7/2 in (a)). Now you try: integral _C y ds along
    the upper half of the unit circle. (2)

           integral _0^1 (t^2 + t) dt = 1/3 + 1/2 = 5/6

    PATH-DEPENDENT, so F is not a gradient field (indeed P_y = 2y != 1 = Q_x).
    Going back along the line reverses the orientation, which flips the sign:
    Now you try: integral _C y dx - x dy along the upper unit semicircle from (1, 0)

D9. Find the upward flux of F = (y, x, z) through the part of the paraboloid
    z = 4 - x^2 - y^2 above the xy-plane.
    Answer: 8pi.
    Teacher explains: For a graph z = g(x, y) oriented UPWARD,
    r(x, y) = (x, y, g), r_x x r_y = (-g_x, -g_y, 1), whose z-component is
    The surface lies over the disc x^2 + y^2 <= 4; in polars:
       flux = integral _0^{2pi} integral _0^2 (4r^2 cos theta sin theta + 4 - r^2) r dr dtheta
    The 4xy term integrates to 0 (integral _0^{2pi} cos theta sin theta dtheta = 0), leaving
       2pi integral _0^2 (4r - r^3) dr = 2pi (8 - 4) = 8pi
    The unnormalised N is used on purpose: n dS = (N/|N|)(|N| dA) = N dA, so
    no square root appears in a flux integral. Common mistake: using the unit

D10. Compute the outward flux of F = (x, y, z) through the closed surface of
     the solid cylinder x^2 + y^2 <= 1, 0 <= z <= 2 by adding the flux through the
     Teacher explains: A closed surface is the union of its pieces; each needs
     its own outward normal.

              flux = 0

     source strength inside. Common mistakes: forgetting the bottom and top;

     surface of the cube [0, 1]^3. (3: only the faces x = 1, y = 1, z = 1
     contribute, 1 each)

     F = r/r^3 has div F = 0 for r != 0, yet its outward flux through every
     sphere x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = a^2 is 4pi. Explain.
     Answer: (a) v = (bz - cy, cx - az, ay - bx), div v = 0, curl v
     = (2a, 2b, 2c). (b) div F = 0 by D2 (n = -3); the flux is 4pi for every
     a because F has a point source at O, where F is not defined.
     Teacher explains: (a) Each component of v has no dependence on its own
     variable, so div v = 0 (a rigid rotation neither compresses nor expands).
     This is why curl measures rotation: half the curl is the angular velocity.
     (b) On the sphere of radius a, n = r/a and F = r/a^3, so
     The flux is the same through every sphere: no source between two spheres
     (div F = 0 there), all of it at the origin, a 'point charge' of strength
     4pi. This is Gauss's law for gravity and electrostatics. Common mistake:
     concluding 'div F = 0 so the flux is 0'; that needs F to be smooth
     everywhere inside. Now you try: the outward flux of r through the sphere
     of radius a. (4pia^3 = 3 x volume)

================================================================================
TOPIC 9.12 - GREEN'S, STOKES' AND GAUSS (DIVERGENCE) THEOREMS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - GREEN'S THEOREM: let D be a bounded region in the plane whose boundary C
    is a piecewise smooth simple closed curve oriented POSITIVELY
    (anticlockwise: the region is on the LEFT as you walk), and let P, Q be
    C^1 on an open set containing D. Then
    Circulation around the edge = total 'scalar curl' inside.
  - FLUX (NORMAL) FORM of Green: with outward unit normal n on C,
    the outer one anticlockwise and each inner one CLOCKWISE (region always on
    the left). Consequence: if Q_x = P_y in the region between two curves,
    the integrals around the two curves (both anticlockwise) are EQUAL; e.g.
    encloses O, and 0 around every curve that does not.
  - STOKES' THEOREM: S an oriented piecewise smooth surface with boundary
    curve C, oriented by the RIGHT-HAND RULE (thumb along n, fingers along C;
    walking along C with head along n, S is on your left); F C^1. Then
    Green's theorem is the special case of a flat S in the xy-plane, n = k.
    a hard surface may be replaced by an easy one (a flat disc) with the same
  - GAUSS / DIVERGENCE THEOREM: E a bounded solid whose boundary S is a
    closed piecewise smooth surface with OUTWARD normal n, F C^1 on an open
    set containing E. Then
    Total outflow through the skin = total source strength inside. For a
    solid between two closed surfaces, the inner one gets the normal pointing
    INTO the hole (away from E).
  - TRICKS: (1) turn a hard line integral into an easy double integral and
    vice versa; (2) CLOSE an open surface with a disc, use Gauss, and subtract
    the disc's flux; (3) cut out a small circle or sphere around a
    and 0 if O is outside.
    'the integral of a derivative over a region = the integral of the
  - Traps: wrong orientation (sign error); applying the theorem when F has a
    singularity inside the region (e.g. at O); using Gauss on a surface that
    is not closed; forgetting the right-hand rule in Stokes; mixing up
    Q_x - P_y with P_y - Q_x.

D1. Verify Green's theorem for P = xy, Q = x^2 on the unit square
    D = [0, 1] x [0, 1], computing both sides.

    Line integral: go anticlockwise round the four sides.
       C_1 bottom  y = 0, x: 0 -> 1   dy = 0,  P = 0:        integral  = 0
       C_2 right   x = 1, y: 0 -> 1   dx = 0,  Q = 1:        integral _0^1 1 dy = 1
       C_3 top     y = 1, x: 1 -> 0   dy = 0,  P = x:        integral _1^0 x dx = -1/2
       C_4 left    x = 0, y: 1 -> 0   dx = 0,  Q = 0:        integral  = 0
    Note on C_3 the limits run from 1 to 0 because we walk leftwards. On each
    side one of dx, dy is zero, which kills a term. Common mistakes: going

D3. Use a line integral to find the area of (a) the ellipse x = a cos t,
    y = b sin t; (b) the astroid x = cos^3t, y = sin^3t; (c) the quadrilateral
    with vertices (0, 0), (3, 0), (4, 2), (1, 3).
    Answer: (a) piab; (b) 3pi/8; (c) 8.
    Teacher explains: Take P = -y/2, Q = x/2 in Green: Q_x - P_y = 1, so
       (a) x dy - y dx = ab cos^2t dt + ab sin^2t dt = ab dt
           area = 1/2 integral _0^{2pi} ab dt = piab
       (b) dx = -3cos^2t sin t dt, dy = 3 sin^2t cos t dt
           x dy - y dx = 3 sin^2t cos^4t + 3 sin^4t cos^2t = 3 sin^2t cos^2t
           area = (3/2) integral _0^{2pi} sin^2t cos^2t dt = (3/2)(pi/4) = 3pi/8
       (c) On a segment from (x_1, y_1) to (x_2, y_2), integral  (x dy - y dx)
           = x_1y_2 - x_2y_1. Add round the polygon (SHOELACE):
           area = 1/2 (0 + 6 + 10 + 0) = 8
    This is how a PLANIMETER measures area by tracing the boundary. Common
    mistake: vertices listed clockwise give a negative sum; take the absolute
    value. Now you try: area under one arch of the cycloid

D4. Prove Green's theorem for a region D that is both of type I and type II.

    y = g_1(x), x from a to b; the top C_3 is y = g_2(x) traversed from b to a;
    the vertical sides (if any) have dx = 0.
    Similarly, writing D = {c <= y <= d, h_1(y) <= x <= h_2(y)}, the right curve is
    such pieces; the integrals along the cuts are traversed twice in opposite
    directions and cancel. The same cancellation trick proves Green for
    regions with holes. Common mistake: forgetting the sign that comes from
    traversing the top curve right to left. Now you try: why do the vertical
