WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - COMPACT: every OPEN COVER of X has a FINITE SUBCOVER. Equivalently
    (FINITE INTERSECTION PROPERTY): every family of closed sets in which any
    finitely many members meet has non-empty total intersection. A subset K
    is compact when it is compact as a subspace (covers by open sets of X
    space are compact; (0, 1), R, Z, an infinite discrete space are not.
  - BASIC THEOREMS: a CLOSED subset of a compact space is compact; a compact
    subset of a HAUSDORFF space is closed; the continuous image of a compact
    space is compact; hence the EXTREME VALUE THEOREM (a continuous
    BIJECTION from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a HOMEOMORPHISM.
    compact metric spaces are UNIFORMLY continuous.
    compact. TYCHONOFF'S THEOREM: an ARBITRARY product of compact spaces is
    compact in the PRODUCT topology (it is equivalent to the axiom of
    choice; it fails for the box topology). Examples: the Cantor space
    {0, 1}^N, the Hilbert cube [0, 1]^N, tori.
  - LOCALLY COMPACT Hausdorff spaces have a ONE-POINT COMPACTIFICATION
  - CONNECTED: X is not the union of two disjoint non-empty open sets
    map X -> {0, 1} (discrete) is constant. The connected subsets of R are
    exactly the INTERVALS. Continuous images of connected spaces are
  - BUILDING connected sets: a union of connected sets with a common point
    finite and arbitrary products of connected spaces are connected.
    COMPONENTS (maximal connected subsets) partition X into closed sets. Q
    and the Cantor set are TOTALLY DISCONNECTED (components are points).
  - PATH-CONNECTED (any two points joined by a continuous path
    path-connected. An OPEN connected subset of R^n is path-connected.
    Connectedness invariants: number of components, CUT POINTS (R - {p} is
  - SEPARATION AXIOMS: T0 (points are topologically distinguishable); T1
    (a point and a closed set not containing it have disjoint
    neighbourhoods); NORMAL (two disjoint closed sets have disjoint
    neighbourhoods). T3 = T1 + regular, T4 = T1 + normal, and
    continuous f : X -> [0, 1] with f = 0 on A and f = 1 on B. In a metric
    space f(x) = d(x, A)/(d(x, A) + d(x, B)). TIETZE EXTENSION: on a normal
    space every continuous f : A -> [a, b] (or R) on a closed set A extends
    to X. URYSOHN METRISATION: a second countable T3 space is metrisable.

D12. State Urysohn's lemma and the Tietze extension theorem. For A = {0} and
     x = 1, 3, -3. Sketch the proof of Urysohn's lemma for a normal space,
     and state the Urysohn metrisation theorem.
     Answer: f(x) = d(x, A)/(d(x, A) + d(x, B)) = |x|/(|x| + d(x, B)):
     f(1) = 1/2, f(3) = 1, f(-3) = 3/8.
     continuous f : X -> [0, 1] with f|A = 0, f|B = 1. (Conversely such an f
     gives the disjoint open sets f^-^1[0, 1/2) and f^-^1(1/2, 1], so this
     CHARACTERISES normality.) In a metric space the formula works because
     the denominator is never 0 (a point cannot be at distance 0 from both
     closed disjoint sets). Here d(x, A) = |x| and
     d(x, B) = max(2 - x, 0):
        x = 1:   1/(1 + 1) = 1/2
        x = -3:  3/(3 + 5) = 3/8
     TIETZE: on normal X, every continuous f : A -> [a, b] on a closed A
     extends to a continuous F : X -> [a, b] (also for R-valued f). On R this
     is just 'join the dots': f(0) = 1, f(1) = -1, f(3) = 2 on A = {0, 1, 3}
     matters: sin(1/x) on (0, 1] has no continuous extension to [0, 1].
     URYSOHN METRISATION: a second countable T3 space is metrisable (it
     embeds in the Hilbert cube via countably many Urysohn functions).
     Common mistakes: using Urysohn in a space that is not normal; forgetting
     that the sets must be disjoint and CLOSED. Now you try: find the Urysohn
     function for A = x-axis, B = {y = 2} in R^2 and evaluate it at (5, 1/2).
     (f = |y|/(|y| + |y - 2|); f(5, 1/2) = (1/2)/2 = 1/4)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: drill the two directions separately - to show NOT compact,
  build one bad cover (usually growing intervals or balls); to show compact,
  quote a theorem (closed and bounded in R^n, closed in compact, image of
  compact, Tychonoff). For connectedness use the 'continuous map to {0, 1}'
  test and the fact that connected pieces never straddle a separation. Keep a
  prove the Lebesgue number lemma via sequential compactness; show that
  Alexander subbase lemma; show the Cantor set is homeomorphic to {0, 1}^N
  and that every compact metric space is a continuous image of it; prove
  Urysohn's lemma in full and deduce Tietze by successive approximation with
  Jones' lemma (a separable normal space has no closed discrete subset of

    between coordinate curves) and AREA dA = sqrt(EG - F^2) du dv. A map that

    k_n = II/I. SHAPE OPERATOR (Weingarten map) S = -dn has matrix

    H = (k_1 + k_2)/2 = (eG - 2fF + gE)/(2(EG - F^2)). Points: ELLIPTIC K > 0,
    HYPERBOLIC K < 0, PARABOLIC K = 0 but II != 0, PLANAR II = 0; UMBILIC
    K = (rt - s^2)/(1 + p^2 + q^2)^2, H = ((1 + q^2)r - 2pqs + (1 + p^2)t)/
    (2(1 + p^2 + q^2)^(3/2)). MINIMAL surfaces have H = 0.
  - STANDARD VALUES: plane K = H = 0; sphere of radius R: K = 1/R^2, |H| = 1/R
    (all points umbilic); cylinder of radius R: K = 0, |H| = 1/(2R); torus
    ((R + r cos v) cos u, (R + r cos v) sin u, r sin v):
    K = cos v/(r(R + r cos v)); catenoid K = -1/cosh^4v, H = 0; helicoid
    (v cos u, v sin u, cu) K = -c^2/(c^2 + v^2)^2, H = 0; pseudosphere K = -1.
  - THEOREMA EGREGIUM (Gauss): K depends only on E, F, G and their
    derivatives, so it is preserved by ISOMETRIES (bending without
    stretching). For F = 0: K = -(1/(2sqrt(EG)))[(E_v/sqrt(EG))_v + (G_u/sqrt(EG))_u];
    for I = du^2 + G dv^2: K = -(sqrtG)_uu/sqrtG; for I = lambda(du^2 + dv^2):
    K = -delta (ln lambda)/(2lambda). Hence no map of a sphere to a plane preserves
    distances, but paper can be rolled into a cylinder or cone (K = 0).
  - GEODESICS and GAUSS-BONNET: the curvature vector of a curve on a surface
    GAUSS-BONNET for a region D bounded by a piecewise smooth simple closed
    = 2 - 2g (genus g): sphere 4pi, torus 0.

D8. Define the second fundamental form, normal curvature and shape operator.
    For the cylinder x = (R cos u, R sin u, v) with inward normal compute II,
    the principal curvatures, K and H, and the normal curvature in the
    direction making angle theta with the circle. Do the same for the sphere of
    radius R, and prove Euler's formula.
    Answer: Cylinder: II = R du^2, k_1 = 1/R, k_2 = 0, K = 0, H = 1/(2R),
    k_n = cos^2theta/R. Sphere: k_n = 1/R in every direction, K = 1/R^2, H = 1/R.
    component along the surface normal n; that component is the NORMAL
       x_u = (-R sin u, R cos u, 0), x_v = (0, 0, 1), n = (-cos u, -sin u, 0)
       x_uu = (-R cos u, -R sin u, 0), x_uv = x_vv = 0
       E = R^2, F = 0, G = 1;  e = R, f = 0, g = 0
    Shape operator [[E, F], [F, G]]^-^1[[e, f], [f, g]] = [[1/R, 0], [0, 0]], so
    k_1 = 1/R (around the circle), k_2 = 0 (along the ruling),
    K = 0, H = 1/(2R). A unit direction at angle theta to the circle is
    (du, dv) = (cos theta/R, sin theta), giving k_n = R cos^2theta/R^2 = cos^2theta/R. EULER'S
    FORMULA in general: the shape operator is self-adjoint with respect to
    I, so it has orthonormal eigenvectors e_1, e_2 with eigenvalues k_1, k_2;
    for w = cos theta e_1 + sin theta e_2, k_n(w) = II(w, w) = k_1cos^2theta + k_2sin^2theta. So k_1,
    k_2 are the max and min of k_n. Sphere (inward normal): n = -x/R gives
    II = I/R, so k_n = 1/R for every direction: every point is UMBILIC,
    K = 1/R^2, H = 1/R. Common mistakes: sign of II depends on the choice of
    n (K does not); computing e with x_u instead of x_uu. Now you try: on the
    cylinder of radius 2, what is the normal curvature at 60 degrees to the
    circle? (cos^260 degrees/2 = 1/8)

    Answer: z = x^2 + y^2 at (1, 0): K = 4/25, H = 6sqrt5/25, k = 2sqrt5/25 and 2sqrt5/5.
    z = xy at (1, 1): K = -1/9, H = -sqrt3/9 (upward normal). Origin: elliptic

    Teacher explains: With x = (u, v, h(u, v)) and p = h_u, q = h_v, r = h_uu,

    At a critical point (p = q = 0) the formulas reduce to the Hessian:

D10. For the torus x(u, v) = ((R + r cos v) cos u, (R + r cos v) sin u,

     Teacher explains:

     the centre of the tube). Then
        x_uu = -(R + r cos v)(cos u, sin u, 0)    e = (R + r cos v) cos v

     and H = (eG + gE)/(2EG) = (R + 2r cos v)/(2r(R + r cos v)). Outer
     equator v = 0: K = 1/(r(R + r)) > 0 (dome-like); inner equator v = pi:

D11. State the Theorema Egregium and explain why it is 'remarkable'. Using
     the formula for orthogonal coordinates compute K for: (a) the sphere
     (c) the catenoid I = cosh^2v (du^2 + dv^2). Deduce that no map from a
     region of the sphere to the plane preserves distances, and that the
     catenoid and helicoid can be locally isometric.
     Answer: (a) 1/R^2; (b) -1; (c) -1/cosh^4v.
     Teacher explains: K was defined with the normal n, i.e. by how the
     surface sits in space. Gauss proved (via the Gauss equations, which
     express x_uu, x_uv, x_vv in terms of the Christoffel symbols of I and the
     coefficients of II, and the compatibility (x_uu)_v = (x_uv)_u) that
        eg - f^2 = (a formula in E, F, G and their first and second
                  derivatives only)   (BRIOSCHI's formula).
     So K is INTRINSIC: an ant measuring lengths on the surface can compute
     it. For F = 0:
        K = -(1/(2sqrt(EG)))[(E_v/sqrt(EG))_v + (G_u/sqrt(EG))_u].
     sqrtG = R sin(u/R), K = 1/R^2.) (b) Conformal lambda = 1/y^2: K = -delta (ln lambda)/(2lambda)
     ln lambda = 2 ln cosh v, delta  = 2 sech^2v, K = -2 sech^2v/(2 cosh^2v)
     = -1/cosh^4v. Consequences: an isometry preserves K; the sphere has
     K = 1/R^2 != 0 = K(plane), so every flat map of the Earth distorts
     distances. The catenoid and helicoid (c = 1) have the same K at
     corresponding points and indeed there is a local isometry: the helicoid
     can be bent into the catenoid. Equal K alone is not always enough, but
     plane' (a cylinder is curved in space but intrinsically flat); mixing
     up E and G in the formula. Now you try: K for I = du^2 + e^(2u) dv^2.

TEACHING TIPS
  first in a neat column, then plug into the formulas; check every cross
  product with a dot product (the result must be perpendicular to both
  the helix, the sphere and the cylinder, where the answers are known. Draw
  the normal and ask 'which way does the surface bend?' to get signs right.
  Harder: prove that a curve with all normal lines through a fixed point is
  a circle; prove that a curve on a sphere satisfies
  Theorema Egregium via the Christoffel symbols; show that a compact surface
  in R^3 has an elliptic point; prove Gauss-Bonnet for a geodesic triangle
  using geodesic polar coordinates (K = -(sqrtG)_rr/sqrtG); and use it to show
  that on a surface with K < 0 two geodesics from a point cannot meet again
  bounding a disc.

================================================================================
TOPIC 10.28 - INTRODUCTION TO ALGEBRAIC TOPOLOGY: HOMOTOPY, FUNDAMENTAL
GROUP, COVERING SPACES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
    a continuous H : X x [0, 1] -> Y with H(x, 0) = f(x), H(x, 1) = g(x). It
    is an equivalence relation. Into a CONVEX set any two maps are homotopic
    by the STRAIGHT-LINE homotopy H = (1 - t)f + tg. f is NULL-HOMOTOPIC if
    it is homotopic to a constant. A map S^1 -> S^1 that is not onto is
    null-homotopic.
    homotopy from id_X to a retraction r : X -> A fixing A. CONTRACTIBLE
    each at double speed: f(2s) for s <= 1/2, g(2s - 1) for s >= 1/2), INVERSE
  - FUNDAMENTAL GROUP pi_1(X, x_0) = path-homotopy classes of LOOPS at x_0 with
    group is independent of the base point up to isomorphism. SIMPLY
    connected (not conversely: S^2).
    and HOMOTOPY EQUIVALENCES induce isomorphisms. If A is a RETRACT of X
    open EVENLY COVERED neighbourhood U: p^-^1(U) is a disjoint union of open
    SHEETS each mapped homeomorphically onto U. Fibres have constant size
    (the number of SHEETS) over a connected base. Examples: R -> S^1,
    S^n -> RP^n (2 sheets); exp : C -> C - {0}. A surjective local
    homeomorphism need NOT be a covering ((0, 3) -> S^1).
    homotopies lift, so path-homotopic paths have lifts with the same
    endpoint. LIFTING CRITERION: f : (Y, y_0) -> (B, b_0) with Y connected and
    Consequences: no RETRACTION D^2 -> S^1; BROUWER'S fixed point theorem in
    dimension 2; the FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF ALGEBRA; Borsuk-Ulam for S^2.
    the FREE PRODUCT. Wedge of n circles: free group F_n; a graph with V
    vertices and E edges: F_(E - V + 1); attaching a 2-cell along a loop w
  - CLASSIFICATION: p_* : pi_1(E, e_0) -> pi_1(B, b_0) is INJECTIVE and the number of
    sheets equals the INDEX [pi_1(B) : p_*pi_1(E)] (E connected). For nice B,
    4-valent tree -> figure eight (F_2).

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw everything - homotopies as films, loops as strings on a
  surface, lifts as paths climbing the helix above the circle. Compute every
  degree by following the lift ('how many times does the string go
  around?'). Keep a table of pi_1 for the standard spaces and use homotopy
  equivalences to reduce new spaces to it (deformation retract first, then
  products or van Kampen). For covers, always check 'evenly covered' with a
  picture of the sheets. Harder: prove that the universal cover of a graph
  is a tree and deduce the Nielsen-Schreier theorem with the rank formula
  n(k - 1) + 1; prove Borsuk-Ulam for S^2 (an odd map S^1 -> S^1 has odd degree)
  and deduce the ham-sandwich theorem; classify all covers of T^2
  (subgroups of Z^2: sigma(n) of index n); compute pi_1 of the complement of the

    with [x : y : z] = [lambdax : lambday : lambdaz] for every lambda != 0. The affine point (x, y)
    is [x : y : 1]; the points [x : y : 0] are POINTS AT INFINITY (one for each
    direction) and together form the LINE AT INFINITY z = 0. RP^n is defined in

  - PRINCIPLE OF DUALITY: interchanging 'point' and 'line', 'lies on' and

    so the group is PGL(n + 1, R) of dimension n^2 + 2n. FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM:
    any n + 2 points in GENERAL POSITION (no n + 1 in a hyperplane) can be sent
    to any other such n + 2 points by exactly one projective transformation.
  - CROSS-RATIO of four points on a line: (a, b; c, d) =
    PROJECTIVELY INVARIANT; distances, ratios and midpoints are not. Under the
    24 permutations it takes the six values lambda, 1/lambda, 1 - lambda, 1/(1 - lambda),
    (lambda - 1)/lambda, lambda/(lambda - 1). (a, b; c, d) = -1 means c, d are HARMONIC CONJUGATES
    with respect to a, b; the midpoint of ab and the point at infinity are
    harmonic.

    from a line (and conversely). PAPPUS: if A, B, C lie on one line and

    det C != 0. The TANGENT at a point p of the conic is the line Cp; for any p

    affine type is decided by the line at infinity: ELLIPSE (0 real points at

    HYPERBOLA (2, B^2 - 4AC > 0).

    NEUTRAL geometry (no parallel axiom) gives angle sum <= pi
    (Saccheri-Legendre). Three constant-curvature geometries: EUCLIDEAN (K = 0,
    one parallel, angle sum pi), HYPERBOLIC (K = -1, infinitely many parallels,
    angle sum < pi), ELLIPTIC/SPHERICAL (K = +1, no parallels, angle sum > pi).

    circumference 2pi sin r, area 2pi(1 - cos r). ELLIPTIC geometry = sphere with

    infinity in the direction (2, -1). (c) [1 : 2 : 1], i.e. (1, 2).

                               = (-4, 2, 0) ~ [2 : -1 : 0]

D7. Explain Euclid's parallel postulate, Playfair's axiom and some statements
    equivalent to it, the Saccheri-Legendre theorem, and how models show the
    postulate is independent. Compare the three classical geometries.
    Answer: See the table and explanation below.
    Teacher explains: Euclid's fifth postulate: if a line crossing two lines
    makes interior angles on one side summing to less than two right angles,
    the two lines meet on that side. With the other axioms (incidence,
    betweenness, congruence, continuity = NEUTRAL geometry) it is equivalent
    to each of:
       the angle sum of every (or of one) triangle is pi;
       a rectangle exists; similar non-congruent triangles exist;
       Pythagoras' theorem; parallel lines are equidistant.
    SACCHERI-LEGENDRE: in neutral geometry every triangle has angle sum <= pi.
    (Idea: repeatedly replace the triangle by one with the same angle sum and
    exterior angle theorem.) For 2000 years people tried to prove the fifth
    postulate from the others. Gauss, Bolyai and Lobachevsky found a
    MODELS of it inside Euclidean geometry. A model makes all the neutral
    axioms true and the parallel postulate false, so if Euclidean geometry is
    consistent, so is hyperbolic geometry, and the postulate cannot be a
    theorem.
                      Euclidean     hyperbolic         elliptic
       curvature K    0             -1                 +1
       parallels      exactly 1     infinitely many    none
       angle sum      = pi           < pi                > pi
       triangle area  any           pi - sum  < pi          sum  - pi (sum  = angle sum)
       circumference  2pir           2pi sinh r          2pi sin r
    (Elliptic geometry also drops the axiom that lines are infinite, since
    great circles are closed.) Common mistakes: saying 'hyperbolic geometry
    has no parallels' (it has too many); thinking the sphere satisfies all
    neutral axioms (two points need not determine a unique great circle unless
    antipodes are identified). Now you try: in hyperbolic geometry, can the
    angle sum of a quadrilateral be 2pi? (No: cut it into two triangles, each
    < pi, so the sum < 2pi - no rectangles.)

================================================================================
TOPIC 10.31 - FRACTALS AND DIMENSION (INTRODUCTION)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A FRACTAL is a set with detail at every scale: typically SELF-SIMILAR
    (made of scaled copies of itself), too irregular for classical geometry,
    defined by a simple recursive rule, and with a FRACTAL DIMENSION larger
    than its topological dimension (often not an integer). Not every fractal
    is exactly self-similar.
    the open middle third of each interval of C_n. C_n has 2^n intervals of
    length 3^-^n, total length (2/3)^n -> 0; the removed lengths add up to 1. C is
    it is compact, uncountable, PERFECT, TOTALLY DISCONNECTED, NOWHERE DENSE,
    of LEBESGUE MEASURE 0, and contains points like 1/4 = 0.0202..._3 that are
    not endpoints. The CANTOR FUNCTION (devil's staircase) is continuous,
    increasing, constant on each removed interval, maps C onto [0, 1].
  - KOCH CURVE: replace the middle third of each segment by two sides of an
    equilateral triangle. After n steps: 4^n segments of length 3^-^n, length
    (8/5)A_0 (A_0 = area of the starting triangle). The limit curve is
    continuous and nowhere differentiable.
  - SIERPINSKI TRIANGLE (3 copies, ratio 1/2), SIERPINSKI CARPET (8, 1/3),
    MENGER SPONGE (20, 1/3), VICSEK fractal (5, 1/3), CANTOR DUST C x C
    (4, 1/3): all have zero area/volume in their ambient space.
  - SIMILARITY DIMENSION: a set made of N copies of itself scaled by r has
    Cantor ln 2/ln 3 ~ 0.6309, Koch ln 4/ln 3 ~ 1.2619, Sierpinski
    ln 3/ln 2 ~ 1.5850, carpet ln 8/ln 3 ~ 1.8928, sponge ln 20/ln 3 ~ 2.7268.
    one value, the HAUSDORFF DIMENSION dim_H F. H^0 counts points, H^1 is length
    do not increase it and BI-LIPSCHITZ maps preserve it; open sets of R^n have
    dimension n, smooth curves 1, smooth surfaces 2. Always
    dim_T F <= dim_H F <= lower dim_B F <= upper dim_B F (dim_T = topological).
    For self-similar sets with the OPEN SET CONDITION (pieces do not overlap
    too much) all these equal the similarity dimension.
  - ITERATED FUNCTION SYSTEMS (IFS): contractions f_1, ..., f_m of a complete
    contraction of the compact sets in the HAUSDORFF METRIC
    fixed point theorem there is a unique non-empty compact ATTRACTOR K with
    F(K) = K, and F^n(A) -> K from any start A, with d_H(F^n(A), K)
    <= r^n d_H(A, K). The CHAOS GAME draws K by random iteration.
  - JULIA and MANDELBROT sets for f_c(z) = z^2 + c: the FILLED JULIA SET K_c =
  - The MAIN CARDIOID of M (attracting fixed point, |2z| < 1) is
    c = mu/2 - mu^2/4, |mu| < 1; the PERIOD-2 BULB (attracting 2-cycle) is the disc
    |c + 1| < 1/4. Period doubling along R accumulates at the Feigenbaum point
    c ~ -1.4012.
  - MEASURING dimension in practice: log-log plots of box counts, of measured

D1. Construct the Cantor set C. Show the removed intervals have total length 1,
    that C consists of the numbers with a ternary expansion using only 0 and 2,
    |C| = |R|; 1/4 = 0.020202..._3.
    3^-^n, so the total removed is
    So C has length 0, yet it is far from empty. TERNARY picture: removing
    (1/3, 2/3) removes exactly the numbers whose first ternary digit must be
    1; removing the middle thirds at step n removes those whose n-th digit
    must be 1. (Endpoints have two expansions: 1/3 = 0.1_3 = 0.0222..._3 - use
    the one without 1s.) Hence
    [0, 1] (every binary sequence occurs), so C is UNCOUNTABLE - as big as R.
    For 1/4: multiply by 3 repeatedly and take integer parts:
       1/4 -> 3/4 (digit 0) -> 9/4 = 2 + 1/4 (digit 2) -> repeat
    in constant 0s or 2s, so 1/4 is not one: C contains far more than the
    endpoints (which are only countably many). Common mistakes: thinking C
    a 1. Now you try: is 1/10 in C? (Yes: 1/10 = 0.00220022..._3)

D2. Prove that C is compact, nowhere dense, perfect and totally disconnected.
    Define the Cantor function F and compute F(1/4), F(1/10), F(1/2) and
    F(2/9). Why is F remarkable?
    Answer: F(1/4) = 1/3, F(1/10) = 1/5, F(1/2) = 1/2, F(2/9) = 1/4. F is
    (a set of full measure).
    choose n with 3^-^n < y - x; x and y lie in different intervals of C_n, and a
    removed gap between them splits C into two relatively open pieces; so the
    only connected subsets are points. NOWHERE DENSE: C is closed and contains
    no interval (any interval has positive length, C has length 0).
    containing x has an endpoint != x within 3^-^n, and endpoints lie in C. The
       F(x) = 0.(a_1/2)(a_2/2)(a_3/2)..._2 ;
    on a removed interval F is constant, equal to its value at the ends. So
       F(1/4) = F(0.0202..._3) = 0.0101..._2 = 1/3,
       F(1/10) = F(0.00220022..._3) = 0.00110011..._2 = 3/15 = 1/5,
               = 0.0111..._2 = 1/2,
       F(2/9) = F(0.02_3) = 0.01_2 = 1/4.
    F is increasing and continuous (points within 3^-^n agree in n ternary
    digits, so their images agree in n binary digits: |F(x) - F(y)| <= 2^-^n).
    length 1, and still F rises from 0 to 1: the fundamental theorem
    Common mistakes: reading a ternary digit 2 as binary 2 (it becomes 1);
    evaluating F on a gap without converting the left end to 0/2 digits.
    Now you try: F(7/9). (7/9 = 0.21_3 lies in the gap (7/9, 8/9) at its left

    Check: A_1 = (4/3)A_0 (three triangles of area A_0/9), A_2 = (40/27)A_0. The
    limit is A_0(1 + 3/5) = (8/5)A_0 = 8sqrt3/20 = 2sqrt3/5 ~ 0.6928. The snowflake
    fits in a disc, so the area had to be finite; the boundary is infinitely
    long because it wiggles at every scale. DIMENSION: the Koch curve is 4

    Now you try: the QUADRATIC Koch curve replaces each segment by 8 segments

    SPONGE: divide a cube into 27, remove the centre cube and the 6 face
    centres (7 cubes): 20 remain, volume (20/27)^n -> 0, s = ln 20/ln 3 ~
    contains curves (the carpet contains the sides of every removed square,
    the Sierpinski triangle all its edges), so s >= 1 = topological dimension
    of those sets. The carpet is universal: every compact 1-dimensional plane
    curve embeds in it; the sponge is universal for curves in space. Common
    mistakes: removing 6 cubes instead of 7 from the sponge (the centre also

    try: the Vicsek fractal keeps the centre and the 4 corner squares of a
    3 x 3 grid. Its dimension? (ln 5/ln 3 ~ 1.4650)

D6. Define box-counting dimension. Compute it for the Cantor set, for
    show.
    Answer: ln 2/ln 3; 1/2; 1. Box dimension is not countably stable and does
    not see the difference between a set and its closure.
       dim_B F = 1/2,
    box dimension fails COUNTABLE STABILITY, and dim_B E = dim_B (closure of
    E). Hausdorff dimension repairs both (countable sets have dim_H = 0), at
    the cost of being harder to compute. In practice (computer, data) box
    counting is what one measures. Common mistakes: counting only the points

D8. Using the properties of Hausdorff dimension find dim_H of: Q; the
    Answer: 0; 1; 1; 2 ln 2/ln 3 ~ 1.2619; 1 + ln 2/ln 3 ~ 1.6309;
    ln 2/ln 3; 1; 2.
    Teacher explains: The toolbox:
       Lipschitz f:         dim f(F) <= dim F; bi-Lipschitz: equal
       open sets of R^n:     dimension n
    Q is a countable union of points (dimension 0 each): dim Q = 0. [0, 1]
    locally a bi-Lipschitz image of a disc: 2. PRODUCTS: C x C (Cantor dust)
    is self-similar with 4 pieces at ratio 1/3: ln 4/ln 3 = 2 ln 2/ln 3 ~
    1.2619 = dim C + dim C; C x [0, 1] is 1 + ln 2/ln 3 ~ 1.6309. (For general
    sets only dim(E x F) >= dim E + dim F holds; equality needs regularity,
    e.g. equal Hausdorff and box dimension for one factor.) Contrast with
    TOPOLOGICAL dimension: C and C x C both have dim_T = 0 (totally
    disconnected), and dim_T <= dim_H always; Mandelbrot's definition of a
    fractal was dim_H > dim_T. Common mistakes: adding dimensions for unions
    (take the maximum); thinking a dimension-0 set must be countable (there are
    uncountable sets of dimension 0, e.g. the Liouville numbers). Now you try:

D9. Define the Hausdorff metric and the Hutchinson operator of an IFS, and
    prove that the operator is a contraction. For the IFS f_1(x) = x/3,
    f_2(x) = x/3 + 2/3 starting from [0, 1], find d_H(F^n[0, 1], C). Give an IFS
    for the Sierpinski triangle and describe the chaos game.
    Teacher explains: For non-empty compact A, B,
    E.g. d_H({0}, [0, 1]) = 1, d_H({0, 1}, [0, 1]) = 1/2. The compact sets with
    d_H(F^n(A), K) <= r^n d_H(A, K). For the Cantor IFS, F^n([0, 1]) = C_n and
    point is 1/2, at distance 1/6 from 1/3 and 2/3. So
    that far from C. SIERPINSKI: with vertices v_1 = (0, 0), v_2 = (1, 0),
    every point lies within tiny distance of K, and the orbit fills K
    densely - the 'random' dots draw the Sierpinski triangle. An IFS is a
    tiny program for a complicated picture (Barnsley's fern uses 4 affine
    maps). Common mistakes: taking d_H as the smallest distance between the
    sets (d_H({0}, [0, 1]) is 1, not 0); forgetting that the attractor does not
    depend on the starting set. Now you try: the attractor of x/2 and
    x/2 + 1/2 on R. ([0, 1])

     That is how computer pictures are made. Orbits of 0:
        c = 1/4: 0, 0.25, 0.3125, 0.3477, ... increases to 1/2 (the fixed
        c = 0.3: 0, 0.3, 0.39, 0.4521, 0.5044, ... no fixed point (z^2 - z +
     For real c the orbit of 0 is bounded exactly for -2 <= c <= 1/4:

D11. Find the region of c for which z^2 + c has an attracting fixed point (the
     main cardioid) and the region with an attracting 2-cycle. Classify
     c = -1/2, -3/4, -1.2, -1.3, 1/4, 1/4 + i/2. Describe J_c for c = 0 and
     c = -2.
     Answer: cardioid c = mu/2 - mu^2/4, |mu| < 1; 2-cycle disc |c + 1| < 1/4.
     -1/2: attracting fixed point; -3/4: on the boundary between cardioid and
     disc; -1.2: attracting 2-cycle; -1.3: neither (period 4 region);
     1/4: cusp, neutral fixed point; 1/4 + i/2: boundary of the cardioid
     Teacher explains: A fixed point z* = z*^2 + c is ATTRACTING when
        c = z* - z*^2 = mu/2 - mu^2/4,   |mu| < 1.
     As mu = e^(itheta) runs round the unit circle this traces a CARDIOID with cusp
     at c = 1/4 (mu = 1) and leftmost point -3/4 (mu = -1). Period 2: the points
     with fc(fc(z)) = z but fc(z) != z satisfy
        (z^4 + 2cz^2 + c^2 + c - z)/(z^2 - z + c) = z^2 + z + c + 1 = 0,
     so z_1 + z_2 = -1, z_1z_2 = c + 1, and the multiplier of the cycle is
     radius 1/4 touching the cardioid at -3/4. Now:
        c = -1/2:  z^2 - z - 1/2 = 0, z* = (1 - sqrt3)/2, mu = 1 - sqrt3 ~ -0.732,
                   |mu| < 1: attracting fixed point.
        c = -3/4:  mu = -1 and also |c + 1| = 1/4: the meeting point.
        c = -1.2:  |c + 1| = 0.2 < 1/4: attracting 2-cycle.
        c = -1.3:  |c + 1| = 0.3 > 1/4: the 2-cycle repels (period doubling at
                   c = -5/4); here a 4-cycle attracts.
        c = 1/4 + i/2: mu = i gives c = i/2 - i^2/4 = 1/4 + i/2, |mu| = 1.
     closed disc and J_0 the unit circle (dimension 1, a smooth curve). For
     c = -2, the substitution z = 2 cos theta gives z^2 - 2 = 2 cos 2theta, so [-2, 2]
     (e.g. c = i: a dendrite; c = -1: the 'basilica'). Common mistakes:
     using |z*| < 1 instead of |2z*| < 1; forgetting to discard the fixed
     points when looking for 2-cycles. Now you try: the multiplier of the
     2-cycle when c = -1. (4(-1 + 1) = 0: superattracting; the cycle is 0, -1)

     giving lengths L = 1600, 1903, 2263, 2691 km. Estimate its fractal
     dimension. Also, box counts for a set in the plane give N(1/3) = 8 and
     N(1/27) = 512: estimate its dimension. Explain the methods.
     Answer: D ~ 1.25; D = ln 64/ln 9 = ln 8/ln 3 ~ 1.8928.

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: build the first three stages of every fractal by hand (Cantor
  on a ruler, Koch and Sierpinski on squared paper) and tabulate pieces,
  itself. Practise ternary expansions (multiply by 3, take integer parts)
  before any Cantor-set question. For box counting draw the grid and count;
  compute the first five iterates in a table and stop as soon as |z| > 2.
  C + C = [0, 2]; prove the Hutchinson operator is a contraction and that
  the attractor of a similarity IFS with the open set condition has
  exponent ln 2/ln 3 but not better; prove that J_c is a Cantor set for
  |c| > 2; and program the chaos game and a Mandelbrot plot, estimating the
  box dimension of the Julia set of z^2 - 1 from the output.

================================================================================
TOPIC 10.32 - PARTIAL DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS: HEAT, WAVE, LAPLACE EQUATIONS;
SEPARATION OF VARIABLES; METHOD OF CHARACTERISTICS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A PDE relates a function of several variables to its partial derivatives.
    ORDER = highest derivative. LINEAR (u and its derivatives appear linearly,
    coefficients depend only on the variables), SEMILINEAR, QUASILINEAR
    (linear in the highest derivatives, e.g. u_t + uu_x = 0) or fully
    NONLINEAR. For linear HOMOGENEOUS equations SUPERPOSITION holds. A problem
    is WELL-POSED (Hadamard) if a solution exists, is unique and depends
    continuously on the data.
  - CLASSIFICATION of Au_xx + Bu_xy + Cu_yy + (lower order) = 0 by the
    = 0 PARABOLIC (heat), < 0 ELLIPTIC (Laplace). CHARACTERISTICS solve
    A(dy/dx)^2 - B(dy/dx) + C = 0; the type can change from region to region
    (Tricomi yu_xx + u_yy = 0).
  - HEAT (diffusion) EQUATION u_t = ku_xx. On 0 < x < L with u(0, t) =
    u(L, t) = 0, u(x, 0) = f(x):
    High modes die fastest; u -> 0. Insulated ends (u_x = 0) give a cosine
    series and u -> the MEAN a_0/2 of f. Non-zero boundary values: subtract the
    STEADY STATE (a straight line for constant end temperatures).
  - HEAT properties: MAXIMUM PRINCIPLE (max of u on the closed rectangle is
    attained at t = 0 or on the ends), hence uniqueness; ENERGY integral u^2 decreases;
    on R, u = (4pikt)^(-1/2)integral  e^(-(x-y)^2/(4kt)) f(y) dy (HEAT KERNEL,
    Gaussian of variance 2kt): infinitely smooth for t > 0, infinite speed of
    propagation; the BACKWARD heat equation is ill-posed.
  - WAVE EQUATION u_tt = c^2u_xx. On R, D'ALEMBERT:
       u = 1/2[f(x - ct) + f(x + ct)] + (1/(2c))integral  (x-ct to x+ct) g(s) ds
    (u(x, 0) = f, u_t(x, 0) = g): two waves travelling at speed c. DOMAIN OF
    DEPENDENCE of (x, t) is [x - ct, x + ct]; finite speed; singularities
    travel along characteristics x +/- ct = const. Energy
    E = 1/2integral (u_t^2 + c^2u_x^2) dx is conserved.
  - STRING with fixed ends u(0, t) = u(L, t) = 0:
       a_n = (2/L)integral  f sin(npix/L), b_n = (2/(npic))integral  g sin(npix/L).
    NORMAL MODES with frequencies nc/(2L) (fundamental c/(2L)), nodes at
    x = mL/n; the motion is periodic with period 2L/c. Equivalent to
    d'Alembert with the ODD 2L-periodic extension of f and g.
    MEAN VALUE PROPERTY (u(centre) = average over any circle), MAXIMUM
    PRINCIPLE (max and min on the boundary), uniqueness of the DIRICHLET
    constant. Rectangle: products sin(npix/a) sinh(npiy/a). Disc of radius a:
    with a_n, b_n the Fourier coefficients of the boundary data (POISSON integral).
  - SEPARATION OF VARIABLES: try u = X(x)T(t); the PDE splits into ODEs linked
    by a SEPARATION CONSTANT -lambda; the boundary conditions give a STURM-LIOUVILLE
       X(0) = X(L) = 0:     lambda = (npi/L)^2, sin(npix/L), n >= 1
       periodic, period 2pi: lambda = n^2, cos nx and sin nx.
    Eigenfunctions are ORTHOGONAL; expand the data in them (FOURIER SERIES)
    average (GIBBS overshoot ~ 9% of the jump).
  - METHOD OF CHARACTERISTICS for a(x, y)u_x + b(x, y)u_y = c(x, y, u):
    along curves with dx/ds = a, dy/ds = b the PDE becomes the ODE
    du/ds = c. Transport u_t + cu_x = 0: u = f(x - ct). u_t + xu_x = 0:
    u = f(xe^(-t)). The general solution contains an arbitrary function of the
    characteristic constant; the data curve must cross each characteristic
    once (not be characteristic).
  - QUASILINEAR / BURGERS u_t + uu_x = 0, u(x, 0) = f(x): u is constant on the
    straight characteristics x = x_0 + f(x_0)t, so u = f(x - ut) implicitly.
    Characteristics cross (a SHOCK forms) at the BREAKING TIME
    RANKINE-HUGONIOT speed s = [F(u)]/[u] = (u_L + u_R)/2 (for flux u^2/2) and
    are admissible only if u_L > u_R; for u_L < u_R a RAREFACTION FAN
    u = x/t fills the gap.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Classify u_xx + 4u_xy + 3u_yy = 0, find its characteristics, reduce it to
    canonical form and find the general solution. Then classify the Tricomi
    equation yu_xx + u_yy = 0.
    Answer: hyperbolic; characteristics y - x = const, y - 3x = const;
    elliptic for y > 0, parabolic on y = 0, hyperbolic for y < 0.
    Teacher explains: A = 1, B = 4, C = 3: B^2 - 4AC = 16 - 12 = 4 > 0, so
    HYPERBOLIC (like the wave equation). Characteristic slopes solve
    so the characteristics are the lines y - x = const and y - 3x = const. Take
    In u_xx + 4u_xy + 3u_yy collect the coefficients:
    u = F(x - ct) + G(x + ct). Tricomi: A = y, B = 0, C = 1, B^2 - 4AC = -4y:
    the type depends on the region - it models transonic flow (subsonic =
    elliptic, supersonic = hyperbolic). Common mistakes: using B^2 - AC (that is
    the rule when the middle term is written 2Bu_xy); forgetting the
    coefficient 4 is the full B. Now you try: classify
    u_xx - 6u_xy + 10u_yy = 0. (36 - 40 = -4 < 0: elliptic)

    lambda <= 0 gives nothing. List the eigenvalues for Neumann, mixed and periodic
    conditions, prove orthogonality of sin(npix/L), and write the formula for
    Fourier sine coefficients. Find the sine series of f(x) = 1 on (0, pi).
    Answer: lambda_n = (npi/L)^2, X_n = sin(npix/L); 1 = (4/pi)(sin x + sin 3x/3 +
    sin 5x/5 + ...).
    Teacher explains: Three cases for the sign of lambda.
       lambda = mu^2 > 0:  X = A cos mux + B sin mux; A = 0; B sin muL = 0 with B != 0
    one gets cos(npix/L), n = 0, 1, 2, ... (lambda = 0, X = 1 now survives); with
    (-pi, pi): lambda = n^2, both cos nx and sin nx. ORTHOGONALITY: for m != n
                                     - cos((m + n)pix/L)] dx = 0,
    L = pi:
       b_n = (2/pi)integral _0^pi sin nx dx = (2/pi)(1 - cos npi)/n = 4/(npi) (n odd), 0 (even).
    At x = pi/2 this gives 1 = (4/pi)(1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - ...), Leibniz's
    pi/4 = 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - .... At x = 0 and pi the series gives 0 (the odd
    extension jumps there), and near the jumps partial sums overshoot to
    ~ 1.179 (GIBBS). Common mistakes: forgetting lambda = 0 in the Neumann case;
    using (1/L) instead of (2/L). Now you try: the sine series of x on
    (0, pi). (2(sin x - sin 2x/2 + sin 3x/3 - ...))

D3. Solve u_t = u_xx on 0 < x < pi with u(0, t) = u(pi, t) = 0 and (a)
    u(x, 0) = 3 sin x - sin 4x, (b) u(x, 0) = 1. In (b) find u(pi/2, 1) and
    describe the long-time behaviour.
    e^(-n^2t) sin nx/n; u(pi/2, 1) ~ 0.4683; u ~ (4/pi)e^(-t) sin x for large t.
                          middle on x only).
    the boundary conditions, so by superposition
    (a) The data is already a sine series: b_1 = 3, b_4 = -1, so
       u = 3e^(-t) sin x - e^(-16t) sin 4x.
    odd n (D2):
       u(x, t) = (4/pi)[e^(-t) sin x + e^(-9t) sin 3x/3 + e^(-25t) sin 5x/5 + ...]
       u(pi/2, 1) = (4/pi)[e^(-1) - e^(-9)/3 + e^(-25)/5 - ...]
                 ~ (4/pi)(0.367879 - 0.000041) ~ 0.4683.
    For t > 0 the series converges extremely fast (e^(-n^2t)), so u is smooth
    even though the data jumps at the ends: DIFFUSION SMOOTHS. After a short
    time only the first mode matters, u ~ (4/pi)e^(-t) sin x, decaying at rate
    lambda_1 = 1 (in general kpi^2/L^2: a rod twice as long cools four times slower).

D4. (a) Solve u_t = u_xx, 0 < x < 1, u(0, t) = 0, u(1, t) = 10, u(x, 0) = 0.
    (b) Solve u_t = u_xx, 0 < x < pi, with insulated ends u_x(0, t) = u_x(pi, t)
    = 0 and u(x, 0) = x, and show the mean temperature is conserved.
    Teacher explains: (a) Separation needs HOMOGENEOUS boundary conditions, so
    v(0, t) = v(1, t) = 0 and v(x, 0) = -10x. Sine coefficients on (0, 1):
       u = 10x - (20/pi)[e^(-pi^2t) sin pix - e^(-4pi^2t) sin 2pix/2 + ...],
    cosine coefficients of x:
       a_0 = (2/pi)integral _0^pi x dx = pi,  a_n = (2/pi)integral _0^pi x cos nx dx
          = 2((-1)^n - 1)/(pin^2) = -4/(pin^2) (n odd), 0 (n even).
    So u -> a_0/2 = pi/2, the AVERAGE of the initial temperature. Directly:
       d/dt integral _0^pi u dx = integral _0^pi u_xx dx = u_x(pi, t) - u_x(0, t) = 0
    - no heat crosses the insulated ends, so the total heat is constant.
    Common mistakes: applying separation straight to non-zero boundary data;

    constant term a_0/2. Now you try: steady state for u(0) = 20, u(pi) = 50.
    (w = 20 + 30x/pi)

D5. Prove the maximum principle for u_t = ku_xx on [0, L] x [0, T] and deduce
    uniqueness; give the energy proof of uniqueness too. Solve the heat
    equation on R with u(x, 0) = e^(-x^2) and comment on the properties of the
    heat kernel.
    Answer: u = (1 + 4kt)^(-1/2) exp(-x^2/(1 + 4kt)).
    Teacher explains: MAXIMUM PRINCIPLE: the maximum of u over the closed
    rectangle is attained on the 'parabolic boundary' (t = 0, x = 0 or
    its max at an interior point or on the top t = T, there v_t >= 0 and
    v_xx <= 0, so v_t - kv_xx >= 0: contradiction. Hence
    has zero data, so max w <= 0 and (applied to -w) min w >= 0: w = 0.
    with the HEAT KERNEL
    For f = e^(-x^2) (a Gaussian of variance 1/2) the variances add:
    1/2 + 2kt = (1 + 4kt)/2, and mass integral f = sqrtpi is conserved, so
       u = (1 + 4kt)^(-1/2) exp(-x^2/(1 + 4kt)).
    backwards is ILL-POSED: sin(nx)/n is small data, but u = e^(n^2t) sin(nx)/n
    solves u_t = -u_xx and explodes. Common mistakes: in the max principle
    forgetting the top side t = T (there v_t >= 0, not v_t = 0); forgetting the
    normalising factor of the kernel. Now you try: u(x, 0) = x^2
    on R. (u = x^2 + 2kt)

D6. Derive d'Alembert's formula for u_tt = c^2u_xx on R. Solve it for (a)
    f = e^(-x^2), g = 0, c = 2; (b) f = 0, g = cos x; (c) f = 1 for |x| < 1 and
    0 otherwise, g = 0, c = 1, and find u(0, 1/2), u(1.5, 1), u(0, 2). Explain
    the domain of dependence.
    Answer: (a) u = 1/2[e^(-(x-2t)^2) + e^(-(x+2t)^2)]. (b) u = cos x sin(ct)/c.
    (c) u(0, 1/2) = 1, u(1.5, 1) = 1/2, u(0, 2) = 0.
    left-moving wave, both unchanged in shape. Fit the data:
    Solve and add:
       u(x, t) = 1/2[f(x - ct) + f(x + ct)] + (1/(2c))integral  (x-ct to x+ct) g(s) ds.
    (a) u = 1/2[e^(-(x - 2t)^2) + e^(-(x + 2t)^2)]: the bump splits into two halves
    moving apart at speed 2. (b) u = (1/(2c))[sin(x + ct) - sin(x - ct)]
    = (1/c) cos x sin ct (a standing wave). (c) Use 1/2[f(x - t) + f(x + t)]:
       u(0, 1/2) = 1/2[f(-1/2) + f(1/2)] = 1/2(1 + 1) = 1
       u(1.5, 1) = 1/2[f(0.5) + f(2.5)] = 1/2(1 + 0) = 1/2
       u(0, 2)   = 1/2[f(-2) + f(2)] = 0   (both halves have passed)
    The corners of the box never smooth out: discontinuities travel along the
    characteristics x +/- t = +/-1 - unlike the heat equation. DOMAIN OF
    DEPENDENCE: u(x_0, t_0) depends only on the data in [x_0 - ct_0, x_0 + ct_0]
    (the base of the backward characteristic triangle); the RANGE OF INFLUENCE
    of a point x_1 is the forward cone |x - x_1| <= ct. Signals travel at speed
    exactly c. Common mistakes: forgetting the 1/2; integrating g over
    [x - t, x + t] when c != 1. Now you try: f = x^2, g = 0. (u = x^2 + c^2t^2)

D7. Solve the string problem u_tt = 4u_xx, 0 < x < pi, u(0, t) = u(pi, t) = 0,

    = 4[u_x u_t]_0^pi = 0, since u_t = 0 at fixed ends. At t = 0:

    divide by sinh npi. Now you try: u(x, 0) = sin x, u = 0 on the other sides.
    (u = sin x sinh(pi - y)/sinh pi)

D10. Solve Laplace's equation in the unit disc with (a) u(1, theta) = cos^2theta,
     (b) u(1, theta) = sin^3theta, by separation in polar coordinates. Verify the mean
     value property in (a) and state the Poisson integral formula and the
     compatibility condition for the Neumann problem.
     Answer: (a) u = 1/2 + 1/2r^2 cos 2theta = 1/2 + 1/2(x^2 - y^2), u(0) = 1/2.
     (b) u = (3r sin theta - r^3 sin 3theta)/4.
     r = 0 keeps r^n and 1:
     where a_n, b_n are the Fourier coefficients of the boundary data. (a)
     cos^2theta = 1/2 + 1/2 cos 2theta, so u = 1/2 + 1/2r^2 cos 2theta; in Cartesian form
     r^2 cos 2theta = x^2 - y^2, u = 1/2 + 1/2(x^2 - y^2), clearly harmonic. MEAN VALUE:
     u = (3r sin theta - r^3 sin 3theta)/4. By the maximum principle
     |u| <= max|sin^3theta| = 1 in the disc. POISSON: summing the series,
     at r = 0 the kernel is 1: the mean value property again. NEUMANN: data
     no solution. For the EXTERIOR r > 1 keep r^-^n: data cos theta gives cos theta/r.
     Common mistakes: keeping r^-^n inside the disc (singular at 0); using
     cos^2theta as a single mode instead of expanding it. Now you try: disc of
     radius 2 with u(2, theta) = sin 2theta. (u = (r^2/4) sin 2theta = xy/2)

D11. Use the method of characteristics to solve (a) u_t + 2u_x = 0,
     u(x, 0) = e^(-x^2); (b) u_t + u_x = -u, u(x, 0) = f(x); (c) u_t + xu_x = u,
     u(x, 0) = x^2; (d) 2u_x + 3u_y = 0, u(0, y) = y.
     Answer: (a) e^(-(x - 2t)^2); (b) e^(-t)f(x - t); (c) x^2e^(-t);
     (d) y - 3x/2.
     Teacher explains: For a u_x + b u_t = c, the left side is the derivative
     of u along the curves with dx/ds = a, dt/ds = b. So: (1) find the
     CHARACTERISTIC curves, (2) solve the ODE for u along each, (3) use the
     data where each curve starts. (a) dx/dt = 2: x = x_0 + 2t, and du/dt = 0:
     u is constant, = e^(-x_0^2) = e^(-(x - 2t)^2). The profile moves right at
     speed 2 without changing shape (TRANSPORT). (b) Same lines x = x_0 + t;
     characteristic, u constant along it: u = G(3x - 2y). Data at x = 0:
     (2(-3/2) + 3(1) = 0). WARNING: data given on a characteristic curve is
     either inconsistent or insufficient: for u_t + 2u_x = 0 data on the line
     x = 2t cannot determine u elsewhere. Common mistakes: solving for x_0 with
     the wrong sign (x_0 = x - 2t, not x + 2t); forgetting the source term on
     the right. Now you try: yu_x - xu_y = 0. (Characteristics x^2 + y^2 = const;
     u = F(x^2 + y^2))

D12. For Burgers' equation u_t + uu_x = 0: (a) show u = f(x - ut) and solve
     with f(x) = -x; (b) find the breaking time for f(x) = e^(-x^2); (c) solve the
     Riemann problems u_L = 1, u_R = 0 and u_L = 0, u_R = 1.
     Answer: (a) u = -x/(1 - t), blows up at t = 1; (b) t* = sqrt(e/2) ~ 1.1658;
     (c) a shock x = t/2; a rarefaction u = 0 (x < 0), x/t (0 <= x <= t),
     1 (x > t).
     Teacher explains: Along dx/dt = u we have du/dt = u_t + uu_x = 0, so u is
     constant on each characteristic, and therefore dx/dt is constant: the
     characteristics are STRAIGHT LINES x = x_0 + f(x_0)t. Hence
     u(x, t) = f(x_0) with x_0 = x - ut: u = f(x - ut), implicitly. (a)
     x = x_0(1 - t) meet at x = 0 when t = 1: the slope becomes infinite.
     fluid behind catches up with slower fluid ahead - a SHOCK. (c) Write the
     equation as a CONSERVATION LAW u_t + (u^2/2)_x = 0. Across a jump the
     RANKINE-HUGONIOT condition gives the speed
        s = [u^2/2]/[u] = (u_L + u_R)/2.
     For u_L = 1 > u_R = 0 the characteristics collide: shock x = t/2 with u = 1
     behind, 0 ahead. For u_L = 0 < u_R = 1 they diverge, leaving an empty
     wedge 0 < x < t filled by the RAREFACTION FAN u = x/t (itself a solution:
     u_t + uu_x = -x/t^2 + (x/t)(1/t) = 0). A shock there would also satisfy RH
     but violates the ENTROPY condition u_L > u_R (characteristics must run
     INTO shocks). This models traffic jams and gas dynamics. Common mistakes:
     using the characteristic speed u instead of the average for the shock;
     u_R = 1. (2)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: write the recipe for separation of variables on the board
  (separate -> eigenvalue problem -> time/space ODE -> superpose -> Fourier
  coefficients) and follow it every time; always make the boundary
  conditions homogeneous first by subtracting a steady state. Keep a table of
  the four standard eigenvalue problems and of five Fourier series. Check
  every answer by substituting it into the PDE, the boundary conditions and
  the initial data. For characteristics draw the (x, t) plane with the
  characteristic lines before any algebra; for d'Alembert draw the backward
  triangle. Harder: prove the mean value property and the strong maximum
  principle for harmonic functions; derive the Poisson integral formula by
  summing the geometric series; solve the heat equation with a source by
  Duhamel's principle; solve the wave equation in 3D by Kirchhoff's formula
  (Huygens' principle) and compare with 2D by descent; separate the Laplace
  equation in spherical coordinates (Legendre polynomials) and in a cylinder
  (Bessel functions); and show that the Riemann problem for Burgers with
  u_L > u_R has infinitely many weak solutions, of which the entropy
  condition picks one.

================================================================================
TOPIC 10.33 - QUALITATIVE THEORY OF ODEs: PHASE PLANE, STABILITY, BIFURCATIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
    its PHASE PORTRAIT: the picture of all solution curves (TRAJECTORIES,
    ORBITS) in the phase space. An EQUILIBRIUM (fixed point, critical point)
    is a point x* with f(x*) = 0. By uniqueness (f of class C^1) trajectories
    never cross, and solutions starting at an equilibrium stay there.
    left where f < 0. Solutions are monotone, can never oscillate, and tend to
    stable and moreover x(t) -> x* for all x(0) near x*; UNSTABLE if not stable.
    A centre is stable but not asymptotically stable.
    real eigenvalues; e^(alphat)(c_1 cos betat + c_2 sin betat)-type solutions for
    lambda = alpha +/- ibeta; (c_1 + c_2t)e^(lambdat) for a repeated eigenvalue with one
    negative real part.
    DEGENERATE (improper) NODE; delta  = 0 a LINE of equilibria. For delta  > 0:
    at (1, 0), i.e. the sign of a_2_1 (positive: anticlockwise).
    J = Df(x*). HARTMAN-GROBMAN: if x* is HYPERBOLIC (no eigenvalue of J with
    nodes, spirals and their stability survive). A linear CENTRE, or a zero
    eigenvalue, is NOT decided by linearisation.
  - NULLCLINES: the x-nullcline is the curve f_1 = 0 (flow vertical there), the
    y-nullcline g = 0 (flow horizontal); equilibria are their intersections.
    Stable and unstable MANIFOLDS of a saddle (tangent to the eigenvectors)
    act as SEPARATRICES between basins of attraction.
  - CONSERVATIVE SYSTEMS: a FIRST INTEGRAL (conserved quantity) H has
    dH/dt = 0 along solutions; orbits lie on level curves of H. For
    and closed orbits around (c/d, a/b). A non-degenerate minimum of H is a
    true (nonlinear) centre.

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always start by finding equilibria and drawing nullclines with
  little arrows (up/down between y-nullclines, left/right between
  x-nullclines); in one dimension draw the graph of f(x) and read the arrows
  off its sign. Put a poster of the trace-determinant plane on the wall: the
  one dot. Check rotation with the velocity at (1, 0). Stress that a linear
  centre and a zero eigenvalue always need an extra tool (energy, first
  integral, Lyapunov function). Harder: prove Hartman-Grobman fails for
  decide super/sub-criticality of a Hopf bifurcation; study the index of a
  saddle and a node with the winding number; find a trapping region for the
  experimenting numerically with the Lorenz equations.

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
    TRUNCATION (discretisation) error (cutting a series or a limit short).
    digits). Floating-point addition is not associative. CATASTROPHIC
    CANCELLATION: subtracting nearly equal numbers loses relative accuracy;
    cure it by algebra (conjugates, identities, x_2 = c/(a x_1)).
  - CONDITIONING vs STABILITY: the CONDITION NUMBER of a problem,
    magnified (a property of the PROBLEM); an algorithm is STABLE if it does
    not add much more error than the conditioning forces. ORDER OF
  - ROOT FINDING: BISECTION (f continuous, f(a)f(b) < 0): after n halvings
    |c_n - r| <= (b - a)/2^n, always converges, linearly. FIXED-POINT iteration
    (CONTRACTION), there is a unique fixed point and |x_n - x*| <= L^n|x_0 - x*|
    multiplicity m; may diverge from a bad start. SECANT: order
    (1 + sqrt5)/2 ~ 1.618, no derivative needed.
    linear interpolation with spacing h: |error| <= h^2M_2/8.
  - RUNGE'S PHENOMENON: high-degree interpolation at equally spaced nodes can
    diverge near the ends (1/(1 + 25x^2) on [-1, 1]); CHEBYSHEV NODES
  - QUADRATURE with h = (b - a)/n: TRAPEZOID T = h[f_0/2 + f_1 + ... + f_n/2],
    Simpson 3, n-point GAUSS 2n - 1 (2-point: nodes +/-1/sqrt3, weights 1).
    RICHARDSON / ROMBERG: (4T(h/2) - T(h))/3 cancels the h^2 term (= Simpson).
    O(h^2), GLOBAL error O(h) (first order); HEUN (improved Euler) and MIDPOINT
    methods are second order; classical RK4
    y_{n+1} = y_n + h(k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4)/6 is fourth order. Multistep:
    y_{n+1} = (1 + hlambda)y_n, stable iff |1 + hlambda| <= 1 (for real lambda < 0: h <= 2/|lambda|).
    BACKWARD EULER y_{n+1} = y_n/(1 - hlambda) and the TRAPEZOIDAL rule are
    A-STABLE (stable for every h > 0). STIFF problems (eigenvalues of very
    different sizes) need implicit methods.
  - DIRECT LINEAR ALGEBRA: GAUSSIAN ELIMINATION = LU FACTORISATION A = LU
    (L unit lower triangular holding the multipliers); cost ~ 2n^3/3 flops,
    each triangular solve ~ n^2. PARTIAL PIVOTING (largest pivot in the column,
    PA = LU) keeps multipliers <= 1 and is needed for stability. CHOLESKY
    +/- product of the pivots.
  - ITERATIVE METHODS: JACOBI and GAUSS-SEIDEL converge for every start when
    A is strictly diagonally dominant (in general iff the spectral radius of
    with shift sigma finds the eigenvalue nearest sigma. GERSHGORIN: every eigenvalue

D1. Using 4-significant-digit rounding arithmetic, solve x^2 - 56x + 1 = 0 by
    the usual formula and then in a way that avoids cancellation. Explain
    machine epsilon and why one answer is bad.
    Answer: Formula: x_1 = 55.98, x_2 = 0.02000 (relative error ~ 12%).
    Better: x_2 = 1/x_1 = 0.01786 (true value 0.017863...).
    Teacher explains: x = 28 +/- sqrt783, and sqrt783 = 27.982137... rounds to 27.98.
       x_1 = 28 + 27.98 = 55.98        (true 55.982137...)   fine
       x_2 = 28 - 27.98 = 0.02000      (true 0.0178628...)   bad
    The subtraction is EXACT; the damage was done earlier, when sqrt783 was
    rounded. Its absolute error (about 0.0021) is small compared to 27.98 but
    huge compared to the difference 0.0179: the leading digits cancel and
    only rounding noise survives. That is CATASTROPHIC CANCELLATION, relative
    error (0.02 - 0.017863)/0.017863 ~ 0.120. Cure: the product of the roots
    is c/a = 1, so
       x_2 = 1/x_1 = 1/55.98 = 0.01786
    correct to 4 digits (no subtraction of close numbers). The same trick
    gap between 1 and the next floating-point number; every operation is
    2.2 x 10^-^1^6). Four-digit arithmetic here has u = 5 x 10^-^4. Common
    mistakes: blaming the subtraction itself; thinking more digits always
    fix cancellation (they only postpone it). Now you try: evaluate
    sqrt(x + 1) - sqrtx for x = 10^6 stably. (1/(sqrt(x + 1) + sqrtx) ~ 4.99999875 x 10^-^4)

    h = 0.05 and by the central difference with h = 0.1; derive the error
    terms, apply Richardson extrapolation, and explain why h cannot be made
    arbitrarily small in floating point. Also define the condition number of
    evaluating f and compute it for sqrtx and for x - 1 near x = 1.001.
    0.0691), central D_0(0.1) ~ 2.722815 (error 0.00453); Richardson
    double precision.
    (in D_0 the even terms cancel). Numbers with e = 2.718282:
       D_0(0.1)  = (3.004166 - 2.459603)/0.2 = 2.722815     error 0.0045
    Halving h halves the forward error (order 1) as predicted (~ h e/2).
    2(2.787386) - 2.858842 = 2.715930. ROUNDING: f(x + h) and f(x) carry
    errors ~ u|f|, so the quotient has an extra error ~ 2u|f|/h. Total
    E(h) ~ Mh/2 + 2u|f|/h is minimised at h ~ 2sqrt(u|f|/M) ~ 2sqrtu ~ 2 x 10^-^8
    here; with h = 10^-^1^2 the computed derivative is wrong in the 4th digit.
    CONDITION NUMBER: relative change of f over relative change of x,
    so evaluating x - 1 at 1.001 magnifies relative errors 1001 times
    (cancellation again, a property of the problem). Common mistakes:
    taking h as small as possible; confusing ill-conditioning with
    instability. Now you try: forward difference for f(x) = x^2 at x = 3,

D5. Find the interpolating polynomial through (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 2), (3, 5) in
    Lagrange form and in Newton form, and evaluate at x = 1.5. Prove that the
    interpolating polynomial is unique.
    Answer: p(x) = (7/6)x^3 - 5x^2 + (35/6)x + 1
    = 1 + 2x - (3/2)x(x - 1) + (7/6)x(x - 1)(x - 2); p(1.5) = 2.4375.
       L_0 = -(x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3)/6     L_1 = x(x - 2)(x - 3)/2
       L_2 = -x(x - 1)(x - 3)/2           L_3 = x(x - 1)(x - 2)/6
    NEWTON: build the divided-difference table, each entry = (lower right -
    upper right)/(span of x's):
       x   f     [ , ]   [ , , ]   [ , , , ]
       0   1
                  2
       1   3             -3/2
                 -1                  7/6
       2   2               2
                  3
       3   5
    e.g. f[0, 1, 2] = (-1 - 2)/(2 - 0) = -3/2, f[0, 1, 2, 3] = (2 - (-3/2))/3
    = 7/6. The top diagonal gives the coefficients:
       p = 1 + 2x - (3/2)x(x - 1) + (7/6)x(x - 1)(x - 2)
    Adding a new point adds just one term: that is the advantage of Newton's
    form. At 1.5: 1 + 3 - (3/2)(0.75) + (7/6)(1.5)(0.5)(-0.5) = 4 - 1.125 -
    0.4375 = 2.4375. UNIQUENESS: if p and q both interpolate, p - q has degree
    <= 3 and 4 roots, so p - q = 0. Common mistakes: dividing by the gap
    between neighbours instead of the whole span; evaluating Newton's form
    with the wrong product factors. Now you try: data (2, 1/2), (2.5, 2/5),
    (4, 1/4) from f = 1/x; find p(3). (p = x^2/20 - 17x/40 + 23/20; p(3) =
    13/40 = 0.325, true 1/3)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: let the student run every method on a calculator or in a few
  lines of Python and PRINT the error column: seeing the error halve
  (bisection, Euler), square (Newton) or fall by 16 (Simpson, RK4 when h is
  halved) makes the idea of 'order' concrete. Always compare with an exact
  answer before trusting a method. Keep a card with the error formulas:
  Euler global O(h). Stress the difference between a badly conditioned
  PROBLEM and an unstable ALGORITHM, with the quadratic formula and the
  matrix [[1, 1], [1, 1.0001]] as the two standard examples. Harder: prove
  that Simpson's rule is exact for cubics and derive its error by Peano
  kernels; prove that the secant order is the golden ratio; show that
  Gauss nodes are the roots of Legendre polynomials; derive the stability
  region of RK4 in the complex plane; implement Gaussian elimination with
  partial pivoting and measure its growth factor; prove that Gauss-Seidel
  converges for symmetric positive definite matrices; and compare QR with
  the normal equations for an ill-conditioned least squares problem.

================================================================================
TOPIC 10.35 - PROBABILITY THEORY II: JOINT DISTRIBUTIONS, MOMENT GENERATING
FUNCTIONS, LAW OF LARGE NUMBERS, CENTRAL LIMIT THEOREM
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - JOINT DISTRIBUTIONS: discrete (X, Y) has a JOINT PMF p(x, y) =
    f_X(x) = integral f(x, y) dy (integrate out the other variable, with the right
    limits when the support is not a rectangle).
    (rectangle) support. A triangular support (e.g. 0 < x < y < 1) always
    means DEPENDENT. Functions of independent variables are independent.
  - CONDITIONAL distributions: p_{Y|X}(y|x) = p(x, y)/p_X(x), f_{Y|X}(y|x) =
    f(x, y)/f_X(x). CONDITIONAL EXPECTATION E[Y|X] is a random variable;
    TOWER LAW E[E[Y|X]] = E[Y]; LAW OF TOTAL VARIANCE Var Y = E[Var(Y|X)] +
    independent. COVARIANCE Cov(X, Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y], bilinear;
    Var(aX + bY) = a^2Var X + b^2Var Y + 2ab Cov(X, Y). CORRELATION
  - TRANSFORMATIONS: for (U, V) = T(X, Y) one-to-one,
    f_{X+Y}(z) = integral f_X(x)f_Y(z - x) dx (CONVOLUTION) for independent X, Y.
    MIN/MAX of iid: P(max <= z) = F(z)^n, P(min > z) = (1 - F(z))^n; the min of
  - MOMENT GENERATING FUNCTION M_X(t) = E[e^(tX)] (finite near 0):
    e^(mut + sigma^2t^2/2); Uniform(a, b) (e^(bt) - e^(at))/(t(b - a)). Hence sums of
    independent Poissons are Poisson, of normals normal, of n Exp(lambda) Gamma(n, lambda),
  - INEQUALITIES: MARKOV P(X >= a) <= E[X]/a (X >= 0, a > 0); CHEBYSHEV
    P(|X - mu| >= ksigma) <= 1/k^2; CHERNOFF P(X >= a) <= min_t e^(-ta)M(t).
    points of F); convergence in distribution to a CONSTANT implies in
    probability. Convergence in probability does not imply E X_n -> E X.
    error ~ sigma/sqrtn). Fails for the Cauchy distribution (no mean).
    (np, n(1 - p) >= 10, say) and Poisson(lambda) (lambda large) with CONTINUITY
    CORRECTION +/-0.5. Proof idea: MGF of the standardised sum

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A fair coin is tossed three times. X = number of heads in the first two
    tosses, Y = total number of heads. Find the joint pmf, the marginals,
    whether X and Y are independent.
    Answer: p(0, 0) = p(0, 1) = 1/8, p(1, 1) = p(1, 2) = 1/4, p(2, 2) =
    Y = 2: X = 1 w.p. 2/3, X = 2 w.p. 1/3 (E[X|Y = 2] = 4/3). Dependent.
    Teacher explains: Write Y = X + T with T the third toss, independent of X.
    P(X = 0, 1, 2) = 1/4, 1/2, 1/4 and Y = X or X + 1 with probability 1/2
    each:
                Y = 0   Y = 1   Y = 2   Y = 3  |  p_X
       X = 0     1/8     1/8      0       0    |  1/4
       X = 1      0      1/4     1/4      0    |  1/2
       X = 2      0       0      1/8     1/8   |  1/4
       p_Y       1/8     3/8     3/8     1/8   |   1
    Marginals are row and column sums. E X = 1, E Y = 3/2,
    (check: Cov(X, X + T) = Var X + Cov(X, T) = 1/2 + 0). Var X = 1/2,
    column Y = 2 by p_Y(2) = 3/8: (1/4)/(3/8) = 2/3 and (1/8)/(3/8) = 1/3, so
    p_X(0)p_Y(2) = 3/32 != 0 (one zero cell with nonzero marginals is enough).
    Common mistakes: using the conditional table without renormalising;
    thinking Cov > 0 needs a causal link. Now you try: E[X | Y = y] for each
    y. (0, 1/3, 4/3, 2, i.e. 2y/3)

D2. Let f(x, y) = c(x + y) for 0 <= x, y <= 1. Find c, the marginals,
    independent?
    Answer: c = 1; f_X(x) = x + 1/2; P(X + Y <= 1) = 1/3; P(X > 1/2) = 5/8;
    Teacher explains: Normalise:
       integral _0^1integral _0^1 (x + y) dy dx = integral _0^1 (x + 1/2) dx = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1,  so c = 1
    Marginal: f_X(x) = integral _0^1 (x + y) dy = x + 1/2, and by symmetry f_Y(y) = y + 1/2.
    f_X f_Y = (x + 1/2)(y + 1/2) != x + y (try x = y = 0): DEPENDENT. For the
    triangle x + y <= 1 let y run from 0 to 1 - x:
       integral _0^1 integral _0^{1-x} (x + y) dy dx = integral _0^1 [x(1 - x) + (1 - x)^2/2] dx
                                 = 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3
    P(X > 1/2) = integral _{1/2}^1 (x + 1/2) dx = [x^2/2 + x/2] from 1/2 to 1 = 1 - 3/8
    = 5/8. Moments:
       E X = integral  x(x + 1/2) dx = 1/3 + 1/4 = 7/12
       E X^2 = integral  x^2(x + 1/2) dx = 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12,  Var X = 5/12 - 49/144 = 11/144
    Common mistakes: forgetting to use the limits of the region in
    P(X + Y <= 1); declaring independence because the formula 'looks
    separable'. Now you try: f(x, y) = 4xy on the unit square. (c = 4;
    f_X = 2x; independent; P(X + Y <= 1) = 1/6)

D3. (X, Y) is uniform on the triangle 0 < x < y < 1. Find f(x, y), both
    marginals, f_{Y|X}, E[Y | X], and verify the tower law and the law of
    total variance for Y.
    Answer: f = 2; f_X(x) = 2(1 - x), f_Y(y) = 2y; Y | X = x ~ U(x, 1),
    E[Y|X] = (1 + X)/2; E Y = 2/3 both ways; Var Y = 1/24 + 1/72 = 1/18.
    Teacher explains: Area 1/2, so f = 2 on the triangle. Integrate out with
    the correct limits (draw the triangle!):
       f_X(x) = integral _x^1 2 dy = 2(1 - x),   f_Y(y) = integral _0^y 2 dx = 2y
    Conditional: f_{Y|X}(y|x) = 2/(2(1 - x)) = 1/(1 - x) on x < y < 1: uniform on
    (x, 1). Hence E[Y | X = x] = (1 + x)/2 and Var(Y | X = x) = (1 - x)^2/12.
    TOWER: E X = integral  2x(1 - x) dx = 1/3, so E[E[Y|X]] = (1 + 1/3)/2 = 2/3, and
       E[Var(Y|X)] = E[(1 - X)^2]/12 = (integral  2(1 - x)^3 dx)/12 = (1/2)/12 = 1/24
       Var(E[Y|X]) = Var X/4;  E X^2 = 1/6, Var X = 1/6 - 1/9 = 1/18;  -> 1/72
       sum = 1/24 + 1/72 = 1/18
    is not a rectangle, so X and Y are dependent (f_X f_Y = 4y(1 - x) != 2).
    Common mistakes: integrating over [0, 1] for both variables; forgetting
    that E[Y|X] is a function of X. Now you try: N ~ Poisson(3) customers,
    each spends X ~ Exp with mean 2 independently; mean and variance of the

    and derive Var(aX + bY). Show that uncorrelated does not imply
    independent. Compute Var(2X - 3Y + 1) when Var X = 4, Var Y = 1,
    Cov(X, Y) = -1.
    Answer: proof below; Var(2X - 3Y + 1) = 37.
    Teacher explains: Bilinearity: Cov(aX + bY, Z) = a Cov(X, Z) + b Cov(Y, Z)
    and Cov(X, X) = Var X, so
       Var(aX + bY + c) = a^2Var X + b^2Var Y + 2ab Cov(X, Y)
    (constants do not change variance). Here
    CAUCHY-SCHWARZ: with centred X_0 = X - mu_X, Y_0 = Y - mu_Y, the quadratic
       q(t) = E[(Y_0 - tX_0)^2] = Var Y - 2t Cov + t^2 Var X >= 0 for all t
    means q(t_0) = 0 for some t_0, so Y_0 = t_0X_0 with probability 1: Y = aX + b
    Y = X^2. E X = 0, E[XY] = E X^3 = 0, so Cov = 0; but P(X = 0, Y = 1) = 0 !=
    (1/3)(2/3): dependent. Correlation measures only LINEAR association.
    Common mistakes: Var(X - Y) = Var X - Var Y (the variances ADD);
    forgetting the factor 2 on the covariance. Now you try: Var X = 4,

D5. X, Y are independent Exp(1). Find the joint density of U = X + Y and
    V = X/(X + Y), and deduce their distributions. State the Jacobian method.
    Answer: f_{U,V}(u, v) = u e^(-u) for u > 0, 0 < v < 1: U ~ Gamma(2, 1),
    V ~ U(0, 1), and U, V are independent.
    Teacher explains: METHOD: if (u, v) = T(x, y) is one-to-one and smooth
    with inverse x(u, v), y(u, v), then
    Invert: x = uv, y = u(1 - v). Jacobian:
         = -uv - u(1 - v) = -u,    |J| = u
    It factorises on a rectangle: U has density u e^(-u) (Gamma(2, 1)), V is
    uniform on (0, 1), and they are independent. Meaning: given the total
    waiting time of two Poisson arrivals, the first arrival is uniformly
    placed. The same method with polar coordinates proves the Box-Muller
    region. Now you try: U = X + Y, V = X - Y for iid N(0, 1). (|J| = 1/2;
    U, V independent N(0, 2))

D6. (a) Find the density of the sum of two independent U(0, 1) variables by

       0 <= z <= 1:  integral _0^z 1 dx = z;       1 <= z <= 2:  integral _{z-1}^1 1 dx = 2 - z
    A triangle: the sum of two flat distributions is already peaked (the
       P(min > t) = (e^(-t/1000))^3 = e^(-0.003t)
    so min ~ Exp(0.003), mean 1000/3 ~ 333.3 h, and P(min > 500) = e^(-1.5) ~
    0.2231. MAX: P(max <= t) = (1 - e^(-t/1000))^3. For the mean use

D10. Prove Markov's and Chebyshev's inequalities. For X ~ Exp(1) compare the
     bounds for P(X >= 3) with the exact value. How many tosses of a coin
     guarantee (by Chebyshev) that the proportion of heads is within 0.05 of
     p with probability at least 0.95? Compare with the CLT answer.
     Answer: Markov 1/3, Chebyshev 1/4, exact e^-^3 ~ 0.0498. Chebyshev:
     n >= 2000; CLT: n >= 385.
     expectations: E X >= a P(X >= a). CHEBYSHEV: apply Markov to (X - mu)^2 with
     a = k^2sigma^2:
        P(|X - mu| >= ksigma) = P((X - mu)^2 >= k^2sigma^2) <= sigma^2/(k^2sigma^2) = 1/k^2
     Exp(1) has mu = sigma = 1:
        Markov:     P(X >= 3) <= 1/3
        Chebyshev:  P(X >= 3) <= P(|X - 1| >= 2) <= 1/4
        exact:      e^-^3 ~ 0.0498
     The bounds are crude because they hold for EVERY distribution with that
     384.16, so n = 385. Chebyshev is guaranteed but wasteful; the CLT is
     approximate but realistic. Common mistakes: using Markov for a
     variable that can be negative; forgetting that Chebyshev bounds a
     TWO-sided event. Now you try: E X = 5, Var X = 4: bound P(|X - 5| >= 4)
     and P(1 < X < 9) from below. (<= 1/4; >= 3/4)

D12. State the central limit theorem and sketch its proof with MGFs. Use it
     with a continuity correction for P(X >= 60) when X ~ Bin(100, 0.5), and
     for P(S <= 330) when S is the total of 100 fair dice.
     Answer: (S_n - nmu)/(sigmasqrtn) -> N(0, 1). P(X >= 60) ~ P(Z >= 1.9) ~ 0.0287
     Z_n = (S_n - nmu)/(sigmasqrtn) -> N(0, 1) in distribution, whatever the shape of the
     mean 0, variance 1, M_Y(s) = 1 + s^2/2 + o(s^2). Then
        M_{Z_n}(t) = [M_Y(t/sqrtn)]^n = [1 + t^2/(2n) + o(1/n)]^n -> e^(t^2/2)
     the N(0, 1) MGF; a continuity theorem turns MGF convergence into
     convergence in distribution. BINOMIAL: X = sum of 100 Bernoulli(0.5),
     mu = 50, sigma = 5. X is integer valued, so P(X >= 60) = P(X > 59.5):
        P(Z >= (59.5 - 50)/5) = P(Z >= 1.9) = 0.0287      (exact 0.0284)
     Without the correction, P(Z >= 2) = 0.0228, noticeably worse. DICE: one
     die has mu = 3.5, sigma^2 = 35/12; for 100 dice E S = 350, Var S = 291.67,
     sd 17.078:
     Common mistakes: dividing by sigma instead of sigmasqrtn (or sigma/sqrtn for a mean);
     applying the continuity correction in the wrong direction; using the
     CLT for n = 3 with a skewed distribution. Now you try: sum of 100 iid
     Exp(1): P(S > 110). (mu = 100, sigma = 10: P(Z > 1) ~ 0.1587)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always DRAW the support before integrating a joint density,
  shade the event, and write the limits from the picture; build joint pmf
  tables with row and column totals. Keep a one-page MGF table and practise
  'multiply and recognise'. For the CLT, drill the single recipe:
  mean nmu, variance nsigma^2, standardise, continuity correction if integer,
  emerging; running averages of coin tosses show the LLN (and that the
  deviation S_n - n/2 does NOT shrink). Harder: prove the tower law from the
  definition; derive the bivariate normal conditional density by completing
  Borel-Cantelli; prove Lyapunov's or Lindeberg's CLT; find the limit law of
  the maximum of n iid Exp(1) minus ln n (Gumbel); and show by a Cauchy
  example why the CLT needs a finite variance.

TOPIC 10.36 - MATHEMATICAL STATISTICS: ESTIMATION, MAXIMUM LIKELIHOOD,
HYPOTHESIS TESTING, CONFIDENCE INTERVALS, REGRESSION

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A RANDOM SAMPLE X_1, ..., X_n is iid from a model f(x; theta). A STATISTIC is a
    its standard deviation is the STANDARD ERROR (SE).
    for sigma^2 (the 1/n version has bias -sigma^2/n); S is biased for sigma. A biased
    estimator can have smaller MSE. RELATIVE EFFICIENCY = ratio of variances.
    estimator attaining it is EFFICIENT. Under regularity the MLE is
    means (pooled or not) and of proportions; PAIRED data: work with the
    differences. MEANING: the procedure covers the true theta in 95% of repeated
    n = (zsigma/E)^2 (for proportions (z/E)^2p(1 - p) <= (z/E)^2/4).
  - HYPOTHESIS TESTS: null H_0 and alternative H_1 (one- or two-sided); TEST
    STATISTIC; REJECTION REGION; TYPE I error (reject a true H_0, probability
    alpha = SIGNIFICANCE LEVEL); TYPE II error (accept a false H_0, probability beta);
    POWER = 1 - beta; P-VALUE = probability, under H_0, of a result at least as
    extreme as observed; reject when p <= alpha. A two-sided level-alpha test rejects
    theta_0 exactly when theta_0 is outside the 100(1 - alpha)% interval (DUALITY).
    'Not rejected' is not 'proved true'.
  - NEYMAN-PEARSON LEMMA: for simple H_0: theta = theta_0 vs H_1: theta = theta_1 the most
    powerful level-alpha test rejects when L(theta_1)/L(theta_0) > k. LIKELIHOOD RATIO TEST
  - STANDARD TESTS: z-test (sigma known or large n); one-sample, PAIRED and
    TWO-SAMPLE (pooled s_p^2 = ((n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2)/(n_1 + n_2 - 2), or
    parameters) and INDEPENDENCE in an r x c table (E = row total x column
    total/n, df = (r - 1)(c - 1)); expected counts should be >= 5.
    R^2 = SSR/SST = r^2 (r = S_xy/sqrt(S_xx S_yy)).
    UNBIASED ESTIMATOR (BLUE). Residual df = n - (number of beta's).

    (bias, MSE, consistency); give the numbers for n = 10.
    Answer: E S^2 = sigma^2. T_1: unbiased, MSE theta^2/(3n); T_2: bias -theta/(n + 1), MSE
    2theta^2/((n + 1)(n + 2)); T_3: unbiased, MSE theta^2/(n(n + 2)). For n = 10:
    theta^2/30 ~ 0.0333theta^2, theta^2/66 ~ 0.0152theta^2, theta^2/120 ~ 0.0083theta^2. All consistent;
    T_3 is best.
    so dividing by n - 1 gives E S^2 = sigma^2. (We lose one degree of freedom
    P(M <= m) = (m/theta)^n, density nm^n^-^1/theta^n, so
       E M = ntheta/(n + 1),   E M^2 = ntheta^2/(n + 2),   Var M = ntheta^2/((n + 1)^2(n + 2))
       MSE(M) = Var M + theta^2/(n + 1)^2 = 2theta^2/((n + 1)(n + 2))
    n = 10: 0.0333theta^2, 0.0152theta^2, 0.0083theta^2. T_2 is biased yet beats the
    unbiased T_1; T_3 removes the bias and is best (its MSE falls like 1/n^2,
    not 1/n). All MSEs -> 0, so all three are CONSISTENT. Common mistakes:
    thinking 'unbiased' means 'good'; forgetting the bias term in the MSE.
    Now you try: is T = (X_1 + 2X_2)/3 unbiased for mu, and what is its

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: insist on the same three lines for every problem: MODEL (what
  is random, which parameter), PIVOT or TEST STATISTIC with its
  distribution under H_0, and CONCLUSION in words. Simulate 100 confidence
  intervals on a screen and count how many miss the true mean; simulate a
  test many times under H_0 to see that it rejects about 5% of the time.
  always write ln L before differentiating and check the support. For
  regression, compute S_xx, S_xy, S_yy in a table and draw the scatter plot
  and the Rao-Blackwell theorem; show that the LRT for a normal mean is the
  t-test; derive Wilks' theorem in one dimension by Taylor expansion; prove
  Gauss-Markov in matrix form; and explore multiple testing (Bonferroni) and
  Bayesian credible intervals as alternatives to the frequentist ideas.

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - BAYESIAN VIEW: the parameter theta is treated as random. A PRIOR density pi(theta)
    expresses belief before the data; the LIKELIHOOD L(theta; x) = f(x | theta) comes
    from the model; BAYES' THEOREM gives the POSTERIOR
    where m(x) = integral  f(x | theta)pi(theta) dtheta is the MARGINAL LIKELIHOOD (evidence). Work
    'up to proportionality' and recognise the kernel of a known density.
  - CONJUGATE PRIORS (posterior in the same family as the prior):
       Binomial(n, theta), prior Beta(a, b)  -> Beta(a + k, b + n - k)
       a precision-weighted average of prior mean and sample mean.
    (Gamma(alpha, beta) uses the RATE beta: mean alpha/beta, variance alpha/beta^2.) Beta(a, b) has mean
    a/(a + b), mode (a - 1)/(a + b - 2) for a, b > 1, variance
    ab/((a + b)^2(a + b + 1)).
  - POINT ESTIMATES are BAYES RULES for a loss: POSTERIOR MEAN (squared loss),
    POSTERIOR MEDIAN (absolute loss), POSTERIOR MODE = MAP (0-1 loss). A
    HPD = highest posterior density, the shortest). The POSTERIOR PREDICTIVE
    is f(y | x) = integral  f(y | theta)pi(theta | x) dtheta (Beta-binomial: P(next success) =
    Jeffreys gives Beta(1/2, 1/2) for a binomial theta, lambda^(-1/2) for a Poisson mean.
  - BAYESIAN TESTING: POSTERIOR ODDS = BAYES FACTOR x PRIOR ODDS, with
    B_0_1 = m_0(x)/m_1(x). For simple hypotheses B_0_1 is the likelihood ratio.
    Bayes factors and p-values can disagree strongly (LINDLEY's paradox: a
    the true theta and the prior's influence vanishes.
    R^2 = ESS/TSS = 1 - RSS/TSS (= r^2 in simple regression); ADJUSTED
    t = (b - beta_0)/SE(b) ~ t(n - 2); overall F = (ESS/(p - 1))/(RSS/(n - p));
    NESTED F = ((RSS_red - RSS_full)/q)/(RSS_full/(n - p)) ~ F(q, n - p); in
    simple regression F = t^2. CONFIDENCE interval for the mean response at x_0:
  - MODELLING: a factor with k levels needs k - 1 DUMMY variables (k dummies
    plots for curvature, non-constant variance, outliers; MULTICOLLINEARITY
    of 1 + theta_1z + ... + thetaqz^q lie outside the unit circle. AR(p):
    cuts off after lag p for AR(p); the ACF of AR decays geometrically.

D1. A coin with unknown head-probability theta has prior Beta(2, 2). In 10 tosses
    it shows 7 heads. Derive the posterior, and find the posterior mean, mode
    and variance, the MLE, and the probability that the next toss is a head.
    Answer: theta | x ~ Beta(9, 5). Mean 9/14 ~ 0.643, mode 2/3 ~ 0.667, variance
    3/196 ~ 0.0153; MLE 0.7; P(next head | data) = 9/14 ~ 0.643.
    Teacher explains: Write prior and likelihood, dropping constants that do
    not involve theta:
    theta^8(1 - theta)^4 is the kernel of Beta(9, 5), so the constant must be 1/B(9, 5);
    no integration is needed. In general Beta(a, b) -> Beta(a + k, b + n - k):
    'a counts prior heads, b prior tails'. Summaries of Beta(9, 5):
       mean = 9/14 ~ 0.643       mode = (9 - 1)/(9 + 5 - 2) = 8/12 = 2/3
    The MLE k/n = 0.7 ignores the prior; the posterior mean
    is a weighted average of prior mean 1/2 and MLE 0.7 with weights prior
    'sample size' a + b = 4 and data size n = 10: the SHRINKAGE towards the
    prior. Predictive: P(head | x) = integral  theta pi(theta | x) dtheta = E(theta | x) = 9/14. Note
    the mode with a FLAT prior Beta(1, 1) would equal the MLE 0.7. Common
    mistakes: adding k to b; forgetting that Beta(a, b) has exponents a - 1,
    b - 1; quoting the mode when the question asks for the Bayes estimate
    under squared loss (the mean). Now you try: prior Beta(1, 1), 3 successes
    in 5 trials. Posterior and its mean? (Beta(4, 3), mean 4/7 ~ 0.571)

D3. Counts of accidents per week are Poisson(lambda). The prior is Gamma(3, 1)
    (shape 3, rate 1). Five weeks give 2, 4, 3, 5, 1. Find the posterior, its
    mean, mode and variance, and the posterior predictive probability of no
    accident next week. Which estimate minimises expected squared error, and
    which absolute error?
    Answer: lambda | x ~ Gamma(18, 6); mean 3, mode 17/6 ~ 2.833, variance 1/2;
    P(Y = 0 | x) = (6/7)^1^8 ~ 0.0624. Squared loss: the posterior mean 3;
    absolute loss: the posterior median (~ 2.94).
    Teacher explains:
    so the prior acts like beta = 1 extra week with alpha = 3 extra accidents.
       mean alpha/beta = 18/6 = 3,  mode (alpha - 1)/beta = 17/6,  variance alpha/beta^2 = 18/36
    Predictive for next week: P(Y = 0 | x) = E(e^(-lambda) | x)
    (the Gamma integral with rate 7). Compare the 'plug-in' answer e^(-3) ~
    0.0498: the predictive is larger because it allows for uncertainty in lambda
    (the predictive is NEGATIVE BINOMIAL, more spread than Poisson). Why mean
    for squared loss: E((lambda - d)^2 | x) = Var(lambda | x) + (E(lambda | x) - d)^2, least at
    d = E(lambda | x). For absolute loss the derivative of E|lambda - d| is
    P(lambda < d) - P(lambda > d), zero at the median. Common mistakes: using the
    SCALE parametrisation (then mean = alphatheta) without saying so; adding the
    number of observations to alpha. Now you try: prior Gamma(2, 1), data 0, 1,
    0, 2. (Gamma(5, 5), posterior mean 1)

D4. A coin is tossed 12 times and shows 9 heads. Compare H_0 : theta = 1/2 with

    ~ 0.146. The data favour H_1 only weakly.
    Teacher explains: The Bayes factor compares how well each hypothesis
    PREDICTED the data:
       m_0(x) = C(12, 9)(1/2)^1^2 = 220/4096 ~ 0.0537
    every k is equally likely). So
    Posterior odds = B_0_1 x prior odds = 0.698 x 1, so
       P(H_0 | x) = 0.698/(1 + 0.698) = 2860/6956 ~ 0.411.
    The p-value: P(X >= 9) + P(X <= 3) = 2(220 + 66 + 12 + 1)/4096 = 598/4096
    ~ 0.146. Here both say 'not much evidence', but in large samples a
    p-value of 0.05 can go with P(H_0 | x) > 1/2 (Lindley's paradox): the
    p-value measures surprise under H_0 alone, the Bayes factor weighs H_0
    against a specific H_1. Rough scale (Jeffreys/Kass-Raftery): B_1_0 of 1-3
    'barely worth mentioning', 3-20 positive, 20-150 strong, > 150 very
    strong. Common mistakes: reading the p-value as P(H_0 | x); using an
    improper prior under H_1 (the Bayes factor is then undefined). Now you
    favouring H_0)
