WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
    equality/inequality CONSTRAINTS. FORMULATION: name the decision variables,
    write the objective, every constraint, and the sign conditions x >= 0.
  - The FEASIBLE REGION {x : Ax <= b, x >= 0} is a convex POLYHEDRON; its corner
    points are VERTICES (extreme points). FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM: if an LP has an
    optimal solution it has one at a vertex; an LP is either INFEASIBLE,
    UNBOUNDED, or has an optimum. In two variables solve GRAPHICALLY: draw the
    region, then slide the objective line (or evaluate every vertex).
  - With A of size m x n and rank m, a BASIC SOLUTION sets n - m NONBASIC
    variables to 0 and solves for the m BASIC ones; a BASIC FEASIBLE SOLUTION
    (BFS: all >= 0) is exactly a vertex. There are at most C(n, m) of them. A
    DEGENERATE BFS has a basic variable equal to 0.
    all objective-row entries are >= 0, STOP: optimal; (2) otherwise the
    ENTERING variable has the most negative entry; (3) RATIO TEST: among rows
    with positive entry in that column, the smallest rhs/entry picks the
    LEAVING variable (if no entry is positive the LP is UNBOUNDED); (4)
    PIVOT: make the pivot 1 and clear its column; repeat. A zero reduced cost
    for a nonbasic variable at the optimum signals MULTIPLE OPTIMA.
    Degeneracy can cause CYCLING; BLAND'S RULE (smallest index) prevents it.
  - ARTIFICIAL VARIABLES for >= and = rows: TWO-PHASE method (Phase I
    The dual of the dual is the primal.
    both optimal). STRONG DUALITY: if either has a finite optimum, both do
    COMPLEMENTARY SLACKNESS: feasible x, y are optimal iff
  - SENSITIVITY: the optimal dual values are SHADOW PRICES: the increase in
    slack columns of the final tableau. A new activity with column a and
    balls, polyhedra, cones of PSD matrices are convex; intersections of
    convex sets are convex; unions usually are not. CONVEX FUNCTION:
    f(lambdax + (1 - lambda)y) <= lambdaf(x) + (1 - lambda)f(y) (JENSEN); STRICTLY convex with <
    for x != y; f concave iff -f convex.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE

D1. A firm makes doors (x) and windows (y). Profit is 3 per door and 5 per
    window (thousands). Plant 1 has 4 hours: a door needs 1 h. Plant 2 has 12
    hours: a window needs 2 h. Plant 3 has 18 hours: a door needs 3 h, a
    window 2 h. Formulate the LP and solve it graphically.
    Answer: max z = 3x + 5y s.t. x <= 4, 2y <= 12, 3x + 2y <= 18, x, y >= 0.
    Optimum x = 2, y = 6, z = 36.
    Teacher explains: Step 1, variables: x doors, y windows per week. Step 2,
    objective: profit 3x + 5y. Step 3, one constraint per resource, and
    x, y >= 0 because negative production is meaningless. Draw the lines
    x = 4, y = 6, 3x + 2y = 18 (through (6, 0) and (0, 9)); the feasible
    region is the pentagon with vertices
       (0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 3), (2, 6), (0, 6)
    ((4, 3): x = 4 in 3x + 2y = 18; (2, 6): y = 6 in 3x + 2y = 18). Evaluate:
       z(0, 0) = 0,  z(4, 0) = 12,  z(4, 3) = 27,  z(2, 6) = 36,  z(0, 6) = 30
    The best is 36 at (2, 6). Equivalently slide the ISO-PROFIT line
    3x + 5y = k (slope -3/5) upward: the last point it touches is (2, 6),
    where the lines y = 6 (slope 0) and 3x + 2y = 18 (slope -3/2) meet; -3/5
    lies between them, confirming the vertex. At the optimum plants 2 and 3
    are fully used (BINDING constraints) and plant 1 has 2 hours spare
    (SLACK 2). Common mistakes: forgetting x, y >= 0; checking only the
    intercepts; reading off a point that is not feasible. Now you try: max
    x + y s.t. x + 2y <= 4, 3x + y <= 6, x, y >= 0. (x = 8/5, y = 6/5, z = 14/5)

D2. (a) Put in standard form: min 2x_1 - x_2 s.t. x_1 + x_2 >= 2, x_1 - x_2 <= 3,
    x_1 >= 0, x_2 free. (b) Prove that if a linear objective attains a maximum
    over a bounded polyhedron, it attains it at a vertex. (c) Give
    two-variable examples of an infeasible LP, an unbounded LP, and an LP with
    multiple optima.
    below.
    Teacher explains: (a) Four moves: min -> max by negating the objective;
    <= gets a SLACK s_1 added. The optimal value of the original problem is
    MINUS the maximum found. (b) A bounded polyhedron P is the convex hull of
    idea uses vertices plus extreme rays; this is why the simplex method may
    move only between vertices.) (c) INFEASIBLE: x + y <= 2 and x + y >= 3.
    MULTIPLE OPTIMA: max 2x + 4y s.t. x + 2y <= 5, x + y <= 4, x, y >= 0: the
    objective is parallel to x + 2y = 5 and every point of the segment from
    (0, 5/2) to (3, 1) gives 10. Note an unbounded REGION does not mean an
    unbounded LP: min x + y over the same region has optimum 0 at (0, 0).
    allows x_2 <= 0); forgetting to change the sign of the final answer after
    min -> max. Now you try: how many basic solutions can
    x_1 + x_2 + s_1 = 4, x_1 + 3x_2 + s_2 = 6 have, and how many are feasible?
    (C(4, 2) = 6; 4 feasible: (0, 0), (4, 0), (3, 1), (0, 2) in (x_1, x_2))

D3. Solve the LP of D1 by the simplex method, showing every tableau, and read
    off the optimal dual values.
    Answer: two pivots (x_2 enters/s_2 leaves, then x_1 enters/s_3 leaves);
    x_1 = 2, x_2 = 6, s_1 = 2, z = 36; dual values y = (0, 3/2, 1).
    Teacher explains: Add slacks: x_1 + s_1 = 4, 2x_2 + s_2 = 12,
    3x_1 + 2x_2 + s_3 = 18, and write z - 3x_1 - 5x_2 = 0 as the bottom row.
       basis   x_1    x_2    s_1    s_2    s_3  | rhs
       s_1       1     0     1     0     0  |   4
       s_2       0     2     0     1     0  |  12
       s_3       3     2     0     0     1  |  18
       z       -3    -5     0     0     0  |   0
    Start: BFS x = 0, z = 0. Most negative: -5, so x_2 ENTERS. Ratios:
    s_1 row has 0 (skip), s_2: 12/2 = 6, s_3: 18/2 = 9. Smallest 6: s_2 LEAVES;
    the pivot is 2. Divide row 2 by 2, then clear the x_2 column:
       s_1       1     0     1     0     0  |   4
       x_2       0     1     0    1/2    0  |   6
       s_3       3     0     0    -1     1  |   6
       z       -3     0     0    5/2    0  |  30
    Now x_1 enters (-3). Ratios: s_1: 4/1 = 4, s_3: 6/3 = 2, so s_3 leaves,
    pivot 3:
       s_1       0     0     1    1/3  -1/3 |   2
       x_2       0     1     0    1/2    0  |   6
       x_1       1     0     0   -1/3   1/3 |   2
       z        0     0     0    3/2    1  |  36
    No negative entries remain: optimal, x_1 = 2, x_2 = 6, z = 36 (the vertex
    found in D1; the path was (0, 0) -> (0, 6) -> (2, 6)). The entries under
    Why the ratio test: x_1 may increase only until the first basic variable
    hits 0; the smallest ratio is that point. Common mistakes: choosing the
    leaving row by the largest ratio or including rows with 0 or negative
    entries; forgetting to update the z-row. Now you try: max 2x_1 + 3x_2 s.t.
    x_1 + x_2 <= 4, x_1 + 3x_2 <= 6, x_1 <= 3. (x_2 in/s_2 out, x_1 in/s_1 out;
    x = (3, 1), z = 9)

D4. Use the two-phase method to solve min z = 2x_1 + 3x_2 s.t. x_1 + x_2 >= 4,
    x_1 + 3x_2 >= 6, x_1, x_2 >= 0.
    Answer: Phase I reaches w = 0 at x = (3, 1); Phase II confirms it is
    optimal: min z = 9 at (3, 1).
    Teacher explains: The origin is infeasible, so there is no obvious
    starting BFS. Subtract surpluses and add ARTIFICIALS:
       x_1 + x_2 - e_1 + a_1 = 4,    x_1 + 3x_2 - e_2 + a_2 = 6
    Phase I: minimise w = a_1 + a_2, i.e. maximise -w. Expressing w in the
    nonbasic variables, w = 10 - 2x_1 - 4x_2 + e_1 + e_2, gives the bottom row:
       basis   x_1    x_2    e_1    e_2    a_1    a_2  | rhs
       a_1       1     1    -1     0     1     0  |   4
       a_2       1     3     0    -1     0     1  |   6
       -w      -2    -4     1     1     0     0  | -10
    x_2 enters; ratios 4/1 = 4, 6/3 = 2: a_2 leaves.
       a_1      2/3    0    -1    1/3    1   -1/3 |   2
       x_2      1/3    1     0   -1/3    0    1/3 |   2
       -w     -2/3    0     1   -1/3    0    4/3 |  -2
    x_1 enters; ratios 2/(2/3) = 3, 2/(1/3) = 6: a_1 leaves.
       x_1       1     0   -3/2   1/2   3/2  -1/2 |   3
       x_2       0     1    1/2  -1/2  -1/2   1/2 |   1
       -w       0     0     0     0     1     1  |   0
    w = 0: a feasible BFS x = (3, 1) exists. Phase II: delete the artificial
    columns, restore the real objective max -z = -2x_1 - 3x_2 (row 2, 3, 0, 0),
    and price out the basic columns (subtract 2 x row x_1 and 3 x row x_2):
       -z       0     0    3/2   1/2  |  -9
    All entries >= 0, so the BFS is optimal: min z = 9. The entries 3/2, 1/2
    under the surplus columns are the dual values (see D6). If Phase I had
    ended with w > 0, the LP would be INFEASIBLE. Common mistakes: forgetting
    to express w in terms of the nonbasic variables (the bottom row must have
    zeros under basic columns); using a surplus as a starting basic variable
    (it would be -4 < 0). Now you try: min x_1 + x_2 s.t. 2x_1 + x_2 >= 4,
    x_1 + 2x_2 >= 4. (x = (4/3, 4/3), z = 8/3)

D5. Show how the simplex method detects (a) unboundedness, using max x_1 + x_2
    s.t. x_1 - x_2 <= 1, -x_1 + x_2 <= 2; (b) multiple optima; (c) degeneracy, using
    max 3x_1 + 2x_2 s.t. x_1 + x_2 <= 4, 2x_1 + x_2 <= 8, x_1 <= 4. Explain cycling and
    Bland's rule.
    Answer: (a) after one pivot x_2 has reduced cost -2 but no positive entry
    in its column: unbounded along x = (1 + t, t). (b) a nonbasic variable
    with reduced cost 0 at the optimum. (c) three-way tie in the ratio test;
    the new BFS x = (4, 0) has basic variables equal to 0; optimum z = 12.
    Teacher explains: (a) Tableau with slacks s_1, s_2; x_1 enters (tie -1, -1,
    take the lower index); the only positive entry in its column is in row
    s_1 (ratio 1). After the pivot:
       x_1       1    -1     1     0  |   1
       s_2       0     0     1     1  |   3
       z        0    -2     1     0  |   1
    x_2 should enter (-2), but its column (-1, 0) has no positive entry: no
    constraint stops x_2 growing. Setting x_2 = t keeps x_1 = 1 + t, s_2 = 3,
    has reduced cost 0, pivoting it in changes the vertex but not z: for
    max 2x + 4y in D2(c) the optimum (0, 5/2) has a zero entry for x, and
    entering x leads to (3, 1). (c) For x_1 the ratios are 4/1, 8/2, 4/1: a
    TIE. Whichever row leaves, the other two basic variables become 0:
    x = (4, 0) is a DEGENERATE vertex, where three constraint lines meet.
    Here z = 12 is already optimal (x_2 has reduced cost +1). In general a
    degenerate pivot can leave z unchanged (a step of length 0), and a
    sequence of such pivots can return to an earlier basis: CYCLING.
    BLAND'S RULE (enter the lowest-index improving variable, break ratio
    ties by lowest index) provably prevents cycling. Common mistakes:
    declaring unboundedness when the entering column has a positive entry
    somewhere; thinking degeneracy means infeasibility. Now you try: max
    x_1 + 3x_2 s.t. -x_1 + x_2 <= 2, x_1 - 2x_2 <= 4. (x_2 enters, s_1 leaves; then
    x_1 has reduced cost -4 with column (-1, -1): unbounded)

D6. State the rules for writing the dual, prove weak duality for
    dual of D4 graphically, checking that the optimal values agree.
    Answer: dual of D4: max 4y_1 + 6y_2 s.t. y_1 + y_2 <= 2, y_1 + 3y_2 <= 3,
    y >= 0; optimum y = (3/2, 1/2), value 9 = min of D4.
    Teacher explains: Each primal constraint gets a dual variable (a price);
    each primal variable gives a dual constraint. Transpose A, swap b and c,
    swap max and min; the signs follow the table
       max problem          min problem
    Weak duality: for x feasible in (P) and y feasible in (D),
    a max with <= constraints and y >= 0:
       max 4y_1 + 6y_2  s.t.  y_1 + y_2 <= 2,  y_1 + 3y_2 <= 3,  y >= 0
    Vertices: (0, 0): 0; (2, 0): 8; (0, 1): 6; intersection of the two lines:
    and y = (3/2, 1/2) are exactly the numbers under e_1, e_2 in D4's final
    tableau. Interpretation: if the constraints are nutrient requirements
    and x amounts of foods, y are the prices a pill-maker can charge per unit
    nutrient. Common mistakes: forgetting to transpose A; mixing up the sign
    rules for >= constraints in a max problem. Now you try: write the dual of
    max 3x_1 + 5x_2 s.t. x_1 <= 4, 2x_2 <= 12, 3x_1 + 2x_2 <= 18, x >= 0.

D7. State the strong duality theorem and prove complementary slackness. Use
    it to verify that x = (5/2, 3/2, 0) is optimal for max 3x_1 + 2x_2 + 4x_3
    s.t. x_1 + x_2 + 2x_3 <= 4, 2x_1 + 3x_3 <= 5, 2x_1 + x_2 + 3x_3 <= 7, x >= 0.
    Answer: optimal, with dual y = (2, 1/2, 0) and common value 21/2.
    Teacher explains: STRONG DUALITY: if (P) has an optimal solution then so
    does (D) and the values are equal (proof: the final simplex tableau
    SLACKNESS: for feasible x, y the proof of weak duality gives
    only on a fully used resource, a positive activity only if it breaks
    5 (tight); row 3: 5 + 3/2 = 13/2 < 7 (slack), so y_3 = 0. x_1, x_2 > 0, so
    the first two dual constraints are tight:
    optimal. If the forced y had failed feasibility, x would NOT be optimal.
    constraints give y_3 = 5/2, y_1 = 3 - 15/2 < 0: not dual feasible, so no)

    0 (y = 6) and -3/2 (3x + 2y = 18): 0 <= c_1/5 <= 3/2, i.e. 0 <= c_1 <= 7.5.
    in resources at shadow prices; profit 4 > 5/2, so reduced cost -3/2 < 0
    and bringing it in raises z. At profit 2 it would not be worth it. Common
    mistakes: applying a shadow price outside its range (at b_2 = 20 the
    answer is not 36 + 3); forgetting that shadow prices of nonbinding
    constraints are 0. Now you try: range of b_3 keeping the same basis?

D9. Define convex sets and functions. Prove: (a) the intersection of convex
    sets is convex; (b) a sublevel set {x : f(x) <= c} of a convex f is
    convex; (c) the maximum of convex functions is convex. Then decide by the
    Hessian whether f = x^2 + xy + y^2, g = x^2 - y^2, h = x^2/y (y > 0) and
    Answer: proofs below; f convex (strictly), g not, h convex, k convex.
    [x, y], so the intersection does. (b) If f(x), f(y) <= c then
       f(lambdax + (1 - lambda)y) <= lambdaf(x) + (1 - lambda)f(y) <= lambdac + (1 - lambda)c = c.
    for 2 x 2: diagonal entries >= 0 and determinant >= 0):
       f: H = [[2, 1], [1, 2]], det 3 > 0, trace 4 > 0   -> PD, strictly convex
       g: H = [[2, 0], [0, -2]], eigenvalues +/-2          -> neither (a saddle)
       h: H = (2/y^3)[[y^2, -xy], [-xy, x^2]], det 0, diagonal >= 0 -> PSD, convex
          0 and 2p(1 - p) >= 0                             -> convex
    k is the 'soft maximum', a smooth convex approximation of max(x, y).
    Note: a convex function need not be differentiable (|x|) and a function
    with convex sublevel sets need not be convex (x^3 on R). Common mistakes:
    'det >= 0 so PSD' without checking the diagonal ([[-1, 0], [0, -1]] has
    det 1); thinking the union of convex sets is convex. Now you try: is
    x^2 + 4xy + y^2 convex? (No: H = [[2, 4], [4, 2]] has eigenvalues 6, -2)

D10. (a) Prove that for convex f every local minimum is a global minimum, and
     that a strictly convex f has at most one minimiser. (b) Minimise
     f(x, y) = x^2 + 5y^2 by gradient descent from (5, 1) with alpha = 0.05, by
     exact line search, and by Newton's method. (c) Apply Newton to
     f(x) = e^x - 2x from x_0 = 0.
     Answer: (a) proofs below. (b) GD: (4.5, 0.5), (4.05, 0.25),
     (3.645, 0.125), ...; exact line search first step alpha = 1/6 to
     (10/3, -2/3); Newton reaches (0, 0) in one step. (c) 1, 0.7358, 0.6940,
     0.69315 -> ln 2.
     Teacher explains: (a) Let x* be a local minimum: f(x*) <= f(z) for
     z = (1 - t)x* + ty with small t > 0, are within r of x*, and
        f(z) <= (1 - t)f(x*) + tf(y) < f(x*),
     a contradiction. If x != y were two minimisers of a strictly convex f,
     gradient step with alpha = 0.05 is x <- x - 0.1x = 0.9x, y <- y - 0.5y = 0.5y:
        (5, 1) -> (4.5, 0.5) -> (4.05, 0.25) -> (3.645, 0.125)
     y converges fast, x slowly: the CONDITION NUMBER 10/2 = 5 of the
     Hessian makes the level sets elongated ellipses. Convergence needs
     |1 - 2alpha| < 1 and |1 - 10alpha| < 1, i.e. alpha < 2/L = 0.2. Exact line search
          = (10/3, -2/3),  f: 30 -> 100/9 + 20/9 = 40/3
     Newton: step -Q^-^1g = -(10/2, 10/10) = -(5, 1), landing exactly at
        x_1 = 1,  x_2 = 2/e ~ 0.7358,  x_3 ~ 0.6940,  x_4 ~ 0.6931475
     The number of correct digits roughly doubles each step (QUADRATIC
     convergence) near ln 2 ~ 0.6931472. Common mistakes: stepping in the
     y <- -1.5y, diverging). Now you try: two GD steps for f = x^2 + y^2 with
     alpha = 0.25 from (4, 2). (x <- 0.5x: (2, 1), (1, 0.5))

D11. State the KKT conditions. Solve (a) min x^2 + y^2 s.t. x + y >= 2;
     (b) min (x - 3)^2 + (y - 2)^2 s.t. x + y <= 2, x >= 0; (c) min x + y s.t.
     x^2 + y^2 <= 2, giving the multipliers and explaining their meaning.
     Answer: (a) (1, 1), lambda = 2, value 2. (b) (3/2, 1/2), lambda_1 = 3, lambda_2 = 0,
     value 9/2. (c) (-1, -1), lambda = 1/2, value -2.
     ACTIVE constraints. All three problems are convex, so a KKT point is the
     global minimum. (a) Write g = 2 - x - y <= 0. Stationarity:
     If lambda = 0 then x = y = 0, infeasible (0 + 0 < 2). So the constraint is
     g_2 = -x. Try g_1 active, lambda_2 = 0:
     consistent). Value (3/2)^2 + (3/2)^2 = 9/2. It is the projection of (3, 2)
     onto the half-plane. (c) g = x^2 + y^2 - 2: 1 + 2lambdax = 0, 1 + 2lambday = 0, so
     lambda > 0, x = y = -1/(2lambda), active: 2x^2 = 2, x = -1 (x must be negative),
     lambda = 1/2. MEANING: lambda is the shadow price of the constraint: in (a), with
     x + y >= c the optimum is c^2/2, whose derivative at c = 2 is 2 = lambda. Common
     mistakes: wrong sign of lambda (check lambda >= 0 with g <= 0 written correctly);
     accepting a KKT point of a NON-convex problem as a global minimum

D12. Define the Lagrange dual function and prove it is concave and gives a
     lower bound. Compute the dual of (a) min x^2 s.t. x >= 1 and (b) the LP
     condition, including (c) min x s.t. x^2 <= 0.
     attained; Slater fails.
     For each fixed x, L is AFFINE in lambda, and an infimum of affine functions
     is concave - even if the original problem is not convex. Lower bound: if
     (a) L = x^2 + lambda(1 - x) is minimised at x = lambda/2:
        g(lambda) = lambda^2/4 + lambda - lambda^2/2 = lambda - lambda^2/4
     b - Ax <= 0 (multiplier y >= 0) and -x <= 0 (multiplier s >= 0):
     feasible point is 0, p* = 0. L = x + lambdax^2, minimised at x = -1/(2lambda):
     AND a dual optimum for convex problems; here no x has x^2 < 0, and the
     dual optimum is missing. For non-convex problems a DUALITY GAP d* < p*
     can occur. Common mistakes: maximising L over x instead of minimising;
     forgetting lambda >= 0. Now you try: dual function of min x^2 + y^2 s.t.
     x + y >= 2. (g(lambda) = 2lambda - lambda^2/2, max 2 at lambda = 2 = p*)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always draw the two-variable picture first and label every
  vertex with its objective value - the simplex method is just a walk along
  these vertices, and each tableau can be matched to a corner of the
  drawing. Insist on the three questions of each simplex step: who enters
  (most negative), who leaves (smallest nonnegative ratio over POSITIVE
  entries), and what is the pivot. For duality, keep the sign table on the
  wall and check every dual with weak duality on one feasible pair. For
  convexity, a sketch of the function and one chord settles most questions;
  for two variables compute the Hessian and test trace and determinant.
  Harder: prove Farkas' lemma from the separating hyperplane theorem and
  deduce strong LP duality; show the simplex method can take exponentially
  many steps (Klee-Minty) while interior-point methods are polynomial;
  prove that gradient descent on an L-smooth, mu-strongly convex function
  converges linearly with factor (1 - mu/L); derive the KKT conditions from
  Farkas; and show that support vector machines and least squares with

TOPIC 10.39 - OPERATIONS RESEARCH: TRANSPORTATION, ASSIGNMENT, NETWORK FLOWS,
QUEUEING

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
    source or destination with zero costs. A BFS has m + n - 1 basic cells
    (one equation is redundant) forming a TREE (no loop); fewer positive
    INTEGER optimal solutions (TOTAL UNIMODULARITY).
  - INITIAL BFS: NORTH-WEST CORNER (ignores costs), LEAST-COST (cheapest
    cell first), VOGEL'S APPROXIMATION METHOD (VAM: PENALTY = difference of
    the two smallest costs in each row and column; allocate in the cheapest
    cell of the line with the largest penalty) - VAM is usually best.
    OPTIMAL. Otherwise enter the most negative cell, trace its unique
    CLOSED LOOP (+ - + - alternating on basic cells), shift theta = the smallest
    (highly degenerate, so solved by the HUNGARIAN METHOD instead).
  - HUNGARIAN METHOD: (1) subtract each row minimum, then each column
    minimum; (2) cover all zeros with the MINIMUM number of lines; (3) if
    n lines are needed, an optimal assignment exists among the zeros; (4)
    otherwise subtract the smallest uncovered entry from every uncovered
    entry, ADD it at line intersections, and repeat. Correctness: adding a
    constant to a row or column changes every assignment's cost equally
    rows/columns of zeros); FORBIDDEN pairs (cost M, a huge number).
  - SHORTEST PATHS: DIJKSTRA's algorithm (nonnegative weights) makes one
    label PERMANENT per step (the smallest temporary label) and updates
    neighbours d(v) <- min(d(v), d(u) + w(u, v)); O(n^2). With NEGATIVE
    weights use BELLMAN-FORD (n - 1 rounds of relaxing every edge; a further
    improvement signals a negative cycle).
  - MAXIMUM FLOW: a flow respects CAPACITIES 0 <= f(e) <= c(e) and
    CONSERVATION at every node except s and t. FORD-FULKERSON: repeatedly
    find an AUGMENTING PATH in the RESIDUAL network (forward residual
    c - f, backward residual f) and push its bottleneck. EDMONDS-KARP
    (shortest augmenting paths, BFS) runs in O(VE^2). An s-t CUT (S, T) has
    capacity the sum of capacities of edges from S to T.
  - MAX-FLOW MIN-CUT THEOREM: the maximum flow value equals the minimum cut
    capacity; at termination, S = nodes reachable from s in the residual
    flow (so bipartite MATCHING is a flow problem).
  - OTHER NETWORK MODELS: MINIMUM SPANNING TREE (KRUSKAL: add the cheapest
    edge not forming a cycle; PRIM: grow one tree by the cheapest edge
    leaving it; n - 1 edges); CRITICAL PATH METHOD (CPM): forward pass
    ES, EF = ES + duration; backward pass LF, LS = LF - duration;
    TOTAL FLOAT = LS - ES; CRITICAL activities have zero float and the
    project length is the longest path. MIN-COST FLOW generalises
    transportation, assignment and shortest paths.
  - QUEUEING BASICS: KENDALL notation A/B/c/K (M = Markovian, i.e. POISSON
    arrivals / EXPONENTIAL service; D = deterministic; G = general). A
    POISSON process of rate lambda: counts in time t are Poisson(lambdat),
    inter-arrival times are Exp(lambda) and MEMORYLESS, P(T > s + t | T > s) =
    P(T > t). LITTLE'S LAW: L = lambdaW, Lq = lambdaWq, and W = Wq + 1/mu.
    beats separate queues.
    lambda_eff = lambda(1 - P_K) in Little's law. M/G/1 (POLLACZEK-KHINCHINE):
    the M/M/1 queue. COST models balance service cost against waiting cost.

D1. Three factories S1, S2, S3 supply 7, 9, 18 units; four warehouses D1-D4
    need 5, 8, 7, 14. Unit costs:
              D1   D2   D3   D4 | supply
       S1     19   30   50   10 |   7
       S2     70   30   40   60 |   9
       S3     40    8   70   20 |  18
    demand     5    8    7   14 |  34
    Find initial basic feasible solutions by the north-west corner, least
    cost and Vogel methods and compare their costs.
    Answer: NW corner 1015; least cost 814; VAM 779 (the optimum is 743,
    see D2).
    Teacher explains: The problem is balanced (34 = 34). A BFS needs
    m + n - 1 = 6 basic cells. NORTH-WEST CORNER: start at S1D1, allocate as
    much as possible, then move right (demand still open) or down:
       S1D1 = 5, S1D2 = 2, S2D2 = 6, S2D3 = 3, S3D3 = 4, S3D4 = 14
       cost 95 + 60 + 180 + 120 + 280 + 280 = 1015
    It never looks at costs (S3D3 at 70!). LEAST COST: fill the cheapest
    available cell each time: S3D2 = 8 (cost 8), S1D4 = 7 (10), S3D4 = 7
    (20), S2D3 = 7 (40), S3D1 = 3 (40), S2D1 = 2 (70): cost 814. VOGEL: the
    PENALTY of a line is (second smallest - smallest) cost, the regret of
    not using its cheapest cell.
       step 1: rows 9, 10, 12; columns 21, 22, 10, 10. Max 22 (D2):
               S3D2 = 8 (D2 done)
       step 2: rows 9, 20, 20; columns 21, 10, 10. Max 21 (D1): S1D1 = 5
       step 3: rows 40, 20, 50; columns 10, 10. Max 50 (S3): S3D4 = 10
       step 4: rows 40, 20; columns 10, 50. Max 50 (D4): S1D4 = 2
       step 5: only S2 left: S2D4 = 2, S2D3 = 7
       cost 64 + 95 + 200 + 20 + 120 + 280 = 779
    avoids the choices that would later force expensive cells. Common
    mistakes: recomputing penalties with deleted rows/columns still
    included; allocating in the line with the largest penalty but not in
    its CHEAPEST cell. Now you try: NW corner for supplies 30, 20, demands
    25, 25, costs [[5, 3], [4, 7]]. (x_1_1 = 25, x_1_2 = 5, x_2_2 = 20, cost 280;
    the optimum is 180)

    10); reduced costs 32, 42, 19, 18, 11, 52, all >= 0: OPTIMAL,

D3. (a) Supplies 50, 40 and demands 30, 40: how do you balance the problem?
    (b) Supplies 20, 30, 50, demands 40, 30, 30, costs [[2, 3, 1], [5, 4, 8],

       v_3 = 1, u_3 = 7, v_1 = -2, v_2 = 6 - 7 = -1, u_2 = 4 + 1 = 5
          S2D3 = 8 - 6 = 2

    has entries 0, 1 and each column has one 1 in a supply row and one in a

D4. Assign four workers W1-W4 to jobs J1-J4 at minimum total cost:
              J1   J2   J3   J4
       W1     10   19    8   15
       W2     10   18    7   17
       W3     13   16    9   14
       W4     12   19    8   18
    Answer: W1-J4, W2-J1, W3-J2, W4-J3; total 15 + 10 + 16 + 8 = 49.
    Teacher explains: Row minima 8, 7, 9, 8; subtract them. Then column
    minima of the result (2, 7, 0, 5); subtract:
       W1   0  4  0  2
       W2   1  4  0  5
       W3   2  0  0  0
       W4   2  4  0  5
    Cover all zeros with as few lines as possible: column J3, row W3,
    column J1 - 3 lines < 4, so no complete zero assignment yet (W2 and W4
    both need J3). The smallest uncovered entry is 2 (W1J4). Subtract 2 from
    every uncovered entry and add 2 where lines cross (W3J1, W3J3):
       W1   0  2  0  0
       W2   1  2  0  3
       W3   4  0  2  0
       W4   2  2  0  3
    Minimum cover: column J3, rows W1, W3 - still 3 lines. Smallest
    uncovered entry 1 (W2J1); subtract from uncovered, add at crossings
    (W1J3, W3J3):
       W1   0  2  1  0
       W2   0  1  0  2
       W3   4  0  3  0
       W4   1  1  0  2
    Now 4 lines are needed. Assign where forced: W4 has one zero (J3); then
    W2 must take J1; W3 takes J2; W1 takes J4. Original costs:
    15 + 10 + 16 + 8 = 49. Why it works: subtracting a constant from a row
    lowers EVERY complete assignment by that constant, so the optimal
    assignment is unchanged, and an all-zero assignment in a nonnegative
    matrix is clearly optimal. The adjustment step is 'subtract k from the
    uncovered rows, add k to the covered columns': it keeps entries >= 0 and
    creates a new zero. Common mistakes: covering with more lines than
    necessary; forgetting to ADD at intersections; reading costs from the
    reduced matrix. Now you try: costs [[9, 2, 7], [6, 4, 3], [5, 8, 1]].
    (W1-J2, W2-J1, W3-J3: 2 + 6 + 1 = 9)

D6. Find shortest distances from A to all nodes of the undirected network
    with edges AB 4, AC 2, BC 1, BD 5, CD 8, CE 10, DE 2, DF 6, EF 2, using
    Dijkstra's algorithm. Prove the algorithm correct, and show why it fails
    with negative edges.
    Answer: d(B) = 3 (A-C-B), d(C) = 2, d(D) = 8 (A-C-B-D), d(E) = 10,
    d(F) = 12 (A-C-B-D-E-F).
    Teacher explains: Keep temporary labels; each step make the smallest
    one permanent and update its neighbours.
       permanent  A 0:  temp B 4, C 2
       permanent  C 2:  B min(4, 2 + 1) = 3, D 2 + 8 = 10, E 2 + 10 = 12
       permanent  B 3:  D min(10, 3 + 5) = 8
       permanent  D 8:  E min(12, 8 + 2) = 10, F 8 + 6 = 14
       permanent  E 10: F min(14, 10 + 2) = 12
       permanent  F 12
    Record the predecessor with each improvement and trace back: F <- E <-
    D <- B <- C <- A. Correctness (induction): when u gets the smallest
    temporary label d(u), any other path to u must leave the permanent set
    at some node x with label >= d(u) and then add NONNEGATIVE edges, so it is
    no shorter. That argument breaks with negative weights: with edges
    s->a 4, s->b 5, b->a -3, a->t 2, Dijkstra fixes a at 4 and t at 6, but
    s-b-a-t costs 4. BELLMAN-FORD (relax every edge n - 1 times) handles
    negative weights, and a further improvement in round n reveals a
    negative cycle (then 'shortest' is undefined). Common mistakes: making
    a label permanent before it is the smallest; updating permanent
    labels; forgetting to keep predecessors. Now you try: directed edges
    S->A 7, S->B 2, S->C 3, A->D 4, B->A 3, B->D 8, C->D 6, C->E 2, D->T 3, E->T 9,
    E->D 1; shortest S->T. (9, via S-C-E-D-T)

D7. In the network with arcs (capacities) s->a 10, s->c 10, a->b 4, a->c 2,
    a->d 8, c->d 9, d->b 6, b->t 10, d->t 10, find a maximum flow by the
    Ford-Fulkerson method with shortest augmenting paths, find a minimum cut,
    and prove the max-flow min-cut theorem.
    Answer: maximum flow 19 (augmenting paths s-a-b-t 4, s-a-d-t 6,
    s-c-d-t 4, s-c-d-b-t 5); minimum cut S = {s, c}: arcs s->a and c->d,
    capacity 10 + 9 = 19.
    Teacher explains: Augment along paths with spare capacity; the amount is
    the BOTTLENECK.
       s-a-b-t: min(10, 4, 10) = 4       (a->b full)
       s-a-d-t: min(6, 8, 10) = 6        (s->a full)
       s-c-d-t: min(10, 9, 4) = 4        (d->t full)
       s-c-d-b-t: min(6, 5, 6, 6) = 5    (c->d full)
    Total 19. In the residual network from s only c is reachable (s->c has 1
    unit left, but c->d is full and a->c carries no flow to cancel), so
    S = {s, c}. Its outgoing arcs s->a (10) and c->d (9) are saturated, and
    no flow runs back from T into S: the cut capacity is 19 = the flow.
    PROOF of the theorem. For any flow f and cut (S, T), conservation gives
       value(f) = f(S -> T) - f(T -> S) <= c(S, T)          (weak duality)
    If no augmenting path exists, let S = nodes reachable from s in the
    would be reachable) and every arc T -> S carries 0 (else its tail would
    be reachable through the backward residual arc). So value(f) = c(S, T):
    the flow is maximum and the cut minimum. Conversely a maximum flow has
    least 1, so the method terminates with an INTEGER flow. BACKWARD residual
    arcs matter: they let later paths undo bad earlier choices. Common
    mistakes: counting arcs from T to S in the cut capacity; forgetting
    backward arcs; stopping when no FORWARD-only path exists. Now you try:
    s->a 3, s->b 2, a->b 1, a->t 2, b->t 3. (max flow 5, min cut {s})

D8. (a) Find a minimum spanning tree of the network of D6 by Kruskal's and
    Prim's algorithms and justify the greedy choice. (b) A project has
    activities A (3 days), B (2), C (4, after A), D (5, after A and B), E (2,

       A 0-3,  B 0-2,  C 3-7,  D 3-8,  E 7-9,  F 9-12,  G 8-11

       B LF = LS(D) = 4 so 2-4, A LF = min(LS C, LS D) = 3 so 0-3

D9. Customers arrive as a Poisson process of rate lambda = 6 per hour.
    (a) P(no arrival in 10 minutes)? (b) P(exactly 2 arrivals in 20
    minutes)? (c) Service times are exponential with mean 4 minutes: given
    that a service has lasted 5 minutes, P(it lasts 6 more)? (d) State and
    justify Little's law and use it: 12 arrivals per hour each spend 15
    minutes in a shop; how many are inside on average? (e) Decode M/M/3/10.
    Answer: (a) e^-^1 ~ 0.368; (b) 2e^-^2 ~ 0.271; (c) e^(-1.5) ~ 0.223; (d)
    L = lambdaW = 3; (e) Poisson arrivals, exponential service, 3 servers, at
    most 10 in the system.
    Teacher explains: For a Poisson process the number of arrivals in time
    t is Poisson(lambdat). (a) lambdat = 6 x 1/6 = 1: P(0) = e^-^1 ~ 0.3679 - which is
    also P(inter-arrival time > 10 min), since gaps are Exp(6). (b) lambdat = 2:
    P(2) = e^-^22^2/2! = 2e^-^2 ~ 0.2707. (c) MEMORYLESS: for T ~ Exp(mu),
       P(T > s + t | T > s) = e^(-mu(s + t))/e^(-mus) = e^(-mut).
    The past 5 minutes are irrelevant: P(T > 6) = e^(-6/4) = e^(-1.5) ~
    0.2231. This is why M/M queues are MARKOV chains: the state n (number
    in system) is all we need. (d) LITTLE: L = lambdaW for any stable system
    under the 'number in system' curve counts customer-time; it equals
    L = 12 x 1/4 = 3. The same law applies to the queue alone (Lq = lambdaWq) and
    to the servers (average busy servers = lambda/mu). (e) Kendall A/B/c/K:
    arrival process / service distribution / number of servers / capacity;
    omitted K means infinite. Common mistakes: mixing time units (lambda per
    hour, t in minutes); using Little's law with the offered lambda when
    customers are turned away (use lambda_eff). Now you try: L = 5, lambda = 20 per
    hour: W? (15 minutes)

     lambda = 8 per hour, mu = 10 per hour find P_0, P(n >= 3), L, Lq, W, Wq and
     P(time in system > 1 hour).
     Lq = 3.2, W = 0.5 h, Wq = 0.4 h, P(W > 1) = e^-^2 ~ 0.135.
     Teacher explains: The number in system is a BIRTH-DEATH process: up at
     rate lambda, down at rate mu (when n >= 1). In steady state the flow across
     the cut between n and n + 1 balances:
     Lq = 0.64/0.2 = 3.2, W = 1/2 h = 30 min, Wq = 0.4 h = 24 min; check
     is Exp(mu - lambda) (FCFS): P(W > 1) = e^(-2) ~ 0.1353. The formulas explode
     try: lambda = 3, mu = 4 per hour: L, Lq, W, Wq. (3, 2.25, 1 h, 0.75 h)

D11. Arrivals at lambda = 8 per hour are served by two clerks, each with
     exponential rate mu = 5 per hour, from ONE queue (M/M/2). Find P_0, the
     probability of waiting, Lq, L, Wq, W. Compare with (a) one fast clerk of
     rate 10 and (b) two separate M/M/1 queues each receiving 4 per hour.
     Answer: P_0 = 1/9, P(wait) = 32/45 ~ 0.711, Lq = 128/45 ~ 2.844,
     L = 40/9 ~ 4.444, Wq = 16/45 h ~ 21.3 min, W = 5/9 h ~ 33.3 min.
     (a) W = 30 min, Wq = 24 min. (b) W = 60 min, Wq = 48 min.
     Teacher explains: a = lambda/mu = 1.6 (the average number of busy clerks),
        L = Lq + a = 2.844 + 1.6 = 4.444
        Wq = Lq/lambda ~ 0.356 h,  W = Wq + 1/mu = 0.356 + 0.2 = 0.556 h
     (a) One clerk twice as fast (D10): W = 0.5 h, Wq = 0.4 h - shorter
     total time (service itself is quicker) but LONGER wait in the queue.
     (b) Separate queues: each M/M/1 with lambda = 4, mu = 5 has W = 1/(5 - 4) =
     1 h: much worse, because one clerk can sit idle while the other has a
     queue. Lesson: POOLING (a single queue) is always better than separate
     Now you try: lambda = 4, mu = 5, c = 2. (P_0 = 3/7, Lq = 16/105 ~ 0.152,
     W = 5/21 h ~ 14.3 min)

D12. (a) A one-chair barber with room for 3 customers in total (M/M/1/3)
     has lambda = 8, mu = 10 per hour. Find P_0, the blocking probability, the
     effective arrival rate, L and W. (b) State the Pollaczek-Khinchine
     formula and find Lq for lambda = 8 per hour with constant service time
     6 minutes (M/D/1), and for service with mean 12 minutes and standard
     deviation 6 minutes at lambda = 4 per hour. (c) Choose the service rate mu of
     an M/M/1 system with lambda = 8 to minimise 2mu + 16L per hour.
     Answer: (a) P_0 = 125/369 ~ 0.339, P_3 = 64/369 ~ 0.173, lambda_eff ~ 6.61,
     L = 452/369 ~ 1.225, W ~ 0.185 h ~ 11.1 min. (b) M/D/1: Lq = 1.6 (half of
     M/M/1's 3.2); second case Lq = 2, Wq = 0.5 h. (c) mu* = 16, cost 48.
        P_0 = 1/(1 + 0.8 + 0.64 + 0.512) = 1/2.952 = 125/369 ~ 0.3388
        P_3 = 0.512 x 0.3388 = 64/369 ~ 0.1734  (arrivals finding it full leave)
     No stability condition is needed (finite states). Customers who
     actually enter arrive at lambda_eff = lambda(1 - P_3) = 8 x 0.8266 ~ 6.61 per
     and Little with lambda_eff: W = L/lambda_eff ~ 0.185 h. Using lambda = 8 would be wrong.
     (b) For M/G/1 with service mean 1/mu and variance sigma^2,
     sigma = 0.1 h: Lq = (16 x 0.01 + 0.64)/0.4 = 2, Wq = Lq/lambda = 0.5 h. (c)
     mu - 8 = 8, mu* = 16; C = 32 + 16 = 48 per hour (in general
     mu* = lambda + sqrt(c_wlambda/c_s)). Common mistakes: using lambda instead of lambda_eff; in
     P-K using the standard deviation instead of the variance. Now you try:
     M/M/1/2 with lambda = 4, mu = 5: P_0 and P_2. (25/61 ~ 0.410, 16/61 ~ 0.262)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: do every transportation problem in a single tableau drawn
  basic cells; count m + n - 1 before every MODI step. For the Hungarian
  method, practise covering zeros on paper with coloured lines, and always
  go back to the ORIGINAL matrix for the final cost. For networks, keep a
  table of labels (Dijkstra), draw residual arrows in a second colour (max
  flow), and do the CPM forward and backward passes in a two-row box above
  and get everything else from Little's law. Harder: prove that
  transportation matrices are totally unimodular; show the Hungarian
  theorem from max-flow min-cut; show that Ford-Fulkerson can fail to
  terminate with irrational capacities; derive the waiting-time
  distribution of M/M/1 (FCFS) and the Erlang C formula; and prove
  Burke's theorem that the departures of M/M/1 form a Poisson process,
  which makes tandem queues (Jackson networks) tractable.

================================================================================
TOPIC 10.40 - GAME THEORY: STRATEGIC GAMES, NASH EQUILIBRIUM, ZERO-SUM GAMES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A STRATEGIC (NORMAL-FORM) GAME has PLAYERS i = 1, ..., n, STRATEGY SETS
    written as a BIMATRIX: row player's strategies are rows, column player's
    are columns, and each cell shows (u_1, u_2). Players choose simultaneously,
    know the game, and are rational (maximise expected payoff).
    DOMINANT strategy dominates all others. ITERATED ELIMINATION OF STRICTLY
    DOMINATED STRATEGIES (IESDS) never removes a Nash equilibrium and its
    result does not depend on the order; weak elimination can remove
    equilibria and is order-dependent. A strategy may also be dominated by
    a MIXED strategy.
    UNILATERAL deviation. In a bimatrix, mark each column's best u_1 and each
    row's best u_2; cells with both marks are the PURE NE.
  - CLASSIC GAMES: PRISONER'S DILEMMA (dominant strategies lead to a NE that
    is not PARETO optimal), BATTLE OF THE SEXES and STAG HUNT (coordination,
    several NE), CHICKEN / HAWK-DOVE (anti-coordination), MATCHING PENNIES
    (no pure NE). A NE need not be efficient, unique or exist in pure
    strategies.
    every pure strategy used with positive probability gives the SAME
    expected payoff, and unused ones give no more. Each player's mix is
    chosen to make the OPPONENT indifferent.
  - 2 x 2 RECIPE: if the row player uses T with probability p, the column
    similarly q from the row player's payoffs. SUPPORT ENUMERATION handles
    larger games: guess supports, solve the indifference equations, check
    probabilities >= 0 and no profitable pure deviation.
  - NASH'S THEOREM: every finite game has at least one NE in mixed
    strategies (proof: Brouwer's or Kakutani's fixed point theorem applied
    to the best-response map). Generically the number of NE is ODD.
  - CONTINUOUS GAMES: find best-response functions from first-order
    conditions and intersect them. COURNOT duopoly with price P = a - Q and
    competition with equal costs: p = c (zero profit).
  - ZERO-SUM game: u_2 = -u_1, described by the payoff matrix A to the row
    player (maximiser); the column player minimises. LOWER VALUE
    strategies.
  - VON NEUMANN'S MINIMAX THEOREM: with mixed strategies
    strategies are the NE of the zero-sum game; all NE give the value v and
  - SOLVING: first look for a saddle point; remove DOMINATED rows (smaller
    everywhere) and columns (larger everywhere). 2 x 2 without a saddle
    [[a, b], [c, d]]: p = (d - c)/(a - b - c + d),
    q = (d - b)/(a - b - c + d), v = (ad - bc)/(a - b - c + d). 2 x n or
    m x 2: GRAPHICAL method (lower envelope of lines, highest point).
    Adding a constant k to all entries adds k to v; multiplying by lambda > 0
    multiplies v by lambda.
  - LP FORMULATION: after adding a constant to make v > 0, the row player
    theorem is LP strong duality.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Two suspects may Cooperate (stay silent) or Defect (confess). Payoffs
    (years in prison as negative numbers):
                  C          D
       C      (-1, -1)   (-3, 0)
       D      (0, -3)    (-2, -2)
    Define a strategic game and dominance, find each player's dominant
    strategy and the Nash equilibrium, and explain why the outcome is not
    Pareto optimal. What changes if the game is repeated a known finite
    number of times?
    Answer: D is strictly dominant for both; the unique NE is (D, D) with
    (-2, -2), which is Pareto dominated by (C, C) with (-1, -1). Finite
    repetition still gives (D, D) every round (backward induction).
    Teacher explains: A strategic game lists players, strategy sets and
    payoffs; players choose at the same time. Compare the row player's
    payoffs column by column:
       against C: D gives 0 > -1;   against D: D gives -2 > -3
    So D is better whatever the other does: STRICTLY DOMINANT. By symmetry
    the same holds for the column player. Rational players therefore play
    (D, D). It is a Nash equilibrium: from (D, D) a unilateral switch to C
    gives -3 < -2. Yet both prefer (C, C): the equilibrium is not PARETO
    OPTIMAL. Individual rationality and collective rationality clash - the
    model of arms races, price wars, over-fishing. Why cooperation cannot be
    enforced by promises: at (C, C) each player gains by deviating (0 > -1).
    With a known last round, D is dominant in the last round; then in the
    second-last round the future is fixed, so D again, and so on backwards.
    (With an infinite horizon and patient players, strategies like
    TIT-FOR-TAT or GRIM TRIGGER can sustain cooperation.) Common mistakes:
    thinking a NE must be the 'best' outcome; checking only one column for
    dominance. Now you try: change (C, C) to (3, 3) and (D, D) to (1, 1),
    with (C, D) = (0, 4), (D, C) = (4, 0). Dominant strategies? (D still
    strictly dominant for both: 4 > 3 and 1 > 0; NE (D, D))

D2. Apply iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies to
                  L        C        R
       T       (4, 3)   (5, 1)   (6, 2)
       M       (2, 1)   (8, 4)   (3, 6)
       B       (3, 0)   (9, 6)   (2, 8)
    Justify the procedure, and explain why weak dominance needs care. Show
    also that a strategy can be dominated by a mixed strategy only.
    Answer: C is dominated by R; then M and B by T; then R by L. The game
    solves to (T, L) with payoffs (4, 3).
    Teacher explains: At the start NO row is dominated (M and B beat T in
    column C). But the column player's C gives (1, 4, 6), less than R's
    (2, 6, 8) in every row: remove C.
       remaining  T: (4, 3), (6, 2)   M: (2, 1), (3, 6)   B: (3, 0), (2, 8)
    Now T's payoffs (4, 6) beat M's (2, 3) and B's (3, 2): remove M and B.
    Finally the column player, facing only T, compares L = 3 with R = 2:
    remove R. Result (T, L). Justification: a rational player never uses a
    strictly dominated strategy, and if everyone KNOWS the others are
    rational (common knowledge of rationality) the reduced game is the real
    one. Strict IESDS never deletes a NE and the order is irrelevant.
    WEAK dominance: in the game [[(1, 1), (0, 0)], [(0, 0), (0, 0)]], B is
    weakly dominated by T, yet (B, R) is still a NE; eliminating weakly
    dominated strategies can delete equilibria and its result can depend on
    the order. MIXED DOMINANCE: in the zero-sum-style payoffs to the row
    player T = (3, 0), M = (0, 3), B = (1, 1), no pure strategy dominates B,
    but 1/2T + 1/2M gives (1.5, 1.5) > (1, 1), so B is strictly dominated by a
    mixture. Common mistakes: comparing the row player's payoffs across a
    ROW instead of down a column; deleting a strategy that is only better
    'on average'. Now you try: in
    [[(1, 0), (1, 2), (0, 1)], [(0, 3), (0, 1), (2, 0)]] run IESDS.
    (R dominated by C for the column player; then B by T; then L by C:
    outcome (T, C))

D3. Define Nash equilibrium and best response. Find all pure-strategy NE of
    (a) Battle of the Sexes [[(2, 1), (0, 0)], [(0, 0), (1, 2)]];
    (b) Stag Hunt [[(4, 4), (0, 3)], [(3, 0), (3, 3)]];
    (c) Chicken [[(0, 0), (-1, 1)], [(1, -1), (-10, -10)]] (rows/columns:
    Swerve, Straight); (d) Matching Pennies [[(1, -1), (-1, 1)],
    [(-1, 1), (1, -1)]].
    Answer: (a) (T, L), (B, R). (b) (Stag, Stag), (Hare, Hare). (c) (Swerve,
    Straight), (Straight, Swerve). (d) none.
    Teacher explains: s* is a NE if every player's strategy is a best
    underline the row player's best payoff in each COLUMN and the column
    player's best payoff in each ROW; a cell with both underlined is a NE.
       (a) col L: best u_1 = 2 (T); col R: 1 (B). row T: best u_2 = 1 (L);
           row B: 2 (R). Double marks: (T, L), (B, R).
       (b) both (Stag, Stag) = (4, 4) and (Hare, Hare) = (3, 3): each is a
           best response to itself. (Stag, Stag) is Pareto better, but
           (Hare, Hare) is SAFER: Hare guarantees 3.
       (c) against Swerve, Straight is best (1 > 0); against Straight,
           Swerve is best (-1 > -10): NE at the two asymmetric cells.
       (d) in every cell one player wants to switch: no pure NE.
    Interpretation: a NE is a 'self-enforcing agreement' - nobody wants to
    break it alone. It is a STEADY STATE, not a prediction of how play
    starts; games with several NE need a selection argument (focal points,
    Pareto dominance, risk dominance). Common mistakes: underlining the
    column player's payoffs down columns; forgetting that both inequalities
    must hold. Now you try: [[(1, 1), (2, 0)], [(0, 2), (3, 3)]]. (Pure NE
    (T, L) and (B, R))

D4. Two firms choose quantities q_1, q_2 >= 0; price P = 100 - (q_1 + q_2); each
    has unit cost 10. Find the best-response functions, the Cournot-Nash
    equilibrium, price and profits, and compare with the monopoly
    (collusive) outcome and with Bertrand price competition.
    (1800 total). Monopoly: Q = 45, P = 55, profit 2025 (1012.5 each if
    shared). Bertrand: P = 10, profits 0.
    Teacher explains: Firm 1's profit pi_1 = (100 - q_1 - q_2 - 10)q_1 =
    (90 - q_2)q_1 - q_1^2, concave in q_1. First-order condition:
    (and 0 if q_2 >= 90). By symmetry BR_2(q_1) = (90 - q_1)/2. A NE is an
    intersection of the best-response curves:
    monopolist maximises (90 - Q)Q: Q = 45, P = 55, profit 2025 > 1800.
    Splitting it (22.5 each, profit 1012.5) is better for both, but it is
    NOT an equilibrium: BR_1(22.5) = 33.75, so each firm cheats - a
    Prisoner's Dilemma. BERTRAND: if firms set prices and the cheaper takes
    the whole market, any price above 10 can be undercut slightly, so the
    unique NE is p_1 = p_2 = 10 with zero profit (the Bertrand paradox). Common
    symmetry before differentiating (that gives the monopoly answer). Now

D5. Explain mixed strategies and the indifference principle, and find the
    mixed NE of Battle of the Sexes [[(2, 1), (0, 0)], [(0, 0), (1, 2)]]
    with the expected payoffs. Draw the best-response correspondences and
    show that the game has exactly three NE.
    Answer: row plays T with p = 2/3, column plays L with q = 1/3; each
    expects 2/3. Together with (T, L) and (B, R): three NE.
    Teacher explains: A mixed strategy is a probability vector over pure
    strategies; payoffs become expected values. If the row player mixes
    T and B with positive probabilities in a best response, both must give
    the SAME expected payoff (otherwise shift weight to the better one).
    So each player's mix is chosen to make the OTHER indifferent. Column
    player's payoffs when row plays T with probability p:
    Row player's payoffs when column plays L with probability q:
    Expected payoffs: row 2q = 2/3, column p = 2/3 - worse for both than
    either pure NE, because they miscoordinate with probability
    (2/3)(2/3) + (1/3)(1/3) = 5/9. Best responses: BR_1(q) = B for q < 1/3,
    anything for q = 1/3, T for q > 1/3; BR_2(p) = R for p < 2/3, anything
    at 2/3, L for p > 2/3. In the unit square the two 'Z'-shaped graphs
    cross at (p, q) = (0, 0), (1, 1) and (2/3, 1/3): three NE. Common
    mistakes: solving for p using the ROW player's own payoffs; reporting
    'q = 1/3' as the probability of R. Now you try: Stag Hunt
    [[(4, 4), (0, 3)], [(3, 0), (3, 3)]]: mixed NE. (Stag with probability
    3/4 each: 4p = 3; payoff 3)

D8. Hawk-Dove: two animals contest a resource worth V = 4; fighting costs
    C = 6. Payoffs: (H, H) = ((V - C)/2, (V - C)/2) = (-1, -1), (H, D) =
    (4, 0), (D, H) = (0, 4), (D, D) = (2, 2). Find all NE, the symmetric
    mixed NE in general (V < C), and the expected payoff. Explain why the
    mixed strategy is evolutionarily stable. Also find the mixed NE of
    Chicken from D3.
    Answer: pure NE (H, D), (D, H); symmetric mixed NE: H with probability
    V/C = 2/3, expected payoff 2/3. Chicken: Swerve with probability 9/10,
    expected payoff -1/10.
    Teacher explains: Best responses: against H, D (0 > -1); against D, H
    (4 > 2): pure NE at the asymmetric cells. Mixed: opponent plays H with
    probability p; indifference
       H: p(V - C)/2 + (1 - p)V      D: (1 - p)V/2
    Payoff: D earns (1 - p)V/2 = (1/3)(2) = 2/3 (and so does H). In a
    population where the fraction of hawks is p, hawks do better when
    p < 2/3 and doves do better when p > 2/3, so the population is pushed to
    2/3: an EVOLUTIONARILY STABLE STRATEGY (ESS): sigma is ESS if, for every
    mutant mu != sigma, u(sigma, sigma) > u(mu, sigma), or u(sigma, sigma) = u(mu, sigma) and
    u(sigma, mu) > u(mu, mu). With x, y the hawk probabilities of the player and
    the opponent, u(x, y) = 2 + 2x - 2y - 3xy; for a mutant playing H with
    probability m, u(m, sigma) = u(sigma, sigma) = 2/3 (indifference), and
       u(sigma, m) - u(m, m) = 4/3 - 4m + 3m^2 = 3(m - 2/3)^2 > 0  (m != 2/3),
    so the mix is an ESS. Chicken: column swerves with probability q; row
    taking p = C/V; forgetting the factor 1/2 in (V - C)/2. Now you try: V = 2,
    C = 8: mixed NE. (H with probability 1/4)

D9. For the zero-sum game with payoff matrix (to the row player)
       A = [[-3, -2, 6], [2, 0, 2], [5, -2, -4]]
    find the maximin and minimax values, a saddle point, and the value.
    saddle point gives optimal pure strategies.
    Answer: maximin 0 (row 2), minimax 0 (column 2); saddle point
    (row 2, column 2); value 0.
    Teacher explains: The row player (maximiser) considers the worst case of
    each row:
       row minima: -3, 0, -4   -> maximin v^- = 0 (row 2)
    The column player (minimiser) considers the worst case of each column:
    column: a SADDLE POINT. Row 2 guarantees at least 0; column 2 holds the
    row player to at most 0; neither can do better, so the value is 0 and
    The left side does not depend on k, the right side not on i: take max
    a_{i*j} >= a_{i*j*} >= a_{ij*} for all i, j, so row i* guarantees a_{i*j*}
    equality. Several saddle points always have the same value (and are
    'announces' first loses, so players must MIX. Common mistakes: taking
    column MINIMA for the minimiser; confusing whose payoff the matrix
    shows. Now you try: A = [[4, 2, 3], [5, 3, 6], [1, 0, 2]].
    (Row minima 2, 3, 0; column maxima 5, 3, 6; saddle (2, 2), value 3)

D10. Solve the zero-sum game A = [[3, -1], [-2, 4]] in mixed strategies,
     derive the general 2 x 2 formulas, and explain why they fail for
     A = [[2, 1], [3, 4]].
     Answer: p = (3/5, 2/5), q = (1/2, 1/2), v = 1. The second matrix has a
     saddle point (row 2, column 1), value 3; the formula would give
     nonsense.
     Teacher explains: No saddle: row minima -1, -2 (v^- = -1), column maxima
     each column his expected payoff is
        column 1: 3p - 2(1 - p) = 5p - 2
        column 2: -p + 4(1 - p) = 4 - 5p
     He wants to maximise the smaller of the two; at the optimum they are
     player with column 1 probability q:
        row 1: 3q - (1 - q) = 4q - 1      row 2: -2q + 4(1 - q) = 4 - 6q
     Both guarantee 1: the value is v = 1. General [[a, b], [c, d]] without
     saddle point: equating gives
        p = (d - c)/(a - b - c + d),  q = (d - b)/(a - b - c + d),
        v = (ad - bc)/(a - b - c + d);
     minima 1, 3, column maxima 3, 4: saddle at a_2_1 = 3. The formula gives
     p = (4 - 3)/(2 - 1 - 3 + 4) = 1/2 - wrong: row 2 dominates row 1, so
     p = 0. ALWAYS check for a saddle point first. Common mistakes: mixing
     up p (row) and q (column) formulas; forgetting to verify that 0 < p < 1.
     Now you try: A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]]. (p = 1/4, q = 1/2, v = 5/2)

D11. Solve the 2 x 4 zero-sum game A = [[2, 3, 1, 5], [4, 1, 6, 0]] by the
     graphical method.
     Answer: v = 17/7; row player (5/7, 2/7); column player uses columns 2
     and 3 with probabilities 5/7 and 2/7 (columns 1 and 4 unused).
     Teacher explains: No saddle: row minima 1, 0 (v^- = 1), column maxima 4,
     column gives a straight line in p:
        col 1: 2p + 4(1 - p) = 4 - 2p      col 2: 3p + (1 - p) = 1 + 2p
        col 3: p + 6(1 - p) = 6 - 5p       col 4: 5p
     The column player will pick the lowest line, so the row player
     maximises the LOWER ENVELOPE. Sketch the four lines on 0 <= p <= 1. The
     envelope is col 4 on [0, 1/3] (5p = 1 + 2p at p = 1/3), col 2 on
     [1/3, 5/7] and col 3 on [5/7, 1]; it rises and then falls, so its peak
     is where col 2 and col 3 cross: 1 + 2p = 6 - 5p, p = 5/7, height
     1 + 10/7 = 17/7. Check the other lines there: col 1: 4 - 10/7 = 18/7 >
     (5/7, 2/7). The column player uses only the two lines through the
     peak, columns 2 and 3; solve the 2 x 2 game [[3, 1], [1, 6]]:
        q = (6 - 1)/(3 - 1 - 1 + 6) = 5/7 for column 2,
     For an m x 2 game draw the column player's lines instead and take the
     LOWEST point of the UPPER envelope. Common mistakes: maximising the
     upper envelope; using columns that do not pass through the optimal
     point. Now you try: A = [[1, 3, -1], [2, -2, 4]]. (p = 3/5, v = 1,
     column player 1/2 on columns 2 and 3)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always write the game as a bimatrix with the row player's
  payoff FIRST, and practise the underline method until pure equilibria can
  be read off in seconds. For mixed equilibria repeat the slogan 'my mix
  makes YOU indifferent' and check the answer by computing both expected
  payoffs. For zero-sum games follow a fixed order: saddle point? ->
  dominance -> 2 x 2 formula or graph -> LP. Drawing the lines of the
  graphical method on squared paper builds intuition for the lower envelope.
  Harder: prove Nash's theorem with Kakutani's fixed point theorem; prove
  the minimax theorem from the separating hyperplane theorem without LP;
  show the Lemke-Howson algorithm finds a NE of a bimatrix game and explain
  why computing one is PPAD-complete; study subgame perfection and backward
  induction in extensive-form games (Stackelberg leader q = 45, follower
  22.5 in D4's market); analyse the infinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma
  and the folk theorem; and verify that the mixed Hawk-Dove equilibrium is
  an ESS while the mixed Stag Hunt equilibrium is not.

TOPIC 10.41 - CLASSICAL MECHANICS / MATHEMATICAL PHYSICS (LAGRANGIAN AND
HAMILTONIAN MECHANICS)

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - GENERALISED COORDINATES q_1, ..., q_n describe a system with n DEGREES OF
    FREEDOM; HOLONOMIC constraints (f(r, t) = 0) remove coordinates, so a
    pendulum needs only theta. The set of all q is CONFIGURATION SPACE; (q, p) is
    PHASE SPACE (dimension 2n; 6N for N free particles in space).
    paths with fixed ends. This gives the EULER-LAGRANGE EQUATIONS
    form in EVERY coordinate system; adding dF(q, t)/dt to L changes nothing.
    (ignorable) coordinate does not appear in L, and then its momentum is
    CONSERVED. NOETHER'S THEOREM: each continuous symmetry of L gives a
    conserved quantity (translation -> linear momentum, rotation -> angular
    momentum, time translation -> energy).
    and the constraints do not depend on time; otherwise (rotating hoop)
    h != T + V but may still be conserved.
  - CONSTRAINT FORCES by LAGRANGE MULTIPLIERS: keep extra coordinates and use
    parabola (E = 0), hyperbola (E > 0); a = -k/(2E), T = 2pisqrt(ma^3/k).
    Two bodies reduce to one of REDUCED MASS mu = m_1m_2/(m_1 + m_2).
    antisymmetric, bilinear, obeys Leibniz {fg, h} = f{g, h} + {f, h}g and
    POISSON'S THEOREM: the bracket of two conserved quantities is conserved.
  - CANONICAL TRANSFORMATION (q, p) -> (Q, P): keeps Hamilton's equations;
    test (one degree of freedom) {Q, P} = 1 (Jacobian determinant 1).
  - LIOUVILLE'S THEOREM: the Hamiltonian flow preserves phase-space AREA
    S = alphaq - alpha^2t/(2m).

D4. Find the curve y(x) > 0 through (-1, cosh 1) and (1, cosh 1) whose
    rotation about the x-axis gives the least area. Compute the area of the
    catenoid(s) and compare with the Goldschmidt solution (two discs).
    Answer: catenaries y = c cosh(x/c) with c cosh(1/c) = cosh 1: c = 1 (area
    pi(2 + sinh 2) ~ 17.677) and c ~ 0.7021 (area ~ 17.734). The two discs
    have area 2pi cosh^21 ~ 14.961, less than either: the global minimum is
    the discs; y = cosh x is only a local minimum.
    Beltrami:
    Symmetry gives d = 0; the end condition is c cosh(1/c) = cosh 1. The
    function f(c) = c cosh(1/c) has a minimum ~ 1.509 at c ~ 0.834 (where

    c = 1 and c ~ 0.7021. For c = 1:
    The deeper catenary (c ~ 0.702) has area ~ 17.734 and is not even a
    local minimum (it has a conjugate point). The GOLDSCHMIDT solution -
    the two end discs of radius cosh 1 joined along the axis - has area
    2pi cosh^21 ~ 14.961, which is smaller. It is not a smooth graph, so
    Euler-Lagrange cannot find it. If the rings are pulled further apart
    (so that the height lies below the minimum of f) no catenary exists at
    all: the soap film breaks. Lesson: the Euler-Lagrange equation finds
    candidates; it does not guarantee a global minimum. Common mistakes:
    finding one root of c cosh(1/c) = h and stopping; forgetting the factor
    2pi. Now you try: which c makes y = c cosh(x/c) pass through (+/-1, 1.6)?
    (Solve c cosh(1/c) = 1.6: two roots, c ~ 0.634 and c ~ 1.126; the second

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: drill the three-line routine - write F, compute F_y and
  order equation into a first-order one. Always check boundary conditions
  last and ask 'is it really a minimum?' by testing one nearby function
  numerically. Draw the brachistochrone and the catenary. Harder: prove the
  integrated Euler-Lagrange equation for C^1 extremals; show that the
  catenoid ceases to exist when the rings are more than about 1.3255 radii
  series; derive Snell's law from Fermat's principle; show that the Jacobi
  equation is the linearisation of Euler-Lagrange about the extremal; and
  explain why the direct method (lower semicontinuity + compactness) proves
  fails at x = 0 where the coefficient x^2 degenerates.

RAMSEY THEORY

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
    form: the number with NONE of the properties is N - S_1 + S_2 - ... =
    Truncating gives the BONFERRONI inequalities (alternately upper and
    lower bounds).
    (STIRLING numbers of the 2nd kind); DERANGEMENTS
    equal/adjacent objects; FORBIDDEN POSITIONS via the ROOK POLYNOMIAL
    symmetry maps one to the other, so we count ORBITS.
  - BURNSIDE'S LEMMA (Cauchy-Frobenius): number of orbits
    A colouring with k colours is fixed by g iff it is constant on each
    CYCLE of g, so |Fix(g)| = k^(c(g)), c(g) = number of cycles.
    of r^a b^c ... counts the orbits with a red, c blue, ....
    each; n even (n/2)x_2^(n/2) + (n/2)x_1^2x_2^((n-2)/2) (BRACELETS). Cube
    rotations (24) on faces: (x_1^6 + 3x_1^2x_2^2 + 6x_1^2x_4 + 6x_2^3 + 8x_3^2)/24, giving
    (k^6 + 3k^4 + 12k^3 + 8k^2)/24 colourings. Graphs on 4 vertices = 11 (S_4 on
    the 6 edges).
  - BLOCK DESIGNS: a 2-(v, k, lambda) design / BIBD(v, b, r, k, lambda) has v points,
    b blocks of size k, every point in r blocks and every PAIR of points in
    exactly lambda blocks. Counting: bk = vr and lambda(v - 1) = r(k - 1). Incidence
    r >= k); b = v is SYMMETRIC (then any two blocks meet in lambda points).
    BRUCK-RYSER-CHOWLA: a symmetric (v, k, lambda) with v even needs k - lambda to be
    a square (v odd: x^2 = (k - lambda)y^2 + (-1)^((v-1)/2) lambdaz^2 has a nonzero
    integer solution).
    (mod 6), with b = v(v - 1)/6, r = (v - 1)/2. FANO plane STS(7).
    PROJECTIVE PLANE of order n: 2-(n^2 + n + 1, n + 1, 1), symmetric (any two
    lines meet in one point); exists for every prime power n; none for n = 6
    (BRC) or n = 10 (computer search). AFFINE plane of order n: 2-(n^2, n, 1),
    n^2 + n lines in n + 1 parallel classes.
  - LATIN SQUARES: n x n arrays with each symbol once per row and column.
    Two are ORTHOGONAL if the n^2 ordered pairs are all different. At most
    n - 1 MUTUALLY ORTHOGONAL LATIN SQUARES (MOLS); n - 1 exist for prime
    plane of order n. Order 6: no pair (EULER'S 36 OFFICERS, Tarry 1900).
  - RAMSEY THEORY: R(s, t) is the least N such that every red/blue colouring
    of the edges of K_N has a red K_s or a blue K_t. PIGEONHOLE is the base.
    R(3, 3) = 6 (the pentagon shows R > 5). R(s, t) <= R(s - 1, t) + R(s, t - 1)
    (strict if both are even), so R(s, t) <= C(s + t - 2, s - 1). Known:
    R(3, 4) = 9, R(3, 5) = 14, R(4, 4) = 18, R(3, 3, 3) = 17; 43 <= R(5, 5) <= 46.
    reals has a monotone subsequence of length n + 1 (sharp); SCHUR - any
    finite colouring of {1, ..., N} (N large) has a monochromatic x + y = z
    (S(2) = 4, S(3) = 13); VAN DER WAERDEN - monochromatic arithmetic
    progressions (W(2, 3) = 9); happy ending: 5 points in general position
    contain a convex quadrilateral.
  - TRAPS: forgetting the alternating signs or the S_0 term; double counting
    orbits (not dividing by |G|, or dividing without Burnside); wrong cycle
    types (a 180 degrees face rotation of a cube has two FIXED faces); checking only
    necessary conditions for designs and claiming existence.

D3. Count the surjections from a 6-set onto a 3-set and find S(6, 3). Then
    count the ways of rolling a total of 15 with three dice, using PIE on

    of i values leaves (3 - i)^6 functions, so
       surjections = 3^6 - C(3, 1)2^6 + C(3, 2)1^6 - C(3, 3)0^6

D4. For the integers 1, ..., 100 and the properties 'divisible by 2, 3, 5',
    find how many have exactly 0, 1, 2, 3 of the properties, using the
    three workers A, B, C to three jobs 1, 2, 3 when A cannot do job 1, B
    cannot do jobs 1 or 2, and C cannot do job 3.
    Answer: E_0 = 26, E_1 = 48, E_2 = 23, E_3 = 3; one assignment (A2, B3, C1).
    Teacher explains: S_0 = 100, S_1 = 50 + 33 + 20 = 103,
    S_2 = 16 + 10 + 6 = 32 (multiples of 6, 10, 15), S_3 = 3 (multiples of 30).
       E_0 = 100 - 103 + 32 - 3 = 26
       E_1 = S_1 - 2S_2 + 3S_3 = 103 - 64 + 9 = 48
       E_2 = S_2 - 3S_3 = 32 - 9 = 23
       E_3 = S_3 = 3
    non-attacking rooks on forbidden squares. The square C3 shares no row
    or column with the others, so the rook polynomial factorises:
       board {A1, B1, B2}: r_1 = 3, r_2 = 1 (A1 with B2)  ->  1 + 3x + x^2
       board {C3}:                                      ->  1 + x
       R(x) = (1 + 3x + x^2)(1 + x) = 1 + 4x + 4x^2 + x^3.
    Common mistakes: letting two rooks share a row (that is not a valid
    partial assignment); multiplying rook polynomials of boards that share a
    row or column. Now you try: how many of 1, ..., 100 are divisible by at
    least two of 2, 3, 5? (E_2 + E_3 = 26)

D5. State and prove Burnside's lemma. Use it to count the necklaces of 6
    beads in 2 colours (rotations only), and the bracelets (rotations and
    reflections).
    Teacher explains: Count the pairs (g, x) with gx = x in two ways:
    NECKLACE: G = C_6 (rotations by 0, 1, ..., 5 places). A rotation by r
    places has gcd(r, 6) cycles, each of length 6/gcd(r, 6); a colouring is
    fixed iff constant on cycles, so |Fix| = 2^gcd(r, 6):
       r = 0: 2^6 = 64    r = 1, 5: 2^1 = 2 each    r = 2, 4: 2^2 = 4 each
       r = 3: 2^3 = 8
       orbits = (64 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 4 + 2)/6 = 84/6 = 14.
    BRACELET: G = D_6 adds 6 reflections. Three pass through two opposite
    beads (2 fixed beads + 2 swapped pairs: 4 cycles, 2^4 = 16 each); three
    pass between beads (3 swapped pairs: 2^3 = 8 each):
       orbits = (84 + 3 x 16 + 3 x 8)/12 = 156/12 = 13.
    Only one pair of necklaces merges into a bracelet: the chiral pair
    BBWBWW and its mirror image BBWWBW (read around the ring). Common
    mistakes: dividing 2^6 = 64 by 6 (not an integer - orbits have different
    sizes); miscounting the cycle structure of reflections. Now you try:
    necklaces of 5 beads in 3 colours. ((3^5 + 4 x 3)/5 = 255/5 = 51)

D8. Define a BIBD(v, b, r, k, lambda). Prove bk = vr and lambda(v - 1) = r(k - 1), and
    Fisher's inequality b >= v. Find the parameters of the design of lines of
    the affine plane of order 3, and describe the Fano plane.
    Answer: proofs below; AG(2, 3): (9, 12, 4, 3, 1); Fano (7, 7, 3, 3, 1).
    Teacher explains: DOUBLE COUNTING. (1) Count pairs (point, block) with
    the point in the block: by blocks bk, by points vr, so bk = vr. (2) Fix a
    v - 1 points Q lies with P in lambda blocks, giving lambda(v - 1); each of the r
    blocks through P has k - 1 other points, giving r(k - 1). FISHER: let N
    counts blocks containing both P and Q: r on the diagonal, lambda off it:
    Its eigenvalues are r - lambda + lambdav = rk (on the all-ones vector) and r - lambda
    (v - 1 times), so det = rk(r - lambda)^(v-1). Since k < v, lambda(v - 1) = r(k - 1)
    the solutions of ax + by = c (k = 3); any two points determine one line
    (lambda = 1). Then r = lambda(v - 1)/(k - 1) = 8/2 = 4 and b = vr/k = 36/3 = 12:
    points 1, ..., 7, lines {1,2,4}, {2,3,5}, {3,4,6}, {4,5,7}, {5,6,1},
    {6,7,2}, {7,1,3} (translates of {1, 2, 4} mod 7, because the differences
    of {1, 2, 4} give every nonzero residue exactly once: a DIFFERENCE SET).
    v = b = 7, r = k = 3, lambda = 1: SYMMETRIC, the projective plane of order 2.
    Common mistakes: confusing r (blocks per point) with k (points per
    block); assuming the necessary conditions guarantee existence. Now you
    try: does a 2-(16, 6, 1) design exist? (r = 15/5 = 3, b = 16 x 3/6 = 8 < 16:
    violates Fisher, no)

    (mod 6). Construct STS(9). Find the parameters of a projective plane of
    order n and explain why there is none of order 6.
    of AG(2, 3); projective plane: v = b = n^2 + n + 1, k = r = n + 1, lambda = 1;
    order 6 is excluded by Bruck-Ryser-Chowla.
    Teacher explains: For k = 3, lambda = 1: r = (v - 1)/2 must be an integer, so v
    is ODD; b = vr/3 = v(v - 1)/6 must be an integer, so 3 | v(v - 1), i.e.
    (Kirkman 1847 proved these v all work.) STS(9): write the points as a
    3 x 3 grid
       1 2 3
       4 5 6
       7 8 9
    Triples: 3 rows, 3 columns, 3 'diagonals' {1,5,9}, {2,6,7}, {3,4,8} and
    3 anti-diagonals {3,5,7}, {1,6,8}, {2,4,9}: 12 = 9 x 8/6 triples, and
    every pair appears once (e.g. 1 and 6 only in {1,6,8}). PROJECTIVE PLANE
    of order n: every line has n + 1 points, any two points on one line, any
    two lines meet in one point. Through a point P there are n + 1 lines,
    each with n further points, so v = 1 + (n + 1)n = n^2 + n + 1 = b. Order 6:
    v = 43, k = 7, lambda = 1 symmetric with v odd; BRC requires a nonzero
    solution of x^2 = 6y^2 - z^2 (since (v - 1)/2 = 21 is odd), i.e.
    x^2 + z^2 = 6y^2. Take a solution with gcd(x, y, z) = 1. Squares are 0 or
    so 3 | y, contradicting gcd 1. No solution, so no plane of order 6 -
    matching Tarry's result that there are not even two orthogonal Latin
    squares of order 6. Common mistakes:
    also counts. Now you try: how many triples in STS(15), and through each
    point? (b = 15 x 14/6 = 35, r = 7)

D10. Define orthogonal Latin squares. Prove that there are at most n - 1
     mutually orthogonal Latin squares of order n, and construct a complete
     set of MOLS of order 5. Explain the link with projective planes.
     Teacher explains: L and M (n x n, symbols 0, ..., n - 1) are ORTHOGONAL
     when the pairs (L(i, j), M(i, j)) run through all n^2 pairs exactly once.
     Renaming symbols in one square keeps orthogonality, so we may make the
     FIRST ROW of every square 0, 1, ..., n - 1. Now look at cell (2, 1)
     (second row, first column). In each square it cannot be 0 (column 1
     already has 0 at the top). If two squares had the same symbol s there,
     the pair (s, s) would occur twice: at (1, s + 1) and at (2, 1). So
     the squares have DIFFERENT symbols from {1, ..., n - 1} there: at most
     (a != 0) is Latin (a != 0 is invertible mod p). For a != b, given a pair
     (s, t), the system ai + j = s, bi + j = t has the unique solution
     i = (s - t)(a - b)^-^1, j = s - ai: orthogonal. For p = 5 this gives 4 MOLS;
     for instance L_1 has rows 01234, 12340, 23401, ... and L_2 has rows
     01234, 23401, 40123, 12340, 34012. Over GF(q) the same works for prime
     n exists (rows, columns and each square's symbols give the n + 1
     parallel classes of an affine plane of order n). Mod 4 the recipe fails
     (a = 2 is not invertible), but GF(4) gives 3 MOLS of order 4. Euler
     (Bose-Shrikhande-Parker 1959). Common mistakes: using Z_4 or Z_6 as if
     they were fields; normalising rows but forgetting cell (2, 1) is
     restricted. Now you try: are L_1 and L_3 (ai + j mod 4) orthogonal of
     order 4? (No: a - b = 2 is not invertible mod 4; e.g. pairs repeat)

D11. Prove R(3, 3) = 6. Prove R(s, t) <= R(s - 1, t) + R(s, t - 1) and deduce
     R(s, t) <= C(s + t - 2, s - 1). Show that R(3, 4) <= 9.
     Answer: proofs below; R(3, 4) <= 9 (in fact = 9).
     Teacher explains: R(3, 3) <= 6: in a red/blue K_6 take a vertex v; it has
     5 edges, so by PIGEONHOLE at least 3 have the same colour, say red to
     a, b, c. If any of ab, bc, ca is red, it forms a red triangle with v;
     otherwise abc is a blue triangle. R(3, 3) > 5: colour the pentagon's
     5 sides red and its 5 diagonals blue: the red graph is a 5-cycle and
     the blue graph is another 5-cycle (the pentagram), and neither contains
     a triangle. RECURRENCE: let N = R(s - 1, t) + R(s, t - 1) and colour K_N.
     A vertex v has N - 1 neighbours, so it has either at least R(s - 1, t)
     red neighbours or at least R(s, t - 1) blue ones (else
     N - 1 <= R(s - 1, t) - 1 + R(s, t - 1) - 1). In the first case the red
     neighbours contain a red K_{s-1} (add v: red K_s) or a blue K_t; the
     second case is symmetric. Since R(2, t) = t = C(t, 1) and Pascal's rule
     C(s + t - 2, s - 1) = C(s + t - 3, s - 2) + C(s + t - 3, s - 1), induction
     gives R(s, t) <= C(s + t - 2, s - 1). R(3, 4) <= R(2, 4) + R(3, 3) = 4 + 6
     = 10. Improve to 9: suppose K_9 has no red K_3 and no blue K_4. Each vertex
     has <= 3 red neighbours (4 red neighbours: if two are joined red we have
     a red triangle, otherwise they form a blue K_4) and <= 5 blue neighbours
     (6 blue neighbours contain a red K_3 or a blue K_3, giving a blue K_4 with
     v). Degree 8 forces exactly 3 red and 5 blue at every vertex; but then
     the red graph has 9 x 3/2 red edges, not an integer. Contradiction.
     (The circulant graph on Z_8 with red differences +/-1, 4 shows R(3, 4) > 8.)
     Common mistakes: in R(3, 3) taking only 2 same-coloured edges; mixing
     up which colour is required for which clique. Now you try: bound
     R(4, 4) by the recurrence. (R(3, 4) + R(4, 3) = 18, and R(4, 4) = 18)

  check small cases by listing (D_3 = 2, 3 dice totalling 15). For symmetry
  counting, physically list the rotations of a cube with a real die and
  write the cycle type of each before substituting; a Burnside sum that is
  not divisible by |G| signals an error. For designs, drill the two counting
  on the lattice of subsets and show that PIE is its special case; derive
  degree n over GF(q); prove that an affine plane of order n gives n - 1
  MOLS; prove Schur's theorem from R(3, 3, ..., 3); and show via Goodman's
  formula that every 2-colouring of K_6 has at least two monochromatic
  triangles.

TOPIC 10.44 - MATHEMATICAL LOGIC: PROPOSITIONAL AND PREDICATE LOGIC,

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - PROPOSITIONAL SYNTAX: formulas are built from ATOMS p, q, r, ... by the
    things by recursion on formulas and prove them by INDUCTION on formulas.
  - SEMANTICS: a VALUATION v assigns T/F to the atoms and extends by truth
  - NORMAL FORMS: every truth function is given by a DNF (OR of the true
    rows' MINTERMS) and a CNF (AND of clauses ruling out the false rows).
    There are 2^(2^n) truth functions of n atoms. FUNCTIONALLY COMPLETE sets:
    functions). POST'S criterion: complete iff not inside one of the five
    classes (0-preserving, 1-preserving, monotone, self-dual, affine).
    subset is (consequence: an infinite graph is k-colourable iff every
    finite subgraph is). SAT is decidable (by truth tables; NP-complete).
  - FIRST-ORDER (PREDICATE) LANGUAGE: constant, function and relation
    is allowed only if t is FREE FOR x (no variable of t gets captured):
    rename bound variables first.
  - STRUCTURES: a structure M has a non-empty DOMAIN and interprets each
    (equisatisfiable, not equivalent).
    (HENKIN's proof: add witnesses, extend to a maximal consistent set, build
    the term model). The valid sentences are recursively enumerable, but by
    CHURCH-TURING (1936) not decidable.
    every infinite cardinality (in particular a countable one: SKOLEM'S
    PARADOX for ZFC). Consequences: 'finite', 'connected', 'torsion',
    'well-ordered' are not first-order expressible; PA and Th(N) have
    NONSTANDARD models; an infinite structure is never characterised up to
    isomorphism by first-order sentences.
    proofs as numbers (e.g. 2^(a_1)3^(a_2)5^(a_3)...); 'x codes a proof of the
    formula coded by y' is a computable relation, REPRESENTABLE in Q, giving
    CONSISTENT, EFFECTIVELY AXIOMATISED (recursively enumerable) and contains
    'I am not provable', and is true in N if T is sound). SECOND
    INCOMPLETENESS THEOREM: such T (extending PA) does not prove its own
    consistency Con(T). TARSKI: arithmetical truth is not definable in
    arithmetic.
  - LIMITS OF THE HYPOTHESES: true arithmetic Th(N) is complete (but not
    geometry are complete and DECIDABLE. Natural independent statements:
    Con(PA), GOODSTEIN'S theorem and PARIS-HARRINGTON (true, unprovable in
    PA); CH and AC are independent of ZF(C).
    completeness (of a logic: provable = valid) vs completeness (of a
    theorems do not say every theory is incomplete (they need the
    hypotheses), nor that mathematics is inconsistent.

    law ((p -> q) -> p) -> p are tautologies. Decide whether
    Answer: both tautologies; the first consequence holds; the second fails
    at p = q = r = F.
    Teacher explains: A tautology must be T in all rows. For the first,
    the only way an implication X -> (p -> r) is false is X true and p -> r
    row makes it false: tautology (the TRANSITIVITY of ->). Peirce's law:
       p  q  | p -> q | (p -> q) -> p | ((p -> q) -> p) -> p
       T  T  |   T   |      T      |         T
       T  F  |   F   |      T      |         T
       F  T  |   T   |      F      |         T
       F  F  |   T   |      F      |         T
    Consequence 1: we need every row with (p -> q) -> r true to make
    p -> (q -> r) true. The conclusion is false only at p = T, q = T, r = F;
    there p -> q = T, so the premise is T -> F = F. So no counter-row: the
    consequence HOLDS. Consequence 2: try to make the premise true and the
    conclusion (p -> q) -> r false: need r = F and p -> q = T. Take p = q = F:
    premise p -> (q -> r) = F -> ... = T, conclusion (F -> F) -> F = T -> F = F.
    with 'F -> anything = F'; declaring a consequence valid after checking a
    the first disjunct is T, if q = F the second is T)

    majority function maj(p, q, r) (true when at least two arguments are
    Teacher explains: Let f be a truth function of p_1, ..., p_n. For each row
    The OR of all these minterms is true exactly in the rows where f is

    sufficient, condition.
    has finitely many classes, and the number of classes is the number of

  - A CONTEXT-FREE GRAMMAR (CFG) G = (V, sum , R, S) has rules A -> alpha; L(G) is
    the set of terminal strings DERIVABLE from S. Context-free languages

    context-free but not regular. A grammar is AMBIGUOUS if some string has
  - A TURING MACHINE (TM) has a finite control, an infinite tape and a
    states. On an input it accepts, rejects or LOOPS for ever. L is
    RECOGNISABLE (recursively enumerable) if some TM accepts exactly L; L is
    DECIDABLE (recursive) if some TM accepts L and HALTS on every input.
    Multitape and nondeterministic TMs recognise the same languages.
  - CHURCH-TURING THESIS: 'algorithm' (effective procedure) = Turing
    machine. It is a thesis (a definition backed by evidence: lambda-calculus,
    recursive functions, register machines all give the same class), not a
    theorem.
  - UNDECIDABILITY: there are countably many TMs but uncountably many
    languages, so most languages are not even recognisable. The HALTING
    are recognisable but UNDECIDABLE (proof by DIAGONALISATION). L is
    complement of A_TM is not recognisable.
    undecidable, B is undecidable. RICE'S THEOREM: every non-trivial
    property of the LANGUAGE L(M) of a TM is undecidable. Other undecidable
    problems: E_TM, EQ_TM, Post correspondence, ambiguity of CFGs, EQ_CFG,
    Hilbert's tenth problem (integer roots of polynomials).
    single-tape TM in O(t(n)) steps; input size n = number of SYMBOLS (bits),
    not the size of the numbers.
    problems; robust across reasonable models). Examples: sorting, shortest
    paths, 2-colouring, 2-SAT, matching, linear programming, PRIMES (AKS
    2002), gcd (Euclid, O(n) divisions for n-bit numbers).
  - NP = problems whose YES-instances have a CERTIFICATE (witness) of
    polynomial length checkable in polynomial time by a VERIFIER;
    equivalently decided by a NONDETERMINISTIC TM in polynomial time.
    P != EXPTIME by the TIME HIERARCHY THEOREM.
  - P VS NP: is every problem with quick-to-check answers also quick to
    solve? Open (a Clay Millennium Problem). If ANY NP-complete problem is
    in P, then P = NP. Most believe P != NP; much of cryptography assumes it
    (and more). Pseudo-polynomial algorithms (subset sum in O(nT)) do not
    show P = NP, because T is exponential in its number of bits.
