D10. Define the oriented intersection number I(X, Z) of compact oriented
     submanifolds of complementary dimension. On the torus T^2 = R^2/Z^2 let
     a, b be the closed curves given by straight lines in the directions
     (1, 2) and (3, 1). Compute I(a, b) and the number of intersection
     points. Explain why I(X, X) for the diagonal of M x M, or for the zero
     Answer: I(a, b) = det [[1, 3], [2, 1]] = -5; 5 points, all with the same
     intersection point p gets the sign +1 if (oriented basis of T_pX,
     oriented basis of T_pZ) is an oriented basis of T_pN, else -1;
     transverse, then use the cobordism argument). Torus: a line of
     direction (p, q) closes up after one period and meets a line of
     direction (r, s) at points whose number is |ps - qr| (the area of the
     parallelogram they span, in units of the torus area). At each point
     the tangent vectors are (1, 2) and (3, 1), with
        det [[1, 3], [2, 1]] = 1 - 6 = -5 < 0,
     so every crossing has sign -1 and I(a, b) = -5, with exactly 5 points.
     Order matters: I(b, a) = +5 (for curves in a surface, I(b, a) =
     -I(a, b)). No homotopy can reduce the number of crossings below 5,
     since I is invariant. The mod 2 intersection number is 1, so a and b
     can never be pulled apart. Self-intersection: push the zero section Z
     of TM off itself using a vector field v (the graph of v); the new copy
     meets Z exactly at the zeros of v, with sign = index. So I(Z, Z) =
     = L(f), the LEFSCHETZ number. Common mistakes: forgetting orientation
     signs (then the count is not invariant); computing ps + qr. Now you
     point)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw everything in the plane first: critical values of
  functions R -> R and R^2 -> R, curves crossing or touching the x-axis, and
  arrows of vector fields on a small circle (count how often the arrow
  turns). For degrees on S^1, always plot the lifted angle g(theta) and count
  the crossings of a horizontal line with the sign of the slope. Keep a
  maps, sources, saddles). Harder: prove Sard's theorem in general (the
  Milnor proof by induction on dimension); prove the easy Whitney
  embedding theorem into R^(2m+1); prove the Borsuk-Ulam theorem (a map
  S^2 -> R^2 identifies some pair of antipodal points) using mod 2 degree;
  prove the Hopf theorem that maps S^n -> S^n are classified up to homotopy
  by degree; compute the linking number of the Hopf link by the Gauss
  diagonal.

================================================================================
TOPIC 11.18 - UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH PROJECT / THESIS; READING CLASSIC PAPERS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - THE PROJECT: choosing a question that is small, well defined and new
    to the student (not necessarily to the world); agreeing it with a
    supervisor; a written plan with milestones (reading, first results,
    draft, final version, talk); a weekly log of what was tried,
    including failures; regular meetings with a written agenda.
  - FINDING LITERATURE: MathSciNet and zbMATH (reviews, citation
    tracking forwards and backwards), arXiv (preprints; the math.XX
    categories), the Mathematics Subject Classification (MSC2020: e.g.
    11 number theory, 05 combinatorics, 60 probability, 62 statistics,
    94 information theory, 03 logic, 68 computer science, 01 history),
    OEIS for integer sequences, survey articles, textbooks, and the
    original papers.
  - READING A PAPER: three passes - (1) title, abstract, introduction,
    statements of the main theorems, conclusion; (2) the definitions,
    examples and structure of the proofs; (3) every line, reconstructing
    each proof with the book closed, checking small cases, filling gaps,
    and noting what each hypothesis is used for. Read old papers in a good
    translation with modern notation beside them, and know how rigour and
    notation have changed.
  - CLASSIC PAPERS TO KNOW: Euclid, Elements IX.20 (infinitely many
    Euler product); Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae 1801 (congruences,
    quadratic reciprocity, Gauss sums); Abel 1826 and Cauchy's error on
    function); Cantor 1874 and 1891 (uncountability, the diagonal
    probabilistic lower bound for Ramsey numbers).
  - EXPERIMENTAL MATHEMATICS: compute small cases, tabulate, look up the
    sequence, GUESS a formula, test it on further cases, then PROVE it.
    Patterns can fail late (n^2 + n + 41 at n = 40, circle regions at n = 6,
    Fermat numbers at n = 5, Goldbach's 'other' conjecture at 5777, Euler's
    sum-of-powers conjecture); finite checking is never a proof.
    extreme case, work backwards, find an invariant, draw a picture, drop
    a hypothesis and look for a counterexample, strengthen the induction
    hypothesis, find an analogous solved problem.
  - PROOF CHECKING: spot the flawed step in a false proof (division by
    zero, invalid algebra for complex numbers, induction with a broken
    base or step, rearranging divergent series, pointwise versus uniform
    limits, reading a figure); check every quantifier; test the
    statement on examples and on the edge cases of its hypotheses.
  - WRITING: structure of a thesis (abstract, introduction with the main
    results, background, main chapters, examples, conclusion and open
    questions, bibliography); definition-theorem-proof style with
    motivation; LaTeX (amsmath, amsthm environments, \label and \ref,
    BibTeX), correct notation (\sin, \log, \mathbb{R}, \left( \right),
    braces for multi-character exponents); figures produced by code.
  - INTEGRITY: cite every source, including web pages and software;
    quote exactly; never present someone else's proof as your own;
    declare the use of computer algebra and AI tools; keep data and code
    so results can be reproduced.
  - PRESENTING: a 20-minute talk has one main idea, a worked example and
    a sketch (not a full proof); anticipate questions in the oral
    examination (viva): definitions, why each hypothesis is needed, what
    fails without it, what the next question would be.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Reconstruct Euclid's proof (Elements IX.20) that there are
    misreading, with a counterexample, and give a second proof (Euler's
    or one using n! + 1).
    Teacher explains: Euclid's statement: 'prime numbers are more than any
    assigned multitude of primes'. Given any finite list p_1, ..., p_n of
    NOT in the list; no finite list contains all primes. The proof is
    constructive but does not claim N is prime:
       2 + 1 = 3, 7, 31, 211, 2311 are prime, but
    Second proof: for n >= 2, any prime factor of n! + 1 exceeds n (every
    k <= n divides n!), so there are primes larger than every n. Euler's
    theorem in modern form, identify the key idea (a number coprime to
    all listed primes), and look for variants. Common mistakes: 'Euclid
    proved it by contradiction' (his proof is direct); claiming the
    Euclid numbers are prime. Now you try: adapt the proof to show there
    the list)

D2. Reconstruct Euler's 1734/35 solution of the Basel problem from the
    1735 and how was it justified later? Check the result numerically by
    partial sums, and estimate the tail.
    Weierstrass's factorisation theorem (1876). S_1_0 ~ 1.549768, error
    ~ 1/10.5 ~ 0.0952.
    Teacher explains: sin x/x has zeros exactly at x = +/-npi (n >= 1) and value
    1 at 0. Euler treats it like a polynomial with these roots:
    Compare coefficients of x^2. From the Taylor series sin x/x =
    1 - x^2/6 + x^4/120 - ..., the coefficient is -1/6. In the product, the
    function is NOT determined by its zeros (e^x sin x/x has the same
    zeros); one needs the Weierstrass (or Hadamard) product theorem, or a
    different proof (Fourier series of x^2, Parseval, or a double integral).
    Euler himself checked his answer numerically to many decimals - a
    model of experimental mathematics. Partial sums: S_1_0 = 1.549768,
    1/(N + 1) and 1/N (compare with integral  dx/x^2) and ~ 1/(N + 1/2): for N = 10,
    pi^2/6 - S_1_0 = 0.095166 ~ 1/10.5 = 0.095238. Common mistakes: comparing
    x^4 coefficients without the cross terms; thinking Euler's argument was
    accepted unquestioned (Daniel Bernoulli objected). Now you try:

D3. Explain Cantor's diagonal argument (1891) that the set of infinite
    binary sequences is uncountable, apply it to a given list, and deduce
    that R is uncountable and that |A| < |P(A)| for every set A. How does
    it differ from his 1874 proof?
    Answer: the diagonal sequence differs from the n-th listed sequence
    Teacher explains: Suppose s_1, s_2, s_3, ... lists ALL binary sequences.
    Define d by d_n = 1 - s_n(n). Then d != s_n for every n (they differ at
    place n), contradicting completeness of the list. Example:
       s_1 = 0 1 0 1 1 ...
       s_2 = 1 1 0 0 1 ...
       s_3 = 0 0 0 1 0 ...
       s_4 = 1 0 1 1 1 ...
       s_5 = 0 1 1 0 0 ...
    diagonal 0 1 0 1 0, so d begins 1 0 1 0 1. To pass to R, map a
    ambiguity): injective into [0, 1/2]. General theorem: if f : A -> P(A),
    |P(A)|. The 1874 proof used nested intervals: given a sequence of
    reals, build nested closed intervals each avoiding the next term,
    and use completeness - the same idea as in 10.1 D4. The 1891 argument
    is purely combinatorial and applies to ANY set; the same 'diagonal'

D4. Reconstruct Turing's 1936 proof that the halting problem is
    undecidable. Explain how a halting decider would settle Goldbach's
    conjecture, and why this shows the problem cannot be 'just hard'.
    Answer: a decider H yields a program D that halts on its own code iff
    it does not halt: contradiction.
    Teacher explains: Suppose a program H(P, x) always halts and outputs
    'yes' iff program P halts on input x. Build D(P): run H(P, P); if the
    answer is 'yes', loop forever; if 'no', halt. Now run D on its own
    Contradiction, so H cannot exist. This is Cantor's diagonal again:
    list programs P_1, P_2, ... and make D differ from P_n on input P_n. The
    halting set is still SEMI-decidable: run P and say yes if it stops;
    what cannot be done is to say no correctly in general. Goldbach: let
    G search n = 4, 6, 8, ... and halt at the first even n that is NOT a
    prime-type statements are harder). Turing's paper also defined
    computable numbers and answered Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem: no
    algorithm decides provability in first-order logic. Common mistakes:
    thinking the proof shows that some SPECIFIC program's halting is
    unknowable (for each fixed program the answer is simply yes or no);
    confusing 'undecidable' with 'unprovable'. Now you try: is it
    decidable whether a program halts within 10^6 steps? (yes: run it for
    10^6 steps)

D6. Shannon (1948) characterised entropy by three properties: continuity,
    monotonicity in n for uniform distributions, and the GROUPING rule.
    State the grouping rule, check it for (1/2, 1/3, 1/6), and compute the
    entropy per letter and total information of the strings BANANA and
    MISSISSIPPI (using letter frequencies). What are the limitations of
    this measure?
    Answer: H(1/2, 1/3, 1/6) = H(1/2, 1/2) + 1/2H(2/3, 1/3) ~ 1.45915 bits;
    BANANA 1.45915 bits per letter (~ 8.755 bits in total); MISSISSIPPI
    1.82307 bits per letter (~ 20.054 bits).
    Teacher explains: GROUPING: a choice may be made in stages; if we first
    decide between the first outcome and 'one of the others', then choose
    among the others, H must be the weighted sum of the stage entropies.
    Check: left side 1/2 log_2 2 + (1/3) log_2 3 + (1/6) log_2 6 = 0.5 + 0.52832
    theorem (Appendix 2 of the paper): the only functions with the three
    satisfies A(mn) = A(m) + A(n) by grouping, and monotonicity forces
    A(n) = K log n; rational p follow by grouping, real p by continuity.
    BANANA: frequencies A 3/6, N 2/6, B 1/6, the same as above: 1.45915
    bits per letter, x6 = 8.755. MISSISSIPPI: I 4, S 4, P 2, M 1 out of 11:
    1.82307 per letter, x11 = 20.054. Limitations: letter frequencies
    ignore order (ANANAB gets the same value), so this is only a
    single-letter model; English has ~ 4.1 bits per letter from letter

    used (Shannon 1951). Common

    Now you try: entropy per letter of ABRACADABRA. (~ 2.04037 bits)

    Compute the largest n for which the exact inequality
    2^(k/2) and with the known R(4, 4) = 18.
    Answer: k = 4: n = 6; k = 5: n = 11; k = 10: n = 100 (against 2^5 = 32).
    So R(4, 4) > 6, R(5, 5) > 11, R(10, 10) > 100.
    Teacher explains: Colour each edge of K_n red or blue independently
    with probability 1/2. A fixed set of k vertices is monochromatic with
       C(n, k)2^(1 - C(k,2)) < 2^(1 + k/2)/k! < 1 for k >= 3.
    Exact values: k = 4, C(6, 4)/32 = 15/32 < 1 but C(7, 4)/32 = 35/32:
    n = 6. k = 5: C(11, 5)/512 = 462/512 < 1, C(12, 5) = 792 > 512: n = 11.
    k = 10: C(100, 10)/2^4^4 ~ 0.984 < 1, C(101, 10)/2^4^4 ~ 1.092: n = 100.
    The method proves EXISTENCE without constructing a colouring - no
    explicit construction of comparable quality is known. For k = 4 it is
    weak (R(4, 4) = 18), but asymptotically it gives the exponential lower
    factor 2 (red OR blue); believing the union bound needs independence
    (it does not). Now you try: expected number of monochromatic triangles
    in a random 2-colouring of K_6. (C(6, 3)/4 = 5)

D8. EXPERIMENTAL MATHEMATICS. Place n points on a circle in general
    position and join all pairs; count the regions for n = 1, ..., 6. Show
    why the guess 2^n^-^1 fails, find the correct formula and prove it.
    Answer: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 31; regions = C(n, 4) + C(n, 2) + 1 (57 for
    n = 7, 99 for n = 8).
    Teacher explains: Drawing gives 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, then 31, not 32 -
    count carefully with n = 6 in general position (no three chords
    through one point). Finite differences of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 31:
       1, 2, 4, 8, 15 -> 1, 2, 4, 7 -> 1, 2, 3 -> 1, 1
    The fourth differences look constant, which suggests a polynomial of
    degree 4 in n. Proof by counting: each new
    crossing point and each new chord adds one region. Start with 1
    region (the disc). Each chord, drawn one at a time, adds 1 + (number of
    crossings on it). The chords are C(n, 2), the crossings C(n, 4) (every
    4 points give exactly one crossing of the two 'diagonals'). So
       regions = 1 + C(n, 2) + C(n, 4).
    Euler's formula V - E + F = 2 for the planar graph.) Lesson: five
    matching values of a sequence prove nothing; a PROOF must explain the
    count. Common mistakes: using a regular hexagon (three diagonals meet
    at the centre: 30 regions); stopping the experiment at n = 5. Now you
    try: predict n = 10. (1 + 45 + 210 = 256 = 2^8, a coincidence)

D10. Cauchy's Cours d'analyse (1821) 'proved' that a convergent series of
     continuous functions has a continuous sum. Abel (1826) gave the
     (-pi, pi], locate the flaw in Cauchy's argument, and state the
     corrected theorem. Then find the flawed step in the 'proof' that all
     horses have the same colour.
     Answer: the sum is x/2 on (-pi, pi) and 0 at x = pi: discontinuous at
     odd multiples of pi. The flaw: the N needed depends on x (pointwise,
     not uniform, convergence). Horses: the step n = 1 -> 2 fails (the two
     subsets do not overlap).
     Teacher explains: The Fourier series of x/2 on (-pi, pi) is
     but the sum jumps from pi/2 to -pi/2 across x = pi. Cauchy argued:
     s = s_N + r_N; s_N is continuous and r_N is small for large N, so s is
     continuous. The gap: 'r_N is small' was used simultaneously at x and
     at nearby points x + h with ONE N - true only if sup_x |r_N(x)| -> 0,
     i.e. UNIFORM convergence. Near x = pi the remainder of Abel's series
     stays of size about pi/2 however large N is (Gibbs phenomenon).
     Corrected theorem (Weierstrass, Seidel, Stokes): a uniform limit of
     continuous functions is continuous. HORSES: 'In any set of n + 1
     horses remove one horse, the rest have one colour; remove another,
     the rest have one colour; the two groups overlap, so all have one
     colour.' For n + 1 = 2 the groups {h_1} and {h_2} do not overlap: the
     mistakes: looking for the error in the base case (P(1) is true); in
     Cauchy's case 'blaming' the continuity of the terms. Now you try:

     c) -1 = (-1)^(2/2) = ((-1)^2)^(1/2) = 1

       i) terms -> 0 is necessary, not sufficient (harmonic series)
       j) arc length is not continuous under uniform convergence
       l) finite checking is not proof; n = 40 fails
       m) needs uniform convergence (Abel's counterexample)
       n) valid, once 0.999... is defined as the limit of the partial sums
          (the manipulations are those of convergent series)
       o) the meeting point lies OUTSIDE the triangle; the figure is wrong
       p) confuses sensitivity with PPV; the base rate matters (Bayes)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: read one classic proof a week in a modern edition and
  re-write it in the student's own words and notation, with every
  implicit step made explicit; always compute examples before and after
  reading a proof. Keep a research diary from the first day, and meet
  the supervisor with written questions. Make the student type every
  solution in LaTeX from the start, so that the thesis is not a
  last-minute typing exercise. For experimental work, insist on 'guess,
  test on NEW cases, then prove', and on keeping the code. Harder: read
  Riemann's 1859 paper and check the functional equation numerically;
  read Turing 1936 and program a universal Turing machine; reproduce a
  table from Shannon 1948; find in the OEIS a sequence with a conjectured
  formula and try to prove it; write a 20-page expository essay on one
  classic theorem with its history, modern proofs and open questions, and
  give a 20-minute talk on it to a non-specialist audience.

================================================================================
END OF STAGE 11 - READINESS CHECKLIST FOR STAGE 12
================================================================================
The student is ready for Stage 12 (master's / first-year graduate
coursework and qualifying exams) when they can usually:
  Analysis
  [ ] Build Lebesgue measure, decide measurability, and justify every
      exchange of limit, sum, derivative and integral with the monotone
      and dominated convergence theorems and Fubini-Tonelli
      density and duality
  [ ] Work in Banach and Hilbert spaces: operator norms, projections,
      orthonormal bases, adjoints, and apply Hahn-Banach, the open mapping
      and closed graph theorems and uniform boundedness
  Number theory and arithmetic geometry
  [ ] Compute rings of integers, discriminants, norms and traces, factor
      primes into prime ideals and compute small class numbers
  [ ] Use Dirichlet series, Euler products and arithmetic functions, and
  [ ] Add points on elliptic curves, count points over finite fields and
      find torsion subgroups over Q
  Geometry, algebra and topology
  [ ] Work with charts, smooth maps, tangent spaces, vector fields, flows
      and Lie brackets on manifolds
  [ ] Find Lie algebras of matrix groups, compute exponentials, brackets
      and dimensions of classical groups
  [ ] Use Noetherian rings, localisation, prime spectra and Krull
      dimension
  [ ] Build character tables of small groups and decompose
      representations using orthogonality
  [ ] Compute genera of curves (degree formula, Riemann-Hurwitz) and use
      Riemann-Roch on Riemann surfaces
  [ ] Use regular values, transversality, Sard's theorem and degree
  Applied and discrete mathematics
  [ ] Classify Markov chain states, find stationary distributions and
      hitting probabilities, and use Poisson processes and random walks
  [ ] Analyse fixed points, periodic orbits, bifurcations, Lyapunov
      exponents and fractal dimensions of dynamical systems
  [ ] Prove structural results about graphs (planarity, colouring,
      matchings, flows) and run and analyse the standard graph algorithms
  [ ] Compute entropy, mutual information and channel capacity, build
      optimal codes and state Shannon's coding theorems
  [ ] Carry out multivariate analysis (multivariate normal, PCA,
      discriminant analysis) and fit and validate basic learning models
  Research
  [ ] Read a classic paper critically, test conjectures by computation,
      find counterexamples, and write a clear, correctly referenced
      project report in LaTeX, then present it in a talk

Graduate real, functional and complex analysis, graduate algebra,
algebraic topology, differential geometry, measure-theoretic probability
and PDE - together with a first specialisation - are the main new work
of Stage 12.

================================================================================
  STAGE 12: MASTER'S / FIRST-YEAR GRADUATE - QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS
  PhD coursework and qualifying exams
================================================================================

How to use this file (note for the parent / teacher)
----------------------------------------------------
- There are 30 topics (12.1 to 12.30, the same as in topic.txt), in two
  groups: the Core graduate sequence (12.1-12.13: real, functional and
  complex analysis, several complex variables, graduate algebra,
  homological algebra, sheaves, commutative algebra, algebraic topology,
  differential geometry, Lie theory, measure-theoretic probability and
  PDE) and the Specialisation foundations (12.14-12.30: algebraic
  geometry, algebraic and analytic number theory, representation theory,
  harmonic analysis, stochastic calculus, ergodic theory, logic, category
  theory, combinatorics, numerical analysis, optimisation, statistics,
  mathematical physics, mathematical finance, inverse problems and
  algorithms).
  Each topic has:
    * WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN   the checklist of definitions, theorems,
                                  standard examples, counterexamples and
                                  methods in that topic
    * PART A - DESCRIPTIVE        12 questions (D1-D12): proofs,
                                  explanations, derivations and worked
                                  numerical problems, each with the answer
                                  and "Teacher explains" (the method step
                                  by step as a teacher shows it on the
                                  board, common mistakes, and a "Now you
                                  try" question)
    * PART B - MATHEMATICAL ONLY  12 questions (M1-M12): pure drills with
                                  answers. Most have many parts (a, b,
                                  c ...) so that EVERY case of the topic is
                                  practised again and again, from the
                                  easiest to the hardest - not just one
                                  example of each idea.
    * TEACHING TIPS               what to do if the student struggles, and
                                  how to make it harder
- In total: 360 descriptive + 360 mathematical questions, then a mixed
  revision test (equal descriptive and mathematical parts, two questions
  from every topic in each part) and a readiness checklist for Stage 13.
- Level: first-year graduate / qualifying-exam mathematics. The core
  sequence (12.1-12.13) is what a typical PhD qualifying exam covers; the
  specialisation foundations are chosen by research area.
- What is new in Stage 12: SYNTHESIS AND ABSTRACTION. Theorems of Stage 11
  become tools; the student learns to recognise the same structure
  (a functor, a spectral decomposition, a cohomology theory, a
  martingale, a variational principle) in many guises, and to solve
  qualifying-exam problems quickly and completely.
- Conventions: as in A11.txt. N = {1, 2, 3, ...}; log = ln unless a base is
- Method: for every theorem know its hypotheses and a counterexample when
  one is dropped; for every computation know which theorem justifies it.
  Use Python/SageMath/Macaulay2/R to CHECK calculations; write every
  solution in LaTeX. Practise past qualifying exams under time limits.
- Do 3 hours a day: 2 descriptive questions (full written proof) and
  2-3 drills per session, plus a weekly timed mixed paper.
- Revise Stage 11 (A11.txt) whenever the student finds something
  difficult: 11.1-11.3 before 12.1, 12.2, 12.12, 12.13, 12.18; 11.4-11.5
  before 12.15-12.16; 11.6-11.7, 11.17 before 12.9-12.11; 11.8-11.9 before
  12.5-12.8, 12.14, 12.17; 11.12-11.13 before 12.12, 12.19, 12.20;
  11.14-11.16 before 12.23-12.30.

  - RADON MEASURES on a locally compact Hausdorff (LCH) space: Borel,

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep three pictures on the board - a DENSITY (a smooth hill,
  continuous measure living on a null set) - and classify every measure
  into these three pieces before computing anything; most Radon-Nikodym
  and Lebesgue-decomposition questions are then just "read off the
  density, list the atoms, look for a Cantor-like remainder". Insist on
  checking sigma-finiteness before quoting uniqueness or Radon-Nikodym, and
  AC. For Riesz, always ask "which points are evaluated, which parts are
  integrated?" and remember that dual norms are total variations. Harder:
  prove the Hahn decomposition via the lemma in D4 in full detail; prove
  Riesz-Markov-Kakutani from Urysohn's lemma and partitions of unity;
  prove the Besicovitch or Vitali covering theorem for Radon measures and
  deduce differentiation of arbitrary Radon measures on R^n; show that a
  function F is AC iff it is continuous, BV and maps null sets to null
  convexity; and show that M(X) is the dual of C_0(X) but C_0(X) is not
  reflexive unless X is finite.

TEACHING TIPS
  reduce a Dirichlet or Schwarz problem to the disc centred at 0 by an
  automorphism first. For conformal maps, track three boundary points and
  one interior point through every brick. For products and partial
  choose the convergence factors, then fix the leftover entire function
  by growth (Hadamard or Liouville) and parity. For elliptic functions,
  draw the period parallelogram and count zeros and poles before
  computing anything; for Riemann surfaces, list branch points including
  Schwarz-Christoffel formula; prove Picard's little theorem via the
  modular function lambda or Bloch's theorem; prove Hadamard's factorisation
  as a sheaf of germs; and derive the Legendre relation and the
  sigma-function product formula.

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw everything in the (|z|, |w|) quadrant or the log plane
  (x, y) = (log|z|, log|w|): polydiscs are rectangles, the ball is a
  quarter circle, {|zw| < 1} is a half-plane, the Hartogs figure is an L,
  and "domain of convergence" / "domain of holomorphy" for Reinhardt
  domains means "log image convex" - the child can SEE the envelope of
  holomorphy as a convex hull. Always check holomorphy by writing f in z
  and test psd with trace and determinant; for Levi forms first find the
  on t only. For Weierstrass preparation, first compute f(0, w) to get
  the order k, then find the k small roots as series in z. Harder: prove
  Hartogs' theorem on separate analyticity (via Baire and Hartogs'
  biholomorphic by comparing automorphism groups at 0; prove the Oka
  Noetherian and a UFD, and prove Riemann's extension theorem across an
  analytic hypersurface and across analytic sets of codimension >= 2.

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep a small zoo on the board and test every statement on
  it: S_3 (solvable, not nilpotent), Q_8 and D_8 (nilpotent, not abelian),
  A_4 (a normal Sylow 2 but not nilpotent), A_5 (simple), Z/2 over Z/6
  (projective, not free), Q over Z (flat and injective, not projective),
  what kills it?"; for Tor and Ext write the resolution 0 -> Z ->m Z ->
  Z/m -> 0, DELETE Z/m, apply the functor and take homology. In category
  theory, draw the universal-property triangle before naming the object.
  prove that a finite group is nilpotent iff all maximal subgroups are
  characters; prove the structure theorem via Smith normal form over a
  Euclidean ring and then a PID; prove the snake lemma and the long exact
  sequence of Tor and Ext; show Ext^1 classifies extensions (Baer sum);
  prove that every module embeds in an injective one (Q/Z-duality); and
  prove the Yoneda lemma and the adjoint functor characterisation of
  limits.

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
    CHAIN HOMOTOPIC maps (f - g = dh + hd) induce the SAME map. A
    QUASI-ISOMORPHISM is a chain map inducing isomorphisms on all H_n.
  - EXACTNESS TOOLS: the SNAKE LEMMA (a map of short exact sequences gives
    FIVE LEMMA, and the LONG EXACT HOMOLOGY SEQUENCE of a short exact
    module), INJECTIVE modules (Hom(-, I) exact; BAER'S CRITERION: enough
    and an injective RESOLUTION ("enough projectives/injectives").
  - COMPARISON THEOREM: a map M -> N lifts to a chain map between
    for F left exact (Hom(M, -), Hom(-, N), fixed points), R^nF(M) =
    R^0F = F, and a short exact sequence gives a LONG EXACT SEQUENCE.
    DIMENSION SHIFTING: if 0 -> K -> P -> M -> 0 with P projective then
    resolution of M OR an injective resolution of N. Over Z: Ext^1(Z/n, A)
    Hom(Q, Z) = 0).
  - EXT^1 CLASSIFIES EXTENSIONS: equivalence classes of 0 -> N -> E -> M -> 0
  - HOMOLOGICAL DIMENSIONS: pd M = shortest projective resolution; id N;
    resolutions ... -> R ->x R ->x R -> k -> 0).
  - KOSZUL COMPLEX: for x_1, ..., x_n in R = k[x_1, ..., x_n] it is a free
    (i + j = n, resp. n - 1). GROUP COHOMOLOGY H^n(G, M) = Ext^n_ZG(Z, M),
    H_n(G, M) = Tor_n^ZG(Z, M); for cyclic G periodic of period 2.
  - HOMOTOPY CATEGORY K(A): complexes, maps modulo homotopy; TRIANGULATED
  - DERIVED CATEGORY D(A) = K(A)[quasi-isos^-^1] (Verdier localisation,
    Ext^n(M, N) (0 for n < 0); D(A) is triangulated but NOT abelian. Total

     the general principle Hom_D(M, N[n]) = Ext^n(M, N), with composition

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: drill the two "master computations" until automatic - for
  M = Z/m resolve by 0 -> Z ->m Z -> Z/m -> 0 and read off Tor_1 = A[m], Ext^1 =
  A/mA - and insist every answer comes from an explicit resolution, not
  from memory ("resolve, delete, apply F, take homology"). Always write
  the long exact sequence with all six or nine terms and label every map
  before chasing; check answers by balance (resolve the other variable)
  and by Euler characteristics. For extensions, draw the pushout and
  compute the order of a lifted generator. For derived categories start
  Z[1] before any abstraction. Harder: prove the horseshoe lemma and the
  comparison theorem in full; prove Baer's criterion via Zorn; show that
  Ext^1 classes form a group under the Baer sum and that Yoneda Ext agrees
  with derived-functor Ext; prove Tor commutes with filtered colimits and
  deduce flat = torsion-free over a PID; compute Ext*_k[x]/(x^2)(k, k) as
  a ring; build the Grothendieck spectral sequence and derive the Lyndon-
  Hochschild-Serre and base-change spectral sequences; verify the
  octahedral axiom for cones in K(A); prove Hom_D(M, N[n]) = Ext^n(M, N)
  via K-projective resolutions; and show that every triangulated category
  that is abelian is semisimple.

     f) f^-^1 is an exact functor.      g) f_* is an exact functor.
     j) The constant sheaf Z_R is flasque.
     o) On a simply connected, locally path-connected space every locally
        constant sheaf is constant.
     p) Two locally constant sheaves with isomorphic stalks are
        isomorphic.
     r) Fine sheaves on paracompact Hausdorff spaces are acyclic.
     s) On an irreducible space H^i(X, A_X) = 0 for i > 0.
     u) Every sheaf embeds in a flasque sheaf.
     y) Sheaf cohomology of Z_X equals singular cohomology for every X.
     Answers:
       a) F: P(R) = Z, P(U) = 0 (U != R)       b) T
       e) F: the exp-image on C*               f) T
       l) F: H^1(R, j_!Z_{(0,1)}) = Z            m) F: S^2 with hemispheres
       n) T              o) T
       q) F: 0 near 0, 1 near 1 on K = {0, 1} (identity theorem)
       r) T              s) T (A_X is flasque)  t) F: see c)
       u) T (Godement)   v) T
       y) F: the Cantor set (M9 r)); true for locally contractible
          paracompact X

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: make every abstract statement concrete on three test cases
  on C* (surjective on stalks, not on sections), and j_*Z, j_!Z for j :
  first: exactness, injectivity and isomorphism are stalkwise, while
  whether every intersection is acyclic (Leray) before trusting the
  answer; for local systems on S^1 just remember ker(T - 1), coker(T - 1).
  Harder: prove that injective sheaves are flasque and flasque sheaves
  Hausdorff spaces; construct the equivalence between local systems and
  and prove Grothendieck's vanishing theorem on noetherian spaces.

TOPIC 12.8 - COMMUTATIVE ALGEBRA: NOETHERIAN AND ARTINIAN RINGS, PRIMARY
DECOMPOSITION, INTEGRAL EXTENSIONS, NULLSTELLENSATZ, DIMENSION THEORY,
COMPLETIONS

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - Rings are commutative with 1. A module M is NOETHERIAN if it satisfies
    the ascending chain condition (ACC) on submodules, equivalently every
    submodule is finitely generated, equivalently every non-empty family of
    Noetherian ring is Noetherian. Z, fields, PIDs, k[[x]] are Noetherian;
    k[x_1, x_2, ...], the ring of all algebraic integers and C([0, 1]) are not.
    Hence every finitely generated algebra over a field or over Z, and all
    its quotients and localizations S^-^1A, are Noetherian. A subring of a
  - ARTINIAN = descending chain condition (DCC). In an Artinian ring every
    prime is maximal, there are finitely many maximal ideals, and the
    Jacobson radical (= nilradical) is nilpotent. AKIZUKI-HOPKINS: A is
    Artinian ring is uniquely a finite product of Artinian LOCAL rings
    then p = sqrtq is prime (q is p-primary). An ideal whose radical is a
    need not be primary, and an ideal with prime radical need not be
    primary: (x^2, xy) has radical (x) yet is not primary.
  - LASKER-NOETHER: in a Noetherian ring every ideal is a finite
    intersection of primary ideals (via irreducible ideals). A MINIMAL
    UNIQUENESS: the components belonging to MINIMAL primes are unique;
    + a_n = 0, equivalently A[b] is a finitely generated A-module
    (determinant trick). Integral elements form a subring (the INTEGRAL
    CLOSURE); integrality is transitive. A domain is NORMAL if it is
    integrally closed in its fraction field; UFDs are normal. The integral
    GOING DOWN holds if in addition A is a normal domain and B is a domain
    (or B is flat over A).
  - NOETHER NORMALIZATION: a finitely generated k-algebra A contains
    algebraically independent y_1, ..., y_d with A finite (integral) over
    k[y_1, ..., y_d]; d = tr.deg_k Frac(A) for a domain = dim A. ZARISKI'S
    LEMMA: if a field K is a finitely generated k-algebra then K/k is
    finite.
  - NULLSTELLENSATZ (k algebraically closed): WEAK form: the maximal ideals
    of k[x_1, ..., x_n] are exactly (x_1 - a_1, ..., x_n - a_n); a system of
    STRONG form: I(V(I)) = sqrtI (proof: RABINOWITSCH trick with an extra
    the nilradical equals the Jacobson radical. Over R it fails:
    HEIGHT ht p = dim A_p. dim k[x_1, ..., x_n] = n, dim Z = 1, dim Z[x] = 2,
    dim of a field or Artinian ring = 0, dim A/I = max over the minimal
    primes of I. For a finitely generated k-domain, ht p + dim A/p = dim A.
    A Noetherian ring can have infinite dimension (Nagata's example), but a
    Noetherian local ring has finite dimension.
  - KRULL'S PRINCIPAL IDEAL THEOREM: in a Noetherian ring a minimal prime
    over (f) has height <= 1 (= 1 if f is a non-zero-divisor); the HEIGHT
    THEOREM: a minimal prime over (f_1, ..., f_r) has height <= r. In a
    (embedding dimension). A is REGULAR if equality holds; regular local
    rings are domains (and UFDs).
    e = MULTIPLICITY (e = 1 for a regular local ring; e = the order of the
    lowest-degree term for a plane curve singularity, e.g. e = 2 for the
    cusp y^2 = x^3 at the origin).
    k[[x_1, ..., x_n]] = completion of k[x_1, ..., x_n] at (x_1, ..., x_n). For A
    generated M, completion is exact (ARTIN-REES LEMMA), and KRULL'S
    non-zero constant term; the node y^2 = x^2(1 + x) is irreducible in
    k[x, y] (localized) but splits into two branches in k[[x, y]].

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: work first in k[x, y] with MONOMIAL ideals, where everything
  can be drawn as a staircase: the length of k[x, y]/I is the number of
  boxes under the staircase, the radical is read off from the axes, and
  primary decomposition is "one piece per corner"; then move to Z and Z[i]
  (primary decomposition = prime factorization, lying over = factoring p).
  Before quoting a theorem, check its hypotheses aloud (Noetherian?
  integral? k algebraically closed? A normal?) - every standard
  counterexample above breaks exactly one of them. Harder: prove
  Lasker-Noether via irreducible ideals and the characterization Ass =
  {primes of the form (I : x)}; prove the Artin-Rees lemma via the blow-up
  ideal theorem with symbolic powers and lengths; prove Noether
  normalization over a finite field; prove that the Hilbert-Samuel
  function is eventually a polynomial of degree dim A (the dimension
  a Noetherian local ring is regular iff its completion is; and construct
  Nagata's Noetherian ring of infinite dimension.

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) Homotopy equivalent spaces have isomorphic homology groups.
     b) Spaces with isomorphic homology groups are homotopy equivalent.
     c) Spaces with isomorphic cohomology RINGS are homotopy equivalent.
     f) H^1(X; Z) is torsion-free for every X.
     g) H_1(X; Z) is torsion-free for every X.
     j) Every closed manifold is Z/2-orientable.
     k) pi_n(X) is abelian for n >= 2.
     m) The cup product is commutative.
     p) The Hurewicz map pi_2(X) -> H_2(X) is an isomorphism for every
        path-connected CW complex X.
     q) A map of CW complexes inducing isomorphisms on all pi_n is a
        homotopy equivalence.
     r) A map inducing isomorphisms on all H_n is a homotopy equivalence.
     s) Every covering map induces isomorphisms on pi_n for n >= 2.
     t) If M^4 is a closed simply connected 4-manifold then H_2(M) is free.
     u) A finite CW complex has finitely generated homotopy groups.
     v) If L(f) = 0 then f has no fixed point.
     Answers:
       a) T
       d) T (Hurewicz gives all pi_n = 0, then Whitehead)
       e) F: P minus an open ball is acyclic but pi_1 != 0
       f) T (Hom(H_1, Z) and Ext(H_0, Z) = 0)
       g) F: RP^2
       h) F: H^2(RP^2) = Z/2 but H_2(RP^2) = 0 (the Ext term)
       i) F: RP^2, Klein bottle (H_n = 0 when non-orientable)
       j) T
       k) T
       l) F: pi_3(S^2) = Z
       n) T (fixed-point-free maps are homotopic to the antipodal map)
       p) F: pi_2(T^2) = 0 but H_2(T^2) = Z (needs simple connectivity)
       q) T (Whitehead's theorem)
       r) F: a degree-1 map P -> S^3 (true for simply connected complexes)
       s) T
       v) F: the identity of a circle has L = 0 and fixes every point

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: make the student compute H_* of every space in M1 from a
  CW structure before touching any theorem, always writing the cellular
  chain complex as a row of Z's with the maps written on the arrows, and
  reading off kernels and cokernels (Smith normal form for matrices).
  Then insist on three reflexes: "homology is homotopy-invariant, so first
  simplify the space" (deformation retract, quotient by a contractible
  subcomplex); "cohomology = homology with torsion shifted up one
  picture and always ask whether a covering or a fibration is available.
  Harder: prove the Mayer-Vietoris sequence from the snake lemma and the
  small-simplices lemma; prove excision; derive the cellular boundary
  convex open sets in R^n; show that the Hopf invariant is 1 for the
  Hopf maps and use Steenrod squares (Adams) to show it is odd only for
  n = 2, 4, 8, so that R^n is a division algebra only for n = 1, 2, 4, 8;
  compute H*(CP^n) via the Gysin sequence; prove Freudenthal's suspension
  theorem and compute pi_4(S^3) = Z/2; show that the Borsuk-Ulam theorem
  follows from the ring H*(RP^n; Z/2); and compute pi_2 of a non-simply
  connected complex as a Z[pi_1]-module.

TOPIC 12.10 - DIFFERENTIAL TOPOLOGY AND GEOMETRY: MANIFOLDS, VECTOR BUNDLES,

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - SMOOTH MANIFOLD of dimension n: a Hausdorff, second-countable space
    Hausdorff matters: the line with two origins is locally Euclidean but
    not a manifold. PARTITIONS OF UNITY exist on every manifold.
    IMMERSION (dF injective), SUBMERSION (dF surjective), EMBEDDING
    (immersion + homeomorphism onto image). INVERSE FUNCTION THEOREM,
    RANK THEOREM. REGULAR VALUE THEOREM: if c is a regular value of F :
    M -> N then F^-^1(c) is an embedded submanifold of dimension dim M -
    dim N. SARD: critical values have measure 0. WHITNEY: every n-manifold
    embeds in R^2^n.
  - MATRIX GROUPS: GL(n) (dim n^2), SL(n) = det^-^1(1) (n^2 - 1), O(n) (n(n -
    1)/2, tangent space at I = skew matrices), U(n) (n^2), SU(n) (n^2 - 1),
    Sp(2n, R) (n(2n + 1)); Grassmannian G_k(R^n) has dimension k(n - k).
  - VECTOR FIELDS AND FLOWS: a vector field X is a section of TM; its
    [X, Y] = 0 iff the flows commute; [X, Y] measures the failure of the
    distribution is integrable iff it is closed under brackets.
    bundle (= tautological bundle over RP^1) is non-trivial; TS^1, TS^3, TS^7
    unique antiderivation with df = differential, d^2 = 0), PULLBACK F*
    CARTAN'S MAGIC FORMULA L_X = d i_X + i_X d. In R^3, d on 0-, 1-, 2-forms
    is grad, curl, div, and d^2 = 0 is curl grad = 0, div curl = 0.
  - ORIENTATION AND INTEGRATION: M is orientable iff it has a nowhere-zero
    Gauss, classical Stokes, FTC are special cases). Consequence: on a
    star-shaped open set every closed k-form (k >= 1) is exact. HOMOTOPY
    dimensions C(n, k); genus-g surface sum _g: 1, 2g, 1; RP^n: R in degree 0
    (and n if n is odd); CP^n: R in even degrees 0, ..., 2n; Klein bottle:
    1, 1, 0; R^2 minus k points: 1, k.
    plane (dx^2 + dy^2)/y^2 with cosh d(z, w) = 1 + |z - w|^2/(2 Im z Im w),
    of 1-forms); the difference of two connections is a tensor, but the
    Christoffel symbols are NOT a tensor. PARALLEL TRANSPORT along curves;
    R_{cdab}, first Bianchi R(X,Y)Z + cyclic = 0; n^2(n^2 - 1)/12 independent
    Ric = (n - 1)g, s = n(n - 1)), R^n (0), H^n (-1). For surfaces K = Gauss
    curvature, s = 2K; THEOREMA EGREGIUM: K is intrinsic (mean curvature is
    sum - pi = integral _T K dA (sphere: excess = area; H^2: defect = area).
    energy/length; constant speed. Examples: lines in R^n, great circles on
    const on surfaces of revolution. HOPF-RINOW: for connected M, metric
    then any two points are joined by a minimizing geodesic.
    (antipodes on S^n at distance pi) - past one a geodesic stops minimizing.

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep ONE worked model for every concept and return to it -
  and Gauss-Bonnet; H^2 for negative curvature and "straight lines that
  writing dx, dy in the new variables, then expanding the wedge (never
  memorize Jacobians), and always check an answer with Stokes or
  cohomology, first ask "what is it homotopy equivalent to?" and then use
  Mayer-Vietoris only on the small pieces. Harder: prove Sard's theorem
  and the Whitney embedding theorem; prove de Rham's theorem via good
  compactly supported cohomology; derive the second variation formula
  and use it to prove Bonnet-Myers and Synge's theorem; prove Cartan-
  Hadamard; compute the curvature of a U(1) connection on the Hopf bundle
  and show (i/2pi)integral F = -1 (Chern-Weil); and show that S^n has a nowhere-zero
  vector field iff n is odd.

================================================================================
TOPIC 12.11 - LIE GROUPS AND LIE ALGEBRAS: STRUCTURE, ROOT SYSTEMS,
CLASSIFICATION OF SEMISIMPLE LIE ALGEBRAS, REPRESENTATIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - LIE GROUP: a group G that is a smooth manifold with smooth
    multiplication and inversion. Its LIE ALGEBRA g = T_eG with the
    GL(n) (a matrix group, closed by CARTAN'S CLOSED SUBGROUP THEOREM
    [X, Y] = XY - YX. Standard list: gl(n) (n^2), sl(n): tr X = 0 (n^2 - 1),
    with velocity X; exp is a local diffeomorphism at 0; det e^X = e^(tr X).
    BAKER-CAMPBELL-HAUSDORFF: log(e^X e^Y) = X + Y + 1/2[X, Y] + (1/12)([X,
    [X, Y]] + [Y, [Y, X]]) + ..., so the bracket determines the group law
    near e. exp is onto for compact connected G but NOT for SL(2, R):
    Ad : G -> GL(g), Ad(g)Y = gYg^-^1, and d(Ad) = ad, ad X(Y) = [X, Y].
    if G is SIMPLY CONNECTED every Lie algebra homomorphism g -> h lifts to
    a group homomorphism G -> H. Every finite-dimensional real Lie algebra
    ADO'S THEOREM: every Lie algebra embeds in some gl(n)); the connected
    pi_1(SO(3)) = Z/2; the universal cover of SL(2, R) is not a matrix group.
  - ABSTRACT LIE ALGEBRAS (over a field, here R or C): bilinear,
    alternating bracket with the JACOBI identity. Ideals, quotients, ad.
    strictly upper triangular n_n (nilpotent), upper triangular b_n (solvable,
    not nilpotent), aff(1): [x, y] = y (solvable), e(2) (solvable).
  - ENGEL: g is nilpotent iff ad X is nilpotent for every X. LIE'S THEOREM
    upper triangular in some basis; so [g, g] is nilpotent. Fails over R
    (so(2) on R^2). The RADICAL rad g = largest solvable ideal; g is
    SEMISIMPLE if rad g = 0 (equivalently no nonzero abelian ideals).
    tr(XY); sp(2n): (2n + 2) tr(XY); gl(n): 2n tr(XY) - 2 tr X tr Y.
    negative definite (su(2): signature (0, 3); sl(2, R): (2, 1)).
  - WEYL'S THEOREM: every finite-dimensional representation of a semisimple
    Lie algebra over C is COMPLETELY REDUCIBLE (proof: the CASIMIR element
    solvable algebras: b_2 on C^2 has an invariant line with no invariant
    complement.
  - CARTAN SUBALGEBRA h (maximal toral: abelian, ad-semisimple) of a complex
    angles 90 degrees, 60 degrees/120 degrees, 45 degrees/135 degrees, 30 degrees/150 degrees, length ratios^2 1, 2, 3. The
    Weyl chambers. Rank 2: A_1 x A_1, A_2, B_2, G_2 (4, 6, 8, 12 roots).
    l(2l + 1), l(2l + 1), l(2l - 1), 78, 133, 248, 52, 14; dim g = rank +
  - REPRESENTATIONS OF sl(2, C): for each n >= 0 exactly one irreducible
    V(n), dim n + 1, h-eigenvalues (WEIGHTS) n, n - 2, ..., -n, basis
    the centre of the simply connected group. THEOREM: finite-dimensional
    sl(3): dim V(a, b) = (a + 1)(b + 1)(a + b + 2)/2 (3, 8, 6, 10, 27, ...).
  - COMPACT LIE GROUPS: bi-invariant HAAR measure; averaging gives an
    invariant inner product, so every representation is unitary and
    completely reducible (the UNITARY TRICK transfers this to sl(n, C)).
    coefficients of irreducibles are dense in L^2(G). MAXIMAL TORUS T:
    sin((n + 1)theta)/sin theta, Haar density (2/pi)sin^2theta dtheta on [0, pi]. SO(3) has
    irreducibles only of ODD dimension 2l + 1 (spherical harmonics).

       d) T (Ado's theorem + Lie III)      e) F: SU(2) and SO(3)
       f) F: b_2 on C^2                      g) T (Weyl)
       i) T (Cartan's criterion)           j) F: so(2) on R^2
       l) T (it is a sum of some of the simple factors)
       o) F: in A_1 x A_1, alpha + beta is not a root; also alpha + alpha = 2alpha
       q) T (commuting operators have a common eigenvector)
       t) T

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: make everything concrete in sl(2) and sl(3) first - write
  draw the six roots of A_2 as a hexagon before ever saying "root system";
  then draw B_2 (a square with its diagonals) and G_2 (a star of David with
  a hexagon) and read off angles and length ratios from the pictures.
  For every representation question, insist on the routine "list the
  weights with multiplicities, peel off the highest weight, repeat", and
  algebra visible: SU(2) -> SO(3) is the example to return to whenever
  someone claims the Lie algebra determines the group. Harder: prove
  Engel's and Lie's theorems and Cartan's criterion; prove Weyl's
  theorem with the Casimir element; show dim g_alpha = 1 and that the roots
  form a root system; complete the classification of connected Dynkin
  diagrams by excluding every tree outside the list; prove the Weyl
  character formula via the Weyl integration formula for a compact group
  (or via Verma modules and the Casimir), derive Kostant's multiplicity
  formula, and show that |P/Q| equals the order of the centre of the
  simply connected group (Z/n for SU(n), Z/4 or Z/2 x Z/2 for Spin(2n)).

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     c) If E[X | Y] = EX then X and Y are independent.
     e) Every L^1-bounded martingale converges in L^1.
     f) Every UI martingale converges a.s. and in L^1.
     h) The last time before 10 that a random walk visits 0 is a
        stopping time.
     i) Brownian motion is a.s. differentiable at t = 0.
     j) Brownian paths have finite total variation on [0, 1].
     k) B_t^2 is a martingale.
     l) Convergence in distribution implies convergence in probability.
     n) A pointwise limit of characteristic functions is a ch.f.
     s) Every tight sequence of laws on R has a weakly convergent
        subsequence.
     Answers:
       a) T        b) T
       c) F: Z ~ N(0, 1), X = Z, Y = Z^2: E[X | Y] = 0 = EX, yet X and Y
          are dependent
       g) F: simple random walk stopped at the first hit of 1
       h) F: deciding it requires the future path
       i) F: B_t/t = W_{1/t} with W = time inversion, a BM, and
       j) F (quadratic variation 1 forces infinite variation)
       m) F: X_n = Z, Y_n = -Z, Y = Z (sum 0, not 2Z)
       q) F: symmetric X with P(|X| > x) ~ 1/(x ln x) (only the converse
          direction holds)
       r) F: X_n = n w.p. 1/n (M8 p))     s) T (Helly-Prokhorov)
       t) T

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: teach conditional expectation first on FINITE partitions
  random variable; then treat the general definition as the same idea
  step. Before every optional stopping argument, have the student WRITE
  bounded increments) holds, and keep the doubling-strategy walk as the
  warning example. For Brownian motion, reduce everything to Gaussian
  vectors with covariance min(s, t), and draw the reflected path. For
  (not tight), N(0, n) (limit not continuous at 0) and "n w.p. 1/n"
  (means do not converge) as the three standard pathologies. Harder:
  series and prove Kolmogorov's continuity criterion; prove the strong
  Markov property and the full reflection principle for the joint law
  of (M_t, B_t); prove nowhere differentiability (Paley-Wiener-Zygmund)
  and the law of the iterated logarithm; prove Lindeberg-Feller and the
  Berry-Esseen bound; prove Prokhorov's theorem and Donsker's invariance
  principle; establish the martingale central limit theorem and
  Azuma-Hoeffding; and study backward martingales to prove the SLLN and
  de Finetti's theorem.

TEACHING TIPS
  a one-line polar-coordinates or scaling computation instead of
  memorising. For every boundary-value problem insist on the same four
  written lines: (1) multiply by v and integrate by parts, (2) name the
  space (Dirichlet in the space, Neumann in the form), (3) check bounded +
  equations, always compute the energy identity first and solve one
  separation-of-variables example by hand, contrasting e^(-k^2t) (heat:
  smoothing, decay) with cos kt (wave: no smoothing, conservation). Harder:
  prove the Gagliardo-Nirenberg-Sobolev inequality for p = 1 and bootstrap
  it to all p < n; prove Morrey's estimate via averages over balls; prove
  the trace theorem on a half-space; carry out the full difference-
  quotient proof of boundary H^2 regularity after flattening the boundary;
  construct weak solutions of the heat and wave equations by Galerkin
  approximation with all energy estimates; prove the mountain pass theorem
  from the deformation lemma and apply it to -delta u = |u|^{p-1}u for 1 < p <
  (n + 2)/(n - 2); and show via Pohozaev's identity that there is no
  non-trivial solution in a star-shaped domain at the critical exponent.

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
    I(Z) = {f : f|_Z = 0}. The V(J) are the closed sets of the ZARISKI
    TOPOLOGY (noetherian, not Hausdorff; on A^1 the closed sets are the
    finite sets and A^1). HILBERT'S NULLSTELLENSATZ: I(V(J)) = sqrtJ, so
    set is a finite union of irreducible components.
  - REGULAR FUNCTIONS AND MORPHISMS: k[V] = k[x_1, ..., x_n]/I(V); the
    category of affine varieties is anti-equivalent to finitely generated
    reduced k-algebras. DIMENSION = Krull dimension of k[V] = tr.deg of the
    function field k(V); a hypersurface in A^n has dimension n - 1. A
    cusp y^2 = x^3 (k[t^2, t^3] != k[t]).
    a connected projective variety are constant. VERONESE v_d : P^n -> P^N
    meet in exactly de points counted with multiplicity.
    space m/m^2 equals r, iff O_{X,p} is a regular local ring. Examples:
    node y^2 = x^2(x + 1), cusp y^2 = x^3, cone x^2 + y^2 = z^2; the singular locus
    is a proper closed subset.
  - SCHEMES: Spec A = prime ideals with closed sets V(a), basic opens D(f),
    structure sheaf with O(D(f)) = A_f and stalks O_p = A_p. A SCHEME is a
    locally ringed space locally isomorphic to some Spec A; morphisms of
    schemes (Spec Z, Spec Z[x], Spec Z[i] -> Spec Z with fibres over p).
    reduced, integral, noetherian, separated, proper, finite type.
  - SHEAVES: presheaf F(U) with restrictions; SHEAF = locality + gluing.
    is surjective iff surjective on stalks, NOT on sections (exp : O -> O*
    Div/Prin; Cartier divisors; Cl = Pic on smooth (locally factorial)
    cone xy = z^2 is Z/2 while its Pic is 0; Pic of a Dedekind ring = its
    class group. H^0(P^n, O(d)) = forms of degree d, dim C(n+d, n).
    resolutions); a short exact sequence of sheaves gives a LONG exact
    separated noetherian scheme for quasi-coherent F. GROTHENDIECK
    d >= 0; h^n(O(d)) = h^0(O(-d-n-1)) (nonzero only for d <= -n - 1); K_{P^n}
    of transcendence degree 1. deg div(f) = 0. GENUS g = h^1(O_C) = h^0(K_C).
    Smooth plane curve of degree d: g = (d - 1)(d - 2)/2 (so no smooth
    K = O(a + b - 4), 2g - 2 = ab(a + b - 4).
    gaps at each point.
  - MAPS OF CURVES: a non-constant f : X -> Y is finite and surjective, deg
    degree 2g + 1 or 2g + 2, has genus g and 2g + 2 Weierstrass points;
    every genus-2 curve is hyperelliptic. No non-constant map P^1 -> curve
    of genus >= 1. HURWITZ: |Aut C| <= 84(g - 1) for g >= 2 (Klein quartic:
    168). CANONICAL EMBEDDING of a non-hyperelliptic curve in P^(g-1).

TEACHING TIPS
  every abstract statement land on four test cases: A^1 (Spec k[x]), P^1,
  until the "negative-exponent monomials" picture of H^n(P^n, O(d)) is
  automatic; then every genus in the course comes from a short exact
  sequence 0 -> O(-d) -> O -> O_C -> 0 plus Serre duality. For curves drill
  what e?" before quoting Riemann-Hurwitz. For surfaces, write K, C^2 and
  of genus g >= 2 has at most (g - 1)g(g + 1) Weierstrass points counted
  with weight and that |Aut C| <= 84(g - 1); derive surface Riemann-Roch
  from curve Riemann-Roch and adjunction; prove the Hodge index theorem
  from Riemann-Roch; show every smooth cubic surface is P^2 blown up at 6
  points and compute the incidence graph of its 27 lines (the
  theoretic fibres of Spec Z[x]/(f) -> Spec Z to see ramification as
  geometry.

================================================================================
TOPIC 12.15 - ALGEBRAIC NUMBER THEORY: DEDEKIND DOMAINS, RAMIFICATION, CLASS
GROUPS, DIRICHLET UNIT THEOREM, LOCAL FIELDS, p-ADIC NUMBERS, ADELES AND
IDELES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - NUMBER FIELD K: a finite extension of Q, [K : Q] = n = r_1 + 2r_2 (r_1
    real embeddings, r_2 pairs of complex ones). RING OF INTEGERS O_K = the
    elements whose monic minimal polynomial lies in Z[x] (the integral
    = (-1)^r_2. If disc(f) is squarefree, or f is Eisenstein at every
    p with p^2 | disc(f), then O_K = Z[alpha].
  - DEDEKIND DOMAIN: a Noetherian, integrally closed domain in which every
    non-zero prime is maximal. O_K is Dedekind; so is every PID and the
    coordinate ring of a smooth affine curve. MAIN THEOREM: every non-zero
    ideal factors UNIQUELY as a product of prime ideals; the fractional
    ideals form a free abelian group I_K on the primes; "to contain is to
    PID. Non-examples: Z[sqrt-3] (not integrally closed: (2, 1 + sqrt-3)^2 =
    2(2, 1 + sqrt-3)), k[x, y] (dimension 2).
    (3, 1 - sqrt-5): unique factorisation is restored at the level of ideals.
    for EVERY alpha.
  - QUADRATIC AND CYCLOTOMIC LAWS: in Q(sqrtd), p odd splits / is inert /
    (mod 4).
  - CLASS GROUP Cl(K) = I_K/P_K (fractional ideals modulo principal ones);
    MINKOWSKI BOUND: every class contains an integral ideal of norm <= M_K =
    (n!/n^n)(4/pi)^r_2 sqrt|d_K|; so Cl(K) is generated by primes of norm <= M_K.
    d = -1, -2, -3, -7, -11, -19, -43, -67, -163 (Heegner-Stark-Baker).
  - GEOMETRY OF NUMBERS: MINKOWSKI'S THEOREM: a convex, centrally symmetric
    R^r_1 x C^r_2. Consequences: finiteness of h_K, |d_K| > 1 for K != Q
    (so some prime ramifies), HERMITE: finitely many K with |d_K| <= X.
    with weight 2 at complex places): kernel = mu_K, image a full lattice
    quadratic). N(u) = +/-1 for units.
  - UNITS IN PRACTICE: imaginary quadratic: O^x = {+/-1}, except mu_4 in Q(i),
    1 + sqrt2, 2 + sqrt3, (1 + sqrt5)/2, 5 + 2sqrt6, 8 + 3sqrt7, 3 + sqrt10, (3 + sqrt13)/2.
    is isosceles, every point of a ball is its centre). OSTROWSKI: every
    8 (p = 2).
  - LOCAL FIELDS: fields complete for a discrete valuation with finite
    residue field (equivalently, non-discrete locally compact fields != R,
    residue field k, n = ef. For each n there is a UNIQUE unramified
    extensions for p odd, 7 for p = 2.
    (Selmer: 3x^3 + 4y^3 + 5z^3 = 0).
    respect to O_v (all but finitely many coordinates integral), topology
    product topology (NOT the subspace topology of A_K: inversion would not
    formula, K^x discrete, and J^1/K^x is COMPACT (this one fact contains both
    the finiteness of h_K and the unit theorem).

D7. State and prove Minkowski's convex body theorem. Use it (a) to prove
    that |d_K| > 1 for every number field K != Q, so that some prime
    ramifies in K.
    covol p. The disc a^2 + b^2 < 2p has area 2pip > 4p, so it contains (a, b)

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample or reason for F.
     i) pi(x) < li(x) for all x >= 3.
     k) The Legendre sieve with z = sqrtx gives pi(x) ~ x/log x.
     m) Every odd n >= 7 is a sum of three primes.
     n) Bombieri-Vinogradov implies GRH.
     o) The non-trivial zeros are symmetric about Re s = 1/2.
     p) A Dirichlet series with non-negative coefficients can be analytic
        at its real abscissa of convergence.

        Hardy-Littlewood conjecture.
     Answers:

       c) F (Euler)               d) T (Brun)
       i) F: Littlewood, sign changes infinitely often
                                     ~ 1.123x/log x; the error dominates
       l) F: parity problem (Selberg's lambda(n) example)
       m) T (Vinogradov for large n; Helfgott for all)
       n) F: it is an average over q only
       p) F (Landau's theorem)    q) F: the constant is ineffective
       s) T                       t) F: it is 4 times too large

TEACHING TIPS
  and translate every question into it before computing. Drill partial
  summation until it is automatic, since nearly every asymptotic in M5
  is one line of it. For the functional equation, have students first
  sieves, do Legendre by hand for x = 100 before any theory: the error
  local factors p by p. Harder: prove the zero-free region
  Siegel's theorem and explain its ineffectivity; derive the large sieve
  via Gallagher's lemma and deduce Bombieri-Vinogradov from Vaughan's
  identity; prove Selberg's G(z) >= log z carefully and the Brun-
  Titchmarsh inequality; carry out Vinogradov's minor arc estimate; and
  read Maynard's bounded gaps proof as a multidimensional Selberg sieve.

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - REPRESENTATIONS: a continuous homomorphism pi : G -> GL(V) (V complex,
    usually finite-dimensional). Subrepresentations, irreducibility,
    irreducible (C algebraically closed). Hence irreps of ABELIAN groups are
    1-dimensional; the centre acts by a scalar (central character).
  - COMPACT GROUPS: a compact group has a unique bi-invariant HAAR
    invariant inner product, so every finite-dimensional representation is
    UNITARISABLE and COMPLETELY REDUCIBLE (orthogonal complements of
    R (or of the algebraic group G_a) is not completely reducible.
  - PETER-WEYL THEOREM (G compact): matrix coefficients of irreps are
    with ONB {sqrt(dim pi) pi_ij}; characters form an ONB of the L^2 class
    functions. Consequences: every compact Lie group has a faithful finite-
    finite; for G = U(1) it is Fourier series. For a closed subgroup K,
    the multiplicity of V_pi in L^2(G/K) is dim V_pi^K (FROBENIUS RECIPROCITY):
  - SU(2) AND SO(3): the irreps of SU(2) are V_n = homogeneous polynomials
    of degree n in two variables, dim n + 1, one for each n >= 0, with
    SO(3) = SU(2)/{+/-1} are the V_n with n even (dims 1, 3, 5, ...; "integer
    spin"). WEYL INTEGRATION on SU(2): integral  f dg = (2/pi)integral _0^pi f(theta) sin^2theta dtheta for
    class functions; on SO(3) the density of the rotation angle is
    (1 - cos theta)/pi.
    reducible.
    For each n >= 0 there is exactly one irrep V(n) of dim n + 1, basis
    2fe acts on V(n) by n(n + 2).
    {f.d. irreps}. The weights of L(lambda) are W-invariant with multiplicities
    FREUDENTHAL or KOSTANT; for GL_n they are Kostka numbers.
  - COMPACT CONNECTED LIE GROUPS: maximal torus T, all maximal tori
    dominant weights in the character lattice X*(T) (THEOREM OF THE
    HIGHEST WEIGHT); WEYL INTEGRATION FORMULA integral _G f = (1/|W|)integral _T f(t)
    V_n). Non-compact simple groups such as SL(2, R) have NO non-trivial
    finite-dimensional unitary reps; their unitary irreps are infinite-
    dimensional (principal and discrete series).
    Jordan decomposition; unipotent radical R_u(G) = largest connected
    normal unipotent subgroup. G is REDUCTIVE if R_u(G) = 1 (GL_n, SL_n, PGL_n,
    reductive: G_a, the Borel B of upper triangular matrices, unipotent U_n.
    reducible (linearly reductive).
    for GL_n: lambda_1 >= ... >= lambda_n in Z^n; polynomial ones = partitions, dimension by
    Specht_lambda as GL_n x S_k-modules.
  - CHARACTERISTIC p: complete reducibility FAILS; the Weyl module Sym^n(k^2)
    F, K^{+/-1} with KEK^-^1 = q^2E, KFK^-^1 = q^-^2F, EF - FE = (K - K^-^1)/(q -
    K^-^1. q-INTEGERS [n] = (q^n - q^-^n)/(q - q^-^1) = q^{n-1} + ... + q^{1-n}.
    all f.d. reps are completely reducible and tensor products obey
    Clebsch-Gordan. QUANTUM CASIMIR C = EF + (q^-^1K + qK^-^1)/(q - q^-^1)^2;

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: reduce everything to WEIGHTS. A representation of SU(2) or
  repeatedly peeling off the highest string, and a character is just this
  multiset written as a Laurent polynomial. Draw the weight diagrams of
  let students find tensor products by adding diagrams before touching
  formulas. Always check a decomposition by dimension, and every Haar
  first at q = 1 and only then insert q-integers. Harder: prove Peter-Weyl
  via compact convolution operators; derive the Weyl integration formula
  from the map G/T x T -> G and prove the Weyl character formula from it
  (Weyl's original analytic proof); prove the denominator identity and
  an irrep is real, quaternionic or complex (Frobenius-Schur indicator);
  prove Borel-Weil for SL_2 via H^0(P^1, O(n)); verify Steinberg's tensor
  product theorem for SL_2 in characteristic 3 up to n = 8; and construct
  equation.

D6. Solve the geometric Brownian motion dS = muS dt + sigmaS dB. For S_0 = 100,

    Answer: S_t = S_0exp((mu - sigma^2/2)t + sigmaB_t); 110.517, 108.329, 498.464
    Teacher explains: Apply Ito to Y = ln S: dY = dS/S - 1/2(dS)^2/S^2 =

    a.s., so (1/t)ln S_t -> mu - sigma^2/2; if mu < sigma^2/2 then S_t -> 0 a.s. even

D7. Solve the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck SDE dX = -thetaX dt + sigma dB, X_0 = x, theta > 0.
    Find the mean, variance, the stationary distribution and the
    stationary covariance. Evaluate for theta = 2, sigma = 1, x = 3, t = 1.
    sigma^2(1 - e^{-2thetat})/(2theta)); stationary N(0, sigma^2/(2theta)); covariance
    (sigma^2/2theta)e^{-theta|t-s|}; numbers 0.40601 and 0.24542.
    Teacher explains: Integrating factor, exactly as for the linear ODE:
    d(e^{thetat}X_t) = thetae^{thetat}X dt + e^{thetat}dX = sigmae^{thetat} dB (no Ito correction
    because e^{thetat} has zero quadratic variation). Integrate and multiply by
    e^{-thetat}. The stochastic integral has deterministic integrand, so X_t is
    N(0, sigma^2/(2theta)); starting from this law, the process is stationary. For
    s < t, X_t = e^{-theta(t-s)}X_s + (independent noise), so Cov(X_s, X_t) =
    e^{-theta(t-s)}Var X_s = (sigma^2/2theta)e^{-theta(t-s)}. Numbers: 3e^{-2} ~ 0.40601,
    (1 - e^{-4})/4 ~ 0.24542 (close to the stationary value 1/4 already).
    Mean reversion half-life: ln 2/theta ~ 0.347. Common mistakes: variance

    try: theta = 1, sigma = sqrt2, x = 0: Var X_1. (1 - e^{-2} ~ 0.86466)

D8. State the existence and uniqueness theorem for SDEs and prove the
    uniqueness part. Then show why each hypothesis matters: (a) dX = X^2 dt,
    X_0 = 1; (b) dX = 3X^{2/3} dt, X_0 = 0; (c) Tanaka's dX = sgn(X) dB.
    explodes at t = 1; (b) two solutions 0 and t^3; (c) weak solution but no
    pathwise uniqueness, no strong solution.
    Teacher explains: THEOREM: if |b(t,x) - b(t,y)| + |sigma(t,x) - sigma(t,y)| <=
    UNIQUENESS: if X, Y are solutions, X_t - Y_t = integral (b(X) - b(Y)) ds +
    integral (sigma(X) - sigma(Y)) dB. Using (a + b)^2 <= 2a^2 + 2b^2, Cauchy-Schwarz on the
    ds-part and the Ito isometry on the dB-part,
    EXISTENCE: Picard iterates X^{n+1} = X_0 + integral b(X^n) + integral sigma(X^n) dB satisfy
    E sup|X^{n+1} - X^n|^2 <= C(Ct)^n/n! (Doob's inequality), summable, so they
    converge a.s. uniformly (Borel-Cantelli). (a) b = x^2 is only locally
    Lipschitz, no linear growth: X = 1/(1 - t) blows up at t = 1. (b) b =
    3(t^3)^{2/3}) solve it. (c) Given any BM W, X = W solves the SDE with
    solves it with the same B (sgn is odd, up to the null set {X = 0}),
    so pathwise uniqueness fails, and B = |X| - L generates only the
    filtration of |X|, so X is not adapted to B: no strong solution.
    Common mistakes: thinking local Lipschitz alone prevents explosion.
    Now you try: explosion time of dX = X^2 dt, X_0 = 2. (1/2)

TEACHING TIPS
  it is automatic, and make every Ito computation a three-column table
  f_t, f_x, 1/2f_xx before writing df; check each answer by taking
  expectations (the dB-part must vanish, e.g. E B_t^4 = 3t^2) or by
  simulation. Always say which interpretation (Ito or Stratonovich) is
  meant, and derive integral B dB from left, right and midpoint sums at least once
  by hand. For SDEs, look first for an integrating factor (linear), then a
  log (multiplicative), then f(B) (try Y = f(X) with Ito). For finance,
  derive the Black-Scholes PDE from the hedge before memorising d_1, d_2,
  and check prices with put-call parity. Harder: construct the Ito
  representation theorem; prove Girsanov and Novikov; prove the Picard
  existence theorem and Yamada-Watanabe; show Tanaka's SDE has no strong
  solution; derive Tanaka's formula and the occupation-time formula for
  local time; prove the Feynman-Kac formula with killing and use it for
  the arcsine law; price barrier options by the reflection principle and
  Girsanov; derive Kramers' escape rate by solving the mean exit-time
  ODE asymptotically; and prove that Euler-Maruyama has strong order 1/2 and
  Milstein order 1.

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: begin every problem by drawing the map (graph of 2x mod 1,
  the rotation as a clock hand, the cat map stretching a square) and by
  asking three questions in order: "which measure is preserved?" (always
  test PREIMAGES of intervals or cylinders), "what are the invariant
  functions?" (use Fourier series for rotations, doubling and toral maps,
  and look for finite orbits of frequencies) and "do correlations decay?"
  exact). Keep the three model examples in mind: rotation (ergodic, zero
  entropy, not mixing), doubling map/Bernoulli shift (mixing, entropy
  Birkhoff is an a.e. statement and that unique ergodicity is what lets
  us talk about SPECIFIC orbits (Weyl, Benford). Harder: prove Kac's
  lemma and the ergodic decomposition; show that weak mixing is
  equivalent to the absence of non-constant eigenfunctions and to
  ergodicity of T x T; prove Weyl's polynomial equidistribution via
  Furstenberg's skew products and van der Corput; prove the
  Kolmogorov-Sinai theorem and Rohlin's formula for the Gauss map;
  compute the entropy of a hyperbolic toral automorphism with Markov
  partitions; study Ornstein's theory and the Halmos-von Neumann
  correspondence principle and multiple recurrence.

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - FIRST-ORDER LOGIC: a language L (constants, function and relation
    theory has a model, via Henkin constants and a maximal consistent set).
  - COMPACTNESS: T has a model iff every finite subset does. Consequences:
    nonstandard models of Th(N) and of R (infinitesimals); "finite",
    "torsion", "connected graph", "well-ordered" are NOT first-order
    axiomatizable; a theory with arbitrarily large finite models has an
    finite subgraph is).
    (downward; Tarski-Vaught test). Skolem's "paradox": ZFC, if consistent,
    has a countable model although it proves R uncountable.
    countable models.
  - TYPES AND QUANTIFIER ELIMINATION: a (complete) n-type over A is a
    maximal consistent set of formulas in x_1..x_n with parameters in A;
    formula is T-equivalent to a quantifier-free one: DLO, ACF (Chevalley:
    constructible sets), RCF (Tarski-Seidenberg: semialgebraic sets),
  - ZFC: Extensionality, Foundation, Pairing, Union, Power set, Separation
    (schema), Replacement (schema), Infinity, Choice. ZFC is not finitely
    and limit ordinals; transfinite induction and recursion. ORDINAL
    definable subsets of L_alpha) is an inner model of ZFC + V = L + GCH, so
    inaccessible exists". Hierarchy (increasing strength): inaccessible <
    Mahlo < weakly compact < measurable < strong < Woodin < supercompact.
    no nontrivial j : V -> V (in ZFC).
    computable (diagonalisation). A set is computable iff it and its
    TARSKI: truth in N is not arithmetically definable. Complete decidable
  - PROOF THEORY: sequent calculus LK; GENTZEN'S HAUPTSATZ (cut
  - TRUE BUT UNPROVABLE COMBINATORICS: GOODSTEIN'S THEOREM (every Goodstein
    notation) is unprovable in PA (Kirby-Paris), as are the hydra game and
    eventually dominates every PA-provably total function.

  are one argument; have students write the four side by side. (3) WELL-
  FOUNDEDNESS: ordinal arithmetic, rank, Goodstein and Gentzen all rest on
  "no infinite descending sequence of ordinals" - drill Cantor normal form
  (absorption rule: a smaller term is swallowed by a later larger one)
  until it is automatic. For computability, insist on "to show I is hard,
  reduce K TO I" and count quantifiers for the arithmetical hierarchy.
  Harder: prove the completeness theorem by Henkin's method; prove
  theorem (an injective polynomial map C^n -> C^n is onto) via ultraproducts
  of the algebraic closures of F_p; prove the delta -system lemma and the
  forcing theorem; show that adding a Cohen real makes the set of
  ground-model reals meagre; prove the Friedberg-Muchnik theorem with a
  lemma and the derivability conditions; and prove Goodstein's theorem is
  unprovable in PA by showing it implies Con(PA) via the Wainer hierarchy.

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) Every monomorphism in Set is injective.
     b) A morphism that is both mono and epi is an isomorphism.
     c) Every epimorphism in Ring is surjective.
     d) Right adjoints preserve colimits.
     e) A fully faithful, essentially surjective functor is an
        equivalence (assuming choice).
     f) Equivalent categories are isomorphic.
     g) Left adjoints, when they exist, are unique up to natural iso.
     h) Every forgetful functor to Set has a left adjoint.
     i) The natural map V -> V** is an isomorphism for every vector space.
     k) Grp is an abelian category.
     l) Finitely generated free abelian groups form an abelian category.
     m) Every projective Z-module is free.
     n) Every flat Z-module is projective.
     o) Hom(A, -) is exact for every abelian group A.
     q) Tor_1^Z(A, B) = 0 whenever A is torsion-free.
     s) Representable functors Hom(A, -) preserve limits.
     t) The Yoneda embedding preserves colimits.
     u) Every monad arises from an adjunction.
     v) Products and equalizers give all small limits.
     w) Ext^n_R(A, B) may be computed from a projective resolution of A or
        an injective resolution of B.

     Answers:
       d) F: U : Grp -> Set does not preserve coproducts
       g) T        h) F: U : Field -> Set
       i) F: infinite-dimensional V (not onto)      j) T
       k) F: not additive (Z/2 * Z/2 != Z/2 x Z/2)
       l) F: there x2 : Z -> Z is mono and epi (its cokernel is 0) but
          not an iso
       m) T (submodules of free modules over a PID are free)
       n) F: Q         o) F: Hom(Z/2, -) on Z -> Z/2
       p) F: x2 on Z, tensored with Z/2
       r) F in general: this is the Whitehead problem, independent of ZFC
          (Shelah); T for countable A (Stein)
       u) T (Kleisli or Eilenberg-Moore)             v) T
       w) T (Ext is balanced)                        x) F: F_2 x F_3

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw EVERY definition as a diagram and make the student
  chase it with elements in Set, Ab and a poset before going abstract; a
  poset is the best laboratory (limits = inf, colimits = sup, adjunctions
  the three reflexes: "what does Hom out of / into it classify?" (Yoneda:
  Hom(Z, G) = G, Hom(Z[x], R) = R), "left adjoints are free and preserve
  colimits, right adjoints are forgetful and preserve limits", and, for
  Tor/Ext, "resolve, DELETE the module, apply the functor, take homology"
  - always starting with 0 -> Z ->(xm) Z -> Z/m -> 0 and the answer Z/gcd.
  in Ring). Harder: prove the adjoint functor theorems (general and
  compactifications; prove Beck's monadicity theorem and show CHaus is
  monadic over Set; prove the snake lemma in an arbitrary abelian
  category and explain how Freyd-Mitchell justifies element chases;
  prove the comparison theorem, the horseshoe lemma and the balancing of
  Ext and Tor; show Ext^1 with the Baer sum is a group isomorphic to
  derived-functor Ext^1; compute group cohomology of cyclic groups via the
  cohomology is Ext and Tor.

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: for every probabilistic argument insist on the same four
  lines on the board - "the random object is ...", "the bad events are
  ...", "their expected number / total probability is ...", "so some
  outcome ..." - and let the child compute the numbers (C(100, 10) against
  2^4^4, 120/16 for tournaments) before any asymptotics. In extremal
  layer, polarity graph) and only then look for the double count or the
  chain argument that matches it. For tableaux, draw the Young diagram and
  write the hook lengths in the cells; for Burnside, fill in a table of
  group elements and fixed points. Harder: prove the general (asymmetric)
  Frankl-Wilson theorem and deduce Kahn-Kalai's counterexample to
  Borsuk's conjecture; prove RSK is a bijection and the Jacobi-Trudi
  identity; and derive the Frobenius character formula relating Schur
  functions and irreducible characters of S_n.

    (re-entrant corners, u ~ r^(2/3)) reduce the rate; 1D P1 is exact at
  - SPECTRAL ACCURACY: Fourier coefficients of a periodic f decay like
    strip; truncation error then decays faster than any power of N. A
    jump gives O(1/k) coefficients and the GIBBS overshoot ~ 8.95% of the
    jump.
    coincide (ALIASING); the trapezoidal rule is spectrally accurate for
    periodic analytic f; FFT costs O(N log N); spectral differentiation
    Fourier-GALERKIN, COLLOCATION (pseudospectral) and TAU methods.
    cos(jpi/N); interpolation at Chebyshev points has LEBESGUE CONSTANT
    O(log n) (equispaced: ~2^n, Runge phenomenon for 1/(1 + 25x^2));
    differentiation matrix D_N with (D_N)_0_0 = (2N^2 + 1)/6; eigenvalues of
    D_N^2 grow like N^4 (explicit time steps O(N^-^4) for diffusion).
    linear well-posed problems the LAX EQUIVALENCE THEOREM: a consistent
    scheme converges iff it is stable.
    1 + O(delta t). Heat equation, r = delta t/h^2: FTCS g = 1 - 4r sin^2(theta/2), stable
    iff r <= 1/2; BTCS and CRANK-NICOLSON unconditionally stable (CN is
    O(delta t^2 + h^2) but not L-stable: g(pi) -> -1 for large r). theta-method stable
    for all r iff theta >= 1/2.
    domain of dependence must contain the true one) is NECESSARY; FTCS is

    linear monotone schemes are at most first order.

TEACHING TIPS
  with the matrix tridiag(-1, 2, -1). Have students assemble it by hand
  as a finite element matrix, derive it by Taylor series as a finite
  difference matrix, find its eigenvalues (4/h^2)sin^2(kpih/2) with the
  needs O(1/h) steps. For stability questions always write "insert
  g^ne^(ijtheta)" and use e^(itheta) - 2 + e^(-itheta) = -4 sin^2(theta/2). Harder: prove
  the Bramble-Hilbert lemma and the scaling argument behind interpolation
  estimates; analyse the inf-sup (LBB) condition for mixed methods and
  Stokes (why P1-P1 fails and Taylor-Hood P2-P1 works); derive
  equivalence theorem via the uniform boundedness principle; show that
  Joukowski map; prove the optimal SOR formula from Young's relation
  combining the smoothing and approximation properties.

     Teacher explains: (a) Let V(t, x) be the optimal cost-to-go from x at
     time t. BELLMAN: over a short interval [t, t + h] use u, then act
     optimally:

     (For infinite horizon and autonomous data V has no t.) The costate of
     PMP is p = V_x along optimal paths. (b) Guess V = px^2. HJB: 0 = min_u

     p^2x^2 + 2px^2, i.e. p^2 - 2p - 3 = 0, p = 3 or -1. The value function
     cost 3x_0^2. (The root p = -1 gives the destabilising feedback u = x.)
     I = 0 with P = [p_1 p_2; p_2 p_3]. Entry (1, 1): 1 - p_2^2 = 0; entry (1, 2):
     characteristic polynomial s^2 + sqrt3 s + 1, roots (-sqrt3 +/- i)/2 (damping
