TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw pictures before formulas - a convex set with a point
  outside and its projection, the tangent line lying under a convex graph,
  the "slope-y line pushed up until it touches the graph" for f*, and the
  feasible polygon with a sliding objective line for LP. Make the student
  single time, and check all four KKT conditions in a table. For control
  problems insist on the routine: rank test -> pole placement or Riccati ->
  check closed-loop eigenvalues; for PMP: write H, costate equations,
  minimise H over U, then use boundary conditions. Always ask "is the
  negative?" before claiming asymptotic stability. Harder: prove the
  Hahn-Banach separation theorem in finite dimensions and derive Farkas
  and LP strong duality from it; prove Fenchel-Moreau (f** = f for closed
  convex f); prove the O(1/k) rate of gradient descent and Nesterov's
  {(g(x) + s, f_0(x) + t)}; derive the Jacobi condition and the Weierstrass
  excess function; prove sufficiency of the Kalman rank condition via the
  Gramian; prove Lyapunov's converse theorem for linear systems (P =
  value functions, then study the viscosity-solution theory that handles
  non-smooth value functions such as T(x) = |x|.

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - SUFFICIENCY: T(X) is SUFFICIENT for theta if the law of X given T does not
    depend on theta. FACTORISATION THEOREM (Fisher-Neyman): T is sufficient iff
    f_theta(x) = g_theta(T(x))h(x). T is MINIMAL sufficient if it is a function of
    every sufficient statistic; criterion: f_theta(x)/f_theta(y) is free of theta iff
  - COMPLETENESS: T is complete if E_theta g(T) = 0 for all theta forces g(T) = 0
    a.s. BASU: a complete sufficient T is independent of every ANCILLARY
    Uniform(theta, theta + 1)).
    contains an open set. Members: Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson,
    geometric, normal, gamma, beta. Non-members: Uniform(0, theta), Cauchy
    (support depends on theta, or no finite-dimensional sufficient statistic).
    an unbiased function of a COMPLETE sufficient statistic is the unique
    UMVUE. Method: find complete sufficient T; either guess an unbiased
    g(T) or Rao-Blackwellise a crude unbiased estimator.
    regularity: common support, differentiation under integral ). For n iid
    estimator (essentially only in exponential families with the natural
    statistic). Fails for Uniform(0, theta), where variance is O(1/n^2).
  - NEYMAN-PEARSON LEMMA: for simple H_0: theta_0 vs H_1: theta_1 the test rejecting
    when f_1(x)/f_0(x) > k (randomising on equality) with size alpha is MOST
    RUBIN: "reject when T > c" is UMP for one-sided H_0: theta <= theta_0 vs theta > theta_0.
    Two-sided UMP tests generally do NOT exist (restrict to unbiased tests).
    equivalent: Wald and score (Rao) tests. The normal-mean LRT is the
    expected loss pointwise: posterior MEAN (squared loss), MEDIAN
    (absolute loss), MODE (0-1 loss, limit), E[thetaw]/E[w] (weighted squared
    loss). Conjugate pairs: Beta-binomial, Gamma-Poisson, Gamma-
    exponential, Normal-normal. Classification: Bayes classifier
    argmax P(Y = k | x), Bayes risk E[1 - max_k P(Y = k | X)].
    A Bayes rule with CONSTANT risk (or whose Bayes risk equals its sup
    risk) is minimax and its prior is LEAST FAVOURABLE; e.g. (X + sqrtn/2)/
    (n + sqrtn) for binomial. Unique Bayes rules are ADMISSIBLE. STEIN: X is
    dominates X for d >= 3; X remains minimax, so minimax != admissible.
  - PAC LEARNING: a class H of classifiers is PAC learnable if for every
    plus union bound). NO FREE LUNCH: the class of all functions on an
    infinite domain is not PAC learnable.
  - VC DIMENSION: H SHATTERS {x_1, ..., x_m} if it realises all 2^m
    Values: thresholds 1, intervals 2, half-spaces in R^d d + 1, axis boxes
    loss multiplies R by at most L; R(conv F) = R(F).
    soft-thresholding and sparsity; STRUCTURAL RISK MINIMISATION trades
    empirical risk against capacity; ridge = MAP with Gaussian prior,
    lasso = MAP with Laplace prior; lambda chosen by cross-validation.
  - KERNELS: k is a (positive-definite) kernel iff every Gram matrix
    (Moore-Aronszajn: unique RKHS H_k with reproducing property f(x) =

D10. Compute the VC dimension of (a) intervals on R, (b) half-planes in R^2,
     (c) axis-aligned rectangles in R^2. Prove the Sauer-Shelah lemma and
     state the fundamental theorem of PAC learning.
     Teacher explains: To show VCdim = d: exhibit ONE shattered set of size
     d and show NO set of size d + 1 is shattered. (a) Two points x < y:
     all four labellings are realised by intervals. Three points x < y < z
     cannot get (+, -, +): an interval containing x and z contains y.
     (b) Three non-collinear points: every labelling is cut off by a line.
     Four points: if three are collinear, label the middle one -; else
     one lies in the triangle of the others (label it - and the others +)
     or they are in convex position (label diagonals alike: XOR) - this is
     Radon's theorem. (c) Four points in a diamond
     (+/-1, 0), (0, +/-1) are shattered. For five points take the leftmost,
     rightmost, top, bottom ones (<= 4 points); any rectangle containing
     them contains the fifth, so label it -. SAUER-SHELAH by induction on
     |H_1| + |H_2|, VCdim H_1 <= d and VCdim H_2 <= d - 1 (if H_2 shattered T,
     d the following are equivalent - uniform convergence, agnostic PAC
     2) + 1 exactly. Common mistakes: showing "some set of size d + 1 is
     not shattered" (you need EVERY set); equating VC dimension with the
     try: VCdim of discs in R^2. (3)

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) The MLE is always unbiased.
     b) A sufficient statistic of the same dimension as theta always exists.
     c) A complete sufficient statistic is minimal sufficient.
     d) A minimal sufficient statistic is complete.
     e) A UMVUE exists for every g(theta).
     g) The MLE is always unique and consistent.
     h) There is a UMP test of mu = 0 vs mu != 0 for N(mu, 1).
     i) The Neyman-Pearson test is most powerful among level-alpha tests.
     j) A unique Bayes rule is admissible.
     k) Minimax estimators are admissible.
     l) The posterior mean is Bayes under absolute loss.
     m) VC dimension equals the number of parameters.
     n) A binary class is PAC learnable iff its VC dimension is finite.
     o) ERM over all measurable functions generalises.
     q) Sums and products of kernels are kernels.
     r) The difference of two kernels is a kernel.
     s) Ridge regression has a unique solution even when p > n (lambda > 0).
     t) Lasso and ridge solutions are both linear in y.
     Answers:
       b) F: Cauchy location needs all n order statistics
       c) T (Bahadur)
       e) F: 1/p in Bin(n, p) has no unbiased estimator at all
       f) F: Var of the UMVUE is theta^2/(n(n + 2)) = o(1/n)
       g) F: Uniform(theta, theta + 1) (non-unique); Neyman-Scott (inconsistent)
       h) F: the one-sided MP tests differ
       i) T         j) T
       k) F: X for N(theta, I_3) (James-Stein dominates it)
       l) F: the posterior median
       n) T (fundamental theorem)
       o) F: it memorises the sample (no free lunch)
       p) T         q) T (Schur product theorem)
       r) F: k - 2k = -k has negative diagonal
       s) T         t) F: lasso is non-linear (soft-thresholding)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: begin every estimation question by writing the likelihood
  and FACTORISING it - the sufficient statistic, the exponential-family
  form, the MLE equation and the Fisher information all fall out of that
  single line. Keep a table of the six workhorse families (Bernoulli,
  UMVUE and conjugate prior, and test every theorem on the uniform first:
  it is the counterexample to CR, to sqrtn asymptotics and to the "natural
  statistic" folklore. For tests, always draw the likelihood ratio as a
  function of the statistic before choosing the rejection region. In
  learning theory insist on the three-step pattern "one hypothesis
  check VC claims with "one set shattered, every larger set not". Harder:
  of the MLE via Kullback-Leibler (Wald); derive Wilks' theorem from the
  quadratic expansion of the log-likelihood; prove Stein's lemma and the
  James-Stein risk formula; prove the upper bound in the fundamental
  via a shattered set; prove Talagrand's contraction lemma; prove
  Moore-Aronszajn and Mercer's theorem; and derive the SVM dual to see
  kernels and margins appear together.

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: tie every abstract statement to a 2 x 2 example first -
  Pauli matrices for observables and uncertainty, the Bloch ball for
  density matrices, the round sphere for Christoffel symbols and holonomy
  Hamiltonian flows. Insist on writing the conventions at the top of
  anti-Hermitian or d - ieA): most "wrong" answers in this topic are sign
  slips. In GR, first identify the conserved quantities (Killing vectors)
  and reduce to a one-dimensional effective potential; in gauge theory,
  compute D^2 before anything else. Harder: prove von Neumann's
  extension theorem and Stone's theorem; derive the Schwarzschild metric
  from the vacuum equations and prove Birkhoff's theorem; show the
  Kruskal extension is maximal; prove Darboux's theorem by Moser's
  trick; prove Arnold-Liouville; construct the BPST instanton and check
  about the Atiyah-Singer index theorem as the common home of
  instantons, Chern numbers and anomalies.

D1. One-period binomial model: S_0 = 100, u = 1.2, d = 0.9, gross interest
    R = 1.05. (a) Prove that the model is arbitrage-free iff d < R < u.
    (b) Price a call with K = 100 by replication and by risk-neutral
    expectation. (c) Price the put and verify put-call parity.
    Answer: (a) proof below. (b) delta  = 2/3, B = -57.1429, C_0 = 9.5238,
    q = 1/2. (c) P_0 = 4.7619; C_0 - P_0 = 4.7619 = 100 - 100/1.05.
    Teacher explains: (a) A portfolio (delta  shares, B in the bank) with value
    zero today has B = -delta S_0 and value tomorrow delta S_0(u - R) in the up state,
    delta S_0(d - R) in the down state. If R <= d, delta  = 1 gives two non-negative
    values, at least one positive (u > d): arbitrage. If R >= u, take delta  = -1.
    If d < R < u the two values have opposite signs for any delta  != 0: no
    arbitrage. (b) Replicate: delta S_0u + BR = C_u = 20, delta S_0d + BR = C_d = 0.
    -60/1.05 = -57.1429. Then C_0 = delta S_0 + B = 66.6667 - 57.1429 = 9.5238.
    Any other price is an arbitrage (sell the dearer of call and
    replicating portfolio, buy the cheaper). Risk-neutral form: substitute
    delta  and B into delta S_0 + B to get C_0 = (qC_u + (1 - q)C_d)/R with
    probability p to discount expected payoffs (p never enters); forgetting
    that B is borrowed (negative). Now you try: same model, digital claim
    paying 1 in the up state. (q/R = 0.47619)

D7. Cox-Ross-Rubinstein: with delta t = T/n, u = e^(sigmasqrtdelta t), d = 1/u, R =
    e^(rdelta t), (a) show q -> 1/2 and that the risk-neutral log-return has
    mean ~ (r - sigma^2/2)delta t and variance ~ sigma^2delta t; (b) explain why the binomial
    call price converges to Black-Scholes; (c) tabulate the CRR price for
    S = K = 100, r = 0.05, sigma = 0.2, T = 1, n = 1, 2, 4, 10, 100, 1000.
    Answer: (c) 12.1623, 9.5405, 9.9705, 10.2534, 10.4306, 10.4486 -> 10.4506.
    Teacher explains: (a) Expand: u ~ 1 + sigmasqrtdelta t + sigma^2delta t/2, d ~ 1 - sigmasqrtdelta t +
    sigma^2delta t/2, R ~ 1 + rdelta t, so q = (R - d)/(u - d) ~ (sigmasqrtdelta t + (r - sigma^2/2)delta t)/
    (2sigmasqrtdelta t) = 1/2 + ((r - sigma^2/2)/(2sigma))sqrtdelta t -> 1/2. The log-step X = +/-sigmasqrtdelta t has
    E^Q X = (2q - 1)sigmasqrtdelta t ~ (r - sigma^2/2)delta t and Var X = sigma^2delta t(1 - (2q - 1)^2) ~
    sigma^2delta t. (b) ln(S_n/S_0) is a sum of n i.i.d. steps with total mean -> (r -
    sigma^2/2)T and variance -> sigma^2T; by the Lindeberg CLT it converges in law to
    N((r - sigma^2/2)T, sigma^2T), the Q-law of ln(S_T/S_0) in Black-Scholes. The
    payoff is continuous and dominated by S_T (uniformly integrable), so
    the discounted expectations converge. (c) n = 1: u = 1.2214, q =
    0.57749, C = 12.1623; the table oscillates (even/odd n) and converges

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) The binomial price of a call depends on the real probability p.
     b) If d < R < u then the one-period binomial model is complete.
     c) Every arbitrage-free market is complete.
     d) In an incomplete market every claim has infinitely many
        arbitrage-free prices.
     e) The risk-neutral measure Q is equivalent to P.
     f) The Black-Scholes call price is increasing in sigma.
     g) The Black-Scholes call price is increasing in mu.
     h) An American put on a non-dividend stock is never exercised early.
     i) An American call on a dividend-paying stock is never exercised
        early.
     j) Put-call parity holds for American options.
     k) The call price is a convex function of K.
     m) Delta-hedging in discrete time removes all risk.
     o) The HJB equation always has a classical C^{1,2} solution.
     p) The Merton fraction depends on the investor's wealth (CRRA).
     q) If an EMM exists in a finite market, there is no arbitrage.
     r) A positive local martingale is a martingale.
     Answers:
       a) F: q = (R - d)/(u - d) does not involve p
       b) T (two states, two assets)
       c) F: the trinomial model M4 a)
       d) F: replicable claims (e.g. the stock, the bond) have one price
       e) T (same null sets; needed for FTAP)
       g) F: mu does not appear in the formula
       h) F: Tree A of M2 (exercise at S_1 = 80)
       i) F: just before a large dividend, e.g. S = 100, K = 50, a
          dividend of 60 an instant before T: exercise now gives 50, waiting
          gives 0
       j) F: only bounds S - K <= C_Am - P_Am <= S - Ke^(-rT)
       k) T (butterflies have non-negative prices)
       o) F: degenerate problems need viscosity solutions (exit from
          (-1, 1) with speed |u| <= 1: V = 1 - |x|, not C^1 at 0)
       q) T (FTAP I, easy direction)
       r) F: it is only a supermartingale; 1/|B_t| for 3-d Brownian
          motion started away from 0 is a strict local martingale

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: begin with the one-period binomial model and do every idea
  there first - replication, the no-arbitrage inequality d < R < u, the
  risk-neutral q, state prices, completeness (count states versus
  assets) - and only then pass to trees, where backward induction is the
  same computation repeated. Insist that "risk-neutral" is a pricing
  device, not a belief: make students compute P(S_T > K) and Q(S_T > K)
  side by side. For Black-Scholes, derive the PDE by delta-hedging on the
  board and the formula by the expectation; check every answer with
  control, always write the HJB, minimise pointwise, then try an ansatz
  (quadratic for LQ, power for CRRA). Harder: prove FTAP I for discrete
  prove the Snell-envelope characterisation and show that the American
  put's exercise boundary is increasing in t; compute the Vasicek bond
  option (Jamshidian) and derive the HJM drift condition; prove the
  verification theorem carefully and solve Merton's problem with
  consumption by duality (convex conjugate of U); show that the
  viscosity solution of a degenerate HJB is the value function.

TOPIC 12.29 - INVERSE PROBLEMS AND UNCERTAINTY QUANTIFICATION: ILL-POSEDNESS,
SVD AND THE PICARD CONDITION, TIKHONOV AND TRUNCATED SVD, PARAMETER CHOICE,
BAYESIAN INVERSION, MCMC, MONTE CARLO, POLYNOMIAL CHAOS, SENSITIVITY,
TOMOGRAPHY

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - WELL-POSEDNESS (HADAMARD): the problem Ax = b, A : X -> Y, is well posed
    if a solution EXISTS for every b, it is UNIQUE, and it depends
    CONTINUOUSLY (stably) on b. Otherwise it is ILL-POSED. Standard ill-
    posed problems: differentiation of noisy data, the backward heat
    equation, deconvolution, Fredholm equations of the FIRST kind integral k(x,
    y)f(y)dy = g(x) with smooth kernel, computerised tomography.
  - COMPACT OPERATORS ARE BAD TO INVERT: if A : X -> Y is compact and
    injective with infinite-dimensional range, then A^-^1 : R(A) -> X is
    UNBOUNDED and R(A) is not closed. In finite dimensions the inverse is
    with sigma_n -> 0. Example: Vf(x) = integral _0^x f on L^2(0, 1) has sigma_n =
    2/((2n - 1)pi), v_n = sqrt2 cos((n - 1/2)pix), u_n = sqrt2 sin((n - 1/2)pix).
    coefficients of the data must decay FASTER than the singular values.
    SEVERELY ill-posed: sigma_n ~ e^(-cn) (backward heat: sigma_n = e^(-n^2pi^2T)).
    iteration count is the parameter (SEMI-CONVERGENCE, early stopping).
    SATURATION rate of Tikhonov (TSVD and Landweber do not saturate).
  - PARAMETER CHOICE. DISCREPANCY PRINCIPLE (Morozov): pick alpha with
  - BAYESIAN INVERSE PROBLEMS: unknown x and data y = G(x) + e are random;
    is the SOLUTION; point estimates are the MAP (mode) and the
    CONDITIONAL MEAN (CM), uncertainty is described by credible regions.
    Under mild conditions the posterior is Lipschitz in y in the Hellinger
    distance: the Bayesian problem is WELL POSED.
    prior needs a TRACE-CLASS covariance (e.g. eigenvalues k^(-s), s > 1).
  - MCMC: build a Markov chain with the posterior pi as invariant law.
    pi(y)q(y, x)/(pi(x)q(x, y))); DETAILED BALANCE pi(x)P(x, y) = pi(y)P(y,
    acceptance does not degenerate as the dimension grows. Diagnose
    the error is O(N^(-1/2)) INDEPENDENT of the dimension; CLT gives the
    variables, control variates (optimal c = Cov(f, g)/Var g), stratified
    sampling, IMPORTANCE SAMPLING (E_p f = E_q[f p/q]) for rare events;
    quasi-Monte Carlo O((log N)^d/N); multilevel Monte Carlo.
    smooth f; number of terms of total degree <= p in d variables is
    (d + p)!/(d! p!). Coefficients by projection (quadrature), regression,
    (line integrals; X-ray CT via Beer-Lambert I = I_0e^(-integral mu)). FOURIER
    (Ram-Lak filter); plain backprojection R^#Rf = f * (1/|x|) blurs.
    R smooths by half a derivative: mildly ill-posed of order 1/2
    (singular values ~ m^(-1/2)); limited-angle CT is severely ill-posed.

D8. (a) Describe the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm and prove that the
    target pi satisfies detailed balance, hence is invariant. (b) On the
    states {1, 2, 3} with pi = (0.2, 0.3, 0.5), propose each of the other
    two states with probability 1/2. Write the transition matrix P and
    check piP = pi. (c) Explain why random-walk Metropolis degenerates in
    high dimensions and how pCN fixes this. (d) A chain behaves like an
    AR(1) process with lag-one correlation 0.9. How many effectively
    independent samples are in N = 10 000 steps?
    with probability a(x, y) = min{1, pi(y)q(y, x)/(pi(x)q(x, y))}, else
    stay at x. For y != x the transition density is P(x, y) = q(x, y)a(x,
    y), so
       pi(x)P(x, y) = min{pi(x)q(x, y), pi(y)q(y, x)},
    which is SYMMETRIC in (x, y): pi(x)P(x, y) = pi(y)P(y, x). Summing (or
    invariant; with irreducibility and aperiodicity the chain converges
    to pi and ergodic averages converge (LLN for Markov chains). Crucially
    only RATIOS pi(y)/pi(x) are needed: the normalising constant (the
    evidence) is never computed. (b) The proposal is symmetric, so a =
    size of random-walk Metropolis must shrink like d^(-1/2) to keep a
    fixed acceptance (optimal ~ 0.234), so mixing slows down; for a
    dimensions, with dimension-independent acceptance. (d) For AR(1),
    autocorrelation time). ESS = 10 000/19 ~ 526. Common mistakes:
    forgetting to count the rejected step as a repeated sample (the chain
    must STAY at x); using the Metropolis ratio with a non-symmetric
    proposal without the q-correction. Now you try: pi = (0.5, 0.25, 0.25)

D11. Sensitivity analysis. Let Y = X_1 + 2X_2 + 3X_1X_2 with X_1, X_2
     independent N(0, 1). (a) Compute the local sensitivities at the mean
     (0, 0). (b) Compute the ANOVA decomposition, the first-order Sobol'
     indices S_1, S_2, the interaction index S_1_2 and the total indices.
     additive.
     2/7, S_1_2 = 9/14, S_T1 = 5/7, S_T2 = 13/14.
     and 2 at the origin: a local analysis ranks X_2 first and sees NO sign
     of the dominant interaction. (b) ANOVA (Hoeffding) decomposition: f_0
     = EY = 0; f_1(X_1) = E[Y|X_1] - f_0 = X_1; f_2(X_2) = 2X_2; f_1_2 = Y - f_0 - f_1 -
     f_2 = 3X_1X_2. The terms are mutually orthogonal (each has zero mean in
     each of its own variables), so Var Y = V_1 + V_2 + V_1_2 = 1 + 4 + 9 =
     14. In chaos language Y = He_1(X_1) + 2He_1(X_2) + 3He_1(X_1)He_1(X_2): the
     variance is the sum of squared coefficients. First order: S_1 =
     Var(E[Y|X_1])/Var Y = 1/14 ~ 0.071, S_2 = 4/14 ~ 0.286; interaction
     S_1_2 = 9/14 ~ 0.643. Total: S_T1 = (V_1 + V_1_2)/Var Y = 10/14 ~ 0.714,
     S_T2 = 13/14 ~ 0.929. Interpretation: fixing X_1 alone removes on
     average only 7% of the variance, but fixing everything EXCEPT X_1
     still leaves 71% on average: X_1 acts through the interaction.
     Estimators: pick-freeze (Saltelli/Jansen) with two sample matrices;
     from a PCE for free. Common mistakes: ranking inputs by derivatives
     at one point for a non-linear model; applying Sobol' indices to
     correlated inputs (the decomposition is no longer orthogonal).
     Now you try: Y = X_1X_2 with X_1, X_2 independent U(0, 1). Find S_1, S_2,
     S_1_2. (Var Y = 7/144, V_1 = V_2 = 1/48: S_1 = S_2 = 3/7, S_1_2 = 1/7)

D12. Tomography. (a) Compute the Radon transform of the indicator of the
     disc |x| <= r and of f(x) = e^(-|x|^2) in R^2. (b) Prove the Fourier
     backprojection formula and explain why plain backprojection blurs.
     (d) Why is CT only mildly ill-posed, while limited-angle CT is
     severely ill-posed?
     Answer: (a) 2sqrt(r^2 - s^2) for |s| <= r (0 otherwise); sqrtpi e^(-s^2).
     (1-D transform in s); R^#Rf = f * (1/|x|).
     (a) Disc: the chord at distance |s| <= r has length 2sqrt(r^2 - s^2). For
     sqrtpi e^(-s^2), independent of theta (radial f). Check: integral Rf ds = integral f (both pi
     where h_theta(s) = (1/(2pi))integral |sigma|(Rf)^(theta, sigma)e^(isigmas)dsigma is the projection
     FILTERED with the ramp |sigma|. The outer integral is the BACKPROJECTION
     integral f(x + y)/|y| dy (polar coordinates again): a convolution with 1/|x|,
     the image is blurred. The ramp filter undoes this. (d) The factor
     are sqrt(4pi/(m + 1)) (multiplicity m + 1), decaying like m^(-1/2):
     MILDLY ill-posed, and the ramp filter amplifies noise only linearly
     in frequency (so in practice it is cut off: Ram-Lak, Shepp-Logan
     wedge; recovering it elsewhere is ANALYTIC CONTINUATION, and the
     singular values decay exponentially: severely ill-posed. Common
     mistakes: forgetting |sigma| (the Jacobian of polar coordinates);
     integrating theta over [0, 2pi) without halving. Now you try: Rf(theta, s)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always go to SVD coordinates first - write every problem
  of TSVD, Tikhonov and Landweber filters on a log axis. For the
  Bayesian part insist on the slogan "precisions add" and check every
  scalar posterior with the Kalman gain; for MCMC run the 3-state
  example by hand before any continuous one. Harder: prove the
  convergence-rate theory of general spectral filters and the
  order optimality of the discrepancy principle; prove the saturation
  of Tikhonov; show Hellinger well-posedness of the Bayesian posterior
  (Stuart's theorem) and that the pCN kernel is prior-reversible;
  fail in function space; derive Sobol' indices from a multivariate
  PCE; prove the Radon inversion formula in R^n with the Riesz
  potential and compute the SVD of the Radon transform on the disc
  using Zernike polynomials.

TOPIC 12.30 - ALGORITHMS AND COMPUTATIONAL COMPLEXITY (GRADUATE): ASYMPTOTICS
AND RECURRENCES, AMORTISED ANALYSIS, GRAPH ALGORITHMS, DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING,
NETWORK FLOWS AND LP DUALITY, RANDOMISED AND APPROXIMATION ALGORITHMS, P, NP,
NP-COMPLETENESS, SPACE COMPLEXITY, HIERARCHY THEOREMS, BPP, THE POLYNOMIAL
HIERARCHY, INTERACTIVE PROOFS AND PCP

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - RECURRENCES: T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), a >= 1, b > 1, critical exponent
  - AMORTISED ANALYSIS: aggregate, accounting (credits) and POTENTIAL
    counter (<= 2 flips), multipop stack, union-find with rank and path
    compression O(alpha(n)), splay trees O(log n), Fibonacci heaps (insert,
    decrease-key O(1), extract-min O(log n)).
  - GRAPH ALGORITHMS: BFS/DFS in O(V + E); DFS gives topological sort,
    cycle detection (back edges), strongly connected components. DIJKSTRA
    (weights >= 0) O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap, O(E + V log V) with a
    Fibonacci heap; BELLMAN-FORD O(VE), detects negative cycles; FLOYD-
    WARSHALL O(V^3). MST: CUT PROPERTY (the lightest edge across any cut is
    in some MST); Kruskal O(E log V), Prim; Cayley: K_n has n^n^-^2 spanning
    trees.
  - DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING: optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems;
    write the recurrence, the table, the order of evaluation. LCS and edit
    distance O(mn); 0/1 knapsack O(nW) (PSEUDO-polynomial: W is exponential
    in its bit length); matrix-chain O(n^3); rod cutting, coin change, LIS.
  - NETWORK FLOWS: flow conservation, capacity constraints, residual graph.
    MAX-FLOW MIN-CUT: the maximum flow value equals the minimum s-t cut
    capacities: terminates, INTEGRAL max flow), Edmonds-Karp (shortest
    (max matching = min vertex cover in bipartite graphs), Hall, Menger.
    optima if either is feasible and bounded); COMPLEMENTARY SLACKNESS.
    Simplex is exponential in the worst case (Klee-Minty) but ellipsoid
    (Khachiyan) and interior-point (Karmarkar) are polynomial. Totally
    unimodular constraint matrices give integral vertices; the dual of
    max-flow is (fractional) min-cut.
  - RANDOMISED ALGORITHMS: LAS VEGAS (always correct, random time) vs
    MONTE CARLO (bounded time, small error). Tools: linearity of
    Quicksort: E[comparisons] = 2(n + 1)H_n - 4n ~ 2n ln n; Karger min cut
    succeeds with probability >= 1/C(n, 2); SCHWARTZ-ZIPPEL: a nonzero
    polynomial of degree d vanishes at a random point of S^n with
    probability <= d/|S|; Miller-Rabin; Freivalds.
  - APPROXIMATION ALGORITHMS: ratio alpha = ALG/OPT (>= 1 for minimisation).
    Vertex cover 2 (maximal matching, or LP rounding at 1/2); greedy set
    cover H_n <= 1 + ln n; metric TSP 2 (MST doubling) and 3/2 (Christofides);
    general TSP has NO constant approximation unless P = NP; knapsack FPTAS;
    MAX-CUT 1/2 (random) and 0.878 (Goemans-Williamson); MAX-3SAT 7/8.
    NP-complete problems (self-reducibility).
    LEVIN: SAT (and 3SAT) is NP-complete. Chain: 3SAT <= INDEPENDENT SET <=
    VERTEX COVER, CLIQUE; 3SAT <= 3-COLOUR, HAM-CYCLE <= TSP, 3SAT <= SUBSET-SUM
    <= KNAPSACK, PARTITION. 2SAT, HORN-SAT, 2-colouring, matching are in P.
    LADNER: if P != NP there are NP-intermediate problems.
    coNSPACE(s), so NL = coNL. PATH (directed s-t connectivity) is
    NL-complete; undirected connectivity is in L (Reingold). TQBF and
    generalised geography are PSPACE-complete.
  - HIERARCHY THEOREMS (diagonalisation): TIME: f time-constructible and
    P^B != NP^B, so relativising arguments cannot settle P vs NP.
  - PROBABILISTIC CLASSES: BPP (two-sided error <= 1/3), RP (one-sided,
    zero error). AMPLIFICATION: majority of k runs has error <= e^(-k/18).
  - INTERACTIVE PROOFS: IP = languages with a probabilistic polynomial-time
    verifier talking to an all-powerful prover, completeness >= 2/3,
    protocol; IP = PSPACE (Lund-Fortnow-Karloff-Nisan, Shamir); MIP = NEXP.
  - PCP THEOREM: NP = PCP(O(log n), O(1)): proofs checkable by reading O(1)
    random bits of the proof. Equivalent to NP-hardness of GAP versions of
    P = NP (so the random assignment is optimal).

D3. Run Dijkstra from s on the directed graph s->a 4, s->b 1, b->a 2, a->c 1,
    b->c 5, c->d 3, b->d 8. Prove that Dijkstra is correct for non-negative
    weights, show it fails with the negative edge set s->a 2, s->b 3, b->a -2,
    and state the cut property of minimum spanning trees.
    Answer: extraction order s, b, a, c, d with d = 0, 1, 3, 4, 7.
    Teacher explains: Dijkstra keeps tentative distances d(v), repeatedly
    extracts the unfinished vertex with the smallest d and relaxes its
    out-edges: d(v) <- min(d(v), d(u) + w(u, v)). Run: start d(s) = 0.
    Extract s: d(a) = 4, d(b) = 1. Extract b (1): d(a) = min(4, 1 + 2) = 3,
    d(c) = 6, d(d) = 9. Extract a (3): d(c) = min(6, 4) = 4. Extract c (4):
    d(d) = min(9, 7) = 7. Extract d (7). Final distances s 0, b 1, a 3, c 4,
    d 7; shortest path to d is s->b->a->c->d. CORRECTNESS (invariant: when u is
    unfinished vertex and x its finished predecessor; x was correct when
    >= 0 are used here: the rest of the path from y to u is non-negative).
    Then y, not u, has the smaller key: contradiction. NEGATIVE EDGES: s->a 2,
    s->b 3, b->a -2: Dijkstra finalises a at 2, but s->b->a costs 1. Use
    Bellman-Ford: V - 1 rounds of relaxing every edge; a further improvement
    in round V proves a negative cycle. CUT PROPERTY: for any partition
    argument: add it to an MST, the cycle created crosses the cut again at
    an edge no lighter, remove that one). Kruskal and Prim are both
    repeated applications. Common mistakes: "re-weighting by adding a
    constant to every edge fixes negative weights" (it penalises paths
    with many edges); forgetting that Dijkstra's bound uses the heap
    (O((V + E) log V)). Now you try: add the edge d->a of weight -5. What
    does Bellman-Ford report? (the negative cycle a->c->d->a of weight -1)

D5. (a) Find a maximum flow and a minimum cut in the network with arcs
    s->a 10, s->b 10, a->b 2, a->t 4, a->c 8, b->c 9, c->t 10. (b) Show on the
    "diamond" s->a, s->b, a->b, a->t, b->t (all capacity 1) why back edges of
    the residual graph are needed. (c) Prove weak LP duality and verify
    strong duality and complementary slackness for max 3x_1 + 2x_2 subject
    to x_1 + x_2 <= 4, x_1 + 3x_2 <= 7, x_1 <= 3, x >= 0.
    Answer: (a) 14, cut S = {s, a, b, c}; (b) greedy s-a-b-t blocks, the
    residual path s-b-a-t fixes it: value 2; (c) x = (3, 1), y = (2, 0, 1),
    both optima 11.
    Teacher explains: (a) Augment: s->a->t (4), s->a->c->t (6), s->b->c->t (4).
    Total 14. Now the arcs a->t (4) and c->t (10) into t are saturated, so
    the cut S = {s, a, b, c}, T = {t} has capacity 4 + 10 = 14. Any flow <=
    any cut (the flow must cross the cut), so 14 is maximal and this cut
    is minimal: MAX-FLOW = MIN-CUT. (b) If we first push 1 along s->a->b->t,
    no s-t path with spare capacity remains in the original graph, yet the
    maximum is 2. In the RESIDUAL graph the arc a->b has a reverse arc b->a
    of capacity 1, and s->b->a->t augments: the flow on a->b is cancelled,
    has no s-t path; the set S reachable from s is then a minimum cut.
    using x >= 0 in the first step and y >= 0 in the second. Here the dual
    is min 4y_1 + 7y_2 + 3y_3 subject to y_1 + y_2 + y_3 >= 3, y_1 + 3y_2 >= 2, y >= 0.
    At x = (3, 1): constraints 1 and 3 are tight, constraint 2 has slack
    (6 < 7), so COMPLEMENTARY SLACKNESS forces y_2 = 0; x_1, x_2 > 0 force both
    dual constraints to be tight: y_1 + y_3 = 3, y_1 = 2, so y = (2, 0, 1).
    Dual value 8 + 0 + 3 = 11 = primal value 9 + 2: both are optimal.
    Max-flow is an LP whose dual is a fractional min cut; its constraint
    matrix is totally unimodular, which is why min-cut is integral.
    Common mistakes: counting arcs from T back to S in the cut capacity;
    forgetting the sign conditions in the dual. Now you try: the maximum
    number of edge-disjoint s-t paths in K_4. (3 = the minimum edge cut)

D7. (a) Prove that taking both endpoints of a maximal matching is a
    2-approximation for vertex cover, and that the bound is tight. (b) Run
    greedy set cover on U = {1, ..., 6}, S_1 = {1, 2, 3, 4}, S_2 = {1, 2, 5},
    S_3 = {3, 4, 6}. (c) Prove the MST-doubling algorithm is a
    2-approximation for metric TSP and that general TSP has no
    polynomial-time alpha-approximation for any constant alpha unless P = NP.
    Answer: (a) |C| = 2|M| <= 2 OPT; tight on K_(n,n). (b) greedy uses 3
    sets, OPT = 2. (c) cost <= 2 MST <= 2 OPT; reduction from Hamiltonian
    cycle.
    Teacher explains: (a) Let M be a maximal matching and C its 2|M|
    endpoints. C is a cover: an uncovered edge could be added to M,
    contradicting maximality. Any cover must contain an endpoint of each
    edge of M, and these edges are disjoint, so OPT >= |M|. Hence |C| <=
    2 OPT. On K_(n,n) a perfect matching gives 2n while OPT = n. (b) Greedy
    picks the set covering the most uncovered elements: S_1 (4 new), then S_2
    covers {5} and S_3 covers {6}: 3 sets. OPT = {S_2, S_3}. In general greedy
    is within H_n <= 1 + ln n (charge each element 1/(number newly covered));
    (c) Deleting an edge of the optimal tour gives a spanning tree, so
    MST <= OPT. Walk around the doubled MST (cost 2 MST) and SHORTCUT
    repeated vertices; the triangle inequality says shortcuts never
    increase cost, so the tour costs <= 2 OPT. Without the triangle
    inequality: given a graph G on n vertices, give its edges weight 1 and
    non-edges weight alphan + 1. If G has a Hamiltonian cycle, OPT = n;
    otherwise every tour costs > alphan. An alpha-approximation would distinguish
    the cases, deciding HAM-CYCLE. (Christofides adds a minimum perfect
    matching on odd-degree vertices instead of doubling: ratio 3/2.) Common
    mistakes: bounding ALG against an unknown OPT without a LOWER BOUND
    (matching, MST, LP value); using a greedy "highest degree vertex"
    of vertex cover on K_n: the LP value and OPT. (n/2 with all x = 1/2; OPT
    = n - 1)

D10. State and prove the deterministic time hierarchy theorem and derive
     PSPACE? Explain why diagonalisation alone cannot resolve P vs NP.
     Teacher explains: Let f be time-constructible. Build D: on input w of
     steps (a universal machine simulates t steps in O(t log t) time, so D
     runs in O(f(n))); if M accepts within the budget, REJECT, otherwise
     time g with g = o(f/log f) (Sipser's form; essentially g log g =
     o(f)). Simulating M costs c_M steps of the budget per step of M, with
     c_M depending on M only, so for k large c_M g(n) < f(n)/log f(n): the
     one inclusion is strict, though nobody knows which. LIMITS:
     Baker-Gill-Solovay give oracles A (a PSPACE-complete language) with
     P^A = NP^A and B with P^B != NP^B. Simulation-and-flip arguments work
     relative to every oracle, so they cannot separate P from NP. Common
     g log g = o(f): 2n^2 log n is not o(n^2 log n)); forgetting
     DTIME(n^3)? (yes: n^2 log n^2 = o(n^3))

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) If f = O(g) then 2^f = O(2^g).
     b) f = O(g) or g = O(f) for any two positive functions.
     c) Every recurrence T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) falls under one of the three
        master cases.
     d) Amortised O(1) per operation means every operation is O(1).
     e) Dijkstra is correct with negative edges if there are no negative
        cycles.
     f) If all capacities are integers then there is an integral maximum
        flow.
     g) Ford-Fulkerson always terminates.
     h) The simplex method runs in polynomial time.
     i) An O(nW) algorithm for knapsack shows P = NP.
     j) A greedy algorithm is optimal for coin change with any coin set.
     m) 2SAT is NP-complete.
     n) NP = coNP is known to be false.
     o) NPSPACE != PSPACE.
     t) IP = NP.
     u) Metric TSP has a 2-approximation, so general TSP does too.
     v) A Monte Carlo algorithm can be turned into a Las Vegas one if
        answers can be verified quickly.
     Answers:
       a) F: f = 2n, g = n
       b) F: f = n^(1 + sin n) and g = n oscillate
       c) F: 2T(n/2) + n/log n
       e) F: s->a 2, s->b 3, b->a -2
       f) T (integrality theorem)
       g) F: irrational capacities (Zwick's example) may not terminate
       h) F: Klee-Minty cubes (though LP is in P via the ellipsoid method)
       i) F: pseudo-polynomial, W is exponential in its bit length
       j) F: {1, 3, 4} and 6 (greedy 3 coins, optimum 2)
          nontrivial B), and HALT is undecidable
       n) F: it is open (it would follow from P = NP)
       o) F: Savitch gives NPSPACE = PSPACE
       p) T (time hierarchy)
       s) T (collapse lemma)
       u) F: no constant ratio unless P = NP (HAM-CYCLE gap reduction)
       v) T (rerun until the verified answer appears)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: for every recurrence, draw the recursion tree and write the
  cost of the first three levels before naming a case; for every
  amortised claim, first compute the total cost of a concrete sequence
  (16 inserts, 16 increments), then find the potential. For DP insist on
  the four-line template "subproblem, recurrence, order, answer" and fill
  a small table by hand. For reductions, draw the arrow "known hard ->
  new problem" and check both directions of the "iff" on a tiny instance
  EXP with the known separations (L != PSPACE, P != EXP) in red. Harder:
  prove Cook-Levin in full (tableau of configurations); prove the
  integrality of max flow via total unimodularity; prove the H_n bound for
  greedy set cover by LP duality (dual fitting); prove
  P/poly by a union bound; prove Karp-Lipton; work through the sumcheck
  theorem is equivalent to NP-hardness of gap-MAX-3SAT.

Scoring guide (out of 120):
  104-120 Ready for Stage 13 (PhD research years).
  77-103  Nearly there - revise the topics of the missed questions for
          three or four weeks, then try those questions again.

          again in a month.

  more practice writing complete proofs, as in a qualifying exam; strong
  in A but weak in B means more drill practice for speed and accuracy.

================================================================================
END OF STAGE 12 - READINESS CHECKLIST FOR STAGE 13
================================================================================
The student is ready for Stage 13 (PhD research years) when they can
usually:
  Core analysis
  [ ] Use abstract measures, signed measures, Radon-Nikodym derivatives,
      differentiation of measures and the Riesz representation theorem
  [ ] Work with weak and weak* topologies, compact operators and their
      spectra, Banach algebras, distributions and Sobolev spaces
  [ ] Apply the Riemann mapping theorem, harmonic functions, Weierstrass
      and Mittag-Leffler, analytic continuation, Riemann surfaces and
      elliptic functions
  [ ] Explain what is new in several complex variables: Hartogs
      phenomena, Reinhardt domains, pseudoconvexity
  [ ] Use Fourier analysis on groups, maximal functions, singular
  Algebra and geometry
  [ ] Use solvable and nilpotent groups, modules, tensor products, exact
      sequences and the language of categories
  [ ] Compute Ext and Tor, use long exact sequences and derived functors,
      and explain the idea of the derived category
  [ ] Work with sheaves, stalks, sheafification and sheaf cohomology
  [ ] Use Noetherian and Artinian rings, primary decomposition, integral
      extensions, the Nullstellensatz, dimension theory and completions
  [ ] Compute singular and cellular homology and cohomology, cup
  [ ] Work with manifolds, vector bundles, differential forms, de Rham
      cohomology, connections, curvature and geodesics
  [ ] Handle root systems, the classification of semisimple Lie algebras
      and highest-weight representations, including the Weyl formulas
  [ ] Use functors, natural transformations, the Yoneda lemma,
      adjunctions, limits and abelian categories fluently
  Probability and PDE
  [ ] Use conditional expectation, martingales and optional stopping,
      Brownian motion, weak convergence and characteristic functions
  [ ] Find weak solutions of elliptic, parabolic and hyperbolic PDEs with
      Sobolev spaces, Lax-Milgram, regularity and variational methods
  [ ] Apply the ergodic theorems, recurrence, mixing and entropy
  Specialisations
  [ ] Work with varieties and schemes, sheaf cohomology on projective
      space, curves and surfaces, and Riemann-Roch
  [ ] Handle Dedekind domains, ramification, class groups, units, p-adic
      and local fields, adeles and ideles
      of sieve methods and the circle method
  [ ] Work with representations of compact Lie groups and algebraic
      groups, and know what a quantum group is
  [ ] Use model theory, ZFC and ordinals, forcing and independence,
      computability and the incompleteness theorems
  [ ] Apply the probabilistic method, extremal and algebraic
      combinatorics
  [ ] Analyse finite element, spectral and iterative methods for PDEs and
      linear systems, with error and convergence estimates
  [ ] Use convex analysis, duality, KKT conditions and optimal control
  [ ] Use estimation theory, hypothesis testing, VC dimension and
      generalisation bounds
  [ ] Explain the mathematical frameworks of quantum mechanics, general
      relativity, gauge theory and symplectic geometry
  [ ] Price derivatives by no-arbitrage, Black-Scholes and stochastic
      control
  [ ] Regularise ill-posed inverse problems and quantify uncertainty
      with Bayesian methods
  [ ] Design and analyse algorithms, prove NP-completeness and reason
      about complexity classes
  Research skills
  [ ] Pass written and oral qualifying exams in the core sequence, read
      graduate monographs and recent papers in one specialisation, and
      present a seminar talk on a research paper

Stage 13 turns from coursework to research: depth in one or two frontier
areas (arithmetic and algebraic geometry, advanced topology, geometric
analysis, operator algebras, advanced probability, and more), awareness
of the great open problems, and the skills of the working mathematician
- reading papers critically, choosing a problem with an advisor, writing,
presenting, collaborating, teaching, and writing and defending an
original doctoral thesis.

================================================================================
  STAGE 13: PhD RESEARCH YEARS - QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS
  Frontier topics and research skills
================================================================================

How to use this file (note for the parent / teacher)
----------------------------------------------------
- There are 32 topics (13.1 to 13.32, the same as in topic.txt), in two
  groups: the Advanced research-level topics (13.1-13.22: algebraic and
  arithmetic geometry, automorphic forms, advanced algebraic and geometric
  topology, quantum topology, mirror symmetry, advanced differential
  geometry, index theory, operator algebras, nonlinear PDE, dynamical
  systems, advanced probability, optimal transport, topological data
  analysis, higher categories, additive combinatorics, geometric group
  theory, mathematics of machine learning, formal verification, quantum
  information and the great open problems) and the Research skills
  (13.23-13.32: reading papers, literature search, choosing a problem,
  examples and counterexamples, writing, presenting, collaboration and
  ethics, teaching, the thesis, and life after the PhD).
  Each topic has:
    * WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN   the checklist of definitions, theorems,
                                  standard examples, counterexamples and
                                  methods in that topic
    * PART A - DESCRIPTIVE        12 questions (D1-D12): proofs,
                                  explanations, derivations and worked
                                  numerical problems, each with the answer
                                  and "Teacher explains" (the method step
                                  by step as a teacher shows it on the
                                  board, common mistakes, and a "Now you
                                  try" question)
    * PART B - MATHEMATICAL ONLY  12 questions (M1-M12): pure drills with
                                  answers. Most have many parts (a, b,
                                  c ...) so that EVERY case of the topic is
                                  practised again and again, from the
                                  easiest to the hardest - not just one
                                  example of each idea.
    * TEACHING TIPS               what to do if the student struggles, and
                                  how to make it harder
- In total: 384 descriptive + 384 mathematical questions, then a mixed
  revision test (equal descriptive and mathematical parts, two questions
  from every topic in each part) and the final checklist of the whole
  programme.
- Level: PhD research. The expectation (topic.txt) is DEPTH IN ONE OR TWO
  of 13.1-13.22 and working AWARENESS of the others: a student should be
  able to do every "Part B" drill in every topic, and every "Part A"
  question in the topics of their own research area.
- The research-skill topics (13.23-13.32) are also practised with
  mathematics: every question there is attached to real computations,
  proofs, estimates or small research tasks, so the skills are learned by
  doing mathematics, not by reading advice.
- What is new in Stage 13: FROM LEARNING TO CREATING. Stage 12 taught the
  student to solve qualifying-exam problems; Stage 13 teaches the student
  to compute invariants in the modern theories, to test conjectures on
  examples, to find counterexamples, and to write and defend new results.
- Conventions: as in A12.txt. N = {1, 2, 3, ...}; log = ln unless a base is
  decimals with ~.
- Method: for every theorem know its hypotheses, the simplest example
  where it applies and the simplest example where it fails. Check every
  computation with software (SageMath, Macaulay2, Magma/PARI, GAP, Lean,
  Python) and write every solution in LaTeX.
- Do 3-4 hours a day: 1-2 descriptive questions (full written proof or
  essay) and 2-3 drills, plus one research paper per week read with the
  method of 13.23.
- Revise Stage 12 (A12.txt) whenever the student finds something
  difficult: 12.14-12.16 before 13.1-13.3; 12.9-12.10 before 13.4-13.9;
  12.2, 12.12-12.13 before 13.10-13.14; 12.21-12.23 before 13.16-13.18;
  12.26 before 13.19; 12.21 before 13.20; 12.27 before 13.21.

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always draw the picture first - Mumford's arithmetic
  ramification happens - and reduce every scheme question to commutative
  algebra of a ring and its primes. For cohomology, drill three moves
  until automatic: Serre's table for P^n, the ideal-sheaf sequence 0 -> O(-d)
  adjunction; every genus, h^0 and Hilbert polynomial in this topic comes
  from these. Before any moduli count, subtract the automorphism group;
  before any intersection count, check properness and transversality,
  and when in doubt compute Tor. Keep a "sanity table" of Betti numbers
  and point counts (P^n, curves, G(2, 4), cubic surfaces) - the Weil
  conjectures tie them together. Harder: prove the valuative criterion
  principle; compute the normal bundle of the twisted cubic; and verify
  Serre's Tor formula on the two-planes example by writing out the
  Koszul complex explicitly.

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep one "running example" on the board all term - the
  curve 11a, y^2 + y = x^3 - x^2 - 10x - 20 - and attach every new notion to
  it: its discriminant -11^5 and j (D1), its 5-torsion point (D2), its
  point counts a_2 = -2, a_3 = -1, a_5 = 1 (D3), its split multiplicative
  reduction at 11 (D5), its BSD quotient 1/5 (D7), its modular form
  (D11). Students then see that "elliptic curve", "modular form" and
  "Galois representation" are three descriptions of the same list of
  numbers a_p. Drill point counting by hand for p <= 13 until Hasse's
  bound and the recursion for #E(F_{p^k}) are automatic, and always
  check a model is minimal before reading off reduction types. Harder:
  prove Mordell-Weil for E/Q via 2-descent and heights; derive the
  Eichler-Shimura relation T_p = F + V on J_0(N) and deduce a_p(f) = a_p(E)
  for X_0(11); prove the valence formula and the dimension formula for
  for several curves; read Ribet's level-lowering statement and check
  that the Frey curve satisfies its hypotheses; and verify numerically
  the Sato-Tate moments 1, 2, 5 (Catalan numbers) for 37a with the
  primes up to 10^4.

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: run one example through every language of the topic
  before any theory - the curve 11a. Count points mod 2 and 3 by hand,
  3pi/4 at 2 and the Steinberg component at 11, write its Frobenius
  polynomial X^2 + 2X + 2, see its Newton polygon (supersingular at 2),
  its Hodge-Tate weights {0, 1} on H^1, and its motive h^1(E) with
  Z(T) = (1 + 2T + 2T^2)/((1 - T)(1 - 2T)). Keep a single sign convention
  Satake computation, and always check Ramanujan (|alpha| = 1) and
  t_H = t_N as a free sanity test. For period rings, memorize the four
  bad extensions) and place every new example between them. For motives
  names what the point counts already show. Harder: prove the Euler
  product and functional equation for L(f, s) via the Mellin transform

  in rank 2 is exactly "Newton above Hodge" and classify all 2-dimensional
  crystalline representations with HT weights {0, k - 1} (the
  Breuil / Berger-Li-Zhu picture); compute H^1_f via the Bloch-Kato
  exponential; prove Manin's identity principle and the blow-up formula
  for Chow motives; and verify the Bloch-Kato conjecture numerically for

WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
    E^1 = homology of the graded pieces and, for a bounded filtration,
  - SERRE SPECTRAL SEQUENCE: F -> E -> B a fibration, B path-connected with
    pi_1(B) acting trivially on H_*(F) (e.g. B simply connected):
    H_*(E) -> H_*(B) and H_*(F) -> H_*(E); TRANSGRESSION d^n : E^{0,n-1} ->
    E^{n,0}. Consequences: Gysin sequence (sphere bundles, Euler class),
  - STANDARD SERRE COMPUTATIONS: S^1 -> S^{2n+1} -> CP^n gives H*(CP^n) =
    pi_4(S^3) = Z/2 and the first p-torsion of pi_*(S^3) is Z/p in pi_{2p}(S^3).
  - ATIYAH-HIRZEBRUCH SPECTRAL SEQUENCE for a generalized cohomology h*:
    H^p(X; Z) in even q, 0 in odd q; d_3 = Sq^3_Z (integral lift of Sq^3),
    the first possible differential. It COLLAPSES if H*(X; Z) is torsion
    free or concentrated in even degrees; rationally always.
  - TOPOLOGICAL K-THEORY: K(X) = Grothendieck group of complex vector
    REAL KO has period 8: KO^{-n}(pt) = Z, Z/2, Z/2, 0, Z, 0, 0, 0
  - CHERN CHARACTER ch : K(X) -> H^{ev}(X; Q), a ring map with ch(L) =
    image of ch is exactly H^{2n}(S^{2n}; Z) and ch_n = +/-c_n/(n - 1)!, so
    c_n of a bundle on S^{2n} is divisible by (n - 1)! (Bott).
    ONE (Adams, Adams-Atiyah): f : S^{4n-1} -> S^{2n} with H(f) odd exists
    only for 2n = 2, 4, 8; hence R^n is a division algebra, S^{n-1} is an
    H-space, or S^{n-1} is parallelizable only for n = 1, 2, 4, 8.
  - STABLE HOMOTOPY: FREUDENTHAL: pi_{n+k}(S^n) -> pi_{n+k+1}(S^{n+1}) is
    iso for n >= k + 2; stable stems pi_k^s = Z, Z/2, Z/2, Z/24, 0, 0, Z/2,
    Z/240, (Z/2)^2, (Z/2)^3, Z/6, Z/504 (k = 0, ..., 11), generated in low
    KO, Thom spectra MO, MSO, MU. BROWN: cohomology theories are
    represented by spectra.
  - J-HOMOMORPHISM J : pi_k(SO) -> pi_k^s; for k = 4s - 1 its image is
    cyclic of order the denominator of B_{2s}/4s: 24, 240, 504, 480, 264.
    Z[c_1, ..., c_n]. SPLITTING PRINCIPLE: compute with Chern roots.
  - STANDARD VALUES: w(RP^n) = (1 + a)^{n+1}; c(CP^n) = (1 + x)^{n+1};
    p(CP^n) = (1 + x^2)^{n+1}; p(HP^2) = 1 + 2u + 7u^2; w(S^n) = 1 but
    R^{2^{r+1}-2}, nor embed in R^{2^{r+1}-1} (Whitney's bounds are sharp).
    S^{2n} is almost complex only for n = 1, 3.
    INTEGER on spin manifolds); TODD Td_1 = c_1/2, Td_2 = (c_1^2 + c_2)/12 (=
    Characteristic NUMBERS are cobordism invariants (Pontryagin); THOM:
    Quillen: the universal formal group law).
  - EXOTIC SPHERES: the signature theorem shows the boundary of the E_8

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw every spectral sequence as a grid on squared paper
  first - mark the nonzero entries, then draw the arrows allowed by the
  bidegree and ask "what MUST die, given what I know about the total
  SU(3)). Keep a small table of standard values on the wall: stable
  stems up to 11, K and KO of a point, w(RP^n), c(CP^n), p(CP^n), p(HP^2),
  computation against a known example (CP^2, K3, HP^2). For characteristic
  classes, always reduce to line bundles (splitting principle) and
  expand power series with truncation at the top degree; for mod 2
  binomials use Lucas' theorem. Harder: prove the multiplicativity of
  the Serre SS and derive H*(K(Z, 3); Z) in degrees <= 8; compute
  K*(SU(3)/SO(3)) and exhibit a nonzero d_3 in the AHSS; prove Bott
  periodicity via the clutching argument of Atiyah-Bott; derive the
  vector-field number from Clifford modules and the J-homomorphism on
  real projective spaces; compute the Adams E_2-term through stem 13 by

    Nielsen-Thurston, give the stretch factor of the Anosov one, and
    compute H_1 of the two mapping tori and their geometries.

    equal [[0,1],[-1,0]], (T_aT_b)^3 = -I. (c) A = [[2,1],[1,1]] Anosov,
    lambda = (3 + sqrt5)/2, H_1(T_A) = Z, geometry Sol; B = [[0,1],[-1,1]] periodic
    of order 6, H_1(T_B) = Z, geometry E^3 (flat).
    Teacher explains: (a) T_a is the identity outside an annulus around
    a. A curve x crossing a transversally once is cut and re-glued after

    then T_aT_bT_a = [[0,1],[-1,0]]. T_bT_a = [[1,1],[-1,0]], T_bT_aT_b =

    Teacher explains: (a) Check the three Reidemeister moves locally,
    with the colours outside the disc fixed. R1: the kink has one crossing
    with over = under_1 = x so under_2 = 2x - x = x: colourings match. R2:
    two crossings with over arc x and incoming y: the middle arc is
    forced to be 2x - y and the outgoing arc 2x - (2x - y) = y: a
    bijection. R3: top strand x over middle y and bottom z, y over z. One
    first, 2x - y and 2x - z, then 2(2x - y) - (2x - z) = 2x - 2y + z. Same
    outgoing colours, and the interior arc is determined, so colourings
    = 9 colourings (6 nontrivial). Figure-eight, arcs A, B, C, D:
       2A = B + C,  2C = D + A,  2B = C + D,  2D = A + B.

    3 it has rank 3, only the 3 constant colourings; mod 5 rank 2, 5^2 = 25

    knotted, and 3_1 != 4_1 (9 != 3). (c) lk = 1/2 sum  signs over crossings

  them before meeting new ones: colourings (9 and 3), delta  (t - 1 + t^-^1 and
  -t + 3 - t^-^1), det (3 and 5), sigma (-2 and 0), V (chiral versus
  versus Anosov), geometry (Seifert versus hyperbolic), and surgery (+/-1
  on the trefoil gives sum (2,3,5) and sum (2,3,7)). Insist on a table of sign
  S^3_{-p/q}(O) = L(p, q)) and on sanity checks: delta (1) = +/-1, V(1) = 1,
  b_2. For 4-manifolds, always classify the form first (rank, sigma, type,
  definite?) and only then ask which theorem (Freedman, Rokhlin,
  Donaldson, Furuta, SW) is relevant. Harder: prove that Seifert's
  algorithm gives minimal genus for alternating diagrams; prove the
  structure of the spinor bundle; derive the Thom conjecture from the
  adjunction inequality via blow-ups; show that the figure-eight complement
  is the union of two ideal tetrahedra and compute its cusp shape; and
  construct an exotic R^4 from Donaldson's theorem plus Freedman's work.

    Reidemeister moves is a chain-homotopy statement (Khovanov, Bar-Natan).
    0, shifted by 0 + 2: q^0 + q^2. Degree 1: ker(delta , -delta ) = {(a, a)} has dim 2 =
    (deg 0), shifted by 2 + 2: q^6 + q^4 in homological degree 2. Kh = 1 + q^2
    theory leaves two generators in homological degree 0 at q^{s-1}, q^{s+1}
    = q^1, q^3: s = 2, and |s| <= 2g_4 gives g_4 >= 1 (the Seifert genus is 1).
    g_4(T(2, 5)) = 2: the Milnor conjecture for this knot.
    Common mistakes: forgetting the shifts (the answer then depends on the
    diagram); reading Kh at t = +1 instead of t = -1 for the Euler
    characteristic; thinking Kh is determined by V (5_1 and 10_1_3_2 share V
    up to mirroring but have different Kh).
    Now you try: Kh(left trefoil) and s(T(3, 4)).
    (q^-^1 + q^-^3 + t^-^2q^-^5 + t^-^3q^-^9; s = (3 - 1)(4 - 1) = 6)

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) The Kauffman bracket is invariant under all Reidemeister moves.
     b) The Jones polynomial distinguishes the two trefoils.
     c) V_K(t) = V_K(t^-^1) for every knot K.
     d) V(K_1 # K_2) = V(K_1)V(K_2).
     e) span V_K = c(K) for every knot K.
     f) Mutant knots have the same Jones polynomial.
     g) There is a nontrivial link with the Jones polynomial of an
        unlink.
     h) dim TL_n = n! for generic d.
     i) Every invertible solution of the YBE gives representations of
        all braid groups B_n.
     j) U_q(sl_2) is cocommutative.
     l) In SU(2)_k the quantum dimension [k + 2] vanishes.
     m) In a 2D TQFT, Z(T^2) = dim Z(S^1).
     n) Every commutative Frobenius algebra is semisimple.
     o) 2D Dijkgraaf-Witten theory distinguishes D_4 from Q_8.
     p) 3D Dijkgraaf-Witten theory distinguishes D_4 from Q_8.
     q) In a 3D TQFT with Z(S^2) = C, Z(M # N) = Z(M)Z(N).
     r) Verlinde dimensions dim V(sum _g) are nonnegative integers.
     s) For SU(2)_k, TV(M) = |RT(M)|^2.
     t) Khovanov homology determines the Jones polynomial.
     u) The Jones polynomial determines Khovanov homology.
     v) Khovanov homology detects the unknot.
     w) The Rasmussen invariant gives g_4(T(p, q)) = (p - 1)(q - 1)/2.
     x) Every surgery presentation of S^3 is the empty link.
     Answers:
       a) F: R1 multiplies it by -A^{+/-3}
       b) T: t + t^3 - t^4 vs t^-^1 + t^-^3 - t^-^4
       c) F: the trefoil
       d) T
       e) F: 8_1_9 (span 5, crossing number 8)
       f) T (e.g. Kinoshita-Terasaka and Conway knots)
       g) T (Eliahou-Kauffman-Thistlethwaite; for knots it is open)
       h) F: dim TL_3 = 5 < 6 = 3! (Catalan numbers)
       i) T
       k) T         l) T ([k + 2] = sin pi/sin(pi/(k + 2)) = 0)
       p) T: Z(RP^3) = 3/4 vs 1/4
       r) T         s) T (Turaev-Walker, Roberts)
       t) T (graded Euler characteristic)
       u) F: 5_1 and 10_1_3_2 have equal V (up to mirror) but different Kh
       v) T (Kronheimer-Mrowka)
       w) T
       x) F: the +/-1-framed unknot also gives S^3 (Kirby blow-up)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep one worked example alive through the whole topic -
  the trefoil. Compute its bracket by hand from the eight states, then
  recompute it from the braid sigma_1^3 in TL_2, then from the R-matrix trace
  [3]q^-^3 - q^-^9, then read it off Khovanov's cube as the Euler
  characteristic of q + q^3 + t^2q^5 + t^3q^9; seeing the SAME polynomial four
  times is what makes "quantum invariant" concrete. Always write down the
  conventions first (A versus t, which smoothing is A, sign of the
  writhe, t^{1/2} = -q or -q^-^1) and check them on the Hopf link before any
  long computation. For TQFT, draw the surfaces: every 2D identity is a
  and Z(sum  x S^1) = dim is "bend and close". For Verlinde and DW, test
  (must give dim Z(S^1)). Harder: prove the Kauffman-Murasugi-Thistlethwaite
  theorem via adequacy; derive the universal R-matrix of U_h(sl_2) and
  of 2D TQFTs from the normal form of surfaces; show TV_{Vec_G} = DW and
  that Rep D(G) is modular; prove the Verlinde formula from the modular
  S-matrix and compute the SU(2)_k genus-2 dimension C(k + 3, 3) in
  closed form; prove invariance of Khovanov homology under R1 and R2 by
  Gaussian elimination, and use Lee's spectral sequence to prove Milnor's
  conjecture g_4(T(p, q)) = (p - 1)(q - 1)/2.

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep one table on the wall - the Hodge diamond of a CY
  3-fold with h^{1,1} and h^{2,1} boxed, the quintic's numbers (1, 101,
  -200) and its mirror's (101, 1, 200) - and insist that every new
  example be placed in it by the same two steps: a Chern class
  other number. For enumerative problems always write the dimension
  count first (2n - 3 - d for lines, 3d - 1 points for plane curves,
  wrong number of conditions. Do Schubert calculus with Chern roots and
  the four G(2,4) numbers (sigma_1^4 = 2, sigma_1_1^2 = sigma_2^2 = sigma_1^2sigma_1_1 = 1), and check
  every localization with integral _{P^n}H^n = 1 before trusting a sign convention.
  For periods, turn every hypergeometric series into its coefficient
  ratio, then read off theta-operator, radius and exponents. For HMS on the
  torus draw the lines on a square and count intersections. Harder:
  derive the Aspinwall-Morrison 1/k^3 from the obstruction bundle on
  reflection in the vanishing S^3); verify Batyrev's formula for the
  sextic in P(1,1,1,1,2) with its resolved polytope; and state and check
  Polishchuk-Zaslow's identification of m_2 with theta-function products.

  - TOEPLITZ INDEX: for f : S^1 -> C* continuous, T_f = P M_f on the Hardy
    -wind(f) (so T_z = S has index -1); for matrix-valued F, ind T_F =
    -wind(det F). T_fT_g - T_{fg} is compact. Fred(H) classifies K-theory:
    odd order is elliptic in dimension n >= 2 (S^{n-1} is connected).

    index independent of s: ind P = dim ker P - dim ker P* (both spaces

    the symbol; a formally self-adjoint P : E -> E has index 0; every

    has index 0 (false for pseudodifferential ones, cf. Toeplitz).

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: build everything on the single identity "index = dim ker
  - dim coker, and it does not move under deformation". Start with
  matrices (index = p - q), then the shift and Toeplitz operators (index
  = -winding number, a picture of a loop around 0), then d/dtheta + a on the
  circle, then the four classical operators with a table on the board:
  top-degree part only, the correct normalisation (p_1 = c_1^2 - 2c_2, x/2
  the S^2 computation by hand with Euler-Maclaurin before any theory.
  Harder: prove the Toeplitz index theorem in full and deduce Bott
  periodicity for pi_1(GL(C)); prove McKean-Singer and compute a_1 for a
  general Laplace-type operator; work through Getzler's rescaling and
  Mehler's formula to prove the local index theorem for the spin Dirac
  operator; derive the Atiyah-Bott fixed point formula from the heat
  kernel and recover the Weyl character formula for SU(3) on the flag
  manifold; prove Rokhlin's theorem via the quaternionic structure and
  Milnor's exotic spheres via the signature theorem; read the APS paper
  theorem to see why determinant line bundles and anomalies appear.

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: work first entirely in finite dimensions, where every
  statement can be checked by hand: a finite-dimensional C*-algebra is
  and multiplicities), its K_0 is Z^k counted by ranks, a state is a
  irrational rotation algebra A_theta with its trace - and test every new
  theorem on them. For spectra and norms insist on the question "is the
  inside the disc and put in the minus sign; for UHF questions, factor
  the supernatural number into primes and check the unit class; for
  Jones indices, list 4cos^2(pi/n) = 2 + 2cos(2pi/n) for n <= 10 once and for
  all. Harder: prove the Gelfand-Naimark-Segal theorem in full and the
  Kaplansky density theorem; prove Cuntz's computation K_0(O_n) = Z/(n -
  1) via the Toeplitz-Cuntz extension; derive the Pimsner-Voiculescu
  sequence from the Toeplitz algebra of a crossed product; prove Jones'
  theorem that indices below 4 lie in {4cos^2(pi/n)} using the positivity
  of the Temperley-Lieb trace; show that the Powers factors R_lambda are
  pairwise non-isomorphic by computing Connes' S invariant; prove the
  Connes distance formula for a compact spin manifold; compute the
  Connes-Chern character of the Dirac operator on T^2 and show that the
  2-cocycle on A_theta is integral on K_0 (the integer quantum Hall effect).

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: start every problem with SCALING - replace u by lambda^betau(lambdax,
  lambda^2t) and see which terms balance: this single computation produces p*,
  the critical exponent (n + 2)/(n - 2), s_c for NLS and heat, the
  Navier-Stokes. Then keep a small zoo of explicit solutions on the board
  and verify each by hand: the bubble 3^{1/4}(1 + r^2)^{-1/2}, Liouville's
  log(8/(1 + r^2)^2), x/|x|, the catenoid and Scherk's surface, the
  shrinking sphere r^2 = r_0^2 - 2nt, the grim reaper, Burgers' shock and
  fan, the KdV soliton, Poiseuille, Lamb-Oseen and Taylor-Green. For
  existence questions ask the three direct-method questions (coercive?
  weakly lsc? compact?) and look for the Pohozaev or Gauss-Bonnet
  obstruction before trying to construct anything. For fluids, always
  check div u = 0 first and remember that div u = 0 kills both the
  nonlinearity and the pressure in energy estimates. Harder: prove the
  mountain pass theorem via the deformation lemma and check Palais-
  Smale for subcritical powers; prove De Giorgi's theorem (Caccioppoli,
  monotonicity formula and use it to classify compact self-shrinkers
  Leray's existence theorem by Galerkin approximation and Aubin-Lions
  compactness, and the Ladyzhenskaya-Prodi-Serrin weak-strong
  uniqueness; and study the proof of the Caffarelli-Kohn-Nirenberg
  suitable weak solutions.

    1)/r^2, so the multiplier
                    = r^2 - 2r(r + 1) + 4(r + 1) = -r^2 + 2r + 4.

D12. (a) State the KAM theorem and Moser's twist theorem; why do tori
    confine the motion for n = 2 degrees of freedom but not for n >= 3?
    (b) For the standard map F(theta, p) = (theta + p + K sin theta, p + K sin theta)
    (mod 2pi) show det DF = 1, find the fixed points, their residues R =
    (2 - tr)/4 and stability, and do the same for the period-2 orbit
    resonant circle p = pi of the unperturbed map? (d) What is known about
    the last invariant circle?
    Answer: (b) (0, 0): R = -K/4, hyperbolic; (pi, 0): R = K/4, elliptic
    for 0 < K < 4; period 2: tr = 2 - K^2, R = K^2/4, elliptic for 0 < K <
    2. (c) >= 2 period-2 orbits survive. (d) the golden circle, broken at
    K ~ 0.9716; none for K > 63/64.
    is a local diffeomorphism, most tori qualify: the complement has
    0, keeps the invariant curves with Diophantine rotation numbers.
    Energy surfaces have dimension 2n - 1 and tori dimension n; a torus
    separates only if n = 2n - 2, i.e. n = 2, so for 2 degrees of freedom
    each orbit is trapped between two KAM tori and the actions stay close
    to their initial values forever. For n >= 3 ARNOLD DIFFUSION may
    occur (at most exponentially slowly for steep H_0: Nekhoroshev).
    (b) DF = [[1 + K cos theta, 1], [K cos theta, 1]], det = 1 (F is the kicked
    = 2 + K, R = -K/4 < 0: hyperbolic. At (pi, 0) tr = 2 - K, R = K/4:
    vanishes; DF(pi)DF(0) = [[1 - K, 1], [-K, 1]][[1 + K, 1], [K, 1]] =
    [[1 + K - K^2, 2 - K], [-K^2, 1 - K]], tr = 2 - K^2, R = K^2/4.
    (c) At K = 0 the circle p = pi consists of period-2 points (rotation
    circles turning slower and faster: for small K > 0 at least two
    period-2 orbits survive; the one in (b) is elliptic, its partner
    hyperbolic, and the circle becomes a chain of islands.
    golden-mean circle is the last to break, at K_c ~ 0.971635
    (numerical); MATHER: no rotational invariant circles for K > 4/3;
    MACKAY-PERCIVAL: none for K > 63/64. They become CANTORI.
    Common mistakes: using DF at one point of the cycle only; believing

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: start every problem by finding the fixed and periodic
  points and computing their multipliers or eigenvalues: that single
  habit classifies saddles and sinks, predicts bifurcations of the
  logistic map, locates the cardioid and bulbs of M, and gives Greene
  residues of the standard map. Draw three pictures side by side - the
  cat map stretching a square, the Julia set of z^2 - 2 as the interval
  [-2, 2] with w + 1/w, and the integrable twist map with circles of
  rational and irrational rotation number - and show how the same idea
  (hyperbolicity versus quasi-periodicity) organizes all three halves of
  the topic. Insist on counting correctly: 2^n versus 2^n - 1, closed words
  1) and ask how small the denominator can be. Harder: prove the stable
  manifold theorem by the graph transform; prove structural stability
  of Anosov diffeomorphisms from the shadowing lemma; construct a Markov
  partition for the cat map and compute its SFT; prove Sharkovskii's
  density of repelling cycles in J and the Fatou-Shishikura bound for
  attracting cycles; prove Siegel's theorem with a KAM-type Newton
  scheme; and prove the Moser twist theorem or Arnold's theorem on
  analytic circle diffeomorphisms, estimating the loss of analyticity
  strip at each step.

PART A - DESCRIPTIVE

D1. Let H be an NxN Wigner matrix (real symmetric or Hermitian, entries
    independent up to symmetry, mean 0, off-diagonal variance 1, all
    the Catalan number, and (1/N)E tr X^{2k+1} -> 0. (b) For the GUE
    Answer: (a) see below. (b) E tr H^4 = 2N^3 + N, so (1/N)E tr X^4 = 2 +
    Teacher explains: (a) Expand
    complete graph with vertices {1, ..., N}. Since entries have mean 0
    and are independent, a walk contributes 0 unless every edge it uses
    is traversed at least twice. Then it uses at most k distinct edges,
    and a connected graph with <= k edges has at most k + 1 vertices,

    ~ 0.162; p_c >= 1/mu ~ 0.379.
    there is an open self-avoiding path of length n from 0. There are
       theta(p) <= sigma(n)p^n <= (4/3)(3p)^n -> 0 for p < 1/3.
    UPPER BOUND: place the DUAL lattice Z^2 + (1/2, 1/2); declare a dual edge
    open iff the primal edge it crosses is closed, so the dual is bond

    iff 0 is surrounded by a dual circuit of dual-open (primal-closed)

    Fix m; the event that the box B(m) is surrounded by a closed dual
    for m large when 3(1 - p) < 1. With positive probability all edges
    of B(m) are open AND no such circuit exists (FKG, or independence of
    the finitely many edges given a large enough m), so theta(p) > 0 for
    p > 2/3.
    (b) Let R be [0, n + 1]x[0, n]. Its dual R* is a rotated copy: the
    dual edges crossing edges of R form an nx(n + 1) grid. Exactly one
    of the two events "open left-right crossing of R" and "dual-open
    top-bottom crossing of R*" occurs (the "Hex lemma"). At p = 1/2 the
    dual has the same law and R* is R rotated by 90 degrees, so both have the
    same probability, which must therefore be 1/2. HARRIS (1960): theta(1/2) =
    0, hence p_c >= 1/2; KESTEN (1980): p_c <= 1/2, so p_c = 1/2. Kesten used
    RSW estimates, FKG and Russo's formula (sharp threshold).
    mu ~ 2.638 (connective constant), the same argument gives theta(p) = 0
    for p < 1/mu ~ 0.379, and dually p_c <= 1 - 1/mu ~ 0.621.
    Common mistakes: forgetting that dual-open means primal-CLOSED;

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep one "master picture" per subject on the board. For
  random matrices: the semicircle with its Catalan moments and the
  equation G = 1/(z - G); every computation (moments, outliers theta + 1/theta,
  free sums) reduces to manipulating G. For percolation: the tree, where
  everything is a Galton-Watson generating function, and then Z^2 with its
  dual lattice, where every question is "is there an open crossing or a
  closed dual circuit?". For SLE: the vertical slit sqrt(z^2 + 4t) and the
  one computation Var = integral integral p_s^2 = integral p_{2s}(0)ds, which explains both the
  answer sqrt(t/pi) and the failure in d >= 2. For large deviations: the
  Legendre transform of log E e^{thetaX} and the tilted coin. Insist that
  from a convention. Harder: prove the semicircle law via the resolvent
  with RSW and a sharp-threshold (Russo, KKL) argument; derive Cardy's
  formula from Smirnov's parafermionic observable; prove Beffara's lower
  bound on SLE dimension or the locality of SLE_6 by comparing Loewner
  chains; construct the Cole-Hopf solution of KPZ and show the moment
  Sanov from it, and compute the Freidlin-Wentzell quasi-potential for a
  non-gradient drift (e.g. a rotation plus a gradient).

D1. (a) State the Monge and Kantorovich problems and explain why the
    relaxation is needed: give a pair with no admissible map, and a pair
    where the Monge infimum is not attained. Prove that an optimal plan
    exists for c continuous and bounded below on compact X x Y. (b) With
    [[1, 3], [2, 5]], find all couplings and the optimal one. (c) Solve
    the 3 x 3 assignment problem for C = [[4, 1, 3], [2, 0, 5], [3, 2, 2]]
    (uniform weights 1/3).
    1/4}, cost 31/4 + a, optimal a = 0, value 13/4. (c) sigma = (1->2, 2->1, 3->3),
    total 5, i.e. optimal cost 5/3.
    Teacher explains: (a) MONGE: minimize integral c(x, T(x)) dmu(x) over maps T
    gives the plan (id x T)#mu, so Kantorovich <= Monge. No admissible map:
    measures on {+/-1} x [0, 1], c = |x - y|^2. Every map moves each point a
    horizontal distance 1, so cost >= 1; zig-zag maps sending [k/N,
    (k+1)/N] alternately left and right (stretched vertically by the
    factor 2) cost 1 + O(1/N^2) -> 1, but cost exactly 1 would force
    horizontal moves, which split mass. The Kantorovich plan that sends
    half of each point left and half right costs 1: attained.
    marginals are fixed; closed since marginals pass to weak limits), and
    by bounded continuous functions). A minimizing sequence has a
    convergent subsequence whose limit is optimal.
    (b) Row sums (1/2, 1/2), column sums (1/4, 3/4): P_1_1 = a forces P_1_2 = 1/2 - a,
    P_2_1 = 1/4 - a, P_2_2 = 1/4 + a with 0 <= a <= 1/4. Cost = a + 3(1/2 - a) + 2(1/4 - a)
    + 5(1/4 + a) = 13/4 + a. Note the coefficient of a is C_1_1 + C_2_2 - C_1_2 -
    C_2_1 = 1 > 0 (swap test): minimize a, optimal P = [[0, 1/2], [1/4, 1/4]],
    value 13/4. This plan splits x_2: no Monge map exists here at all.
    (c) By Birkhoff-von Neumann an optimal plan is a permutation. Row
    minima (1, 0, 2) sit in columns 2, 2, 3: conflict in column 2. Try
    1->2, 2->1, 3->3: 1 + 2 + 2 = 5. Certificate (dual, see D2): u = (0, -1,
    4, (1,3): 2 <= 3, (3,1): 3 <= 3, (3,2): 1 <= 2, (2,3): 1 <= 5) with
    other five permutations cost 6, 6, 7, 9, 11: 5 is the unique min).
    Common mistakes: thinking Monge >= Kantorovich can be strict in nice
    cases (for atomless mu and continuous c they agree); forgetting that
    weights must be matched exactly (a plan, not just a matching of
    points); using the row minima greedily.
    anti-diagonal, total 10 - the anti-sorted pairing, since c = xy is
    submodular.)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: start every problem by drawing the two measures as piles
  of sand and holes on a line and asking "who goes where?"; in 1D the
  answer is always "sort and pair" for convex costs, so let the child
  compute many W_1 = integral |F - G| and quantile integrals before touching
  higher dimensions. Keep the 2 x 2 swap test C_1_1 + C_2_2 vs C_1_2 + C_2_1 on
  the board - it is cyclical monotonicity in miniature, and it explains
  duality (potentials), assortative matching and why concave costs cross.
  In R^n, reduce to three model cases: translations (W_2 = |shift|),
  dilations (Gaussians, the Bures formula) and radial maps (match the
  mass of balls), and always check the answer is the GRADIENT OF A
  CONVEX function (symmetric PSD Jacobian). For flows, first write the
  For Sinkhorn, do two iterations by hand on a 2 x 2 example. Harder:
  prove Kantorovich duality via Fenchel-Rockafellar or via c-cyclical
  version without moments; derive the Bures-Wasserstein formula and the
  Riemannian structure on Gaussian covariances; prove displacement
  the JKO scheme for Fokker-Planck; show linear convergence of Sinkhorn
  in the Hilbert metric; prove Talagrand from LSI (Otto-Villani) and
  isoperimetry from the Knothe map; and read how Lott-Sturm-Villani
  obtain Bishop-Gromov and Brunn-Minkowski from CD(K, N).

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw everything. For each point cloud draw the growing
  literally watch components merge and holes open and close; write each
  simplex with its filtration value before touching a matrix. Drill the
  triangle at its circumradius if acute and at half its longest side if
  not, and a lower-star simplex at its highest vertex. For H_0 always use
  the elder rule and the minimum spanning tree; for H_1 count beta_1 = E - V +
  (components) - (filled triangles that kill loops). Compute bottleneck
  distances by listing, for each point, "match it or send it to the
  diagonal at cost half its length", and check the answer against the
  stability bound. Harder: prove the stability theorem through the
  interleaving and the isometry theorem (induced matchings of Bauer-
  Lesnick); prove Gabriel's theorem for A_n zigzags; show that the rank
  invariant is complete for one parameter but not for two, and find a
  circle passes through S^1, S^3, S^5, ... (Adamaszek-Adams); implement
  the reduction algorithm with clearing and compare homology with
  cohomology on the regular 12-gon; and design a permutation test using
  mean persistence landscapes to compare two samples of point clouds.
